Missing いけない: “早く帰らないと” may be considered incomplete in JLPT written language, unless a conversational context allows the omission.
59.notes:
• Colloquial contraction: ～ないと (with the rest omitted) often comes with an urgent intonation.
• To negate an obligation, use a double negative: 行かなくてもいい (don't have to go), not 行かないといけないの否定 directly.
• Past obligation: ～ないといけなかった states a reason/objective circumstance; polite: ～ないといけませんでした.

examples.jp: この書類は今週中に提出しなくてはいけない。
examples.tr: This document must be submitted within this week.

examples.jp: 入場するには会員でなくてはいけません。
examples.tr: You must be a member to enter.

examples.jp: 製品は安全でなくてはいけない。
examples.tr: Products must be safe.

examples.jp: 健康のために、定期的に運動しなくてはいけない。
examples.tr: For your health, you must exercise regularly.

examples.jp: ダイエットしなくてはいけません。
examples.tr: I have to go on a diet.

examples.jp: この中からえらばなくてはいけませんか。
examples.tr: Do I have to choose from among these?

60.explain:
Polite: change いけない → いけません to suit business/public settings.
The obligation is usually based on rules/policies; it carries little personal emotion.
To negate an obligation, use ～ なくてもいい ／～ 必要はない ; do not use いけない in a double-negative form.
In official normative documents, there is a tendency to switch to ～なければならない.

• Obligation based on rules, procedures, or general requirements: “must ...”.
• Neutral; can be used with strangers/customers in the polite form: ～なくてはいけません.
• Expresses a necessary condition: if you don't do it, it is “not OK/not allowed”.
• Focus on actions: mainly used with verbs; with A/N, used when talking about meeting a condition/standard.

rows: <ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>しなければならない。
もう<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくちゃいけない。
<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>歩<rt>ある</rt></ruby>くことだ。

mistakes: Dropping “で” with N/na: ×会員なくてはいけない → 〇会員でなくてはいけない.
Sounds stiff when used for personal requests: with friends, use ～なくちゃいけない.
Wrong negation: ×行かなくてはいけないくない → 〇行かなくてもいい／行く必要はない.
Confusing it with べきだ on the exam: べきだ means “should”, not “must”.
60.notes:
• Fast pronunciation: ～なくてはいけない → ～なくちゃいけない in conversation.
• Past tense for an obligation already fulfilled: ～なくてはいけなかった（had to ...）.
• Combined with other particles: どうしても行かなくてはいけない（must go no matter what）.

61.name: ～ね　right?

examples.jp:
A: まいにち　10じまではたらきます。
A: たいへんですね。
examples.tr:
A: I work until 10 every day.
A: That must be tough.

examples.jp:
A: やまださんのでんわばんごうは　871の　6813です。
B: 871の　6813ですね。
examples.tr:
A: Yamada's phone number is 871-6813.
B: 871-6813, right?

61.explain: ね is used at the end of a sentence to show that the speaker expects the listener's agreement, or to confirm or remind.

examples.jp:
A: このしゅくだいはどうですか。
B: とてもむずかしいです。
examples.tr:
A: How is this homework?
B: It's very difficult.

examples.jp:
A: このまちはどうですか。
B: しずかです。
examples.tr:
A: How is this town?
B: It's quiet.

62.explain: どう： used to ask about impressions, opinions, feelings, or the nature of a thing or matter.
62.notes:
Xはどうですか (question pattern using どう to ask about state/evaluation) means This grammar pattern is used to ask about the state, condition, or evaluation of something. It translates to 'How is X?' or 'What do you think about X?'
Structure: Xはどうですか
The phrase combines the topic particle は with どう, which means 'how' or 'in what way,' followed by ですか to form a polite question. It is commonly used to inquire about someone's opinion, condition, or the state of something in a neutral and polite manner.

examples.jp: 今年は去年より暑い。
examples.tr: This year is hotter than last year.

examples.jp: このスマホは前のモデルより軽い。
examples.tr: This smartphone is lighter than the previous model.

examples.jp: 私は弟より背が高い。
examples.tr: I am taller than my younger brother.

examples.jp: 彼は私より日本語が上手だ。
examples.tr: He is better at Japanese than I am.

examples.jp: バスは電車より時間がかかる。
examples.tr: The bus takes longer than the train.

examples.jp: AとBとでは、Aのほうが人気がある。
examples.tr: Between A and B, A is more popular.

63.explain:
より can be replaced by よりも to emphasize the contrast.
With nouns of time/place, は is often omitted:今年は去年より～.
When answering a どちら question, のほうが is natural: AのほうがBより～/Aのほうが～.
Negative comparison: AはBほど～ない (A is not as ～ as B).

Expresses “A is more than B in terms of ～”. より is placed after the reference target to compare the difference.
The clause after より is the point of reference; the predicate applies to A.
Combine with degree adverbs (ずっと,少し, かなり, やや) to quantify the difference.
With verbs: compares the frequency/degree of an action (食べる/使う/勉強する...).

rows: この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>はあれより<ruby>厚<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>ほど<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>くない。
<ruby>犬<rt>いぬ</rt></ruby>のほうが<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>より<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きだ。
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>より<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>び？ (criticism)

mistakes: Swapping A and B by mistake: × BはAより… (the meaning becomes B is more than A) → note “AはBより…”.
Using を after より: × Aよりを… → より does not take を; it is followed by the predicate.
Confusing it with ほど in affirmative sentences: × AはBほど高い → ほど is used with the negative when comparing more/less.
Leaving out のほうが when answering a comparison question makes the sentence unnatural in conversation.
63.notes:
Chained comparison: AはBよりCより～ can be ambiguous; it is better to split the sentence or use数値 to make it clear.
With numerical data, state it directly:去年より3%増えた。
Comparing yourself over time:前より/以前より/昔より +形容詞/動詞.

64.name: ～よ　～you know, I tell you

examples.jp:
A: このでんしゃはこうしえんへいきますか。
B: いいえ、いきません。つぎの「ふつう」ですよ。
examples.tr:
A: Does this train go to Koshien?
B: No, it doesn't. It's the next “local” train, you know.

64.explain: ～よ　emphasizes a piece of information for the listener.

examples.jp:
A: カリナさんのかばんはどれですか。
B: あの赤くて、大きいのです。
examples.tr:
A: Which bag is Karina's?
B: It's that big red one.

65.explain:
Replaces a noun that appeared earlier.

の～：the ~ one

66.name: Using quantities and counters
66.meaning: Position of the counter in the sentence: after Nを/が, before V

examples.jp:
A: つくえのうえにビールがなんぼんありますか。
B: ろっぽんあります。
examples.tr:
A: How many bottles of beer are there on the desk?
B: There are six.

examples.jp:
A: かいぎしつになんにんいますか。
B: よにんいます。
examples.tr:
A: How many people are in the meeting room?
B: There are four.

66.explain: Quantities and counters always come after the particle.

67.name: Expressing the number of times
67.meaning:
Used to talk about how many times you do something.
なんかい：How many times?

examples.jp: 私は一週間に二回映画を見ます。
examples.tr: I watch movies twice a week.

examples.jp: ナムさんは一か月に一回田舎へ帰ります。
examples.tr: Nam goes back home to the countryside once a month.

68.name: Particles used with means of transportation
68.meaning:
Get on (a vehicle/train) ~
Get off (a vehicle/train) ~
Change (vehicles/trains) from ~ to ~
～を leave, get out of ~
～に into, onto ~
68.connection: N(means of transportation) + に + 乗ります / N + を + 降ります / N1 + から + N2 + に + 乗り換えます

examples.jp:
でんしゃにのります。
でんしゃをおります。
でんしゃからバスにのりかえます。
examples.tr:
I get on the train.
I get off the train.
I change from the train to a bus.

69.name: N が A of emotion, degree
69.meaning: N is A (adjectives of emotion/degree: 頭がいい)

examples.jp: わたしはかんじがへたです。
examples.tr: I'm bad at kanji.

examples.jp:
A: あなたはなにがきらいですか。
B: わたしはたばこがきらいです。
examples.tr:
A: What do you dislike?
B: I dislike cigarettes.

69.explain: が： used with adjectives that express emotion or degree.

70.name: N1(person/thing/place) の N2 position
70.meaning:
On/above　した：Under/below
In front　うしろ：Behind
Right　ひだり：　Left
Inside　そと：Outside
Next to
Next to ( side by side)
Near
Between

examples.jp: わたしのうちはこうえんのちかくにあります。
examples.tr: My house is near the park.

examples.jp: ミラーさんはかいぎしつにいます。
examples.tr: Mr. Miller is in the meeting room.

71.meaning: The particle に indicates the place N1 where N2 ends up after the action V is performed.
71.connection: N1 (place) + に + N2 + を + V

examples.jp: ここに車を止めてください。
examples.tr: Please park your car here.

examples.jp: ここに住所を書いてください。
examples.tr: Please write your address here.

examples.jp: 北海道は雪が多いです。
examples.tr: Hokkaido gets a lot of snow.

examples.jp:
A: マリアさんはどうですか。
B: めがおおきくて、はだがしろいです。
examples.tr:
A: What is Maria like?
B: Maria has big eyes and fair skin.

examples.jp:
A: ゆみこさんはどのひとですか。
B: かみがくろくて、ながいひとですよ。
examples.tr:
A: Which one is Yumiko?
B: The person with long black hair.

examples.jp: へやのなかにテレビやれいぞうこなどがあります。
examples.tr: In the room, there are things like a TV and a refrigerator.

examples.jp: スーパーでにくやたまごなどをかいました。
examples.tr: At the supermarket, I bought things like meat and eggs.

73.explain:
Used to list nouns.
For the last N, we do not use や but use など to end the list. など comes before the appropriate particles, depending on the verb at the end of the sentence.
や + など gives a sense of “just examples”, suitable when you do not need to (or cannot) list everything.
In conversation, you can use just や without adding など if the list is implicitly clear.
など comes after the last item in the list, or after a single item, to mean “for example”.
When talking about people: avoid Nなど if you do not want to sound impolite; “先生など” can sound belittling.
73.notes:
original notes: “NやNなどのN” is often used in headings/reports: “AやBなどの影響”.
“などと +言う/思う” carries a quoting nuance with a dismissive tone:彼が天才だなどと言う。 (implies skepticism).
When the list is long, you can use “などを中心に/などについて”.
meaning_vi: A conjunctive particle that connects a noun with another noun. Used to list a few things out of many.
examples: 1. ①　秋葉原や　原宿。
Akihabara and Harajuku.

74.name: Joining simple sentences into a compound sentence
74.meaning: Joining compound sentences: Vて/Aくて/Naで/Nで join clauses with the same topic

examples.jp: 毎日　６じにおきて、朝ご飯をたべて、それからがっこうへ行きます。
examples.tr: Every day I get up at 6, eat breakfast, and then go to school.

examples.jp: 私は会社員で、田中さんは医者です。
examples.tr: I am an office worker, and Mr. Tanaka is a doctor.

examples.jp: 私はフンで、がくせいです。
examples.tr: I'm Hung, and I'm a student.

examples.jp: この木はながくて、おもいです。
examples.tr: This piece of wood is long and heavy.

examples.jp: この所はきれいで、しずかです。
examples.tr: This place is beautiful and quiet.

74.explain:
Used to form a compound sentence.
With V: use Vて to list actions in sequence.With N: it can be used not only for sentences with the same topic but also to join sentences with different topics.With A: only used to join adjectives that are similar in meaning.

75.name: Joining several kinds of things with different quantities
75.meaning: Listing several kinds of things with different quantities (N1を…とN2を…)
75.connection: ～は + N1を/が + [quantity] + と + N2を/が + [quantity] + V

examples.jp: 机の上に卵がにことパンがひとつとコーヒーが一杯あります。
examples.tr: On the desk there are two eggs, one piece of bread, and a cup of coffee.

examples.jp:
A: りんごをふたつとバナナをさんぼんください。
B: はい、わかりました。
examples.tr:
A: Two apples and three bananas, please.
B: Certainly.

75.explain: The particle depends on the verb at the end of the sentence.

examples.jp: あめがふっています。
examples.tr: It's raining.

examples.jp: ミラーさんがいませんね。
examples.tr: Mr. Miller isn't here, is he?

77.meaning: The particle に indicates the place where the subject ends up after performing the action V.

examples.jp: ここに入ってはいけません。
examples.tr: You must not go in here.

examples.jp: このいすに座ってもいいですか。
examples.tr: May I sit on this chair?

77.explain:
Verbs used:
Nに～
はいります enter N
すわります sit on N
のります get on N (vehicle/train)
のぼります climb N (mountain)
つきます arrive at N
77.notes:
meaning_vi: Move to N (NにV of movement: 日本に行く)
explain: The particle に indicates the destination and is used in place of the direction particle へ.
Verbs such as いきます/きます/かえります/しゅっちょうします can be used with both Nへ and Nに.
examples: 1. A: どこかで　財布を　落として　しまったんです。
B: それは　大変ですね。すぐ　交番に　行かないと。
I've gone and dropped my wallet somewhere.
That's terrible. You need to go to the police box right away.

78.name: Nは～にいます/あります N is at ～
78.meaning: N is located at… (います for people and living things, あります for objects)
78.connection: N + は + N (place) + に + います / あります

examples.jp:
A: にほんごのほんはどこにありますか。
B: つくえのうえにあります。
examples.tr:
A: Where is the Japanese book?
B: It's on the desk.

examples.jp:
A: ねこはどこにいますか。
B: はこのなかにいます。
examples.tr:
A: Where is the cat?
B: It's in the box.

78.explain: Used to emphasize the location of an object that both the speaker and the listener know about.

79.name: Equal comparison

examples.jp: Aさんは　Bさんとおなじぐらいせがたかいです。
examples.tr: A is about as tall as B.

examples.jp: Aさんは　Bさんとおなじとしです。
examples.tr: A is the same age as B.

79.explain: N 1 and N 2 are the same (in some property or characteristic)

80.name: Less-than comparison

examples.jp: バナナはりんごほどたかくないです。
examples.tr: Bananas are not as expensive as apples.

examples.jp:
A: Aさんのへやはどうですか。
B: Aさんのへやは　Bさんのへやほどひろくないです。
examples.tr:
A: What is A's room like?
B: A's room is not as spacious as B's room.

80.explain: ほど used with a negative ending means that N 1 does not have the property A as much as N 2 .

81.name: Turning the object into the topic
81.meaning: When we want to take the direct object in a “NをV” sentence and make it the topic, we replace the particle を with は and move Nは to the beginning of the sentence.
81.connection: N + を + V → N + は + V (moving the object up to become the topic)

examples.jp:
ここに荷物を置かないでください。
荷物はここに置かないでください。
examples.tr:
Please don't put your luggage here.
As for your luggage, please don't put it here.

examples.jp:
会社の食堂で昼ごはんを食べます。
昼ごはんは会社の食堂で食べます。
examples.tr:
I eat lunch at the company cafeteria.
As for lunch, I eat it at the company cafeteria.

examples.jp: 日本へ行きたいです。
examples.tr: I want to go to Japan.

examples.jp: 何が食べたいですか。
examples.tr: What do you want to eat?

examples.jp: 今日は早く帰りたくないです。
examples.tr: I don't want to go home early today.

examples.jp: 子どものとき、犬を飼いたかったです。
examples.tr: When I was a child, I wanted to have a dog.

examples.jp: 彼は新しいスマホを買いたがっています。
examples.tr: He seems to want to buy a new smartphone.

examples.jp: 水が飲みたいです。
examples.tr: I want to drink some water.

82.explain:
Basic politeness in everyday communication; with superiors/customers, use ～たいと思っております／～させていただきたいです to sound softer.
Asking about the listener's wishes: ～たいですか／何が～たいですか; more formal: ～たいでしょうか／～たいですかね.
To emphasize a lasting desire: ～たいと思っています (an intention that has already formed); light and spontaneous: ～たいです.
In complex sentences: can be used before から・ので・けど to give a reason/suggestion:早く帰りたい ので、先に失礼します。

Expresses the speaker's subjective desire or intention “want to do V”; polite with です.
Restriction on the subject: usually used for the first person; asking the second person is fine; for the third person, use ～たがる／～たがっています to make it objective.
Grammatical nature: ～たい is an i-adjective and conjugates like an い-adj (たくない・たかった...).
Particles: the object often changes from を → が when emphasizing the desire toward the target.
Nuance: direct and natural; more formal: ～たいと思っています／～たいと考えています.

rows: Describes a third party, based on observation
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りたがっている。
The target is a noun, not an action
<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>がほしい。
Vたいと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う／と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っている
<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>したいと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています。

mistakes: Using it directly for the third person: ×彼は帰りたいです → ◯彼は帰りたがっています.
Mixing up particles: ×水を飲みたい (not wrong), but it is more natural when asking/answering about preferences:水が飲みたい.
Conjugating it like a noun/na-adjective: ×行きたいですな → ◯行きたいです.
Mixing it up with欲しい: ×食べ物がたい → ◯食べ物がほしい／寿司を食べたい.
JLPT: often tests conjugating たい like an い-adj and distinguishing ～たい vs ～たがる.
82.notes:
It is unnatural to state a strong desire directly to a superior: “休みたいです” → consider “体調が優れないので、お休みをいただきたいです”。
Avoid “～たいですと思います” (redundant); “～たいと思います” is enough.
Verbal nouns with する: Nを/が＋したい (勉強をしたい／勉強がしたい) are both correct; が emphasizes the desire.
When asking about general preferences:何がしたい？ (casual) instead of何をしたい？ sounds natural.

examples.jp: あしたテストがありますから、こんばん、勉強しなければなりません。
examples.tr: I have a test tomorrow, so I have to study tonight.

examples.jp: 病気ですから、くすりをのまなければなりません。
examples.tr: I'm sick, so I have to take medicine.

86.connection: あまり + [negative predicate] (Vません / Aくない / Naではない / Nがない)

examples.jp: 時間があまりありません。
examples.tr: I don't have much time.

examples.jp: この映画はあまり面白くありません。
examples.tr: This movie isn't very interesting.

examples.jp: 肉はあまり食べません。
examples.tr: I don't eat meat very much.

examples.jp: 日本語はあまり難しくないです。
examples.tr: Japanese isn't very difficult.

examples.jp: ここは人があまりいません。
examples.tr: There aren't many people here.

examples.jp: 昨日は勉強をあまりしませんでした。
examples.tr: I didn't study much yesterday.

86.explain:
Used to soften the degree of negation and to be polite in communication.
With na-adjectives: ではありません (polite), じゃない (casual).
With nouns of quantity: Nが/は あまり ありません to say “there isn't much/aren't many …”.
Not used for absolute emphasis. To emphasize “almost not”, use ほとんど～ない.

Expresses a degree/duration/frequency LOWER than expected: “not very …/not much …”.
Must be used with the negative form: ありません／ない. Using the affirmative is incorrect in this meaning.
Scope: applies to verbs (actions, frequency), adjectives (degree), and nouns of quantity/existence.
The nuance is gentle and neutral; it is not an absolute negation (unlike全然～ない: “not at all”).
Colloquial variant: あんまり (casual). Polite: ～ません／～ではありません.

rows: あまり～ない／ありません
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>はあまり<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くない。
Compared with an expected/previously mentioned level
この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>はそんなに<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しくない。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>はほとんどテレビを<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ない。
<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>が<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby>わからない。
あんまり<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しくないよ。

mistakes: Using the affirmative after あまり: × あまり食べます → it must be ○ あまり食べません.
Forgetting to change the i-adjective ending: × あまり高いない → ○ あまり高くない.
Confusing it with全然/ほとんど in degree of negation; choosing wrongly gives the wrong nuance.
Wrong particle for existence: ×人はあまりありません → people are living beings → いません.
86.notes:
In spoken language, あまり may be slightly clipped before ない: “あまり食べない → まり食べない” (not recommended in exams).
With i-adjectives, both くない and くありません are correct; choose according to the level of politeness.
With quantity words/counters:数はあまり多くない(the number is not large) → more natural when you add evaluative words多く/少なく.

examples.jp: りんごはいくつありますか。
examples.tr: How many apples are there?

examples.jp: ケーキをいくつ食べましたか。
examples.tr: How many pieces of cake did you eat?

examples.jp: みかんをいくつ買いましたか。
examples.tr: How many mandarin oranges did you buy?

examples.jp: 失礼ですが、おいくつですか。
examples.tr: Excuse me, but may I ask how old you are?

examples.jp: ここに箱がいくつありますか。
examples.tr: How many boxes are there here?

examples.jp: いくつかの質問があります。
examples.tr: I have a few questions.

87.explain:
Friendly and neutral; when politeness or sensitivity is needed (asking someone's age), use おいくつですか and add the softener失礼ですが.
If the exact unit is needed, use何＋counter: ビンは何本ですか。
In written language, いくつか has a gentle nuance of “a few”, without specifying an exact number.

いくつ asks about an unspecified quantity and is usually used for small items that can be counted directly.
It can replace何＋counter in basic communication; however, with specific units (本、枚、冊…),何＋counter is more natural.
おいくつですか is used politely to ask someone's age (especially older people).
いくつか (noun) means “a few, some”.

rows: <ruby>卵<rt>たまご</rt></ruby>はいくつありますか。
Specific about the type of unit
<ruby>卵<rt>たまご</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby><ruby>個<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ですか。
あなたは<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby><ruby>歳<rt>さい</rt></ruby>ですか。
<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>ですが、おいくつですか。

mistakes: Confusing it with いくら (price): × これはいくつですか → ○ これはいくらですか。
Forgetting to use a counter when needed: × ペンはいくつですか (ambiguous) → ○ ペンは何本ですか。
Using いくつ to ask an older person's age without politeness; use おいくつですか／何歳ですか instead.
87.notes:
When the quantity is large/not directly countable, switch to どのくらい/どれくらい: どのくらい買いましたか。
Avoid asking someone's age directly when it is not necessary; if you must ask, use おいくつですか to be polite.
In answers, use数字＋counter or a plain number: 3つ／三つ (both kanji and native Japanese forms are fine at N5).

examples.jp: いつか日本へ行きたいです。
examples.tr: I want to go to Japan someday.

examples.jp: いつか自分の店を持ちます。
examples.tr: Someday I will have my own shop.

examples.jp: いつかは家を買いたいです。
examples.tr: Eventually, I want to buy a house.

examples.jp: いつかの写真を見つけました。
examples.tr: I found a photo from some time ago.

examples.jp: その約束をいつか果たします。
examples.tr: I will keep that promise someday.

examples.jp: いつか会いましょう。
examples.tr: Let's meet up someday.

88.explain:
Creates a vague but positive feeling; often used with きっと／必ず to strengthen the commitment.
Use いつかの when talking about an unspecified day in the past that is implicitly shared between the speaker and the listener.
When stating long-term goals, いつかは is placed before the topic to emphasize “sooner or later …”.

Indicates an unspecified point in time in the future (usually) or in the past (when using いつかの). Translation: “someday”.
Carries a nuance of hope/dreams/long-term direction when used with ～たい, ～つもり, ～ます.
いつかは means “eventually …”, emphasizing inevitability without making clear when.
Not used to ask “when”; that is いつ (interrogative).

rows: いつか<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>したい。
Indicates frequency, not a vague point in time
いつも<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいです。
いつでも<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>してください。

mistakes: Confusing it with the interrogative いつ (when): × いつか来ますか (vague) when a specific appointment is needed → ○ いつ来ますか。
Using いつか in a context that requires a clear promise of time (listening section) → trap: the “unspecified” answer choice is more correct.
Confusing いつも/いつでも with いつか because they all contain いつ: pay attention to frequency vs a vague point in time.
88.notes:
To make a goal more concrete, add a vague time reference:将来/いつの日か日本で働きたい。
Avoid overusing it in schedules that require a time commitment; いつか is so vague that it may be taken as evasive.
In spoken language, いつかさ… can introduce an old story/a memory (casual).

examples.jp: 何かあったら、いつでも連絡してください。
examples.tr: If anything comes up, please contact me anytime.

examples.jp: 私はいつでも行けます。
examples.tr: I can go anytime.

examples.jp: この店はいつでも開いています。
examples.tr: This shop is always open.

examples.jp: 困ったら、いつでも手伝いますよ。
examples.tr: If you're ever in trouble, I'll help you anytime.

examples.jp: 質問はいつでも大丈夫です。
examples.tr: You can ask questions anytime.

89.explain:
Used to show flexibility:予約は いつでも 変更できます (You can change your reservation at any time).
Polite/encouraging: いつでもどうぞ／いつでもお越しください sounds friendly and warm.
In advertising/services: サポートは いつでも OK (24/7 support).
Rarely used directly with the negative; when negated, it is more natural to shift the meaning: いつでもは行けません (I can't go just any time) rather than a total negation.

Main meaning: “anytime”, expressing ability/willingness/permission at any point in time.
Polite nuance: often used when making a suggestion or an invitation, or when talking about flexibility of time.
Different from “いつも”: いつでも = “any time is fine (your choice)”; いつも = “always (habit/frequency)”.
Often used with verbs of ability/availability:行ける,会える,使える,開いている,連絡する,手伝う.
Often used in invitations/services: いつでもどうぞ／いつでもお越しください。

rows: いつも <ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きする
いつか <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい
いつでもいい／<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>
<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>は いつでもいいです

mistakes: Confusing it with いつも: いつでもは行きます (wrong meaning) → いつも行きます (I always go).
Unnatural total negation: × いつでも行けません → いつでもは行けません (I can't go just any time).
Position: place it right before the verb/predicate; avoid inserting it in the middle of a long noun phrase, which causes ambiguity.
For the advertising sense of “24/7”, use いつでも; for habits/frequency, you must use いつも.
89.notes:
Combining with “Xでも” forms a universal series: いつでも・どこでも・だれでも・なんでも.
In spoken language, “いつでもOK” is colloquial; more formal: “いつでも結構です／差し支えありません”.
Often used with a light condition:困ったら、いつでも～ /必要なら、いつでも～.

examples.jp: 私はいつも7時に起きます。
examples.tr: I always get up at 7.

examples.jp: 彼はいつも元気です。
examples.tr: He is always full of energy.

examples.jp: いつもはバスで行きませんが、今日は行きます。
examples.tr: I don't usually go by bus, but today I will.

examples.jp: 彼女はいつもコーヒーを飲みません。
examples.tr: She never drinks coffee.

examples.jp: この店はいつもにぎやかです。
examples.tr: This shop is always lively.

90.explain:
Very high frequency: almost every time. If you just mean “often”, consider よく／たいてい.
“いつもは” + a present difference: sets up a frame of contrast.
When complaining, いつも can carry a critical nuance:彼は いつも 遅れる (he is always late).

Meaning: “always/regularly”, indicating high frequency (almost every time).
“いつもは” is used to state a general habit and then contrast it with the present situation.
Can be used with both the affirmative and the negative: いつも行く／いつも行かない.
Casual/standard nuance, suitable for both written and spoken language.

rows: Neutral, a little weaker than いつも
たいてい <ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる
ふだんは <ruby>早寝<rt>はやね</rt></ruby>です

mistakes: Confusing it with いつでも (availability) → Choose correctly according to the meaning: frequency vs a time of your choice.
Position: place いつも before the predicate; avoid inserting it between the subject and an important particle, which causes ambiguity.
Critical nuance: using いつも + something negative can sound like criticism.
90.notes:
Polite combination: いつもありがとうございます (Thank you for your continued support).
Emphasizing a difference:今日はいつもより寒い (It's colder today than usual).
In letters/business:平素（へいそ）より＝ふだんより (close in meaning to “いつも”).

examples.jp: こちらは田中さんです。
examples.tr: This is Mr. Tanaka.

examples.jp: こちらへどうぞ。
examples.tr: This way, please.

examples.jp: こちらがお手洗いです。
examples.tr: This is the restroom.

examples.jp: こちらの商品はいかがですか。
examples.tr: How do you like this product?

examples.jp: こちらこそ、ありがとうございます。
examples.tr: I'm the one who should be thanking you.

examples.jp: こちらは三名です。
examples.tr: There are three of us.

91.explain:
More polite than これ/ここ/この; suited to service, guidance and refined communication.
Gently giving directions:受付は こちら です。
Introducing someone: こちら は山田課長です。

こちら is a polite demonstrative equivalent to “この/ここ/これ” (but more polite), meaning "this side/this one/this person/our side".
For people: "this person" (polite, courteous).
For places/directions: "this way/this side".
For organizations/groups: "our side/we".
Used in directions, service, on the phone and in introductions.

rows: ここは<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>です。

mistakes: Confusing it with これ/ここ: to say "this is the restroom" politely, say こちらがお手洗いです (not これが…).
Using こちら for things far from the speaker → use あちら/そちら depending on distance/context.
Dropping の when modifying a noun: × こちら部屋→ correct: こちらの部屋。
91.notes:
The phrase こちらこそ is used to reply to thanks/an apology: "the same goes for me".
On the phone/in service:こちらはABC会社でございます。 (This is ABC Company.)
“こちらになります” is a polite way of saying "this is ~" (with a service nuance).

92.connection: さっき + [sentence/clause] / さっきの + N

examples.jp: さっき、田中さんに会いました。
examples.tr: I saw Mr. Tanaka a little while ago.

examples.jp: さっきのメールを見ましたか。
examples.tr: Did you see the email from earlier?

examples.jp: さっきから頭が痛いです。
examples.tr: I've had a headache for a while now.

examples.jp: さっきまで雨でした。
examples.tr: It was raining until just a moment ago.

examples.jp: さっき電話しました。
examples.tr: I called a little while ago.

examples.jp: さっきの写真を送ってください。
examples.tr: Please send me the photo from earlier.

92.explain:
さっき usually goes with the past: さっき行きました／来ました。
さっきから + Vている expresses a state that has continued up to the present.
さっきまで emphasizes that something has just ended.
Casual, used in conversation; in formal situations you can use 先ほど (more polite).

さっき expresses a very recent point in time in the past: "a little while ago, just now". It usually goes with the past tense, or with the progressive when used as さっきから.
さっき: a short, vague time before the present (from a few minutes to a short while).
さっきから: from a while ago until now (continuing).
さっきまで: right up until a little while ago (has just stopped).

rows: たった<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>きました。
<ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>ほどお<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>しました。
もうすぐ<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>まります。
さっきから／さっきまで
Since a while ago / Until a while ago
さっきから<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っています。

mistakes: Wrong tense: × さっき行きます → correct: さっき行きました。
Confusing さっき with もうすぐ (future): × さっき始まります → correct: もうすぐ始まります。
Dropping の when used as a noun modifier: × さっき店→ correct: さっきの店。
92.notes:
How "recent" さっき is depends on the context (usually within the last few dozen minutes).
さっき is not used for the future; for an ongoing present action, use さっきから + Vている.
In business emails, prefer 先ほど for politeness.

examples.jp: 今すぐに来てください。
examples.tr: Please come right now.

examples.jp: 家に帰ったらすぐにシャワーを浴びます。
examples.tr: When I get home, I take a shower right away.

examples.jp: 授業が終わってすぐに帰りました。
examples.tr: I went home right after class ended.

examples.jp: 駅のすぐに近くにコンビニがあります。
examples.tr: There is a convenience store right near the station.

examples.jp: その話を聞いてすぐに涙が出ました。
examples.tr: As soon as I heard that story, tears came to my eyes.

93.explain:
“すぐに” indicates a point in time or a position very close to the present reference point.
It can be placed before a verb or a time noun: すぐに行く／すぐに電話する／帰ってすぐに寝る。
In casual speech, “に” is often dropped: すぐ行くね！ → "I'll be right there!"
“すぐ” emphasizes a sense of speed with no delay; it suits situations where you want to show urgency or immediacy.

① “すぐに” expresses an action that happens right after another one, emphasizing immediacy.
② English meaning: "immediately", "right after", "at once".
③ It can express closeness in both time and space:・Time → the action happens right after.
・Space → "right near", "right next to".
“すぐに” can be used alone or combined with “あとで／前に／近くに” to emphasize the degree of closeness.

rows: Expresses something happening right after an action
Short form of “すぐに”, used in casual conversation
Has not happened yet, but will happen in the near future
Emphasizes an action that has just happened
たった<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りました。

mistakes: Forgetting “に” in written language or on the JLPT:
✕ すぐ行きます → (correct in conversation, but on the JLPT write) ○ すぐに行きます。
Confusing “すぐに” with “もうすぐ”:
すぐに → immediately.
もうすぐ → soon.
“すぐに” is not used with long-lasting actions (such as 勉強しています) — only with actions that start or are brief.
JLPT N5 often asks: choose the right one of “すぐに”, “もうすぐ”, “あとで” to express the exact time.
93.notes:
“すぐに” is an adverb of time and comes before the main verb of the sentence.
It can be used in instructions and urgent directions:火事です！すぐに逃げてください！→ Fire! Get out right now!
At JLPT N5, learners only need to know the basic usage "to do something immediately".
At higher levels, “すぐに” can express a "quick emotional reaction", for example:彼はすぐに怒ります。→ He gets angry easily.

94.connection: ぜんぜん + [negative predicate] (Vません / Aくない / Naではない)

examples.jp: お金がぜんぜんありません。
examples.tr: I have no money at all.

examples.jp: きのうはぜんぜん勉強しませんでした。
examples.tr: I didn't study at all yesterday.

examples.jp: この映画はぜんぜんおもしろくないです。
examples.tr: This movie isn't interesting at all.

examples.jp: 先生の話がぜんぜんわかりませんでした。
examples.tr: I didn't understand the teacher's talk at all.

examples.jp: 日本の冬は寒いけど、ベトナムの冬はぜんぜん寒くないです。
examples.tr: Winter in Japan is cold, but winter in Vietnam isn't cold at all.

94.explain:
Usually comes before a negative verb or negative adjective.
Emphasizes the feeling of "none at all" or "zero degree".
In conversation, "ぜんぜん + positive" can be used, as in “ぜんぜん大丈夫！” (Totally fine!) – however, this is a natural colloquial expression and is not used on the JLPT.
Suits a strong intonation or clear emotion (annoyance, surprise, emphasis).

① “ぜんぜん” is an adverb that emphasizes absolute negation: "not at all", "not in the least".
② Used together with a negative verb or negative adjective to express that an action or state does not happen at all.
③ In modern conversation, “ぜんぜん” is sometimes used with a positive meaning ("very", "totally") for emphasis — but for JLPT N5, you only need to remember the negative meaning.

rows: ぜんぜん + Vない／Adjない
ぜんぜんわかりません。
<ruby>全<rt>まった</rt></ruby>く（まったく） + Vない
Like “ぜんぜん” but used in written language or more formal situations

mistakes: Wrongly using it with an affirmative sentence on the JLPT:
✕ ぜんぜんわかります → ○ ぜんぜんわかりません。
Confusing it with あまり: “ぜんぜん” = not at all, stronger than “あまり”.
Forgetting the negative verb: ✕ ぜんぜん勉強→ ○ ぜんぜん勉強しません。
JLPT N5 often asks: choose the right negative adverb among “あまり”, “ぜんぜん”, “ちょっと”.
94.notes:
「ぜんぜん」 = "completely / totally / not at all" depending on the context.
In kanji it is written 「全然」, but in everyday communication it is usually written in hiragana: 「ぜんぜん」.
In modern Japanese you may hear: 「ぜんぜんOK！」, 「ぜんぜん大丈夫！」 → with the positive meaning "totally fine". However, this is colloquial and is not used in written language or on the JLPT.

examples.jp: こんにちは。そちらは今、何時ですか。
examples.tr: Hello. What time is it there now?

examples.jp: 午後3時ごろそちらへ伺います。
examples.tr: I will visit you around 3 p.m.

examples.jp: 明日はそちらで会いましょう。
examples.tr: Let's meet at your place tomorrow.

examples.jp: そちらの国では春はいつですか。
examples.tr: When is spring in your country?

examples.jp: こちらは晴れです。そちらはどうですか。
examples.tr: It's sunny here. How about there?

examples.jp: 電話ありがとうございます。ABC会社そちらでしょうか。
examples.tr: Thank you for answering. Is this ABC Company?

95.explain:
Polite: そちら is used instead of そっち/そこ to show respect to the listener.
Avoid using it directly to address a person: instead of “そちらは田中さんですか”, use “田中様でいらっしゃいますか”. However, in the context of an organization, “そちらはABC会社ですか” is natural.
Symmetrical set: こちら（our side）– そちら（your side）– あちら（a third party/far from both）.
Goes with the appropriate particle: そちらへ（toward）, そちらに（to/at）, そちらで（doing an action at that place）.

“そちら” is a polite pronoun referring to the listener's side (location, organization, group, situation on their side).
Used on the phone, in emails and in service communication to be more polite than そこ/そっち.
It can indicate a direction/destination (そちらへ), a place (そちらで) or possession (そちらのN).
In conversation, “そちらは？” is used to ask back about the listener's side (weather, situation).

rows: こちらは<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>です。
そちらは<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>ですか。
あちらへお<ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>いします。
そこは<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>い？／そっちどう？
<ruby>貴社<rt>きしゃ</rt></ruby>のご<ruby>担当<rt>たんとう</rt></ruby><ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using そこ/そっち instead of そちら in formal contexts → less polite.
Wrong particle: “そちらで行きます” (incorrect) → should be “そちらへ行きます”.
Addressing the listener as そちら in every situation → can sound rude. Use the name + 様 or a suitable keigo expression.
Mixing up the demonstrative axis: こちら (our side) ≠ そちら (your side) ≠ あちら (over there).
95.notes:
On the phone, you can open with: そちらはABC会社でいらっしゃいますか。
Asking about the weather/situation: そちらはどうですか／そちらの状況はいかがですか。
In service, staff often refer to themselves as こちら and to customers as そちら（のご希望） as an indirect polite form.

examples.jp: 朝ごはんを食べました。それから、学校へ行きました。
examples.tr: I ate breakfast. After that, I went to school.

examples.jp: 宿題をして、それから、テレビを見ます。
examples.tr: I'll do my homework, and then watch TV.

examples.jp: パスポートを取って、それから空港へ行きます。
examples.tr: I'll get my passport, and then go to the airport.

examples.jp: 牛乳を買って、それからパンも買ってください。
examples.tr: Please buy milk, and then buy some bread too.

examples.jp: えっと…それから、質問があります。
examples.tr: Um… and also, I have a question.

96.explain:
Clear time sequence: used to recount steps/activities of a day.
Adding something you just remembered: as a filler when listing things to buy/requests.
In plain writing and everyday conversation, それから is very common and natural.
It does not express a cause-and-result relationship; if needed, use それで／だから.

Meaning: "after that; and then; next". Used to connect actions/ideas in a clear chronological order.
Nuance: stronger in sequence than そして (neutral). Suited to listing things done one after another.
Also used like "oh, and also/by the way" when adding something you just remembered in conversation.

rows: <ruby>掃除<rt>そうじ</rt></ruby>した。それから<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Using それから for a result relationship: incorrect. Use それで/だから.
Confusing it with そして: if you want to emphasize "chronological order", choose それから; そして just connects ideas neutrally.
Repeating それから too often in writing makes the text monotonous; mix in other connectives.
96.notes:
When listing several items in instructions, まず／次に／それから／最後に create a very clear flow.
In conversation, それから can serve as a pause while the speaker thinks of what comes next, helping the rhythm sound natural.
Avoid connecting too many sentences with それから in a row; replace it with それに, そして, そのあと to avoid monotony.

97.connection: たいてい + V / たいてい + [sentence/clause]

examples.jp: 私はたいてい6時に起きます。
examples.tr: I usually get up at 6.

examples.jp: 週末はたいてい家で映画を見ます。
examples.tr: On weekends I usually watch movies at home.

examples.jp: たいていの学生はアルバイトをします。
examples.tr: Most students have part-time jobs.

examples.jp: この店はたいてい空いています。
examples.tr: This shop is usually not crowded.

examples.jp: 日本の夏はたいてい暑いです。
examples.tr: Summers in Japan are usually hot.

97.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence or before the predicate.
A general nuance, not a 100% statement.
Suited to describing habits and tendencies.

Most of the time, the majority of the time; talks about habits and general tendencies.
Stronger than “よく”, weaker than “いつも”.
Not used to mean "approximately (a number)".

rows: よく<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>します

mistakes: Using “たいてい” to estimate a number → wrong function.
Confusing it with “いつも”: its degree is stronger than “たいてい”.
Dropping “の” when used as a modifier: it must be “たいていの人”.
97.notes:
In advertising/news the kanji “大抵” is sometimes used.
“たいていのN” helps limit the scope of the subject: たいていの子ども, たいていの場合.
When you want to be more certain, “ほぼ/ほとんど” may be suitable, but the nuance is different.

98.connection: だいたい + [quantity/N] / だいたい + V

examples.jp: 学校までだいたい20分です。
examples.tr: It's about 20 minutes to school.

examples.jp: この本の内容はだいたい分かりました。
examples.tr: I roughly understood the content of this book.

examples.jp: 昼ごはんはだいたい500円ぐらいです。
examples.tr: Lunch is about 500 yen.

examples.jp: 準備はだいたい終わりました。
examples.tr: The preparations are mostly finished.

examples.jp: だいたいでいいので、数を教えてください。
examples.tr: A rough number is fine, so please tell me how many.

98.explain:
Placed right before the item being estimated or at the beginning of the sentence.
Neutral, usable in almost any situation.
Suited to cases where absolute precision is not needed.

Approximates a quantity/time (about/approximately).
A general assessment, not detailed (generally/broadly).
Not used for "frequency" (unlike “たいてい”).

rows: だいたい<ruby>100人<rt>ひゃくにん</rt></ruby>
たいてい<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>にいる

mistakes: Confusing it with “たいてい” (frequency) → used in the wrong context.
Combining it with an exact number and the word “ちょうど” creates a contradiction.
Dropping “ぐらい/くらい” when you need to emphasize approximation: in many contexts “ぐらい” sounds more natural.
98.notes:
Kanji: 大体; at N5, the kana “だいたい” is preferred.
“だいたい合っている” = roughly correct.
In conversation: “だいたいね…” introduces an idea as "generally speaking…".

examples.jp: 時間がありません。だから、今日は無理です。
examples.tr: I don't have time. So today is impossible.

examples.jp: 危ないです。ですから、近づかないでください。
examples.tr: It's dangerous. So please don't go near it.

examples.jp: 勉強が好きです。だから、よく図書館に行きます。
examples.tr: I like studying. So I often go to the library.

examples.jp: 雨です。だから、傘を持って行きます。
examples.tr: It's raining. So I'll take an umbrella.

examples.jp: 安いです。だから、買います。
examples.tr: It's cheap. So I'll buy it.

99.explain:
Placed after the sentence giving the reason, to lead to the conclusion.
Keep the politeness appropriate to the listener: だから → ですから.
Very natural for answering “どうして？”.

Connects a stated reason (S1) with a result/intention (S2) in the sense of "so/therefore".
Casual and direct; replace it with “ですから” when politeness is needed.
Different from “ので/から” (linking within one sentence) and “それで” (continuation of events).

rows: <ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいです。ですから<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>です。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なので<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だから<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。（Nだから）
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>でした。それで<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>に。

mistakes: Omitting the reason sentence (S1) → “だから” sounds abrupt.
Confusing it with “それで” in narrative writing.
Using “だから” with superiors/customers: not polite enough → change to “ですから”.
99.notes:
For an even softer tone: “ですので” (advanced) instead of “ですから”.
“だからこそ” emphasizes the positive inevitability of the result.
Avoid repeating “だから” too often in one stretch of speech.

examples.jp: だれかがドアをノックしています。
examples.tr: Someone is knocking on the door.

examples.jp: だれかいますか。
examples.tr: Is anyone here?

examples.jp: だれかを探しています。
examples.tr: I'm looking for someone.

examples.jp: だれかに手伝ってもらえますか。
examples.tr: Could I get someone to help me?

examples.jp: これはだれかのかばんです。
examples.tr: This is someone's bag.

examples.jp: 週末、だれかと映画を見に行きます。
examples.tr: This weekend I'm going to see a movie with someone.

100.explain:
Used when the speaker does not know specifically who it is or does not want to say.
In questions, だれか～? suggests there may be such a person (expecting a "yes/no" answer).
In requests/calls for help, だれか～! has an urgent nuance: だれか助けて！
Polite style: どなたか (the polite form of だれか) can be used.
It is not used with the negative to mean "no one"; switch to だれも～ない.

だれか means "someone, somebody" (unspecified).
Usually used in affirmative sentences or questions to talk about a person whose identity is unknown.
Emphasizes "some person among those possible", but not "everyone" (unlike だれでも).
Goes with particles such as が, を, に, と, へ, の depending on its role in the sentence.
だれか + ません/ない is not used to mean "no one"; to say "no one", use だれも～ません/ない.

rows: だれでも <ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>できます。
Must be used with a negative
なにか / どこか / いつか
Like だれか but for things, places, time
なにか <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べます。/ どこか <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。
どなたか いらっしゃいますか。

mistakes: Incorrect: だれか来ません。→ Correct: だれも来ません。 (no one comes)
Confusing だれか with だれでも: だれか入れます (refers to someone) ≠ だれでも入れます (anyone can enter).
Leaving out the appropriate particle: だれかに聞きます, だれかを探します, だれかと行きます.
100.notes:
As a modifier: だれかのN (example: だれかの手紙).
In conversation, the particle can be omitted if the meaning is clear: だれか来た？
Combined with もし: もし だれか困っていたら、助けましょう。 strengthens the hypothetical sense.

examples.jp: この図書館はだれでも入れます。
examples.tr: Anyone can enter this library.

examples.jp: この問題はだれでもわかります。
examples.tr: Anyone can understand this problem.

examples.jp: イベントはだれでも参加できます。
examples.tr: Anyone can take part in the event.

examples.jp: これはだれでも使えるアプリです。
examples.tr: This is an app anyone can use.

examples.jp: 失敗はだれでもあります。
examples.tr: Everyone fails sometimes.

examples.jp: 入口はだれでも分かるように大きい看板があります。
examples.tr: There is a large sign so that anyone can find the entrance.

101.explain:
Used in neutral/objective contexts (advertising, instructions, rules, introductions).
When emphasizing "no restriction on who": だれでもOK, だれでも歓迎.
Avoid using it for very personal/private things that are hard to generalize (e.g., "everyone loves this dish" may sound exaggerated).
Polite form: どなたでも for strangers/customers.

Expresses universality: "anyone can…/everyone…".
Often used in rules, announcements, and descriptions of ease or universality.
Suited to verbs of ability, right of use, degree of ease/difficulty, understanding/knowing.
Not used to say "no one" (in the negative it is easily misread as "not everyone…").
In gentle invitations/suggestions, you can use: だれでも来てください (anyone, please come).

rows: だれかが <ruby>呼<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んでいます。
Must be used with a negative
A specific group, does not mean "anyone"
More polite than だれでも
どなたでも <ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>できます。

mistakes: Confusing it with だれも: "anyone/everyone" must be だれでも, not だれも.
Using だれでも + ません to say "no one" is incorrect; you must use だれも～ません.
Confusing it with みんな: みんな is "everyone" (a specific group), だれでも is "anyone" (open, conditional).
101.notes:
Adding は: だれでもは～ emphasizes a contrasting topic, with an emphatic nuance.
A common modifier form in advertising: だれでも簡単に～できる.
Be careful with the negative: だれでも～ない is usually understood as "not everyone…", not "no one…".

examples.jp: きょうはだれも来ませんでした。
examples.tr: No one came today.

examples.jp: このことをだれも知りません。
examples.tr: No one knows about this.

examples.jp: パーティーでだれとも話しませんでした。
examples.tr: I didn't talk to anyone at the party.

examples.jp: 忙しくて、だれにも会いません。
examples.tr: I'm busy, so I don't see anyone.

examples.jp: その質問にだれも答えられませんでした。
examples.tr: No one could answer that question.

examples.jp: 夜は危ないので、だれも外に出ません。
examples.tr: It's dangerous at night, so no one goes outside.

102.explain:
Used to negate the entire group of people who could be involved.
Adding も creates the nuance "not even one person…".
In spoken language, you can add emphasis with ぜんぜん/まったく (but be careful with the degree): ぜんぜん だれも来ない。
In the past tense: だれも来ませんでした keeps the meaning "no one…(did)".

だれも～ません/ない expresses "no one …".
A form of total negation where the subject is a "person".
Combines with particles depending on the relationship: に → だれにも, と → だれとも.
Not used with the affirmative (だれも～ます/だれも～だ) in modern standard Japanese.
Emphatic when placed at the beginning of a sentence: だれも～ない → strong negation "no one at all".

rows: どこも <ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>いていない。
どなたも いません。

mistakes: Using the affirmative with だれも: Incorrect “だれも来ます” → Correct “だれも来ません”。
Forgetting to change に/と to だれにも/だれとも in the negative.
Confusing it with だれでも～ない: "not everyone…" ≠ "no one…".
102.notes:
If you need "not even once": 一度も～ません (not once), which differs from だれも (target is people).
Do not insert が after だれも when it is the subject of a negative: usually だれも来ません (not だれもが来ません).
When politeness is needed in service: どなたも～ません/いらっしゃいません.

examples.jp: あの人はだれですか。
examples.tr: Who is that person?

examples.jp: これはだれのペンですか。
examples.tr: Whose pen is this?

examples.jp: 入口にだれがいますか。
examples.tr: Who is at the entrance?

examples.jp: だれも来ませんでした。
examples.tr: No one came.

examples.jp: だれか日本語が話せますか。
examples.tr: Can anyone speak Japanese?

examples.jp: 今日はだれと行きますか。
examples.tr: Who are you going with today?

103.explain:
Neutral; can be used in most contexts; for more politeness, use “どなた”.
In yes/no questions, “だれか” is often used to ask about existence: “someone…”.
“だれも” goes with the negative to mean “no one”.

“だれ” is an interrogative pronoun for people: who, which person.
It takes the particle that matches its function: が (subject), を (object), に (target/destination), と (together with), の (possession).
“だれも + Vません” = “no one …”; “だれか” = “someone”.
mistakes: Using “だれも” with the affirmative at the basic level gives the wrong meaning: “だれも来ます” is easily misunderstood; use “みんな来ます” instead.
Forgetting the particle: “だれですか” (correct), but for possession you must use “だれの”.
Confusing “だれ” (who) with “どれ/どの” (which one/which + N): their functions are different.
103.notes:
“だれも +肯定” in casual conversation is sometimes understood as “everyone …”, but at the basic level you should use “みんな” to avoid ambiguity.
In announcements/ceremonies, prefer “どなた”.
On the phone/at the door: “どなたですか？” is very polite.

examples.jp: ときどきジョギングをします。
examples.tr: I sometimes go jogging.

examples.jp: 私はときどきコーヒーを飲みます。
examples.tr: I sometimes drink coffee.

examples.jp: 時々雨が降ります。
examples.tr: It sometimes rains.

examples.jp: 学生のとき、ときどき図書館へ行きました。
examples.tr: When I was a student, I sometimes went to the library.

examples.jp: 彼はときどきは早く帰ります。
examples.tr: He does go home early sometimes.

104.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence to set up the frequency context: ときどき、～。
Placed after the subject to emphasize the subject's habit: 私はときどき～。
ときどきは carries the nuance “every now and then (only a little)…”, creating a contrast with the usual.
Used with verbs/adjectives/nouns: ときどき忙しいです／ときどき雨です。

ときどき expresses a lower frequency than よく, and a higher one than たまに.
Often used in the present tense to talk about habits; can also be used in the past to describe frequency during a period.
Can be placed at the beginning of the sentence, in the middle (before the verb), or after the subject.

rows: いつも<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べます。
よく<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ます。
ときどき<ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>します。
たまに<ruby>外<rt>そと</rt></ruby>で<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べます。

mistakes: Adding a wrong particle: ×ときどきを → ✓ときどき（を is not needed）.
Confusing its position with に/で: ときどき is an adverb of frequency, not a marker of place/point in time.
Wrong kanji: ×時時→ ✓時々.
104.notes:
Kanji spelling: 時々 (the character 時 repeated). Hiragana: ときどき. Avoid the misspelling “時時”.
Used with ことがある to talk about experiences that happen occasionally: ときどき～ことがあります。
No special particle is needed; it is an adverb that stands on its own.

105.meaning: Why ~?（the answer uses ～から — see the entry ～から（reason））
105.connection: どうして + [sentence/clause] + か（answer: ～から(です)）

examples.jp:
A: どうしてきのうはやくかえりましたか。
B: ようじがありましたから。
examples.tr:
A: Why did you go home early yesterday?
B: Because I had something to take care of.

examples.jp:
A: どうしてたべませんか。
B: けさもうあさごはんをたべましたから。
examples.tr:
A: Why aren't you eating?
B: Because I already had breakfast this morning.

examples.jp:
A: どうしてにほんごをべんきょうしていますか。
B: にほんではたらきたいですから。
examples.tr:
A: Why are you studying Japanese?
B: Because I want to work in Japan.

105.explain:
どうして　is a question word asking for the reason. Instead of repeating what the other person said, you can use “どうしてですか” – “Why is that?”
から is used to explain a reason: because ~, so ~. It is also used to answer a question with “どうして” – “why”.

どうして：Why ~
から：Because ~.
～から、～：Because ~, ~

examples.jp: 駅までどうやって行きますか。
examples.tr: How do you get to the station?

examples.jp: このアプリはどうやって使いますか。
examples.tr: How do you use this app?

examples.jp: 東京へはどうやって行くの？
examples.tr: How do you get to Tokyo?

examples.jp: その問題はどうやって解決しましたか。
examples.tr: How did you solve that problem?

examples.jp: 日本語はどうやって勉強したんですか。
examples.tr: How did you study Japanese?

examples.jp: 空港からホテルまでどうやって行けばいいですか。
examples.tr: How should I get from the airport to the hotel?

106.explain:
Polite: どうやってVますか／どうやってVたらいいですか。
Casual: どうやってVるの？／どうやってやる？
Emphasizing a request for advice: どうやって…たらいいですか／どうすればいいですか。
Combined with means: どうやって（電車で／バスで／歩いて）行きますか。
Avoiding long repetition: you can add the place/destination with まで／へ／に to make the meaning clear.

どうやって = by what means, how: asks about the process, means, or route to reach a goal.
Compared with どう: どう is a general “how”, while どうやって emphasizes the specific method.
Often used with verbs of motion (行く、来る), use (使う), making (作る), solving (直す、解決する)…
Can ask about the route (which way to go), the tool (with what), or the sequence (which steps to follow).

rows: With what/by what means of transport
<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く？（<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>で）
どのように<ruby>解決<rt>かいけつ</rt></ruby>しますか。

mistakes: Wrong particle: ×どうやって学校を行きますか → ✓どうやって学校に行きますか。
Confusing it with どう, which is too general, so the answer does not state a specific method.
Using it with あります/います: to ask about moving, use 行きます/来ます, not ×どうやってありますか。
Confusing it with 何で（なにで）: that one only asks about the tool, not the sequence of steps.
106.notes:
Do not use どうやってのN to modify a noun; replace it with どのような/どういう（例：どういう方法）.
何で has 2 readings: なにで = with what; なんで = why (colloquial). Be careful to avoid misunderstanding.
When asking for a route: どうやって行きますか can be answered with a line, a means of transport, or directions.

examples.jp: 週末はどこかへ行きましたか。
examples.tr: Did you go anywhere over the weekend?

examples.jp: 財布をどこかに忘れました。
examples.tr: I left my wallet somewhere.

examples.jp: 暑いですね。どこかで休みましょう。
examples.tr: It's hot, isn't it? Let's take a break somewhere.

examples.jp: この近くにどこか安いレストランはありますか。
examples.tr: Is there a cheap restaurant somewhere around here?

examples.jp: いっしょにどこかへ行きませんか。
examples.tr: Would you like to go somewhere together?

examples.jp: この文、どこか変です。
examples.tr: Something is off about this sentence.

107.explain:
Invitation: どこかへ行きませんか (polite), どこか行かない？ (casual).
Dropping the particle へ in conversation: どこか行く (natural); in formal speech, keep に／へ.
Emphasizing vagueness: avoids being specific, polite in communication (“eat somewhere”, “rest somewhere”).
Not used with total negation. To say “nowhere”, use どこにも～ません.

Main meaning: “somewhere, some place” – the speaker does not (or does not want to) specify a particular place.
Vague, polite/gentle nuance when making a suggestion: used in invitations and when suggesting shared plans.
Combines flexibly with place particles: に／へ (destination), で (place where the action happens), の (noun modifier).
Different from “どこでも” (anywhere – covering everything) and “どこにも～ません” (not … anywhere – total negation).
Common extended meaning (by feel): どこかおかしい／変だ = “something is strange”.

rows: どこかで<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いましょう。
どこにも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。
どこも（＋<ruby>肯定<rt>こうてい</rt></ruby>/<ruby>否定<rt>ひてい</rt></ruby>）
With the affirmative = “everywhere”; with the negative = “nowhere”
どこも<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。／どこも<ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>いていない。

mistakes: Using どこか with total negation: × どこか行きません → for the meaning “not go anywhere”, it must be どこにも行きません.
Confusing it with どこでも: どこか = some place; どこでも = any place is fine.
Forgetting the particle: × どこか行きます → use どこかに/へ行きます (formal).
107.notes:
Colloquial short form: どっか (e.g., どっか行く？). Avoid it in formal written language.
どこかの +人/会社/国: “some person/company/country”.
The meaning “something …”: どこか + Adj（変/不自然/おかしい） is very natural in conversation.

examples.jp: このカードはどこでも使えます。
examples.tr: This card can be used anywhere.

examples.jp: 休みならどこへでも行きたいです。
examples.tr: If I have time off, I'd like to go anywhere at all.

examples.jp: 座る場所はどこでもいいです。
examples.tr: I don't mind where I sit.

examples.jp: 子どもはどこでもすぐ友だちを作ります。
examples.tr: Children make friends quickly wherever they are.

examples.jp: この町ではどこでもWi‑Fiが使えます。
examples.tr: You can use Wi‑Fi anywhere in this town.

108.explain:
Nuance of “no limits, not picky”.
Goes well with permission/ability patterns: ～てもいい／～られる／～ことができる.
With verbs of motion, どこへでも／どこにでも sound more natural when emphasizing the destination.
Avoid using it with the negative; switch to どこにも～ません to express “nowhere”.

Expresses unlimited scope: “anywhere at all…”.
Usually used with the affirmative, ability, permission, gentle commands: 使える／行ける／入れる／座ってください.
To emphasize direction, use どこへでも／どこにでも; if no emphasis is needed, どこでも is still natural.
Not used for total negation (to say “nowhere”, it must be どこにも～ません).

rows: どこへでも／どこにでも
Add へ/に to make the direction clear
どこへでも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。
どこにも<ruby>売<rt>う</rt></ruby>っていません。
Close in meaning to どこでも

mistakes: Wrong negative: × どこでも行きません → ○ どこにも/どこへも行きません.
Forgetting to emphasize direction when needed: with verbs of motion, use どこへでも/どこにでも to make the meaning clear.
Confusing it with どこか (some place) → avoid どこでも when you only want to be vague without covering everything.
108.notes:
Fixed expression: どこでもいい（です）= “anywhere is fine”, common when making a choice.
In advertising/products: どこでも使える／ドア（Doraemon joke） – highlights the “usable anywhere” feature.
Written language usually avoids repeating でも: choose どこでも or どこへでも according to the meaning; do not use both at once unnecessarily.

examples.jp: 今日はどこにも行きません。
examples.tr: I'm not going anywhere today.

examples.jp: 財布がどこにもありません。
examples.tr: My wallet is nowhere to be found.

examples.jp: この本はどこにも売っていません。
examples.tr: This book isn't sold anywhere.

examples.jp: 彼はどこにもいない。
examples.tr: He's nowhere to be found.

examples.jp: 疲れたので、休みの日もどこにも出かけませんでした。
examples.tr: I was tired, so I didn't go out anywhere, even on my day off.

109.explain:
Emphasizes absence/non-occurrence everywhere: add も after どこに.
Polite: どこにも～ません; casual: どこにも～ない／いない／ないです（colloquial).
With searching: ～見つかりません／見つからない to say “can't find it no matter how hard I look”.

Meaning: “not … anywhere”, total negation over the whole scope of places.
Used with verbs of motion (行く/来る/出かける) and verbs of existence/searching (ある/いる/見つかる/売る…).
に emphasizes “at (which) place”/“in which place”; へ emphasizes “direction/destination”.
Style: ません (polite), ない (casual). The JLPT accepts both.

rows: どこへも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。
Colloquial/general; easy to use with “open/closed, there is/there isn't”
どこも<ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>いていない。

mistakes: Using どこでも with the negative: × どこでも行きません → ○ どこにも/どこへも行きません.
Confusing に and へ: for existence/searching, use に; for motion, you can use へ to emphasize direction.
Forgetting to use the negative form: × どこにも行きます → it must be どこにも行きません/行かない.
109.notes:
Has an absolute nuance; add よ/ね to soften it: 今日はどこにも行かないよ。
Distinguish あります/います: inanimate things use ある（ない）, people/animals use いる（いない）.
In a negative question used as an invitation: どこか行きませんか (shall we go somewhere?) is different from どこにも～ません.

110.connection: どこへも + Vません（V of motion）

examples.jp: 休みの日はどこへも行きません。
examples.tr: I don't go anywhere on my days off.

examples.jp: 台風だから、今日はどこへも出かけません。
examples.tr: There's a typhoon, so I'm not going out anywhere today.

examples.jp: 去年はお金がなくてどこへも旅行できませんでした。
examples.tr: Last year I had no money, so I couldn't travel anywhere.

examples.jp: 危ないので、子どもだけではどこへも行かせません。
examples.tr: It's dangerous, so I don't let the children go anywhere on their own.

examples.jp: 今週は忙しくてどこへも行っていません。
examples.tr: I've been busy this week, so I haven't gone anywhere.

110.explain:
Often used with 行く／出かける／旅行する／来る in the negative form.
Polite: ～ません／～ませんでした; casual: ～ない／～なかった.
If you do not need to emphasize “direction”, どこにも行きません is also natural.

Used to negate movement to any place: not going/not coming anywhere.
The particle へ marks the direction/destination clearly; that is why どこへも fits best with verbs of motion.
Similar in meaning to どこにも（行きません）, but different in emphasis: に = “at/to”, へ = “toward”.

rows: どこへも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなかった。
どこにも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。
どこへでも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。
どこも<ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>いていない。

mistakes: Using どこでも with the negative: × どこでも行きません → ○ どこへも/どこにも行きません.
Forgetting へ: × どこも行きません (with motion, written language should use どこへも/どこにも).
Confusing the nuance: どこへも = motion; do not use it for “there isn't/doesn't exist” (use どこにもありません).
110.notes:
In sentences emphasizing a reason: ～ので/から + どこへも行きません (because …, I'm not going anywhere).
A more strongly polite way of saying it: 本日はどこへも伺いません（です） – business context.
Polite affirmative counterpart: どこへでも参ります (humble).

111.connection: どこも + Vません / どこも + [negative predicate]

examples.jp: もう夜遅いので、店はどこも開いていません。
examples.tr: It's already late at night, so none of the shops are open.

examples.jp: この町には静かな所がどこもありません。
examples.tr: There is no quiet place anywhere in this town.

examples.jp: なくした鍵はどこも見つかりません。
examples.tr: I can't find the key I lost anywhere.

examples.jp: 今日はどこも行きません。家で勉強します。
examples.tr: I'm not going anywhere today. I'll study at home.

examples.jp: お正月なのに、コンビニもどこも開いていませんでした。
examples.tr: Even though it was New Year's, nothing was open, not even the convenience stores.

111.explain:
Has a general nuance covering the whole space: “no place is …”.
Suits descriptions of states: 開いていない／混んでいない／売っていない／ない.
With motion, consider the context: in written language/exams, switch to どこへも/どこにも.

Meaning with the negative: “no place …”, covering the whole scope of places.
Often used to describe a general situation: open/closed, there is/there isn't, crowded/empty, available/sold out…
With the affirmative, どこも = “everywhere …”. However, this entry focuses on the negative pattern どこも～ません.
With verbs of motion, どこも行きません sounds natural in conversation, but the JLPT prefers どこへも/どこにも行きません.

rows: どこも<ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>いていない。
どこへも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。
どこでも（＋<ruby>肯定<rt>こうてい</rt></ruby>）
Close in meaning to どこでも

mistakes: Using どこも for motion in academic writing: prefer どこへも/どこにも.
Confusing どこも～ません with どこにも～ません: both are total negation, but どこにも is neutral, while どこも is often used for “general situations”.
Forgetting the negative: × どこもあります → ○ どこもありません.
111.notes:
Often used with もう/全然/まったく for emphasis: もうどこも開いていない。
In sentences that deny an expectation: 探したけど、どこも見つからなかった。
In advice: 今日は危ないからどこも行かないほうがいい。

examples.jp: 駅はどこにありますか。
examples.tr: Where is the station?

examples.jp: 先生はどこにいますか。
examples.tr: Where is the teacher?

examples.jp: どこで昼ごはんを食べますか。
examples.tr: Where will you eat lunch?

examples.jp: 休みの日はどこへ行きますか。
examples.tr: Where do you go on your days off?

examples.jp: あなたはどこから来ましたか。— ベトナムから来ました。
examples.tr: Where are you from? — I'm from Vietnam.

examples.jp: この携帯はどこのブランドですか。
examples.tr: What brand is this phone?

112.explain:
Asking about a static location: どこに あります／いますか。
Asking where an action takes place: どこで Vますか。
Asking about direction/destination: どこへ／どこに 行きますか（へ carries a nuance of direction, に emphasizes the destination).
Polite: ～はどこですか is also used to ask about a location in general (トイレはどこですか).

どこ is the question word “where”; combined with particles, it asks about location, place of action, direction, starting point, and destination.
どこのN asks about the origin/affiliation of a noun: “N from which place/which brand”.
Distinguish あります (inanimate) and います (animate) when asking about location.

rows: More polite than どこ/どれ
お<ruby>手洗<rt>てあら</rt></ruby>いはどちらですか。
どこの<ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby>ですか。

mistakes: Wrong particle: ×どこでいますか → ✓どこにいますか（existence takes に）.
Mixing up に/で: actions must take で, static locations take に.
Confusing あります/います: inanimate things use あります, people/animals use います.
Using へ for a static location is unnatural: ×どこへありますか → ✓どこにありますか。
112.notes:
Asking for a specific address: 住所はどこですか（more natural than どこにありますか）.
For a person/thing that is moving, to ask “where” right now, you still use どこにいますか／どこにありますか depending on animate/inanimate.
In casual conversation: どこ？／どこにいる？

113.meaning:
Which side | has 3 main meanings:
Used to ask about a place (a polite way of saying どこ)
Used to ask about direction.
Used to ask the name of a country, school, company…
113.connection: どちらが + A/V + か / Nは + どちらですか / どちらへ/に + V (asking about direction, polite)

examples.jp: コーヒーと紅茶、どちらが好きですか。
examples.tr: Which do you like, coffee or tea?

examples.jp: 会議室はどちらですか。
examples.tr: Where is the meeting room?

examples.jp: どちらの会社から来ましたか。
examples.tr: Which company are you from?

examples.jp: 駅へはどちらへ行けばいいですか。
examples.tr: Which way should I go to get to the station?

examples.jp: 失礼ですが、どちら様ですか。
examples.tr: Excuse me, but may I ask who you are?

examples.jp: この二つのサイズは、どちらが大きいですか。
examples.tr: Of these two sizes, which one is bigger?

113.explain:
More polite than どっち; can be used in services, at work, and with strangers.
To modify a noun, you must use “の”: どちらのN (not どちら N directly).
To ask about a location/place, use は + どちらですか for a natural, polite question.
Used to ask about direction with へ/に, and about origin with から (どちらからいらっしゃいましたか).

Core meaning: “which one/which way/where” with a polite nuance.
Commonly used for a choice between two options. With more than two, the standard is どれ/どの; however, in polite conversation どちら can still be used, but at JLPT N5 you should follow the “2 options” rule.
Asking about a location/place politely: どこ → どちら (トイレはどちらですか).
Asking which side/which organization something belongs to: どちらの + N (どちらの会社ですか).
When asking about a person very politely: どちら様ですか (Who is this, please?).

rows: Usually 2 options; can be a polite “where”
AとBはどちら？／トイレはどちら？
Does not modify nouns; stands alone
どれがあなたのですか。
Must be followed by a noun
どの<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby>ですか。
Used in ordinary speech; polite → どちら

mistakes: Forgetting “の”: incorrect × どちら会社→ correct ✓ どちらの会社.
Using どちら when there are 3+ options in a JLPT question (trap): choose どれ/どの if there is no “2 options” context.
Confusing どちら (polite “where”) with どこ: in polite conversation, use どちら.
Using どちら with close acquaintances sounds too formal; with friends, どっち/だれ is more appropriate.
113.notes:
In service settings, “お国はどちらですか” sounds very polite and replaces “どこの国”.
“どちら様でいらっしゃいますか” is ultra-polite keigo used on the phone.
With more than two options, the JLPT favors the answer どれ/どの; do not confuse it with どちら unless the context is general politeness.

114.connection: どなた + ですか / どなたが + V + か（polite form of だれ）

examples.jp: 失礼ですが、どなたですか。
examples.tr: Excuse me, but who are you?

examples.jp: こちらはどなたですか。
examples.tr: Who is this?

examples.jp: これはどなたのお荷物ですか。
examples.tr: Whose luggage is this?

examples.jp: どなたか日本語がわかる方はいらっしゃいますか。
examples.tr: Is there anyone here who understands Japanese?

examples.jp: 明日のイベントはどなたでも参加できます。
examples.tr: Anyone can take part in tomorrow's event.

examples.jp: 本日はどなたも入れません。
examples.tr: No one may enter today.

114.explain:
More polite than だれ; safe to use in formal settings.
“どなた様（さま）でしょうか／でいらっしゃいますか” is ultra-polite keigo.
Takes particles such as が/に/の/を depending on its role: どなたが来ますか, どなたに会いますか.
In casual conversation, use だれ to sound more natural.

“どなた” = “who” at a polite/respectful level; used with strangers, guests, and superiors.
Variant meanings: どなたか (someone), どなたでも (anyone), どなたも〜ません (no one).
Combines naturally with keigo: いらっしゃる／お〜になる when the agent is a guest.
Often used on the phone, at reception desks, in shops, and in hospitals.

rows: On the phone, formal business situations
どなた<ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>でしょうか。
Polite, attached to the noun <ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>
どの<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>が<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>ですか。
どんな<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きですか。

mistakes: Confusing affirmative/negative: × どなたでも来ません→ ✓ どなたも来ません.
Using どなた with friends/younger people sounds stiff; use だれ.
Missing the correct particle: × どなた会いますか → ✓ どなたに会いますか.
Mistakenly asking about characteristics with どなた: to ask “what kind of person”, you must use どんな人/どの方.
114.notes:
“どなたでも” is often seen in open announcements: “どなたでも大歓迎”.
With the negative, “どなたも〜ません” = “no one”; do not use “どなたでも〜ません”.
“どなたのご担当者様” sounds redundant; choose one of the two: “ご担当者様” or “どなたがご担当ですか”.

examples.jp:
A: どのくらい日本へ行きますか。
B: 三か月ぐらい行きます。
examples.tr:
A: How long are you going to Japan for?
B: I'm going for about three months.

examples.jp:
A: 大阪から東京まで新幹線でどのくらいかかりますか。
２時間半かかります。
examples.tr:
A: How long does it take from Osaka to Tokyo by Shinkansen?
It takes two and a half hours.

115.explain:
Used to ask about duration or quantity.
You can use either どのくらい or どのぐらい to ask.

どのくらい： how long? how much/how many?
115.notes:
meaning_vi: A question word asking about quantity or degree.
examples: 1. ①　どのぐらい　かかりますか。
How long will it take?
2. ②　毎日　どのぐらい　ねますか。
About how many hours do you sleep every day?
3. ③　うちに　どのぐらい　本が　ありますか。
About how many books are there in your house?
4. ④　夏休みは　どのぐらい　ですか。
How long is the summer vacation?

examples.jp: どの本が一番おもしろいですか。
examples.tr: Which book is the most interesting?

examples.jp: どの部屋ですか。
examples.tr: Which room is it?

examples.jp: どのシャツが田中さんのですか。
examples.tr: Which shirt is Tanaka's?

examples.jp: 先生はどの方ですか。
examples.tr: Which person is the teacher?

examples.jp: 駅はどの辺ですか。
examples.tr: Whereabouts is the station?

examples.jp: ここからどのくらいかかりますか。
examples.tr: How long does it take from here?

116.explain:
Remember that どの is always followed by a noun; if there is none, switch to どれ.
To ask about a person politely: use どの方 instead of どの人.
To ask about degree: どのくらい/どのぐらい goes with V/A/名詞+です.
For origin/affiliation, どこのN is very natural in conversation: どこの会社ですか.

“どの + N” asks you to identify one specific noun among several options: “Which …?”.
“どのくらい/どのぐらい” asks about degree, time, or quantity: “how much/how long”.
It cannot stand alone; if there is no noun, use どれ (which one).
For origin/affiliation, どこのN is usually more natural: どこの国／どこの会社.

rows: どれがあなたのですか。
どこの<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>ですか。
どのくらい<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>？

mistakes: Using どの alone: ×どのが好き？ → ✓ どれが好き？ or ✓ どの映画が好き？
Confusing どの with どこの when asking about origin: ✓ どこの国／会社.
Forgetting the noun after どの, which leaves information missing in JLPT answers.
Confusing どのくらい (degree) with いくつ/いくら (quantity/price). Choose correctly based on the meaning of the question.
116.notes:
“どのくらい” ≈ “どれくらい” (both are common; どれくらい is slightly more colloquial).
For a specific point in time, use “何時／何分／何日” instead of どの.
“どの辺” is casual; the more polite form is “どのあたりですか”.

117.meaning: Which one（pronoun; distinguish from どの + N — see the どの～ entry）
117.connection: どれ + (です/particle)（stands alone, not followed by N）

examples.jp: どれがあなたのくつですか。
examples.tr: Which shoes are yours?

examples.jp: りんごとみかんとバナナ、どれをかいますか。
examples.tr: Apples, mandarin oranges, and bananas — which will you buy?

examples.jp:
A: あなたのかさはどれですか。
B: あかいかさです。
examples.tr:
A: Which umbrella is yours?
B: The red one.

117.explain:
Identifies one item within a group of three or more.

どれ : which one
どのN : which N

examples.jp: この中からどれでも選んでください。
examples.tr: Please choose any one of these.

examples.jp: 色はどれでも同じ価格です。
examples.tr: All the colors are the same price.

examples.jp: プレゼントはどれでもうれしいです。
examples.tr: I'd be happy with any of the presents.

examples.jp: お好きなものをどれでもどうぞ。
examples.tr: Please take whichever you like.

examples.jp: ドリンクはどれでも100円です。
examples.tr: All drinks are 100 yen.

examples.jp: 席はどの席でもいいです。
examples.tr: Any seat is fine.

118.explain:
Friendly; often used when letting someone else choose: “どれでもいいです”.
Natural in instructions/price lists: “どれでも同じ価格”.
“どれでも” is not used to modify a noun directly; change it to “どのNでも”.
If there is no clear list, consider using なんでも (anything at all) instead of どれでも.

“どれでも” expresses no distinction among options that already exist: “any of them is fine”.
Often used with いい／大丈夫／構いません to show agreement/no specific requirement.
When you need to modify a noun, use “どのNでも” instead of “どれでもN”.
The scope of “どれでも” must be a finite set of options that is visible or listed.

rows: Any one of them is fine
どれも<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです／どれも<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きではありません。
Not limited to a specific list
どこでもいい／いつでも<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: ×どれでも席→ ✓どの席でも（modifying a noun requires どのNでも）
Wrong scope: to say “anything at all” in general, use なんでも, not どれでも.
Confusing it with negative どれも: “どれも〜ません” = “none of them”, completely different from “どれでも”.
Using どれでも for places/times: use どこでも／いつでも respectively.
118.notes:
In service settings, “どれでもどうぞ” is a polite way of inviting free choice.
“どれでも +同じ” is common in promotions and combo deals.
With verbs that ask you to choose one, どれでも emphasizes “not being picky”; どれも (affirmative) emphasizes “all are ...” (a different nuance).

examples.jp: 何か食べたいです。
examples.tr: I want to eat something.

examples.jp: 飲み物は何かありますか。
examples.tr: Is there anything to drink?

examples.jp: 何か質問がありますか。
examples.tr: Are there any questions?

examples.jp: 何か手伝いましょうか。
examples.tr: Shall I help you with anything?

examples.jp: 一緒に何か飲みませんか。
examples.tr: Why don't we have something to drink together?

examples.jp: 昨日、何かありましたか。
examples.tr: Did something happen yesterday?

119.explain:
Expresses indefiniteness, keeping politeness and distance: it avoids pointing directly at “a specific X”.
In questions,何か implies an expectation that the answer is “yes”:何か問題がありますか。
を after何か is often dropped in conversation:何か食べる？ (casual).
Used with 〜ませんか to make a gentle invitation/suggestion.
For total negation, use何も～ません, not何か～ません.

何か expresses an unspecified “something”.
Often used in affirmative sentences, exploratory questions, and invitations/suggestions to stay vague and polite.
With あります/います it expresses “there is something” (an object/person/animal) without specifying what.
何か is not used with the negative form to say “not … anything” (use何も～ません in that case).
In negative questions with 〜ませんか,何か softens the sentence: “Shall we …?”

rows: どれか<ruby>選<rt>えら</rt></ruby>んでください。

mistakes: Using何か with a negative to say “not … anything”: ×何か食べません → correct:何も食べません。
Not dropping を is not wrong in spoken language, but in JLPT written language you should be standard:何かを食べます（acceptable),何か食べます（more natural).
Confusing何か and何:
何を飲みますか（what will you drink? a specific question）
何か飲みますか（will you drink anything? a suggestion).
Misreading何かありますか as “is there a specific X?”; it actually asks in general “is there anything (any matter)?”.
119.notes:
“何かありますか” can mean “Did something happen?” depending on the context (not only “Is there anything?”).
“何か＋Nを＋ください” is more polite than “何かください” when you have a kind of thing in mind:何か飲み物をください。
Negative questions with 〜ませんか and何か often carry a nuance of invitation:何か食べませんか（＝let's eat something together）.
In spoken language,何か is sometimes shortened to “なんか” (colloquial), but on the exam you should keep何か.

examples.jp: 今日は何も食べません。
examples.tr: I'm not eating anything today.

examples.jp: ここには何もありません。
examples.tr: There is nothing here.

examples.jp: 何も分かりません。
examples.tr: I don't understand anything.

examples.jp: 休みの日は何もしません。
examples.tr: On my days off, I don't do anything.

examples.jp: もう何もいりません。
examples.tr: I don't need anything anymore.

examples.jp: 昨日のことは何も知りません。
examples.tr: I don't know anything about what happened yesterday.

120.explain:
Emphasizes “not a single thing/doing nothing at all” → a firm, total nuance.
を after何も is usually dropped:何も食べません（more natural than何もを食べません）.
In casual style, use ない:何もない／何もしない。
For general negation of existence,何もありません（there is nothing at all） is very common in announcements/polite answers.

何も～ません/ない is a total negation pattern: “not … anything at all”, “nothing”.
Always used with a verb/adjective in the negative form; not used with the affirmative.
Used with あります/います to say “there is nothing (at all)”.
The degree can be emphasized with supporting words (N4 and above) such as全然/全く; at N5,何も + Vません alone is enough.

rows: Must be used with the negative
どれも<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きじゃない。
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません。

mistakes: Using it with the affirmative: ×何もあります → incorrect. Use the negative:何もありません。
Adding を after何も: ×何もを食べません → を is usually dropped:何も食べません。
Confusing it with何か:
何か食べます（eat something, affirmative)
何も食べません（not eat anything, negative).
Using いません for inanimate objects (×何もいません for objects in a room) → the correct form is何もありません.
120.notes:
“何もない” can stand alone as a complete sentence:何もない（There is nothing at all）.
“何も問題はありません” is grammatically correct:何も＋N＋は＋ありません → “There is no problem at all”.
In a polite answer, you can say: いいえ、何もありません。
With verbs of cognition,何も覚えていません／何も聞いていません are both natural.

examples.jp: 私はなんでも食べます。
examples.tr: I eat anything.

examples.jp: 飲み物はなんでもいいです。
examples.tr: Any drink is fine.

examples.jp: この店はなんでもあります。
examples.tr: This store has everything.

examples.jp: 彼はなんでも知っています。
examples.tr: He knows everything.

examples.jp: 質問があれば、なんでも聞いてください。
examples.tr: If you have any questions, feel free to ask anything.

examples.jp: それはなんでもありません。
examples.tr: It's nothing.

121.explain:
なんでも is used to speak generally, without limiting the options. It suits both polite and casual speech.
なんでもいい shows “not being picky”; add です to be more polite: なんでもいいです。
なんでもない is used to reassure someone or to downplay importance: “it's nothing/it's fine”.
Avoid using なんでも with a ない-type negative to say “not … anything”; use 何も…ない for that meaning.

なんでも expresses an all-inclusive scope: “anything …”, “whatever it is …”. Usually used with affirmative verbs/ adjectives.
なんでもいい: “anything is fine”, showing there is no specific requirement.
なんでもない: a set phrase meaning “it's nothing/it's fine”, not to be understood as “everything is not” (different from the standard negative formula何も…ない).
In everyday speech,なんでも sometimes carries a nuance of exaggeration (“everything …” in a relative sense).

rows: Set phrase, not the ordinary “なんでも + ない” structure
<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>、なんでもないよ
どれでも／どこでも／いつでも／だれでも

mistakes: Incorrect use with a negative: to say “not eat anything” you must use何も食べない, not “なんでも食べない”.
Confusingなんでもない (it's nothing) with “何でもない= not everything…” → the correct understanding is the set phrase “it's nothing”.
Usingなんでも too broadly leads to exaggeration: consider the context (e.g., “なんでも知っている” is an exaggeration).
In questions about a specific choice, use どれでも/どのNでも instead of なんでも.
121.notes:
In spoken language,なんでも can be an exaggeration: “everything …” but understood as “almost everything …”.
At higher levels,なんでも also means “I hear that …” (hearsay), but this is not N5; do not confuse it with the meaning “anything”.
なんでもかんでも is an emphatic form; avoid overusing it in formal written language.

122.connection: なんで + [question] (reason; 何で is also used to ask about means: バスで…)

examples.jp: なんで遅れたんですか。
examples.tr: Why were you late?

examples.jp: 学校へなんで行きますか。— バスで行きます。
examples.tr: How do you get to school? — I go by bus.

examples.jp: なんで日本語を勉強しているんですか。
examples.tr: Why are you studying Japanese?

examples.jp: 今日はなんで来ましたか。—自転車で来ました。
examples.tr: How did you come here today? — I came by bicycle.

examples.jp: なんで笑うの？
examples.tr: Why are you laughing?

examples.jp: 東京へなんで行きますか。—電車で行きます。
examples.tr: How do you get to Tokyo? — I go by train.

122.explain:
To ask for a reason in casual conversation: use なんで +普通形(plain form).
To be more polite: なんで～んですか, or switch to どうして/なぜ.
To ask about means: なんで + V; the answer is usually N + で.
Use rising intonation at the end of the sentence to show it is a question.

なんで(何で) has 2 main meanings at N5:
Why (casual, everyday conversation). Add ～んですか to be polite: なんで～んですか。
By what (means/method): asks about transportation, tools, etc.
Why (casual, everyday conversation). Add ～んですか to be polite: なんで～んですか。
By what (means/method): asks about transportation, tools, etc.
Tell them apart by looking at the answer:
If the answer uses N + で(バスで, はしで, てで, パソコンで) → it asks about means.
If the answer uses ～から／～ので(雨だから,忙しいので) → it asks about the reason.
If the answer uses N + で(バスで, はしで, てで, パソコンで) → it asks about means.
If the answer uses ～から／～ので(雨だから,忙しいので) → it asks about the reason.
In formal contexts or on exams, prefer どうして/なぜ to ask for a reason; なんで leans toward casual.

rows: Casual; can be ambiguous without context
Neutral, more polite than なんで
どうして<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ないんですか
なぜ<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れましたか
どうやって<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きますか

mistakes: Confusing the meanings: なんで = “by what” or “why”. Use the answer (N+で vs ～から/～ので) to tell them apart.
Using なんで in overly formal contexts → it sounds impolite. Use どうして/なぜ instead.
Wrong pronunciation: writing “なにで” when asking for a reason. The common colloquial standard isなんで; “なにで” mainly means “by what”.
122.notes:
Kanji:何で. Common pronunciation:なんで. When it means “by what”, it can also be understood as “by what means”.
In some contexts, なんで asking for a “reason” can sound blunt; avoid using it with superiors you are not close to.
To ask “how” (a process, step by step) → prefer どうやって to avoid ambiguity.

123.name: ～に行く／来る（purpose of movement）
123.connection: Vます(drop ます)・N(action) + に + 行く・来る・帰る

examples.jp:
にほんごをべんきょうしに行きます。
にほんごのべんきょうに行きます。
examples.tr:
I'm going to study Japanese.
I'm going to my Japanese lesson.

123.explain:
に：Indicates the purpose of an action.

V2 in order to do V1.
