V2 is usually a verb of movement such as いきます go, きます come, かえります return, もどります go back…
123.notes:
For verbal nouns （Nする）：there are 2 ways to use them:
Full sentence: N(place)へ Nを Vに 行きます・来ます・帰ります

examples.jp: この映画はほとんど知っています。
examples.tr: I know almost everything about this movie.

examples.jp: 日本語はほとんど話せません。
examples.tr: I can hardly speak Japanese.

examples.jp: ほとんどの学生がテストに合格しました。
examples.tr: Most of the students passed the test.

examples.jp: 今日はほとんど雨が降りませんでした。
examples.tr: It hardly rained at all today.

examples.jp: 休みの日はほとんど毎日公園へ行きます。
examples.tr: On my days off, I go to the park almost every day.

examples.jp: 昨日はほとんど一日中家にいました。
examples.tr: Yesterday I was at home almost all day.

124.explain:
Do not add ない when it is already used before a noun: ほとんどのN (not ほとんどのNない).
To emphasize “almost not”, always use it with the negative form: ほとんど～ない／ありません.
With specific quantities, ほとんど emphasizes “almost all”, while だいたい emphasizes “approximately, about”.
In spoken language, “ほとんどは〜” can be used to state the majority of the subject: ほとんどは学生です (most of them are students).

With the affirmative: “almost all/most”. Example: ほとんど分かる = understand almost everything.
With the negative: “hardly” (a very low degree, close to 0). Example: ほとんど分からない.
ほとんどの + N is used to say “most …”. Avoid using “ほとんどN” directly before a noun in standard written language (except in some special cases).
With time/frequency: ほとんど毎日(almost every day), ほとんど一日中(almost all day).
The quantitative nuance is considerably stronger than だいたい (roughly), close to ほぼ (almost completely).

rows: ほとんどできる／ほとんどできない
Formal, neutral; close to affirmative ほとんど
ほぼ<ruby>完成<rt>かんせい</rt></ruby>した。
Emphasizes estimation; not as strong as ほとんど
About frequency, not an exact proportion
たいてい<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる。
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない。

mistakes: Incorrect use with nouns: × ほとんど学生→ ○ ほとんどの学生(written language). In special cases it may be acceptable in spoken language, but it is not recommended on the exam.
Forgetting the negative when you want to say “hardly”: × ほとんど分かります → ○ ほとんど分かりません.
Confusing it with だいたい: だいたい means “about, roughly” and is not as strong as ほとんど.
Redundant double negative: × ほとんどの人が来ませんない → ○ ほとんどの人が来ません.
124.notes:
ほとんど + ありません/ないです is a very common pair at N5; memorize it as a set phrase.
When describing duration: “ほとんど一日中” is more natural than “ほとんど一日” when you mean “all day”.
“ほとんどNだ” can be heard in spoken language: ここはほとんど外国人だ (almost everyone here is a foreigner), but standard written language prefers ほとんどのN.

examples.jp: この映画はまあまあ面白いです。
examples.tr: This movie is fairly interesting.

examples.jp: 日本語はまあまあ話せます。
examples.tr: I can speak Japanese reasonably well.

examples.jp: テストはまあまあでした。
examples.tr: The test went okay.

examples.jp: この店はまあまあな値段です。
examples.tr: This shop's prices are reasonable.

examples.jp: 彼はテニスがまあまあ上手だ。
examples.tr: He's pretty good at tennis.

examples.jp: まあまあ、落ち着いて。
examples.tr: Now, now, calm down.

125.explain:
Placed before an adjective/verb to indicate an average degree.
In conversation, “まあまあです／まあまあかな” is a safe answer when you don't want to praise or criticize strongly.
The interjection form “まあまあ、…” is used at the beginning of a sentence to ease the mood.
Do not combine it with strong intensifiers such as “とても” or “すごく”.
Politeness: neutral; add です/ます to be polite.

Expresses an average degree: “so-so”, “okay”, “fairly”. Neither very good nor very bad.
Used to be modest or to soften an evaluation, avoiding a strong statement.
As the interjection “まあまあ”, it is used to reassure/calm others: “calm down”.
The nuance depends on the context: mild praise (“pretty good”) or mild criticism (“only so-so”).

rows: More positive than まあまあ
この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>はけっこういい。
なかなか<ruby>面白<rt>おもしろ</rt></ruby>い。

mistakes: Using it with strong intensifiers: ×とてもまあまあ → choose one or the other.
Wrong position: ×静かなまあまあ店→ 〇まあまあな静かな店(but the natural way to say it is usually: まあまあ静かな店).
Confusing まだまだ (still a long way to go) with まあまあ (so-so) → the meanings are different.
Overusing it in formal written language: avoid it in academic texts; replace it with “平均的/可もなく不可もない”.
125.notes:
Colloquial phrases: “まあまあかな…”, “まあまあいける” (eating/ drinking/ doing something is okay).
“まあまあの + N”: まあまあの成績(okay grades).
Do not use “とても” + まあまあ (contradictory degrees).
The repeated interjection “まあ、まあ” has a different role; it is usually written in full as “まあまあ”.

examples.jp: 映画はまだやっています。
examples.tr: The movie is still showing.

examples.jp: もう夜ですが、彼はまだ起きています。
examples.tr: It's already night, but he's still awake.

examples.jp: 私はまだ学生です。
examples.tr: I'm still a student.

examples.jp: 冷蔵庫に牛乳がまだあります。
examples.tr: There's still milk in the fridge.

examples.jp: 宿題はまだですか。— はい、まだです。
examples.tr: Haven't you finished your homework yet? — No, not yet.

examples.jp: 日本語はまだまだ難しいです。
examples.tr: Japanese is still really difficult for me.

126.explain:
Placed right before the element being emphasized (verb, noun, adjective).
Combines naturally with もう for contrast: もう…／まだ…
“まだです” is a polite short form; the full form is usually “まだVていません”.
“まだまだ” expresses modesty/the expectation that there is still a long way to go.

Indicates a state/activity that is ongoing up to the present: “still”, “yet”.
In questions: expresses an expectation about whether a change has happened yet (“… yet?”).
The short answer “まだです” is equivalent to “not (done) yet”.
“まだまだ” raises the degree: still a long way, still a lot.

rows: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>はまだ<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>っている。
もう<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えている。

mistakes: Confusing it with もう: “もう起きています” = already up; “まだ起きています” = still awake.
Using “まだ” but forgetting the correct tense: 〇まだしています／×まだします (different meaning: will not do it yet).
Question: “もう食べましたか。” Answer: “まだです。” (correct); ×“まだ。” in formal situations.
“まだに” is not used at N5 (the pattern いまだに is a higher level).
126.notes:
まだ +可能形: まだ行けます (can still go/still have the energy).
まだ +数量: まだ二人来ます (two more people are still coming).
Avoid using まだ with an unsuitable simple past: ×まだ行った → 〇まだ行っていない/まだ行く。

examples.jp: 宿題はまだしていません。
examples.tr: I haven't done my homework yet.

examples.jp: 雨はまだ降っていません。
examples.tr: It hasn't started raining yet.

examples.jp: 私はまだ行きません。
examples.tr: I'm not going yet.

examples.jp: プレゼントはまだありません。
examples.tr: There's no present yet.

examples.jp: 彼はまだ学生ではありません。
examples.tr: He isn't a student yet.

examples.jp: A: もう食べましたか。 B:いいえ、まだです。
examples.tr: A: Have you eaten yet? B: No, not yet.

127.explain:
Formal: use まだ～ません／まだ～ていません in polite conversation.
Nuance difference:まだ行きません: not going "at this moment".まだ行っていません: up to now "still haven't gone (even once/haven't started)".
まだ行きません: not going "at this moment".
まだ行っていません: up to now "still haven't gone (even once/haven't started)".
Emphasis: まだ + は is used to highlight the topic being contrasted (例:宿題はまだです)。
With time expressions: まだ＋今／今日／この週… emphasizes the sense of "it's not time yet".

Core meaning: まだ indicates that a situation "still" remains unchanged; with the negative (～ません／～ない／～ていません) it means "not yet, still not, has not happened/been completed".
まだ + Vません: emphasizes not-yet at present, implying a decision or schedule: "not doing it right now".
まだ + Vていません: emphasizes the state up to the time of speaking, "still haven't done it/it still hasn't happened", suitable for expressing experience/result.
まだ + N は/が ありません: "there is no N yet". まだ + Aく/では ありません: "not yet (reached the level/state)".
Implied expectation: usually implies that the action will happen in the future (unlike "never").

rows: More natural for saying "haven't done it" up to now
まだ<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べていません
Short answer replacing a full sentence
— もう<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わった？ — いいえ、まだです。

mistakes: Using まだ～ません to express the state of "never having done" → まだ～ていません/～たことがありません is more natural.
Confusing まだあります (still have) with まだありません (don't have yet).
Mixing up まだ and もう: もう～ません = no longer… (unlike まだ～ません = not yet).
Past tense with まだ: avoid まだ行きました (contradictory). Use まだ行っていません or もう行きました.
127.notes:
In casual speech, ～ません ⇄ ～ない: まだ行かない／まだ食べてない.
With verbs of experience: まだ行ったことがありません "have never been there yet".
With quantities: まだ三枚あります "there are still 3 sheets". In the negative: まだ三枚もありません "there aren't even 3 sheets yet".

examples.jp: 電車はもうすぐ来ます。
examples.tr: The train will be here soon.

examples.jp: もうすぐ三時です。
examples.tr: It's almost three o'clock.

examples.jp: もうすぐ春です。
examples.tr: Spring is almost here.

examples.jp: 雨がもうすぐ降ります。
examples.tr: It's going to rain soon.

examples.jp: 山田さんはもうすぐ着きます。
examples.tr: Yamada will arrive soon.

examples.jp: A: いつ出発しますか。 B:もうすぐ出発します。
examples.tr: A: When are we leaving? B: We're leaving soon.

128.explain:
Emphasizes a sense of "imminence": used when the wait is not long.
In formal announcements, まもなく is more appropriate; もうすぐ leans toward conversation.
Can be used with natural phenomena, schedules, and states that are about to change.

Meaning: Expresses something that will happen in the near future, with a sense of "almost there/about to happen".
Casual, neutral nuance; can be used in everyday conversation.
Does not express the past; used with the present/near future or N + です.

rows: もうすぐ<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>まります
Implies "it's time to…", often used with a suggestion
そろそろ<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りましょう
まもなく<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>到着<rt>とうちゃく</rt></ruby>します
Almost instant, stronger than “もうすぐ”

mistakes: Using the past with もうすぐ: × もうすぐ行った → ✓ もうすぐ行きます。
A direct negative is unnatural: × もうすぐ行きません → Say “まだ行きません” (not going yet) or use another expression that fits the context.
Confusing "already" with "soon": もう春です (it's already spring) ≠ もうすぐ春です (spring is almost here).
Confusing degrees of "nearness": すぐ (immediately) is stronger than もうすぐ (soon, not instant).
128.notes:
With potential/plan verbs: もうすぐ行けます (will soon be able to go).
Exclamation: もうすぐだ！ (Almost there!).
In descriptive written language: もうすぐ町が見えてくる (The town will soon come into view).

129.connection: もう + Vた (already…) / もう + Vない (no longer…)

examples.jp: もう食べました。
examples.tr: I've already eaten.

examples.jp: もう宿題をしましたか。
examples.tr: Have you done your homework yet?

examples.jp: もう行きません。
examples.tr: I'm not going anymore.

examples.jp: もうケーキはありません。
examples.tr: There's no more cake.

examples.jp: もう一度お願いします。
examples.tr: Once more, please.

examples.jp: もう少しゆっくり話してください。
examples.tr: Please speak a little more slowly.

129.explain:
Strong affirmative "already done": もう + Vた emphasizes completion.
Definite stop: もう + Vない／Vません shows a decision "not to do it anymore".
Polite: the short reply もういいです (that's enough/no longer needed) in service and shopping.
Casual: もう行った？／もうやらない。

Meaning 1: "already" with the past/completion (happened before the time of speaking).
Meaning 2: "no longer…" with the negative, showing the end of a habit/intention.
Meaning 3: "more, another" in quantity phrases (もう一度: once more; もう少し: a little more).
Implied expectation: a question with もう usually implies the asker thinks it may have already happened.

rows: Completed before the time of speaking
すでに<ruby>発表<rt>はっぴょう</rt></ruby>した

mistakes: Confusing もう～ません (no longer…) with まだ～ません (not yet). The meanings are opposite.
Using もう with the present in the wrong context: “もう行きます” is fine (I'm off/going right now), but it does not mean "already" in the past sense.
Answering “もうです” is unnatural. Use “はい、もうしました／いいえ、まだです”。
Confusing もうすぐ (soon) with もう (already). Example: もう春です (it's already spring) vs もうすぐ春です (spring is almost here).
129.notes:
In yes/no answers:
A: もう食べましたか。 B: はい、もう食べました／いいえ、まだです。
A: もう食べましたか。 B: はい、もう食べました／いいえ、まだです。
もう + non-past present can still mean "right now/soon" in spoken language: もう行くね (I'm off now).
Negative of existence: もうNがない = "there is no more N".

130.connection: もっと + A/Na / もっと + [Adverb] + V

examples.jp: もう少しもっとゆっくり話してください。
examples.tr: Please speak a little more slowly.

examples.jp: この本はおもしろい。もっと読みたい。
examples.tr: This book is interesting. I want to read more.

examples.jp: 今日は寒い。明日はもっと寒いそうです。
examples.tr: It's cold today. I hear it will be even colder tomorrow.

examples.jp: テストまでもっと勉強しましょう。
examples.tr: Let's study more before the test.

examples.jp: 次はもっと大きな声で歌ってください。
examples.tr: Next time, please sing in a louder voice.

examples.jp: 健康のためにもっと野菜を食べたほうがいいです。
examples.tr: For your health, you should eat more vegetables.

130.explain:
Emphasizes an increase: placed right before the word being intensified (A/V/Adv).
Polite: combine with 〜てください／ましょう to soften it. A direct “もっと！” can sound strong.
“もう少し” is milder than “もっと”: もう少し＝a little more; もっと＝considerably more.
With specific quantities: usually “もう＋[number＋counter]”（もう一杯）; “もっと” leans toward general degree (もっと多く).

Core meaning: "more, even more; increasing the degree/amount/speed… compared with now/expectations".
Used to:
Request/advise an increase in degree: もっと静かに、もっと頑張って。
Express a desire: もっと日本語が話せるようになりたい。
Make a progressive comparison:今年は去年よりもっと忙しい。
Request/advise an increase in degree: もっと静かに、もっと頑張って。
Express a desire: もっと日本語が話せるようになりたい。
Make a progressive comparison:今年は去年よりもっと忙しい。
Nuance: the speaker feels something is "not enough/lacking" and wants to "increase" it.
Position: comes before the adjective/adverb/verb it emphasizes.

rows: Written language/explanations; more formal than もっと
さらに<ruby>詳<rt>くわ</rt></ruby>しく<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>する
<ruby>今年<rt>ことし</rt></ruby>はずっと<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>い
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>がもっとも<ruby>速<rt>はや</rt></ruby>い

mistakes: Using it directly before a noun: ✕ もっと日本語→ instead:日本語をもっと勉強する／もっと日本語が話したい.
Confusing it with “もう”: “もう三枚ください”（3 more sheets） is more natural than “もっと三枚ください”.
Wrong superlative combination: ✕ もっと一番速い → いちばん速い（the most）／もっと速い（more）.
Confusing it with “もっとも”: もっと（more） ≠ もっとも（the most / however).
130.notes:
In conversation, “もっと！” can be used on its own as a command/encouragement.
With Aな: change it to Aに (きれいに、上手に) when it modifies a verb: もっときれいに書いて。
“もっと多くのN” (written language): もっと多くの人, but conversation usually uses “もっと人が…/人をもっと…”.
Combined with advice: もっと〜たほうがいい (You should ~ more).

examples.jp: 私は週末、よく公園へ行きます。
examples.tr: I often go to the park on weekends.

examples.jp: 日本の音楽をよく聞きます。
examples.tr: I often listen to Japanese music.

examples.jp: 彼は日本語がよく話せます。
examples.tr: He can speak Japanese well.

examples.jp: すみません、あなたの名前がよく聞こえませんでした。
examples.tr: Sorry, I couldn't hear your name well.

examples.jp: 子どものころ、友だちとよく遊びました。
examples.tr: When I was a child, I often played with my friends.

examples.jp: この映画はよくできています。
examples.tr: This movie is well made.

131.explain:
Position: comes before the verb and modifies the whole action.
With the negative: expresses "not clearly/not well": よくわかりません； for negative frequency, use あまり〜ません.
Slight differences: よく vs たびたび（more formal）; よく vs いつも（always, higher frequency）.

Meaning 1 (N5): frequency "often, frequently". Example: よく行きます（I often go）.
Meaning 2 (N5): degree of quality "well/clearly enough/skillfully". Example: よくわかります（I understand well）.
With the negative: よくわかりません＝"don't understand well", not "don't often understand". To say "not often", use あまり〜ません.
Context determines the meaning: よく飲む（drink often） vs よくできた（well done）.

rows: <ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>をよく<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する
Clearer meaning of "proficient" than よく

mistakes: Using よく＋Vません to say "not often": ✕ よく行きません → 〇 あまり行きません.
Confusing よく with上手に:日本語がよく話せます（natural）;日本語が上手に話せます (OK, but emphasizes "skillfully").
Using it with adjectives of degree: ✕ よく暑い → 〇 とても暑い／よく暑くなります（often gets hot）.
Misunderstanding the meaning: よくわかりません＝don't understand well; not "rarely understand".
131.notes:
The kanji良く is sometimes seen in written language, but hiragana よく is common at N5.
Emphatic intonation can change the nuance: よくやった！（Well done!）.
よくも（N3~）carries a nuance of reproach: よくもそんなことを…（How dare you…）— not part of basic N5.

132.meaning: A way of asking someone to give you something.

examples.jp: わたしにもください。
examples.tr: Please give me some too.

examples.jp: あれをください。
examples.tr: That one, please.

examples.jp: りんごをふたつください。
examples.tr: Two apples, please.

examples.jp: それ、むすこにください。
examples.tr: Please give that to my son.

examples.jp: 神様わたしに時間をください。
examples.tr: God, please give me time.

133.meaning:
something, some animal
somewhere
someone.
… | Indicates things that are not specifically known or have not been determined.

examples.jp: のどがかわきましたから、なにか「を」のみたいです。
examples.tr: I'm thirsty, so I want to drink something.

examples.jp:
A: きのうどこかいきましたか。
B: はい、としょかんへいきました。
examples.tr:
A: Did you go anywhere yesterday?
B: Yes, I went to the library.

133.explain:
Adding か after a question word gives a word meaning "some + question word": for example, なに is "what", so なにか is "something".
The particles へ,を after question word + か can be omitted.

examples.jp: はらださんはえいごがわかります。
examples.tr: Harada understands English.

examples.jp: わたしはなにもわかりません。
examples.tr: I don't understand anything at all.

examples.jp: わたしのうちはほんやとこうえんのあいだにあります。
examples.tr: My house is between the bookstore and the park.

examples.jp: ミラーさんとはらださんのあいだにたなかさんがいます。
examples.tr: Tanaka is between Miller and Harada.

examples.jp: わたしは結婚しています。
examples.tr: I'm married.

examples.jp: わたしは田中さんを知っています。
examples.tr: I know Tanaka.

examples.jp: ミラーさんは大阪に住んでいます。
examples.tr: Miller lives in Osaka.

examples.jp: お母さんは　A病院で働いています。
examples.tr: My mother works at A Hospital.

examples.jp: スーパーでナンプラーが売っています。
examples.tr: Nam pla is sold at the supermarket.

examples.jp: 今、昼ご飯を食べています。
examples.tr: I'm eating lunch now.

136.explain:
Distinguish知る (come to know) vs知っている (know);結婚する (get married) vs結婚している (be married, a state).
Vてある vs Vている: てある emphasizes an intentional result with transitive verbs; ている is neutral/a natural state, or is used with intransitive verbs.
With着る/はく/かぶる... + ている, it expresses "be wearing/have on".
The contracted spoken forms ～てる/～でる are common, but are not used in formal written language.

Progressive: an action at the time of speaking (今勉強しています).
Habit/repeated action: describes regular activities (毎日日本語を勉強しています).
A current state created by a previous action: ドアが開いています (the door is open),結婚しています (got married and is now in that state).
Verbs of perception/knowledge:知っています（know）、知りません（don't know) → use ている to indicate the state of knowing/not knowing.
With verbs of motion:行っています can mean "is going" (with今/これから) or "goes regularly/has gone and is there now", depending on context.

rows: Doing / has done and remains in that state
Transitive verb + object left in a state by someone
Change up to now / from now on
<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>えてきた／<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>えていく。
<ruby>今<rt>こん</rt></ruby>Vている vs Vている
“<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>” makes it clear the action is in progress right now
<ruby>今<rt>こん</rt></ruby><ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>している。

mistakes: Wrong transitive/intransitive verb: ×窓を開いています → ◯窓が開いています /窓を開けています (different meaning).
Confusing知る and知っている: ×彼を知ります → ◯彼を知っています.
Misunderstanding行っている: it can mean "is going/goes regularly/has gone and is there", depending on context.
JLPT: identify the three uses (progressive, habit, state) from context; distinguish ている and てある.
136.notes:
Choose the correct intransitive/transitive verb:窓が開いている（intransitive verb）vs窓を開けている（in the act of opening, a different meaning).
持っている can mean holding/owning; distinguish by context:今チケットを持っている（have it in hand now）.
With instantaneous verbs of change (死ぬ、壊れる…), ている usually indicates the state after the change:彼は死んでいる。

examples.jp: ごはんをたべてから、はをみがきます。
examples.tr: I brush my teeth after eating.

examples.jp: 朝ご飯を食べてから、会社に行きます。
examples.tr: I go to work after eating breakfast.

examples.jp: 日本に来てから、寿司が好きになりました。
examples.tr: Since coming to Japan, I've come to like sushi.

examples.jp: 仕事が終わってから、電話します。
examples.tr: I'll call you after I finish work.

examples.jp: 宿題をしてから、遊んでください。
examples.tr: Please play after you've done your homework.

examples.jp: 手を洗ってからでないと、キッチンに入れません。
examples.tr: You can't enter the kitchen until you've washed your hands.

137.explain:
Emphasizes completion: V1 must finish before V2; suitable for instructions/procedures.
"Right after": add すぐ/すぐに to make the immediacy clear.
In the meaning "ever since", it often goes with それ以来／ずっと to emphasize duration.
Not used to give a reason with a direct command; if you need a reason + request, use ので／から.

Indicates a clear time order: V1 is completed before V2 is done; different from simple listing with ～て.
Used as a time reference point, "ever since": Vてから、ずっと～ (continuously until now).
The negative variants emphasize a prerequisite: ～てからでないと／～てからでなければ.
Usually has the same subject when it is a sequence of one person's actions; with different subjects, it mainly shows the time relationship and does not emphasize cause.

rows: The time gap may be long
<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べた<ruby>後<rt>のち</rt></ruby>で、<ruby>歯<rt>は</rt></ruby>を<ruby>磨<rt>みが</rt></ruby>く。
Condition + result; prior completion not required
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたら、<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して。
<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>してからでないと<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>だ。

mistakes: Confusing it with後で: ×宿題をして後で遊ぶ (sounds disjointed) → ◯宿題をしてから遊ぶ.
Using it for cause: ×雨が降ってから、中止した (emphasizes cause) → use降ったので／から中止した instead.
Different subjects cause ambiguity: prefer the same subject when it is a sequence of personal actions.
JLPT: often tests ～てからでないと／～てからでなければ and the "right after" nuance with すぐ.
137.notes:
In procedures/instruction signs, ～てから sounds polite but clear: “カードを入れてから、暗証番号を押してください”。
In the meaning "ever since", it often goes with a change of state: ～てから、～ようになった／～くなった.
No second “から” is needed: a single “から” after Vて is enough.

examples.jp: こちらに名前を書いてください。
examples.tr: Please write your name here.

examples.jp: ゆっくり話してください。
examples.tr: Please speak slowly.

examples.jp: 写真を撮らないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't take pictures.

examples.jp: もう一度言ってくださいませんか。
examples.tr: Could you please say that once more?

examples.jp: 窓を開けてくれませんか。
examples.tr: Could you open the window for me?

examples.jp: ご確認ください。
examples.tr: Please check.

138.explain:
Used directly toward the listener; with superiors/customers, prefer ～ていただけますか／～てくださいませんか to be more polite.
Add softening openers: すみませんが／恐れ入りますが／よろしければ + ～てください。
The negative uses ないでください (not なくてください).
In instructions/procedures, ～てください is used in sequence: カードを入れてください。次に、暗証番号を押してください。

Makes a polite request or suggestion for the listener to do action V.
The negative “～ないでください” is used to forbid/ask someone not to do something with moderate politeness.
Politeness increases: ～て → ～てください → ～てくださいませんか／～ていただけますか.
In service language/signs, the form お／ご～ください is concise, very polite and formal.

rows: <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せてくださいませんか。
<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>っていただけますか。
Vてくれますか／くれない？

mistakes: Wrong negative: ×来なくてください → ◯来ないでください.
Being too direct with superiors: replace it with ～ていただけますか／～てくださいませんか.
Dropping て: ×窓を開けください → ◯窓を開けてください.
JLPT: distinguish the politeness levels of ください／くれますか／いただけますか; recognize お／ご～ください as standard keigo.
138.notes:
In business emails, the form お／ご～ください is very common: ご返信ください／ご確認ください.
“ください” also means "please give me" with nouns:水をください (outside the scope of Vてください, but common).
Chaining requests: ～て、～てください for coherence; avoid too many consecutive commands, which sounds stiff.

139.meaning: A way of giving someone permission to carry out an action (expressed with a volitional verb).

examples.jp: 外にごみをすててはいけません。
examples.tr: Do not throw garbage outside.

examples.jp: えさをあげてはいけません。
examples.tr: Do not feed the animals.

examples.jp: 戦争をわすれてはいけません。
examples.tr: We must not forget the war.

examples.jp: かのじょの前ではそのことを言ってはいけません。
examples.tr: You must not mention that in front of her.

examples.jp:
A: ここで電話を使ってはいけませんよ。
B: はい。どうもすみません。
examples.tr:
A: You can't use your phone here.
B: Okay. I'm very sorry.

139.explain: Prohibition: not allowing someone to do an action.

140.meaning:
it's OK to ~.
it's all right to ~.
140.connection: Vて + もいい(です) / N + で / Na + で / Aい + い くて / Vても + いいですか・かまいませんか（question asking for permission）

examples.jp:
A: すみませんが、タバコをすってもいいですか。
B: はい、どうぞ。
examples.tr:
A: Excuse me, may I smoke?
B: Yes, go ahead.

examples.jp:
A: すみません、ギターをひいてもいいですか。
B: ええ、いいですよ。
examples.tr:
A: Excuse me, may I play the guitar?
B: Sure, that's fine.

140.explain:
Asking for or giving permission to do an action.
When not giving permission, answer tactfully with すみません、ちょっと…, or answer with a prohibition using the いけません structure in the next grammar point.

examples.jp: ここに入らないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't come in here.

examples.jp: このボタンを押さないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't press this button.

examples.jp: 私の話を途中で止めないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't interrupt me.

examples.jp: 夜遅くテレビを見ないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't watch TV late at night.

examples.jp: 泣かないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't cry.

examples.jp: むりしないでください。
examples.tr: Don't push yourself too hard.

141.explain:
Polite and gentler than “～な！” (harsh command).
Often used on signs, in instructions, or when you want to ask someone to avoid doing something.
In casual speech, it can be contracted to ～ないでね or ～ないで .
例：そんなこと言わ ないでね。→ Don't say that, okay?
Not used with nouns or adjectives – only with verbs .

Expresses a polite request or suggestion for someone not to do an action.
It is the negative form of ～てください(please do…), meaning "please don't…".
The speaker uses it to give a gentle command or a polite reminder in conversation, instructions, or rules.
Mainly used with listeners of equal or lower status (such as friends, students, customers…).

rows: ここに<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>ってください。
Request not to do an action
ここに<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>らないでください。
Imperative form, used toward subordinates or in strong warnings

mistakes: Wrong conjugation of the nai-form:話す →話さないでください(correct),話しないでください(incorrect).
Confusing it with the imperative form “～な！” (rude, impolite).
Forgetting 「で」: ✕行かないください → ○行かないでください.
JLPT N5 often tests: choosing the correct polite negative request structure between ～てください and ～ないでください.
141.notes:
In notices and public signs, you often see the forms:～しないでくださいor～は禁止です(is prohibited).
To say it more gently, you can use:～ないようにしてください（Please try not to…）.
At JLPT N5, this is the basic pattern for expressing a polite negative request.

142.meaning: Shall I do it? | Shall I V ~? | Vましょうか Shall we V ~?
142.connection: Vます (drop ます) + ましょうか

examples.jp: ここで少し休みましょうか。
examples.tr: Shall we take a short rest here?

examples.jp: 荷物を持ちましょうか。
examples.tr: Shall I carry your bags?

examples.jp: 駅まで案内しましょうか。
examples.tr: Shall I show you the way to the station?

examples.jp: 雨ですね。タクシーで行きましょうか。
examples.tr: It's raining, isn't it? Shall we take a taxi?

examples.jp: 飲み物は水にしましょうか。
examples.tr: Shall we go with water for the drinks?

examples.jp: 何かてつだいましょうか。
examples.tr: Shall I help you with anything?

142.explain:
Used with the masu-form of a verb (drop ます) to make a gentle suggestion.
When you mean “I'll do it for you”, add the subject: 私が・こちらが + Vます-drop ます + ましょうか.
Formal and polite; suitable in service/hospitality settings: ご案内し ましょうか。
If you just want to make an ordinary invitation, you can use ～ませんか; if you want to decide together right away, use ～ましょう.

Meaning: “Shall we …?” / “Shall I …?” Used to make a polite suggestion or offer.
Two common nuances:
Suggestion to do something together:一緒に行きましょうか(Shall we go together?).
Suggestion to help:窓を開けましょうか(Shall I open the window?).
Suggestion to do something together:一緒に行きましょうか(Shall we go together?).
Suggestion to help:窓を開けましょうか(Shall I open the window?).
Degree of politeness: more polite than “～しようか”, friendlier than “～ませんか” when you want to take the initiative to help.
A rising intonation at the end of the sentence conveys a soft, suggestive tone.

rows: Inviting someone to do something together
Asks the listener's opinion; polite; less of an offer to help
<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きませんか。
A request, not a suggestion to do something together

mistakes: Wrong verb conjugation: ×行くましょうか → ✓行きましょうか.
Wrong nuance: when offering help, use ～ましょうか (“shall I do it?”); when inviting others to do something, prefer ～ませんか.
Leaving out the subject when offering help in an ambiguous context: use 私が…ましょうか to make the meaning “I will do it” clear.
142.notes:
In service settings, 何かお手伝いしましょうか is a very natural set phrase.
To avoid sounding pushy, you can add もしよろしければ before ～ましょうか.
Not used directly with adjectives/nouns; used only with verbs in the ます form minus ます.

examples.jp: 計画は順調だ。しかし、油断はできない。
examples.tr: The plan is going smoothly. However, we can't let our guard down.

examples.jp: 値段は高い。しかし、品質は抜群だ。
examples.tr: The price is high. However, the quality is outstanding.

examples.jp: データは増えた。しかし、精度は改善されていない。
examples.tr: The amount of data has increased. However, the accuracy has not improved.

examples.jp: 努力した。しかし、結果は出なかった。
examples.tr: I made an effort. However, it did not produce results.

examples.jp: その案は魅力的だ。しかし、リスクが大きい。
examples.tr: That proposal is attractive. However, the risk is high.

examples.jp: 多くの研究がある。しかし、結論は一致していない。
examples.tr: There is a lot of research. However, the conclusions do not agree.

143.explain:
Formal and rational; suitable for transitions, or for stating limitations/exceptions after presenting the main point.
Usually placed at the beginning of a sentence with a comma: しかし、…
In casual conversation, replace it with でも/けど to sound more natural.

Expresses a strong contrast/opposition between S1 and S2; often used to counter an argument, add a limitation, or present an exception.
Formal, objective style; suitable for written language, presentations and news.
Not used for a strong “surprise contrary to expectation” (better: ところが); not as casual as でも/けど.

rows: <ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>。しかし<ruby>課題<rt>かだい</rt></ruby>。
Breaks the flow, at the beginning of a sentence; less formal.
A result strongly contrary to expectation.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。ところが<ruby>閉店<rt>へいてん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だが<ruby>十分<rt>じゅっぷん</rt></ruby>でない。

mistakes: Using しかし in casual conversation sounds stiff; use でも/けど instead.
Confusing しかし with ところが when there is an element of being “contrary to expectation”; a common JLPT trap.
Omitting the comma after しかし makes it hard to read: “しかし、…”.
Using しかし to link a command/request in everyday conversation can sound too formal or unpleasant in nuance.
143.notes:
“しかしながら” is an even more formal variant, often used in academic writing.
In journalism, しかし can open a new paragraph to create a turning point in the argument.
Avoid overusing conjunctions at the beginning of a sentence in consecutive sentences; you can replace them with が/一方で to vary the flow of the text.

examples.jp: もう遅い。じゃ、今日はここまでにしよう。
examples.tr: It's already late. Well then, let's stop here for today.

examples.jp: 雨が降ってきた。じゃ、タクシーで帰ろう。
examples.tr: It's started to rain. Well then, let's take a taxi home.

examples.jp: それは難しい。じゃ、別の方法を試そう。
examples.tr: That's difficult. Well then, let's try another way.

examples.jp: 会議は三時から？じゃ、昼ご飯は早めに食べよう。
examples.tr: The meeting starts at three? Well then, let's eat lunch early.

examples.jp: 現金は持ってない。じゃ、後で振り込むね。
examples.tr: I don't have any cash on me. Well then, I'll transfer the money later.

examples.jp: テストに合格した？じゃ、お祝いしよう！
examples.tr: You passed the test? Well then, let's celebrate!

144.explain:
Used to sum up or make a decision based on the information in S1.
Combines naturally with volition/suggestion: ～しよう／～しませんか／～しましょう。
Casual speech; in formal business settings, prefer それでは／では .
じゃあ feels soft and drawn out; じゃ is short and decisive.
Usually comes at the beginning of a new utterance; avoid inserting it in the middle of a long sentence.

Changing direction/making a decision based on what was just said: “well then / in that case”.
Marks the next step in a process/action: opens a new part after concluding something.
Implies “if that's the case, then”, but conversationally, not as a strict grammatical condition.
Casual, brisk nuance; often used when wrapping up/closing a topic or starting work.
The intonation usually falls slightly after じゃ、, followed by a command, suggestion, volition, or a statement of plans.
Not used to raise a strong counterargument; for clear contrast/concession, use でも/しかし.

rows: The “あ” is drawn out; very conversational
<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わり？ じゃあ、またね。
Well then (a bit more polite than じゃ)
<ruby>締切<rt>しめきり</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>？ それじゃ、<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>ごう。
それでは、<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めます。
では、<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>みます。
それなら、<ruby>別<rt>べつ</rt></ruby><ruby>日<rt>び</rt></ruby>にしよう。

mistakes: Using じゃ in a formal written text → unnatural; choose それでは／では.
Using じゃ for strong contrast → wrong nuance; use でも／しかし instead.
Omitting the period before じゃ、→ breaks the convention for linking sentences: it must be S1。じゃ、S2。
Confusing じゃ with ～じゃない (negative) → different function.
JLPT: recognize the degree of politeness when choosing じゃ vs それでは/では according to a conversational vs formal context.
144.notes:
じゃ can open a sentence to draw attention: じゃ、次は…
Do not confuse it with sentence-final ～じゃ in dialects (elderly/old-fashioned speech). Here it is a sentence-initial conjunction.
In chat, there is a repeated emphatic form: じゃ、じゃ、… to call for attention again; avoid it in formal writing.

examples.jp: 明日は雨だって。それじゃ、ピクニックは中止だね。
examples.tr: I heard it's going to rain tomorrow. In that case, the picnic is off, right?

examples.jp: 申し込みは今日まで？それじゃ、今すぐ送ります。
examples.tr: Applications close today? In that case, I'll send mine right away.

examples.jp: 説明は以上です。それじゃ、確認お願いします。
examples.tr: That concludes my explanation. Well then, please check it.

examples.jp: 準備できた？それじゃ、出発しよう。
examples.tr: Are you ready? Well then, let's head out.

examples.jp: それじゃ、また明日。
examples.tr: Well then, see you tomorrow.

examples.jp: 鍵を忘れたの？それじゃ、私が開けるよ。
examples.tr: You forgot your key? In that case, I'll open it for you.

145.explain:
Natural in casual work settings, friendly internal emails, and small team meetings.
Used at the beginning of a sentence, after the listener has understood “that (それ)”.
Combines well with commands, volition, invitations, and closing remarks.
If you need to be more polite (customers, formal presentations), replace it with それでは .

“Well then / in that case”, based on the information just mentioned (referred to by それ).
Moves on to the next step, starts an action, or gently sums up in conversation.
Moderately more polite than じゃ, less formal than それでは.
Often used to end a topic, say goodbye, or move on to a new part.

rows: <ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わり？ それじゃ、<ruby>解散<rt>かいさん</rt></ruby>。
More formal; used with customers/an audience
それでは、<ruby>質疑<rt>しつぎ</rt></ruby><ruby>応答<rt>おうとう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>移<rt>うつ</rt></ruby>ります。
<ruby>遅<rt>おそ</rt></ruby>い。じゃあ、<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ろう。
Short, slightly stiff; used to lead a program
Clear logical condition, not just a transition
それなら、<ruby>後日<rt>ごじつ</rt></ruby>に。

mistakes: Using それじゃ in a text with a high level of keigo → not formal enough; change it to それでは.
Missing the reference for “それ” (the preceding content is unclear) → the sentence becomes vague.
Confusing its function with それで (so → cause and result) → different logic.
JLPT: recognize the politeness nuance among じゃ／それじゃ／それでは／では according to context.
145.notes:
それじゃ is suitable for ending a call/message: それじゃ、また連絡します。
In many mildly polite contexts, それじゃ is still acceptable, but do not use it in formal speeches.
The sound “じゃあ” makes the sentence less abrupt and friendlier.

examples.jp: 時間になりました。それでは、始めます。
examples.tr: It's time. Well then, let us begin.

examples.jp: ご清聴ありがとうございました。それでは、失礼いたします。
examples.tr: Thank you for your kind attention. Well then, I will take my leave.

examples.jp: 以上で説明を終わります。それでは、質疑応答に移ります。
examples.tr: This concludes my explanation. Well then, we will move on to questions and answers.

examples.jp: 特に問題がなければ、それでは、契約を締結いたします。
examples.tr: If there are no particular problems, then we will conclude the contract.

examples.jp: 本題はここまでです。それでは、まとめに入ります。
examples.tr: That's all for the main topic. Well then, let us move on to the summary.

examples.jp: 本日はありがとうございました。それでは、また次回。
examples.tr: Thank you very much for today. Well then, until next time.

146.explain:
Polite, standard in business/academic settings; suitable for emails, presentations, and MCs.
Placed at the beginning of a sentence, starting a new one; usually followed by a heading, an instruction, or the next step.
Combines well with keigo: ～いたします／～でございます。
If you need something short and moderately formal, consider では、 .

“Well then / Then” with a polite nuance, used to steer things to the next part.
Used to open a new action/topic after completing the previous part.
Closes a conversation, an email, or a meeting in a serious manner.
A proper, standard tone, suitable for business and academic settings.

rows: それでは、<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めます。
Short, slightly stiff; common in written language
Less formal than それでは
それじゃ、また<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>。
Cause → result; different logic from “making a decision”
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。それで、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>した。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。でも、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けない。

mistakes: Using それじゃ instead of それでは in a formal speech → not polite enough.
Confusing それでは with それで (cause-result) → wrong logical relationship.
Omitting the comma after それでは makes the rhythm less natural; there should be a “、”.
JLPT: choose the right level of politeness for the context of a presentation/business email.
146.notes:
それでは often goes with set phrases when opening/closing a meeting.
In written texts, you can start a new line after それでは、 to emphasize the paragraph transition.
Do not overuse it; using it too much can feel “formulaic”.

examples.jp: 会議を開始します。では、最初の議題です。
examples.tr: We will now open the meeting. Now then, the first item on the agenda.

examples.jp: ここまで準備できました。では、実験を始めます。
examples.tr: Preparations are complete up to this point. Now then, we will begin the experiment.

examples.jp: それは確認済みです。では、次の点に移りましょう。
examples.tr: That has already been confirmed. Now then, let's move on to the next point.

examples.jp: 以上です。では、解散します。
examples.tr: That's all. Then, this meeting is adjourned.

examples.jp: 準備はいいですか。では、参ります。
examples.tr: Is everyone ready? Then, here we go.

examples.jp: これが課題です。では、どうすればよいでしょうか。
examples.tr: This is the problem. So then, what should we do?

147.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence, starting a new one; followed by the next part/action.
Suitable for minutes, slides, textbooks, and announcements.
If you want something softer/standard for speeches, use それでは ; if casual, use じゃ／それじゃ .

“Now/Well then/Then”, used to move to the next step and to open/close a part concisely.
Feels like coordinating or official business; not very casual.
Often accompanied by a heading, an instruction, or the next step in a process.

rows: Longer, soft; for speaking in front of an audience
それでは、<ruby>発表<rt>はっぴょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わります。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。それで、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>。
さて、<ruby>本題<rt>ほんだい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>ります。

mistakes: Using では in casual conversation → feels stiff; use じゃ／それじゃ instead.
Confusing では (conjunction) with それで (cause) → wrong sentence logic.
Omitting the comma after では makes the rhythm less natural.
JLPT: choose では when the context is a written text, a presentation, or an official announcement.
147.notes:
では also appears in the conditional structure: ではない／ではありません; do not confuse it with the sentence-initial conjunction.
In MC scripts/slides, では、+ a heading noun is very common: では、まとめ。

examples.jp: 日本語は難しい。でも、面白い。
examples.tr: Japanese is difficult. But it's interesting.

examples.tr: He is kind. But he is sometimes strict.

examples.jp: 予約は満席でした。でも、キャンセル待ちなら可能です。
examples.tr: The reservations were fully booked. But it is possible if you join the waiting list for cancellations.

examples.jp: それは危険だ。でも、必要だ。
examples.tr: That is dangerous. But it is necessary.

examples.jp: 雨だ。でも、練習はやる。
examples.tr: It's raining. But we'll still practice.

148.explain:
Opens the following sentence to present an opposing point, a limitation, or an exception.
Neutral → casual; in more formal writing, consider しかし／だが／とはいえ .
Usually followed by an affirmation of one's position, an alternative solution, or an exception.
Keep the comma after でも so the sentence reads naturally.

Presents a point of contrast/an exception to the previous sentence: “but/however”.
Conversational nuance, softer than しかし／だが, stronger than けど(も) when placed at the beginning of a sentence.
The rhythm “S1。でも、S2。” makes the flow clear and easy to say.
Often used when S2 expresses a volition/evaluation opposed to S1.

rows: しかし、<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>がある。
だが、<ruby>例外<rt>れいがい</rt></ruby>もある。
Soft; usually attached at the end/middle of a sentence
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くつもりだった。ところが、<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Writing one long sentence “…,でも、…” → spoken style; in written language, split it into two sentences.
Confusing “でも” (conjunction) with “N + でも” (suggestion/even) → wrong meaning.
Using でも instead of しかし in a formal text → not formal enough.
JLPT: distinguish でも／しかし／それでも／ところが by the degree of contrast and nuance.
148.notes:
でも at the beginning of a sentence clearly breaks the flow and is easy to use in conversation.
Do not confuse it with N + でも (suggesting “or something”/“even”). The context determines the meaning.
In formal writing, replace it with しかし／とはいえ／一方 depending on your intention.

149.meaning: Emphasizes that an action or event in the second clause takes place after the action or event in the first clause.

examples.jp: 焼いたあとで
examples.tr: After grilling it

examples.jp: ハチが死んだあと（で）渋谷にハチ公像ができた。
examples.tr: After Hachi died, the Hachikō statue was built in Shibuya.

examples.tr: Why don't we go for a drink after work?

examples.tr: Would you like some coffee?

examples.tr: How are your travel plans coming along?

examples.jp: このスープはいかがですか。
examples.tr: How is this soup?

examples.jp: お元気でいらっしゃいますか/お元気はいかがですか。
examples.tr: Are you keeping well? / How have you been?

examples.jp: お土産はいかがですか。
examples.tr: Would you like a souvenir?

150.explain:
“いかが” is used in formal conversation, especially when speaking to customers or superiors, or in service settings.
Placed after a noun or a clause, combined with “は”, “で”, “でしょうか”, etc.
Polite, gentle nuance that shows respect for the listener.
Often used in situations such as offering food or drink, asking for opinions, asking about impressions, and introducing products.

① Used to invite someone to eat, drink, or do something in a polite and refined way.
② A more polite way of saying 「どうですか」– often used in formal communication, customer service, or with superiors.
③ Can be used to ask for an opinion or impression, or to suggest choosing something.
“いかが” is the keigo form (丁寧語) of “どう”.

rows: How is it? / Would you like some?
Neutral; used with friends and equals
コーヒーはどうですか。
How is it? / Would you like some?
コーヒーはいかがですか。
How is it? / What do you think?
Very polite; used in business/customer service
こちらのプランはいかがでしょうか。

mistakes: Confusing “どうですか” with “いかがですか”:
✕ コーヒーはいかが？ (too casual → use どう instead).
○ コーヒーはいかがですか。 (correct, standard politeness).
Wrong context: “いかが” is only used when speaking to superiors or in polite situations.
Omitting “は”: ✕ コーヒーいかがですか → ○ コーヒーはいかがですか。
JLPT N5 often asks you to choose correctly between “どうですか” (casual) and “いかがですか” (polite).
150.notes:
“いかが” = “どう” in meaning but shows a much higher degree of politeness.
When used with “でしょうか”, the politeness increases further: お味はいかがでしょうか。→ Is it to your liking?
Very common in shops, restaurants, hotels, or when introducing products/services.
This form is not used with subordinates or friends (it sounds distant and unnatural).

examples.jp: うまくいくかどうか、わかりませんが、できるだけ、やってみます。
examples.tr: I don't know whether it will go well, but I'll do as much as I can.

examples.jp: たくさんありますから、どうぞ食べたいだけ食べてください。
examples.tr: There's plenty, so please eat as much as you like.

examples.jp: 試験が終わったら、好きなだけ遊びたい。
examples.tr: When the exams are over, I want to have fun as much as I like.

examples.jp: 「食べたいだけ食べていいですよ」
examples.tr: 「You can eat as much as you like.」

examples.jp: 「あしたはできるだけ早く来ます」
examples.tr: 「I'll come as early as possible tomorrow.」

examples.jp: できるだけのことはやったつもりだ。
examples.tr: I believe I did everything I could.

151.explain:
“only” is neutral, without the negative implication of しか～ない; it can go with affirmative or negative statements depending on the content.
Particle position: だけ attaches after the word/phrase to be limited; it can combine with は/も/に/を/が for emphasis (それ だけは、それ だけを …).
VるだけV and できるだけ carry the nuance “as much as possible / as much as you like”.
～だけのN means “belonging only to / enough to ~”, sometimes “worth… to the extent that” depending on the context.

Limitation/Only: only N / only that much / only do V (limitation of scope, quantity, target).
Maximum possible: できるだけ／VるだけV express “as much as possible / as much as you like”.
Emphasizing a minimum/special case: ～だけは (at least / as for ~ in particular), ～だけでも (even just ~ is…).
Neutral nuance; compared with しか～ない, だけ can be used in affirmative sentences, while しか goes with the negative.

rows: Can be used in affirmative sentences
Must go with ～ない; nuance of lack/regret
<ruby>一人<rt>ひとり</rt></ruby>しか<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なかった
Can carry a nuance of too much/bias; also means “about”
お<ruby>菓<rt>かし</rt></ruby><ruby>子<rt></rt></ruby>ばかり<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる

mistakes: Using だけ with a negative to give a “lacking” nuance like しか: “三人だけしか来ない” is a wrong overlap; choose either だけ or しか～ない.
Leaving out the emphasizing particle: to emphasize a minimum/special case, は/も is needed: それだけは言いたい。
Confusing “Vるだけ” (just do) with “VたいだけV” (do as much as you like): the meanings are different.
Misunderstanding “～だけのN”: it can mean “enough to ~” (この成績は合格するだけのレベルだ), not only “belonging only to”.
Confusing it with “～だけに/～だけあって”: these are different patterns; check the context in JLPT questions.
151.notes:
1) It is easy to take ～だけ only as “only” in the restrictive sense.
→ At N3, ～だけ very often expresses degree/scope: できるだけ, 好きなだけ.
2) Distinguish it from ～しか.
→ ～しか always goes with the negative and has a restrictive nuance; ～だけ is neutral and can be positive.
3) Distinguish それだけ from ～だけ.
→ それだけ often means “corresponding to that degree” (pronoun), not the grammar point “only”.

examples.jp:

Vたい behaves like an i-adjective.
In the tai-form, the particle が can be used instead of を.
The tai-form is not used with the verb ある.

examples.jp: 「あしたは８時半に来てください」
examples.tr: 「Please come at 8:30 tomorrow.」

154.explain:
Often found in instructions, schedules and work requests.
“～までには” adds personal emphasis/determination compared with “～までに”.
Not used with nouns expressing a length of time (3時間までに×); use a specific point in time or an event.

• Expresses a deadline: something must be completed before or exactly at that point (the point in time itself included).
• Different from ～まで (until/up to): ～までに targets a “deadline point” and does not express duration.
• Vる＋までに: “before (the time when) … happens”, often used to set a condition for preparation.
• Often used with verbs that express completion: 終える, 提出する, 着く, 用意する,…

rows: Emphasizes the duration up to the point
Emphasizes the deadline point in time
Used for lengths of time, scope
<ruby>3日<rt>みっか</rt></ruby><ruby>以内<rt>いない</rt></ruby>に<ruby>返信<rt>へんしん</rt></ruby>。
Limits the end to that point
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>はここまでで<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わり。
<ruby>今週<rt>こんしゅう</rt></ruby>までには<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>める。

mistakes: Wrong use with a length of time: 3時間までに終わる× → 3時間以内に終わる✓ or 3時間で終わる✓
Confusing ～まで with ～までに: 5時まで来て× (ambiguous meaning) → 5時までに来て✓
Wrong clause with Vる＋までに (using the past): 会議が始まったまでに× → 始まるまでに✓
The JLPT often tests the “deadline” nuance: choose ～までに when there are keywords like “by/no later than/before”.
154.notes:
• The point in time can be an “event”: 試験までに, 雨季までに…
• When the timeline is vague, use “～頃までに” for flexibility: 今月末までに／今月末頃までに.
• In work emails, combine it with “必ず／遅くとも／目安として” to make the deadline clear: 遅くとも金曜までに。

The verb is conjugated in the ta-form + り.
Used for listing actions in no particular sequence.
Used for one or more agents.

V1たり、V2たり、～ する : Doing things like V1 and V2~

159.meaning: Become ~ | Adjで～ - Connecting sentences with na-adjectives | Adjじゃない(ではない) - Negative form of na-adjectives | Adjに V - Adverb form of na-adjectives | Adjになります - Become (na-adjective) | Adjにします - Make something become (na-adjective)

examples.tr: After you wash your hands, they become clean.

examples.jp: この部屋は静かで広い。

159.explain:
An action with a clear purpose, usually with a person/role who carries it out:私がNをAにします.
The noun with を is the target being changed; Aな is the desired new state.
In reminders/signs: 〜にしてください/〜にしましょう are polite and carry a nuance of suggestion/request.
Different nuance: 「Aにします」 (choose) vs 「Aにします」 (make into A). Tell them apart by context and by whether there is a を-target or not.
Used with abstract adjectives (簡単,便利,安全,重大) to talk about optimizing/standardizing.

Expresses an intentional act: changing the state/property of something to some na-adjective.
- Pattern: Nを Aな に します = Make N become A (actively, by the speaker/agent).
Used to “simplify”, “clean up”, “make safe”, “make quiet” a target:簡単・きれい・安全・静か…
Implies a desired goal/standard: the speaker sets the target state and brings it about.
Different from ～になります (natural/unintentional): ～にします emphasizes human intervention, choice and decision.
Also used when choosing an option (with nouns): Aにします “I'll choose A”. With な形容詞, the nuance is “adjusting something so it becomes A”.

rows: There is an agent acting on it
<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>を<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かにする
<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>が<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かになる
い<ruby>形容詞<rt>けいようし</rt></ruby> + くする
Make (with い<ruby>形容詞<rt>けいようし</rt></ruby>)
く form; に is not used
<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>は<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>にします
Habit/goal, not a change of property
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>るようにする

mistakes: Wrongly using い形容詞+ にする (incorrect). Correct: い形容詞+ くする; な形容詞+ にする.
Confusing を and が: it must be NをAにする (not NがAにする).
Confusing it with ～になる:要 distinguish intention (にする) vs natural change (になる).
Machine-translating it as “decide to be A” in every case: with な形容詞 it usually means “make something become A”, while “decide/choose” applies when it is used with nouns.
159.notes:
Some words also have a dedicated adverb form (うまく/きちんと), but 上手に/きちんと have the same adverbial function. Choose according to habit/collocation.
“静かにして”: a fixed command meaning “be quiet”.
“きれい” is a な形容詞 but is also a noun in some structures; as an adverb, always use “きれいに”.
The -的（的） group, such as 積極的・具体的, is often used naturally in the form “～的に”.

examples.jp: 母はこのごろ人の名前を忘れることがあります。
examples.tr: These days my mother sometimes forgets people's names.

examples.jp: 雪の日は道ですべることがありますから、注意してください。

examples.jp: サラはときどき僕の話を聞いていないことがある。
examples.tr: Sara sometimes isn't listening to what I say.

examples.jp: 私は何度も大阪城へ行ったことがあります。
examples.tr: I have been to Osaka Castle many times.

examples.jp:
A「毎朝何時ごろ朝ごはんを食べますか。」
B「いつもは7時に食べますが、時間がない時は食べないこともあります。」
examples.tr:
A: "What time do you usually have breakfast every morning?"
B: "I usually eat at 7, but when I don't have time, I sometimes don't eat."

examples.jp:
A: ナムさんは富士山に登ったことがありますか。
B: はい、一度あります。

160.explain:
Talks about an experience you have had.
The verb あります is not conjugated in the past tense.

Used when you want to talk about things that happen in a special way. Not used with things that happen very frequently. It can also be used in the form ~こともあります as in example ④.

examples.jp: 電車かバスか、どちらで行きますか。
examples.tr: Which will you take, the train or the bus?

examples.jp: 明日行くか行かないか、まだ決めていません。
examples.tr: I haven't decided yet whether I'll go tomorrow or not.

examples.jp: この案が安全か危険かは、専門家に聞いてみましょう。

161.explain:
Neutral; used in both spoken language and written language. To be more formal, you can use AかBかにつきましては…
In direct questions, か appears once before the second choice: Aですか、Bですか。
With long clauses, it is better to repeat everything in full before and after か for clarity.
Often used with は to turn the phrase “AかBか” into a topic: AかBかは〜

Presents a contrasting choice/possibility: “A or B (or C)”.
Used like “whether A or B” together with verbs of perception/uncertainty:分かる、決める、迷う、知る、調べる、考える.
When the second possibility is “not A”, you can use “AかAないか” or shorten it to “Aかどうか”.
In direct questions, “それとも” can be used to connect them: Aですか、それともBですか。
With nouns/na-adjectives, use the plain form before か:静かか静かではないか.

rows: <ruby>寿司<rt>すし</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>天ぷら<rt>てんぷら</rt></ruby>とか
<ruby>紅茶<rt>こうちゃ</rt></ruby>ですか、それともコーヒーですか

mistakes: Confusing AかBか with AやB: か is an exclusive choice; や is listing.
Dropping the second か in long sentences causes ambiguity. Keep the structure balanced: AかBか.
Use かどうか when option B is “not A”, to avoid unnecessary repetition.
In direct questions, do not put か right after A: say “Aですか、Bですか” (not “Aか、Bですか”).
161.notes:
With な形容詞/名詞, the negative form in a contrasting pair usually uses ではない／じゃない:静かか静かではないか.
The second choice can be left out when the context is clear:行くか（どうか）まだ…
In titles/tables, A/B are often written briefly:可/不可,賛成/反対.
meaning_vi: Choice question: …N1 or N2? (～ですか、～ですか)
explain: This is a choice question: N1 or N2.
For this kind of question, we usually answer by choosing one of the options the asker gives.
examples: 1. A: これは　しんぶんですか、ざっしですか。
B: しんぶんです。
A: Is this a newspaper or a magazine?
B: It's a newspaper.
2. A: あなたは　じゅうはっさいですか、はたちですか。
B: わたしは　はたちです。
A: Are you 18 or 20?
B: I'm 20.

166.explain:
けど leans toward conversation; ですけど is polite; だけど is used after Aな/N.
Used to lead into a request/suggestion: すみませんけど、ペンを貸してください。
Used to reduce directness/negation and create a soft feeling.

～けど means “but/although…”. Used to connect two contrasting clauses, to soften a sentence, or as an opener leading into a request/suggestion.
Core meaning: mild contrast, a change of direction.
Conversational, natural nuance, softer than が; ですけど is polite.
Can be placed at the end of a sentence to “trail off”, to hint at something/sound gentle:今日はちょっと…けど。

rows: <ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>いけれど、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。

mistakes: Wrong position of です: × です高いけど → correct:高いですけど。
Using けど in overly formal writing → consider using が/しかし.
Forgetting to conjugate for tense in the first clause: ×行くたけど→ correct:行くけど／行ったけど。
166.notes:
The first clause (before けど) can be a full clause or a noun/adjective phrase:学生ですけど…。
“Trailing off” with けど helps with politeness/reduces pressure:今日は無理ですけど…。
In polite emails you can use けれども/しかしながら (above N5).

167.meaning: Demonstratives. When referring to things they become「これ・それ・あれ・どれ」, when referring to places they become「ここ・そこ・あそこ・どこ」, and when used as a complement to a noun they become「このN・そのN・あのN・どのN」.
167.connection: こ/そ/あ/ど + れ (thing) ・ + の + N ・ ここ/そこ/あそこ/どこ (place) ・ こちら/そちら/あちら/どちら (direction)

examples.jp: このお金

167.notes:
meaning_vi: こ group そ group あ group ど group
things これ それ あれ どれ(Lesson 16)
things/people この N その N あの N どの N(Lesson 16)
places ここ そこ あそこ どこ
direction/
place (polite) こちら そちら あちら どちら
examples: 1. ①　こ～／そ～／あ～／ど～
~ this, ~ that, ~ that over there, ~ which/where
2. ②　「どうしたらいいんですか？」「こうすれば、いいんですよ」
"What should I do?" "Just do it like this."
3. ③　「どんな家に住みたい？」「（遠くの大きな家を指して）あんな家に住みたいなあ」
"What kind of house do you want to live in?" "(pointing at a big house in the distance) I'd like to live in a house like that."
4. ➃　「ああ、そんなにたくさん買っちゃった！もうお金が全然ない」「そんなに買うからだよ」
"Ah, I bought this much! I have no money left at all." "That's because you buy that much."
5. ⑤　「昨日行ったあの店、安くておいしかったね」「そうだね」
"That shop we went to yesterday was cheap and tasty, wasn't it?" "Yeah, it was."
6. ⑥　昨日、新しくできたすし屋に行ってみた。でも、その店は込んでいて、入れなかった。
Yesterday I tried going to a newly opened sushi restaurant. But that restaurant was crowded, so I couldn't get in.

examples.tr: 「If you don't like it, you don't have to eat it.」

examples.tr: 「Can you read kanji?」「Yes, if they're easy kanji, I can read them.」

examples.tr: I plan to go back to my country when winter break comes.

examples.jp: 「この仕事が終わったら帰ってもいいですか」
examples.tr: 「Can I go home after I finish this work?」

169.explain:
V 1 たら、V 2 : Emphasizes that when V 1 is realized, V 2 will happen with certainty.

Means doing or not doing something after the condition in the first clause has been carried out or met.
169.notes:
Note:
「と」や「ば」（５８番）より、会話で使うことが多い。１回だけのことに使うことが多い
Compared with と and ば of grammar point 57, this grammar point is used more in conversation. It is often used with things that happen only once
meaning_vi: Expresses that after ~ is done, … takes place. The ~ part is not a supposition but something already scheduled to be done from now on.
examples: 1. ①3時になったら、休みましょう。
Once it's 3 o'clock, let's take a break.
2. ②この学校を卒業したら、何をしますか。
What will you do after you graduate from this school?
3. ③お湯が沸いたら、火を止めてください。
When the water boils, please turn off the heat.
──────
1. ①もし水がなかったら、私たちは生きられません。
If there were no water, we could not live.
2. ②もし大きい地震が起きたら、すぐ机の下に入ってください。
If a big earthquake happens, get under a desk right away.
3. ③明日天気が良かったら、どこへ行きませんか。
If the weather is nice tomorrow, why don't we go somewhere?

examples.jp: たとえ雨が降っても、試合は行います。
examples.tr: Even if it rains, the match will be held.

examples.jp: 忙しくても、運動するようにしている。
examples.tr: Even when I'm busy, I try to exercise.

examples.jp: 彼が反対でも、計画を進める。
examples.tr: Even if he is against it, I'll go ahead with the plan.

examples.jp: 安くても、品質が悪ければ買わない。
examples.tr: Even if it's cheap, I won't buy it if the quality is bad.

examples.jp: 行けなくても、連絡だけはしてね。
examples.tr: Even if you can't go, at least let me know, okay?

examples.jp: 資料を忘れてもいいから、時間だけは守ってください。
examples.tr: It's fine if you forget the materials, but please at least be on time.

170.explain:
Y is usually the speaker's volition/intention:行く／頑張る／続ける／構わない…
When Y is an objective fact, it can still be used if it states a “no effect” relationship.
Combine it with emphatic words (たとえ／いくら／どんなに／もし) to strengthen the supposition/intensity.
Distinguish it from ～てもいい: adding いい changes the meaning to “it is allowed/it's fine”.

• Main meaning: concession/hypothetical concession, “even if X, Y still…”; Y is not affected by X.
• Scope: can be purely hypothetical (not yet real) or real; different from のに (already real, contrary to expectation).
• Common structures: たとえ～ても, いくら～ても, もし～ても; Y often expresses volition/judgment/habit.
• Variants for permission/no problem: ～てもいい (permission), ～てもかまわない (no problem).

rows: Hypothetical or real; Y is not affected.
A fact contrary to expectation; expresses disappointment/dissatisfaction.
ここに<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>ってもいい？
Emphasizes degree; often used with ない/<ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>.
いくら<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べても<ruby>太<rt>ふと</rt></ruby>らない。
たとえ<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けても<ruby>諦<rt>あきら</rt></ruby>めない。

mistakes: Confusing it with のに: if the sentence has a nuance of regret/going against expectation → choose のに, not ても.
Wrong form with な-adj/N: it must be で＋も (きれいでも), not にも.
Mixing up なくても vs the different structure も…ない; “even if not” is ～なくても, not ～ないでも (except in limited colloquial use).
JLPT: the trap of てもいい (permission) vs ても (concession). Keywords asking for permission/OK → てもいい.
170.notes:
• Adversative pattern in argumentation: 「Aても、Bと言えない」 to negate an inference.
• In ads/slogans: 「どれだけ動いても、快適。」 carries a nuance of a quality guarantee.
• When connecting several concessive clauses: 「安くても、軽くても、丈夫でなければ意味がない。」
meaning_vi: Expresses that things ~ that seem obvious do not actually happen. The ~ part can be an affirmative event as in examples ①②; it can also be a real event as in the example. This sentence pattern is used with words like もし・どんなに・いくら or question words as in examples ②④⑤.
examples: 1. ①後輩「明日雪がふったら、練習は休みですか。」
先輩【いや、雪が降っても、休みじゃないよ。」
Junior: "If it snows tomorrow, will practice be canceled?"
Senior: "No, even if it snows, there's no day off."
2. ②もし暑くても、仕事にはスーツを着ていきます。
Even if it's hot, I wear a suit to work.
3. ③この料理はかんたんです。初めて作っる人でもできます。
This dish is simple. Even someone making it for the first time can do it.
4. ④説明が難しくて、何回読んでも、意味が分かりません。
The explanation is hard to understand; no matter how many times I read it, I don't get the meaning.
5. ⑤山田「ケーキが好きなんでしょう？これ、全部どうぞ。」
トム「え、いくら好きでも、こんなにたくさんは食べませんよ。」
Yamada: "You like cake, right? Please have all of this."
Tom: "Huh? No matter how much I like it, I won't eat this much."

examples.jp: 運動場でサッカーの試合があります。
