171.explain:
•　N is a word for happenings, events or incidents that involve many actions inside them, for example a party, a conference, a criminal case, a natural disaster…
•　”あります” is used with the meaning “to be held”, “to take place/happen”; the place where it happens is marked with で.

～で: At

examples.jp: どうしてもの絵がほしい。借金してでも買いたい。
examples.tr: I really want that painting. I want to buy it even if I have to borrow money.

examples.jp: 多少無理をしてでもこの取引を成功させたい。
examples.tr: I want to make this deal succeed, even if I have to push myself a little.

examples.jp: 法律に反することをしてでも完成させろと、上司に命じられた。
examples.tr: My boss ordered me to get it done even if I had to break the law.

examples.jp: この仕事は徹夜してでも完成させろと、上司に命じられた。
examples.tr: My boss ordered me to finish this work even if I had to stay up all night.

examples.jp: この料理は簡単そうだから、わたしでも作れそうです。
examples.tr: This dish looks easy, so it seems even I could make it.

examples.jp: あの歌手は夏でも首にスカーフを巻いて寝るそうです。
examples.tr: I hear that singer sleeps with a scarf around their neck even in summer.

172.explain:
Gives a suggestion, or a typical example from a certain group of words.
Used when you want to suggest or propose something, or express a desire to someone else.

A
Gives an extreme example or an example that cannot be taken for granted, implying that even in that case, a certain state or action still occurs.
B
Mainly used with the combination "1 + counter" to express the concessive idea that just that much is enough.
C
Gives an example lightly in sentences expressing a suggestion, a request, volition, etc., to give gentle examples.
D
Often used with question words to express the idea of including all targets of the same kind.
172.notes: original explain: ◎ Sentence pattern used when giving an example of something of a low degree

173.connection: Vる / Vない / Nだ / Naだ / Aい + と + [sentence/clause]

examples.jp: このあたりは、３月の終わりごろになるとさくらが咲きます。（自然現象）
examples.tr: In this area, the cherry blossoms bloom around the end of March.（自然現象）

examples.jp: あの角を曲がると駅があります。（道順を言う）
examples.tr: If you turn at that corner, you'll find the station.（道順を言う）

examples.jp: このボタンを押すとおつりが出ます。（機械の操作）
examples.tr: If you press this button, your change comes out.（機械の操作）

examples.jp: 天気がいいと、この窓から富士山が見える。
examples.tr: When the weather is good, you can see Mt. Fuji from this window.

examples.jp: わたしは部屋が静かでないと勉強できない。
examples.tr: I can't study unless my room is quiet.

examples.jp: ２０人以上の団体だと、１割引きになります。
examples.tr: Groups of 20 or more get a 10% discount.

173.explain:
What follows と is something obvious, something that inevitably happens.
The second clause (after と) cannot express volition, wishes, requests, desires, invitations or appeals.

A
Listing things, people, events.
B
Expresses the person (target) together with whom an action is done.
C
Expresses the target an action affects （①）、expresses the standard of comparison (②③）.
D
States a name, the content of what is said or thought, etc..
173.notes:
Note:
後ろに意志、希望、命令、依頼などの表現は続かない
What follows cannot be an expression of volition, expectation, desire or request.
1.  X暑いと窓を開けてください。（→暑かったら～）（→５７番）
X because it's hot, please open the window
2.  X高校を卒業すると、留学するつもりだ。（高校を卒業したら～）（→５７番）
X after I graduate from high school, I plan to study abroad.

174.meaning: When, at the time  ~ | When, at the time
174.connection: V plain form + とき / N + の / Na + な / Aい

examples.jp: コーヒーを飲むとき、さとうをいれます。
examples.tr: I put sugar in when I drink coffee.

examples.jp: 病気のとき、くすりをのまなければなりません。
examples.tr: When you are sick, you have to take medicine.

examples.jp: 日本へ行くとき、パスポートを持っていきます。
examples.tr: When I go to Japan, I take my passport with me.

examples.jp: 日本へ行ったとき、京都を観光しました。
examples.tr: When I went to Japan, I went sightseeing in Kyoto.

examples.jp: 暇なとき、映画を見ます。
examples.tr: When I have free time, I watch movies.

examples.jp: 子どものとき、よく公園で遊びました。
examples.tr: When I was a child, I often played in the park.

174.explain:
Emphasizes the point in time when something happens or an action is done.
Especially with verbs:
When using とき, we look at the order of the actions to put V 1 in the appropriate form.

V 1 た  : After V1, V2 （V 1 happens first）
V 1 る  : Before V1, V2 （V 1 happens later）
れ い１ ：
部屋を　出たとき、ドアを　閉めます。
When (after) I leave the room, I close the door.
The verb with とき is in the ta-form (出た), so 部屋を　出た is understood to happen first and ドアを　閉めます afterward.
れい２：
きのう、家へ帰るとき、パンを　買いました。
Yesterday, when (before) I went home, I bought bread.
The verb with とき is in the る form (帰る), so パンを　買いました is understood to happen first and 家へ帰る afterward.

～とき expresses “when, at the time” of a situation/point in time.
Key difference (verbs):
V-辞書形+ とき: the main action happens before/while V (before the completion of V).
V-た形+ とき: the main action happens after the completion of V.
V-辞書形+ とき: the main action happens before/while V (before the completion of V).
V-た形+ とき: the main action happens after the completion of V.
With adjectives/nouns: there is no “before/after” distinction; it only gives the time setting.

rows: Indicates a point in time, neutral
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>にいました。
A relationship of inevitable condition, not a simple “when”
<ruby>春<rt>はる</rt></ruby>になると、<ruby>桜<rt>さくら</rt></ruby>が<ruby>咲<rt>さ</rt></ruby>く。
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>のときに<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>してください。

mistakes: Wrong point in time: ×日本へ行くとき、写真をたくさん撮りました（meaning after arriving）→ ✓日本へ行ったとき…。
Forgetting の with nouns: ×学生とき→ ✓学生のとき。
Using the wrong tense in the main clause makes the sentence hard to understand; be consistent (past/present).
174.notes:
With verbs of movement (行く、来る、帰る), choose 辞書形/た形 to distinguish “before going” and “after arriving”.
「このとき／そのとき／あのとき」 are phrases meaning “at this time/at that time/at that time (then)”.
「Nとき」 is not used directly; it must be Nのとき (例：朝のとき× →朝は/朝に or 朝起きたとき).

examples.jp: 田中さん：今晩私は出かけます。
examples.tr: Tanaka: I'm going out tonight.

examples.jp: 田中さんは今晩出かけるいました。
examples.tr: Tanaka said that they were going out tonight.

examples.jp: 田中さんは「今晩私は出かけます」と言いました。
examples.tr: Tanaka said, "I'm going out tonight."

examples.jp: ミラー：今日、私は早く帰らなければなりません。
examples.tr: Miller: I have to go home early today.

examples.jp: ミラーさんは彼は今日、早く家へ帰らなければならないと言いました。
examples.tr: Miller said that he had to go home early today.

examples.jp: ミラーさんは「今日、私は早く家へ帰らなければなりません」と言いました。
examples.tr: Miller said, "I have to go home early today."

176.explain:
Used to report some content.
Because it is usually used to report back what was said, it is often used in the past tense: 言いました。

examples.jp: 夕ごはん、どうしますか。
examples.tr: What are we doing about dinner?

examples.jp: この箱はどうしますか。
examples.tr: What would you like to do with this box?

examples.jp: 明日、雨です。ピクニックはどうしますか。
examples.tr: It's going to rain tomorrow. What shall we do about the picnic?

examples.jp: レシートはどうしますか。
examples.tr: What would you like to do with the receipt?

examples.jp: 支払いは現金とカード、どうしますか。
examples.tr: How would you like to pay, cash or card?

examples.jp: この問題、あとでもう一度やりますか。— はい、そうします。
examples.tr: Will you do this problem again later? — Yes, I will.

177.explain:
Used to ask the listener to make a decision; the person asking is neutral.
In casual conversation: どうする？/ どうするの？
Polite: どうしますか; formal service language: どういたしますか。
Common answers are そうします/やめます/あとでにします/こちらにします.

Asks about a decision/the next action: “What will (you/we) do / how will (you/we) do it?”.
Usually follows a context/target that has already been mentioned (an object, a plan, a situation).
In service situations, used to confirm the customer's choice (payment, wrapping, delivery…).
Unlike どうですか (asking for an evaluation), どうしますか focuses on the action/decision.

rows: <ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>は どうしますか。
Focuses on “how is it/is it good”
この<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>は どうですか。
Expects the name of a specific action
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みに なにを しますか。
<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>は どれに しますか。
Polite; the speaker takes part in the decision
<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>は どうしましょうか。

mistakes: Confusing it with どうですか: どうしますか asks about an action, どうですか asks for an evaluation/suggestion.
Missing context indicating the target: saying “どうしますか” on its own is hard to understand; state it clearly as “N は どうしますか”。
Use どうしましょうか when you want to make a suggestion; avoid どうしますか so as not to seem to force a decision.
177.notes:
Sample answers in service situations: “袋は いりますか。— いりません。/ お願いします。/有料ですが どうしますか。— お願いします。”
In a group, どうする？ creates an atmosphere of discussing together; adding ね makes it softer: どうするね is dialect; in standard Japanese, どうするね is nonstandard; use どうする？/どうしようか。
In urgent situations: どうする？！ has a tense nuance: “What do we do now?!”

examples.jp: この服、どうですか。
examples.tr: What do you think of these clothes?

examples.jp: 日本の生活はどうですか。
examples.tr: How is life in Japan?

examples.jp: コーヒーはどうですか。
examples.tr: How about some coffee?

examples.jp: この席はどうですか。
examples.tr: How about this seat?

examples.jp: 旅行はどうでしたか。
examples.tr: How was your trip?

examples.jp: 宿題の進み具合はどうですか。
examples.tr: How is your homework coming along?

178.explain:
Asks generally about quality/impression: どうですか has a neutral, gentle nuance.
Using は to mark the topic (N は どうですか) is more natural than を in this pattern.
In invitations: with rising intonation, in a context that calls for the listener's decision, it is understood as an “invitation/suggestion”.
Typical answers: いいです／だめです／大丈夫です／ちょっと… (a tactful refusal).

Asks for an opinion/evaluation of a person/thing/situation: “how is it?”.
Used as a gentle suggestion: “How about N?” → encourages choosing/trying.
The context determines the meaning: the same sentence can be an “evaluation” or an “invitation/suggestion”.
Made more polite with いかがですか (service, receiving guests).
Unlike どうしますか, どうですか does not require an immediate decision about an action.

rows: この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>は どうですか。
<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>は どうしますか。
Polite form of どうですか
お<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>は いかがですか。
<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ませんか。
Softer than どうですか; often used when weighing options
この<ruby>案<rt>あん</rt></ruby>は どうでしょうか。

mistakes: Confusing it with どうしますか when a specific action is needed; どうですか does not require a decision.
Using を with どうですか in invitations/suggestions: は is more natural (コーヒーは どうですか).
Using どうですか too directly in a formal setting; switch to いかがですか.
178.notes:
Use どうでしたか to ask about a past experience (past).
In service situations: “試飲はいかがですか” (Would you like to try a sample?); polite answers: “結構です/お願いします”。
Avoid repeating どう many times; replace it with いかが or specific adjectives (おいしいですか,便利ですか…).

179.name: ～は［language］で何と／どう言いますか
179.connection: Nは + [language]で + どう/なんと言いますか

examples.jp: 「猫」は英語で何と言いますか。
examples.tr: How do you say 「猫」 in English?

examples.jp: この気持ちは日本語でどう言いますか。
examples.tr: How do you express this feeling in Japanese?

examples.jp: この文は日本語でどう言いますか。
examples.tr: How do you say this sentence in Japanese?

examples.jp: Wi-Fi は日本語で何ですか。
examples.tr: What is Wi-Fi in Japanese?

179.explain:
Formal: X は日本語で何と言いますか／どう言いますか。
Casual: X って日本語で何て言う？／どう言う？
The pattern “X は日本語で何ですか” is suitable when asking about a single word.
When answering, use: 「X」は日本語で「Y」と言います。/ Y と言います。

Asks how to express a word/sentence in a language: “how do you say it”, “what is it called”.
何と言いますか emphasizes “what is said”. どう言いますか emphasizes “how it is said” (the expression).
For single words/phrases, both 何と言いますか／何ですか are natural. For paraphrases/long sentences, どう言いますか is more natural.

rows: X は <ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>と<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いますか
「apple」は<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>と<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いますか。
X は <ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で どう<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いますか
この<ruby>表現<rt>ひょうげん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>でどう<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いますか。
X は <ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>ですか
これは<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>ですか。
Asks for the reading, not the meaning
この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>はどう<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みますか。

mistakes: Wrong particle: ×日本語に何と言いますか → ✓日本語で何と言いますか。
Using どう言いますか for kanji: you need どう読みますか when asking how to read it.
Mixing up 何ですか (what is it) and 何と言いますか (what is it called); both are correct for single words but differ in nuance.
179.notes:
“何と言いますか” is often shortened in pronunciation to “なんと言いますか/何て言いますか”.
Do not confuse どう言う (how to say) with どういうN (what kind of N).
To emphasize the language: X は英語では何と言いますか（in contrast with other languages）.
Original notes: Spelling: 何と言いますか／なんと言いますか are both correct; なんて言いますか leans toward casual conversation.
Fillers such as “ええと/あの/その” often come before なんと言いますか to show hesitation.
When pointing at a specific object, the language can be omitted if the context is clear: これ、なんと言いますか。
To check a word you have just forgotten: 何て言うんでしたっけ (I forgot, what's it called again?)

examples.jp: 毎日、練習をしているけど、なかなか上手になりません。
examples.tr: I practice every day, but I'm just not getting any better.

examples.jp: 休みが十分とれなくて、なかなかかぜが治りません。
examples.tr: I can't get enough rest, so my cold just won't go away.

examples.jp: 宿題がなかなか終わらない。
examples.tr: My homework just won't get finished.

examples.jp: タクシーがなかなかつかまらない。
examples.tr: I just can't catch a taxi.

examples.jp: なぜがなかなかなおらない。
examples.tr: My cold just won't go away.

examples.jp: ダイエットがなかなか成功しません。
examples.tr: My diet just isn't working out.

180.explain:
◎ The situation is not progressing as the speaker expected.

Expresses regret at not being able to do something as one wishes, at not being able to succeed easily.

examples.jp: 毎日８時に家に帰ります。
examples.tr: I go home at 8 o'clock every day.

examples.jp: 今週末、国に帰ります。
examples.tr: I'm going back to my home country this weekend.

examples.jp: お正月は実家に帰ります。
examples.tr: I go back to my parents' home for New Year's.

examples.jp: 授業が終わったら部屋に帰ります。
examples.tr: When class is over, I go back to my room.

examples.jp: 今日は遅くに家に帰ります。
examples.tr: Today I'll get home late.

examples.jp: バスで寮に帰ります。
examples.tr: I go back to the dorm by bus.

182.explain:
に帰る emphasizes that the destination is a place where one “belongs”; へ帰る is also possible but neutrally indicates direction and is less common.
帰る vs 戻る: 戻る means “go back (to the immediately previous position/state)”, not necessarily home.
帰ってくる/帰っていく: nuance of coming toward the speaker/going away from the speaker.
Often used politely in work conversations: 先に失礼して家に帰ります。

Movement back to the starting point/a place one belongs to (home, hometown, room, dorm…).
に marks a specific destination; 帰る expresses “returning” (unlike 行く/来る).
Has a nuance of familiarity when used with 家/実家/故郷.
Can be combined with a point in time or means: ９時に/電車で家に帰ります.

rows: <ruby>９時<rt>きゅうじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>帰宅<rt>きたく</rt></ruby>する

mistakes: Using で instead of に: 家で帰ります (incorrect) → 家に帰ります.
Dropping に with 帰る: 家帰る (often colloquial, but in standard Japanese use 家に帰る).
Confusing 戻る and 帰る: 家に戻る (unnatural except in certain contexts); prefer 家に帰る.
へ帰ります is rarely the best answer on the JLPT; prefer に帰ります.
182.notes:
“国に帰ります” is a familiar phrase for international students; often used with 休み/連休/旧正月.
Add a reason with ので/から/ために: 急用のために国に帰ります。
Different nuance from 戻る: 会社から家に戻る is usually unnatural; use 帰る.

examples.jp: 家に戻ります。
examples.tr: I'm going back home.

examples.jp: 会社に戻ります。
examples.tr: I'm going back to the office.

examples.jp: 休みが終わって、また仕事に戻りました。
examples.tr: The holiday ended, and I went back to work again.

examples.jp: 天気が晴れにに戻りました。
examples.tr: The weather has cleared up again.

examples.jp: 昔の生活に戻りたい。
examples.tr: I want to go back to my old life.

183.explain:
“N + に戻ります” is used for both places and states (physical or abstract).
It is a neutral, polite expression, usable in everyday conversation and written language.
When talking about people, “戻る” has the nuance of “coming back on one's own”; when talking about things or situations, it can mean “returning to how it was”.

① Returning to the starting point: Expresses going back to the original place.
→ “return”, “go back”.
② Returning to a former state: Used when a thing, situation or mood goes back to how it was originally.
→ “return to the original state”, “go back to the previous situation”.
“戻ります” is the intransitive verb form of “戻す” (return, give back). The speaker goes back, or returns to some state, on their own.

rows: Return, go back (to a former place / state)
Going back or returning on one's own
Return home / to one's hometown / to where one belongs
Usually used for people returning to their “starting point”
Someone “returns” an object or a state
<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>棚<rt>たな</rt></ruby>に<ruby>戻<rt>もど</rt></ruby>す。（Put the book back on the shelf）
Emphasizes that the destination is “where one lives” or “one's hometown”

mistakes: Confusing 戻る（go back on one's own）and 戻す（give back, return something）.
Using the wrong particle: it should be に戻る, not へ戻る (although it is sometimes acceptable, “に” is more natural).
Confusing it with 帰る: “戻る” is used for a place you left temporarily and come back to; “帰る” is used for a place you belong to (home, hometown…).
JLPT N5–N4 often tests the difference between “戻る”, “帰る” and “戻す”.
183.notes:
“戻る” can be used in both a physical sense (returning to a place) and an abstract sense (returning to a state, a frame of mind).
Clearly distinguish “戻る” (go back on one's own) and “戻す” (make something go back / return it to someone).
In conversation, “戻ります” is often used in the office: 例：「すぐ戻ります。」→ “I'll be right back.” (when stepping away briefly).

184.connection: [place]に + Nが + あります/います

examples.jp: 教室に学生がいます。
examples.tr: There are students in the classroom.

examples.jp: 冷蔵庫に水があります。
examples.tr: There is water in the fridge.

examples.jp: 公園に犬がいますか。— はい、います。
examples.tr: Is there a dog in the park? — Yes, there is.

examples.jp: 机の上にパソコンがあります。
examples.tr: There is a computer on the desk.

examples.jp: ここは静かな町です。駅はこの近くにあります。
examples.tr: This is a quiet town. The station is near here.

examples.jp: 今日は会議があります。
examples.tr: There is a meeting today.

184.explain:
Typical word order: [Place] に [new subject] が あります／います.
が marks new information; は brings the topic to the front to emphasize the location: 図書館は駅の西にあります.
Politely asking where something is: 〜はどこにありますか。 For people: 〜はどこにいますか。
Very polite: 〜がございます（things/items in service, sales).

Expresses the existence/presence of a thing/person at a specific location.
あります: things, events, inanimate concepts (会議があります＝there is a meeting).
います: people, animals, living things. At the present point in time / temporarily in that position.
Possessive variant: “Nがあります” sometimes expresses “have N” (私には時間があります＝I have time), but for personal belongings 持っています is usually more natural.

rows: <ruby>机<rt>つくえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>があります
N is the topic; emphasizes the location
<ruby>銀行<rt>ぎんこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>の<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>にあります
<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っています
〜にいます vs 〜に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいます
にいます: temporary; <ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいます: place of residence
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>にいます／<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいます
ここは<ruby>図書館<rt>としょかん</rt></ruby>です

mistakes: Confusing が/に: ✕公園が犬にいます → 〇公園に犬がいます.
Using を: ✕部屋を机があります → 〇部屋に机があります.
Confusing あります/います: ✕店に店員があります → 〇店に店員がいます.
Expressing possession: ✕私は車があります → 〇車があります／車を持っています.
Confusing です with あります: ✕机の上は本です（different meaning） → 〇机の上に本があります.
Order of counters: ✕三本の木があります（OK, but emphasizes N）; for existence it is more natural to say: 木が三本あります.
184.notes:
For robots/fictional characters that are “alive”: います is usually used (ロボットがいます) — depends on the context.
Detailed location elements: 上／下／中／隣／前／後ろ＋に indicate spatial relationships: 机の下に箱があります。
“Having time/an event”: 時間があります／試験があります — あります is still used because these are inanimate concepts.

185.meaning: Expresses a feeling or evaluation （すき・きらい・下手・上手）toward an action; the verb expressing that action must be nominalized. Similar to 「～こと」.

examples.jp: 旅行するのが好きです。
examples.tr: I like traveling.

examples.jp: 朝はしるのがすきです。
examples.tr: I like running in the morning.

examples.jp: かれはうんてんするのがへたです。
examples.tr: He is bad at driving.

examples.jp: わたしはおふろに入るのがきらいです。
examples.tr: I hate taking baths.

186.meaning: Marks the subject of a modifying phrase
186.connection: N1の/が + V/A + N2 (subject of the modifying clause)

examples.jp: わたしのすきな喫茶店。
examples.tr: The café I like.

examples.jp: わたしがすきな人はかれですか。
examples.tr: Is he the person I like?

examples.jp: Aクラスは、先生のおもしろいクラスです。
examples.tr: Class A is the class with the fun teacher.

examples.jp: 寝る前に、歯を磨きます。
examples.tr: I brush my teeth before going to bed.

examples.jp: 出かける前に、天気予報を確認してください。
examples.tr: Please check the weather forecast before you go out.

examples.jp: 授業の前に、教室を掃除しました。
examples.tr: I cleaned the classroom before class.

examples.jp: 3時前に戻ります。
examples.tr: I'll be back before 3 o'clock.

examples.jp: 日本へ行く前に、パスポートを作りました。
examples.tr: Before going to Japan, I got a passport.

examples.jp: 食事の前に、手を洗いましょう。
examples.tr: Let's wash our hands before the meal.

187.explain:
Emphasizes preparation/a condition that must be done before another activity.
With habits/rules: ～前に～する has a nuance of advice/instruction.
Polite style: ～前に～してください／お願いいたします。
To say “don't do A before B”, you can use ～までVない or Vないで to show avoiding an action.

Expresses that action B happens before A takes place: A の/辞書形前に、B。
Focuses on preparation/conditions before carrying out the main action.
With a specific time, “X時前に” is more natural than “X時の前に”.
V辞書形+前に: A has not yet happened at the time of B (emphasizes that A is in the future relative to B).

rows: V<ruby>辞書<rt>じしょ</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に
Emphasizes that A has not happened at the time of B
Emphasizes a deadline, not a sequence
<ruby>5時<rt>ごじ</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>
Emphasizes “making use of the time while still …”
Expresses the opposite sequence to “<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に”

mistakes: Wrong verb tense: ×食べた前に → ✓食べる前に.
Using “の” with clock times: ×3時の前に → ✓3時前に／3時までに.
Confusing it with うちに: “make use of the time while you are still free” → ひまなうちに, not “ひまの前に”.
Confusing it with までに: when emphasizing the deadline for handing in an assignment, use までに, not 前に.
187.notes:
Vた +前に is incorrect; you must use V辞書形+前に because action A has not yet happened at the time of B.
With clock times: “X時前に” is natural; “X時の前に” is rarely used and sounds forced.
“以前（いぜん）” = “before, formerly” (the distant past); it is not used like “前に” to show an immediate sequence of actions.

examples.jp: 日本語はたいへんです。
examples.tr: Japanese is hard.

examples.jp: 毎日残業はたいへんです。
examples.tr: Working overtime every day is tough.

examples.jp: 引っ越しはたいへんでした。
examples.tr: Moving was a lot of work.

examples.jp: 朝早く起きるのはたいへんです。
examples.tr: Getting up early in the morning is hard.

examples.jp: それはたいへんですね。手伝いましょうか。
examples.tr: That must be hard. Shall I help you?

examples.jp: この仕事はたいへんではありません。
examples.tr: This job isn't hard.

188.explain:
Use は to mark the topic being evaluated: N は たいへんです. To emphasize the subject in a sentence presenting new information, が can be used (with a different nuance), but the pattern here is は.
Use たいへんですね when hearing about someone else's difficulties, to show politeness and sympathy.
In casual speech: たいへんだ／たいへんだった.
Avoid using たいへん instead of むずかしい when talking purely about “how difficult the material is”. たいへん leans toward “hard work, effort, tiring”.

“たいへん” expresses a degree of difficulty, hardship or seriousness. Used to say that something is “hard/painful/troublesome”.
With “N は たいへんです”: a general evaluation of a subject, job or situation.
With “V の は たいへんです”: emphasizes that a specific action is hard to do.
In unusual situations/accidents, たいへん can mean “serious/terrible”.
The exclamation form “たいへんですね” shows sympathy/politeness in conversation.

rows: <ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>はたいへんです。
この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>はむずかしい。
Spoken language, stronger than たいへん
たいへんに<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいです。

mistakes: Confusing it with むずかしい: “a difficult problem” should be 問題はむずかしい, not たいへん.
Dropping “の” when nominalizing a verb: ×勉強するはたいへんです → ○勉強するのはたいへんです.
Using が instead of は changes the focus of the sentence; with this pattern, keep N は たいへんです to state the topic.
Forgetting to use the polite/past form: たいへんでした (correct) instead of たいへんです (when talking about the past).
188.notes:
たいへん can be used as a polite adverb meaning “very”: たいへんおいしい、たいへん失礼しました.
Social formula: お仕事はたいへんですか (Is your work hard?).
To emphasize a serious incident: たいへんなことになった (Something serious has happened).

189.meaning: Particle indicating the direction of movement. Often used with verbs of movement such as 「行く」「帰る」「来る」

190.explain:
Emphasizes the order of actions.
The tense (future, present, past …) is marked on the second verb. (V2)
The subject of the main clause takes は; the subject of the subordinate clause takes the particle が.

～まえに： Before
A length of time placed directly before まえに usually means: ~ ago.
190.notes:
meaning_vi: Emphasizes that the action or event in the second clause takes place before the action or event in the first clause.
examples: 1. ①　つらくなる　前に
Before it becomes painful.
2. ②　テストを　はじめる　前に　名前を　書いてください。
Please write your name before starting the test.
3. ③　ねる　前に　何をし　ましたか。
What did you do when you slept?
4. ④　食事の　前に　手を　あらいます。
I wash my hands before meals.

191.meaning: This one is more … than that one

examples.jp: 去年より今年のほうが忙しい。

examples.jp: バスより電車のほうが速い。

examples.jp: 日本語より英語のほうが話しやすい。
examples.tr: English is easier to speak than Japanese.

examples.jp: AとBでは、どちらのほうが難しいですか。— Bのほうが難しいです。
examples.tr: Which is more difficult, A or B? — B is more difficult.

examples.jp: 予想より結果のほうが悪かった。
examples.tr: The result was worse than expected.

191.explain:
When the context is clear, you can say: B のほうが ～ (omitting Aより).
Add ずっと/はるかに to emphasize a large difference.
のほうが is common in conversation; formal written language may use other比較的構文, but this pattern is still standard.
Note that A and B must be compared on the same criterion.

States which is superior: “B is more ~ than A”.
The focus is on B（のほう）. The Aより part can be omitted when the comparison is implicit.
Can be used with adjectives, verbs, quantities, frequency…
のほう (the side of …) carries a nuance of choice/comparison and is natural in conversation.

rows: A は B ほど ～ない
A is not as … as B
Focuses on the negative (A falls short of B); softer nuance than the affirmative “B is more than A”.
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>兄<rt>あに</rt></ruby>ほど <ruby>背<rt>せ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>くない。
Advice/choice, not simply a comparison of degree.
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>はタクシーのほうがいい。
Not a comparison of two sides; picks the highest degree among many.
この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby><ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い。

mistakes: Wrong order: “BよりAのほうが” is usually unnatural; the standard is “AよりBのほうが”.
Mixed criteria: A and B must be compared on the same criterion.
Confusing ～のほうがいい (advice) with ～より～のほうが～ (comparison of degree).
Dropping より when the context is not clear makes the sentence ambiguous in reading comprehension.
191.notes:
のほう is a nominalization meaning “side/direction”, which helps set B up naturally as the topic of the comparison.
より can become よりも for emphasis or when a clearer rhythm is needed.
が/は after のほうが: use が when giving new information, and は for contrast/generalization.

192.meaning: The sentence-final particle「よ」is used when giving the listener new information. The sentence-final particle「ね」is used when you want the listener to confirm information the listener already knows.

208.explain:
Polite: できます／できません. Casual: できる／できない.
General ability uses Nができます; a specific action uses Vることができます or可能形V-られる.
In the meaning “be built/appear/form”, the subject is a thing + が:公園ができる,予約ができる (reservations can be made).
To show degree: よくできます (can do well), だいたいできます (can roughly do),少しできます (can do a little).

Ability/possible conditions: “can do ~”, “know how to ~” (ability, skill, conditions that allow it).
Formation/completion/coming into being: “be finished/be born/form” (a different meaning from “can”).
State the scope of ability with a noun: ピアノができます (can play the piano),料理ができます (can cook).
When expressing ability with a specific verb, Vることができます is formal; the plain form used in conversation is the V-可能形:読めます,行けます.

rows: Ability to do a specific action
<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>することができる
V-<ruby>可能<rt>かのう</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby> (<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>める)
Emphasizes change, not simply present ability
<ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>可能<rt>かのう</rt></ruby>だ

mistakes: Wrong particle: using を instead of が for ability. Correct: Nができます.
Confusing the completion meaning: “駅ができました” does not mean “can station”, but “a new station has been built”.
Mistakenly using Nをすることができる (redundant). Usually Vることができる or Nができる is used.
Confusing degree: “少しできます/全然できません” are natural expressions of degree in the JLPT.
208.notes:
Distinguish the two meanings “can do” and “be built/be made” based on the context and the subject.
With people:友だちができる = make a new friend;子どもができる = get pregnant/have a child (be careful with the nuance).
Places/equipment: ここで充電ができます (you can charge here) = the conditions allow it.
Polite negative in public places: 〜ことはできません/ご遠慮ください differ in nuance (prohibition/request to refrain).
explain: Expresses ability or possibility regarding something.
examples: 1. A:　カリナちゃんは　漢字が　できますか。
B:　はい、漢字をよむことが　できます。書くことも　できますよ。
A: Does Karina know kanji?
B: Yes, she can read kanji. She can write them too.
2. A:　カードで　はらうことが　できますか。
B:　はい、できますよ。
A: Can I pay by card?
B: Yes, of course.
explain: ◎ Used with the dictionary form of a verb; means it is possible to do that action.
examples: 1. 屋上から 富士山を 見る ことが できます。
You can see Mt. Fuji from the rooftop.
2. ここから 先は、車で、通る ことが できません。
Beyond this point, cars cannot pass.
explain: Vる + こと + が + できます: more polite than the potential V-られる.
Use に/で to show the place/condition:学校で勉強することができます。
Can be used both for inherent ability and for ability due to circumstances/permission.
examples: 1. 私は泳ぐことができます。
I can swim.
2. この図書館で日本語の本を読むことができます。
You can read Japanese books at this library.
3. ここでは写真を撮ることができません。
You can't take pictures here.
4. 昨日、早く帰ることができました。
Yesterday I was able to go home early.
5. このカードで払うことができますか。
Can I pay with this card?
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
Vる + ことができます | Can do (polite) | Formal, easy to use at N5 | 日本語（にほんご）を話（はな）す ことができます
V可能（かのう）形（けい） (～られる) | Can do | Concise, conversational; higher level | 日本語（にほんご）が話（はな）せる
N + ができます | Can do/know N | Used with nouns of ability | 料理（りょうり） ができます
common_mistakes: Wrong particle: ×日本語を話すができます → ✓日本語を話すことができます.
Omitting こと: ×車を運転ができます → ✓車を運転することができます or車の運転ができます.
Confusing permission and ability: rely on the context/place to understand correctly.
explain: Compared with the V-可能形: ことができる is formal/objective; the V-可能形 is more natural and colloquial:日本語が話せる。
In a nominalized clause, keep the particle order inside:日本語 を 話すことができる (correct); the pattern日本語 が 話せる is used with the potential form.
To express “service availability”: こちらで両替 できます (more natural in instructions).
Combining for emphasis:少しなら/十分に/自由に + できる.
examples: 1. 私は日本語を話すことができます。
I can speak Japanese.
2. ここではWi‑Fiを無料で利用することができます。
You can use Wi‑Fi for free here.
3. 事故のため、今日は運転することができません。
Because of the accident, I can't drive today.
4. このアプリで予約することができる。
You can make reservations with this app.
5. 手術のおかげで、また走ることができるようになった。
Thanks to the surgery, I became able to run again.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
V-ことができる | Can (objective) | Formal; suits written language, announcements | 入場（にゅうじょう）する ことができません
V-可能（かのう）形（けい）（読（よ）める等（ひとし）） | Can (natural) | Colloquial; object changes を→が | 日本語（にほんご） が 話（はな）せる
～てもいい | Allowed to | A different axis of meaning (permission) | ここで写真（しゃしん）を撮（と）っ てもいい
Nができる | Know/be good at/be made | Noun form: 英語（えいご）ができる/ケーキができる | 彼（かれ）は数学（すうがく） ができる
common_mistakes: • Confusing permission vs ability: “入ってもいい” (allowed) ≠ “入ることができる” (able to enter).
• Wrong particle inside the clause: 日本語が話すことができる → should be 日本語を話すことができる.
• Redundancy with サ変: “予約をすることができる” is long; natural: 予約できる / 予約することができる (when formality is needed).
• Too formal in casual conversation: ことができる → use the 可能形 to sound natural.
meaning_vi: Expresses a situation in which an action can always be carried out (①②), or an ability to do something (③). Verbs expressing a person's volitional actions are usually used with this sentence pattern. It is a stiffer way of speaking than ～（され）ます。
examples: 1. ①このコンビニでは24時間買い物ができます。
You can shop 24 hours a day at this convenience store.
2. ②今、この建物の中には入ることができません。
You can't go inside this building right now.
3. ③私は日本の県の名前を全部いうことができます。
I can name all the prefectures of Japan.
meaning_vi: being able to do something…
judging from the situation, being able to do something…
examples: 1. わたしは車の運転ができます。
I can drive a car.
2. リンさんは日本語を話すことができます。
Lin can speak Japanese.
3. 「場所がどこかわかりますから、一人で行くことができます」
“I know where the place is, so I can go by myself.”
4. この図書館は9時まで利用することができます。
This library can be used until 9 o'clock.
5. 「禁煙です。ここではたばこを吸うことはできません」
“No smoking. You can't smoke here.”
6. 「このいすは壊れていますから、座ることはできません。注意してくださいね。」
“This chair is broken, so you can't sit on it. Please be careful.”
meaning_vi: Expresses that something can be done.
examples: 1. ①　何でも　食べられるよ。
I can eat anything.
2. ②　わたしは　何でも　食べる　ことが　できます。
I can eat anything.
3. ➂　いつか　また　会えますよ。
We'll be able to meet again someday.

examples.jp: 彼女は、日本の生活のことをいろいろ教えてくれました。
examples.tr: She taught me a lot about life in Japan.

examples.jp: 彼が、森先生の授業が休みになると知らせてくれました。
examples.tr: He let me know that Professor Mori's class was canceled.

examples.jp: 友だちが宿題を手伝ってくれた。
examples.tr: My friend helped me with my homework.

examples.jp: 先生が発音を直してくれました。
examples.tr: My teacher corrected my pronunciation.

examples.jp: この本を貸してくれて、本当に助かった。
examples.tr: You lent me this book, and it really helped.

examples.jp: ちょっと待ってくれる？
examples.tr: Can you wait a moment?

209.explain:
The subject is the doer (ga/wa) + V-て + くれる; the receiver is I/we (usually omitted).
Shows gratitude and familiarity; switch to くださる when the doer requires respect.
In the request form, add a polite cushion phrase: すみませんが、～て くれますか ／～て くれませんか .
Not used to say “I do something for someone else”; in that case use ～てあげる／～てさしあげる.

• Expresses an action that “someone does (for the benefit of) the speaker or someone in the speaker's group”. Emphasizes the favor and a sense of gratitude/positive evaluation.
• Can be used to make a request in question form: ～てくれる？／～てくれますか (request).
• In emotional contexts: ～てくれてありがとう／～てくれてよかった (expressive).
• When the doer is a superior/customer, change to ～てくださる (honorific); to emphasize that the receiver is me, use ～ていただく (humble).

rows: Someone else does something for me
<ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ってくれた
<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくださった
<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちに<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってもらった
I do something for someone else
The benefit goes from me outward
Humble (I do something for a superior)
<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>してさしあげます

mistakes: Using くれる when the receiver has no connection to the speaker → use あげる/もらう depending on the direction of the favor.
Forgetting to switch to keigo with a superior: × 先生が教えてくれた → ✓ 教えてくださいました／教えてくださった。
Mixing up くれる and もらう when the subject changes: JLPT questions often ask you to change the structure while keeping the meaning.
Using the command form くれ sounds rude; avoid it in polite settings.
209.notes:
• ～てくれるな is a blunt prohibition (don't you do it), often found in rhetoric/classical style/strongly masculine speech; use with care.
• ～てくれてよかった／～てくれてうれしい: a positive emotional nuance about the favor received.
• Changing the viewpoint: with もらう, the receiver is the subject; with くれる, the giver is the subject. Both can describe the same event with different nuances.
meaning_vi: ~smiley1V for me.
explain: Used only for yourself and your family members such as father, mother, older brother, older sister…（ちち、はは、あね、あに、おとうと、いもうと…)
私に can be omitted; in that case the subject takes the particle が.
examples: 1. A:　犬が　かわいいですね。
B:　ええ、姉が　この犬 を　買ってくれましたよ。
A: Your dog is so cute.
B: Yeah, my sister bought it for me.
2. A:　すてきな　セーターですね。
B:　ありがとう　ございます。ママが　送ってくれましたよ。
A: That's a lovely sweater.
B: Thank you. My mom sent it to me.
meaning_vi: The subject of the sentence is not the speaker. The receiver of the thing or action is the speaker or someone psychologically close to the speaker. When receiving from a superior who is not a family member, the pattern くださいます is used.
examples: 1. ①山田さんは私に時計をくれました。
Mr. Yamada gave me a watch.
2. ②先生が妹に本をくださいました。

210.explain:
A casual pattern, usually used between equals or close friends. With superiors or in business, avoid ～てあげる; use ～てさしあげる or a neutral expression instead.
Offering help: ～てあげましょうか can be perceived as "doing someone a favor" if the other person does not need it.
The recipient is always marked with に; the thing/matter helped with is marked with を/に/で depending on the verb.
Not used when the recipient is the speaker; in that case you must use ～てくれる/～てもらう.
Rarely used in formal written language; replace it with an expression that does not take credit for oneself.

• Expresses the action of "doing something for / helping" someone; the doer actively gives a benefit to another person.
• Point of view: from the giver's side. If the speaker is the recipient, use ～てくれる.
• The nuance ranges from friendly to slightly condescending, depending on the relationship. With superiors/customers, use ～てさしあげる (when talking about your own help) or rephrase.
• Can be used for both concrete and emotional actions: 勇気づけてあげる, 相談に乗ってあげる.
• Can express "no need / not worth doing for someone": ～てあげる必要はない／～てあげなくてもいい.

Wrong point of view: when the speaker is the recipient, you must use ～てくれる/～てもらう, not ～てあげる.
Forgetting に for the recipient: 彼に手伝ってあげる (correct), 彼手伝ってあげる (incorrect).
Offering too directly: 手伝ってあげます ⇒ may sound self-important; more neutral: お手伝いしましょうか.
210.notes:
• Tense/politeness follow the auxiliary verb あげる: あげる・あげます・あげた・あげようか.
• Do not combine it with honorific keigo (sonkeigo) toward the target at the same time (avoid 二重敬語).
• In advertising/services, "we do this for you" is usually avoided by emphasizing the customer's benefit without showing the agent.

211.explain:
To emphasize gratitude, add ありがとうございました after the past-tense sentence.
With superiors/customers: prefer いただく to be humble.
に and から: both are possible; に is neutral/standard, から is casual/emphasizes the starting point.
Change it to the potential form (V-て もらえる) to turn it into "could you do this for me?" → a polite request.
The one receiving the benefit is usually 私/私たち (can be omitted). If it is someone else, state it clearly, and the context must show the speaker's point of view.

• Expresses "having someone do V for me/us," showing a benefit to the speaker or the speaker's group.
• The frame "N に V-て もらう" focuses on the recipient of the benefit (the speaker), unlike "N が V-て くれる," which focuses on the giver.
• Often carries a sense of gratitude, a request, or acknowledgment of help. With いただく, the nuance is humble and formal.
• The agent can be a person or an organization: 市役所に手続きをしてもらう（have city hall do the paperwork for you）.
• Not used for unintentional actions or actions with no clear doer. There must be an "agent" with volition/responsibility to do V.

mistakes: Wrong point of view: "母が送ってもらった" is incorrect; it should be "母に送ってもらった".
Confusion with くれる: "田中さんが手伝ってくれた" is correct; with もらう it must be "田中さんに手伝ってもらった".
Using it with an inanimate agent: "雨にやませてもらった" is unnatural.
Forgetting the nuance of benefit: もらう always implies the speaker receives a benefit; it is not neutral like "AはBを直す".
On the JLPT, the trap is usually choosing between てくれる and てもらう based on the subject/point of view in the sentence.
211.notes:
• In formal written language, you may see 〜ていただく with phrases like ご教示, ご確認, ご対応.
• Indirect "request": AさんにBさんを紹介してもらう（have A introduce B）; に is still used for the person doing the action.
• With organizations: 市に許可を出してもらう is natural because it is an "entity with authority." もらう is not used with inanimate things that have no will.
• When chaining several actions done for you: 連絡してもらって、資料も送ってもらった（they contacted me and also sent me the documents）.

212.explain:
A polite, neutral conjecture; suitable for business conversation and speeches.
Asking a polite question: ～でしょうか (softer than ～ますか).
Seeking agreement: ～でしょう？ (↑); sympathy: ～でしょうね (↓).
Goes well with adverbs: たぶん／おそらく／きっと＋～でしょう.
Not used with direct commands/prohibitions: ×「行きなさいでしょう」.

• Polite conjecture/estimate: about 70–80% certainty. Example: 彼は来るでしょう。
• Gently offers a personal judgment, avoiding a strong assertion. Natural in expert statements and weather forecasts.
• Asks for an opinion/conjecture politely with ～でしょうか.
• Seeks agreement/emphasizes something obvious with ～でしょう？ (rising intonation).
• Emphasizes sympathy/understanding with ～でしょうね／～でしょう（ね） (falling, soft intonation).

mistakes: Confusing it with a strong assertion: ～でしょう is still conjecture, not 100% certainty.
Using ～でしょう？ in formal settings can feel like forcing agreement.
Attaching it to commands/prohibitions is grammatically incorrect.
Confusing the degree: かもしれない (low) ＜ ～でしょう ＜ はずだ／に違いない (high).
212.notes:
• In formal written language, ～でしょう often appears in presentations and forecasts.
• Placed after a number to give an estimate: 30％でしょう (about 30%).
• Avoid using it many times in a short statement, as it can sound like you are avoiding responsibility.
• Expressive use: ～でしょう？ is casual; in formal settings use ～でしょうか／と思います.

214.explain:
Neutral; describes a general method: "how to do, how to use".
"仕方" is often used when talking about a "way/manner" with a nuance of evaluation (good/bad) or in set phrases:仕方がない.
Instructional texts and UIs often use ～方/～かた: ご利用のしかた,使い方ガイド.

• Turns a verb into a noun meaning "the way/style/method of doing V".
• When the direct object of V (with を) attaches to ～方, it usually becomes a noun phrase with の: 漢字を書く → 漢字の書き方.
• Particles for direction/destination/place such as へ/に/で stay as they are, because they belong to the structure of the original V: 駅への行き方, 鍋での作り方.
• ～方 is a noun and can combine with の, は, が, を, に like other nouns.

The door is open  (the current state of the door is open)
1. お皿に　魚が　きってありますから、これから　さしみを　作りましょう。
The fish on the plate has already been cut, so let's make sashimi now.
2. A: ケーキは　どこですか。
B: ケーキは　もう　テープルに　おいてありますよ。
A: Where's the cake?
B: The cake is on the table.

221.name: V (volitional form) と思っています
221.connection: V (volitional form) + と思っています

examples.jp:
A: 今週の週末に何をしますか。
B: 友達とテニスをしようと思っています。
examples.tr:
A: What are you doing this weekend?
B: I'm thinking of playing tennis with a friend.

examples.jp:
A: 夏休みにうみへ行こうと。一緒に行きませんか。
B: すみませんが、私は家族と山にのぼろうと思っています。
examples.tr:
A: I'm thinking of going to the beach during summer vacation. Won't you come with me?
B: I'm sorry, but I'm planning to go mountain climbing with my family.

221.explain:
Expresses the speaker's intention.
• Note:
~思(おも)います：intention at the present point in time.
~思(おも)っています: I have been intending this all along.

222.meaning: Intransitive verb | Expresses the resultant state after some change.

examples.jp: まどが割れています。
examples.tr: The window is broken.

examples.jp: 私の部屋のまどは割れています。
examples.tr: The window in my room is broken.

222.explain:
Describes the state of a thing or a phenomenon.
When describing a state, it is always conjugated in the Vている form.
If we want to emphasize the thing being referred to, we can replace が with は.

223.name: ～ V (potential form)
223.meaning:
can ~ | Potential form of verbs | be able to do something…
considering the situation..be able to do something…
223.connection: Vる → V (potential form) (Group 1: う→える / Group 2: る→られる / する→できる / くる→こられる)

examples.jp:
A: カリナちゃんは漢字がよめますか。
B: はい、漢字がよめます。
examples.tr:
A: Can Karina read kanji?
B: Yes, Karina can read kanji.

examples.jp:
A: すみません、ここではカードがつかえますか。
B: はい、できますよ。
examples.tr:
A: Excuse me, can I use a card here?
B: Yes, you can.

223.explain:
• Presents the ability or capability of some target.
• Talks about a condition, or something that one is permitted to do.

~ V可能(かのう)形(けい): can ~
223.notes:
Note:
When conjugated into the potential form, all verbs become Group 2 verbs.
Only the particle を is replaced by the particle が. Other particles stay the same.
私は　ビールを　のみません。
I don't drink beer.
私は　ビールを　のむことが　できません。
私は　ビールが　のめません。
I can't drink beer.
忙しいですから、いなかへ　帰れません。
I'm busy, so I can't go back to my hometown.
meaning_vi: Can ~
［可能動詞の作り方］
examples: 1. ①　教科書が買える
Can buy a textbook.
2. ②　あの人はフランス語が話せる。
That person can speak French.
3. ③　私は生の魚が食べられない。
I can't eat raw fish.
4. ③　インタネットで予約できる店が増えている。
The number of stores where you can make reservations online is increasing.

examples.jp: 私は部屋をそうじしながら、音楽を聞きます。
examples.tr: I listen to music while cleaning my room.

examples.jp: パンをたべながら、新聞を読まないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't read the newspaper while eating bread.

224.explain:
Tenses and grammar patterns are conjugated on verb V2.
V1  is in the masu-form with ま す dropped

~Vながら: do ~ while ~
224.notes:
Connects verbs expressing a preceding and a following action to express two actions that proceed simultaneously in parallel. In this case, the latter action is the main action, and the former expresses a secondary action that describes, for example, the manner in which the main action is performed. In example ①, 「勉強や仕事をする」 is the main action, and it is carried out accompanied by the action 「音楽を聞く」. In the following sentence, the action of getting on the train and the action of reading a book would be taking place at the same time, so it cannot be interpreted as meaning that the person read a book on the train.
*（誤） 電車に乗りながら本を読んだ。
*（正） 電車に乗って本を読んだ。
!The subject of both clauses is the same, and the pattern usually expresses a person's intentional actions, but as in ⑤⑥, it can also be used with things that can move or change by their own power, such as airplanes or natural phenomena.
*（誤） 私は本を読みながら、彼はウイスキーを飲んだ。

examples.jp: 将来小説家になりたいです。それで今はアルバイトをしながら小説を書いています。
examples.tr: I want to become a novelist in the future. That's why I'm now writing novels while working a part-time job.

examples.jp: 小さい字が見えなくなりました。それで、新しいめがねを買いました。
examples.tr: I can no longer see small print. So I bought new glasses.

examples.jp: 会社が遠い。それで、毎朝早く家を出る。
examples.tr: My office is far away. So I leave home early every morning.

examples.jp:
A: ここはコーヒーもおいしいし、食事もできるし･･･。
B: それで人気があるんですね。
examples.tr:
A: The coffee here is good, and you can have a meal too…
B: So that's why it's popular.

225.explain:
「それで」is a conjunction used to present a result that comes from a cause or reason stated before it.

Used to state the consequence of a matter mentioned in the preceding sentences (factual).
225.notes:
meaning_vi: And so…, therefore… ⏐ explain: Suitable for narrating in a logical sequence; polite and clear.
Used to introduce a suggestion/request based on the preceding reason:故障しました。 それで、修理をお願いしたいのですが。
In conversation, それでね can be used casually to move on to a conclusion/consequence. ⏐ examples: 1. 雨が降っていた。それで、試合は中止になった。
It was raining. So the match was canceled.
2. 頭が痛かった。それで、早退した。
I had a headache. So I left early.
3. プリンターが壊れた。それで、新しいのを買った。
The printer broke. So I bought a new one.
4. 会議が長引いた。それで、連絡が遅れました。
The meeting ran long. That's why I was late getting in touch.
5. それで？彼は何て言ったの。
And then? What did he say? ⏐ comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Key difference | Short example
それで | therefore (result) | Adverb at the start of S2 | 雨（あめ）だ。 それで 遅（おく）れた。
だから/ですから | so | Conjunction, stronger/more direct nuance | だから 遅（おく）れた。
meaning_vi: （1）So, therefore
（2）So, ～? ⏐ explain: (1) expresses a result.
(2) a connective used to ask about the result. 「で」 is used in spoken language.
⏐ examples: 1. 父は働きすぎた。それで病気になった。
My father overworked. As a result, he got sick.
2. 「田中君、インフルエンザにかかったんだって。」
「それで学校を休んだんだね。」
I heard Tanaka caught the flu. So that's why he's absent from school today, huh.
3. 「田中君にお金を貸してくれって言われたんだ。」
「へえー。それで、貸してあげたの」
Tanaka asked me to lend him money. Huh. So, did you lend it to him?
4. 「今日、面接を受けたんだ。」
「で、どうなった。」
I had an interview today. So, how did it go?

226.meaning: Used to add things of the same kind as the words or sentences that come before.

examples.jp: バナナはおいしいです。それに、安いです。
examples.tr: Bananas are delicious. Besides, they're cheap.

examples.jp: 雨が降っているし、それに、風もある。
examples.tr: It's raining, and on top of that, it's windy too.

226.notes:
explain: Position: At the beginning of the sentence (second sentence), followed by a comma: それに、…
Formality: Neutral; works well in everyday conversation and internal emails. In formal documents, そのうえ/さらに may be more appropriate.
Listing chain: Can be used after ～し～し to end the sentence with an extra plus point as a “soft conclusion”.
Information weight: S2 usually points in the same direction and has equal or slightly greater value than S1. ⏐ examples: 1. この店は安い。それに、品質もいい。
This store is cheap. Besides, the quality is good too.
2. 今日は忙しい。それに、会議も三つある。
I'm busy today. On top of that, I have three meetings.
3. この本は読みやすい。それに、図が多くて理解しやすい。
This book is easy to read. What's more, it has a lot of diagrams, so it's easy to understand.
4. 彼は経験が豊富だ。それに、人柄もいい。
He has a wealth of experience. Besides, he has a good personality too.
5. 交通費は会社が出す。それに、昼食も支給される。
The company pays for transportation. In addition, lunch is provided.
6. このパソコ ⏐ comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Key difference | Short example
それに | Adds information | Neutral, “equal-level” addition. | 安（やす）い。 それに 早（はや）い。
そして | And, then | Neutral link in sequence; little emphasis on adding. | 説明（せつめい）

examples.jp: 地下鉄のほうが早く着きます。
examples.tr: The subway will get you there faster.

227.explain: ◎ Used when making a comparison and a judgment against something else. In some cases, the thing being compared is omitted.

examples.jp:
A: あめはもうやみましたか。
B: いいえ、まだふっていますよ。
examples.tr:
A: Has the rain stopped yet?
B: No, it's still raining.

examples.jp:
A: このはさみをしまいましょうか。
B: いいえ、まだ使っていますからそのままにしておいてください。
examples.tr:
A: Shall I put these scissors away?
B: No, I'm still using them, so please leave them as they are.

228.explain: Describes a state or an action that is still in progress.

230.name: Imperative form
230.connection: Vる → V (imperative form) (Group 1: う→え / Group 2: る→ろ / する→しろ / くる→こい)

examples.jp: 閉めろよ。
examples.tr: Close it!

examples.jp: いやならやめろ！
examples.tr: If you don't like it, then quit!

examples.jp: たのむ。来るな！
examples.tr: Please, I'm begging you. Don't come!

examples.jp: えんりょしないでもっと飲めよ。
examples.tr: Don't hold back, drink more!

231.name: Question word＋でも
231.meaning: Question word + でも: anyone/anything/anywhere… at all

examples.jp: こまったときは、いつでも言ってください。
examples.tr: Please tell me anytime you're in trouble.

examples.jp: 何でも買ってあげますよ。
examples.tr: I'll buy you anything you want.

examples.jp: これは、どこでも買えます。
examples.tr: You can buy this anywhere.

examples.jp: この店は品物は何でも１００円です。
examples.tr: Everything in this store is 100 yen.

examples.jp: 彼は有名な人だから、だれでも知っています。
examples.tr: He's famous, so everyone knows him.

examples.jp: 「何時ごろ電話しましょうか」「何時でもいいですよ」
examples.tr: 「Around what time should I call?」「Any time is fine.」

231.explain:
◎ 「Question word + ても」means that something applies in every case.

Question word + ても
231.notes:
meaning_vi: Follows question words such as 「何」「いつ」「どこ」「だれ」 to express an unspecified meaning.
examples: 1. ①　何でも　言ってください。
Please say anything.
2. ②　いつでも　電話してください。
Please call anytime.
3. ③　旅行は　どこでも　だいじょうぶです。
For the trip, anywhere is fine.
4. ④　だれでも　来てください。
Anyone is welcome to come.
original examples: 1. コンサートのチケットがとれるなら、どんな席でもかまわない。
If I can get concert tickets, any seat is fine.
2. 「待ち合わせは何時にしますか」「何時でもいいですよ」。

232.name: Question word＋～ても

examples.jp: どんなに時間がかかっても、見つけるつもりです。
examples.tr: No matter how long it takes, I intend to find it.

examples.jp: 何が起きても、もうおどろきません。
examples.tr: Whatever happens, nothing will surprise me anymore.

232.explain: ◎ Even if the situation changes, the conclusion does not change.

233.meaning: Used to give permission to someone or make someone do an action. Not used toward friends or superiors. Usually used toward subordinates. It also expresses cause and result.

examples.jp: 買いに行かせる
examples.tr: make someone go and buy something

examples.jp: 山田先輩は田中さんにビールを買いに行かせた。
examples.tr: Yamada-senpai made Tanaka go and buy beer.

examples.jp: お酒が飲めない人に、無理にお酒を飲ませてはいけません。
examples.tr: You must not force people who can't drink to drink alcohol.

examples.jp: 急に国に帰って、母をびっくりさせた。
examples.tr: I suddenly went back to my home country and surprised my mother.

examples.jp: アメリカの経済の悪化が、世界の経済を混乱させた。
examples.tr: The worsening of the American economy threw the world economy into turmoil.

examples.jp: 社長は、その仕事を田中さんにやらせた。
examples.tr: The company president had Tanaka do that job.

233.explain: ◎ 「～（さ）せる」is a sentence pattern that expresses acting on another person to force them, or to bring about some state or result.

rows: <ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>が<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めさせる
<ruby>上司<rt>じょうし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>残業<rt>ざんぎょう</rt></ruby>させられる

mistakes: Wrong particle for the person made to act: using を instead of に. Correct: 先生は学生に発表させた.
Confusing the nuance: whether “させる=permission” or “forcing” must be judged from context; exams test this inference.
Wrong form of 来る: it is “来させる(こさせる)”, not “来らせる”.
Mixing up the double objects: 私は息子に宿題をさせる (correct); changing the order easily causes confusion.
233.notes:
meaning_vi: Make / have … do …
explain: “Forcing” vs “permission” depends on the context, the accompanying words (許可・命令) and the nuance of the verb.
In polite/humble speech, the speaker uses “Vさせていただく/もらう” to ask for or receive permission to do something.
With verbs of motion (行く/帰る), the person made to act usually takes に:子どもに行かせる.
Expressing causing an emotion: Aを驚かせる／喜ばせる (surprise A / make A happy).
examples: 1. 先生は学生にスピーチをさせた。
The teacher made/let the students give a speech.
2. 部長は私を先に帰らせてくれた。
The department manager let me go home first.
3. 親は子どもに自分で決めさせるべきだ。
Parents should let their children decide for themselves.
4. その映画は多くの人を泣かせた。
That movie made many people cry.
5. 少し考えさせてください。
Please let me think about it for a bit.

234.meaning: Is doing, has done (state) | expresses habit | Doing…, repetition, state

examples.jp: ゴッホもまた、パリの風景を描いている。
examples.tr: Van Gogh, too, painted scenes of Paris.

examples.jp: こちらのお寺は、14世紀末に建てられましたが、1952年に火事で焼けて、その後、建て直されています。
examples.tr: This temple was built at the end of the 14th century, but it burned down in a fire in 1952 and was later rebuilt.

examples.jp: 彼は今、資料を読んでいる。
examples.tr: He is reading documents now.

examples.jp: 私は田中さんを知っている。
examples.tr: I know Mr. Tanaka.

examples.jp: 彼女は大阪に住んでいる。
examples.tr: She lives in Osaka.

examples.jp: 窓が開いている。
examples.tr: The window is open.

234.explain:
Be careful to distinguish “doing” from “being in a state”:開けている (is opening it) vs開いている (is already open).
With punctual verbs (know, understand), 〜ている = state:知っている＝know;分かっている＝already understand.
Shortened spoken forms: 〜てる／〜てます are used a lot in casual/polite conversation.
To express one's occupation or current habits, 〜ている is more natural than the simple present tense.

• Progressive: an action in progress. 例：今、昼ご飯を食べている。
• Resultant state (punctual verbs): 結婚している（is married, in the state of being married）, 知っている（know）.
• Habit/repetition: 毎朝走っている（I run every morning）.
• State of existence/location: 東京に住んでいる, 電車に乗っている.
• With intransitive verbs of change: ドアが開いている（the door is open) → the state after opening.

rows: Resultant state intentionally brought about by someone
A preparatory action, not a state
Point in time of an action
<ruby>直前<rt>ちょくぜん</rt></ruby>/<ruby>最中<rt>さいちゅう</rt></ruby>/<ruby>直後<rt>ちょくご</rt></ruby>: Vる/ている/たところだ
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べているところだ。
Does not emphasize a continuing state

mistakes: Confusing 〜ている with 〜てある: 花が飾ってある（someone has decorated with them in advance）≠ 花が飾っている（rarely used, easy to get wrong).
Machine translation “am knowing”: 知っている does not mean “am knowing” but “know”.
Using 〜ている with punctual verbs such as 死ぬ, 着く… usually does not give the progressive meaning (着いている = has arrived and is there).
234.notes:
• “行っている/来ている” has two meanings: the state of being there (went and is there now) or a habit. Example: その店によく行っている（habit）／田中さんは今、出張に行っている（is currently away on a business trip）.
• Shortened spoken forms: している → してる, していない → してない. In formal language, avoid contractions.
• Combined with progression: ～てきている（gradually …）, ～ていく／～てくる with a nuance of time direction/viewpoint.

examples.jp: 雨がふったので、旅行は中止になってしまいました。
examples.tr: Because it rained, our trip ended up being canceled.

examples.jp: 早く買わないと、なくなってしまいますよ。
examples.tr: If you don't buy it soon, it'll be gone.

examples.jp: この本はおもしろかったから、１日で読んでしまいました。
examples.tr: This book was so interesting that I read it all in one day.

examples.jp: 「作文、もう書いた？」「うん、書いてしまったよ」
examples.tr: 「Have you written your essay yet?」「Yeah, I've finished it.」

examples.jp: 「８時のバスはもう出ましたか」「ええ、もう出てしまいましたよ」
examples.tr: 「Has the 8 o'clock bus already left?」「Yes, it's already gone.」

examples.jp: 今日は10キロ以上歩いたので疲れてしまった。
examples.tr: I walked more than 10 km today, so I'm worn out.

235.explain:
To sound “lighter” in conversation, use ちゃう／じゃう; in formal speech, use しまう.
Adding adverbs creates nuance: うっかり／つい／いつの間にか + ～てしまう.
When narrating consequences: ～てしまって… and then state the bad or awkward result.

There are 3 meanings:
1.Expresses that you are doing something and intend to finish it.
A:昼(ひる)ごはんを食(た)べに行(い)きませんか。
A: Shall we go get lunch?
B: すみません。今(いま)これを　コピーしてしまいますから。
B: Sorry, I'm going to finish copying this now.
2.Expresses that something has finally been done and completed.
A：先週(せんしゅう)貸(か)した本(ほん)は　もう読(よ)みましたか。
A: Have you finished reading the book I lent you last week?
B: はい、全部(ぜんぶ)読(よ)んで　しまいました。
B: Yes, I've read the whole thing.
3.Expresses the speaker's embarrassment or regret about something that happened.
A: どう　したんですか。
A: What happened?
B:指(ゆび)を切(き)って　しまったんです。
B: I accidentally cut my finger.
A: どう　したんですか。
A: What happened?
B: どこかで　さいふを　なくして　しまいました。
B: I lost my wallet somewhere.

rows: <ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わる。
Colloquial form of てしまう

mistakes: Assuming it is negative by default: incorrect; it can simply mean “finish doing completely”.
Wrong contraction: ～で→じゃう, not ちゃう (例: 閉めて→閉めちゃう; 出して→出しちゃう; 読んで→読んじゃう).
Confusing it with ～終わる and ～きる in questions that ask you to choose the nuance of completion.
235.notes:
• しまった can stand alone as an exclamation; no preceding verb is needed.
• When describing an undesirable habit, ～てしまいがち (tendency) can be used.
• With もう, the nuance of completion is strong: もう食べてしまった（have already eaten it all).

examples.jp: べんきょうしなさい。
examples.tr: Study.

examples.jp: 食べなさい
examples.tr: Eat.

examples.jp: 静かにしなさい。
examples.tr: Be quiet.

examples.jp: ここに名前を書きなさい。
examples.tr: Write your name here.

examples.jp: 危ないから手をつないで歩きなさい。
examples.tr: It's dangerous, so hold hands while you walk.

examples.jp: 早くお風呂に入りなさい。
examples.tr: Hurry up and take your bath.

236.explain:
Mild emphasis/pressure: used when an action is needed right away, especially in safety situations.
Can be softened with よ/ね:片付け なさいね。/早く寝 なさいよ。
Instructional texts: ～しなさい was often replaced by ～しなさいこと in older books; nowadays ～こと/～こと is commonly used。
Combined with an indirect prohibitive adverb: もうそれ以上言わ ないで、早く謝り なさい。

• A directive command or reminder addressed to subordinates or people close to you (children, students, subordinates).
• The nuance is stronger than ～てください (asking/request), but softer than 命令形（～しろ／～しなさい＜～しろ）.
• Often used in education, in announcing rules, or when emphasizing something that "should be done right away".
• Not used with superiors/customers; use ～てください／ご～ください instead。

rows: <ruby>命令<rt>めいれい</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby>（～しろ／～こい）
Very strong/rough, mostly male speech only, rough spoken language
Not a direct command; expresses a general judgment
もっと<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>すべきだ。
Written regulations; not used in face-to-face conversation
<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>金曜<rt>きんよう</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>うこと。

mistakes: Wrong form: × 書くなさい → ○ 書きなさい（drop ます).
Using it with superiors is rude; choose ～てください／ご覧ください…
Confusion with prohibition: "～な" is a prohibition, not ～なさい.
Pronunciation of 来なさい: きなさい, not こなさい.
Overuse makes the sentence sound harsh; avoid it in customer service.
236.notes:
• Colloquial contracted form: しな／やりな（with a casual nuance).
• "～なさいませ" appears in old-fashioned retail service language: ご利用なさいませ（very polite, old style).
• Combining with prohibition: ～てはいけません／～ないでください to prohibit, and ～なさい to indicate what should be done.

examples.jp: 飲み物は用意しているので、買わなくてもいいです。〈動詞ない形 ＋〉
examples.tr: Drinks have been prepared, so you don't have to buy any.〈動詞ない形 ＋〉

examples.jp: １日泊まるだけなので、部屋は広くなくてもいいです。〈Aく ＋〉
examples.tr: I'm only staying one night, so the room doesn't have to be large.〈Aく ＋〉

examples.jp: きれいでなくてもいいので、タオルを貸してください。〈Naな ＋ で〉
examples.tr: It doesn't have to be clean, so please lend me a towel.〈Naな ＋ で〉

examples.jp: 心配しなくてもいいよ。
examples.tr: You don't need to worry.

examples.jp: 今日は無理に来なくてもいいです。
examples.tr: You don't have to force yourself to come today.

examples.jp: このイベントは会員でなくてもいい。
examples.tr: You don't have to be a member for this event.

237.explain:
Polite: ～なくても いいです ／～なくても かまいません .
Gentle; reassures or relaxes a requirement.
With A/N: expresses a minimum standard that does not need to be met.
To emphasize "should not": use ～ないほうがいい instead of ～なくてもいい.

• Gives permission not to do an action or have a quality / does not require it: "you don't have to ...".
• Reduces the burden and presents an option; it does not completely negate doing the action.
• Practical opposite of ～なくてはいけない／～なければならない.
• Often used in instructions, soft rules, and customer service.

rows: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくてはいけない。
<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>する<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない。
<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しなくてもかまいません。
<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby><ruby>更<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>かししないほうがいい。

mistakes: Forgetting "で" with N/na: ×会員なくてもいい → 〇会員でなくてもいい.
Confusion with "should not": ×行かなくてもいい（when you mean "you shouldn't go"）→ 〇行かないほうがいい.
Wrong level of politeness: with customers use ～なくてもかまいません instead of ～なくてもいいよ.
In exams, a double-negative trap: "必ずしも～なくてもいい" = "you don't necessarily have to ...".
237.notes:
• Past form/hypothetical: 来なくてもよかった（didn't need to come). Easily confused with the regret expression ～ばよかった.
• Polite double negative: ～なくてもよろしい（very polite, used in written notices).
• Emphasizing the option: ～ても～なくてもいい（Either doing it or not doing it is fine）.

examples.jp: 彼より彼女のほうが話が上手です。
examples.tr: She is a better talker than he is.

examples.tr: Walking is better than going by bus.

238.explain: ◎ A sentence pattern that compares two things to show which one is superior or inferior.
238.notes:
meaning_vi: Used to compare two things or matters, where one (noun ②) exceeds the other (noun ①) in degree: (noun ②) > (noun ①). Usually not used in negative sentences.
examples: 1. ①私より弟のほうが背が高いです。
My younger brother is taller than me.
2. ②前のテキストのほうがこのテキストよりよかったです。
The previous textbook was better than this textbook.
3. ③私はご飯よりパンのほうをよく食べます。
I eat bread more often than rice.

examples.jp: 授業のあとで、先生に質問します。
examples.tr: After class, I'll ask the teacher a question.

examples.jp: 昼ごはんを食べたあとで、散歩しました。
examples.tr: After eating lunch, I took a walk.

examples.jp: 仕事のあとで、一杯飲みに行きませんか。
examples.tr: Would you like to go for a drink after work?

examples.jp: このあとで会議があります。
examples.tr: There is a meeting after this.

examples.jp: 雨のあとで、空気がきれいになります。
examples.tr: After the rain, the air becomes clean.

examples.jp: 手を洗ったあとで、料理を始めてください。
examples.tr: Please start cooking after you have washed your hands.

239.explain:
In spoken language "あとで" is common; in written language "あとに/後に" can be used.
"で" emphasizes the setting in time in which B happens "after A"; "に" emphasizes the point in time.
Do not use ～のあとで with a specific clock time: use 3時以降／3時のちに（formal）/3時過ぎに instead.
Natural order: A finishes safely and then B happens; suited to actions that need preparation beforehand.

Expresses that action B happens after A has been completed: A の/た あとで、B。
There may or may not be a time gap between A and B; it does not have to be "right after".
Difference from ～てから: ～てから often suggests "right after / do it and then immediately".
With numerical time expressions (3時,三日,三時間): use ～後（ご）/ ～以降 instead of ～のあとで.

rows: After V (then immediately / as a basis)
Used with quantities: <ruby>三日<rt>みっか</rt></ruby><ruby>後<rt>ご</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Wrong tense: ×食べるあとで → ✓食べたあとで.
Using it with a clock time: ×3時のあとで会いましょう → ✓3時以降に会いましょう.
Confusion with ～てから: when "right after" is required, choose ～てから, not ～たあとで.
A noun that is not an event: ×机のあとで掃除する → ✓掃除のあとで休む／机を片付けてから休む.
239.notes:
"あとで" on its own = "later / in a while": あとで電話します。
"直後（ちょくご）" = "right after":試合の直後にインタビューがあった。
"のちに" (後に・のちに) formal/literary:彼はのちに大統領となる。

examples.jp: 明日は雨かしら。
examples.tr: I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: この服、彼に似合うかしら。
examples.tr: I wonder if these clothes will suit him.

examples.jp: 時間に間に合うかしら。
examples.tr: I wonder if we'll make it in time.

examples.jp: どうしたらいいかしら。
examples.tr: I wonder what I should do.

examples.jp: 本当に大丈夫なのかしら。
examples.tr: I wonder if it's really all right.

240.explain:
Feminine, gentle nuance; men usually use かな/かなあ.
Used in casual, everyday conversation; in work or formal exchanges use でしょうか/かどうか.
Add ね to soften it: ～かしらね; add のかしら for a nuance of explaining/emphasizing the reason behind the conjecture.

• A sentence-final particle meaning "I wonder…"; often used by women; similar to かな (neutral/used more by men).
• Expresses gentle reflection without requiring a direct answer; used when talking to yourself or when asking for someone's opinion in an indirect way.
• The intonation usually rises at the end of the sentence when it is a real question: ～かしら↑
• In polite speech, use ～でしょうか（ね） instead of ～ですかしら to avoid sounding stylistically off.

rows: <ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>だろうか
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>でしょうか

mistakes: × 本当ですかしら → ○ 本当かしら／本当でしょうか.
Using it with superiors/customers: avoid ～かしら and choose でしょうか.
Men who use it too much sound stylistically off; use かな instead.
240.notes:
• In polite letters, replace it with でしょうか／お伺いできますでしょうか to suit the style.
• Polite expressions like "～してもよろしいかしら" exist in the speech of middle-aged and older women.
• Archaic form: ～かしらん (literary, playful/old-fashioned).

241.meaning: A casual way of expressing that you are wondering to yourself. ③ expresses hesitation about what to do.; I hope… (in the form ～ないかな(あ))
241.connection: V/A plain form + かな(あ) / N/Na + かな(あ)

examples.jp: 入れるかな
examples.tr: I wonder if I can get in.

examples.jp: 明日は晴れるかなあ。
examples.tr: I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.

examples.jp: 行こうかな。どうしよかな。
examples.tr: Maybe I'll go. What should I do?

examples.jp: なんか、おもしろいことないかなあ。
examples.tr: I wish something interesting would happen.

examples.jp: あしたのパーティー、行こうかなあ、やめようかな、どうしようかな
examples.tr: Tomorrow's party... should I go, or skip it? What should I do?

examples.jp: 「この問題、ちょっと難しいけど、できるかな」「できるよ、きっと」
examples.tr: "This problem is a bit hard, but I wonder if I can do it." "You can, I'm sure."

241.explain:
Used at the end of a sentence with a light, rising-and-falling tone; usually when talking to yourself or to people close to you.
Not used to question someone directly; for a polite question use ～でしょうか／ますか.
Traditionally women used かしら; nowadays かなあ is used by both men and women, and かな (without あ) is more neutral.
かなあ is usually preceded by the plain form; です／ます + かなあ exists but is slightly formal and not very natural in written language.

rows: <ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>かしら。
<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いだろうか。

mistakes: Using かなあ to ask a stranger directly → not polite enough. Use ～でしょうか／ますか instead.
Wrong polite form: ×静かだかなあ → 〇静かかなあ (colloquial).
Confusion with a question using か: かなあ needs no "?" and does not require an answer.
JLPT: distinguish かなあ (spoken language) from だろうか (written language) and かしら (feminine nuance).
241.notes:
meaning_vi: I wonder…, probably…
examples: 1. 明日、晴れるかなあ。
I wonder if it'll be sunny tomorrow.
2. 彼、来てくれるかなあ。
I wonder if he'll come.
3. 日本語、もっと上手に話せるかなあ。
I wonder if I'll be able to speak Japanese better.
4. この問題、間に合うかなあ。
I wonder if I'll finish this problem in time.
5. 値段、もう少し安くならないかなあ。
I wish the price would come down a little more.
6. 大丈夫かなあ…。
I wonder if it's all right… meaning_vi: Won't it…?, I hope…, will it… or not? ⏐ explain: Used to express your own hope, or your own doubt about some matter
It mostly implies worry or unease about what is happening ⏐ examples: 1. バス、早く来ないかなあ。
I wish the bus would come soon.
2. この実験、うまくいくかな。
I wonder if this experiment will go well.
3. 今日、富士山が見えるかなあ。
I wonder if we'll be able to see Mt. Fuji today.

examples.jp: 夕方、雨が降るかもしれません。
examples.tr: It might rain this evening.

examples.jp: 彼が言っていることは正しいかもしれない。
examples.tr: What he's saying might be right.

examples.jp: よく練習したので強くなった。あしたの試合は勝てるかもしれない。
examples.tr: We practiced hard, so we've gotten stronger. We might be able to win tomorrow's match.

examples.jp: 「来週はひまですか」
examples.tr: "Are you free next week?"

examples.jp: 「アリさん、まだ来ませんね。遅いですね。」
examples.tr: "Ali still hasn't come, has he? He's late."

examples.jp: 頭が痛い。きのう、あまり寝ていないからかもしれない。
examples.tr: I have a headache. It might be because I didn't sleep much last night.

242.explain:
A reserved nuance that avoids asserting; suitable when you want to be polite/not impose.
In reports/academic writing, it can be replaced with 可能性がある (formal).
Degree of certainty: に違いない ＞ だろう／でしょう ＞ かもしれない.

• Expresses a judgment about possibility, with lower certainty than だろう／でしょう.
• Often combined with adverbs: もしかすると／もしかしたら／ひょっとすると to emphasize "who knows".
• The past is used to make a conjecture about something that already happened: 行ったかもしれない／学生だったかもしれない.

rows: <ruby>本物<rt>ほんもの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない

mistakes: × 学生ですかもしれない → ○ 学生かもしれない.
な形容詞 in the present does not take だ: × 静かだかもしれない → ○ 静かかもしれない.
Forgetting "だった" in the past: × 学生だかもしれなかった → ○ 学生だったかもしれない.
242.notes:
• Spelling: かも知れない (kanji) is also correct; it is usually written かもしれない (hiragana).
• Not used directly before a command/order; if needed, change it to a mild recommendation.
• Adding たぶん tends to be redundant; it is more natural with もしかしたら/ひょっとすると.

243.meaning: whether or not (+ verb, + i-adjective / na-adjective)

examples.jp: 席が空いているか、わかりません。
examples.tr: I don't know whether there are any free seats.

examples.tr: Please ask whether they have other colors.

examples.tr: I haven't decided where to go yet.

examples.jp: いつ退院できるか、はっきりしません。
examples.tr: It's not clear when I'll be able to leave the hospital.

243.explain:
◎ The adverbial particle「か」 placed at the end of a sentence indicates that something is unclear. In this structure, the「ということが」or「ちうことを」that would originally follow「か」is dropped.
◎ Often used with questions.
