examples.jp: 明日はよていがあって、行けません。
examples.tr: I have plans tomorrow, so I can't go.

examples.jp: ここにおくと、なくなるしんぱいがあります。
examples.tr: If you leave it here, there's a risk it'll get lost.

245.explain: ◎ 「ある」expresses possession, like「持っている」. Besides concrete objects, it can be used with abstract things or things with a psychological meaning.

examples.jp: もう一度説明させてください。
examples.tr: Please let me explain once more.

examples.jp: 少し休ませてください。
examples.tr: Please let me rest for a bit.

examples.jp: 先に帰らせてください。
examples.tr: Please let me go home first.

examples.jp: 写真を撮らせてください。
examples.tr: Please let me take a photo.

examples.jp: 今日は欠席させてください。
examples.tr: Please allow me to be absent today.

examples.jp: この件について発言させていただけますか。
examples.tr: Would you allow me to speak on this matter?

248.explain:
Formal: ～させていただけますか／～させていただきたいです。
Casual: ～させて（もらって）／～させてね（within your own group).
In business: as a humble announcement, "ご連絡 させていただきます "。
Avoid using it with来る: "来させてください" sounds awkward; people usually say "伺わせてください／行かせてください".

• Asks the listener for permission for the speaker to do an action: "let me …/please allow me to …".
• Emphasizes the speaker's volition/intention more than ～てもいいですか (which only asks whether it is allowed).
• The nuance can be somewhat strong/imposing; in formal contexts use ～させていただけますか to soften it.
• Used for actions the speaker does themselves; not used to "ask someone else to do something".

rows: <ruby>発言<rt>はつげん</rt></ruby>させてください。
<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>を<ruby>外<rt>はず</rt></ruby>させてもらえますか。
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>させていただけますか。
ここに<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>ってもいいですか。
Asks the listener to do it
<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ってください。

mistakes: Using it to ask someone else to do something: ×説明させてください＝please explain to me → wrong meaning; this pattern means "let me explain".
Wrong causative: ×見らせてください → ✓見させてください；×行きさせて → ✓行かせてください。
Too direct with superiors/customers: switch to ～させていただけますか.
The JLPT often asks you to distinguish it from ～てもいいですか (neutral permission) and ～てください (request).
248.notes:
• "～させていただく" should be used when: there is permission, it benefits the listener, or the speaker is grateful; avoid overusing it for no reason.
• Combines with keigo nouns: ご挨拶／ご連絡／ご報告＋させていただく.
• Negative causative asking permission: ～させないでください（please don't make/let me do it; please let me not do it） is rare; consider the context carefully.
meaning_vi: asking for permission.
examples: 1. 「疲れたので、少し休ませてください」
「I'm tired, so please let me rest for a bit.」
2. 「そのゲーム、おもしろそうね。わたしにもやらせて」
「That game looks fun. Let me play too.」
3. 「いつもごちそうになっているので、たまにはわたしに払わせてください」
「You always treat me, so please let me pay once in a while.」
meaning_vi: Could you let me ~?
explain: Used to ask the other person for permission to do something yourself.
They all mean the same thing, but the level of politeness differs. Specifically:
Vさせて　ください　＜　Vさせて　もらえます　＜　Vさせて　もらえませんか。
See also: review how to conjugate verbs in the causative form (使役形）：See
examples: 1. ちょっと気分が悪いので、早く帰らせてください。
I'm not feeling very well, so please let me go home early.
2. あなたの会社のお話を聞かせてください。
Please tell me about your company.
3. 手を洗わせてください。
Please let me wash my hands.

249.connection: V causative form + られる / くる + こさせられる / やる + やらせられる

examples.jp: 子どものころ、嫌いな野菜を無理やり食べさせられた。
examples.tr: When I was a child, I was forced to eat vegetables I didn't like.

examples.jp: 上司に休日出勤を頼まれて、結局働かされることになった。
examples.tr: My boss asked me to come in on my day off, and I ended up being made to work.

examples.jp: この映画は社会問題について考えさせられる。
examples.tr: This movie makes you think about social issues.

examples.jp: 事故の影響で遠回りさせられて、到着が遅れた。
examples.tr: Because of the accident, we were made to take a detour and arrived late.

examples.jp: 彼の失敗談にはつい笑わされる。
examples.tr: His stories about his failures always make me laugh.

249.explain:
Passive + forced nuance: usually comes with feelings of displeasure, annoyance, or reluctance.
In written/argumentative language, 〜させられる can be used abstractly (状況に〜させられる), weakening the nuance of "someone forces you" and emphasizing "the circumstances make you".
The contracted form -される of五段 verbs is natural in conversation:行かされる,書かされる,待たされる (from待たせられる).

• 〜させられる: "be made/forced to do…"; the subject feels reluctant/unwilling.
• Common formula: Nは/が Nに Vさせられる (be made to do V by N).
• With 五段 verbs: the contracted form 〜される (行かされる, 書かされる, 読まされる) is very common in spoken language; the full form 〜せられる is more formal.
• Some fixed expressions mean "make you think/feel": 考えさせられる, 感心させられる, 驚かされる (from 驚く).

rows: Does not mean "be forced to do"
The subject is the one who causes the action
Have someone do something for you
No sense of being forced by someone

mistakes: Confusing 五段 forms: 書く → 書かされる (colloquial) / 書かせられる (formal). Avoid "書きさせられる" (incorrect).
Missing the agent marker に: "上司に残業させられた" (correct); dropping に can make it ambiguous.
Confusing the meaning with 〜なければならない: "行かなければならない" is obligation, without the nuance of "being forced by someone" that "行かされる" has.
The JLPT often asks about the easily confused pair 考えさせられる vs 考えられる (ability/inference). Distinguish them by context.
249.notes:
• 待たされる is the established form in practice (considered more natural than 待たせられる).
• Emotion verbs often use the form 〜させられる/〜される to say "made to feel": 考えさせられる, 驚かされる, 感動させられる.
• Avoid repeating a long subject: compared with Aさんに私は行かされるより, "私はAさんに…" is more concise.
meaning_vi: Be made to do something => Can't help (feeling)~
explain: ◎ The「られる」 part of the passive is attached after the「させる」 of the causative pattern. 「びっくりさせられる」(be made to jump in surprise) expresses the same event as 「びっくりする」(be surprised), but adding「～させられる」adds a feeling of unexpected, involuntary surprise.
examples: 1. 青木さんのまじめなことには、みんな感心させられている。
Everyone can't help admiring how hardworking Mr. Aoki is.
2. 山の上から見た景色の美しさには、感動させられました。
I couldn't help being moved by the beauty of the view from the top of the mountain.

examples.jp: 作品を通してしか、彼のことを知ることができない。
examples.tr: I can only get to know him through his works.

examples.jp: 時間もないし、彼に頼むしか方法がない。
examples.tr: There's no time, so the only option is to ask him.

examples.jp: お金が100円しか残っていない。
examples.tr: Only 100 yen is left.

examples.jp: ここでしか買えない限定商品だ。
examples.tr: It's a limited-edition item you can only buy here.

examples.jp: 今日は時間がないから、コンビニでしか食べられない。
examples.tr: I don't have time today, so I can only eat at a convenience store.

examples.jp: 彼しか知っていない秘密だ。
examples.tr: It's a secret that only he knows.

250.explain:
しか comes after a noun/quantity/pronoun indicating a place, and before a negative verb.
Keep the relational particles before しか when needed:日本 でしか 見られ ない ,今日 までにしか でき ない .
Different from だけ: だけ is neutral, while しか has the nuance of “there is nothing else”.
V-辞書形+ しかない expresses reluctance.

• Limitation of scope: “only … and not … (there is nothing else)”.
• Stronger nuance than だけ: しか emphasizes a sense of lack/dissatisfaction.
• V-辞書形 + しかない has the idiomatic meaning “the only option is to …”.
• Must be used with the negative form (ない/ありません/できない…), not with the affirmative.

rows: Expresses an equivalent meaning with a different structure.
ほかに<ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>がない。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>ほかに<ruby>頼<rt>たよ</rt></ruby>れる<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>はない。
Have no choice but to / cannot help but
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>延期<rt>えんき</rt></ruby>せざるを<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>ない。

mistakes: Using the affirmative with しか: 水しか飲む（wrong）→ 水しか飲まない.
Wrong particle position: 水をしか飲まない（extra を）→ 水しか飲まない.
Confusing it with “だれも～ない”: “だれしか～ない” is not used; the correct forms are だれもいない／彼しかいない.
Forgetting to keep the relational particle: ここしか買えない（ambiguous）→ ここでしか買えない.
250.notes:
• The subject is often omitted in conversation: これしかない（this is all there is）.
• With people/animals: ～しかいない is used very naturally: 会場にはスタッフしかいない。
• Emphasize the limitation with “たった/わずか + 数量 + しか + ない”.

251.connection: V/A plain form + し / N・Na + だし

examples.jp: 遠いし、にもつも重かったので、つかれました。
examples.tr: It was far, and my luggage was heavy too, so I got tired.

examples.jp: ゆうべは、暑いし、となりもうるさくて、よくねむれませんでした。
examples.tr: Last night it was hot, and the neighbors were noisy too, so I couldn't sleep well.

251.explain: ◎ 「し」, as used in「忙しいですし」or「お金もありません」, is used when stating one after another several things of the same kind.

rows: <ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>な<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い
<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>たりする

mistakes: Dropping だ with な形容詞/N: ×便利し → 便利だし.
Confusing it with ～て for giving reasons. The JLPT often requires choosing し when “multiple reasons” are needed.
Ending with し in formal written language can lack coherence if there is no clear conclusion.
251.notes:
meaning_vi: Both… and…, and also…
explain: When persuading/giving reasons, put the strongest element at the end of the chain to lead to the conclusion.
In formal writing, the last one can be replaced with ～上に／さらに for better flow.
Avoid overusing し clauses in one long sentence.
examples: 1. このアプリは無料だし、使いやすいし、おすすめです。
This app is free and easy to use, so I recommend it.
2. 駅に近いし、静かだし、ここに住みたい。
It's close to the station and quiet, so I want to live here.
3. 今日は雨だし、寒いし、家にいよう。
It's raining today, and it's cold too, so let's stay home.
4. 時間もないし…また今度。
There's no time anyway… next time, then.

examples.jp: この歌は聞いたことがあります。
examples.tr: I've heard this song before.

examples.jp: 富士山に登ったことがありますか。
examples.tr: Have you ever climbed Mt. Fuji?

examples.jp: わたしは高校生のとき、１年間アメリカで勉強したことがあります。
examples.tr: When I was in high school, I studied in America for a year.

examples.jp: 「この歌を知っていますか」「はい、前に一度聞いたことがあります」
examples.tr: “Do you know this song?” “Yes, I've heard it once before.”

examples.jp: わたしはまだ一度も雪を見たことがありません。
examples.tr: I have never seen snow, not even once.

examples.jp: 富士山に登ったことがある？
examples.tr: Have you ever climbed Mt. Fuji?

252.explain:
Often used with words indicating the number of times:一度／何回も／数回／一回も…ない to make clear how often the experience happened.
Polite form: 〜たことが あります ／〜たことが ありません .
When asking about experience: 〜たことが ありますか ？ is the polite, neutral pattern.

• Vたことがある expresses a past experience without a specific point in time, focusing on “whether one has ever done it or not”.
• Negative: Vたことがない = has never had that experience at all.
• Not used with very specific events/clear points in time (昨日/先週…), because that contradicts its “non-specific time” nature.
• Different from plain Vた: Vた tells of something that happened once (a time may be given); Vたことがある emphasizes the experience of having done it.

rows: <ruby>寿司<rt>すし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べたことがある
Can be tied to a specific point in time
<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>寿司<rt>すし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べた
<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>経験<rt>けいけん</rt></ruby>がある

mistakes: Attaching a specific point in time: “昨日富士山に登ったことがある” (unnatural) → “昨日登った” or “富士山に登ったことがある”.
Confusing it with habit: “よく行く” ≠ “行ったことがある”. One is frequent, the other is an experience one has had.
Dropping こと is inappropriate in formal written language: “食べたことある” is colloquial; the JLPT requires the full form.
Incorrect double negative: “一度も行ったことありません” (correct), not “一度も行ったことないです” in standard exam language (keep the level of politeness consistent).
252.notes:
• Adding a broad time frame is still fine: 子どものころに、海外へ行ったことがある (childhood, not a specific point in time).
• With もう/まだ: もう行ったことがあります (have already been)／まだ行ったことがありません (have still never been).
• In natural conversation, ことが is often omitted: 食べたことある？ (colloquial).

examples.jp: 明日は朝早いから、もう寝たほうがいいですよ。
examples.tr: You have to get up early tomorrow morning, so you'd better go to bed now.

examples.jp: 寝る前はあまり食べないほうがいいです。
examples.tr: It's better not to eat much before going to bed.

examples.jp: 頭が痛いなら、今日は早く寝たほうがいいよ。
examples.tr: If you have a headache, you'd better go to bed early today.

examples.jp: その件は、上司に相談したほうがいいと思う。
examples.tr: I think you should talk to your boss about that matter.

examples.jp: 無理して働かないほうがいいです。
examples.tr: It's better not to push yourself too hard at work.

examples.jp: 英語と日本語なら、日本語で書くほうがいい。
examples.tr: Between English and Japanese, it's better to write in Japanese.

253.explain:
Advice of a moderate degree, friendly; in polite contexts, ～ほうがよい/よろしいです can be used.
Avoid using it directly with superiors/customers unless asked; replace it with a soft suggestion: ～てはいかがでしょうか, ～たらいかがですか.
Not used for strict rules/norms (use ～べきだ/～ねばならない).

• Gives advice or a recommendation that is personal/based on experience.
• Affirmative: V-たほうがいい; Negative: V-ないほうがいい (more common than V-なかったほうがいい).
• V-るほうがいい is used for an objective comparison of two options, not necessarily direct advice.
• Strength: ～たほうがいい < ～べきだ (strong, normative) / softer: ～たらどう/～たらいい.
• Usually used in the present tense; the implied subject is “you/I/we”.

rows: <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>めに<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったほうがいい。
<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby><ruby>更<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>かししないほうがいい。
<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったらどう？
<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>より<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くほうがいい。
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るべきだ。

mistakes: Using V-るほうがいい as general advice → for positive advice, prefer V-たほうがいい.
Using it with a subject that does not fit the social context (speaking directly to a superior) → not polite enough.
Confusing it with ～べきだ: when the question calls for a soft recommendation, choose ～たほうがいい.
253.notes:
• In conversation, add よ/ね/よね to adjust the degree of familiarity and certainty.
• Avoid V-なかったほうがいい (unnatural); use V-ないほうがいい.
• With nouns/choices, use ～にしたほうがいい to recommend a choice: Aにしたほうがいい。

examples.jp: 健康のために、毎日走っています。
examples.tr: I run every day for my health.

examples.jp: 将来医者になるために、いっしょうけんめい勉強しています。
examples.tr: I'm studying hard so that I can become a doctor in the future.

examples.jp: 漢字がなかなか覚えられません。それで、覚えるために何回も書いて練習しています。
examples.tr: I just can't memorize kanji. So, to memorize them, I'm practicing by writing them over and over.

examples.jp: 父は家族のためにいっしょけんめい仕事をしています。
examples.tr: My father works hard for our family.

examples.jp: これは日本語を勉強する人のための辞書です。
examples.tr: This is a dictionary for people who study Japanese.

examples.jp: わたしは会社のために、働きたくありません。自分のために働きます。
examples.tr: I don't want to work for the company. I work for myself.

254.notes:
Note:
「ために」の前に,可能形、ナイ形など使えない。
The potential form or the ない-form of a verb cannot be used before 「ために」。
1.  X日本語が話せるために、毎日練習します。　→日本語が話せるように～
X To be able to speak Japanese, I practice every day. → To be able to speak Japanese…
2.  X　かぜをひかないために、注意してください。　→　かぜをひかないように～(→　N3)
X To not catch a cold, please be careful. → To not catch a cold…
◎ A sentence pattern expressing cause or reason. Used with the plain form of verbs and「N＋の」.
1. かぜを 引いたため、昨日は 休みました。
I caught a cold, so I took yesterday off.
2. 大雪の ため、電車が 止まって います。
The trains have stopped because of heavy snow.
More formal than ので/から when stating a cause; often used in announcements, signs, and the news.
For purpose, it is more formal than ～ように; suitable when the verb is volitional and there is a specific goal.
Do not use ために (purpose) with non-volitional/potential verbs such as分かる、見える、起きる… (switch to ～ように).
1. A:　なんの　ために　貯金していますか。
B:　将来　自分の店を　持つために、貯金しています。
A: What are you saving money for?
B: I'm saving money so that I can have a shop of my own in the future.
2. A:　健康の　ために、　何か　していますか。
B:　いいえ。でも、来週から　毎朝　走ろうと。
A：Do you do anything for your health?
B: No. But starting next week, I'm planning to go running every morning.
3. 家族の　ために、うちを　建てます。
I'm going to build a house for my family.
──────
1. 日本に留学するために、日本語を勉強している。
I'm stud

255.meaning: Should V ~ | It would be good if…

examples.jp: 疲れているなら、少し休んだらいいですよ。
examples.tr: If you're tired, you should rest a little.

examples.jp: 日本で働けたらいいな。
examples.tr: I wish I could work in Japan.

examples.jp: この問題はどうしたらいいですか。
examples.tr: What should I do about this problem?

examples.jp: 雨がやんだらいいのに。
examples.tr: I wish the rain would stop.

examples.jp: 時間があったらいいですね。
examples.tr: It would be nice if we had time, wouldn't it?

examples.jp: もっと早く相談したらよかったね。
examples.tr: We should have asked for advice sooner, shouldn't we?

255.explain:
Gives light, polite advice: Vたらいいですよ／と思います。
For wishes, add な(あ)/のに to heighten the emotion:会えたらいいな／雨ならやんだらいいのに。
Asking for an opinion: どうしたらいいですか／いつ行っ たらいいですか。
Should not be used directly with superiors when it risks sounding like a command; use softer patterns such as ～ていただけますか or ～たらいかがですか.

• Advice/suggestion: “It would be good to …” → softer than 〜たほうがいい, suited to lightly polite communication.
• Personal wish: “If only/I wish …” → used with な(あ)/ね to express feeling: 会えたらいいな。
• Asking how to deal with something: “どうしたらいいですか” is a fixed pattern for asking for advice.
• The たら condition means “it would be good if that condition happened” (supposition/possibility).

rows: Hoping it happens on its own, non-volitional
<ruby>病院<rt>びょういん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったほうがいい
Spoken language, more direct than たらいい

mistakes: Confusing the “advice” function with the “wish” function: judge by the context and the sentence ending (ですよ vs な/のに).
Too direct with superiors → not polite enough; consider ～たらいかがですか/～ていただけますか.
Confusing it with 〜たほうがいい (stronger) in advice sentences in sensitive situations.
255.notes:
• “〜たらいいのに” often expresses regret or a desire that is hard to fulfill.
• When asking for instructions, “どうしたらいいですか” is more natural than “どうすればいいですか” in spoken language; both are correct.
• Don't use “〜たらいい！” as a command; add ですよ/と思います to soften it.
meaning_vi: It would be good if… / should…
explain: Light advice, less imposing than ～べきだ or ～ほうがいい.
The question form “～ばいいですか” is commonly used when you want the listener to show you how to solve something.
～ばいいのに carries a feeling of reproach/regret; be careful using it with older people/superiors.
～ばよい is formal/very polite, used in written language and at work.
examples: 1. 疲れたら、休めばいい。
When you get tired, just rest.
2. 「駅はどう行けばいいですか」「この道をまっすぐいけばいいですよ」
"How do I get to the station?" "Just go straight along this road and you'll get there."
──────
1. どうすればいいですか。
What should I do?
2. 迷ったら、先生に聞けばいい。
If you're unsure, just ask the teacher.
3. そんなに心配しなければいい。
You don't need to worry that much.
4. もっと勉強すればいいのに。
You should study more (you really ought to).
5. 雨なら、無理に行かなければいい。
If it rains, you don't have to go.
6. 今回は謝ればいいだけだ。
This time, all you need to do is apologize.
comparison: Pattern | Nuance | Difference | Short example
～ばいい | Light advice/sufficient condition | Soft, not forcing | 早（はや）く寝（ね）れ ばいい。
～たらいい | Equivalent, natural in spoken language | Hypothetical, after the condition happens | 早（はや）く寝（ね）たらいい。
～ほうがいい | Stronger advice | Compares 2 options, clearly implies “should” | 早（はや）く寝（ね）たほうがいい。
～べきだ | Obligation/norm | Strong, based on principle | 守（まも）るべきだ。
～てもいい | Permission | Not advice; it is permission | 帰（かえ）ってもいい。
common_mistakes: • Misreading it as a command: ～ばいい does not mean “must”; it is only a light suggestion.
• Confusing it with ～てもいい (permission) → different function.
• Wrong ば形 conjugation of godan verbs: 書く→書けば; 買う→買えば; 行く→行けば.
• Wrong nuance: for a strong suggestion, choose ～ほうがいい／～べきだ instead of ～ばいい.
explain: ～Vば いいです： Should V ~
Used to ask for or give advice.
Usage is the same as NVTたら　いいです。
examples: 1. A:　本を　借りたいんですが、どう　すれば　いいですか。
B:　受付で　カードを　作って　もらって　ください。
A: I'd like to borrow a book. What should I do?
B: Please have a card made at the reception desk.
2. A:　友達が　結婚します。どんな物を　あげれば　いいですか。
B:　ワインを　あげれば　いいですよ。
A: My friend is getting married. What kind of thing should I give ?
B: Wine would be good.
explain: For your own wishes: ～といい んですが / のですが (polite, with a slight sense of worry).
For other people: ～といい ですね (polite, as a well-wish).
Giving advice: ～といい ですよ / よ (casual). Can be replaced with ～たらいい／～ばいい.
The content should be a future event; for the past, use ～とよかった (how nice it would have been) to express regret.
examples: 1. 試験、うまくいくといいですね。
I hope your exam goes well.
2. 忘れ物が見つかるといいんですが。
I hope the lost item turns up.
3. 時間があるといいね、映画に行こう。
I hope we have time. Let's go see a movie.
4. 風邪なら、今日は早く休むといいですよ。
If it's a cold, you should rest early today.
5. 英語は毎日少しずつ続けるといいよ。
With English, it's good to keep at it a little every day.
6. 明日は晴れだといいなあ。
I hope it's sunny tomorrow.
──────
1. ①いい仕事が見つかるといいですね。
I hope you find a good job.
2. ②運動会の日、雨が降らないといいですけど｡｡｡
I hope it doesn't rain on the day of the sports festival.
3. ③のどが痛いの？悪いかぜでないといいけど｡｡｡
Do you have a sore throat? I hope it's not a bad cold.
4. ④部屋がもっと広いといいけどなあ。
I wish the room were bigger.
5. ⑤ホームステイの家族がみんな親切だといいなあ。
I hope everyone in my homestay family is kind.
comparison: Pattern | Function | Difference | Short example
～といい（ですね） | Well-wishing/hope | For other people; polite. | 合格（ごうかく）だ といいですね。
～といい（んですが） | Hope (for oneself) | With a nuance of longing and worry. | 雨（あめ）がやむ といいんですが。
～たらいい／～ばいい | Suggestion | Similar to advice; sometimes more direct. | 休（やす）ん だらいい よ。
～ますように | Prayer/wish | More formal, leaning toward prayer. | 合格（ごうかく）し ますように。
～といい vs ～たい | Wish/hope vs desire | ～たい is the speaker's volition; ～といい is hoping for something beyond one's control. | 休（やす）み たい ／休（やす）み だといい。
common_mistakes: • Using ～といいです for your own wishes sounds stiff; more natural: ～といいんですが。
• Using ～といい to give overly direct advice in formal contexts; consider ～たらいかがでしょうか。
• Using ～といい for something fully under your own control → unnatural (×「早く寝るといいんですが」). Use ～ばいい／～たほうがいい instead。
• Confusing it with ～ますように (prayer). The JLPT tests the politeness nuance and the target (oneself vs other people).
meaning_vi: 「～ことを望んでいる。」 ～には話者自身の意志的行為を表す言葉は来ない。
I hope ~.
~ is not a word expressing a volitional act of the speaker themselves.
examples: 1. 疲れているようですね。あしたはゆっくり休むといいですよ。
You seem tired. You should take a good rest tomorrow.
2. その仕事、気が進まないのなら引き受けなければいいんじゃないですか。
If you don't feel like doing that job, why not just turn it down?
3. 申込書の書き方がわからなければ、事務の人に聞いてみたらいいですよ。
If you don't know how to fill out the application form, try asking someone in the office.
──────
1. 先生「このクラスも今日でお別れです。いつかまたみんなで会えるといいですね。」
Teacher「Today is also the day we say goodbye to this class. I hope we can all meet again someday.」
2. 最近ずっと体の調子が悪い。悪い病気でなければいいが…。
I haven't been feeling well for a while now. I hope it's nothing serious….
3. あした入学試験だ。頑張ろう。合格できたらいいなあ。
Tomorrow is the entrance exam. Let's do our best. I hope I can pass.
meaning_vi: Expresses advice or a suggestion.
（～ばいい）／（～たらいい）／（～と）+いい
examples: 1. ①　買えばいい／買ったらいい／買うといい
You should buy it.
2. ②　「日本語がうまくなるには、どうしたらいいですか。」
「日本人(にほんじん)と友達(ともだち)になるといいですよ。」
"What should I do to get better at Japanese?"
"You should make friends with Japanese people."
3. ③    勉強したくないなら、学校をやめればいい。
If you don't want to study, you should just quit school.
4. ➃　食べたくないなら、食べなければいい。
If you don't want to eat, you don't have to.
meaning_vi: I wish…, if only… it would be good (といい/たらいい)

examples.jp: 彼に聞けば、わかるだろう。
examples.tr: If you ask him, he'll probably know.

examples.jp: 田中さんたちは、もう東京に着いているだろう。
examples.tr: Tanaka and the others have probably already arrived in Tokyo.

examples.jp: 明日は雪が降るだろう。
examples.tr: It will probably snow tomorrow.

examples.jp: 彼はもう家に着いているだろう。
examples.tr: He has probably already gotten home.

examples.jp: そんな計画はうまくいかないだろう。
examples.tr: That kind of plan probably won't work.

examples.jp: 君もそう思うだろう？
examples.tr: You think so too, right?

256.explain:
Casual speech/male speech: ～だろう／～だろ？; polite style: ～でしょう／～でしょうか.
Combined with adverbs of conjecture: おそらく／たぶん ～だろう (raising/lowering the degree of certainty).
Avoid ～だろうですか. A polite question must be ～でしょうか.

• Conjecture with a moderate degree of confidence: “probably/ must be”.
• Used as a confirmation tag/a tag seeking agreement (especially in male speech): ～だろう？ “right?”.
• ～だろうか: wondering to oneself, deliberating; formal written language often uses ～であろう/～であろうか.
• More direct, stronger nuance than でしょう. In polite conversation, use でしょう.
mistakes: Wrong form: × 静かだだろう → 静かだろう.
Mixing styles: × でしょうだろう (mixed up). Choose one consistent style.
Using だろうか for a polite question to a superior can sound somewhat stiff; prefer でしょうか.
Confusing its degree of certainty with ～かもしれない in trick questions about confidence level.
256.notes:
• Formal written form: ～であろう (same meaning, elevated style).
• Negative question: ～ないだろうか often means “isn't it the case that …?”.
• In polite communication, switch to ～でしょう to avoid sounding rough. | Variant: （～だろう）と思う — the speaker's conjecture

257.meaning:
「～と言っている・～と聞いた。」「～と」のくだけた話し言葉で。②③④⑤のように、後の動詞（言っている・聞いたなど）をよく省略する。④のように、言った言葉に直接「って」をつけることもある。
Says that ~ / I heard that ~.
This is a word used in spoken language, a colloquial variant of ～と.
In examples ②③④, the verb that follows, いっている／きいた…, is often omitted.
In some cases, って is attached directly to the exact words that were said, as in example ④.

examples.jp: 「お母さん、お父さん、きょうは遅くなるって」
examples.tr: "Mom, Dad says he'll be late today."

examples.jp: 「田中さん、行くって？」「ううん、行かないって」
examples.tr: "Did Tanaka say they're going?" "No, they said they're not going."

examples.jp: 「学校で習ったんだけど、このあたりは昔、海だったんだって」
examples.tr: "I learned this at school: apparently this area used to be sea a long time ago."

examples.jp: 「天気予報、なんて言ってた？」「晴れるって。それに、暑いって。」
examples.tr: "What did the weather forecast say?" "It said it'll be sunny. And hot, too."

examples.jp: 久しぶりにテイさんからメールが来たよ。元気だって。
examples.tr: I got an email from Tei for the first time in ages. Tei says everything's fine.

examples.jp: 小川さん、今日は休むって言ってたよ。
examples.tr: Ogawa said they're taking today off.

257.explain: A casual way of passing on hearsay or what someone else said (“I heard…/they said…”). Used a lot in conversation.
257.notes:
1) Easily confused with the quotation particle と.
→ ～って is the colloquial form of と言って／という, used to report what was said/information.
2) Pay attention to the spoken-language context.
→ Often appears in conversation; not preferred in formal written language.
3) The two usages are easily confused.
→ It can mean “I heard…” or “they said…” (quoting), depending on the sentence.

examples.jp: メールを送ったつもりだったが、届いていなかった。
examples.tr: I thought I had sent the email, but it never arrived.

examples.jp: バッグにさいふを入れたつもりだったが、買いものをしようとしたら、なかった。
examples.tr: I was sure I had put my wallet in my bag, but when I went to buy something, it wasn't there.

examples.jp: この問題はわかっているつもりだったが、テストでは間違えてしまった。
examples.tr: I thought I understood this problem, but I got it wrong on the test.

examples.jp: まだ若いつもりだったのに、電車の中で席を譲られてショックだった。
examples.tr: I still thought of myself as young, so it was a shock when someone gave up their seat to me on the train.

examples.jp: 私は人より絵が上手なつもりだったが、美術大学に進学したら、もっとすごい人がおおぜいいた。
examples.tr: I believed I was better at drawing than others, but when I went on to art college, there were lots of people who were far more talented.

examples.jp: ぼくは彼女とは友達のつもりなのに、彼女はぼくと結婚したいらしい。困ったなあ。
examples.tr: I see her as just a friend, but she apparently wants to marry me. What a pain.

258.explain:
Used for personal intentions; should not be imposed on the listener (avoid using it as a command).
To soften it: ～つもりだが／けど… (I intend to…, but…).
Vたつもり: nuance of self-justification/misunderstanding; often used with が/のに to state contrast.
Negative “～つもりはない”: strong, a firm refusal to do something.
Unnatural when asserting someone else's firm intention without a source: use ～つもりだそうだ／らしい.

• Personal intention/plan: the speaker intends to do / not to do something.
• Subjective/mistaken judgment: Vたつもりだ = thinking you did something when in fact you didn't, or it isn't so.
• Degree of certainty: stronger than “～と思う” in volition, weaker than “～予定だ” (a plan with a concrete schedule).
• With a third-person subject: usually the hearsay/conjecture form “～つもりらしい／～つもりだという” is used.
• Often followed by a contrasting clause: ～つもりだったのに (I meant to… but…).

rows: <ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby><ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>するつもりだ
<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>だ
<ruby>意向<rt>いこう</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby>＋と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こうと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う
<ruby>節約<rt>せつやく</rt></ruby>するつもりで<ruby>歩<rt>ある</rt></ruby>く

mistakes: Using ～つもり for someone else's intention without a quotation or conjecture marker → unnatural or impolite.
Confusing ～つもりだ with ～予定だ: when the question calls for an official schedule, choose ～予定だ.
Mixing up V-たつもり (thought you had done it) with V-てしまった (ended up doing / did by accident) → different nuances.
Using つもり directly with an adjective → not used; switch to つもりで (adverbial) or another expression.
258.notes:
Note:
●主語が三人称（彼、彼女、田中さんなど）のときは使えない。
Cannot be used when the subject is third person (he, she, Mr. Tanaka, etc.).
1.  X彼は来年アメリカに留学するつもりです。
X He intends to study in the US next year.
2.  　→彼は来年アメリカに留学するつもりだと言っています。
→ He says he intends to study in the US next year.
Note:
●自分の意志で決められないことには使えない。
Cannot be used for things that cannot be decided by your own will.
1.  X　わたしは来年大学に合格するつもりです。
X I intend to pass the university entrance exam next year.
2.  X わたしは交通事故にあわないつもりです。
X I intend not to have a traffic accident.

259.meaning:
～するのが難しくてこまる
Doing ~ is difficult and troublesome

examples.jp: 個人的なことなので職場の人には頼みづらい。
examples.tr: It's a personal matter, so it's hard to ask people at work.

examples.jp: ここは黒板の字が見づらい位置です。
examples.tr: From this spot, it's hard to see what's written on the blackboard.

260.meaning: Do and then go / continue onward

examples.jp: 高くなっていく
examples.tr: to keep getting higher

examples.jp: 世界全体で量が減っているので、石油の価格はこれから高くなっていくだろう。
examples.tr: Since the amount is decreasing worldwide, the price of oil will probably keep rising from now on.

examples.jp: このままの生活をしていたら、どんどん太っていきますよ。
examples.tr: If you keep living like this, you'll get fatter and fatter.

examples.jp: もっと上手になれるよう、努力していくつもりです。
examples.tr: I intend to keep working hard so that I can get even better.

examples.jp: この作家は、これから有名になっていくでしょう。
examples.tr: This writer will probably become famous from now on.

examples.jp: これから日本語の勉強を続けていくつもりです。
examples.tr: I intend to continue studying Japanese from now on.

260.explain:
Direction “moving away”: in contrast with ～てくる (toward the speaker/the present).
When talking about strategies or visions: ～していく emphasizes continuity and initiative.
With a change of state: ～く/～に + なっていく is used for the future; ～なってきた is used for a change that has progressed up to the present.
The contracted spoken form ～てく is common, but should be avoided in formal written language.

• Spatial direction: the action moves away from the speaker/reference point (走っていく, 持っていく).
• Temporal direction: a process/degree of change will continue from now into the future (増えていく, 良くなっていく).
• Sequence of actions: do something and then go (食べていく can mean “eat and then go / go on”).
• Nuance of progression, long-term, long-range plans (この活動を続けていくつもりだ).

rows: From now on; leaving the point of origin
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くなっていく／<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っていく
Has progressed until now; approaching the speaker
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くなってきた／<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってくる
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>ける
Preparing beforehand, does not show direction/future progression

mistakes: Confusing the direction with ～てくる: ×持ってくる when you are “taking it away”; it must be 持っていく.
Using ～ていく for past up to present: “has gradually … until now” requires ～てきた.
Confusing it with ～続ける: ～ていく has a future-oriented nuance, not just simple continuation.
Overusing the contraction ～てく in formal written language.
260.notes:
• With verbs of motion, ～ていく can also mean “do something and then leave”: 食べていく, 見ていく.
• In narration, the past ～ていった/～ていった often describes moving away from the scene.
• Avoid using ～ていく for sudden, instantaneous events; it suits tendencies and progression better. | Meaning: moving away from the speaker (space) / change from now on (time)

261.meaning: Wanting someone to do something | Want (someone) to do…

examples.jp: 静かにしてほしいんですが。
examples.tr: I'd like you to be quiet, please.

examples.jp: 明日は早く来てほしい。
examples.tr: I want you to come early tomorrow.

examples.jp: 子どもたちに本をもっと読んでほしい。
examples.tr: I want the children to read more books.

examples.jp: 彼が元気になってほしい。
examples.tr: I hope he gets better.

examples.jp: ここではタバコを吸わないでほしい。
examples.tr: I'd like you not to smoke here.

examples.jp: この件、今日中に確認していただきたいです。
examples.tr: I would like you to check this matter by the end of today.

261.explain:
Casual: Vてほしい／Vないでほしい。Polite: Vてほしいです。Very polite: Vていただきたいです。
Indirect, softer: ～てもらえるとありがたい／助かります。
When hoping for something natural (rain stopping), use が:雨 が やん でほしい。
Emphasizing strong emotion can sound demanding; consider the context.

• Expresses a desire/request for someone else to do an action (or for something to happen).
• The subject is usually the speaker (I/we). For a general desire: みんなに分かってほしい。
• Strength depends on the context: statement (hope), suggestion (request), complaint (don't do…).
• に marks “the person being asked”; が marks “the agent of the desired action/event”.

rows: Direct desire; the subject is the speaker.
The subject is the speaker; not used for others.
Want to have someone do it for you
More polite/tactful; emphasizes receiving a benefit.
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>してもらいたい。
Would like to have it done (keigo)
<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>していただきたいです。

mistakes: Using てほしい for a third party's desire → unnatural; to say “A wants B to do” you need たがっている/ほしがっている: 彼は私に来てほしがっている。
Confusing it with たい: “I want you to help” must be 手伝ってほしい, not 手伝いたい。
Leaving out に/が makes the agent ambiguous: “誰にしてほしいのか” needs to be clear.
JLPT: politeness trap – choose ていただきたい when addressing a superior/customer.
261.notes:
• When speaking directly to the listener, add a polite opener: すみませんが／恐れ入りますが／できれば…＋Vていただきたい。
• “人に” vs “人が”: with a specific agent, both are possible; に emphasizes the person being asked, が emphasizes the event happening.
• In business writing, avoid commands: prefer 「ご対応いただけますと幸いです」。

examples.jp: このボタンを押してみてください。
examples.tr: Please try pressing this button.

examples.jp: 辛そうだけど、少し食べてみる。
examples.tr: It looks spicy, but I'll try a little.

examples.jp: 新しいアプリを使ってみたが、意外と便利だ。
examples.tr: I tried the new app, and it's surprisingly handy.

examples.jp: サイズが合うか着てみませんか。
examples.tr: Would you like to try it on to see if the size fits?

examples.jp: 先生に聞いてみよう。
examples.tr: Let's try asking the teacher.

examples.jp: 新しいざっしを買ったので、すぐ読んで見ました。
examples.tr: I bought a new magazine, so I tried reading it right away.

262.explain:
Friendly; reduces the pressure of deciding (“just try it first”).
Often used as てみてください (please try), てみませんか (invitation), てみたい (desire).
Not used when the action is serious/high-risk (in that case use検討する/試みる...).

～てみる expresses “trying” an action to check the result/possibility/experience. みる here is an auxiliary verb meaning “try and see”, different from 見る “look”. The action is usually small-scale and exploratory, with no commitment to a result.
• Emphasizes experience: doing something to find out the result (アウトカム未知).
• Goes well with polite suggestions/recommendations in conversation.
• Distinguish from 試す/試みる: てみる is more casual/lighter; 試みる is very formal, written language.

rows: Emphasizes the intention at that point in time
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>しようとする
<ruby>新<rt>しん</rt></ruby><ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>試<rt>ため</rt></ruby>す

mistakes: Attaching てみる to the potential form: ×食べられてみる → 〇食べてみる (てみる itself already carries the sense of trying).
Using てみる for actions that cannot be “tried”: ×死んでみる (unnatural/pragmatically inappropriate).
Confusing it with ようとする: てみる is trying (actually done), ようとする is “to intend, to be about to”.
262.notes:
• てみる combines well with “trial” adverbs: とりあえず/まず/一度/少し.
• Negative: Vてみない (spoken) or Vてみません (polite negative, invitation form) means “why not try?”.
• When the goal is “checking whether something is possible”: ～かどうか + Vてみる is very natural. Example: 動くかどうか試しに動かしてみる。

examples.jp: 明日、パーティーに行くので、服を出しておいた。
examples.tr: I'm going to a party tomorrow, so I got my clothes out ahead of time.

examples.jp: お客さんが来るので、部屋のそうじをしておかなければならない。
examples.tr: Guests are coming, so I have to clean the room beforehand.

examples.jp: あした友だちが来るので、飲み物と食べ物をたくさん買っておきました。
examples.tr: My friends are coming tomorrow, so I bought lots of drinks and food in advance.

examples.jp: 「来週は第3課を読みますから、ことばの意味を調べておいてください」
examples.tr: “We'll read Lesson 3 next week, so please look up the meanings of the words beforehand.”

examples.jp: 卒業する前に、運転免許を取っておこうと思います。
examples.tr: I'm thinking of getting my driver's license before I graduate.

examples.jp: 「使ったものは、元の場所に戻しておいてください」
examples.tr: “Please put the things you used back where they were.”

263.explain:
Emphasizes “preparation” when there is a clear future purpose: 〜ために／〜に備えて + Vておく.
Request form: 〜しておいてください（please do it in advance / leave it as is）。
Contracted spoken forms are very common: しとく、買っとく、やっといて。
“Leave as is” often appears with そのままにしておく／開けておく／つけておく（leave on）.

Preparing in advance
1.
A:会議(かいぎ)の前(まえ)に　なにを しておきますか。
A: What should we prepare before the meeting?
B:資料(しりょう)を　コピーしておきます。
B: I'll make copies of the documents beforehand.
2.
A:旅行(りょこう)に行(い)く前(まえ)に何(なに)を　しておいたら　いいですか。
A: What should I do before going on a trip?
B: ホテルを予約(よやく)しておいたら　いいですよ。
B: You should book a hotel in advance.
Used to deal with a situation after doing an action, or to offer a temporary solution.
1.
A: この本(ほん)は　どう　しましょうか。
A: What should I do with this book?
B:読(よ)んだら、本棚(ほんだな)に戻(もど)しておいてください。
B: When you've finished reading it, please put it back on the bookshelf.
2.
A: ナイフと　フォークは　どこに　しまいましょうか。
A: Where should I put away the knives and forks?
B:元(もと)の所(ところ)に　しまっておいてください。
B: Please put them back where they were.
Keeping or maintaining a certain state.
1.
A:片付(かたづ)けましょうか。
A: Shall I tidy up?
B: もうすぐ会社(かいしゃ)に行(い)く時間(じかん)ですから、そのままに　しておいてください。
B: It's almost time to go to work, so please just leave it as it is.
2.
A:窓(まど)を　しめてもいいですか。
A: May I close the window?
B: すみません、ちょっと　あついですから、そのまま　あけておいてください。
B: Sorry, it's a bit hot, so please leave it open.
We can conjugate the verb おく into the appropriate forms.

rows: Do in advance, leave as is
<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>用意<rt>ようい</rt></ruby>しておく。
Existing result; does not emphasize “the future”
<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>置<rt>お</rt></ruby>いてある。

mistakes: Confusing it with 〜てある: “already there” (結果状態) uses てある; “do in advance” (intentional, future-oriented action) uses ておく. The JLPT often sets traps: ドアが（開けてある／開けておく）.
Using ておく for actions with no sense of “preparation” sounds forced.
Forgetting the “leave as is” nuance: 片付けないでおく（deliberately not tidying up) differs from 片付けていない（simply the state of not having tidied up).
263.notes:
• With devices/electricity: つけておく（turn on in advance）、消しておく（turn off in advance）、充電しておく（charge in advance） are very natural.
• The negative ないでおく has a deliberate nuance of “leaving it for later”: 今は触らないでおく。
• In business email: あらかじめ共有しておきます（I am sharing this in advance） is a polite set phrase.
meaning_vi: Expresses doing something so that there are no difficulties later, or so that something is thoroughly prepared. As in example ④, this sentence pattern is sometimes also used to mean keeping a state as it is. Usually used with verbs expressing volitional actions.
examples: 1. ①荷物をかばんに入れておきます。
I'll put my things in the bag in advance.
2. ②ごみを外に出しておきましょう。
Let's take the trash outside beforehand.
3. ③旅行の話はサラに伝えておいたよ。
I already told Sarah about the trip.
4. ④窓はそのまま開けておいてください。
Please leave the window open as it is.
The structure「Nを～ておく」expresses an action prepared in advance for the future. The structure「Nが～てある」expresses the result of an action.
1. ①　書いておく／書いてある
Write in advance / Is written
2. ②　他の人のかさと間違えないように、ここに名前を書いておこう／買いとこう。
Let's write our names here so we don't mix up our umbrellas with other people's.
3. ③　明日から国に帰るので、お土産を買っておいた。
I'm going back to my country tomorrow, so I bought souvenirs in advance.
4. ➃　これはだれのかさだろう？あっ、ここに名前が書いてある。
Whose umbrella is this? Oh, there's a name written here.

264.meaning: Do and come back / gradually become…

examples.jp: 友だちからまた電話がかかってきた。
examples.tr: My friend called me again.

examples.jp: これは、母が送ってきた国の食べ物です。
examples.tr: This is food from my home country that my mother sent me.

examples.jp: ちょっとコンビニで飲み物を買ってくるね。
examples.tr: I'm just going to pop out and buy a drink at the convenience store.

examples.jp: 資料をプリントしてきますから、少々お待ちください。
examples.tr: I'll go print out the documents and be right back, so please wait a moment.

examples.jp: 雨が急に降ってきた。
examples.tr: It suddenly started raining.

examples.jp: このところ、物価が上がってきた。
examples.tr: Prices have gone up lately.

264.explain:
Common in spoken language:行ってくる (I'm going out for a bit and will be back), いってきます (set phrase when leaving home).
Emphasizes the result “has arrived / up to the present”: ～てきた is often used with verbs of change:増える／減る／慣れる／分かる／見えてくる.
Compared with ～ていく:寒くなって きた : it has started getting cold up to now.これからもっと寒くなって いく : it will get colder from now on.
寒くなって きた : it has started getting cold up to now.
これからもっと寒くなって いく : it will get colder from now on.
Used with verbs of motion/bringing:持ってくる,連れてくる,呼んでくる.

• It is not just “come”, but “an event/action/change happens and its result is present with the speaker or at the present time”.
• Two major groups of meaning:

Spatial meaning: 行ってくる, 買ってくる, 持ってくる (go do something / bring it here).
Temporal/abstract meaning: ～てきた (has gradually), ～ていく (will gradually from now on). くる points toward the present, いく toward the future/moving away.

• Spatial meaning: 行ってくる, 買ってくる, 持ってくる (go do something / bring it here).
• Temporal/abstract meaning: ～てきた (has gradually), ～ていく (will gradually from now on). くる points toward the present, いく toward the future/moving away.
• The form てきている emphasizes a state that has begun and continues up to the present.

rows: Progression moving away from the present
<ruby>気温<rt>きおん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>下<rt>さ</rt></ruby>がっていく
Intention to try; unrelated to direction
<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってくる vs <ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っていく
ここに<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってきて／あちらへ<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っていって

mistakes: Mixing up てくる and ていく in temporal direction: ✕ これから寒くなってきます (hasn't happened yet) → ✓ なっていきます.
Using てくる with verbs that have no sense of progression makes it hard to understand: ✕ 知ってきた → usually 分かってきた/理解できるようになってきた.
Confusing “bring here” vs “take away”: ここに持っていって is the wrong direction; it must be 持ってきて.
The JLPT often tests the contrast: 降ってきた (started raining) vs 降っている (is raining) vs 降っていく (rarely used).
264.notes:
• With emotions/perception: 実感してきた, 見えてきた (has gradually become clear).
• Causative form + くる in spoken language: 待たせてきてごめん (went to do X before coming, making you wait).
• 電話してくる contains the meaning “call (toward me)”; 電話していく is rare and has a different meaning.
meaning_vi: Expresses a change of state that has occurred up to the present or up to a certain point in time.
V:　太って　+　くる
explain: Expresses emotions, states, or natural phenomena that arise or increase gradually over time. Emphasizes the process of “gradually appearing”.
examples: 1. 健康に関心を持つ人が増えてきました。
More and more people have become interested in their health.
2. ４月に入って、だんだん暖かくなってきました。
Now that it's April, it has been getting gradually warmer.
──────
1. 悲しくて、涙が出てきた。
I was so sad that tears started to come.
2. こう暑いと、じっとしていても汗が出てくる。
When it's this hot, you start sweating even if you stay still.
3. そのときはあまり感じなかったが、あとになって怒りがわいてきた。
I didn't feel much at the time, but later anger welled up in me.
4. しばらくしてから、優勝の喜びがこみあげてきた。
After a while, the joy of winning welled up.
──────
1. ①　痛くなってきた
It has started to hurt
2. ②　石油の値段がだんだん高くなってきた。
The price of oil has gradually gone up.
3. ③　運動しなかったので、だんだん太ってきた。
I didn't exercise, so I gradually gained weight. | Meaning: toward the speaker (space) / change from the past up to now (time)

265.connection: Vても / Aくても / N・Naでも + [sentence/clause]

examples.jp: 「今からタクシーで行けば間に合いますか」
examples.tr: 「If I take a taxi now, will I make it in time?」

examples.jp: 「この仕事は経験がなければできませんか」
examples.tr: 「Is it impossible to do this job without experience?」

examples.jp: 「あしたはわたしの誕生日です。いそがしくても、かならず来てくださいね」
examples.tr: 「Tomorrow is my birthday. Even if you're busy, be sure to come, okay?」

examples.jp: 「どんなにきらうでも、野菜は健康のために食べたほうがいいですよ」
examples.tr: 「No matter how much you dislike them, you should eat vegetables for your health.」

examples.jp: いろいろな理由があって、勉強がしたくてもできない子どもたちがたくさんいる
examples.tr: For various reasons, there are many children who can't study even though they want to.

examples.jp: 「林さんのおじいちゃん、いくつになってもお元気でいいですね」
examples.tr: 「Mr. Hayashi's grandfather is still so healthy no matter how old he gets. That's wonderful.」

265.explain:
Emphasizes that something “has no effect / does not change the decision”.
Often used with emphatic words: たとえ／いくら／どんなに／もし.
Can be used with commands/advice, but is more natural when stating a position:雨でも来てください（acceptable), though the style is a bit stiff.

• Concession/concessive condition: “even if … still …”; the result is not affected by the condition in the first clause.
• Used for suppositions or for real, repeated situations.
• With a question word＋でも/ても it means “no matter how … / regardless of …”: 何をしても, いつでも.

rows: A fact contrary to expectation; nuance of dissatisfaction.
<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるとしても<ruby>頑張<rt>がんば</rt></ruby>る。
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>くたって<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>わない。

mistakes: Wrong conjugation: ×高いでも → correct: 高くても; ×静かくても → correct: 静かでも.
Confusing it with ～のに (a fact contrary to expectation). ～ても can be a supposition; ～のに is a fact.
Using ～てもいい instead of ～ても when you mean “even if … still …” → wrong meaning.
Mistaken “雨でても” (wrong connection) → correct: 雨でも.
265.notes:
• N/Na＋でも, Aい→Aくても, Vて＋も: be careful to change each word type correctly.
• Negative: Aくなくても, Na/N＋じゃなくても, Vなくても.
• Fixed emphatic phrases: たとえ～ても／いくら～ても／どんなに～ても.

266.connection: V/A plain form + ではないか / N・Na + ではないか

examples.jp: それは少し危険ではないか。
examples.tr: Isn't that a little dangerous?

examples.jp: 彼はもう帰ったのではないか。
examples.tr: Hasn't he already gone home?

examples.jp: いいじゃないか！この案で行こう。
examples.tr: Isn't that great! Let's go with this plan.

examples.jp: 時間に遅れるなんて、社会人としてどうかじゃないか。
examples.tr: Being late — isn't that questionable for a working adult?

examples.jp: 皆さん、もう一度考え直そうではないか。
examples.tr: Everyone, let's reconsider this once more.

examples.jp: 彼は忙しいのではないかと思う。
examples.tr: I think he may be busy.

266.explain:
Rising intonation at the end of the sentence → asking/inviting agreement; falling intonation → exclamation, criticism, praise.
のではないか is more objective/softer than the direct ではないか.
V-ようではないか is used in speeches and rallying calls; in everyday life it is replaced by ～よう（よ）/ ～ようか.
じゃないか is versatile: agreement, criticism, dissatisfaction, praise depending on the context.

• Rhetorical question/affirmation seeking agreement: “Isn't it…?”, “Wouldn't it be…?”. High degree of certainty; the speaker wants the listener to agree.
• Emphasis of emotion (praise/disapproval/criticism): the voice falls at the end of the sentence, making it an exclamation: “That's good!”, “It's already late!”.
• Suggestion/call to action (V-ようではないか): “Let's …!”. Speech or slogan style.
• Formality: ではないか (formal/written) > じゃないか (spoken language). The form のではないか is used when a long clause serves as the subject.

rows: Does not directly seek agreement; neutral
Softer and more objective than ではないか; used with clauses
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>すぎるのではないか。
Casual; sounds more feminine with rising intonation
また<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れたじゃないか！

mistakes: Confusing it with だろう: ではないか seeks agreement or expresses exclamation; だろう only expresses conjecture.
Wrongly dropping “の/ん”: with V/いA you need のではないか (not Vではないか).
Wrong intonation distorts the meaning: rising → question; falling → criticism/praise.
Using じゃないか in formal written language: choose ではないか / のではないか instead.
266.notes:
• In journalism and editorials, ではないか is often used to lead an argument and call on readers to agree.
• んじゃないか (contracted form of ＝のではないか) is common after verbs/adjectives: 難しいんじゃないか.
• Avoid repeating では: with N/なA + のではないか you need “なの”: 静かなのではないか.
• Using じゃないか in complaints can easily sound aggressive; consider the relationship and intonation.

examples.jp: この辺りは昔、広い野原だったという。
examples.tr: It is said that this area was once a wide field.

examples.jp: この祭りは村で古くから行われてきたという。
examples.tr: It is said that this festival has been held in the village since ancient times.

examples.jp: 豆腐は1300ねんぐらい前に中国から日本に伝わったという。
examples.tr: It is said that tofu came to Japan from China about 1300 years ago.

examples.jp: 今度の試験は、かなりむずかしいということだ。
examples.tr: I hear that the next exam will be quite difficult.

examples.jp: 先生がこくさいかいぎにでるので、こうぎは休みになるという話だ。
examples.tr: I heard that the lecture will be canceled because the professor is attending an international conference.

examples.jp: パンダの赤ちゃんが生まれたというニュースを見ました。
examples.tr: I saw the news that a baby panda was born.

267.explain:
NというN: used for naming, identifying or introducing. Natural, not too stiff.
文というN: puts the information of a whole sentence in to modify nouns such as噂・話・意見・考え・事実…
ということ／というの: nominalizes so the sentence can act as subject/object; more formal than っていうこと.
というのは: introduces a definition or explanation; what follows is the content that clarifies the meaning.
“～という”: at the end of a sentence it means “I hear/it is said that”, more formal than って.
Avoid overusing っていう in academic texts or written exams.

• Links content (a name, information, a clause) to a noun in the sense of “called/is called/is said to be/such as”.
• Before a noun: NというN or ClauseというN → “N (that is) called …”, “N (that) … is said to be …”.
• With ということ／というの: nominalizes a clause → turns the whole sentence into a “fact/thing”.
• というのは: opens an explanation/definition, close to “that is/meaning”.
• The spoken っていう makes sentences more natural in conversation, but avoid it in formal writing or official presentations.
• Nuance: neutral; “～という” has a sense of relaying transmitted information or naming objectively.

rows: <ruby>富士山<rt>ふじさん</rt></ruby>という<ruby>山<rt>やま</rt></ruby>
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>したということ
Reports information; does not modify N
A single word; no preceding clause needed
いわゆる<ruby>名門<rt>めいもん</rt></ruby><ruby>校<rt>こう</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Confusing ということ (nominalization) with と言う (to say that): ということ does not need an agent who “says” something.
Using っていう in JLPT N2/N1 writing: prefer という／とされる／とのことだ.
Missing “だ” before という with nouns/na-adjectives: 彼は元気だという噂 (do not drop だ in formal written language).
Confusing という with そうだ (hearsay): というN modifies a noun; そうだ cannot.
Using というのは without a following explanation leaves the sentence incomplete.
267.notes:
• The preceding clause (before という) can be in the past, affirmative or negative: 来なかったという噂, 高くないという評価…
• ということだ can also mean “that means/the conclusion is”: 3割引ということだ → “that is, 30% off”.
• というより／というか: shifts or adjusts what was said; strong conversational nuance.
• Use brackets「…」+ という to quote a title or proper name exactly.

examples.jp:
A: この漢字はどういう意味ですか。
B: 使うなという意味です。
examples.tr:
A: What does this kanji mean?
B: It means “Do not use.”

examples.jp:
A: このマークはどういう意味ですか。
B: 洗濯機で洗えるという意味です。
examples.tr:
A: What does this mark mean?
B: It means it can be washed in a washing machine.

268.explain: Used to explain the meaning of a word or sentence.

examples.jp: どっちが悪いんじゃなくて、二人とも悪いんです。
examples.tr: It's not that one of them is to blame; they're both to blame.

examples.jp: かさが ３本ありますが、３本ともこわれています。
examples.tr: There are three umbrellas, but all three are broken.

269.explain: ◎ Used with the plural of people and things; it means「どちらも」.
269.notes: Attaches to the 「－く」 and 「かろう」 forms of i-adjectives. In spoken language, 「－くても」 is the usual form. ① means 「そのように見積もっても」 and is followed by an expression estimating a quantity. 「多くとも１０人」「長くとも３０分」「遅くとも５時までに」 are similar usages. When 「－かろうと」 is repeated twice, as in ③, 「も」 is often omitted.

examples.jp: これは間違っていると思います。
examples.tr: I think this is wrong.

examples.jp: 医者になりたいと思っています。
examples.tr: I'd like to become a doctor.

examples.jp: この案が一番現実的だと思います。
examples.tr: I think this plan is the most realistic.

examples.jp: 明日は雨だと思う。傘を持っていこう。
examples.tr: I think it'll rain tomorrow. I'll take an umbrella.

examples.jp: 彼は真面目だと思わない。
examples.tr: I don't think he's serious.

examples.jp: 彼が来るとは思わなかった。
examples.tr: I didn't think he would come.

270.explain:
“～と思います” is polite and less imposing; used in meetings and discussions.
“～と思う” is neutral/spoken. Combine it with “たぶん/おそらく/きっと” to adjust the degree of certainty.
Intention: Vようと思う/と思っています. If the intention is formed right now:今から勉強しようと思う。

• Expresses a subjective opinion or conjecture: “I think that/I believe that”.
• With volitional verbs: ～ようと思う shows a momentary intention; ～ようと思っています shows an established intention.
• Negative: ～ないと思う (think that … not) vs ～とは思わない (do not go so far as to think …) differ in strength and emphasis.
• In spoken language, んです/けど is often added to soften the statement: ～と思うんですが…

rows: <ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>そうと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています
<ruby>有効<rt>ゆうこう</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>える
<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>のように<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う

mistakes: Dropping だ in the wrong place: 彼は医者だと思う (written). In spoken language both are possible: 医者だと思う／医者と思う.
Mistaking と for a condition: と here is always the quotation particle for 思う.
Intention: ～と思う vs ～と思っています → choose correctly according to the context, “right now” or “already decided”.
Negative: choose ～ないと思う or ～とは思わない to express the degree of negation that fits the JLPT question.
270.notes:
• In the first person, “私は” is usually omitted: 私は行くと思う → 行くと思う.
• “～だと思う” with na-adjectives/N: in conversation だ may be dropped, but keep だ in written exams.
• と here is the quotation particle, not a condition.
• Scope of negation: AはBだと思わない (do not think A is B) differs from AはBではないと思う (think A is not B) in focus.
meaning_vi: Expresses the speaker's thoughts and feelings.
examples: 1. ①　3月30日ごろだと　おもいます。
I think it's probably around March 30.
2. ②　はなさんは　来ないと　おもいます。
I think Hana won't come.
3. ③　ちょっと　ねだんが　高いと　おもいます。
I think the price is a little high.
4. ④　日本語と　英語と　どちら　かんたんだ　とおもいますか。
Which do you think is easier, Japanese or English?

examples.jp:
田中：　お弁当を行きますよ。
A: 田中さんはなんと言っていましたか。
B: お弁当を買いに行くと言っていました。
examples.tr:
Tanaka: I'm going to get a bento.
A: What did Tanaka say?
B: Tanaka said they were going to buy a bento.

examples.jp:
A: 山田さんはいますか。
B: 今出かけています。３０分ぐらいで戻ると言っていました。
examples.tr:
A: Is Yamada here?
B: Yamada is out right now, but said they'd be back in about 30 minutes.

271.explain:
Used to relay the words of a third party.
• ～と　言いました: used for quoting.
• ～と　言っていました: used for passing on a message

～と言(い)っていました： ~ said that ~
271.notes:
meaning_vi: An expression used when relaying what someone else said earlier. The question form of this pattern uses なんと, as in example ③.
examples: 1. ①トムさんは今日休むと言っていました。
Tom said he would be off today.
2. ②サラさんは最近忙しいと言っていました。
Sarah said she has been busy lately.
3. ③山田「お父さんから電話？何と言っていた？」
トム「今日は晩ご飯はいらないと言っていましたよ。」
Yamada: "A call from Dad? What did he say?"
Tom: "He said he won't need dinner tonight." | Plain form: ～と言っていた

272.meaning:
「～と、世界の人たちが言っている。」
It is said that ~ .
272.connection: V plain form + と言われている / N + だ / Na + だ / Aい

examples.jp: 今年は黒い服が流行すると言われている。
examples.tr: It is said that black clothes will be in fashion this year.

examples.jp: 納豆は体にいいと言われている。
examples.tr: Natto is said to be good for your health.

examples.jp: 今度の大会では中川選手が優勝するだろうと言われています。
examples.tr: It is said that Nakagawa will probably win this tournament.

272.notes: Used when talking about widely held views or reputations.

273.meaning: read as ~ ・ ～と書いてあります : It says ~

examples.jp:
A: あそこに何とてあるんですか。
B: 「使用禁止」と書いてあります。
examples.tr:
A: What does it say over there?
B: It says 「使用禁止」 (Do not use).

examples.jp:
A: あの漢字は何と読むんですか。
B: 「えいぎょうちゅう」と読みます。
examples.tr:
A: How do you read that kanji?
B: It's read 「えいぎょうちゅう」.

273.explain:
～と読(よ)みます: read as ~
～と書(か)いてあります： It says ~

examples.jp: この本は、明日までに図書館に返さなければなりません。
examples.tr: I have to return this book to the library by tomorrow.

examples.jp: 部屋のそうじをしなければならないので、早く帰りました。
examples.tr: I had to clean my room, so I went home early.

examples.jp: 労働法を遵守しなければならない。
examples.tr: Labor laws must be observed.

examples.jp: 応募書類は日本語でなければならない。
examples.tr: Application documents must be in Japanese.

examples.jp: 安全基準は常に満たされなければならない。
examples.tr: Safety standards must be met at all times.

examples.jp: 明日までに報告書を提出しなければなりません。
examples.tr: I have to submit the report by tomorrow.

274.explain:
Strength: stronger than ～なくてはいけない in terms of normativity.
Politeness: ～なければ なりません in formal dialogue; past ～なければ ならなかった .
It can sound like a command; when speaking to a superior or a customer, consider switching to ～ていただけますか／～てください（softer, but no longer meaning “must”).
When stating rules or provisions, this is the precise choice.

• Expresses strong obligation required by laws, regulations or responsibility: “must/have to ...”.
• Formal, objective; suitable for policy documents, reports and public statements.
• Emphasizes the consequence of not doing it: breaking the law, failing to meet standards.
• The subject is usually an organization or individual bound by a standard; rarely used to give direct orders to the listener.

rows: Softer/more neutral; spoken language and work
<ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>しなくてはいけない。
Archaic/official; used in slogans and official documents
Moral standard, not a legal obligation
<ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るべきだ。
Have no choice but to/cannot help but
<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>せざるを<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>ない。

mistakes: Forgetting “で” with N/na: ×日本語なければならない → 〇日本語でなければならない.
Confusing the nuance with べきだ in inference questions: べきだ ≠ legal obligation.
Wrong negative: ×行かなければならないくない → 〇行かなくてもいい／行く必要はない.
Using it directly to the listener sounds rude: switch to a polite request if the goal is to ask a favor.
274.notes:
• To negate an obligation, use ～なくてもいい／～必要はない, not the negative ならない.
• In headings and regulations, the contracted form without a subject is common: ～しなければならない。
• Two variants with the same meaning of obligation: ～なければならない ≈ ～いけない; they differ mainly in a stiffer or softer nuance.

examples.jp: 日本史や地理などを勉強した。
examples.tr: I studied things like Japanese history and geography.

examples.jp: 私などはまだまだ未熟です。
examples.tr: Someone like me still has a lot to learn.

examples.jp: 彼の前で嘘をつくなど許されない。
examples.tr: Something like lying in front of him is unacceptable.

examples.jp: 合格できるなど思っていなかった。
examples.tr: I never imagined I'd be able to pass.

examples.jp: 天才などという言葉は簡単には使うべきではない。
examples.tr: A word like “genius” should not be used lightly.

275.explain:
Humble self-reference:私 など ／私 などは … shows humility.
Contempt/belittling: あいつ など …（that guy…） has a contemptuous nuance; use it with care.
Strong negation: ～ など ない／ありえない emphasizes "no way".
In listing: AやB など means "etc." as examples, not an exhaustive list.
More formal than なんか／なんて; suitable for written language, documents and exams.

• Listing representative examples: "such as…, etc." Often used with や／とか for a soft listing.
• Nuance of belittling/contempt or humility: when attached to a word referring to oneself (私など), or when dismissing something as trivial or worthless.
• In written language, など can follow a clause (V辞書形など) to give an evaluation of an action or ability, often together with ない.
• Formality: neutral→formal; more polite than なんか／なんて.

rows: <ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>や<ruby>雑誌<rt>ざっし</rt></ruby>などを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>なんて<ruby>大嫌<rt>だいきら</rt></ruby>いだ。
<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない？

mistakes: Using など with contempt toward the listener or a superior → impolite. Avoid: あなたなど…
Mistaking など for an exhaustive listing. In fact it gives representative examples, not the whole set.
Wrong combination with verbs: Vます＋など is unnatural; use V辞書形＋など／～するなど.
In a negative sentence, forgetting ない loses the "no way" nuance.
275.notes:
• In research and academic writing, など is often used to mark a non-exhaustive list: 例：温度、湿度、気圧など。
• With quantities/estimates: 10人など（about 10 people） is less common than ほど/くらい but does occur.
• Fixed phrases carrying an evaluation: ～するなどもってのほか（out of the question）.

examples.jp: この肉は硬くて食べにくい。
examples.tr: This meat is tough and hard to eat.

examples.jp: 丈夫で割れにくいカップはありませんか。
examples.tr: Do you have any cups that are sturdy and hard to break?

examples.jp: この字は小さすぎて読みにくい。
examples.tr: These characters are too small and hard to read.

examples.jp: その靴は滑りにくいから山登りに向いている。
examples.tr: Those shoes don't slip easily, so they're good for mountain climbing.

examples.jp: 彼には頼みにくい雰囲気がある。
examples.tr: There's something about him that makes it hard to ask him for things.

examples.jp: 油汚れは水だけでは落としにくい。
examples.tr: Oil stains are hard to remove with water alone.

276.explain:
Used in advertising and product reviews:汚れにくい／壊れにくい／傷つきにくい.
When talking about feelings and relationships:言いにくい／聞きにくい express hesitation and delicacy.
Negative: ～にくくない（not hard to do）; Past: ～にくかった.
Combine with adverbs:非常に／かなり／ちょっと + ～にくい to adjust the degree.

• Expresses that “V is hard to do”, due to objective or subjective factors: technique, environment, properties of the target.
• Expresses a tendency or property: 見にくいデザイン（a design that is hard to look at）, 汚れが取れにくい（stains are hard to remove）.
• Different from “難しい”: ～にくい describes difficulty in performing a specific action V; 難しい means difficult in general.
• Compared with ～づらい: ～にくい is more neutral/objective; ～づらい leans toward the speaker's feelings (psychological or physical sensation).

rows: <ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いづらい<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>だ。
Written language; used with <ruby>許<rt>ゆる</rt></ruby>しがたい／<ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたい
<ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたい<ruby>事実<rt>じじつ</rt></ruby>。
Not attached directly to an action V
この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。
<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みやすい<ruby>文章<rt>ぶんしょう</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Wrong form: × 読むにくい → ○ 読みにくい（drop ます）.
Confusing it with 難しい: generally “hard to solve” → 難しい; “hard to do V” → ～にくい/～づらい.
Expressing the negative: 読みにくくない（not hard to read）, not × 読みにくいない.
Confusing the nuance with ～づらい: psychological/hesitation → prefer ～づらい; physical/objective property → ～にくい.
276.notes:
• Inflects like an い-adjective: にくい→にくくない／にくくて／にくかった… used flexibly in complex sentences.
• Avoid redundancy冗長: instead of とてもとても読みにくい, use 非常に/かなり + 読みにくい.
• When describing UI/UX: 見やすさ/見にくさ are measures of how easy or hard something is to read or see.

277.meaning: Nothing but…, all the time…, full of… (repeating one action / all of one kind)

examples.jp: 年をとると、記憶力は衰えるばかりだ。
examples.tr: As you get older, your memory just keeps declining.

examples.jp: この数年、性格は苦しくなるばかりだ。
examples.tr: Over the past few years, life has only gotten harder.

examples.jp: せっかく覚えた日本語も、使わなければ忘れていくばかりだ。
examples.tr: Even the Japanese you worked so hard to learn will just keep slipping away if you don't use it.

examples.jp: 仕事も私生活もうまくいかない。ストレスがたまるばかりで、いやになってしまう。
examples.tr: Neither work nor my private life is going well. The stress just keeps building up, and I'm getting fed up.

examples.jp: 退職してから、貯金は減るばかりだ。
examples.tr: Since I retired, my savings have done nothing but decrease.

examples.jp: このままでは、被害は広がるばかりだ。
examples.tr: If things go on like this, the damage will only spread.

277.explain:
Tense, form : Usually present; the past is used to describe a tendency that continued up to a certain point in time.
Topic : Usually social phenomena, indicators, health conditions, costs…
Nuance : With the tendency meaning, usually negative or worrying; with the “all that remains” meaning, neutral or positive.
Not used with single, momentary actions that do not imply a tendency.

• One-directional tendency: Describes a state progressing in one direction (usually bad) that the speaker can hardly influence. Close in meaning to ～一方だ, but ～ばかりだ usually has a clearer negative nuance.
• All that remains (the last task): Everything is ready; the only thing left is to do V. Nuance of “having reached the final step”.
• Pragmatics: Often used in written language, news and commentary. Avoid it for strongly positive tendencies (～一方だ is more natural).
• Different from ～たばかりだ: ～たばかりだ = “just did…”, indicating a point in time; whereas ～ばかりだ = a tendency or the remaining task.

mistakes: Confusing ばかり and だけ: ばかり often has a critical nuance; in neutral sentences use だけ.

Confusing the two meanings of Vるばかりだ: rely on the context, “tendency” or “only the task remains”.
Confusing ばかり and だらけ: だらけ is used only for negative things, “full of/covered in”.

• When you need to emphasize escalation: “～増える一方でなく、増えるばかりだ” – choose “ばかりだ” if you want a negative nuance.
• With abstract nouns: 不安・負担・圧力・赤字・被害・緊張 combine naturally with “増す/高まる/広がる＋ばかりだ”.

280.explain:
Neutral: it only indicates a state that is maintained; it carries no criticism in itself.
Vないまま often carries a feeling of regret or something missing.
In instructions: そのままにしておいてください (please leave it as it is).
Compared with っぱなし: まま is neutral; っぱなし implies neglect/negative nuance (開けっぱなし: left wide open).

～まま expresses “keeping the original state” unchanged. It is a grammatical noun (名詞), so it takes の/な/だ. The tense and aspect of the main sentence determine the overall time; まま only marks the background state.
• Vたまま: emphasizes “after V is done, leaving that state as it is”.
• Vないまま: “without having done V, leaving things as they are...”, often implying regret or something missing.
• Nのまま / Aなまま: keeping an existing quality or characteristic.

rows: ドアを<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けっぱなし
About a “way/standard”, not a state kept unchanged
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>したとおりに

mistakes: Using Vる + まま carelessly: ×食べるまま → 〇食べたまま / 食べないまま.
Confusing it with っぱなし: in exam questions, っぱなし usually requires a sense of “neglect/annoyance”.
Confusing its meaning with とおり: ～まま does not mean “following instructions” but “keeping the state unchanged”.
280.notes:
• The tense of the main clause determines the time: 開けたままにしていた (had left it open), 開けたままだ (is still open).
• Vる + まま is hardly ever used, except in fixed phrases such as 思うまま（に） (as one thinks), 言うまま (as told), but these are really nominalizations.
• In written language, そのまま/このまま can omit a known subject, which is very natural.
meaning_vi: This sentence pattern is used to express that a state continues as it is without changing. It is often used when an unchanging state leads to an undesirable situation.
examples: 1. ①昨日、窓を開けたまま寝ました。

281.explain:
Based on intuitive feeling/direct evidence (what you see or hear). Not used for pure rumor (use らしい) or strong logical inference (はずだ/に違いない).
Casual, everyday; in formal writing, replace it with ようだ/かのようだ to be more polite.
Do not attach the polite form before みたい: say 雨が降るみたいです (correct), avoid 雨が降りますみたいです (incorrect).
When modifying a noun: N/Adj + みたいな + N. When indicating manner: ～みたいに + V/Adj.
Negative: ～ないみたいだ; past: ～だったみたいだ; conjecture about something that already happened: ～していたみたいだ.

• Meaning 1 (comparison/like): Expresses similarity in appearance or nature. Example: 子どもみたいだ (looks like a child).
• Meaning 2 (conjecture based on observation): “Seems / It looks like”, based on signs you see or hear (not 100% certain). Example: 雨が降るみたいだ.
• Colloquial nuance, more casual than ようだ; lower degree of certainty than に違いない/はずだ.
• Before a noun: use みたいな + N; before a verb/adjective: みたいに + V/A.
• In polite sentences you can use みたいです; formal written language usually prefers ようだ.

rows: Used in written language, more objective
Based on information heard / characteristic features
Colloquial; nuance of “having a touch of”
Looks about to / based on what you see
Based on direct perception that something is about to happen

mistakes: Incorrect polite form: × 降りますみたいだ → ✓ 降るみたいです.
Confusing it with らしい (hearsay): 彼は結婚したらしい (I heard) ≠ 彼は結婚したみたいだ (there are signs that suggest it).
Forgetting to switch to みたいな/みたいに when modifying: × 子どもみたい声 → ✓ 子どもみたいな声.
JLPT: you need to distinguish ～ようだ/～みたいだ/～らしい/～そうだ (様態/伝聞). Pay attention to the context and the source of the information.
281.notes:
• Grammatically, みたい works like a “na-adjective” when modifying (みたいなN) and like an adverb with みたいに.
• In conversation, you can add なんか/どうやら to strengthen the nuance: なんか雨が降りそうな/みたいな感じ.
• Inverted for emphasis: 本当みたいだね, 嘘みたいだ.
• Avoid contradictory conjecture: きっと～みたいだ (unnatural); using たぶん/どうやら with みたいだ is more natural.
meaning_vi: Like ~, it seems that ~
explain: Expresses a judgment based on signs but not certain. Usually based on what you see, hear, or feel; conversational nuance.
Expresses a strong feeling or impression that makes the speaker think so, “just as if…”, even though in reality it is not quite so. Subjective in nature.
Used to give a typical, representative example (“like…, such as…”). Close in meaning to ～ような; helps the listener picture it easily.
examples: 1. 彼は小さい時はとてもわかいくて、女の子みたいだとよく言われたそうだ。
I hear that when he was little he was so cute that people often said he looked like a girl.
2. 理由はわからないけど、彼女、怒っているみたい。
I don't know why, but she seems to be angry.

1. 「星がたくさん出ている。あしたも晴れみたい」

meaning_vi: Comparison, simile (not reality), similar to ～
examples: 1. まだ2月なのに、今日は暖かくて春のようです。

2. あの二人はまるで兄弟のように中がいいです。

meaning_vi: A way of comparing something by using something else that is similar.
examples: 1. ①　鬼のように　おこっていました。

2. ②　あつい！5月なのに、夏みたいですね。

Hana is as beautiful as an actress.
4. ➃　かわいい　手！　もみじみたいな　手ですね。
What cute hands! They're like maple leaves.
meaning_vi: Used when the speaker makes a conjecture from their own personal observations. In formal, serious contexts, ～みたいです should not be used.
examples: 1. ①この肉は少し古いようです。変なにおいがします。

2. ②健君は本が好きなようですね。いつも何か読んでいます。

283.explain:
Evaluating quality: 読みやすい文章／使いやすいツール (positive nuance, emphasizing UX).
Combined with adverbs of degree: 非常に／とても／かなり + ～やすい.
Negative: ～やすくない (not easy); past: ～やすかった.
When talking about human tendencies: 忘れやすい／太りやすい／怒りやすい (tend to V easily).

• Expresses “easy to V” or “having a tendency/property to V easily”.
• Used both for actions (読みやすい, 使いやすい) and for properties/physical characteristics (壊れやすい, 乾きやすい).
• Compared with 易しい（やさしい）: different meanings. 易しい = “easy” in terms of difficulty; ～やすい = “easy to V” in terms of the tendency to carry out a specific action.
• Often objective/useful when describing products, design, and UX.

rows: <ruby>読<rt>読</rt></ruby>みにくい<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>。
Not “easy to V” but “tends to V often”
An independent adjective, not attached directly to an action V

283.notes:
• Can be combined with negative adverbs: 必ずしも～やすいとは限らない (not necessarily easy to…).
• In marketing: “持ちやすい/読みやすい/掃除しやすい” are common UX keywords.
• When describing risks: 壊れやすい → an accompanying warning should be added so it is not taken as positive.

Passive: Agent: N + に/によって + V-られる. によって is used when neutral/objective (発見される,建設される). The topic is usually the target that is affected, marked with は/が.

With 一段: 食べ られる (can eat). Colloquial: 食べ れる (avoid in formal written language).

Honorific: Usually replaced with お/ご～になる to sound natural: お読みになります（＝読まれる）.

• Passive: The subject receives the action. Includes:

Direct passive: 私は先生に褒められた (I was praised).
Indirect/suffering passive (迷惑の受身): 雨に降られて困った (I was troubled by the rain).
Possessive passive: 私は子どもに泣かれた (my child cried and it troubled me).

• Direct passive: 私は先生に褒められた (I was praised).
• Indirect/suffering passive (迷惑の受身): 雨に降られて困った (I was troubled by the rain).
• Possessive passive: 私は子どもに泣かれた (my child cried and it troubled me).
• Ability: Ability, or conditions under which something is possible/impossible. With 一段 the forms are identical, so it is easily confused with the passive; resolve it by context, the subject (が), and complements.
• Spontaneous: Thinking/remembering/feeling naturally. Has a nuance of “unintentional”.
• Honorific: Elevates the subject (a superior) with V-れる/られる. Avoid overusing it as “二重敬語”.

rows: More formal/standard; with <ruby>一段<rt>いちだん</rt></ruby> identical to the passive
<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>が<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>せる/<ruby>話<rt>ばなし</rt></ruby>せます
Objective/formal; suits サ<ruby>変<rt>へん</rt></ruby>: <ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>することができる
<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>することができる
<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>はお<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みになります
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>られてしまった

mistakes: Confusing the ability form of 五段 verbs: 読まれる (passive) ≠ 読める (ability).
Using を in ability sentences: 日本語を話せる → 日本語が話せる is better (more natural).
Overusing ～られる as an honorific in every situation; in business, use お/ご～になる.
Confusing に and によって: specific people usually take に; inventions/works take によって.
284.notes:
• Passive/ability ambiguity with 一段 is resolved by context and particles: 魚が食べられる (ability) vs 魚は猫に食べられる (passive).
• 来れる (これる) is the colloquial form of 来られる (こられる) for ability; avoid it in formal language.
• Avoid “二重敬語”: 召し上がられる is usually considered excessive; use 召し上がる.
• News/science prefer the objective passive with によって: この星は1950年に発見された。
meaning_vi: Passive expression
examples: 1. ①　母に怒られる
Get scolded by my mother
2. ②　夜遅く家に帰ったら、母に怒られた。

285.explain:
Friendly/polite in conversation. With superiors, avoid ～んだ (rude); use ～んです/～のです.
Asking for a reason gently: どうして来なかった んですか。
Leading into a request/suggestion: ～んですが/～んですけど +依頼/質問.
Emphasizing feelings/situations: ～たい んです , ～ている んです .
Formal written language prefers ～のです/～のである (rarely used in spoken language).

～んですか。
1.Conjecture, or confirming information based on what you have heard or seen.
A:　Bさんは時々(ときどき)大阪弁(おおさかべん)を使(つか)いますね。大阪(おおさか)に住(す)んでいたんですか。
A: You sometimes use Osaka dialect, B. Did you use to live in Osaka?
B:　ええ、１５さいまで大阪(おおさか)に住(す)んでいました。
B: Yes, I lived in Osaka until I was 15.
2.Wanting the speaker to give more information about what you have heard or seen
おもしろい　デザインの靴(くつ)ですね。どこで買(か)ったんですか。
Those shoes have an interesting design. Where did you buy them?
3.Wanting the listener to explain the reason for what you have heard or seen.
Use どうして　～んですか。
どうして遅(おく)れたんですか。
Why were you late?
4.Wanting the listener to explain a situation
A:　どう　したんですか。
A: What's wrong?
B:　おなかが　いたいんです。
B: I have a stomachache.

rows: いつがいいでしょうか。

mistakes: Incorrect connection after N/Adj-na: 学生んです × → 学生なんです 〇; 便利んです × → 便利なんです 〇.
Using ～んだ with superiors → rude. Choose ～んです/～のです.
Overusing ～んですが in formal documents → replace it with ～のですが/～しかし.
Confusing its function with ～から: ～んです emphasizes “explanation”, not just a plain link between cause and result.
285.notes:
Note: Used when you want to know more about special information; using it inappropriately will make the listener uncomfortable.
✖この問題(もんだい)、難(むずか)しいんですか。
Is this exercise hard? (Implying the exercise is easy, so how can you be so slow?)
～んです。
Presents a reason, adding a reason for what you said before (It's because ~).
Ex. 1:
A:　どうして遅(おく)れたんですか。
Why were you late?
B:　バスが来(こ)なかったんです。
The bus didn't come.
Ex. 2:
A:　よく　カラオケに行(い)きますか。
Do you often go to karaoke?
B:　いいえ、あまり行(い)きません。
No, I don't go much.
カラオケが好(す)きじゃないんです。
Because I don't like karaoke.
Note: Not used in sentences that simply describe a fact.
✖わたしは　ミラーなんです。

287.explain:
Used to emphasize surprise or suddenness; the speaker usually did not anticipate it.
Rarely used with verbs for long-term, planned activities (勉強し出す sounds like “suddenly started studying”).
Often accompanied by adverbs:突然,急に, いきなり, とたん(に).
The subject can be inanimate (rain, wind) or animate (people, animals).

• Expresses the sudden onset of an action/state, often hard to control.
• Often used with natural phenomena, emotions, and impulsive behavior: 雨が降り出す, 子どもが泣き出す, 彼が歌い出す.
• Has a stronger nuance than ～始める (neutral, not necessarily sudden).
• Some verbs with 出す have become “lexicalized” with their own meanings: 言い出す (blurt out an idea/proposal), 切り出す (broach a subject), 思い出す (remember – does not follow the V-ます+出す pattern).

rows: No emphasis on suddenness; a process
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>める
Gradual change, tendency up to the present
<ruby>言<rt>いいだす</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt></rt></ruby>す/<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す
<ruby>話題<rt>わだい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す

mistakes: Confusing it with compound words meaning “take out”: 取り出す/持ち出す do not mean “start”.
Using it with stative verbs: ×知り出す／×要り出す → unnatural.
Confusing the nuance with ～始める: the JLPT often requires choosing -出す when there is an adverb like 急に/突然.
Wrong form: ×泣く出す → ○泣き出す (continuative form).
287.notes:
• -出す attaches to the continuative form (ます-form minus ます) of Group I/II/III verbs: 笑い出す, し出す; 来(き)出す is rarely used.
• Many combinations are natural, but avoid attaching it to stative verbs or cognitive verbs such as 知る, 分かる (×知り出す).
• In spoken language, -出す adds a sense of drama to a narrative.
explain: ◎ Indicates that an action or some change suddenly begins. Used in spoken language.
examples: 1. 雨が ふり出したから、早く 帰りましょう。
It's started raining, so let's hurry home.
2. 彼女が 急に 泣き出したので、みんな おどろきました。
She suddenly started crying, so everyone was surprised.

examples.jp: おばあさんは、しずかに話し始めました。

288.explain: ◎ Combines with the masu-form of a verb to express starting some action. Used as in「読み始める、食べ始める」(start reading, start eating).

examples.jp: 宿題をやり終わったら、ゲームしてもいい。

289.explain:
Used to emphasize that something is entirely finished, usually followed by the next step or marking a milestone of progress.
Unnatural with punctual verbs or verbs with no clear process (×知り終わる, ×思い終わる).
In spoken language, it is often combined with ところ/ばかり to emphasize the point in time right after finishing.

• Expresses completion of the whole action stated by the verb: “finish doing, end …”.
• Usually used with actions that have duration/a process: 読む, 書く, 食べる, 片付ける.
• ～終える is more formal and emphasizes “finishing completely”; ～終わる is neutral and everyday.
• Different from ～切る: ～切る emphasizes “thoroughly, completely used up/exhausted”, stronger than simple completion.

rows: Nuance of “managed to finish”; written language
<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>る／<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れ<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>る
<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>り<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げる／<ruby>仕上<rt>しあ</rt></ruby>げる

mistakes: Using it with punctual verbs: ×知り終わる → use 分かった/理解できた.
Confusing it with ～切る: 食べ終わる (finish eating) ≠ 食べ切る (eat it all up).
Wrong form: ×読み終わりますた → ○読み終わりました.
JLPT: easy to fall into the trap with “～終える” in formal writing; choose the nuance that fits the context.
289.notes:
• The auxiliary “～終わる” is intransitive (needs no direct object), but if the base V is transitive, there can still be an object: 宿題をやり終わる.
• “～終わったところ/ばかり” indicates the point in time right after completion, often followed by another event.
• For large tasks, ～終える is more formal in reports: 手続きを完了し、審査を終えました。
