〇 あした雨(あめ)が降(ふ)っても、サッカーを　します。
Even if it rains tomorrow, we will play soccer.
✖あした雨(あめ)が降(ふ)るのに、サッカーを　します。
meaning_vi: Expresses that something ~ that seemed natural to expect did not actually happen. This pattern is often used to convey the speaker's surprise, regret, dissatisfaction or complaint. Usually, sentences expressing the speaker's wish or intention, or calling on or urging the other person to act
examples: 1. ①昨日宿題をやったのに、持ってきませんでした。
Even though I did my homework yesterday, I didn't bring it.
2. ②雨が降っていないのに、あの人は傘をさしています。
Even though it isn't raining, that person is using an umbrella.
3. ③このかばんはまだ新しいのに、もう壊れました。
This bag is still new, and yet it has already broken.
4. ④花ちゃんはまだ3歳なのに、漢字がわかる。
Hana is only 3 years old, and yet she understands kanji.
5. ⑤はな「お兄ちゃん、雨が降っているよ。」
けん「本当？あーあ、今日は運動会なのに。」
Hana: "Hey, it's raining."
Ken: "Really? Oh no, and today is sports day..."

374.name: ～のに［time・cost］

examples.jp: 京都に行くのに、２時間半かかります。
examples.tr: It takes two and a half hours to get to Kyoto.

examples.jp: 会場に入るのに、このハガキがいります。
examples.tr: You need this postcard to enter the venue.

374.explain: ◎ 「の」 means 「こと」; expresses how much time or cost is needed to do that thing. Used with the dictionary form of verbs.

375.meaning: Emphasizes the subject: the thing/person... is N (～のはNです)

examples.jp: 私が生まれたのは海に近くて、きれいな町です。
examples.tr: The place where I was born is a beautiful town near the sea.

examples.jp: １年で一番忙しいのは　１２月です。
examples.tr: The busiest month of the year is December.

examples.jp:
A: バンコクで生まれたんですか
B: いいえ、生まれたのはチェンマイです。
examples.tr:
A: Were you born in Bangkok?
B: No, I was born in Chiang Mai.

375.explain: This sentence pattern is a way of emphasizing N.

376.name: ～の［sentence-final particle］

examples.jp: お母さん、今日、学校でおもしろいことがあったの。
examples.tr: Mom, something funny happened at school today.

examples.jp: さくらさん、今日は何時ごろに家に帰るの？
examples.tr: Sakura, around what time are you coming home today?

376.explain: ◎ A shortened form of 「のです」, used between people who are close. With a falling intonation it is an affirmative statement (the subject is female), and with a rising intonation it becomes a question.

377.name: ～ば［hypothetical condition］

examples.jp: これを読めば、わかります。
examples.tr: If you read this, you'll understand.

examples.jp: 練習をすれば、うまくなります。
examples.tr: If you practice, you'll get better.

examples.jp: 安ければ、買うつもりです。
examples.tr: If it's cheap, I plan to buy it.

377.explain: ◎ 「～ば」 is a hypothetical condition pattern; 「A ば、B」 means "when in situation or circumstance A, then B". 「～ば」 is formed by changing the conjugation of a verb or adjective into

examples.jp: わたしは彼女ほど頭がよくありません。
examples.tr: I'm not as smart as she is.

examples.jp: 実際は、口で言うほど簡単なことじゃないです。
examples.tr: In reality, it's not as simple as it sounds.

378.explain: ◎ 「～ほど」 is a pattern expressing comparison; the second clause is in the negative form.
378.notes: In the form 「ＸはＹほど…ない」, it expresses that, taking Ｙ as the standard, Ｘ is at or below Ｙ. For example, 「ＸはＹほど大きくない」 amounts to 「ＸはＹより小さい」. However, whereas 「ＸはＹより…」 simply compares the two, when the sentence pattern 「ＸはＹほど…ない」 is used, it can carry the meaning "both Ｘ and Ｙ are..., but when compared". For example, example ① implies 「今年の夏も暑いが、去年よりましだ」.

examples.jp: ３つめのバス亭でおりてください。
examples.tr: Please get off at the third bus stop.

examples.jp: 手紙の ２枚めにそう書いてありました。
examples.tr: It was written that way on the second page of the letter.

379.explain: ◎ Expresses order, counting from the first.

examples.jp: おいしくて、３個もたべました。
examples.tr: They were so good that I ate three of them.

examples.jp: ねぼうして、２０分もおくれてしまった。
examples.tr: I overslept and ended up being a full 20 minutes late.

examples.jp: 漢字が少し読めるようになりました。
examples.tr: I've become able to read a little kanji.

examples.jp: インターネットでよやくできるようになった。
examples.tr: It has become possible to make reservations online.

examples.jp: 最近、父とよく話すようになりました。
examples.tr: Recently, I've started talking with my father a lot.

381.explain: ◎ Expresses a change: a new situation arises that did not exist before. Attaches to the potential form and the dictionary form of verbs.

383.meaning: Please try to make sure that ~

examples.jp: 毎日運動するようにしてください。
examples.tr: Please try to exercise every day.

examples.jp: あした絶対時間に遅れないようにしてください。
examples.tr: Please make absolutely sure you aren't late tomorrow.

383.explain:
～ようにしてください： Please try to make sure that ~
Guide & explanation
Politely asks someone to do or not do something.
It is softer than ～Vてください or ～Vないで　ください。

384.meaning: Try to... | make an effort so that ~

examples.jp: 野菜を食べるようにする
examples.tr: To make a point of eating vegetables

examples.jp: 健康のために、野菜を食べるようにしています。
examples.tr: I make a point of eating vegetables for my health.

examples.jp: 健康のために、お酒を飲み過ぎないようにしてください。
examples.tr: For your health, please try not to drink too much alcohol.

examples.jp: 「これからは遅刻しないようにします」
examples.tr: 「I'll try not to be late from now on」

examples.jp: 暑いときは、水をたくさん飲むようにしましょう。
examples.tr: When it's hot, let's make sure to drink plenty of water.

examples.jp: 習ったことばすぐに使ってみるようにしています。
examples.tr: I make a point of trying out words I've learned right away.

384.explain:
Emphasizes personal effort; polite when giving advice: ～ようにしてください/お願いします。
～ようにしている expresses a current habit; ～ようにした is the action of starting a habit.
Not used with spontaneous/uncontrollable change (in that case use ～ようになる).

• Expresses “try to...”, “take care to...”, aiming to form a habit or make sure a behavior happens.
• Does not guarantee the result; emphasizes the effort/awareness of the agent.
• The form ～ようにしている emphasizes a maintained, regular state.
• Used for actions that can be controlled by personal volition.

rows: The result of a decision; does not emphasize daily effort.
<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby><ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>ることにした。
Come to / start having a habit
A change of state as a result (usually objective); does not emphasize effort.
<ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べるようになった。
The moment just before doing something; not building a habit.
<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きようとしたが、<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>かった。
Doing something once as a trial; does not emphasize persistence.
<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>試<rt>ため</rt></ruby>してみる。

mistakes: Using it with an uncontrollable verb: × 雨が降るようにする → contradictory (you cannot control the rain).
Confusing it with ～ようになる: × 日本語が話せるようにする (one's own effort) → ○ 日本語が話せるようになる (a resulting change).
Forgetting to switch to the correct negative: × 忘れるようにする → ○ 忘れないようにする。
Using ～ことにする instead of ～ようにする when talking about a habit lacks the nuance of “effort to maintain”.
384.notes:
• Collocations with an intentional nuance: 心がける・意識する・努める are also close in meaning to ～ようにする.
• In instructions/notices: ゴミは持ち帰るようにしてください。 is very common.
• Duration/frequency can be added: 毎日／できるだけ／必ず + ～ようにする。
meaning_vi: So as not to ~, lest ~
explain: ◎ Expresses an effort to avoid a bad result or situation.
examples: 1. 私は、いつも約束の時間に遅れないようにしている。
I always take care not to be late for appointments.
2. あまり疲れないようにしたほうがいいですよ。
You should take care not to get too tired.
Try not to forget your things
2. 毎食後、歯をみがくようにしています。
I brush my teeth after every meal

385.name: ～ように（purpose）
385.meaning: So that, in order to, as | so that ~ | In order to..., so as to...

examples.jp: 忘れないように、カレンダーに予定を書いておく。
examples.tr: I write my plans on the calendar so that I don't forget.

examples.jp: 皆に聞こえるように、もう少し大きな声で話してください。
examples.tr: Please speak a little louder so that everyone can hear.

examples.jp: 健康でいられるように、毎日歩いている。
examples.tr: I walk every day so that I can stay healthy.

examples.jp: 先生に静かにするように注意された。
examples.tr: I was told by my teacher to be quiet.

examples.jp: 合格できますように。
examples.tr: I hope I pass.

examples.jp: 子どものように笑った。
examples.tr: (They) laughed like a child.

385.explain:
The first clause (before “ように”) expresses a target state/ability; the second clause is the action/measure taken to reach that target.
For indirect requests: use “～ように言う/頼む/注意する” to be polite and less direct.
“～ますように” has a humble/polite nuance, often used in writing/emails and prayers.
“N のように/ような” creates a simile; do not confuse it with “ようだ” (judgment / seeming to be like).

• “So that / in order that ...”: aims at reaching a state/ability (being able to hear, see, do...). Often used with potential verbs or results not directly controlled by volition (聞こえる・見える・できる・間違えない...).
• “Like / similar to ...”: used with nouns/“ような/ように” to make a metaphorical comparison.
• The wishing structure “～ますように”: expresses a polite wish.
• In messages/indirect commands: ～ように言う／頼む expresses “do / don't” indirectly and politely.

rows: The agent volitionally performs the target action directly.
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くために<ruby>貯金<rt>ちょきん</rt></ruby>する。
Used with ability/result, not directly controlled.
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けるように<ruby>貯金<rt>ちょきん</rt></ruby>する。
A judgment, different from the actual comparison “ように/ような”.
More casual than “ように/ような”.
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもみたいに<ruby>笑<rt>わら</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れないようにしてください。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～ために: purpose directly controlled by volition → use ために; ability/result → use ように.
Using “ように” with a volitional target verb without the potential form: 日本に行くように勉強する（more natural: 行けるように/合格するために）.
Confusing “ように” (comparison) with “ようだ” (conjecture): 子どものように（like a child）≠ 子どものようだ（looks like a child).
Forgetting the Vない形 for a negative goal: 遅れないように（so as not to be late), not 遅れるように.
385.notes:
• When the goal is an ability/permission: 聞こえる・見える・できる・分かる go with “ように”.
• The two main uses of “ように” (purpose and comparison) are often tested against “ために” and “ようだ/みたい”.
• In safety instructions/signs: 火の取り扱いに注意するように（please be careful when handling fire）.

386.connection: N + の + ようだ / V plain form + ようだ

examples.jp: このパンはすごくかたくて、石のようです。
examples.tr: This bread is really hard, like a stone.

examples.jp: ゆめのように楽しい毎日でした。
examples.tr: Every day was as fun as a dream.

examples.jp: すごくつかれていたので、けさは死んだようにねむっていました。
examples.tr: I was really tired, so I slept like the dead this morning.

386.explain:
◎ ｢Xのよう｣ means resembling something else (X). ｢女の子のよう｣ means [That child is actually a boy but looks like a girl]
◎ In addition, ｢よう｣ can be attached to the plain form of a verb to express a similar meaning.

387.name: ～よう［purpose・result］
387.connection: Vる / Vない (non-volitional) + ように

examples.jp: よごれないように、紙でつつんでください。
examples.tr: Please wrap it in paper so it doesn't get dirty.

examples.jp: 合格するよう、毎日、勉強しています。
examples.tr: I study every day so that I can pass.

387.explain: ◎ 「よう」 is used with the dictionary form of verbs to indicate the purpose or result of an action. 「～よう＋V」 and 「～ように＋V」 have the same meaning.
387.notes: A written-language expression of 「だろうか」. Expresses a question or a rhetorical question. ②～④ are examples of rhetorical questions and can be interpreted as 「…だろうか。いやそうではない」. The plain style is more commonly used.

388.name: ～らしい［conjecture］
388.connection: V・Aい plain form + らしい / N・Na + らしい

examples.jp: 山下さんが会社をやめるらしいと、みんなが言っています。
examples.tr: Everyone is saying that Yamashita is apparently quitting the company.

examples.jp: 彼女は M大学に合格したらしいです。
examples.tr: Apparently she passed the entrance exam for M University.

388.explain: ◎ Means 「そう思われる」; expresses a judgment based on some information. It conjugates like an adjective, with the forms 「～らしい、～らしくない、～らしかった」.
388.notes: Attached to the end of a sentence, it expresses that the speaker considers the content to be fairly certain. The basis for that judgment is objective, such as information from outside or observable facts, not mere imagination. For example, in ①, the judgment 「雨らしい」 is based on the information from the weather forecast. In ⑤, the judgment 「試験がうまくいかなかったらしい」 comes from the situation 「帰ってくるなり部屋に閉じ込もってしまった」. For the difference from 「みたいだ」 and 「そうだ」, see 「みたいだ２」.

examples.jp: まだ、はっきりしません。４、５日中に返事をします。
examples.tr: It's not clear yet. I'll give you an answer within four or five days.

examples.jp: 今月中にこの部屋を出ます。
examples.tr: I'll move out of this room within this month.

examples.jp: 今日中にゴミを捨ててください。
examples.tr: Please throw out the trash by the end of today.

389.explain: ◎ 「～中」 in an expression like 「２，３日中」 means "within that period of time."
389.notes:
meaning_vi: Means doing something within a certain time limit, or while a certain ongoing state continues. 「中」 has two readings: 「ちゅう」 and 「じゅう」.
examples: 1. ①　今日中に
Within today.
2. ②　夏休み中に　一回　会いましょう。
Let's meet once during summer vacation.
3. ➂　授業中に　地震が　ありました。
There was an earthquake during class.
4. ➃　外出中に　どろぼうが　入った。
A thief broke in while I was out.

391.name: Honorific language (sonkeigo) of Vてください
391.meaning: The honorific language (sonkeigo) of Vてください

examples.jp: 係りの者にて来ますので、ちょっとお待ちください。
examples.tr: Someone in charge will be with you shortly, so please wait a moment.

examples.jp: このボールペンをお使いください。
examples.tr: Please use this ballpoint pen.

examples.jp: 変な音がしますね。どこか壊れたようです。
examples.tr: There's a strange noise, isn't there? Something seems to be broken.

examples.jp: 変な味がします。このミルクは古いようです。
examples.tr: It tastes strange. This milk seems to have gone off.

examples.jp: ２階のほうで何か音がしますね。
examples.tr: I hear some kind of sound from upstairs, don't you?

examples.jp: この牛乳、ちょっと変なにおいがします。
examples.tr: This milk smells a little strange.

examples.jp: このスープ、リンゴのような味がします。
examples.tr: This soup tastes like apples.

examples.jp: どんな味がするか、食べてみました。
examples.tr: I tried eating it to see what it tasted like.

393.explain:
◎ Perceiving a sound, smell or taste through the senses.

Something can be perceived, such as a taste, smell or sound (expresses a normal property)
393.notes: Attached to nouns such as におい、かおり、味、昔、感じ、気、寒気、吐き気, it expresses that sensation or perception.

394.meaning: decide on / choose ~ | Decide to choose...

examples.jp: 注文は何にしますか。— カレーにします。
examples.tr: What would you like to order? — I'll have the curry.

examples.jp: 会議は来週の火曜日にします。
examples.tr: We'll set the meeting for next Tuesday.

examples.jp: 部屋を明るくします。
examples.tr: I'll make the room brighter.

examples.jp: 音量を小さくします。
examples.tr: I'll turn the volume down.

examples.jp: 髪型を短めにします。
examples.tr: I'll have my hair cut a bit short.

examples.jp: 無駄遣いをしないことにします。
examples.tr: I've decided not to waste money.

394.explain:
Nにします is very natural and polite in service conversations, with the nuance “I'll take / choose...”.
にします (setting) expresses a decision by the speaker/group; moderately formal.
Change of state: を+Adj-na/N+にします; with Adj-i, くします is required.
ことにします expresses a personal decision; ようにします emphasizes the effort to maintain a habit.

Immediate/situational choice (ordering food, choosing an option): Nにします.
Setting a time/point:会議は３時にします (we decide on 3 o'clock).
Intentional change: を + N/Adj-na にします; with Adj-i use くします.
A decision as a personal commitment: Vる/ない + ことにします (I've decided to...); softer than に決めます.

rows: <ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きすることにします
<ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きするようにします
になる vs にする
<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かになる／<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かにする

mistakes: Adj-i + にします (wrong):早いにします→早くします.
Confusing にします and に決めます: when the question requires a decisive nuance, choose に決めます.
Missing を when changing an object:部屋にします(ambiguous) →部屋をきれいにします.
Using にします instead of ことにします for a decision about behavior:毎日走るにします(wrong) →毎日走ることにします.
394.notes:
In restaurants, question patterns: お飲み物は何にしますか／お決まりですか。
にします can go with degree adverbs:少なめにします／辛さは控えめにします。
Setting options/technical settings:画面の明るさを50％にします。

395.meaning: After, just | Just ~ | Just…, right after…

examples.jp: 先生にお願いしたところ、快く引き受けてくださった。
examples.tr: When I asked my teacher, they kindly agreed to do it.

examples.jp: 先生のお宅へ伺ったところ、あいにく先生はお留守だった。
examples.tr: When I visited my teacher's home, unfortunately my teacher was out.

examples.jp: 一口食べてみたところ、とてもおいしかった。
examples.tr: I tried a bite, and it was delicious.

examples.jp: 調べてみたところ、意外な事実がわかった。
examples.tr: When I looked into it, I found out a surprising fact.

examples.jp: 久しぶりに体重を測ったところ、やはり増えていた。
examples.tr: I weighed myself for the first time in a while, and sure enough, I had gained weight.

examples.jp: 担当者に聞いたところ、本日は不在とのことだった。
examples.tr: When I asked the person in charge, I was told they were out today.

395.explain:
Emphasizes the result or discovery immediately after the action.
The second clause usually uses the past tense; the sentence is narrative and objective.
Not used to talk about habits/regular repetition.
More formal than ～たら in written language when reporting the results of a check/lookup.

• Expresses a result/phenomenon that occurs, or information discovered, right after doing action V.
• Often used with verbs of trying/looking up/short actions: 〜てみる、尋ねる、調べる、連絡する、申し込む…
• Has the nuance of “a single, specific occasion, a new discovery”, unlike expressions of habit.
• Often combines with verbs of perception/judgment: 分かった、気づいた、見つかった、断られた、判明した…

rows: Do A, then find out/get result B
<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>い<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わせたところ、<ruby>満席<rt>まんせき</rt></ruby>だった。
<ruby>外<rt>そと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たら、<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。
<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べてみたら、<ruby>美味<rt>おい</rt></ruby>しかった。
Indicates only a point in time, does not imply a result
V-る/ている/た + ところ
Different time axis: るところ（about to）, ているところ（in the middle of）, たところ（just finished）
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べているところ。
Even if you do A, (it is no use)
Completely different meaning (supposition + negation of the effect)
<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>ったところで、<ruby>許<rt>ゆる</rt></ruby>されない。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～たら: when the question asks you to emphasize the “discovered result”, ～たところ is the better choice.
Using ～たところ for a habit/repeated action → wrong nuance.
Confusing ～たところ with the conjunction ところで “by the way” in conversation.
Leaving out the correct particle after ところ (に/へ/を) distorts the meaning of the time context.
395.notes:
• Verbs expressing an intention to try, 〜てみる + たところ, form a natural collocation when reporting results.
• V-たところに/へ expresses “just as … , … came”; V-たところを emphasizes the point in time of being caught/targeted.
• In business reports, ～たところ is often followed by a conclusion/suggestion.

examples.jp: すみません、この席を譲ってくれませんか。
examples.tr: Excuse me, could you let me have this seat?

examples.jp: 窓を開けてくれませんか。ちょっと暑いので。
examples.tr: Could you open the window? It's a bit hot.

examples.jp: もう一度ゆっくり説明してくれませんか。
examples.tr: Could you explain it once more, slowly?

examples.jp: その資料、メールで送ってくれませんか。
examples.tr: Could you send me that document by email?

examples.jp: 写真を撮ってくれませんか。
examples.tr: Could you take a picture for me?

examples.jp: 道に迷ってしまって、駅まで案内してくれませんか。
examples.tr: I've gotten lost. Could you show me the way to the station?

396.explain:
A cushion phrase is often added: すみませんが／申し訳ないですが／恐れ入りますが + V-て くれませんか to make it less direct.
Compared with くれますか, くれませんか is softer because it is a negative question, expressing the expectation “if possible”.
In casual speech it can be shortened to くれない？; the strongly masculine 〜てくれ (a blunt command) should be avoided.

• Asks the listener to do something “for my/our benefit”. More direct than ～てもらえませんか (receiving), but still polite.
• Effective when the listener has the ability/authority to decide on the action. An apology can be added as a prefix to make it softer.
• Has a slightly “direct request” nuance, so be careful when speaking to superiors/clients; ～ていただけませんか／～てくださいませんか is better.

rows: <ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれませんか
Could I receive the favor of having it done
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>してもらえませんか
ご<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>していただけませんか
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せてくださいませんか
ちょっと<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくれる？

mistakes: Using it with superiors/clients sounds not formal enough → choose 〜ていただけませんか／〜てくださいませんか.
Confusing it with 〜てもらえませんか in JLPT questions on the nuance of “receiving” vs “doing for”.
Leaving out the polite cushion phrase makes the sentence sound abrupt: add すみませんが／恐れ入りますが.
Confusing who benefits: 〜てくれませんか means “do it for me”; it is not used when the benefit has nothing to do with the speaker.
396.notes:
• Adding a reason with ので／から makes it easier to accept: ドアを閉めてくれませんか。寒いので。
• Avoid using it for requests backed by authority in business; use 〜ていただけますでしょうか／〜てくださいませんか instead.
• In casual internal chat with close colleagues, 〜てくれますか is a balanced choice between politeness and naturalness.
meaning_vi: Could you help me?
explain: Softly polite; gives the listener a sense of choice (they can refuse).
The goal is directly related to the speaker's benefit (asking someone to do something for you).
In business emails/phone calls, combine it with いただけますと幸いです to increase politeness: ご対応いただけますと幸いです。
When asking for something that causes a lot of trouble, add an apology/compensation: お忙しいところ恐れ入りますが…
Not used for firm internal commands (use 〜てください instead in close superior–subordinate relationships).
examples: 1. すみませんが、この書類を確認してもらえませんか。
Excuse me, could you check this document for me?
2. 恐れ入りますが、明日までにご連絡してもらえませんか。
I'm sorry to trouble you, but could you contact me by tomorrow?
3. 田中さんに会議で説明してもらえませんか。
Could we ask Mr. Tanaka to explain it at the meeting?
4. もう少しゆっくり話してもらえませんか。
Could you speak a little more slowly?
5. この写真、メールで送ってもらえませんか。
Could you send me this photo by email?
6. 駅まで案内してもらえませんか。
Could you show me the way to the station?
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
V-て もらえませんか | Polite request | Standard, soft | 手伝（てつだ）って もらえませんか
V-て いただけませんか | Very polite request | Highly humble | ご確認（かくにん）して いただけませんか
V-て くれませんか | Direct request | Less humble | 説明（せつめい）して くれませんか
V-て くれない？ | Casual | Used with friends | 貸（か）して くれない？
V-させて もらえませんか | Asking permission to do something yourself | From the viewpoint of the person asking to act | 少（すこ）し休（やす）ませて もらえませんか
common_mistakes: • Confusing who is asked: when speaking to A, attaching に to A in a direct request is unnecessary. “説明してもらえませんか” is enough; “あなたに説明してもらえませんか” sounds distant.
• Using 〜てもらえませんか with someone of much higher status may lack humility; switch to 〜ていただけませんか.
• Confusing it with 〜てください (command). The JLPT often tests the nuance: ください is a mild command; もらえませんか is a soft request.
• Leaving out a polite opening phrase in a formal context (seen as impolite). Add すみませんが／恐れ入りますが.
meaning_vi: Expresses a casual way of making a request (when asking family or close friends)
examples: 1. ①　手伝ってもらえない（かな）？
Could you help me?
2. ②　宿題が分からないんだけど、ちょっと教えてもらえる？
I don't understand the homework. Could you explain it to me a bit?
3. ③　『日本語スピードマスター』って本、見せてもらえないかな？
Could you show me the book called "Nihongo Speed Master"?
meaning_vi: Could you… for me? (casual request) | More polite: ～てくださいませんか

examples.jp: 雪の日は道が滑りやすいです。
examples.tr: On snowy days, the roads are slippery.

examples.jp: この鉛筆はみじかくて、かきにくいです。
examples.tr: This pencil is short and hard to write with.

398.explain:
～Vやすいです： easy to  ~
～Vにくいです： Hard to  ~
Treat the phrases ～Vやすい, ～Vにくい as an i-adjective.

examples.jp: 今からかみを切るところです。
examples.tr: I'm about to cut my hair now.

examples.jp: これから食べるところだ。
examples.tr: I'm just about to eat.

examples.jp: 出発するところに、上司から電話が入った。
examples.tr: Just as I was about to leave, I got a call from my boss.

examples.jp: 寝るところを、子どもに起こされた。
examples.tr: Just as I was about to go to sleep, I was woken up by my child.

examples.jp: 今、会議室へ入るところです。あとで掛け直します。
examples.tr: I'm just about to go into the meeting room. I'll call you back later.

examples.jp: 帰るところだったが、急用ができた。
examples.tr: I was about to go home, but something urgent came up.

399.explain:
Used when an action is just about to happen; the degree of “closeness” is higher than with “V-るとき”.
“ところだった” expresses that you almost did something (but did not).
With “ところに/を/で”: the choice of particle clarifies the relationship between the two events (arrival/interruption/setting).
In conversational style, ちょうど/今/これから are often added for emphasis.

• V-るところ: “about to/just at the start of” an action; immediate and imminent.
• Used with different particles to show the relationship with another event: に (something happens at just that moment), を (being affected), で (setting).
• Compared with “～とき”: “～るところ” puts more emphasis on “just before”, closer to the point in time.
• Often used with words indicating a point in time such as これから, 今, ちょうど, まさに.

rows: Immediate, close to the point in time
A period of time in progress
Emphasizes volition; not necessarily as imminent as “ところ”

mistakes: Confusing “ところ” meaning “place” with “point in time”. Use the preceding verb to tell them apart.
Using “V-るところ” for an action that is still far from starting → unnatural. Use “V-るとき/前に” instead.
Wrong particle: ×出るところを雨が降った → ○出るところに雨が降ってきた.
The JLPT often tests the three patterns V-る/V-ている/V-た + ところ through the accompanying context (ちょうど/今/さっき).
399.notes:
• “ところ” originally means “place/point”; here it means “point in time”.
• “ところを失礼します” is a polite expression used when interrupting, based on “V-るところを”.
• Easily combines with passive/potential states to describe being affected just as you are about to do something.

examples.jp: このいすはちょっとたかいですから、ひくくします。
examples.tr: This chair is a little high, so I'll make it lower.

examples.jp: 娘が帰る前に、この部屋をきれいにしておきます。
examples.tr: I'll get this room cleaned up before my daughter comes home.

400.explain: The agent acts directly on a target and changes it.

401.connection: Vます + すぎだ / Aい (drop い)・Na + すぎだ

examples.jp: 昨日はちょっと食べすぎました。
examples.tr: I ate a little too much yesterday.

examples.jp: 彼はちょっとたべすぎです。
examples.tr: He eats a little too much.

examples.jp: このシャツは、わたしにはちょっと大きすぎます。
examples.tr: This shirt is a little too big for me.

examples.jp: 食べすぎて、おなかが痛くなってしまいました。
examples.tr: I ate too much and ended up with a stomachache.

examples.jp: 先月はお金を使いすぎてしまいました。今月は貯金しようと思います。
examples.tr: I spent too much money last month. I think I'll save this month.

examples.jp: この問題はわたしには難しすぎる。ぜんぜんわからない。
examples.tr: This problem is too hard for me. I don't understand it at all.

401.explain:
◎ Adding「すぎ」to a verb or adjective in the MASU form expresses an excessive degree. Verbs become 働きすぎ」「食べすぎ」, and adjectives become「高すぎ」「長すぎ」. It can be used both as a noun「～すぎ」 and as a verb「～すぎる」.

• Indicates a degree beyond the norm: “too…”, usually undesirable.
• Can be used with V/A; すぎる itself is a verb and can take the negative form or the potential form; the volitional form is rarely used.
• To distinguish “too much” (多すぎる) from “not enough” (少なすぎる), both use すぎる.

rows: <ruby>過度<rt>かど</rt></ruby>なN/<ruby>過剰<rt>かじょう</rt></ruby>なN
<ruby>過剰<rt>かじょう</rt></ruby>な<ruby>反応<rt>はんのう</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Mixing up the form: ×高いすぎる → 高すぎる.
Adding だ with な形容詞: ×静かだすぎる → 静かすぎる.
Confusing it with ～にすぎない in reading comprehension because 過ぎる/過ぎない share the same kanji.
401.notes:
Note:
●　「～すぎ」という名詞の形でも使う。
the noun form [すぎ」 is also used
1.食べすぎ飲みすぎは体に良くありません。
Eating and drinking too much is not good for your health.
2.  テレビの見すぎに注意しましょう。
Be careful not to watch too much TV.

402.name: ～そうだ（hearsay）
402.meaning: I hear that ~（passing on reported information from another source）
402.connection: V/A plain form・Naだ・Nだ + そうだ・そうです

examples.jp: 天気予報によると、明日は雨が降るそうです。
examples.tr: According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: 田中さんは来月結婚するそうだ。
examples.tr: I heard Tanaka is getting married next month.

examples.jp: あの店のラーメンはとてもおいしいそうですよ。
examples.tr: I hear the ramen at that shop is really good.

402.explain:
Passes on information the speaker has learned without adding a personal opinion.

To state the source of the information, add ～によると、at the beginning of the sentence.
Nによると： According to ~
～そうです： I hear ~

This expression describes signs that something is about to happen, as in example ①, predictions about the nature or state of things after observing them, as in examples ②③, or judgments and premonitions based on the outward appearance or condition of things, as in examples ④⑤．

examples.jp: さっきご飯を食べたばかりなのに、もうお腹が空いてしまった。
examples.tr: I ate just a little while ago, but I'm already hungry.

examples.jp: 先月結婚したばかりなので、まだ新しい生活に慣れていない。
examples.tr: I only got married last month, so I'm not used to my new life yet.

examples.jp: 買ったばかりのおもちゃがもう壊れてしまった。
examples.tr: The toy I just bought has already broken.

examples.jp: 今年完成したばかりだ
examples.tr: It was just completed this year.

examples.jp: 引っ越したばかりなので、まだ部屋に何もない。
examples.tr: I just moved in, so there's nothing in my room yet.

examples.jp: さっき聞いたばかりの名前を、もうわすれてしまった。
examples.tr: I've already forgotten the name I heard just a moment ago.

403.explain:
Expresses that an action or event happened not long ago, as felt by the speaker.
Vたところ：The event really has just happened.

Vたばかり：The speaker feels that the event has just happened, regardless of when it actually happened.
Often used in the following structures:

Vたばかりなのに、～　Even though (I) just V, ~

Vたばかりなので、～　Because (I) just V, ~
◎ 「ばかり」expresses that there has been no time for anything else to happen; here it means "right after something happened".

•
Expresses an action that happened recently; the time that has passed from the action to the present is very short.

• Natural translations: “just…”, “only just…”, “recently…”.
• Does not emphasize the exact time (not specifically how many minutes or hours), but emphasizes the feeling that “it happened not long ago”.
• Often used to explain the reason for not being used to something, not being good at it yet, or not being able to do something yet.

rows: Subjective feeling; the exact time is not specified
Just finished / just at the moment of finishing
Emphasizes the point in time “right after finishing”
<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったばかりに、<ruby>怒<rt>おこ</rt></ruby>られた。
More formal than Vたばかり
<ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったばかりです。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～たところ (which specifies the point in time right after an action).
Using it for an action that happened too long ago (such as 2 years ago) → unnatural.
Confusing it with ～たばかりに (cause – bad result).
The JLPT often tests the distinction between たばかり・たところ・たところに・たところで.
403.notes:
•
Subjective: the length of “just” can vary depending on how one feels (e.g. someone who moved to Japan 3 months ago can still say 来たばかり).
• Often used to justify or explain the reason for “not being able to do it yet, not being used to it yet”.
• Signals a state that is new and not yet settled.

405.meaning: Ended up…, have gone and… (casual form of ～てしまった)

examples.jp: 宿題、もう終わっちゃった。
examples.tr: I've already finished my homework.

examples.jp: ごめん、君のプリン食べちゃった。
examples.tr: Sorry, I ate your pudding.

examples.jp: 寝坊しちゃって、電車に乗り遅れた。
examples.tr: I overslept and missed the train.

examples.jp: 財布を落としちゃったみたい。
examples.tr: I think I dropped my wallet.

examples.jp: その話、つい言っちゃった。
examples.tr: I let that slip without thinking.

examples.jp: 本、電車で読んじゃったから、もう返せるよ。
examples.tr: I finished reading the book on the train, so I can give it back now.

405.explain:
Simple completion: does not necessarily involve regret (もうやっ ちゃった よ).
Regret/carelessness: often used with つい、うっかり、気づかずに…
Casual, used with friends/acquaintances; at work, use ～てしまいました to be polite.

• Completing/finishing an action fully (neutral completion).
• Doing something by mistake, with regret, unintentionally (unintentional/mistake nuance), depending on context and intonation.
• Spoken language, casual; not suitable for formal writing (use ～てしまった there).

rows: Can be used in written language and at work
また<ruby>寝坊<rt>ねぼう</rt></ruby>しちゃうよ。

mistakes: Using it in formal writing: × 提出が遅れちゃった → instead: 遅れてしまいました。
Confusing じゃった/ちゃった: 読む→読んじゃった (correct), × 読んちゃった (incorrect for 読む because it is 読んで).
Assuming it always means “regret”: in fact it depends on context and may simply mean “done”.
The JLPT often tests recognizing contractions in fast conversation; pay attention to the sound changes て→ちゃ, で→じゃ.
405.notes:
• A rising intonation/a “あっ” in front strengthens the nuance of “oops/oh no”.
• The contracted negative is rare in standard usage: ～ちゃわない（＝てしまわない）; usually avoided in academic writing.
• It can still be used in casual internal emails, but consider the recipient and the company culture.

406.connection: [sentence/clause] + っていう / N + っていう + N

examples.jp: 彼は「今日は無理」って言ってた。
examples.tr: He said, "I can't today."

examples.jp: このアプリ、使いやすいっていう評判だよ。
examples.tr: I hear this app is easy to use.

examples.jp: 田中っていう医者を知ってる？
examples.tr: Do you know a doctor called Tanaka?

examples.jp: SDGsっていうのは何の略ですか。
examples.tr: What does SDGs stand for?

examples.jp: 明日は休みだって。どこ行く？
examples.tr: I heard tomorrow's a day off. Where should we go?

examples.jp: それっていうの、どういう意味？
examples.tr: What does that so-called thing mean?

406.explain:
Spoken language: って／っていう lowers assertiveness, creating a soft/indirect feel.
In formal speech/standard writing: use と言う／という instead of っていう.
At the end of a sentence, just って means “I hear/I was told that …” in conversation.

• Marks the quotation of an utterance/opinion: “that …”, “said that …”.
• Introduces a definition/topic: “what is called …”, “about …”.
• Naming/identifying: “a person/thing/object called …”.
• Character: very colloquial, softens the statement, sometimes roundabout to avoid being direct.

rows: <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>っていう<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>
Strongly expressive; a different function from quotation.
もう<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いてるってば！

mistakes: Wrong style: using っていう in a thesis/formal exam → change it to という.
Wrong NっていうN structure: × っていう田中人 → 田中っていう人.
Misunderstanding だって: it can mean “I hear” or “because”; rely on the JLPT context to choose the correct meaning.
406.notes:
• Avoid repeating っていう several times in a row in one written sentence; replace it with という/と/の: × AっていうBっていうC → AというBのC.
• In formal naming (self-introductions): ～と申します is very polite.
• だって at the end of a sentence can mean “I hear that …” or “because …” (different grammar).

407.meaning: In the middle of ~ | Right while…

examples.jp: 今かみを切っているところです。
examples.tr: I'm in the middle of cutting my hair right now.

examples.jp: 彼に電話したら、ちょうど食事をしているところでした。
examples.tr: When I called him, he was just in the middle of eating.

examples.jp: 今、バスを待っているところで、もう少しで着きます。
examples.tr: I'm waiting for the bus right now, so I'll be there shortly.

examples.jp: 今、会議をしているところです。後でかけ直します。
examples.tr: I'm in a meeting right now. I'll call you back later.

examples.jp: ちょうど出かけているところに、部長が来た。
examples.tr: The department manager came by just while I was out.

examples.jp: 説明しているところを、邪魔しないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't interrupt me while I'm explaining.

407.explain:
Add 今／ちょうど／まさに to emphasize “right at this moment”.
In polite style, add です/おります: ただいま対応し ているところでございます。
Compared with 〜ている, 〜ているところ emphasizes the moment and is suitable when you need to decline/explain politely.
Often used with sudden interrupting events such as 電話が鳴る、来客が来る、メールが届く…

• Emphasizes the point in time of being “in the middle of” doing an action, often to explain why you cannot do something else or to describe an interruption.
• With ところに/へ: expresses another event happening at exactly that point in time (the phone rings, someone arrives…).
• With ところを: emphasizes being affected during the process (being disturbed, being caught…).
• With ところで: the place/time setting of the ongoing action.

rows: <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べているところ。
これから<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけるところ。
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>着<rt>ちゃく</rt></ruby>いたところ。
Stronger emphasis, often tied to nuisances
<ruby>食事<rt>しょくじ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>最中<rt>さいちゅう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>。
Does not emphasize “right at this moment”

mistakes: Confusing it with 最中に: 〜ているところに also works, but 最中に is stronger about “right in the middle” and is often used with nuisances.
Using ところ with stative verbs: 知っているところ is rarely natural; just use 知っています.
The JLPT often asks you to distinguish Vるところ／Vているところ／Vたところ based on the time context.
407.notes:
• The particle after ところ changes the nuance: ところに（an event arrives）／ところを（being affected）／ところで（setting).
• In business emails: ただいま確認しているところで、判明次第ご連絡いたします is the standard expression.
• Not used with stative verbs that have no clear process (知っているところ is usually unnatural).

examples.jp: 私が寝ている間に、雪が降った。
examples.tr: It snowed while I was sleeping.

examples.jp: 父が留守にしている間に、泥棒が入った。
examples.tr: A burglar broke in while my father was away from home.

examples.jp: 映画を見ている間に、スマホが鳴った。
examples.tr: My phone rang while I was watching a movie.

examples.jp: 子どもが遊んでいる間に、夕飯を作ってしまった。
examples.tr: I finished making dinner while the children were playing.

examples.jp: 会議の間に、重要なメールが届いた。
examples.tr: An important email arrived during the meeting.

408.explain:
Adding a clear time marker makes the sentence tighter: その間に／この間に（during that time）。
B is usually something sudden that does not last; if it lasts, switch to 〜間.
Can be used with the negative:見ている間に気づかなかった（didn't notice while watching）。

• Expresses that event B happens at some point during the period in which A is continuing.
• Mainly used when B is a short action/situation that ends quickly (鳴る、来る、起きる、入る…).
• When A is a lasting state (寝ている、留守にしている、会議中…), 〜間に is very natural.
• If B lasts throughout the whole period A, use 〜間 (without に).

rows: B happens at one point during A
<ruby>昼寝<rt>ひるね</rt></ruby>している<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもが<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>んでいる<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>を<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>る。
While A still holds / Before A changes
<ruby>若<rt>わか</rt></ruby>いうちに<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>する。
Right in the middle of A
<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>最中<rt>さいちゅう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Confusing 〜間 with 〜間に: if B lasts, do not use に. Incorrect example: 勉強している間に音楽を聞いた → better: 勉強している間、音楽を聞いた。
Using 〜うちに for a situation with no “change”: 映画を見ているうちに電話が鳴った → more natural with 〜間に.
The JLPT often asks you to choose between 〜間／〜間に／〜うちに based on whether clause B is a “point” or a “span”.
408.notes:
• N with a time-span meaning: 留守の間に／授業の間に／休憩の間に are very natural.
• In conversation, “この間” usually means “recently/the other day,” which is different from “間に”. Avoid confusing them.
• In written language, for coherence B can be placed before A: 電話が、映画を見ている間に、鳴った。

409.meaning: Expresses that something has been completed early, as in examples ①②, or regret that it is impossible to return to a previous state, as in examples ③④.

examples.jp: レポートは明日出してしまいます。
examples.tr: I'll get the report submitted tomorrow.

examples.jp: 今日買った本はもう読んでしまった。
examples.tr: I've already finished reading the book I bought today.

examples.jp: あの人の名前を忘れてしまいました。
examples.tr: I've forgotten that person's name.

examples.jp: あ、白い服が汚れてしまいますよ。
examples.tr: Oh, your white clothes are going to get dirty!

410.meaning: The sentence pattern ～てもいいです expresses permission or concession. ~てはいけません　expresses prohibition.

examples.jp: 安い部屋を探しています。狭くてもいいです。
examples.tr: I'm looking for a cheap room. It's fine if it's small.

examples.jp: 花ちゃん、一人で川に行ってはいけないよ。
examples.tr: Hana, you mustn't go to the river by yourself.

examples.jp: 入社試験の時の服は、Tシャツではいけません。
examples.tr: For the company entrance exam, a T-shirt is not acceptable.

examples.jp:
トム「ここに座ってもいいですか。」
女の人「ええ、どうぞ。」
examples.tr:
Tom: "May I sit here?"
Woman: "Yes, go ahead."

411.meaning: Expresses cause or reason. In many cases this pattern is used more than ~から／～ので　to state the cause or reason for certain feelings or emotions. After this pattern, besides words expressing emotion such as こまる、さびしい, etc., there are also words expressing the inability to carry out a

examples.jp: 今日はたくさん仕事があって、大変でした。
examples.tr: I had a lot of work today, so it was tough.

examples.jp: 友達がいなくて、寂しい。
examples.tr: I have no friends, so I'm lonely.

examples.jp: 心配で、よく眠れませんでした。
examples.tr: I was worried, so I couldn't sleep well.

examples.jp: 教えてくれて、ありがとう。
examples.tr: Thank you for telling me.

examples.jp: 遅れて、すみませんでした。
examples.tr: I'm sorry I was late.

412.connection: Vると/Vたら/Vば + いい（expectation, wish）

examples.jp: 「お母さんの病気、早くよくなるといいですね」
examples.tr: "I hope your mother gets well soon."

examples.jp: 「あしたは運動会だそうですね。雨が降らなければいいですね」
examples.tr: "I hear tomorrow is the sports day. I hope it doesn't rain."

examples.jp: 今年は就学金がもらえるといいなあ。
examples.tr: I hope I can get a scholarship this year.

examples.jp: 来年は家族で海外旅行ができたらいいなあ。
examples.tr: It would be nice if our family could travel abroad next year.

412.notes: Used both for advice/suggestion (～たらいいですよ) and for expectations/wishes

413.meaning: Just when, right in the middle of | at the time~

examples.jp: 今から会議に入るところです。
examples.tr: I'm about to go into a meeting now.

examples.jp: ちょうど説明しているところなので、少し待ってください。
examples.tr: I'm just in the middle of explaining, so please wait a moment.

examples.jp: 先ほど申し込みを終えたところです。
examples.tr: I've just finished applying a moment ago.

examples.jp: 家を出るところに雨が降り出した。
examples.tr: It started to rain just as I was leaving the house.

examples.jp: お忙しいところを恐れ入りますが、こちらにご署名ください。
examples.tr: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but please sign here.

examples.jp: これから家を出るところです。
examples.tr: I'm about to leave the house now.

413.explain:
Add a time word: これから/ちょうど/たった今to make the meaning of about to/in the middle of/just clear.
In emails/at work: the opening phrase “お忙しいところ恐縮ですが…” is very polite.
V-たところ: often states a discovery/result right after an experience:調べ たところ、～が分かった。
V-るところ is rarely used with lasting actions; it suits the moment of starting.

- “ところ” marks the point/stage (time point) of an action: before it starts (V-る), while it is happening (V-ている), just after it ends (V-た).
- V-たところ emphasizes “just now” more than たばかり (it feels more immediate). V-ているところ emphasizes the immediacy of “right in the middle of”.
- With particles:
- ところに/へ: just when (something comes/goes) “arrived just as … was …”.
- ところを: even though (in a state), another action has an effect; also used in keigo “お忙しいところを…” (apologizing/thanking).
- ところで: has the conjunction meaning “by the way” (not the time aspect of V); be careful to distinguish it.

rows: The exact moment it is happening
Emphasizes being uninterrupted; usually with Nの/V-ている
<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>最中<rt>さいちゅう</rt></ruby>に
Unrelated to the time aspect of V
ところで、<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>議題<rt>ぎだい</rt></ruby>は…

mistakes: Confusing V-たところ with たばかり: the JLPT often tests the “immediate” nuance of たところ.
Mixing up ところで (conjunction) with ところ＋particle: their functions are completely different.
Using V-るところ for a lasting action (×明日旅行に行くところだ) → better to use 前/直前/行くところ “right when about to go” with the context “今/これから”.
Forgetting the correct particle: 来たところに電話が… / 邪魔しているところをすみません。
413.notes:
- The pattern “V-たところ、～” is often used in reports/conclusions: “After doing V, (I) found out/realized…”. This is a structure that states the result of a short investigation/test.
- “ところを” goes with verbs of apologizing/thanking: お忙しいところを申し訳ありません／ありがとうございます。
- Note the ambiguity of V-るところ: add a time adverb “今から/これから/ちょうど” to make it clear it means “about to”.

examples.jp: 高木さんはきのう、あした８時に来ると言いました。でも、まだ来ません。
examples.tr: Yesterday, Mr. Takagi said he would come at 8 tomorrow. But he hasn't come yet.

examples.jp: テレビのニュースで、けさ早く千葉で地震があったと言っていました。
examples.tr: The TV news said there was an earthquake in Chiba early this morning.

examples.jp: きのうの天気予報で、しばらく雨が続くだろうと言っていました。
examples.tr: Yesterday's weather forecast said the rain would probably continue for a while.

examples.jp: 「来週テレビがあると聞きましたが。本当ですか」
examples.tr: "I heard there's a TV (program) next week. Is that true?"

examples.jp: 母の手紙に、先週の祭りはとてもにぎやかで楽しかったと書いてありました。
examples.tr: My mother's letter said that last week's festival was very lively and fun.

414.notes:
Note:
●　「　」があるときは、「　　」の中はていねい体でもよい
when there is 「　　」, the polite form can also be used inside 「　　」。
1.高木さんはきのう、「あした８時に来ます」と言いました。
Yesterday Mr. Takagi said, 「I will come at 8 tomorrow.」

examples.jp: 健康のために、夜9時以降は食べないことにする。
examples.tr: For my health, I've decided not to eat after 9 p.m.

examples.jp: お金を貯めたいので、外食はしないことにした。
examples.tr: I want to save money, so I decided not to eat out.

examples.jp: 今月は無駄遣いをしないことにしている。
examples.tr: This month, I make a point of not wasting money.

examples.jp: 忙しいので、週末の旅行には行かないことにする。
examples.tr: I'm busy, so I'll decide not to go on the weekend trip.

examples.jp: 今日は甘い飲み物は買わないことにした。
examples.tr: Today I decided not to buy any sweet drinks.

415.explain:
Used for personal decisions; emphasizes the speaker's volition/control.
To be polite to the listener: 〜ことにしました（I have decided…）.
Can go with a reason/motive before or after: 〜ので／〜ために + ないことにする.
In a promise to oneself: よし、今日は文句を言わ ないことにする ！

• Expresses a subjective decision by the speaker: “decide not to do V”.
• The form 〜ことにした emphasizes the point in time when the decision was made in the past; 〜ことにしている emphasizes a present habit/rule.
• Can be used for a temporary decision (today) or a long-term one (from now on) depending on context.
• Different from 〜ないことになる: 〜ないことにする means deciding oneself; 〜ないことになる means it is decided by circumstances/rules.

rows: It is decided that one will not do
V-る/ない + ことにしている
<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べないことにしている
<ruby>喫煙<rt>きつえん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>許可<rt>きょか</rt></ruby>しないこととする

mistakes: Confusing it with 〜ないことになる: exam questions often require distinguishing who makes the decision. “会社の方針で飲まないことになった”（because of the company) ≠ “自分で飲まないことにした”.
Use 〜ことにした when telling about a past decision; use 〜ことにする when declaring/setting a rule in the present.
Wrong tense: attaching だ after ことにする is incorrect. There is no “〜ないことにするだ”.
Overusing it with non-volitional behavior: “雨を見ないことにする” is meaningless; use it only for behavior that can be controlled.
415.notes:
• This negative form often goes with consumption/health/bad habit behaviors: 飲まない・食べない・買わない・行かない・言わない.
• To emphasize that it is temporary: 今日は〜しないことにする; long-term: これからは〜しないことにする.
• In conversation, it can be used as a “reminder to oneself,” with a nuance of determination.

examples.jp: 今日は無理をしないほうがいいよ。
examples.tr: You shouldn't push yourself too hard today.

examples.jp: その話は部長には言わないほうがいい。
examples.tr: You'd better not tell the department manager about that.

examples.jp: 夜は一人で出歩かないほうがいいです。
examples.tr: It's better not to go out alone at night.

examples.jp: 空腹でその薬を飲まないほうがいい。
examples.tr: You shouldn't take that medicine on an empty stomach.

examples.jp: 初対面ではあまり踏み込んだ質問はしないほうがいい。
examples.tr: It's better not to ask very personal questions when meeting someone for the first time.

examples.jp: 雨が強いから、今日は行かないほうがいいと思います。
examples.tr: The rain is heavy, so I think you'd better not go today.

416.explain:
Polite: ～ないほうがいいです; Neutral: ～ないほうがいいよ; Softened: ～ないほうがいいと思います。
Used when the listener is free to decide; avoid using it with superiors (switch to ～てはいかがですか/おすすめしません).
When comparing two options, both can be stated:行くより行か ないほうがいい。
Often accompanied by a reason: ～から/ので/ほうがいい。
Not used for actions that have already happened (for regret, use ～ないほうがよかった).

• Advice/suggestion: “You shouldn't do …” based on experience, common sense, or the speaker's opinion.
• Softer nuance than a command; often used when giving personal advice, about health care or safety.
• Shows a choice: between two possibilities, the option of “not doing” is better.
• Not used for an organization's absolute prohibitions (then use ～てはいけない/禁止).
• Often accompanied by ですよ/と思います/かもしれません to reduce directness.
• Compared with ～べきではない: weaker, less moralizing/judgmental; leans toward practical advice.

rows: Affirmative counterpart. Stronger than ～たらどう
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>たほうがいい。
Better not to do it (less bad)
Strong negative comparison, usually when both options are bad
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をつくくらいなら<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>わないほうがましだ。
Strong, with a moral/rule-based judgmental nuance
<ruby>差別<rt>さべつ</rt></ruby><ruby>的<rt>てき</rt></ruby>な<ruby>発言<rt>はつげん</rt></ruby>はするべきではない。
～ないほうが<ruby>無難<rt>ぶなん</rt></ruby>だ/<ruby>身<rt>み</rt></ruby>のためだ
Not doing it is safe/good for you
Stronger than ～ないほうがいい, a warning
<ruby>夜中<rt>やちゅう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>出歩<rt>である</rt></ruby>かないほうが<ruby>無難<rt>ぶなん</rt></ruby>だ。
General set phrase; not only advice to “not do”
<ruby>関<rt>かか</rt></ruby>わらないに<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>したことはない。

mistakes: Wrong form: using 辞書形 instead of ない形. Correct: 行かないほうがいい (not 行くほうがいい when you mean “should not”).
Confusing it with absolute prohibition: ～てはいけない is stronger and more rule-like.
Not distinguishing regret: if it already happened, use ～ないほうがよかった.
Irregular verbs: する→しないほうがいい；来る→来ない（こない）ほうがいい。
Rude when said to a superior/customer: change it into an indirect suggestion to be polite.
416.notes:
• Writing: both ほう and 方 are seen; in formal written language 方 is usually used.
• To be even more polite: ～ないほうがよろしいかと思います。
• Add grounds from experience: ～ないほうがいいですよ、前に失敗しましたから。
• In conversation, drop です to sound casual: ～ないほうがいいよ。

417.connection: Vなければいけない → Vなきゃいけない（contraction; 急がなきゃ）

examples.jp: そろそろ寝なきゃいけない。
examples.tr: I have to go to bed soon.

examples.jp: 締め切りだから急がなきゃ。
examples.tr: The deadline's here, so I've got to hurry.

examples.jp: 明日、早く起きなきゃいけないんだ。
examples.tr: I have to get up early tomorrow.

examples.jp: そんなに食べなくちゃいけない？
examples.tr: Do I have to eat that much?

examples.jp: 子どもを迎えに行かなきゃならない。
examples.tr: I have to go pick up my child.

examples.jp: 雨が降りそう。洗濯物を入れなきゃ。
examples.tr: Looks like it's going to rain. I've got to bring the laundry in.

417.explain:
Very colloquial; used in conversation, chat, and quick notes. Avoid it in formal documents.
The ending is often omitted when the context is clear: もう出かけ なきゃ。High sense of urgency.
Combines well with ちょっと／やっぱ／もう／そろそろ to sound natural: もう行かなきゃ。

• Expresses the meaning “must/have to” in a casual way, in everyday conversation.
• Origin: なきゃ＝なければ (contraction) → “If (you) don't …, it's not OK” → implies having to do it.
• Softer nuance than ～なければならない; the casual equivalent of ～ないといけない/～なくてはいけない.

rows: <ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らなければならない
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>しなくちゃ

mistakes: Confusing it with the prohibition ～てはいけない: the meaning is completely different.
Using it in formal written language (essays/applications): change it to ～なければならない／～ないといけません.
Writing the original form incorrectly: なきゃ＝なければ, なくちゃ＝なくては; avoid the combination “なきゃては”.
Omitting the ending on an exam: もう出かけなきゃ… → if it is not conversation, write it out in full to avoid losing points.
417.notes:
• Sound changes in conversation: ～なきゃ → ～なきゃぁ／～なきゃね to soften.
• The information focus is usually placed before なきゃ for emphasis: 絶対今日中に終わらせなきゃ。
• Negating the obligation uses a different structure: 行かなくてもいい／行かなくてはならないの否定ではない.

examples.jp: 明日早く起きなくちゃいけない。
examples.tr: I have to get up early tomorrow.

examples.jp: 締め切りまでに提出しなくちゃいけない。
examples.tr: I have to submit it by the deadline.

examples.jp: ここは静かでなくちゃいけないから、電話は外でして。
examples.tr: It has to be quiet here, so make your calls outside.

examples.jp: もう行かなくちゃ！
examples.tr: I've got to go now!

examples.jp: 連絡しないと（いけない）。
examples.tr: I have to get in touch (with them).

418.explain:
Formality: spoken language. In written language/formal situations, prefer ～なくてはいけない／～なければならない.
Person: usually I/we; rarely used to directly order the listener (it sounds harsh). For gentle advice: ～ほうがいい/～たほうがいい.
Negating the obligation: use ～ なくてもいい (no need to), not the negative of いけない.
Polite: ～なくちゃ いけません can be used, but it mixes colloquial and polite; normally use ～なくてはいけません.

• Main meaning: obligation/requirement at a casual level: “have to ...”, “definitely have to ...”.
• Nuance: softer than ～なければならない; has the feel of “reminding oneself”, “group rules”, or “strong advice” in conversation.
• Source of the obligation: can be oneself, a schedule, not-very-formal rules, the family/friend context.
• Omission of いけない: when the speaker is in a hurry/noting something to do, they just say ～なくちゃ／～なきゃ.

rows: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>さなくてはいけない。
<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>基準<rt>きじゅん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らなければならない。
Not absolutely obligatory, leans toward opinion
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るべきだ。
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくてもいい。

mistakes: Forgetting “で” before なくちゃいけない with N/na: ×静かなくちゃいけない → 〇静かでなくちゃいけない.
Using it as a direct command to a superior: sounds rude. Switch to ～てください or ～ていただけますか.
Confusing it with negating the obligation using いけない: ×行かなくちゃいけなくない → 〇行かなくてもいい.
Formal writing: avoid ～なくちゃ in reports/written exams; use ～なくてはいけない／～なければならない.
418.notes:
• Basis: ～なくちゃ is a contraction of ～なくては. “ちゃ” comes from “ては” → “ちゃ”.
• ～ないと (いけない/だめ) is very common; when the latter part is omitted, the context supplies the meaning “have to”.
• With Aい/N/na: the meaning “need to (be in a state) ...” is often used when describing conditions to be met: 安くなくちゃいけない (it has to be cheap).
• In polite communication with customers/partners, avoid ～なくちゃ; choose ～なくてはいけません.

419.meaning: The sentence pattern ～なくてもいいですexpresses lack of necessity or concession. ～なければなりませんexpresses necessity, an obligation to do something.

examples.jp: いいホテルはありませんか。駅に近くなくてもいいです。
examples.tr: Is there a good hotel? It doesn't have to be close to the station.

examples.jp: お母さん、はこ、ない？丈夫でなくてもいいよ。
examples.tr: Mom, do we have a box? It doesn't have to be sturdy.

examples.jp: Eメールの返事を書かなければなりません。
examples.tr: I have to write a reply to the email.

examples.jp: ここのサインはあなたのでなければなりません。
examples.tr: The signature here must be yours.

examples.jp:
医者「もう薬を飲まなくともいいですよ。」
病気の人「そうですか。ああ。よかった。」
examples.tr:
Doctor: "You don't need to take the medicine anymore."
Patient: "Really? Oh, what a relief."

420.meaning: Turns a verb into a noun.

examples.jp: 私は本を読むの（/こと）が好きです。
examples.tr: I like reading books.

examples.jp: 一人で生活するの（/こと）はさびしいが、自由でいい。
examples.tr: Living alone is lonely, but it's nice because you're free.

examples.jp: 私は文章を読むの（/こと）は得意ですが、書くの（こと）は苦手です。
examples.tr: I'm good at reading texts, but I'm bad at writing.

examples.jp: 「チンさんが来月結婚するの（/こと）を知っていますか」
examples.tr: "Do you know that Mr. Chin is getting married next month?"

420.notes:
Note:
●次のような文では、「こと」しか使えない。
In sentences like the following, only 「こと」 can be used
1.  わたしの趣味は映画を見ることです。
My hobby is watching movies
2.  わたしが日本へ来た目的は、日本語の勉強をすることです。
My purpose in coming to Japan is to study Japanese.

examples.jp: 夏休みの間に、祖父母の家へ行った。
examples.tr: During summer vacation, I went to my grandparents' house.

examples.jp: 子供が寝ている間に、洗濯を済ませた。
examples.tr: I finished the laundry while my child was sleeping.

examples.jp: 留守の間に、泥棒が入った。
examples.tr: A burglar broke in while I was away.

examples.jp: 会議の間に、一度だけ電話が鳴った。
examples.tr: During the meeting, the phone rang only once.

examples.jp: 在学の間に、交換留学を経験した。
examples.tr: While I was a student, I took part in an exchange program abroad.

421.explain:
Emphasizes a “point” within a span: used for a single event that cuts into a lasting period.
Neutral formality: works well in both spoken and written language; on signs, ～中/～の際 are often used instead depending on context.
Leans toward a lasting background state: before ～の間に there is usually a noun expressing a time span that lasts.

• “While/during”: expresses an action/event that happens at some point within the stated time period.
• Time coverage: ～間に leans toward “a point/a few times within the span,” unlike ～間, which emphasizes “throughout, in parallel”.
• Natural combinations: time nouns (休み、会議、授業、在学) or Vている to express a lasting state.
Core difference: A間、B (B takes place throughout A). A間に、B (B happens once/a few times during A).

rows: Within span A, B happens (a few times)
A point in time within a span
<ruby>授業<rt>じゅぎょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>にメモした
<ruby>授業<rt>じゅぎょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby><ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かにしていた
While A still holds / before state A changes
<ruby>若<rt>わか</rt></ruby>いうちに<ruby>挑戦<rt>ちょうせん</rt></ruby>する

mistakes: Mixing up 間 and 間に: a lasting event must use 間, a point event uses 間に.
Using Vる + 間に with a punctual verb sounds awkward: ×帰る間に 盗まれた → ○帰っている間に? In practice, use ～うちに/～とちゅうで depending on the meaning.
Forgetting 「の」 after a noun: ×夏休み間に → ○夏休みの間に.
421.notes:
• Vている + 間に is more natural than Vる + 間に with verbs of duration: 彼がいる間に vs 彼がいている間に (both are seen, but Vている makes the state clear).
• Nouns expressing states: 留守/在学/勤務/出張 など go very well with ～の間に.
• “この間” also means “recently”; but “この間に” emphasizes a specific period that has just passed.

422.name: ～は…が＋adjective／stative verb
422.meaning: Talks about a state or property. Indicates that 「～」 is the whole and 「・・・」is a part.

examples.jp: 兄は背が高いです。わたしは髪が長いです。父は声が大きいです。
examples.tr: My older brother is tall. I have long hair. My father has a loud voice.

examples.jp: （わたしは）おなかが痛いです/目が疲れました/熱があります。
examples.tr: (I) have a stomachache / my eyes are tired / I have a fever.

examples.jp: わたしの部屋は窓が大きいです。
examples.tr: My room has big windows.

examples.jp: あのスーパーの野菜は値段が安くて新鮮です。
examples.tr: The vegetables at that supermarket are cheap and fresh.

examples.jp: この公園は緑が多くて、気持ちがいいです。
examples.tr: This park has lots of greenery and feels pleasant.

examples.jp: 東京は車が多いですが、わたしのふるさとは車が少ないです。
examples.tr: Tokyo has a lot of cars, but my hometown has few.

423.meaning: Should be, ought to be | Surely ~
423.connection: V・Aい plain form + はずだ / Na + な / N + の

examples.jp: 今日は祝日のはずだ。
examples.tr: Today should be a holiday.

examples.jp: 彼はもう駅に着いているはずだ。
examples.tr: He should have arrived at the station by now.

examples.jp: パスポートはこの引き出しにあるはずだ。
examples.tr: The passport should be in this drawer.

examples.jp: そんな高い店には学生は行かないはずだ。
examples.tr: Students wouldn't go to such an expensive place.

examples.jp: 彼は来るはずだったが、来なかった。
examples.tr: He was supposed to come, but he didn't.

examples.jp: それは彼のミスのはずがない。
examples.tr: There's no way that was his mistake.

423.explain:
The basis for the inference needs to be clear (a timetable, what someone said, experience).
More refined when speaking politely: ～はずです／～はずでしょう（softer）.
Expresses a contradiction: ～はずなのに + a result contrary to expectation.
Strong negation: ～はずがない ＞ ～ないはずだ in terms of negative nuance.
Avoid using it for requests/commands; it is a judgment, not volition.

- Meaning: “Surely/by rights… (according to common sense, a plan, or a reason)”. The degree of conviction is higher than だろう/でしょう, based on clear grounds (information, a schedule, logic).
- Nuance: An assertion with grounds. In the negative ～はずがない, it is a strong negation because it goes against common sense/the grounds.
- Tense: ～はずだった expresses “should have/was planned”, often used with が／のに to state a contrary result.
- Combinations: Can be used with ある/いる/可能・受身・使役, etc.

rows: Strong, based on intuition/evidence; close to はずだ but with a more subjective, assertive nuance
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>犯人<rt>はんにん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない。
Moral norms/rules, not a logical prediction
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るべきだ。
Strong negation, more colloquial than ～はずがない
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるわけがない。

mistakes: Wrong linking particle with nouns: use Nのはずだ, not Nはずだ.
Confusing it with だろう/でしょう: when the question requires “firm grounds” → choose ～はずだ.
Confusing the past: 来るはずだった（expectation in the past）≠ 来たはずだ（conjecture that it happened）.
Combining it with a command/request is unnatural: × 来るはずだ、来なさい。
423.notes:
• N + の + はずだ is the standard form; avoid N + はずだ (without の) in formal written language.
• “来るはずだった” expresses an expectation at a point in time in the past; “来たはずだ” is a conjecture that something has surely happened.
• ～はずがない emphasizes negation based on common sense/what is known; it is stronger than ～ないはずだ.
• In polite speech: ～のはずです/～のはずではありません are used at work and in emails.

424.name: ～は～に　（causative-passive form）
424.meaning: An expression combining the causative and the passive. Indicates having to do something because someone forced you to, or an emotion arising from some trigger.
424.connection: N1は + N2に + V causative-passive form

examples.jp: クリーニング代を払わされました。
examples.tr: I was made to pay the cleaning fee.

examples.jp: わたしは子どものころよく兄に泣かされた。
examples.tr: When I was a child, my older brother often made me cry.

examples.jp: 高校で毎日　10キロも走らされた。
examples.tr: In high school, I was made to run as much as 10 km every day.

examples.jp: いつもかのじょに待たされる。
examples.tr: I'm always kept waiting by her.

426.connection: N1は + N2ほど + A negative (～くありません/～ない)

examples.jp: 私は兄ほど背が高くありません。
examples.tr: I'm not as tall as my older brother.

examples.jp: 日本語は英語ほど発音が難しくない。
examples.tr: Japanese isn't as hard to pronounce as English.

examples.jp: 今年は去年ほど雪が降りません。
examples.tr: It doesn't snow as much this year as it did last year.

examples.jp: この問題は思ったほど複雑ではありません。
examples.tr: This problem isn't as complicated as I thought.

examples.jp: 彼は私ほどコーヒーを飲まない。
examples.tr: He doesn't drink as much coffee as I do.

426.explain:
Polite form/written language: ～くありません／～ではありません; spoken language: ～くない／～じゃない.
You can add それほど/思ったほど to adjust the standard of comparison: “not to that degree/not as much as I thought”.
The word order is fixed: AはBほど…ない. Do not move B into the subject position.

• “A is not as … as B” (comparison of inferiority in the negative form).
• ほど expresses “to the degree of B”; add ない/ありません to negate the degree of A compared with B.
• Used naturally for both qualities (tall, difficult) and actions (eat, study, speak).

rows: A is not as … as B
Negative form of the comparison of inferiority
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>ほど<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>くない
States the greater side, not used in the negative
<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>のほうが<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>い
～ほどではない／ほどでもない
Compares the degree with an abstract standard
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>するほどではない
More casual, with a nuance of approximation
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>と<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じくらい<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い

mistakes: Wrong な-form: “親切くない” → correct: “親切ではない”.
Confusing the order: “BはAほど…” is not equivalent; A must stay as the item that is less.
Confusing it with より: AはBより～ is used when A is more than B, not as the negative form of inferiority.
Dropping ほど: “AはBない” is incorrect; ほど is the core of the comparison.
426.notes:
• With Aな/N: use ではない/ではありません, not ～くない.
• The subjective evaluation expressions “思ったほど～ない/予想したほど～ない” are very natural in essays.
• A can be omitted when the context is clear: 思ったほど難しくない。

427.name: ～ば（conditional form）
427.connection: Vば / Aければ / N・Naなら(ば) + [sentence/clause]

examples.jp: ８時にうちを出れば、８時１５分の電車に間に合うでしょう。
examples.tr: If you leave home at 8:00, you'll probably make the 8:15 train.

examples.jp: 「日本語の新聞が読めますか」「ええ、辞書を使えば」
examples.tr: "Can you read Japanese newspapers?" "Yes, if I use a dictionary."

examples.jp: 天気がよければ、ここから富士山を見ることができます。
examples.tr: If the weather is good, you can see Mt. Fuji from here.

examples.jp: 「食べたくなければ、食べなくてもいいですよ」
examples.tr: "If you don't want to eat it, you don't have to."

examples.jp: 「今度の日曜日、もしひまなら遊びに来てください」
examples.tr: "If you're free this Sunday, please come over."

examples.jp: 日本語が上手でなければこの仕事はできません。
examples.tr: If your Japanese isn't good, you can't do this job.

427.notes:
Note:
●文末は過去形にならない。（＝結果が出ている文には使えない）
The end of the sentence cannot be in the past.(=cannot be used in a sentence where the result has already appeared)
X　クーラーをつけらば、すぐに涼しくなった。
X if I turn on the air conditioner, it immediately became cool
〇クーラーをつければ、すぐに涼しくなるだろう。
〇 If you turn on the air conditioner, it will probably get cool right away.
〇クーラーをつけたら、すぐに涼しくなった。
〇 when I turned on the air conditioner, it quickly became cool.

428.name: ～ます in polite speech
428.meaning: Polite form within compound sentences: ～まして/～ますので/～ますのに

examples.jp: ハンスがゆうべ熱を出しまして、けさもまだ下がらないんです。
examples.tr: Hans ran a fever last night, and it still hasn't gone down this morning.

examples.jp: きょうは学校を休ませますので、先生によろしくお伝えください。
examples.tr: I'm keeping my child home from school today, so please pass that on to the teacher.

428.explain: In spoken language, verbs are sometimes used like this: V ます まして、Vますので、Vますのに… to make speech sound more formal and polite.

429.meaning: A sentence pattern expressing a time limit. ～まで is usually followed by sentences expressing a continuous action or state. へまでに is usually followed by sentences expressing a momentary action.
429.connection: N/Vる + まで + [continuing action] / N/Vる + までに + [action at a point in time]

examples.jp: 飛行機の出発時間までここで待っています。
examples.tr: I'll be waiting here until the plane's departure time.

examples.jp: この仕事が終わるまで帰らないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't go home until this work is finished.

examples.jp: 20日までに旅行のお金を払います。
examples.tr: I'll pay for the trip by the 20th.

examples.jp: お客さんが来るまでに部屋を片付けてね。
examples.tr: Tidy up the room by the time the guests arrive, okay?

430.meaning: It seems…, apparently… | It looks like ~
430.connection: V・Aい plain form + ようだ / Na + な / N + の

examples.jp: 部屋の電気がついている。アリさんは部屋にいるようだ。
examples.tr: The light in the room is on. Ali seems to be in the room.

examples.jp: 田中さんは歌が好きなようです。よく歌っています。
examples.tr: Tanaka seems to like singing. They're often singing.

examples.jp: 「この地図を見てください。駅はここからあまり遠くないようですよ」
examples.tr: "Please look at this map. It seems the station isn't very far from here."

examples.jp: 「このノート、だれのでしょうか」「テイさんのノートのようですよ。ここにTと書いてありますから」
examples.tr: "Whose notebook is this?" "It seems to be Tei's notebook, because it says T here."

examples.jp: のどが痛い。かぜがひいたようだ。
examples.tr: My throat hurts. I seem to have caught a cold.

examples.jp: 「オウさん、このごろやせたようですね。どうしたのですか」
examples.tr: "Ou, you seem to have lost weight lately. What happened?"

430.explain:
“～ようだ” is neutral and can be used in written language. Polite: ～ようです.
Comparison with “～みたいだ”: みたいだ is casual and colloquial; ようだ is more formal.
Use “～のように/～のような” when you want to turn it into an adverbial/attributive modifier.
When the degree of certainty is low or to soften the sentence, you can use: ～ようだと思う, ～ように感じる.
To describe a clearly visible appearance, そうだ（様態） is more natural:雨が降り そうだ (it looks like it's going to rain).

• Conjecture based on sensory/indirect evidence: “it seems/apparently”. Example: 声からすると彼のようだ。
• Metaphor/comparison: “like”. Example: 綿のように柔らかい。
• Describes outward appearance/a general impression, more objective than みたいだ in written language/for JLPT scoring.
• The form ～ように also indicates a goal/manner (a different meaning from conjecture): 間違えないように書く。

rows: <ruby>日本人<rt>にほんじん</rt></ruby>らしい<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>。
A source of information, not personal conjecture

mistakes: Wrong connection: 学生だようだ × → 学生のようだ 〇.
Confusing it with そうだ（様態）: “looks like it's going to rain” → 降りそうだ, not 降るようだ.
Overusing みたいだ in JLPT style: prefer ようだ/ようです in standard answers.
Forgetting to switch to Aな/ Nの when used as an attributive modifier: 夢のような vs 夢ような ×.
430.notes:
• “かのようだ” strengthens the metaphorical nuance, written language: 何も知らないかのようだ。
• “～ようでは/ようじゃ” states a condition leading to a negative evaluation: そんなに勉強しないようでは合格できない。
• “～ようなら/ようだったら” is a hypothetical condition based on a judgment: 雨のようなら中止します。
• Watch the connection: Nのようだ, Aなようだ (not Nだようだ / Aだようだ).

432.meaning: A way of quoting a command, advice, or a request.

examples.jp: 考えるように言われました。
examples.tr: I was told to think about it.

examples.jp: 先生に宿題を忘れないように言われました。
examples.tr: My teacher told me not to forget my homework.

examples.jp: 明日は、いつもより　30分早く来るように言われた。
examples.tr: I was told to come 30 minutes earlier than usual tomorrow.

examples.jp: となりの人に、もう少し静かにするように言われた。
examples.tr: The person next to me told me to be a little quieter.

433.name: ～ように（wish）
433.meaning: Expresses a wish that something will become ~. Often used with verbs that do not include the speaker's volition (non-volitional verbs, verbs with a potential meaning (①）or verbs whose subject is a third person (②), etc.).
433.connection: Vるように / Vないように + [sentence/clause]

examples.jp: 話がよく聞こえるように、前の方に座りましょう。
examples.tr: Let's sit toward the front so that we can hear the talk well.

examples.jp: いい風が入るように、窓を大きく開けた。
examples.tr: I opened the window wide to let a nice breeze in.

examples.jp: 雪の日、学校に遅れないように、早く家を出ました。
examples.tr: On the snowy day, I left home early so that I wouldn't be late for school.

examples.jp: けがをしないように、気をつけてね。
examples.tr: Be careful not to get hurt, okay?

434.connection: V plain form + らしい らしく らしくない / N / Na / Aい

examples.jp: 大山さんは拾ってきたネコを育てているそうだ。いかにも動物好きな彼らしい。
examples.tr: I heard that Oyama is raising a cat he found. That's just like him, being such an animal lover.

examples.jp: 「そのセーターの色、春らしくてすてきね」
examples.tr: "The color of that sweater is so springlike and lovely."

examples.jp: 「就職したのだから、もっと社会人らしくしなさい」
examples.tr: "You've got a job now, so act more like a working adult."

examples.jp: 彼女は体がじょうぶで、病気らしい病気をしたことがない。
examples.tr: She's very healthy and has never had what you'd call a real illness.

examples.jp: 彼は来ないらしい。
examples.tr: Apparently he isn't coming.

examples.jp: 明日は寒くなるらしいよ。
examples.tr: I hear it's going to get cold tomorrow.

434.explain:
Hearsay “らしい” expresses a conjecture based on a source (a rumor/what someone said); the speaker does not assert it with certainty.
“～そうだ” (hearsay) has the nuance of directly reporting what someone else said; “らしい” is indirect and softer, showing that the speaker is piecing together sources.
In the meaning “typical of”, “～らしい” is an i-adjective and can be conjugated as らしく, らしさ.

• Meaning 1 (hearsay): Based on information heard/an indirect source → “it seems/I heard that …”. A moderate degree of certainty, a conjecture from a source.
• Meaning 2 (typicality): Expresses being “truly/befitting” a noun according to a model/social characteristics.
• N/Na before らしい: do not use だ. Example: 便利らしい（do not say 便利だらしい）.

rows: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>によると、<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みだそうだ。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るようだ／みたいだ。
Colloquial, sometimes with a critical nuance
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもっぽい<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Adding “だ” before らしい: ×便利だらしい → ○便利らしい。
Confusing “らしい” (hearsay) with “そうだ（様態）” meaning “looks like”: 雨が降りそうだ ≠ 雨が降るらしい.
Confusing “子どもらしい”（truly childlike, positive) with “子どもっぽい”（childish, can have a critical nuance).
434.notes:
1) It is easy to confuse ～らしい (befitting/typical) with ～らしい (I heard).
→ Here ～らしい expresses “full of the character of, true to the characteristics of N”.
2) It is not used to pass on rumors.
→ Rumors/hearsay usually use: 普通形＋らしい.
3) Often used with nouns of role, personality, or style.
→ The meaning is close to “suitable for, worthy of” (にふさわしい).

examples.jp: 仕事が忙しいと、昼ご飯を食べないことがある。
examples.tr: When I'm busy with work, I sometimes don't eat lunch.

examples.jp: この道は冬になると凍結することがある。
examples.tr: This road sometimes freezes over in winter.

examples.jp: 外国人にはこの漢字が読めないことがある。
examples.tr: Foreigners sometimes can't read this kanji.

examples.jp: 人によっては生魚が苦手なことがある。
examples.tr: Some people don't like raw fish.

examples.jp: たまに電車が遅れることがある。
examples.tr: Trains are occasionally late.

examples.jp: 疲れすぎて、眠れないことがある。
examples.tr: Sometimes I'm so tired that I can't sleep.

435.explain:
Often used with:時々, ときどき, たまに, まれに, よく (less often),人によっては,場合によっては.
In descriptions/rules: ～では…ことがある states a general possibility.
The negative “ないことがある” is softer than “ない”: “there are times when … not”.
Formal: ～ことがあります (~ます) keeps it polite in reports/presentations.

• An action/event happens “at times/sometimes” (not regularly, depending on the situation).
• Used to state a general possibility of occurrence, without committing to a specific frequency.
• A polite expression that reduces absoluteness; suitable when you want to soften a statement.
• The negative ないことがある states exceptions: “there are also times when … not”.

rows: A phenomenon that recurs under certain conditions
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れることがある
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったことがある
Somewhat stiff/more objective, used in instructions
<ruby>認証<rt>にんしょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>する<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>がある
<ruby>週末<rt>しゅうまつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>たりする

mistakes: Confusing it with V-たことがある (experience): “日本へ行くことがある” ≠ “行ったことがある”.
Using the absolute simple present instead of the softening pattern: “必ず遅れる” → use “遅れることがある” when you are not sure.
Adding the wrong subject: “人は～ことがある” is too general; use a specific setting: この地域では～ことがある。
435.notes:
• If you add も: V-ることもある → “there are also times when”, emphasizing one possibility among many.
• In technical documents/customer service, “～ことがあります” is used to avoid legal risk (no absolute commitment).
• Put “ごくまれに/稀に” in front to lower the probability: ごくまれにエラーが発生することがある。

examples.jp: 今年から毎日英語を勉強することにする。
examples.tr: Starting this year, I'll study English every day.

examples.jp: 健康のため、酒を飲まないことにした。
examples.tr: I decided not to drink for the sake of my health.

examples.jp: 節約のため、外食は週一回にすることにしている。
examples.tr: To save money, I make it a rule to eat out only once a week.

examples.jp: 雨が強いので、今日は車で行くことにする。
examples.tr: It's raining hard, so I'll go by car today.

examples.jp: この件は、なかったということにしよう。
examples.tr: Let's just say this never happened.

436.explain:
First person in the present/past tense: emphasizes personal volition. With a third person, context is needed to show their intention.
～ことにしている expresses a habit and can be used with frequency words:毎日/いつも/なるべく.
In conversation, ～ことにする can carry the nuance of “having just decided”: よし、これにする！
Often appears with a reason: ～ので/ために + ことにする.

• Expresses a deliberate decision by the speaker/agent after consideration.
• ～ことにしている: the decision has turned into a personal habit/rule, still maintained by oneself.
• ～ということにする: to treat as…, used for a “temporary agreement/assumption”.
• An active nuance, in contrast to ～ことになる (a decision made by outside parties/a process).

rows: It has been decided/end up having to
A decision made by outside parties/a process
<ruby>転勤<rt>てんきん</rt></ruby>することになった
Emphasizes effort, not necessarily a firm decision
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>るようにする
A nuance of “consider it as” rather than deciding to do
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>したということにする

mistakes: Confusing it with ことになる: “会社が決めた” → you must use ことになる, not ことにする.
Using ことにしている for a fresh decision: when you have just decided, ことにした is more natural.
Third person without grounds for their intention: 彼は来ることにした (needs context/a source of information).
Confusing it with ようにする: ようにする emphasizes effort, not a firm decision.
436.notes:
• In group plans, using ～ことにする sounds like you decided on your own; more polite: ～ことにしませんか (shall we decide on it together?).
• Nuance of timing: ことにした (already decided) vs ことにする (deciding right now/about to decide).
• When reporting someone else's volition, add ようだ/という: 彼は留学することにしたようだ。

437.meaning: Means doing something before the action in the first clause is carried out.
437.connection: Vる + とき（the action in the second clause happens first）

examples.jp: 行くとき
examples.tr: When going

examples.jp: ごばんを食べるとき「いただきます」と言う。
examples.tr: We say 「いただきます」 when we eat a meal.

examples.jp: 明日家を出るとき電話しますね。
examples.tr: I'll call you tomorrow when I leave the house.

examples.jp: きのうねるときめざまし時計をセットした。
examples.tr: Yesterday, when I went to bed, I set my alarm clock.

437.notes: Takes the dictionary form of a verb expressing an action and indicates that another act or event takes place before that action is performed, or simultaneously in parallel with it. ① and ② are examples of the former, ③ and ④ of the latter.

438.connection: Vる + ときに（not yet happened） / Vた + ときに（already happened）

examples.jp: 日本へ行くときに、カメラを買った。
examples.tr: I bought a camera before I went to Japan.

examples.jp: 日本へ行ったときに、カメラを買った。
examples.tr: I bought a camera when I was in Japan.

examples.jp: 出かけるときは、電気を消してください。
examples.tr: Please turn off the lights when you go out.

examples.jp: 子どものときに、よく川で遊んだ。
examples.tr: When I was a child, I often played in the river.

examples.jp: 忙しいときほど、休憩が大事だ。
examples.tr: The busier you are, the more important it is to take breaks.

examples.jp: 困ったときには、遠慮なく相談してください。
examples.tr: When you're in trouble, please feel free to talk to us.

438.explain:
Used to set a time reference for the main action; the “とき(に)” clause can come either before or after.
With verbs of motion such as行く/来る/帰る: V-るとき usually = “before going/coming/returning”, V-たとき = “after having gone/come/returned”.
“に” is usually used when the main action happens exactly at that reference (a point in time); “に” is omitted when speaking in general (habits, situations).
Do not use “とき” for a strong cause-and-result relationship (use ～ので/から instead) or for conditions (see ～たら/～と).

• Expresses “when/at the time …” – a point in time at which another action/event takes place.
• V-るとき(に): the time reference is before or just before the action happens (for movement/going somewhere, it is usually understood as “before”).
• V-たとき(に): the time reference is after the action has taken place.
• “に” makes the “point” nature of the time clear; without “に” the meaning does not change much and has a more general nuance.
• The tense in the “とき” clause is relative tense, determining the before/after relationship with the main clause.

rows: A point in time; the tense in the subordinate clause determines before/after
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くとき/<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>ったとき
About to/right at the moment of starting
Closer to the moment than “とき” (immediacy)
Extends over a period of time, not a point
<ruby>授業<rt>じゅぎょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>けているあいだ
<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったら、<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して
Clearly indicates an absolute temporal relationship
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>する<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に/<ruby>後<rt>ご</rt></ruby>で

mistakes: Confusing V-るとき with V-たとき: 日本へ行くとき/行ったとき mean before going/after arriving.
Forgetting “の” with nouns: ×子どもとき → ○子どものとき.
Using “とき” instead of “あいだ” with an ongoing action: ×勉強するときずっと → ○勉強しているあいだずっと.
Overusing “に”: not grammatically wrong, but it can make the style heavy; choose according to nuance.
JLPT: trick questions often change the tense in the “とき” clause to test your understanding of the before/after relationship.
438.notes:
• The tense in the “とき” clause is relative: 現在形 does not only mean “present” but “simultaneous/before” depending on the verb.
• With adjectives/nouns: Aい/ Aな/ Nの + とき expresses a state as a time reference.
• “ときどき” is an adverb meaning “sometimes”, not the structure “とき + とき”.

examples.jp: 今、会議中（ちゅう）です。
examples.tr: We're in a meeting right now.

examples.jp: 授業中にスマホを使ってはいけません。
examples.tr: You must not use your smartphone during class.

examples.jp: 日本では、桜は3月から4月中（じゅう）に咲きます。
examples.tr: In Japan, cherry blossoms bloom from March through April.

examples.jp: 一日中（じゅう）雨が降っていた。
examples.tr: It was raining all day long.

examples.jp: 世界中（じゅう）の人々が注目している。
examples.tr: People all over the world are paying attention.

439.explain:
N + ちゅう : Used for a state in progress → “in the middle of…”.
Example:使用中（in use）,勉強中（studying）.
N + じゅう : Indicates the whole scope → “throughout…”, “all over…”.
Example:一年中（all year round）,日本中（all over Japan）.
When it is hard to tell them apart, you can rely on the meaning of the sentence or the dictionary reading.

•
① In the middle of…（～しているところ）：expresses an action or state in progress.
“While…”, “in the middle of…”.

•
② The whole / throughout / all over…（～の全体）：expresses the whole scope of time/space.
“Throughout…”, “all over…”.

•
Pronunciation:

・Depending on the word it attaches to, it is read ちゅう or じゅう.
・N + ちゅう：in progress (授業中, 使用中, 会議中).
・N + じゅう：throughout, the whole scope (一日中, 世界中, 年中).
