Natural in conversation; in formal written language, consider ほど when talking about degree.

Approximation: indicates an approximate quantity/time (3時間くらい = about 3 hours).
Degree, intensity: states a threshold, “to the point that…” (泣きたいくらい嬉しい = so happy I want to cry).
Minimum/expected level: with せめて/少なくとも, expresses “at least…”.
Nuance: くらい has a standard nuance; ぐらい leans more toward spoken language (see the comparison section).

rows: Standard; works well for both degree and quantity
to the point of; as … as
More formal; used in the negative structure “Aほど～ない”
<ruby>想像<rt>そうぞう</rt></ruby>したほど<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しくない
Only attaches to a point in time; not used for quantities

mistakes: Doubling approximation words: “3時ごろくらい” is incorrect; choose one: “3時ごろ” or “3時くらい”.
Using くらい for the negative comparison “Aくらい～ない” is unnatural; use “Aほど～ない”.
Confusing “only” with “about”: “三人だけ” (only 3 people) differs from “三人くらい” (about 3 people).
Forgetting the emphatic particle: to emphasize a minimum, you need “～くらいは”: これくらいは覚えよう。
525.notes:
“これくらい/それくらい/あれくらい/どれくらい” are very common phrases in questions and answers about degree/quantity.
In minimum comparisons: “これくらいはできるでしょ” stresses the lowest expected level.
“Vるくらいなら～” is a conditional pattern meaning “if it comes to having to V, I would rather ~” (a separate, advanced grammar point).
meaning_vi: About…; around… (estimate)
To the point of… (degree)
Only about…; nothing much (low evaluation)
explain: Expresses a rough estimate of quantity/time/distance… (not exact).
Expresses a strong degree: “to the point of…”. Comes after a clause/verb/adjective to emphasize degree.
Used to downplay: “only about…”. Often carries a nuance of low evaluation or treating something as insignificant.
examples: 1. ここから駅まで１０分ぐらいだ。
It's about 10 minutes from here to the station.
2. もう動けないくらい疲れた。
I'm so tired I can't move anymore.
3. ライバルに負けた。悔しくて泣きたいぐらいだ。
I lost to my rival. I'm so frustrated I could cry.
4. 彼くらいの背の高さなら、棚に手が届くだろう。
Someone about as tall as him could probably reach the shelf.
5. かぜくらいで仕事を休めない。
I can't take time off work for just a cold.
6. これぐらいの傷なら医者に行かなくてもいいだろう。
With a cut like this, you probably don't need to see a doctor.
7. 半年勉強したので、簡単な会話くらいならできる。
I've studied for half a year, so I can at least handle simple conversation.
8. 忙しくても、電話をするくらいの時間はあるはずだ。
Even if you're busy, you should have at least enough time to make a phone call.
9. 「こんなことを知らないのは君くらいだよ」
“You're probably the only one who doesn't know this.”
meaning_vi: 「～と同じ程度だ・～と同じ程度に…。」 程度の強さを表すために、ある状況に例えて言うときに使う。⑥のように、「～かと思うくらい・かと思うほど」の形でもよく使う。
To the same degree as ~ / just like ~.
Used when comparing something to a certain state in order to show degree.
The expression ～ かと思うくらい・～かと思うほど, as in example ⑥, is also often used.
examples: 1. この店のパンはおいしい。毎日食べたいくらいだ。
The bread at this shop is delicious. So good I want to eat it every day.
2. よう子さんの腕は折れそうなくらい細い。
Yoko's arms are so thin they look like they might break.
3. 天気予報によると、今日は台風ぐらいの風が吹くそうだ。
According to the weather forecast, there will be winds as strong as a typhoon today.
4. 傘をさすほどではないが、少し雨が降っている。
It's not enough to need an umbrella, but it's raining a little.
5. 突然立っていられないほどの痛みを背中に感じた。
Suddenly I felt a pain in my back so bad I couldn't stand.
6. さっき地震があった。本棚が倒れるかと思うほど激しく揺れた。
There was an earthquake a moment ago. It shook so hard I thought the bookshelf would fall over.
examples: 1. ①　３時間ぐらい
About 3 hours
2. ②　毎日、日本語を３時間ぐらい勉強しています。
I study Japanese for about 3 hours every day.
3. ②　〈駅で〉
A：すみません、黒(くろ)いかばんを電車(でんしゃ)に忘(わす)れてしまったんですけど。
B：どのくらいの大(おお)きさですか。
A：雑誌(ざっし)ぐらいの大(おお)きさです。（手(て)で示(しめ)して）ええと、これぐらいの。
(At the station)
A: Excuse me, I left a black bag on the train.
B: About how big is it?
A: About the size of a magazine. (Showing with hands) Um, about this big.
meaning_vi: Expresses the degree of something by using an example
examples: 1. ①　死ぬほど
Like dying
2. ②　歯を抜いた時は、死ぬほど痛かったです。
When I had my tooth pulled, it hurt like death.
3. ③　夢に見るくらい彼のことが好きです。
I like him so much that I dream about him.
meaning_vi: 軽い程度・最低限を示す
Indicates a light degree / a minimum degree.
同じ程度の例を示す
Gives an example of the same degree.
examples: 1. 簡単な挨拶ぐらいなら日本語で言える。
If it's just simple greetings, I can say them in Japanese.
2. 今日は少しぐらいお酒を飲んでもいいね。
It's fine to have a little to drink today, isn't it?
3. 日曜日ぐらい休ませてくださいよ。
At least let me have Sundays off.
4. 卵ぐらいの大きさのパンを作った
I made a bread roll about the size of an egg.
5. うちの娘ぐらいの女の子が泣いていた。
A girl about my daughter's age was crying.
6. この車は私にも買えるくらいの値段だ。
This car is priced so that even I can afford it.
meaning_vi: To the extent of, to the point of, about
explain: Used to talk about degree or scale by comparing with things or events
examples: 1. それは米粒くらいの大きさです。
It's about the size of a grain of rice
2. この洗剤は、おもしろいほど汚れが落ちる。
This detergent removes dirt amazingly well
3. あきるほど食べた
I ate until I was sick of it
4. 宿題が多すぎて、泣きたいくらいだ。
There's so much homework I could cry

526.meaning: To tend to ~, to have a tendency to ~

examples.jp: この仕事は、月末に忙しくなる傾向があります。
examples.tr: This job tends to get busy at the end of the month.

examples.jp: 年をとると、早起きになる傾向がある。
examples.tr: As people get older, they tend to wake up early.

526.explain: ◎ Form meaning "usually becomes that way" or "is mostly like that".

examples.jp: 次こそ絶対に合格したい。
examples.tr: Next time, I absolutely want to pass.

examples.jp: この本こそ、私がずっとほしかったものです。
examples.tr: This book is exactly what I've wanted all along.

examples.jp: 「どうぞよろしく」「こちらこそ」
examples.tr: “Nice to meet you.” “The pleasure is mine.”

examples.jp: 今年こそ合格したい。
examples.tr: This year, I really want to pass.

examples.jp: 困ったときこそ助け合おう。
examples.tr: It's precisely in hard times that we should help each other.

examples.jp: 言葉は実際に使って見てこそ身につくのだ。
examples.tr: It is only by actually using a language that you master it.

527.explain:
Attaches directly after a noun/time word to emphasize the focus.
In ～から こそ, the second clause is usually a positive/desired result; the nuance is strongly affirmative.
Does not attach directly after verbs/adjectives (except fixed phrases such as から こそ); nominalize if needed.
Used in polite replies: こちら こそ ／いえいえ、こちら こそ …

• An emphatic particle meaning “precisely/exactly”: makes the preceding element the focus.
• Emphasizing a reason with ～からこそ: strongly affirms the cause-and-effect link (“precisely because… ”).
• Emphasizing a decisive point in time: 今日こそ／今度こそ express determination/high expectations.
• Used in reciprocal politeness: こちらこそ（a reply: I'm the one who should thank you/apologize）.

rows: Weaker emphasis than こそ; こそ marks a strong focus
<ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>はできる → <ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>こそできる
Does not create a central focus like こそ
Fixed phrase (だから + こそ); stronger than だから
だからこそ<ruby>挑戦<rt>ちょうせん</rt></ruby>する

mistakes: Using こそ directly after a verb/adjective: incorrect; use a fixed phrase (からこそ) or nominalize.
Confusing こそ with は: exams often test the emphatic focus nuance of こそ compared with は.
～からこそ usually goes with a positive result; choose the answer with the matching nuance.
527.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～だけ／～こそが.
→ ～こそ is used to emphasize “precisely… (is the one that…)”.
2) Often appears in fixed patterns.
→ Examples: こちらこそ, 今こそ, だからこそ… (emphasizing a reason/point in time).
3) Not a listing pattern.
→ Its main function is emphasis; it adds no new information. meaning_vi: Precisely, precisely because (reason) ⏐ explain: Used for emphasis when the subject is the main agent or main reason, to highlight it ⏐ examples: 1. 明日こそ勉強するぞ！
Tomorrow I'm definitely going to study!
2. 愛情があるからこそ、しかるんです。
It's precisely because I love you that I scold you.

examples.jp: 声が震えていることから、彼女が緊張していることがわかった。
examples.tr: From the way her voice was trembling, I could tell she was nervous.

examples.jp: 遺書があったことから、A氏の死は自殺と断定された。
examples.tr: Because a suicide note was found, Mr. A's death was ruled a suicide.

examples.jp: ～という理由で…と名付けられた
examples.tr: Was named … for the reason ～

examples.jp: その坂は富士山が見えることから冨士見坂と呼ばれるようになった。
examples.tr: That slope came to be called Fujimizaka because Mt. Fuji can be seen from it.

examples.jp: 妹は3月に生まれたことから、「弥生」と名付けられた。
examples.tr: My younger sister was named “Yayoi” because she was born in March.

examples.jp: ～がきっかけで→変化
examples.tr: Triggered by ～ → change

528.explain:
Usually followed by verbs of perception/judgment:分かる・見なされる・考えられる・推測される・判断される.
Use であることから in formal writing when it follows N/na-adj.
Avoid using it to state the reason for the speaker's own action (行く・買う・決める). In that case ので/から is more natural.
Suited to logical explanations in reports, science and news.

～ことから has two main uses:
• Basis for an inference/evaluation: “From the fact that … (we can) conclude/understand that …”. Emphasizes an objective basis.
• Reason for a name/origin: “Because …, it is called/was named …”.
• Formal nuance; common in reports, articles and news bulletins.
• Not used for a direct, volitional cause-and-effect relationship (buying, deciding…). When you need to give the reason for an action, use ので/から.

rows: From the fact that…, hence conclude/name
<ruby>足跡<rt>あしあと</rt></ruby>があることから、<ruby>熊<rt>くま</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かる。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だから、<ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>つ。
Emphasizes the source/basis N rather than a “factual clause”
<ruby>症状<rt>しょうじょう</rt></ruby>からすると、<ruby>風邪<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>だ。
Form that emphasizes the content of the clause
<ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>しているということから、<ruby>増産<rt>ぞうさん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ。

mistakes: Using it for a volitional action: “雨が降っていることから、傘を持っていく” → forced. Change to: 雨が降っているから／ので、傘を持っていく.
Dropping である after N/na in formal writing: “静かだことから” → incorrect; correct: 静かなことから／静かであることから.
Confusing it with からすると: ことから emphasizes a “factual clause”, からすると emphasizes “the source/basis N”.
JLPT: recognize that the following part is often 分かる・見なされる・呼ばれる in order to choose ことから.
528.notes:
• The naming pattern often goes with 呼ばれる／名付けられる／通称〜とされる.
• In essays it makes a good logical connector: データが示していることから、〜と結論づけられる.
• Position: very natural at the beginning of a sentence as a premise.

examples.jp: うれしこいとに、スピ－チ大会の代表に選ばれた。
examples.tr: To my delight, I was chosen to represent us at the speech contest.

examples.jp: 惜しいことに、Aチームは1点差で負けた。
examples.tr: Unfortunately, Team A lost by one point.

examples.jp: 残念なことに、楽しみにしていたキャンプが雨で中止になった。
examples.tr: To my disappointment, the camping trip I had been looking forward to was canceled because of rain.

examples.jp: 驚いたことに、そのコンサートのチケットは１５分で売り切れたそうだ。
examples.tr: Surprisingly, I hear the tickets for that concert sold out in 15 minutes.

examples.jp: うれしいことに、第一志望の大学に合格した。
examples.tr: To my delight, I got into my first-choice university.

examples.jp: 残念なことに、会議は延期になった。
examples.tr: Unfortunately, the meeting has been postponed.

530.explain:
Usually comes at the beginning of a sentence/clause, followed by an objective fact.
Creates a formal, polite tone; suited to essays and presentations.
Not used for direct commands/volition. Used to express an emotion before describing the event.
With Aな you need “な”:残念なことに／幸いなことに.

～ことに: “How … that/It is … that” — puts the speaker's subjective emotion/evaluation at the beginning of the sentence as a formal/written exclamatory frame.
• Goes with adjectives/verbs expressing emotion/evaluation: うれしい・残念だ・残念ながら（different)・困る・驚く・ありがたい・幸いだ・面白い・不思議だ.
• Emphasizes the degree of the speaker's emotion toward the content that follows.
• More formal than て嬉しい/てよかった.

rows: <ruby>幸<rt>さ</rt></ruby>いなことに、<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った。
Vて + <ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しい/よかった
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>して<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しい。
Strong exclamation, often with <ruby>想定<rt>そうてい</rt></ruby><ruby>外<rt>がい</rt></ruby>
なんと<ruby>美<rt>うつく</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>景色<rt>けしき</rt></ruby>だ。

mistakes: Dropping “な” with Aな: “残念ことに” → incorrect; correct: 残念なことに.
Using it with an adjective that carries no emotional nuance (例: 高いことに) → forced. Choose an adjective of evaluation/emotion.
Combining it with a command/volition: “うれしいことに、行きましょう” → unnatural. Separate the emotion and the suggestion using a different structure.
JLPT: recognize the sentence-initial position and the emotion adjective to choose 〜ことに over 〜てうれしい/〜とは.
530.notes:
• “驚いたことに/困ったことに/面白いことに/皮肉なことに” are common phrases in written language.
• It can also go in the middle of a sentence in a subordinate clause: 彼が来なかったのは、残念なことに、連絡が取れなかったからだ。
• With Vた + ことに: the verb should express an experienced emotion (驚く・困る), not an ordinary action verb.

531.meaning: To make a point of doing…, habit

examples.jp: 健康のため、毎朝牛乳を飲むことにしている。
examples.tr: For my health, I make a point of drinking milk every morning.

examples.jp: 田中さんは、帰りが遅くなるときは、必ずメールすることにしているそうだ。
examples.tr: I hear that whenever Tanaka is going to be home late, he always sends an email.

examples.jp: 若いころはオリンピックに出るのが夢で、毎日８時間練習することにしていた。
examples.tr: When I was young, my dream was to compete in the Olympics, so I made it a rule to practice eight hours every day.

examples.jp: 休日は家で仕事をしないことにしているのに、今週はどうしても金曜日に終わらせることができず、持って帰ってきた。
examples.tr: I make it a rule not to work at home on my days off, but this week I just couldn't finish by Friday, so I brought work home.

examples.jp: 健康のために、毎日一万歩歩くことにしている。
examples.tr: For my health, I make it a habit to walk 10,000 steps every day.

examples.jp: 節約のため、外食は週一回だけにすることにしている。
examples.tr: To save money, I make it a rule to eat out only once a week.

531.explain:
Goes with adverbs of frequency/time:毎日/いつも/基本的に/～から.
Has a subjective nuance of a “self-imposed rule”; polite when needed: ～ことにしています.
Not used for natural phenomena/things beyond control: ×雨の日は降ることにしている。
Can be used to mean “pretend/treat as” in humorous or implied contexts:今日は休みってことにしている。

• Expresses a habit set by the speaker themselves and kept up regularly.
• Emphasizes a decision made earlier that is still ongoing. More stable nuance than ～ようにしている (which emphasizes “making an effort”).
• For rules of an organization/regulations, use ～ことになっている, not ～ことにしている.
• Most natural in the first person; other persons need context (a known/reported habit).

rows: <ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby><ruby>更<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>かししないことにしている。
<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby><ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>すことにした。
<ruby>社内<rt>しゃない</rt></ruby>は<ruby>禁煙<rt>きんえん</rt></ruby>ということになっている。
Emphasizes effort, may not be stable yet
<ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きするようにしている。

mistakes: Mixing it up with ～ことになっている: when asked about a “rule”, you must use ～ことになっている.
Mixing it up with ～ようにしている: if the emphasis is on “making an effort” rather than “it has become a habit”, choose ～ようにしている.
Using it for uncontrollable actions is unnatural (e.g., weather, automatic abilities).
Using it for another person without an introducing context → unnatural; add “彼は～としている/彼の習慣では～”.
531.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ことになっている.
→ ～ことにしている is a habit or rule decided by the speaker themselves.
2) Confusing the nuance of “have already decided” with “am maintaining”.
→ This pattern emphasizes setting a rule for yourself and carrying it out as a habit.
3) Avoid using it for rules of an organization or circumstances.
→ External rules usually take ～ことになっている.

532.meaning: As per the rules; scheduled to

examples.jp: 本校では、教室では日本語しか話せないことになっている。
examples.tr: At our school, the rule is that only Japanese may be spoken in the classroom.

examples.jp: 法律では、２０歳未満はお酒を飲んではいけないことになっている。
examples.tr: By law, people under 20 are not allowed to drink alcohol.

examples.jp: 私のうちでは、１月２日に親戚が皆、集まることになっている。
examples.tr: In my family, it's customary for all our relatives to get together on January 2.

examples.jp: あしたはアルバイトの面接に行くことになっている。
examples.tr: I'm scheduled to go to a part-time job interview tomorrow.

examples.jp: 「中村さんとここで１０時に会うことになっていたんですが……」
examples.tr: "I was supposed to meet Mr. Nakamura here at 10, but..."

examples.jp: このマンションではゴミは朝8時までに出すことになっている。
examples.tr: In this apartment building, garbage must be put out by 8 a.m.

532.explain:
Used in workplaces, schools, written rules, announcements, and meetings.
With a time/date: shows a fixed schedule and avoids the nuance of a “personal decision”.
Polite form: ～ことになっております; more formal form in formal written language: ～こととなっております.
Not used for personal habits you set for yourself (in that case use ～ことにしている).
Suits verbs of actions/procedures; rarely used directly with adjectives.

• Expresses a rule, custom, or schedule decided by a group/rule/third party, not by a personal decision.
• Main meaning: “the rule is that…”, “it has been arranged that…”, “it is set that…”.
• Often used for internal rules, regulations, work procedures, meeting schedules, class schedules, flight schedules…
• “Objective/passive” nuance: the speaker only reports an existing rule and cannot change it at will.
• Different from ～ことにしている (a decision set by oneself/a small group).
• Present tense ことになっている implies a rule currently in effect; past ことになった emphasizes “has just been decided”.

rows: <ruby>社内<rt>しゃない</rt></ruby>では<ruby>禁煙<rt>きんえん</rt></ruby>ことになっている。
<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby>は<ruby>砂糖<rt>さとう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>らないことにしている。
<ruby>週末<rt>しゅうまつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>だ。
Focuses on the result of a decision
<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>転勤<rt>てんきん</rt></ruby>することになった。
Formal version of ～ことになっている
<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby><ruby>期限<rt>きげん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>15日<rt>じゅうごにち</rt></ruby>までとなっております。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～ことにしている: for self-imposed habits, ～ことになっている is not used.
Using an adjective directly: incorrect. Switch to a verb/rule: 価格は毎年見直すことになっている.
Forgetting the appropriate tense: to express “it has been decided” but not yet in effect now, use ことになった, not ことになっている.
Attributing personal volition: “明日は休むことになっている” follows a schedule/rule, not “I decided it myself”.
532.notes:
• To emphasize that something has “just” been decided: use the past ことになった; for a rule currently in effect: ことになっている.
• Often used with expressions indicating the source of the rule: 規則で／社内規定で／契約上／法律で + ～ことになっている.
• In service announcements, it can be shortened: ～のみとなっております (only…).
• The logical subject is an organization/rule, but it is usually omitted and a subjectless form is used.

examples.jp: 「時間は十分にあるから、そんなに急ぐことはありませんよ」
examples.tr: "There's plenty of time, so there's no need to hurry like that."

examples.jp: 「彼の招待だから、あなたがお金を払うことはないと思う」
examples.tr: "It's his treat, so I don't think you need to pay."

examples.jp: 「そんなにがったりすることはありませんよ。まだチャンスがあるんだから」
examples.tr: "There's no need to be so disappointed. You still have a chance."

examples.jp: 心配することはないよ。ちゃんと準備してきたから。
examples.tr: There's no need to worry. I've prepared properly.

examples.jp: 焦ることはない。計画どおりに進めよう。
examples.tr: There's no need to rush. Let's proceed as planned.

examples.jp: その問題はすぐに解決できる。泣くことはない。
examples.tr: That problem can be solved right away. There's no need to cry.

533.explain:
Usually follows the dictionary form of a verb. In conversation, よ/ですよ can be added to soften the sentence.
Reassuring, objective nuance; suits announcements/instructions:提出は今日でなくてもいい →今日出す ことはない。
With the meaning “never”, the subject must be a habit/characteristic:彼は遅刻することはない。

• Used to reassure/advise: “there is no need to …”. More objective nuance than ～なくてもいい, more formal in written language.
• Can also express a habit with strong negation: “I never …”. Requires a context of habit/general behavior.
• Not used to say “should not” (moral warning) → use ～べきではない.

rows: <ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>することはない。
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>しなくてもいい。
Vる<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない
<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>ぐ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない。
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をつくべきではない。

mistakes: Confusing it with “should not”: ×遅刻することはない → this means “never late”, not “should not be late”. “Should not” must be 遅刻すべきではない。
Wrong tense: this pattern uses the present; for the past → express it through context: 昨日は急ぐ必要がなかった (～ことはなかった is not used).
Lack of context leads to ambiguity between “no need” and “never”; the JLPT signals it with reassuring keywords (心配/焦る/慌てる) → read it as “no need”.
533.notes:
1) Easy to misread as “there is no such thing/it does not exist”.
→ ～ことはない here means “there is no need/it is not necessary to…”, used to advise or reassure.
2) Often used in conversation, with a light nuance.
→ The meaning is close to “no need to…”.
3) Not used to deny the existence of something.
→ If you want to say “that does not happen”, use a different expression.

534.connection: Aい (drop い) + さ / Na + さ

examples.jp: 工場を見学して、技術の高さに驚いた。
examples.tr: I toured the factory and was amazed by how advanced the technology was.

examples.jp: このコートがあれば、冬の寒さも心配ない。
examples.tr: With this coat, I won't have to worry about the winter cold either.

examples.jp: この山の高さは想像以上だ。
examples.tr: The height of this mountain is beyond what I imagined.

examples.jp: 日本語の難しさを感じている。
examples.tr: I'm feeling how difficult Japanese is.

examples.jp: 彼女の優しさに救われた。
examples.tr: I was saved by her kindness.

examples.jp: 都市の便利さと田舎の静かさ、どちらも捨てがたい。
examples.tr: The convenience of the city and the quiet of the countryside: both are hard to give up.

534.explain:
Used as a noun: takes particles が・は・を・の…, serves as a subject/modifier.
Often comes with a measurement or standard of comparison:高さ3メートル,速さを競う.
With emotions:嬉しさ/悲しさ exist, but when emphasizing the “feeling”, ～み is often more natural.
Neutral style; can be used both in academic/technical contexts (重さ,長さ) and in everyday life (大切さ, ありがたさ).

• Turns an adjective into an abstract noun indicating degree, quality, or attribute: “degree of…/…-ness”.
• Objective nuance, measurable or comparable: 高さ（height）, 速さ（speed）, 大きさ（size）.
• With な形容詞: expresses “…-ness/degree of …”: 静かさ, 便利さ, 真面目さ.
• Distinguish it from ～み: ～さ leans toward the objective/measurable; ～み leans toward feeling/the subjective (詳しく in section 5).
• Often combines with nouns of measurement and standards: 強さ, 弱さ, 深さ, 重さ, 明るさ, 厳しさ.

rows: <ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>性<rt>せい</rt></ruby>・<ruby>硬<rt>かた</rt></ruby><ruby>度<rt>ど</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Confusing it with ～み: “objective vs. subjective”. Example: 誤）その店の安み → More natural: 安さ.
Using ～さ with an unsuitable adjective: 可能さ（可能性 is usually used instead）.
Forgetting the irregular forms: いい→よさ, ない→なさ.
Mechanically translating everything as “-ness” sounds stiff. Be flexible: 高さ=height, 大きさ=size, 便利さ=convenience.
534.notes:
• Many four-kanji words become measurement nouns with ～さ: 深さ, 厚さ, 硬さ, 明るさ… very common in JLPT exams.
• 一番＋～さ: used for superlatives together with nominalization, e.g.: この川は深さが一番だ。
• Not every い形容詞 sounds natural with ～さ; if it feels forced, consider another expression (～み/～性/抽象名詞).

examples.jp: この子はもう６歳だが、まだ自分の名前さえ読めない。
examples.tr: This child is already 6, but still can't even read their own name.

examples.jp: 娘は親にさえ相談せずに留学を決めてしまった。
examples.tr: My daughter went ahead and decided to study abroad without even talking to her parents.

examples.jp: この問題は成績優秀な佐藤君でさえできなかった。
examples.tr: Even Sato, a top student, couldn't solve this problem.

examples.jp: 「運動の苦手な私でさえ、１週間で泳げるようになったのだから、あなたなら３日でだいじょうぶよ」
examples.tr: "Even I, who am bad at sports, learned to swim in a week, so you'll be fine in three days."

examples.jp: 妻は夫の給料がいくらかさえ知らなかった。
examples.tr: The wife didn't even know how much her husband's salary was.

examples.jp: どんなに頼んでも、野口さんは会ってさえくれなかった。
examples.tr: No matter how much I asked, Mr. Noguchi wouldn't even meet me.

535.explain:
Used to emphasize an extreme exception, causing surprise.
In ～さえ～ば, さえ marks the “minimum condition”; this form appears very often in the JLPT.
With が/を: usually dropped, and さえ attaches directly after the noun. With に/で/から/へ: keep the particle + さえ.
Style: さえ is neutral; ですら is formal/written language; でも is lighter.

• Meaning 1: Emphasizes the degree “even” with an extreme example → emphasizes surprise, something unexpected.
• Meaning 2: The sufficient-condition pattern ～さえ～ば “as long as … , …” → identifies the minimum condition to achieve a goal.
• Position: さえ attaches right after the emphasized element (noun/case particle; with verbs use Vます＋さえすれば).
• Stronger nuance than でも; ですら is more formal than さえ.

rows: <ruby>専門<rt>せんもん</rt></ruby><ruby>家<rt>か</rt></ruby>ですら<ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>く
Emphasizes scope; までに has a different meaning
<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>た
<ruby>一回<rt>いっかい</rt></ruby>だけ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>った

mistakes: Wrong position of さえ: it must come right after the emphasized element. 誤）さえ彼に → 正）彼にさえ.
Confusing さえ with だけ: さえ means “even”, だけ means “only”. Their meanings are opposite in many contexts.
Forgetting to drop が/を: 誤）彼をさえ → 彼さえ is usually used.
Confusing ～さえ～ば with ～だけで: both mean “all it takes is”, but ～さえ～ば emphasizes the minimum condition more strongly.
535.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～まで.
→ ～さえ means “even…”, emphasizing something unexpected; it is not a limit “up to the point of”.
2) Easily confused with ～しか.
→ ～さえ: addition (even… also…).
→ ～しか: limitation, always used with a negative.
3) In the conditional form (～さえ…ば), the meaning is different.
→ ～さえ…ば usually means “as long as… then…”; look carefully at the structure.
explain: ◎ By giving an extreme example, shows that things other than the given example are a matter of course. Can also be replaced with ｢～でも｣.
examples: 1. 小学生でさえ簡単に答えられる問題を間違えてしまった。
I got wrong a question that even elementary school students can answer easily.
2. 世の中には、医者でさえ原因がわからない病気がたくさんある。
There are many diseases in the world whose cause even doctors don't know.
meaning_vi: Even, to the point of
explain: Used to show something of an especially high/low degree that certainly can / cannot be done.
examples: 1. ひらがなさえ書けないんですから、漢字なんて書けません。
I can't even write hiragana, so there's no way I can write something like kanji.
2. そんなこと、子どもでさえ知っている。
Even children know that kind of thing.

examples.jp: 買うしかない
examples.tr: Have no choice but to buy it

examples.jp: ここまで頑張ったんだから、最後までやるしかないよ。
examples.tr: You've worked hard to get this far, so you just have to see it through to the end.

examples.jp: チケットを持ってくるのを忘れたので、入口でまた買しかなかった。
examples.tr: I forgot to bring my ticket, so I had no choice but to buy another one at the entrance.

examples.jp: 現金は千円しかない。
examples.tr: I only have 1,000 yen in cash.

examples.jp: 会場には学生しかいない。
examples.tr: There are only students at the venue.

examples.jp: 電車が止まっているから、歩くしかない。
examples.tr: The trains have stopped, so there's no choice but to walk.

536.explain:
When expressing a small/insufficient quantity: N/数量＋しかない.
When expressing an unavoidable choice: Vる＋しかない (“have no choice but to …”).
The nuance is often negative/regretful, but it can also be neutral when stating an objective fact.
In spoken language, しかない is more emphatic than だけだ/だけしかない.

• “Only …” with a nuance of strong negation: rules out every other possibility.
• With nouns/quantities: emphasizes a small amount, “only this much”.
• With verbs: “have no choice but to/there is no other way than …”. Carries a sense of reluctance or inevitability.
• Grammatically: しか always goes with a negative predicate (ない). The fixed phrase “～しかない” creates the meaning of obligation.

rows: Only …; have no choice but to …
Does not need a negative predicate
ほかに<ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>がない
よりほか（は）ない／ほかない
More formal than しかない
Negation in the opposite direction, nuance of obligation
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないわけにはいかない

mistakes: Forgetting the negative predicate: しか always goes with ない. 誤）お金は千円しか → 正）千円しかない。
Confusing it with だけ: だけ does not carry the nuance of constraint/scarcity and does not need ない.
Using しか alone: a noun/quantity/verb must come before しか.
Redundant double negative: しかない is already negative; do not add ありませんか? in the same clause.
536.notes:
• For a polite style: both しかありません/しかないです are acceptable.
• To emphasize scarcity: たった＋数量＋しかない（たった一人しかない）.
• In motivational conversation: “やるしかない！” carries a nuance of determination even though there is no other choice.
examples: 1. ①　野菜しか食べない
Only eat vegetables
2. ②　あの人は肉や魚は食べず、野菜しか食べないそうです。
I hear that person doesn't eat meat or fish, only vegetables.
3. ③　パーティーには二人しか来なかった。
Only two people came to the party.
4. ➃　私のことをこんなにわかってくれるのは、彼女しかいません。
She is the only one who understands me this well.
Variants: ～(より)ほかない・～よりほかしかたがない

examples.jp: 子どもたちにキャンディーを二つずつ配った。
examples.tr: I gave the children two candies each.

examples.jp: 順番に一人ずつ面接室に入ってください。
examples.tr: Please enter the interview room one at a time, in order.

examples.jp: 毎日、漢字を十個ずつ覚えている。
examples.tr: I memorize ten kanji every day.

examples.jp: 少しずつ良くなってきました。
examples.tr: It has been getting better little by little.

examples.jp: この問題は三グループに分けて、各グループに五枚ずつ配ります。
examples.tr: For this problem, we'll split into three groups and hand out five sheets to each group.

examples.jp: お金は月に三万円ずつ貯金している。
examples.tr: I save 30,000 yen each month.

537.explain:
Commonly used in instructions, rules, distribution guidelines, or descriptions of progress.
Emphasizes fairness/regularity; for gradual change it is often used with少しずつ/だんだん.
Place ずつ right after the quantity:一つ ずつ （correct）; ×ずつ一つ（wrong order).

• Even distribution: “each …”, “… per person/per item”.
• Little by little: gradual change/progress over time.
• Position: ずつ comes right after the quantity expression it modifies.

rows: Placed after a quantity; emphasizes distribution/progress
A particle marking units, not necessarily dividing evenly
<ruby>一時間<rt>いちじかん</rt></ruby>ごとに<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>む
<ruby>二日<rt>ふつか</rt></ruby>おきに<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>る
Noun/adverb vocabulary, not attached after a quantity
<ruby>各<rt>かく</rt></ruby>グループに<ruby>五<rt>ご</rt></ruby><ruby>枚<rt>まい</rt></ruby><ruby>配<rt>くば</rt></ruby>る

mistakes: Wrong order: ×ずつ二つ → 二つずつ（correct）.
Dropping the counter when it is needed: ×三ずつ（ambiguous） → 三人ずつ/三個ずつ（clear）.
Confusing it with ごとに: ごとに means “every time/periodically”, not “one per person, one per item”.
The JLPT often tests the position of ずつ in long sentences; rule: always place it right after the quantity phrase it modifies.
537.notes:
• With decimals/ratios: 0.5杯ずつ（half a cup per person）, 3％ずつ（3％ each time）.
• When saying “little by little” in a long process: 少しずつ＋Vていく／Vてくる is a very natural frame.
• In spoken language, ずつ can be emphasized with ずつでも: 少しずつでも前に進もう。

538.connection: Vない (drop ない) + ずに / する → せずに

examples.jp: けさは寝坊して、食事をせずに家を出た。
examples.tr: I overslept this morning and left the house without eating.

examples.jp: 努力せずにいい結果を望むのは、よくないことです。
examples.tr: It's not good to hope for good results without making an effort.

examples.jp: 朝ご飯を食べずに会社へ行った。
examples.tr: I went to work without eating breakfast.

examples.jp: 彼は何も言わずに部屋を出た。
examples.tr: He left the room without saying anything.

examples.jp: 雨が降らなかったので、傘を買わずに済んだ。
examples.tr: Since it didn't rain, I didn't have to buy an umbrella.

examples.jp: スマホを見ずに歩くのは危ない。
examples.tr: Walking without looking at your smartphone is dangerous.

538.explain:
Used to connect a subordinate clause (Vずに、…) placed before the main clause.
More formal than ないで; suits written language/explanations. ないで suits conversation, including commands/requests（～ないでください）.
ずに is not used for direct commands: “Don't …” must use ～ないで（例：撮らないでください）.
With verbs of motion/time, ずに can imply “skipping/jumping over a step”.

• Connects clauses to express that the main action happens while “not doing” action A: “B without A”.
• Emphasizes the absence/exclusion of action A before or at the same time as action B.
• Slightly more formal nuance than ないで; often used in written language, announcements, and essays.
• The fixed pattern ～ずに済む means “get by without having to …/not need to …”.

rows: Doing B without doing A; prohibition
Colloquial; can be used with ～ないでください
<ruby>振<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>り<ruby>返<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ることなく<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>む
<ruby>笑<rt>わらわ</rt></ruby>わずにはいられない

mistakes: Wrong irregular forms: 誤）来りずに×／しずに× → 正）来ずに（こずに）／せずに。
Confusing its role with ないでください: ずに is not used for requests/prohibitions.
Choosing a verb that does not fit “not … but …”, causing a logical contradiction (e.g. 例４ requires a pragmatic reading).
JLPT: often sets traps comparing ずに・ないで・ことなく; pay attention to the formal nuance and the phrase ずに済む.
538.notes:
• ずに can be chained: 連絡もせずに、謝りもせずに、帰った。
• Reordering clauses to emphasize the main clause: ～ずに、…した（written language often places ずに at the beginning of a sentence）.
• With verbs of perception/social behavior, ずに adds a nuance of impoliteness: 挨拶もせずに去る.
meaning_vi: state of not (=ないで）
explain: ◎ Means "not doing ~". Often used in the form「A (し)ないでBです」when 'not doing (A) as usual but doing (B)'.
examples: 1. 彼は 何も 言わずに 行って しまいました。
He left without saying anything.
2. うちの むすこは よく 考えずに 行動する んです。
My son often acts without thinking.
──────
1. わたしはいつも朝ごはんを食べずに会社へ行く。
I always go to work without eating breakfast.
2. 彼女は何も言わずに部屋を出て行った。
She left the room without saying anything.
3. 「準備体操をせずにプールに入ってはいけません」
「You must not get into the pool without warming up first」
4. 「わたしたちのことを忘れずにいてください」
Please don't forget us. meaning_vi: Not doing something (but doing something else) ⏐ explain: Used when we skip an action that we would naturally, normally do ⏐ examples: 1. 辞書を使わずに書いたので、自信がありません。
I wrote it without using a dictionary, so I'm not confident.
2. 昨夜、歯をみがかずに寝てしまった。
Last night I ended up going to bed without brushing my teeth.

examples.jp: 雨のせいで試合が中止になった。
examples.tr: The game was canceled because of the rain.

examples.jp: 彼のミスのせいで、計画が台無しになった。
examples.tr: The plan was ruined because of his mistake.

examples.jp: 徹夜したせいで、今日は眠くてたまらない。
examples.tr: Because I stayed up all night, I'm unbearably sleepy today.

examples.jp: 交通渋滞のせいで遅刻しました。
examples.tr: I was late because of a traffic jam.

examples.jp: この薬のせいで頭が痛くなった。
examples.tr: This medicine gave me a headache.

examples.jp: 雨が多かったせいか、野菜が高い。
examples.tr: Vegetables are expensive, perhaps because there was so much rain.

539.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize the "negativity" of the cause or to imply blame.
Avoid using it with positive results; when the result is good, use ～おかげで.
Usable in both spoken and written language; in formal documents it can be replaced with ～ために／～により to neutralize the nuance.
Usually combined with a specific, clear cause (N/V); rarely used with Aい/Aな.

• Expresses a cause with a negative nuance, assigning blame: "because of/due to ... (bad result)".
• The speaker usually implies reproach, complaint, or a negative feeling about the cause.
• Compared with ～ために/～ので/～から: ～せいで leans toward the emotional sense of "it's the fault of (blameworthy)".
• Often used as N のせいで and Vたせいで when the cause has already happened.
• ～せいか: "maybe it's because of... that...", expresses uncertainty about the cause.

rows: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>のせいで<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れた。
<ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>のおかげで<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>した。
More neutral; usable for both good and bad
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>のために<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>。
Objective reason (ので) / subjective reason (から)
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なので<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>により<ruby>遅延<rt>ちえん</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Forgetting の: ×雨せいで → ✓雨のせいで.
Using it with a good result: ×先生のせいで合格した → ✓先生のおかげで合格した.
Choosing the tense of the cause verb: when the cause has already happened, prefer Vたせいで.
Confusing it with ～ために: the JLPT often tests the difference in nuance between "blaming" (せいで) and "neutral" (ために).
Following せいで with a command/request sounds unnatural: use a clause describing an actual result.
539.notes:
• ～せいだ is the concluding form: "It's because of...". ～せいで links cause and result.
• "気のせい" is an idiom: "just one's imagination/a misperception". Example: 気のせいかもしれない。
• Avoid ～せいで in contexts that require neutrality (reports, news), as the nuance of blame may be inappropriate.
meaning_vi: Because of... / Due to... (bad result, reproach)
Not certain, perhaps because of...
explain: States the cause that led to a bad result, with a nuance of reproach.
Expresses an uncertain conjecture: "perhaps it is because of...", a milder nuance than ～せい.
examples: 1. あの人のせいでみんなが迷惑している。
Everyone is bothered because of that person.
2. 景気が悪いせいでボーナスが減った。
Bonuses were cut because of the poor economy.
3. 試合に負けたのはミスをした私のせいだ。
We lost the game because I made a mistake.
4. 大気汚染が悪化したのは、政府が何の対策も立てなかったせいだ。
Air pollution got worse because the government took no measures at all.
5. 彼女は何でも人のせいにするから嫌われている。
She is disliked because she blames others for everything.
6. 気のせいか、最近父は元気がないようだ。
Maybe it's just my imagination, but my father seems to be in low spirits lately.
7. 年のせいか、このごろ物忘れがひどい。
Maybe it's because of my age, but lately I've been very forgetful.
8. このあたりは気候が温暖なせいか、のんびりしていて暮らしやすい。
Perhaps thanks to the mild climate, this area is relaxed and easy to live in.
meaning_vi: Because, due to
It seems it's because
explain: Used when you want to mention a reason connected to a bad result
Implies reproach
examples: 1. バスが遅れたせいで、約束の時間に間に合わなかった。
Because the bus was late, I didn't make it in time for the appointment
2. 疲れたせいか、頭が痛い。
Maybe because I'm tired, I have a headache
「～の影響で…といういい結果になる（おかげだ）/よくない結果になる（せいだ）。」 …には希望・意向・相手への働きかけなどの文は来ない。
As an effect of ~, it leads to a good result (thanks to) / it leads to a bad result (because of)
… does not take sentences expressing desire, intention, or urging the listener to do something.
1. いい会社に就職が決まったのは先生のおかげです。ありがとうございました。
It's thanks to you, teacher, that I got a job at a good company. Thank you very much.
2. 天気のいい日が続いたおかげで、工事が早く終わった。
Thanks to a stretch of good weather, the construction finished early.
3. 最近忙しかったせいで、かなり疲れている。
Because I've been busy lately, I'm quite tired.

540.meaning: I hear that..., it is said that... (passing on information heard or read)

examples.jp: このデパートでは、若者向けの商品に力を入れているそうだ。
examples.tr: I hear this department store is focusing on products for young people.

examples.jp: さくらさんは、部屋に小さい花をたくさん置いているそうです。
examples.tr: I hear Sakura keeps lots of little flowers in her room.

examples.jp: そのケーキはおいしそうだ。
examples.tr: That cake looks delicious.

examples.jp: 彼は今日は元気そうだ。
examples.tr: He looks well today.

examples.jp: 今にも雨が降りそうだ。
examples.tr: It looks like it's going to rain any minute.

examples.jp: あの店は高くなさそうだ。
examples.tr: That shop doesn't seem expensive.

540.explain:
Direct observation → use 様態: images, sounds, signs right in front of you.
Indirect information → use 伝聞: it is good to state the source (～によると/～では); polite: そうです。
Negative of 様態: V なさそうだ / Aい くなさそうだ / Aな ではなさそうだ .
Combinations: そうに + V:嬉しそうに話す (talk happily). そうな + N:面白そうな本(a book that looks interesting).
そうに + V:嬉しそうに話す (talk happily).
そうな + N:面白そうな本(a book that looks interesting).
Avoid using 様態のそうだ with completed past events or facts that are already clearly known.

• 様態のそうだ: Conjecture based on the senses/signs in front of you. Fits signs that 目で見える・耳で聞こえる. Example: 雨が降りそうだ (dark clouds, strong wind...)
• 伝聞のそうだ: Reports information you have heard. Neutral, does not guarantee reliability. Often used with a source: 新聞によると、〜そうだ。
• Do not use 様態のそうだ for inherent qualities that are hard to observe directly (× 日本は安全そうだ in a general sense; use ようだ/らしい instead).
• Contrast of forms: そうだ(様態) means "looks like it's about to / looks", unlike らしい (rumor/characteristic) and ようだ/みたいだ (metaphor/overall comparison).

rows: V/A + そうだ (<ruby>様態<rt>ようたい</rt></ruby>)
Clause + そうだ (<ruby>伝聞<rt>でんぶん</rt></ruby>)
<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>値上<rt>ねあ</rt></ruby>げするそうだ
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本人<rt>にほんじん</rt></ruby>らしい
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るに<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない

mistakes: Wrong sound change: × いいそうだ → ○ よさそうだ.
Wrong negative: × 降らないそうだ (if 様態) → ○ 降らなさそうだ. Note: 降らないそうだ is 伝聞.
Using 様態 for general information: × 日本は安全そうだ (use ようだ/らしい).
Confusing そうです (polite) with そうだ (plain): the grammar is the same; only the politeness level differs.
540.notes:
• Many nouns describing qualities are actually Aな (元気・幸せ・暇…), so they attach directly to そうだ: 幸せそうだ。
• Colloquial: 死にそう (dead tired), やばそう (looks bad) are used in spoken language.
• 「Aくなさそう」 is more natural than 「Aそうではない」 with Aい.
• 「今にも〜そうだ」 is a frame that emphasizes that something is "about to happen".
meaning_vi: information from letters, magazines, TV, or other people.
examples: 1. ①　弱かったそうだ
I hear (she) was weak.
2. ②　母から聞いたが、姉は子供の時体が弱かったそうだ。
I heard from my mother that my older sister was physically weak as a child.
3. ③　医者に聞いた話では、インフルインザがもう流行しているそうだ。
According to what I heard from the doctor, the flu is already going around.
──────
1. リンさんは子どものころ、サッカーの選手になりたかったそうです。
I hear that as a child, Lin wanted to become a soccer player.
2. 「駅前の新しいレストランに、もう行きましたか」
「Have you been to the new restaurant in front of the station yet?」
3. 「いいえ。でも、チンさんが先週行ったそうです。とてもおいしくて、値段も高くなかったそうです」
「No. But I hear Chin went last week. I hear it was really delicious and not expensive either.」
4. 弟からメールが来た。アリさんはとても歌が上手だそうです。
My younger brother sent an email saying that Ali sings very well.
5. 天気予報によると、明日は一日雨だそうだ。
According to the weather forecast, it will rain all day tomorrow.
6. この本によると、日本では１９５３年にテレビ放送が始まったそうだ。
According to this book, TV broadcasting started in Japan in 1953.
Seems..., I hear...

examples.jp: 工場が停止した。そのために納期が遅れた。
examples.tr: The factory shut down. As a result, the delivery was delayed.

examples.jp: 健康を維持したい。そのために毎朝ジョギングしている。
examples.tr: I want to stay healthy. For that purpose, I go jogging every morning.

examples.jp: 予算が不足している。そのため計画の見直しが必要だ。
examples.tr: The budget is insufficient. Therefore, the plan needs to be reviewed.

examples.jp: 新製品を成功させたい。そのために市場調査を徹底した。
examples.tr: We want the new product to succeed. To that end, we did thorough market research.

examples.jp: 大雪だった。そのために学校は休校になった。
examples.tr: There was heavy snow. Because of that, the school was closed.

541.explain:
A sentence connective more formal than だから／それで; well suited to essays and reports.
When used with the meaning of "purpose", "そのために" comes before the subsequent actions taken to achieve the stated goal.
Avoid repeating "～ため／ので" in both clauses, which sounds heavy: ×雨のため、そのために中止→ ✓雨で、そのため中止。
A comma after "そのため(に)、" makes the flow of the sentence clearer.

• "そのために" has two interpretations:

Result conjunction: "therefore/for that reason".
Purpose: "in order to do that/to achieve that goal".

• Result conjunction: "therefore/for that reason".
• Purpose: "in order to do that/to achieve that goal".
• When it expresses "result", the first clause states the cause/situation; the second clause states the logical consequence.
• When it expresses "purpose", the first clause states the goal; the second clause is the concrete action taken to achieve that goal.
• In written language, "そのため" (without に) is slightly more formal for the meaning "therefore".

rows: Therefore / In order to do that
<ruby>故障<rt>こしょう</rt></ruby>。そのため<ruby>停止<rt>ていし</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>。それで<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>？
だから<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったでしょ。
<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>。その<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby><ruby>判明<rt>はんめい</rt></ruby>。
Attaches directly to V/N: <ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>するために
<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>のために<ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Mixing up the meanings "therefore" and "in order to do that" makes the text ambiguous; the JLPT often tests the context to choose the correct one.
Repeating the cause: ×雨のため、そのために～ → omit one of the cause clauses.
Using "そのために" (purpose) when the previous sentence does not clearly state a goal → causes misunderstanding.
Confusing it with それで/だから in formal written language; prefer そのため/その結果/したがって.
541.notes:
• When "そのために" expresses purpose, it usually refers back semantically to the goal in the previous sentence; make sure the reference is clear to avoid ambiguity.
• In standard style, "そのため、～" may be preferred for the meaning "therefore".
• Placed at the start of a paragraph to shift the topic: state the cause/vision → そのため、方針…
explain: Used as a connective that continues from a previously stated reason or goal and leads on to the result
examples: 1. 隣の駅で事故があったらしい。そのために電車が遅れている。
Apparently there was an accident at the next station. Because of that, the trains are running late.
2. 留学するつもりだ。そのために、バイトしてお金をためている。
I plan to study abroad. For that, I'm working part-time and saving money

examples.jp: 焼きたてのパンは香りがいい。
examples.tr: Freshly baked bread smells wonderful.

examples.jp: 入れたてのコーヒーをどうぞ。
examples.tr: Please have some freshly brewed coffee.

examples.jp: 揚げたてをお持ちします。
examples.tr: I'll bring them out freshly fried.

examples.jp: できたてですから、熱いですよ。
examples.tr: It's freshly made, so it's hot.

examples.jp: 社会人になりたてで、まだ右も左も分からない。
examples.tr: I've only just started working, so I still don't know my way around at all.

examples.jp: 入社したての頃は毎日緊張していた。
examples.tr: When I had just joined the company, I was nervous every day.

542.explain:
Often used for food and "fresh" products: 焼きたて／揚げたて／炊きたて／茹でたて／搾りたて。
Used for a newly reached state: できたて／なりたて／入社したて／結婚したて。
Positive nuance: tasty, fresh, brand-new; sometimes a warning that something is "still hot".
Rarely used with verbs that do not produce a "tangible result" (×食べたて → use 食べたばかり).

• Expresses the state of "having just been done" while the result still keeps its "freshness/newness".
• It is not simply "just happened" in terms of time like 〜たばかり; 〜たて emphasizes the quality of "freshness".
• Lexical restrictions: usually used with verbs that produce a tangible product/result or a new state.

rows: できたて vs できたばかり
できたて: emphasizes being "brand-new"; できたばかり: emphasizes time
できたてのケーキ／できたばかりのケーキ

mistakes: Using たて with an unsuitable verb: × 食べたて → √ 食べたばかり。
Taking たて to mean "recently": たて is not used for something that "just happened" in general (× 昨日起きたて). Use 起きたばかり.
Wrong form with する-verbs: × 勉強したて? → 勉強したて is possible, but 勉強し始めたばかり is more natural depending on the context.
Attaching it directly to an adjective: × 新しいたて → use できたて／作りたて to express "newly made".
542.notes:
• Common fixed combinations: 焼きたて・揚げたて・炊きたて・茹でたて・搾りたて・採れたて／とれたて・できたて・入れたて・なりたて・入社したて・結婚したて。
• Negative/affirmative is expressed with だ/です rather than directly on たて: できたてではない（not freshly made）。
• "覚えたて／習いたて" can be used to emphasize the state of "having just learned (still inexperienced)". explain: Used when an action has just finished
Often used with the meaning "fresh, new, piping hot..." ⏐ examples: 1. 焼きたてのパンはおいしい。
Freshly baked bread is delicious
2. あのスーパーは、とりたての新鮮な野菜を売っている。
That supermarket sells fresh, just-picked vegetables

543.meaning: Used to give an example of the words or sentence that come before.

examples.jp: 日本のスポーツ、例えば、柔道をやってみたいです。
examples.tr: I'd like to try a Japanese sport, for example, judo.

examples.jp: 山田さんはいつも遅く帰る。例えば、昨日は11時に帰った。
examples.tr: Yamada always gets home late. For example, yesterday he got home at 11.

examples.jp: たとえばケーキやチョコレートなど。
examples.tr: For example, cake, chocolate, and so on.

examples.jp: 緊急のとき、たとえば事故や病気のとき。
examples.tr: In an emergency, for example, in case of an accident or illness.

examples.jp: よくおんがくを聞きます。たとえばクラシックやジャズなどです。
examples.tr: I often listen to music. For example, classical, jazz, and so on.

543.notes: Used when showing something mentioned before by giving a concrete example. When a hypothetical case is given as an example, as in ⑤ and ⑥, it is followed by 「とすると」, 「としたら」, etc.

examples.jp: たとえ少々高くても、質のいいものが買いたい。
examples.tr: Even if it's a little expensive, I want to buy something of good quality.

examples.jp: たとえ両親に反対されても、家を出て一人暮らしがしたい。
examples.tr: Even if my parents are against it, I want to leave home and live on my own.

examples.jp: 手紙は、たとえ字が下手でも、手書きのほうが暖かみがある。
examples.tr: Even if your handwriting is poor, a handwritten letter feels warmer.

examples.jp: たとえ小さな子どもでも、ゆっくり話してやればわかるはずだ。
examples.tr: Even a small child should understand if you speak slowly to them.

examples.jp: たとえ雨でも、試合は行います。
examples.tr: Even if it rains, the game will be held.

examples.jp: たとえ失敗しても、挑戦し続ける。
examples.tr: Even if I fail, I will keep trying.

544.explain:
Often used in statements of determination/policy: たとえ〜ても、〜する。
The second clause is rarely a direct request to the listener unless it has a soft nuance: たとえ〜でも、〜してください。
In spoken language, たとえ can be omitted, using only 〜ても/〜でも; adding たとえ adds emphasis.
Combines well with emphatic words: いくら／どんなに／たとえ…

• Expresses hypothetical concession: "Even if ... (still) ...".
• たとえ is an emphatic adverb; grammatically it can be omitted, but it is added to strengthen the emphasis.
• The second clause is usually a volition/determination/evaluation unaffected by the preceding condition.
• Used for hypothetical or possible situations; not used to describe obvious facts.

rows: たとえ is an emphatic adverb
たとえ<ruby>遅<rt>おそ</rt></ruby>くても<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
いくら<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>くても<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>真実<rt>しんじつ</rt></ruby>だたとしても…
More analytical, objective ニュアンス
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くにしても<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ。

mistakes: Wrong particle with N/なA: × たとえ雨ても → √ たとえ雨でも。
Omitting たとえ when the question requires emphasis; on the JLPT, it can be a trap choice between "ても" and "たとえ〜ても".
Using it for obvious facts → unnatural: × たとえ火は熱くても（everyone knows this, so no concession is needed).
A blunt command/prohibition in the second clause: × たとえ遅れても来るな → use a softer expression or change the structure.
544.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ても (ordinary concession).
→ たとえ～ても gives strong emphasis: "no matter what, still...".
2) The second clause is usually a firm conclusion.
→ Often volition/decision/assertion (will still do it, will not change).
3) Not suitable when only stating a slight possibility.
→ For an ordinary "even if... still...", ～ても is enough. meaning_vi: Supposing that... even so... / Even if... still... ⏐ explain: Used when you want to emphasize the assertion of a fact or action regardless of other conditions occurring ⏐ examples: 1. たとえ反対されても留学します。
Even if people are against it, I will study abroad
2. たとえ元気じゃなくても、家族への手紙には元気だと書きます。
Even if I'm not well, I write in letters to my family that I'm fine

545.meaning:
たとえ～しても→（-）の予想(よそう)・判断(はんだん)、たいしたことではない
Even if

examples.jp: 本当のことを言ったところで、だれも信じてくれないだろう。
examples.tr: Even if I told the truth, nobody would believe me.

examples.jp: この病気は手術をしたところで回復は難しいと思われる。
examples.tr: With this illness, recovery is thought to be difficult even with surgery.

examples.jp: 「今から急いだところで間に合わないよ」
examples.tr: "Even if you hurry now, you won't make it."

examples.jp: すんでしまったところは、今さら後悔したところでどうにもならない。
examples.tr: What's done is done; regretting it now won't change anything.

examples.jp: 彼女は体力があるから、2、3日徹夜したところで平気だろう。
examples.tr: She has a lot of stamina, so she'd probably be fine even after staying up two or three nights.

examples.jp: 最後の答えを書いたところで、試験が終わった。
examples.tr: Just as I finished writing the last answer, the exam ended.

545.explain: ◎ The preceding event has just finished when the following event occurs.

examples.jp: 車から降りた途端、海のにおいがした。
examples.tr: The moment I got out of the car, I smelled the sea.

examples.jp: 先生の顔を見た途端、宿題をするのを忘れていたことに気がついた。
examples.tr: The moment I saw my teacher's face, I realized I had forgotten to do my homework.

examples.jp: ドアを開けたとたん、猫が飛び出した。
examples.tr: The moment I opened the door, the cat dashed out.

examples.jp: 席に座ったとたん、電話が鳴り出した。
examples.tr: The moment I sat down, the phone started ringing.

examples.jp: 彼の顔を見たとたん、涙があふれた。
examples.tr: The moment I saw his face, tears welled up.

examples.jp: 家を出たとたん、強い雨が降り出した。
examples.tr: The moment I left the house, it started raining hard.

546.explain:
Has the nuance of narrating a sudden event, quick as "the blink of an eye".
The second clause is not used to express the speaker's intention (commands, advice, invitations...).
Often accompanied by emphatic 副詞: そのとたん(に), ちょうどそのとたん(に).
Often used with verbs of sudden change: 降り出す, 鳴る, 壊れる, 飛び出す, 立ち上がる, こみ上げる.
Has a narrative nuance; suitable for written language and moderately formal speech.

• Expresses something that happens instantly, right after the action in the first clause is finished.
• The second clause is usually an unexpected result, beyond one's intention/control, and very sudden.
• Usually used in the past to narrate events that have happened; rarely used for predicted future events.
• The subjects of the two clauses can differ, but the second clause should not express volition, a command, or an invitation.
• Unlike ～たら/～とすぐ: ～とたん emphasizes suddenness and unexpectedness at that very moment.

rows: Focuses on the instant; the second clause is usually unexpected, beyond one's will
<ruby>外<rt>そと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たとたん、<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>。
General, not necessarily unexpected; allows volition/commands
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたらすぐ<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>して。
Similar meaning, neutral style; does not emphasize "unexpectedness" as strongly
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った<ruby>瞬間<rt>しゅんかん</rt></ruby>、<ruby>恋<rt>こい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>ちた。
V-る/た + かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと/かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>ったら
Nuance of commenting on a quick change; the subject is usually different
<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>いたかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと<ruby>笑<rt>わら</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>到着<rt>とうちゃく</rt></ruby>するや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Using volition/a command in the second clause: × ドアを開けたとたん、入ろう。→ Use instead: 開けたら入ろう。
Using it for a prolonged action: × 仕事を始めたとたん、三時間働いた。→ Not suitable because it is not sudden.
Using the present tense/a future prediction: × 行くとたん、雨が降るだろう。→ Narrating the past is natural.
Confusing it with ～たらすぐ: ～とたん requires unexpectedness; ～たらすぐ is neutral and allows commands.
The subject being the speaker but expressing a sudden sensation is fine: 立ち上がったとたん、めまいがした (not a trap).
546.notes:
• "とたん" can be written in kana: とたんに. The form "そのとたん" refers to exactly the moment just mentioned.
• Negating an unexpected emotion is rare: the second clause is usually an objective occurrence.
• In narratives, "とたん" speeds up the rhythm and creates an unexpected climax.
• Similar structures: "～や/～や否や" is limited to written language; "～か～ないかのうちに" emphasizes an extremely short interval.

examples.jp: 私のおいは、会うたびに背が高くなっている。
examples.tr: Every time I see my nephew, he's grown taller.

examples.jp: 古いアパートなので、車が通るたびに、窓が揺れます。
examples.tr: It's an old apartment, so every time a car goes by, the windows shake.

examples.jp: バーゲンセールのたびに、ついいらないものも買ってしまう。
examples.tr: Every time there's a bargain sale, I end up buying things I don't even need.

examples.jp: 父は旅行のたびに、その土地の名産品をおみやげに買ってきてくれる。
examples.tr: Every time my father goes on a trip, he brings back the local specialty as a souvenir for us.

examples.jp: 辞書を引くたびに新しい発見がある。
examples.tr: Every time I look something up in the dictionary, I discover something new.

examples.jp: 友人たちの活躍を聞くたびに、うれしく思う。
examples.tr: Every time I hear about my friends' success, it makes me happy.

547.explain:
Used to emphasize the "each time" nature of A; B repeats correspondingly and is usually a natural consequence.
Objective, neutral nuance; suitable in both spoken and written language.
Can express emotions or memories that come back each time A happens (見るたびに、思い出す...).
Not used with long-lasting states like いつも～だ (because たびに emphasizes "each time", not "all the time").

• Meaning: "Every time… , …"; emphasizes repetition for each occurrence of A, which brings about B.
• Features:

B happens repeatedly, corresponding to each occurrence of A (regular per occurrence, not necessarily at regular time intervals).
Usually used for events that can be counted in "times"; not used for continuous, long-lasting states.
B can be an emotion that arises spontaneously when A happens: ～を見るたびに、～を思い出す。

• B happens repeatedly, corresponding to each occurrence of A (regular per occurrence, not necessarily at regular time intervals).
• Usually used for events that can be counted in "times"; not used for continuous, long-lasting states.
• B can be an emotion that arises spontaneously when A happens: ～を見るたびに、～を思い出す。
• Restrictions:

Not used when A is something almost constant / without "each time" boundaries.
Rarely used with strong commands; usually comments, habits, emotions.

• Not used when A is something almost constant / without "each time" boundaries.
• Rarely used with strong commands; usually comments, habits, emotions.

rows: Emphasizes "each time"; does not refer to a regular time cycle
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>うたびに、<ruby>笑顔<rt>えがお</rt></ruby>になる。
Used for regular units (<ruby>三時間<rt>さんじかん</rt></ruby>ごとに…)
<ruby>三<rt>さん</rt></ruby>ページごとに<ruby>図<rt>ず</rt></ruby>がある。
Written-language nuance; often used in pairs: うれしいにつけ<ruby>悲<rt>かな</rt></ruby>しいにつけ
<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るにつけ、<ruby>故郷<rt>こきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>春<rt>はる</rt></ruby>になると<ruby>花<rt>はな</rt></ruby>が<ruby>咲<rt>さ</rt></ruby>く。

mistakes: Incorrect use with an adjective: × 高いたびに → correct: 値段が高くなるたびに… (turned into a verb)
Confusion with ～ごとに: if it is not a regular unit (every three hours), prefer ～たびに.
Use for a constant state: × 彼はいつも忙しいたびに → いつも expresses a habit and does not combine with たびに.
B happens only once: × 日本に行くたびに、初めて富士山を見た → logical contradiction.
547.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～とき／～たら.
→ ～たびに means "every time… , …", with regular repetition.
2) The second clause is usually a repeated reaction/result.
→ Usually not used to describe a single occurrence.
3) Avoid using it for something that happened only once.
→ If it only means "after…" (time sequence), use a different pattern.
meaning_vi: 「～のとき、毎回同じように…する。」 毎回同じだということを特に言いたいときに使う。日常の当然のことには使わない。～・ …には状態を表す文は来ない。
When ~, … happens the same way as every time.
This structure is used when you especially want to express that it is the same every time.
This structure is not used for things that are obvious in everyday life.
~ and … do not take sentences expressing states.
examples: 1. この地方は台風が来るたびに大水の害が起こる。
In this region, every time a typhoon comes, there is flood damage.
2. 母は私が電話をかけるたびに、ちゃんとご飯を食べているかと聞く。
Every time I call my mother, she asks whether I'm eating properly.
3. このチームは試合のたびに強くなっていく。
This team gets stronger with every match.
examples: 1. ①　コンビニへ行くたびに
Every time I go to the convenience store...
2. ②　コンビニへ行くたびに、つい買いすぎてしまう。
Every time I go to the convenience store, I end up buying too much.
3. ③　最近、試合のたびにけがをしているので、気をつけよう。
Lately I've been getting injured every time I play a match, so I should be careful. meaning_vi: Every time, each time ⏐ explain: Used when talking about something that usually happens each time a particular situation occurs ⏐ examples: 1. 買い物のたびに、袋をたくさんもらう。
Every time I go shopping, I get lots of bags
2. この曲を聞くたびに、ふるさとを思い出す。
Every time I hear this song, I remember my hometown

examples.jp: 新しいパソコンがほしいけど、まだ買うだけのお金がたまっていない。
examples.tr: I want a new computer, but I still haven't saved enough money to buy one.

examples.jp: ワンさんには、N3に合格するだけの力がある。
examples.tr: Wang has what it takes to pass N3.

548.explain: ◎ Means "enough to do something". This is an expression of degree that follows nouns referring to strength, money, time, courage, determination, etc.

examples.jp: ほこりだらけの部屋／泥だらけのくつ
examples.tr: A dusty room / muddy shoes

examples.jp: 数学の答案は間違いだらけだった。
examples.tr: My math test answers were full of mistakes.

examples.jp: 苦労した祖父の手は固くてしわだらけだ。
examples.tr: My grandfather, who worked hard all his life, has stiff, wrinkled hands.

examples.jp: 山頂までの道は石ころだらけだ。
examples.tr: The path to the summit is covered in pebbles.

examples.jp: 父の部屋は本だらけで足の踏み場もない。
examples.tr: My father's room is so full of books that there's nowhere to step.

examples.jp: 靴が泥だらけだ。
examples.tr: My shoes are covered in mud.

549.explain:
Usually used with nouns that carry a sense of "dirt/errors/problems": 泥、ほこり、シミ、血、ミス、誤字、矛盾、偏見.
Hard to use with a positive meaning: ×賞賛だらけ → sounds odd; ばかり/いっぱい are more suitable.
The form "NだらけのN" is very common in everyday spoken and written language.
Emphasizes a feeling of discomfort, irritation, or disappointment.

• Expresses a state of being "full of, covered in, all over with" something undesirable: dirt, errors, scratches, etc.
• Strong negative nuance: the speaker evaluates it unfavorably (dirty, bad, full of problems).
• Different from "いっぱい/たくさん": emphasizes "everywhere" and "deserving criticism".
• Used for both physical things (泥、血、ほこり) and abstract things (ミス、文法の誤り、矛盾).

rows: Something stuck on a surface (blood, oil); rarely abstract
Spoken/written; used for a uniform theme, not necessarily negative

mistakes: Attaching to verbs/adjectives: × 疲れるだらけ → correct: 疲れだらけの顔 (nominalization).
Use with a positive meaning: × 褒め言葉だらけ → sounds jarring; use 褒め言葉が多い/いっぱい.
Confusion with まみれ: 泥だらけ/泥まみれ are both fine; but ミスまみれ is unnatural, it must be ミスだらけ.
The JLPT often tests the "obligatory negative" nuance of だらけ compared with いっぱい/ばかり.
549.notes:
1) Easily confused: ～だらけ and ～まみれ.
→ ～だらけ: "full of / all", usually with a negative meaning; often used for mistakes, flaws, bad things.
2) Not used for good or neutral results.
→ For "full of people, full of flowers…", a different pattern is usually used depending on the context.
3) Often used with nouns meaning "errors, trouble".
→ For example: 間違いだらけ, ごみだらけ… meaning_vi: Full of, all ～ ⏐ explain: Talks about dirty or unpleasant things that are all over or stuck all over a surface. Or describes something full of bad or unfortunate things. ⏐ examples: 1. この手紙の日本語は間違いだらけだ。
The Japanese in this letter is full of mistakes.
2. ちゃんとたたんでおかなかったから、服がしわだらけになってしまった。
I didn't fold my clothes properly, so they ended up all wrinkled.

550.meaning:
Confirming information
Recalling the past | A spoken-language grammar pattern for asking to confirm information you have forgotten.

examples.jp: 「レポートの提出期限は来週の月曜日だったっけ（／だっけ）」
examples.tr: "The report is due next Monday, right?"

examples.jp: 「試験は何時からだったっけ（／だっけ）」
examples.tr: "What time does the exam start again?"

examples.jp: 「えっ、私、そんなこと言ったっけ」
examples.tr: "Huh? Did I say something like that?"

examples.jp: 「山田さんの家、駅から近かったっけ」
examples.tr: "Yamada's house is near the station, isn't it?"

examples.jp: 「キムさんって、数学が得意じゃなかったっけ」
examples.tr: "Isn't Kim good at math?"

examples.jp: こどものころ、よくこの公園で遊んだっけ。
examples.tr: When I was a child, I used to play in this park a lot.

550.explain:
Used to ask again in order to confirm information you already know or have heard.
Used to recall something that happened in the past.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>だっけ？
Does not necessarily expect an answer from others

mistakes: Use in formal language/exams: × 何時でしょうかっけ → incorrect; choose でしょうか or でしたっけ depending on the context.
Wrong tense combination: × 高いだったっけ → with Aい use 高かったっけ／高いっけ.
Confusing the purpose: ～っけ is "recalling", not a neutral information question.
JLPT listening can trick you with ですか vs でしたっけ; pay attention to the nuance of recalling.
550.notes:
1) The two uses of ～っけ are easily confused.
→ One is asking again to confirm; the other is recalling something to yourself (reminiscing).
2) Used only in spoken language.
→ Common in conversation; not used in formal written language.
3) Usually used with the past form or with content already known.
→ Used when the speaker "knew it but has forgotten / isn't sure".
meaning_vi: …right?, confirming again
explain: Used when the speaker is unsure / vaguely remembers and wants confirmation.
Often used with questions containing question words: 何、どこ、いつ、誰＋～だっけ？
Can be used as a monologue: 電気消したっけ？ (Did I turn off the light?)
examples: 1. 明日の集合時間、何時だっけ？
What time are we meeting tomorrow again?
2. あの店、定休日は火曜だったっけ？
That shop is closed on Tuesdays, isn't it?
3. 彼、結婚してたっけ？
Is he married?
4. この漢字、どう書くんだっけ？
How do you write this kanji again?
5. 出発は９時でしたっけ？
We're leaving at 9, right?
6. ここ、前に来たっけ？それとも初めてだっけ？
Have I been here before? Or is this my first time? explain: Used to confirm a matter, thing, or feature once again
Usually used in everyday, casual spoken language ⏐ examples: 1. 国へ帰るのは、来週だ（った）っけ？
You're going back to your country next week, right?
2. 明日のパーテイーのこと、話し（まし）たっけ？
Did I tell you about tomorrow's party?

examples.jp: この１週間雨が降りっぱなしで、洗濯物が乾かない。
examples.tr: It's been raining nonstop all week, so the laundry won't dry.

examples.jp: 新幹線が込んでいて、大阪まで３時間立ちっぱなしだった。
examples.tr: The Shinkansen was crowded, so I had to stand the whole three hours to Osaka.

examples.jp: 彼女は葉を磨いている間じゅうみずを流しっぱなしにしている。あれは資源の無駄づがいだ
examples.tr: She leaves the water running the whole time she's brushing her teeth. That's a waste of resources.

examples.jp: 新製品の注文が殺到している。朝から電話が鳴りっぱなしだ。
examples.tr: Orders for the new product are pouring in. The phone has been ringing nonstop since this morning.

examples.jp: したまま、後始末をしていない
examples.tr: Left as it is after doing it, without cleaning up afterward

examples.jp: ドアが開けっぱなしだ/開けっぱなしになっている/開けっぱなしの窓
examples.tr: The door is left open / has been left open / a window left open

551.explain:
Often used with verbs that create a state, such as "open/close/put/turn on/turn off/take out/put in": 開ける／閉める／出す／つける／消す／置く／履く など.
A tone of criticism/reminder: ～っぱなしだ/～っぱなしにする carries a negative meaning.
Used for prolonged postures: 立ちっぱなし／座りっぱなし／歩きっぱなし → implies tiredness/discomfort.
Everyday spoken language, not very formal; neutral in written language when describing a situation.

• Meaning 1: Leaving (neglecting) the state after doing V as it is, without dealing with it further. Nuance: carelessness, annoyance, being criticized.

Analysis: emphasizes the resultant state after action V and its unexpectedly long duration.
• Meaning 2: Keep doing V / doing V continuously (for a long time). Nuance: hardship, discomfort, not changing posture/state.
• Grammar: The whole phrase functions as a noun; it can combine with にする／にしておく to emphasize the intention of "just leaving it as is".
• Restrictions: Not used for desirable, positive states (unless there is a clear intention and no criticism).

rows: <ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>のまま<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>る（neutral） vs <ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>履<rt>は</rt></ruby>きっぱなし（slightly critical）
Emphasizes the cutoff point; more written
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>ていったきり<ruby>戻<rt>もど</rt></ruby>らない
Emphasizes repeated/ongoing action; no sense of "neglect"
<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>み<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>ける（keep reading） vs <ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みっぱなし（read and leave it）
A vocabulary word; more formal than ～っぱなし
<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>放置<rt>ほうち</rt></ruby>する

mistakes: Incorrect combination directly with a noun: ×雨っぱなし → it would have to be 雨を降らせっぱなし（unnatural）. Use the correct base verb.
Confusion with ～まま: 開けっぱなし（implies carelessness） ≠ 開けたまま（neutral, descriptive).
Forced use for a positive meaning: ×音楽を流しっぱなしで集中できた → っぱなし usually does not go with a positive result.
Choice of verb: Punctual verbs are hard to use with っぱなし if they do not produce a lasting state.
551.notes:
• Phonetically, the geminate "っ" emphasizes a feeling of "left there / left hanging".
• Often appears in instructions/signs: 水を出しっぱなしにしないでください。
• Usually written in hiragana; the kanji form ～放し is rare and tends to look stiff/hard to read.
• Can be combined as っぱなしにしておく to emphasize "deliberately leaving it as is".

552.meaning: While (you're at it), on the occasion of

examples.jp: 買い物のついでにクリーニング屋に寄って、できあがった洗濯物を受け取ってきた。
examples.tr: While I was out shopping, I stopped by the dry cleaner's and picked up my finished laundry.

examples.jp: 用事で都心へ出たついでに、美術館をのぞいてみた。
examples.tr: While I was downtown on an errand, I took a look around an art museum.

examples.jp: （コピーをしている人に）「すみません、ついでにこれもお願いします。」
examples.tr: (To someone making copies) "Excuse me, could you do this one too while you're at it?"

examples.jp: 「きょうデパートに行ってきてあげる」「いいの、ついでがあるから。」
examples.tr: "I'll go to the department store for you today." "Are you sure?" "It's fine, I'm going that way anyway."

examples.jp: 郵便局に行くついでに、はがきを買ってきて。
examples.tr: While you're going to the post office, could you buy some postcards for me?

examples.jp: 図書館へ本を返すついでに、新刊をチェックした。
examples.tr: While I was returning books to the library, I checked out the new arrivals.

552.explain:
Nuance of "taking the chance / while at it", reducing the sense of making a separate effort for B.
Suitable in both spoken and written language; politeness is not affected.
Often used in gentle requests: ～ついでに、～てくれる？／～ていただけますか。

• Meaning: "While (doing) A, also do B"; B is an additional action done by taking advantage of the opportunity.
• Features:

A is the main purpose; B takes advantage of the opportunity of A (usually by the same person).
Close in time: while going to/arriving at/doing A, or just before/after A.

• A is the main purpose; B takes advantage of the opportunity of A (usually by the same person).
• Close in time: while going to/arriving at/doing A, or just before/after A.
• Restrictions: Not used when B is the main thing and A is just an excuse. Not used when the two subjects are different (unless the context allows it).

rows: While doing A, also do B
B is secondary, done while at it
<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くついでに<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う。
ご<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>かたがた<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>いました。
By the way (topic shift in conversation)
Does not express an A-B action relation
ところで、<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>件<rt>けん</rt></ruby>は？

mistakes: Reversing main and secondary: × 買い物のついでに旅行に行く → a trip cannot be something done "while you're at" shopping.
Different subjects cause ambiguity: × 私が行くついでに、彼が荷物を受け取る → the agent should be the same.
Confusion with ながら: ～ついでに does not express simultaneity, but taking advantage of an opportunity.
JLPT: a trap choosing among ところで/ながら/ついでに; tests understanding of the relation A (main) – B (secondary).
552.notes:
• V辞書形＋ついでに emphasizes "before doing A, also…"; Vた形＋ついでに emphasizes "having done A, also…".
• When making a request, add ついでで悪いけど… to be more polite: "Sorry to ask while you're at it, but…".
• For trips: ～に行くついでに often goes with a destination/route.
meaning_vi: 「～するとき、その期間を利用して…もする。」二つの別々のことを同時にやってしまうと言いたいときに使う。～が本来の行為、…はそれに加えてする、目的のある意志的行為。
When doing ~, take advantage of that opportunity to also do ….
Used when you want to say you get two separate things done at the same time.
~ is the original action; … is an additional action, a volitional action with a purpose.
examples: 1. 散歩のついでにこのはがきをポストに出してきて。
While you're out for a walk, could you drop this postcard in the mailbox?
2. 玄関の掃除をするついでに靴の整理をしよう。
While cleaning the entrance, let's tidy up the shoes too.
3. インターネットで本を注文したついでに新しく出たDVDも調べた。
While ordering a book online, I also looked up newly released DVDs.

examples.jp: 資料を確認しつつ、発表の準備を進める。
examples.tr: I'm preparing my presentation while checking the materials.

examples.jp: 将来に不安を感じつつ、新しい挑戦を始めた。
examples.tr: Although I felt anxious about the future, I started a new challenge.

examples.jp: 危険性を知りつつも、その計画を受け入れた。
examples.tr: Despite knowing the risks, I accepted the plan.

examples.jp: 彼の話を聞きつつ、ポイントをメモした。
examples.tr: I noted down the key points while listening to him.

examples.jp: 反省しつつ、前に進む。
examples.tr: Reflecting on the past while moving forward.

examples.jp: 彼女は体調に不安を抱えつつ、大会に出場した。
examples.tr: Despite worrying about her health, she competed in the tournament.

553.explain:
Formal style, used in reports, essays, and the news.
With the concessive meaning, often used in set phrases: 知りつつ、分かりつつ、危険と知りつつ、心配しつつ.
Not followed directly by a command/volition after つつ; if you need to give instructions, use ～ながら or a separate sentence.
The two parallel actions may not be completely simultaneous but take place in the same period.

• Simultaneity: performing two actions in parallel, consciously. Formal, crisp nuance.
• Concession: "although knowing/aware that ..., ...". Often used with verbs of perception: 知る、思う、感じる、悩む.
• Same subject for both clauses. Unlike ～ながら, つつ is rarely used in everyday conversation.
• Not used for momentary, sudden actions; suitable for prolonged, purposeful processes.

rows: Written language, same subject, no commands
<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聴<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する
Different meaning: a developing change, not "doing while doing"
Written language; does not require the same subject

mistakes: Using different subjects: × 彼は話しつつ、私はメモした → Use ながら or two independent sentences.
Using with punctual actions: × 立ち上がりつつ飛び出した → unnatural.
Adding a command right after つつ: × 注意しつつ来なさい → wrong nuance.
Confusion with つつある: つつ＝simultaneity/concession; つつある＝progression.
553.notes:
• The form "Vます＋つつも" is the classic formula for a contrast between awareness and action.
• Often seen in company documents: 検討しつつ、改善を進める／注意しつつ運用する.
• If the two actions have different agents, switch to ～ながら or a separate clause with its own subject.

554.meaning: In other words, in short, that is

examples.jp: 彼は父の弟、つまり私の叔父です。
examples.tr: He is my father's younger brother; in other words, my uncle.

examples.jp: この店は現金しか使えません。つまり、カードは不可です。
examples.tr: This store only accepts cash. In other words, cards aren't accepted.

examples.jp: 3割引、つまり30％オフという意味です。
examples.tr: It means a three-tenths discount, that is, 30% off.

examples.jp: つまり、今回の失敗は準備不足が原因だということですね。
examples.tr: So in short, this failure was caused by a lack of preparation.

examples.jp: 彼は来ないと言った。つまり、私たちだけで行くことになる。
examples.tr: He said he wasn't coming. That means we'll be going by ourselves.

554.explain:
Usually placed at the beginning of a sentence or mid-sentence, with a comma before/after to separate ideas.
Used in both speech and writing. In formal language, "すなわち/要するに" can replace it depending on the context.
When stating a strong conclusion: つまり～ということだ／わけだ to make the reasoning clear.
Do not say "つまりに/つまりな" (it is not a particle but an adverb/discourse marker).

• Rephrasing/explaining: Used to switch from way of saying A to an easier-to-understand way of saying B.
• Summary/conclusion: Wraps up after presenting reasons and facts.
• Definition/equivalence: "A, that is, B".
• Discourse nuance: Introduces the speaker's conclusion; sounds logical and coherent.

rows: Strong generalization; slightly more formal in writing/speech
<ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに、<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>だ
Outcome after a course of events; not "in other words"
<ruby>結局<rt>けっきょく</rt></ruby>、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなかった
<ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない

mistakes: Confusion with "結局": "結局" is the outcome after a process; "つまり" is rephrasing/equating ideas.
Omitting the preceding clause before "つまり": you need content A to rephrase as B.
Using "つまりに": grammatically incorrect (it does not take a particle).
Overuse in formal written language: consider "すなわち/要するに" depending on the nuance.
554.notes:
• The spelling "詰まり" (noun: blockage) differs from "つまり" (adverb: in short). In conversation, both are pronounced the same and are distinguished by context/kanji.
• When linking explanations smoothly: A。つまり、B。You can also write A、つまり、B for a lighter break.
• Adding "ということだ/わけだ/ってことだ" gives a sense of affirming the inferred conclusion. explain: Used to restate a thing or matter with an equivalent, different way of saying or naming it ⏐ examples: 1. 父の兄、つまり私の伯父は、医者をしている。
My father's older brother, that is, my uncle, is a doctor
2. 田中さんは、携帯もパソコンも持っていない。つまり、メールで連絡はできないのだ。
Tanaka has neither a cell phone nor a computer. In other words, you can't contact him by email

555.meaning: With the intention of, intending to

examples.jp: 冗談のつもりで言ったが、彼を傷つけてしまった。
examples.tr: I meant it as a joke, but I ended up hurting him.

examples.jp: 留学するつもりで英語を勉強している。
examples.tr: I'm studying English with the intention of studying abroad.

examples.jp: 飲んだつもりでそのお金を貯金している。
examples.tr: I'm saving that money as if I had spent it on drinks.

examples.jp: 客のつもりで店内をチェックした。
examples.tr: I checked the inside of the store as if I were a customer.

examples.jp: 正しいつもりで意見を言ったが、反感を買った。
examples.tr: I gave my opinion believing I was right, but it provoked resentment.

examples.jp: 忘れないつもりでメモを取った。
examples.tr: I took notes intending not to forget.

555.explain:
Placed before the main action as an adverbial expressing intention/purpose.
Vたつもりで often goes with verbs of saving/substitution:貯金する・我慢する・控える.
When emphasizing a stance/role: Nのつもりで + an action of observing/evaluating.
Usually subjective; if the purpose is clearly objective, use ～ために.

• States the purpose/intention when performing the main action: “with the intention of …, …”.
• Vたつもりで: “acting as if … had been done, in order to …”, used for saving/substitution.
• Nのつもりで: “playing the role of / assuming one is …”.
• Subjective nuance; differs from ～ために (actual purpose) because it emphasizes “mindset/tendency”.

rows: With the intention of / playing the role of
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>するつもりで<ruby>図書館<rt>としょかん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く
Ends the sentence, not an adverbial
<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby><ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>するつもりだ
<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>のために<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>る
Often goes with V<ruby>可能<rt>かのう</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby>/<ruby>自動詞<rt>じどうし</rt></ruby>
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>できるように<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する
<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>けるつもりでいる

mistakes: Used as a predicate: ～つもりで。× → A main clause must follow.
Confusing it with ～ために: if it shows a subjective mindset → つもりで; if an objective purpose → ために.
Vたつもりで does not mean the action was actually done; many trick questions state “not done, but treated as done”.
Wrong combination: Naだのつもりで × → Naなつもりで ○; Nだのつもりで × → Nのつもりで ○
555.notes:
• N3–N2. Often appears in reading questions when stating “playing the role of a customer/target”.
• Vたつもりで has a nuance of “restraint, substitution” that is very typical in savings ads/slogans.
• The comma can be omitted in short sentences: 冗談のつもりで言ったが…

examples.jp: 身分証を確認してからでないと入れません。
examples.tr: You cannot enter until your ID has been checked.

examples.jp: 工事が終わってからでないと通行できません。
examples.tr: Traffic cannot pass until the construction work is finished.

examples.jp: 親に相談してからでないと決められない。
examples.tr: I can't decide until I've talked it over with my parents.

examples.jp: 20歳になってからでないとお酒は飲めない。
examples.tr: You can't drink alcohol until you turn 20.

examples.jp: このソフトはインストールしてからでないと使えません。
examples.tr: This software cannot be used until it has been installed.

556.explain:
Used in rules, instructions and warnings: ～ません／～できません follows.
The clauses can be reordered to emphasize the procedure:予約してからでないと、受付できません。
Its nuance is more formal/standard than ordinary ないと/なければ because it emphasizes “only after having…”.

• States a necessary condition before carrying out the following action/accepting the following state: “Only after V can…”.
• The main clause usually means “cannot/not allowed/difficult”; it is rarely a direct affirmative.
• Expresses a mandatory sequence, rules, procedures, safety logic.

rows: <ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>してからでなければ<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>できない
Does not emphasize “only after having”; softer
<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>しないと<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れない
Emphasizes a realization/result that newly occurs
<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>して<ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>した
After V… (then do the next thing)
Neutral, often used in formal writing
<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>した<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>決定<rt>けってい</rt></ruby>する

mistakes: Using an affirmative main clause: ×登録してからでないと利用できます → it should be 利用できません.
Confusing the time sequence: the Vて clause is a condition that must be completed first; avoid describing simultaneous actions.
Missing conditional logic: the first clause must be a feasible/controllable action.
Confusing it with て初めて: てからでないと is a mandatory necessary condition; て初めて is a first-time realization/result.
556.notes:
• The main clause is almost always negative/expresses difficulty: ～ない／できない／困る／無理だ.
