• Useful in legal/procedural contexts: 入場、登録、承認、確認、支払い など.
• “じゃないと” is a colloquial variant; avoid it in formal documents. | Variant: ～てからでなければ

examples.jp: これ、食べてごらん。おいしいよ。
examples.tr: Try this. It's good.

examples.jp: もう一度やってごらん。できるはずだよ。
examples.tr: Try it once more. You should be able to do it.

examples.jp: 声を出して読んでごらん。
examples.tr: Try reading it out loud.

examples.jp: 外に出て風を感じてごらん。
examples.tr: Go outside and try feeling the wind.

examples.jp: 自分で考えてごらん。
examples.tr: Try thinking about it yourself.

examples.jp: 危ないから、触らないでごらん？（皮肉）
examples.tr: It's dangerous, so why don't you try not touching it? (sarcastic)

557.explain:
Used only with subordinates/children/people you are close to; not used with superiors/customers.
“～て ごらんなさい ” sounds softer than “～て ごらん ”.
Same function as “～てみなさい”; “～てみる” is voluntary and does not carry a command.
It can sound somewhat imposing if the relationship is not close enough.

• A suggestion/mild command, “try doing … and see”, directed at a listener of lower status or in a close relationship.
• Carries a nuance of encouraging direct experience: trying it to feel/conclude for oneself.
• ～てごらん is an imperative variant of “ご覧になる/ごらん” (to look/see), extended to all verbs via Vて.
mistakes: Using it with superiors/customers: inappropriate. Use “～てください／～ていただけますか”.
Confusing it with “～てみる”: ～てごらん is a command; ～てみる is trying something yourself.
Using the negative “～ないでごらん” in the wrong place can easily sound sarcastic/unpleasant.
Forgetting the polite form “～てごらんなさい” in educational/parent-child contexts.
557.notes:
• Originates from “ご覧なさい” (look!), extended into a mild command pattern for all verbs via Vて.
• In marketing/apps: “まずは無料で試してごらん” sounds quite casual; in standard writing, “お試しください” should be used.
• The interrogative form “～てごらん？” carries a nuance of invitation or sarcasm depending on intonation.

examples.jp: 明日の結果が気になってしょうがない。
examples.tr: I can't stop worrying about tomorrow's results.

examples.jp: 彼のことが羨ましくてしょうがない。
examples.tr: I'm terribly envious of him.

examples.jp: 雨で外出できず、退屈でしょうがない。
examples.tr: I can't go out because of the rain, and I'm bored to death.

examples.jp: 子どもが心配で(は)しょうがない。
examples.tr: I'm worried sick about my child.

examples.jp: 早く会いたくてしょうがない。
examples.tr: I'm dying to see you soon.

examples.jp: 足がかゆくてしょうがない。
examples.tr: My feet are unbearably itchy.

558.explain:
Leans toward colloquial use; used in everyday conversation to emphasize a strong degree.
Usually carries negative emotions; positive emotions are also possible but less common.
“で(は)” after な/N adds emphasis:退屈 では しょうがない (more emphatic than退屈でしょうがない).
Avoid using it to describe objective states/things that are not emotions (×忙しくてしょうがない in the objective sense of having a lot of work; use it only when the speaker feels “miserable because of being busy”).

Expresses a very strong degree of emotion/sensation, “unbearable/hard to stand”, almost beyond control.
• Usually used for spontaneous emotions: うれしい、悔しい、心配だ、恥ずかしい、退屈だ…
• The subject is usually the speaker (or someone whose feelings the speaker can empathize with/sense).
• Colloquial nuance. “～でしょうがない” sounds strongly conversational, while “～しょうがありません” is formal.
• Negative: ～なくてしょうがない (会えなくてしょうがない: not being able to see someone makes me terribly restless).

rows: ～てしょうがない/～で(は)しょうがない
<ruby>不安<rt>ふあん</rt></ruby>で(は)しょうがない
～てたまらない/～でたまらない
More formal than しょうがない
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>くて<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない

mistakes: Wrong form combination: ×嬉しいでしょうがない → 嬉しくてしょうがない; ×静かでしょうがない → 静かで(は)しょうがない.
Describing objective facts instead of the speaker's emotions → unnatural.
Confusing the nuance with ～でならない (more formal) and ～でたまらない (stronger).
JLPT N2: often tests conjugation (くて/で/て) and distinguishing the three patterns ～しょうがない／～たまらない／～ならない.
558.notes:
• “しょうがない” = “仕方がない” (colloquial). In formal written language, prefer “仕方がない/しょうがありません”.
• Often appears in fixed phrases: 気になってしょうがない／心配で(は)しょうがない／退屈で(は)しょうがない。
• When the subject is someone else, a context that allows inference about their feelings is usually needed.

examples.jp: 病気をしてはじめて、健康の大切さに気づいた。
examples.tr: It was only after getting sick that I realized how important health is.

examples.jp: 子供を持ってはじめて、親の苦労がわかった。
examples.tr: Only after having children did I understand how hard my parents had worked.

examples.jp: 一人暮らしをしてはじめて、家事の大変さを知った。
examples.tr: Only after living alone did I learn how hard housework is.

examples.jp: 海外出張に行ってはじめて、英語の必要性を痛感した。
examples.tr: Only after going on a business trip abroad did I keenly feel the need for English.

examples.jp: 病気になってはじめて、健康の大切さが分かる。
examples.tr: Only when you get sick do you understand how important health is.

examples.jp: 先生に注意されてはじめて、自分のミスに気づいた。
examples.tr: Only after the teacher pointed it out did I notice my own mistake.

559.explain:
After ～てはじめて comes a clause of result/first-time realization:分かった／気づいた／実感した／始まる…
Not used for ordinary, repeated results; it emphasizes “for the first time (初めて)”.
Often accompanied by words indicating a first time:初めて; はじめて itself already includes “first time”.
Narrative/reflective nuance; often seen in written language, essays, interviews.

• Meaning: “Only after/when doing X, for the first time…”, emphasizing that it had not happened/not been realized before.
• Scope: Usually goes with a result clause that is a first-time discovery/realization/feeling, or a state that starts to take effect.
• Implied negation of what came before: it implies “not before that” (まだ/全然/分からなかった…).
• Pivotal point in time: X is the trigger point for Y. Not used for obvious everyday things.

rows: Emphasizes the trigger point and “not before that”.
<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>してはじめて、<ruby>自立<rt>じりつ</rt></ruby>した。
Neutral about time; does not emphasize “first time/realization”.
<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べてから<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する。
Emphasizes continuity from that point to the present.
<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby>して<ruby>以来<rt>いらい</rt></ruby><ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>っていない。
The turning point is a change in status/state.
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>になってはじめて<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かる。
<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてみてはじめて<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しさが<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かる。

mistakes: Using it with a result that is not a “first time/realization” → wrong nuance. Replace it with ～てから.
Stating an obvious event/one without a trigger-result relationship → unnatural.
Confusing it with ～て以来 (continuing) in JLPT questions: watch for signals like “until now/ずっと”.
Wrong tense: using Vた + はじめて (×) → it must be Vてはじめて.
559.notes:
• After ～てはじめて, the verb is usually one of perception: 分かる／気づく／感じる／実感する／認識する／始める.
• Useful for skillfully stating a lesson learned from experience in reflective essays: 「失敗してはじめて、改めるべき点が見えた。」
• Do not attach a particle for a specific point in time before はじめて (×昨日してはじめて); use a Vて clause to indicate the turning point.

examples.jp: １時間も待たせたんだから、ワインさんが怒るものしかたがない。
examples.tr: I made Wine-san wait a whole hour, so it can't be helped if Wine-san gets angry.

examples.jp: 人気のコンサートだから、チケットが買えなくてもしかたがない。
examples.tr: It's a popular concert, so it can't be helped if you can't get tickets.

560.explain: ◎ Accepting being told or thought of in that way, even though it is not the best outcome.
560.notes:
meaning_vi: Expresses the feeling of accepting an unsatisfactory result.
examples: 1. ①　行っても仕方（が）ない
I have no choice but to go
2. ②　電車が止まったのなら、遅れても仕方（が）ない。
If the train has stopped, being late can't be helped.
3. ③　家賃が安いんだから、駅から遠くてもしょうがないよ。
The rent is cheap, so it can't be helped if it's far from the station.

561.connection: V (plain form) + ということ / N + だ / Na + だ / Aい

examples.jp: 旅館の人の話では、ここは夏でも寒い日があるということです。
examples.tr: According to the people at the ryokan, there are cold days here even in summer.

examples.jp: けさのニュースでは、きのう有名な作家が亡くなったということです。
examples.tr: According to this morning's news, a famous writer passed away yesterday.

561.explain: ◎ I will tell you what I have learned from information such as people's stories and what I have read.

examples.jp: 長期予報によると、今年の夏は暑いということだ。
examples.tr: According to the long-range forecast, this summer is going to be hot.

examples.jp: 医者の話では、２カ月ぐらいで退院できるだろうということだった。
examples.tr: According to the doctor, I would probably be able to leave the hospital in about two months.

examples.jp: 東京駅のあたりは昔は海だったということだ。
examples.tr: I hear the area around Tokyo Station used to be sea long ago.

examples.jp: 「ニュースで聞いたのですが、来年JRの運賃が値上げされるということですよ」
examples.tr: "I heard on the news that JR fares are going to be raised next year."

examples.jp: ＊「さっき電話があって、山田さんはきょう欠席するとのことです」
examples.tr: "There was a phone call a little while ago saying that Yamada-san will be absent today."

examples.jp: ＊「お嬢さんが大学に合格なさったとのこと、おめでとうございます」
examples.tr: "I hear your daughter passed her university entrance exam. Congratulations."

562.explain:
Used for hearsay: conveying indirect information from newspapers, other people, or official announcements.
Used to summarize or interpret a conclusion after presenting a situation.
Neutral, objective nuance; does not emphasize personal emotions.
In spoken language, it can be used to end a sentence when explaining: “…ということだね”.
Not suitable for commands or personal volition.

～ということだ has two main interpretations depending on the context:
• Conveying information/hearsay: “I hear that…”, “it is reported that…”. The speaker did not witness it directly but relays information from another source.
• Conclusion/interpretation: “that is…”, “that means…”, used to sum up what has just been stated.
In both cases, this pattern has an objective nuance, shows little personal emotion, and is common in written language, news, and logical explanations.

rows: <ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>ということだ。
Only for hearsay; not used for conclusions.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいらしい。
これは<ruby>危険<rt>きけん</rt></ruby>という意味だ。
A conclusion with a more subjective nuance.
だから<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>したわけだ。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～そうだ: if the sentence expresses a conclusion/summary, ～そうだ is not used.
Confusing it with ～わけだ: ～わけだ has a subjective nuance, while ～ということだ is more neutral.
Using it for personal volition: wrong. Example: ❌ 行きたいということだ.
Incorrectly omitting 「だ」 with nouns/na-adjectives in standard written language.
In JLPT reading, if the sentence contains “according to the newspaper, according to the announcement”, choose ～ということだ first.
562.notes:
1) The two meanings of ～ということだ are easily confused.
→ It means “I hear that…” (hearsay) and “that is…” (explanation/definition).
2) Look at the context.
→ If there is a source/something heard: the meaning is “I hear that”.
→ If summarizing or restating: the meaning is “that is”.
3) Easily confused with ～って (colloquial).
→ ～ということだ is more formal and often used in written language. | Spoken variant: ～ってことだ

examples.jp: お祭りと言うと、子供の頃を思い出します。
examples.tr: Festivals remind me of my childhood.

examples.jp: 夏休みと言うと、毎年、家族で旅行に出かけました。
examples.tr: Speaking of summer vacation, my family went on a trip every year.

examples.jp: 夏というと、海や花火を思い出す。
examples.tr: When it comes to summer, I think of the sea and fireworks.

examples.jp: 寿司というと、やっぱり日本でしょう。
examples.tr: When it comes to sushi, Japan is the place, of course.

examples.jp: 京都というと、寺と紅葉が有名だ。
examples.tr: Speaking of Kyoto, it is famous for its temples and autumn leaves.

examples.jp: 引っ越すというと、どこへ行くつもりですか。
examples.tr: You say you're moving. Where are you planning to go?

563.explain:
Placed after a noun/topic just heard or seen, to open an association or ask for clarification.
Often goes with verbs of association:思い出す・連想する・言えば…
When confirming meaning, というと is usually followed by a question/explanation clause.
It feels more casual than といえば in direct conversation; というと leans toward “typical association”.

• Association/typical: from a keyword, states what is commonly associated, a representative example.
• Checking/re-emphasizing content: used when you want to confirm “if you say that, it means…, right?”.
• Conversational nuance; というと emphasizes a topic shift triggered by a keyword just mentioned/heard.

rows: speaking of N, that reminds me…
<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>紅葉<rt>こうよう</rt></ruby>といったら…
spoken form of というと
<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>っていうと<ruby>粉<rt>こな</rt></ruby>もの

mistakes: Using というと to connect two clauses with no association → forced. There should be a clear reminder relationship.
Confusing it with というのは for definitions. というと is not used to define terms.
Confusing the nuance with といったら: というと is neutral; といったら carries strong/excessive emotion.
563.notes:
• Often appears in conversation when hearing a new keyword: A「留学します。」B「留学というと、どこに？」
• というと is not used to define concepts; for definitions use というのは／とは.
• In written language, というと often goes with formulaic phrases: 一般に～といえば／～と聞くと～を連想する。

examples.jp: 「肉じゃが」というのは、肉とジャガイモ、玉ねぎなどを煮た料理です。
examples.tr: 「肉じゃが」 is a dish of meat, potatoes, onions and so on simmered together.

examples.jp: 「成人式」というのは、２０歳になったことを祝う行事です。
examples.tr: The Coming-of-Age Ceremony is an event celebrating turning 20.

examples.jp: 「おもてなし」というのは、相手を思いやる心のことだ。
examples.tr: 「おもてなし」 means a heart that is considerate of others.

examples.jp: 東京というのは、人と情報が集まる都市だ。
examples.tr: Tokyo is a city where people and information come together.

examples.jp: 行けません。というのは、急用ができたからです。
examples.tr: I can't go. That's because something urgent has come up.

examples.jp: 彼が天才だというのは、少し言い過ぎだ。
examples.tr: Saying that he is a genius is a bit of an exaggeration.

564.explain:
After というのは there is usually a sentence giving a definition, stating the essence, or making a general evaluation.
When used to give a reason, the following sentence often ends with からだ／ためだ／わけだ to make the causal relationship clear.
More formal than っていうのは; suitable for documents and lectures.
It can also be used with a clause: S(plain) + というのは、～ (the fact that … is …).

• Defining/explaining a concept: AというのはBだ = “what is called A is B”.
• Introducing a reason: place というのは at the beginning of the sentence that follows, to state the reason for the previous sentence.
• Explanatory, coherent nuance; often used in presentations, writing, or when you want to clarify a term.

rows: <ruby>多様<rt>たよう</rt></ruby><ruby>性<rt>せい</rt></ruby>というのは…
concise, formal; goes with <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>々とは～だ
used to lead into a consequence
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>だ。ということは…
no は; does not define by itself
<ruby>多様<rt>たよう</rt></ruby><ruby>性<rt>せい</rt></ruby>という<ruby>概念<rt>がいねん</rt></ruby>
<ruby>多様<rt>たよう</rt></ruby><ruby>性<rt>せい</rt></ruby>っていうのは…

mistakes: Using というと instead of というのは to define → wrong function.
Forgetting は: “多様性というのは” → without は, the meaning is incomplete in its defining role.
Turning というのは into a long-winded bridge between two sentences that have no reason/definition relationship → wordy, loses coherence.
564.notes:
• Since it gives a definition, avoid an overly specific example right after というのは; state the essence first, then give examples.
• When giving a reason, というのは usually comes at the beginning of a sentence, starting a new one after a period or a paragraph break.
• In negative evaluations, it often goes with ～にすぎない／～とは限らない／～わけではない.
meaning_vi: Defines what something is like. The meaning of ~ is...
examples: 1. ➀　デジカメとは
デジカメ is...
2. ②　デジカメとは、デジタルカメラ（のこと）だ。
デジカメ is a digital camera.
3. ③　「ひそひそ話すって（いうのは）、どんな話し方？」「ほかの人に聞こえないように小さい声で話すことだよ」
"What kind of way of talking is whispering?" "It's talking in a low voice so that other people can't hear."
4. ➃　顔が広いと（いうの）は、いろいろな分野に友達がたくさんいるという意味だ。
Having a wide circle of acquaintances means having many friends in various fields.
Definition variant: N + とは

565.meaning: So-called… | That is, it is precisely…

examples.jp: 彼が来ないというのは本当ですか。
examples.tr: Is it true that he isn't coming?

examples.jp: 彼女が合格したというのを聞いて安心した。
examples.tr: I was relieved to hear that she had passed.

examples.jp: 締め切りが今日までだというので、急いで提出した。
examples.tr: I was told the deadline was today, so I hurried to submit it.

examples.jp: これで十分だというのだ。もう買わなくていい。
examples.tr: This is enough, that's what I'm saying. You don't need to buy any more.

examples.jp: これが正義だというのか。納得できない。
examples.tr: You call this justice? I can't accept that.

examples.jp: 日本へ行くというのが昔からの夢だ。
examples.tr: Going to Japan has been my dream for a long time.

565.explain:
というの has an explanatory/emotional tone; ということ is more objective and abstract.
In casual speech, というの → っていうの; in formal written language, ということ is preferred.
With というのか , intonation is important to express a question with a somewhat contradicting tone.
というので is often used when the reason is indirect information (heard/believed that).

• ① Affirmation / emphasis: Used when the speaker wants to strongly affirm what they just stated or draw a conclusion from previous information.
→ “That is…”, “It means…”.
• ② Conveying information (reported speech): Means “I hear that…”. More formal than「～そうだ」「～らしい」.
• ③ Emphasizing emotion, explaining a reason: May carry surprise, reproach, or an assertion of what is right.
• More formal than というんだ / っていうんだ. Used in written language, speeches, essays, and explanatory texts.

rows: That is…, I hear…, strong affirmation
Formal; the emotion can be strong
<ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>というのだ。
<ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>ということだ。
<ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>そうだ。
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>いというのに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた。

mistakes: Confusing ということ with というの: in academic writing, use ということ and avoid というの.
Attaching です/ます before というの: 来ますというの (unnatural) → 来るというの.
Using というのか too strongly in polite language → it can easily sound aggressive.
565.notes:
• Often used in written language, reports, news, and speeches.
• In casual conversation, Japanese people often say: ～っていうんだ.
• Can carry a judgmental emotion: “You're saying that…?”, “You mean…?”

examples.jp: 担任の山田先生はとても若くて、先生というより友だちみたいだ。
examples.tr: Our homeroom teacher, Yamada-sensei, is very young and seems more like a friend than a teacher.

examples.jp: 社内は冷房が効きすぎていて、涼しいというより寒いくらいだった。
examples.tr: The air conditioning in the office was too strong; it was cold rather than cool.

examples.jp: 試合に負けたことは、残念と言うよりただ悔しい。
examples.tr: Losing the match was not so much disappointing as simply frustrating.

examples.jp: 私にとって留学は、外界で学ぶというより家を出る手段であった。
examples.tr: For me, studying abroad was not so much a way to learn about the outside world as a means of leaving home.

examples.jp: 彼はリーダーというよりムードメーカーだ。
examples.tr: He is not so much a leader as the one who lifts everyone's mood.

examples.jp: この映画は怖いというより悲しい。
examples.tr: This movie is sad rather than scary.

567.explain:
Used to rephrase an expression, emphasizing that B is more fitting than A.
Has a mildly contradicting nuance and is polite if used skillfully; add むしろ to emphasize “contrary to expectation”.
Suitable for describing impressions and evaluations; avoid it when a completely neutral statement is needed.
In spoken language, it can be replaced by というか (lighter) or っていうか (very colloquial).

• Literally “it is more correct to say A than B”, but in actual usage it negates/adjusts A and affirms that B is the more fitting expression. Natural translation: “not so much A as B”, “rather than A, it should be called B”.
• A is a general or old description/label; B is the essence/core point the speaker wants to emphasize.
• Often carries a nuance of rephrasing, correcting oneself, or subjective evaluation; stronger in degree than というか (which works as a filler).
• Often used to compare qualities and impressions: “beautiful… rather than cute”, “hot… rather than warm”.
• With むしろ: highlights the reversal of expectation, “it should really be B”.

rows: Corrects A, affirms that B is more fitting
<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かというより<ruby>寂<rt>さび</rt></ruby>しい
How should I put it, sort of B
<ruby>面白<rt>おもしろ</rt></ruby>いというか<ruby>変<rt>へん</rt></ruby>
<ruby>犬<rt>いぬ</rt></ruby>より<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>き
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>というよりはむしろ<ruby>才能<rt>さいのう</rt></ruby>
If I had to choose, leaning toward B
どちらかといえば<ruby>辛<rt>つら</rt></ruby>い

mistakes: Reversing the order of A/B: it must be “AというよりB” (B is the main point).
Adding an unnecessary だ: “先生だというより” is not wrong, but “先生というより” is usually more natural.
Using it when A and B are not on the same axis of comparison: they should belong to the same category/quality to be logical.
Confusing it with AよりB (ordinary comparison) in JLPT questions: というより has the nuance of “correcting the expression”.
567.notes:
• With nouns/na-adjectives, だ before というより is usually omitted; だというより is not wrong but is more formal.
• A can be fairly negative to set off a positive B (or vice versa) for rhetorical effect.
• In polite disagreement, you can begin with: どちらかというと/私の印象では…＋B。
meaning: 「～という言い方より…という言い方の方が適切だ。」 ～より、もっと適切な言い方（…）を示すときに使う
The expression … is more appropriate than the expression ~.
Used when you want to point out that the expression … is more appropriate than the expression ~.
examples: 1. ぼくと彼が友達？ いや、僕たちは友だちというよりいい競争相手なんだよ。
He and I are friends? No, we're more like good rivals than friends.
2. 美知子は歩くのが速い。歩くというより走るという感じだ。
美知子 walks fast. It's more like running than walking.
3. A 「へえ、この絵、社長に頼まれてかいたんですか。」
B 「頼まれて、というより命令されたんだよ。」

568.meaning: Speaking of… (evoking an association: といえば)

examples.jp: 日本料理といえば、やはりおすしが有名ですね。
examples.tr: Speaking of Japanese food, sushi is the famous one, isn't it?

examples.jp: 「母の日」といえば、カーネーションがすぐに浮かぶけど、ほかの花でもいいんですよ。
examples.tr: Speaking of Mother's Day, carnations come to mind right away, but other flowers are fine too, you know.

examples.jp:
A: 今朝、電車の窓から富士山が見えたよ。すごくきれいだった。
B: そう。富士山っていえば、田中さんが来月登るんだって。
※くだけた会話では「っていえば」になる。
examples.tr:
A: I saw Mt. Fuji from the train window this morning. It was really beautiful.
B: Oh yeah? Speaking of Mt. Fuji, I heard Tanaka is going to climb it next month.
※In casual conversation, it becomes 「っていえば」.

568.explain:
◎ An expression that picks up a word from the flow of the conversation and talks about something related to it.
◎ Mentions something one has been reminded of by something just said in the conversation.
568.notes:
meaning: Speaking of ~, mentioning ~, when it comes to ~
examples: 1. 日本料理といえば、おすしや天ぷらが人気だ。
Speaking of Japanese food, sushi and tempura are very popular.
2. 夏といえば、やっぱり海へ行きたくなる。
Speaking of summer, it makes you want to go to the sea.
3. 日本と言えば、何が思い浮かびますか。
When it comes to Japan, what comes to your mind?
4. 心理学と言えば、確か、田中さんが専門だって言っていた。
Speaking of psychology, that reminds me, I think it's Tanaka's major. | Variant: ～といったら

examples.jp: 「キムさん、大学でロシア語を勉強したそうですね」
examples.tr: "Kim, I hear you studied Russian in college."

examples.jp: 「ええ、でも、勉強したといっても、初級レベルだけなんですよ」
examples.tr: "Yes, but even though I say I studied it, it was only at the beginner level."

examples.jp: 「今度のアパートは駅から遠いのよ」
examples.tr: "My new apartment is far from the station, you know."

examples.jp: 「でも、遠いといっても歩いて１５分なんでしょ」
examples.tr: "But even if it's far, it's only a 15-minute walk, right?"

examples.jp: 「駅の周辺は、昼間はにぎやかだといっても、夜は人通りが少ないんです」
examples.tr: "The area around the station may be lively during the day, but there aren't many people around at night."

examples.jp: この辺りは一戸建てが多く。しかし一戸建てといっても、敷地はせいぜい９０平方メートルぐらいだ。
examples.tr: There are many detached houses in this area. But even though they're detached houses, the lots are about 90 square meters at most.

569.explain:
B uses real information to adjust the expectation set up by A; often appears in explanations and when being modest.
Common in natural conversation; can also be used in neutral written language.
Rarely used to lead into a command/suggestion; usually states facts, evaluations, or habits.

• “Although it is called A… (actually) B”: states a label/concept A, then lowers expectations and clarifies the reality B.
• Emphasizes the gap between a name/stereotype and reality: “it's called cheap, but it's actually not that cheap…”.
• Often used to set a limitation on scope, degree, or exceptions; B is usually information that corrects expectations.
• Concessive nuance, more objective than けど/が, with little strong emotion.

rows: Although it is called A, B
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>といっても<ruby>背<rt>せ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い
<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>とはいえ<ruby>欠点<rt>けってん</rt></ruby>もある
General connective; does not imply a “label” like といっても
Colloquial variant of といっても
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いっていっても<ruby>千<rt>せん</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>

mistakes: B has the wrong function (command/suggestion): avoid “Aといっても、〜してください/〜ましょう”.
Confusing it with とはいえ in terms of style: if the question requires a formal nuance → choose とはいえ.
A is not a “label”, so the sentence sounds forced: prefer A as a general frame and B as the specific reality.
569.notes:
• A is usually a “label/title”: a season, job title, nationality, state…
• When you need to be humble: できるといっても、少しだけです。
• B can express partial negation of the expectation, or give an exception/limiting condition.

570.meaning:
Expresses the meaning “in accordance with ~”
読む／読んだ　+　とおり（に）／とおりだ
予想の　+　とおり（に）／とおりだ
予想　+　とおり（に）／とおりだ
570.connection: Vる + とおりに / V plain form / N + どおりに のとおりに

examples.jp: 先週決めたとおりに、会議は6時から行います。
examples.tr: As we decided last week, the meeting will be held from 6 o'clock.

examples.jp: 先輩に聞いていたとり、石川先生の試験は難しかった。
examples.tr: Just as I had heard from my senpai, Professor Ishikawa's exam was difficult.

examples.jp: 心配していたとおり
examples.tr: Just as I had feared

examples.jp: 先生が黒板に書いたとおりにノートに書いた。
examples.tr: I wrote in my notebook exactly what the teacher wrote on the blackboard.

examples.jp: 説明書のとおりに作ったが、うまくできなかった。
examples.tr: I made it following the instructions, but it didn't turn out well.

examples.jp: 会議は予定どおり終わった。
examples.tr: The meeting ended as scheduled.

570.explain: ◎ Expresses doing something exactly as promised, planned, or instructed.

rows: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>のように<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す
Keeping as is/ as one pleases

mistakes: Confusing “Nどおり” with “Nのどおり”: after a noun to form a compound word, use “どおり”, without inserting “の”.
Using とおり instead of ように when you mean a general “like” → the nuance easily becomes wrong. For example, to describe a style, use ように.
Forgetting “に” with a verb: ×先生が言ったとおり書く → ◯先生が言ったとおりに書く.
Confusing it with “通り” meaning “street”: the 文脈 decides; do not translate mechanically.
570.notes:
examples: 1. わたしが　やった　とおりに、やって　ください。
Please do it exactly the way I did.
2. 見た　とおりに　話して　ください。
Please tell us exactly what you saw.
3. 線のとおりに　紙を　折りました。
I folded the paper along the line.
explain: Also used for commands/instructions: ～とおりにしてください.
Emphasizes exactness according to a model/standard (a drawing, a procedure, instructions).
Meaning “just as expected/planned”: ～のとおりだ/だった.
In casual use, “Nどおり” is common; in formal/precise use, the full “Nのとおり” is used.
Not used for loose “similar” comparisons without a standard; in that case ように is more natural.
examples: 1. 説明書に書いてあるとおりに組み立ててください。
Please assemble it exactly as written in the instructions.
2. 先生が言ったとおりに発音すれば通じます。
If you pronounce it exactly as the teacher said, you'll be understood.
3. 試合は予想どおりの結果になった。
The match ended with the expected result.
4. 写真のとおり、部屋はとても広いです。
Just as in the photo, the room is very spacious.
5. いつもどおり落ち着いてやれば大丈夫だ。
If you stay calm and do it as usual, you'll be fine.
meaning: Exactly as…/Just like…
Just as (expected/planned/instructed/hoped…)
As you have seen/know…
explain: Expresses an action or result that happens exactly as was said, seen, heard, or demonstrated. Emphasizes “exactly like that”.
Used with nouns such as prediction, plan, instruction, order, expectation… to say that the result turned out as anticipated.
A formal expression, often used in presentations: “as you have seen/know/heard…”. Used a lot in polite spoken language and announcements.
examples: 1. 学生たちは、先生が黒板に書いたとおりにノートに写した。
The students copied into their notebooks exactly what the teacher wrote on the blackboard.
2. 外国語だと、なかなか思ったとおりに話すことができない。
In a foreign language, it's hard to speak exactly the way you want.
3. 父は、私たち家族が父の言うとおりにしないと、きげんが悪い。
My father gets in a bad mood if our family doesn't do as he says.
4. 勉強がなかなか予定どおりに進まない。
My studies aren't progressing as planned.
5. 幼い弟は思いどおりにならないと大声で泣く。
Whenever things don't go his way, my little brother cries loudly.
6. 例のとおりに書きなさい。
Write it exactly like the example.
examples: 1. 交番で教えてもらったとおりに歩いていったので、迷わず会場に着いた。
I walked exactly as I was told at the police box, so I got to the venue without getting lost.
2. 初めて作る料理だから、この本に書いてあるとおりのやり方で作ってみよう。
Since it's my first time making this dish, I'll try making it exactly the way this book says.
3. サッカーの試合の結果はわたしたちの期待どおりだった。
The result of the soccer match was just as we had hoped.
explain: An action that is performed continuously
Used to indicate that an action is performed exactly according to the content expressed by the noun.
examples: 1. 友達がかいてくれた地図のとおりに来たが、道に迷った。
I came following the map my friend drew for me, but I got lost.
2. 雪が降ってきた。予定どおりだ。
It has started snowing. Just as predicted.
3. 先生が言ったとおり、試験は難しかった。
Just as the teacher said, the exam was difficult.
meaning: As, just like
explain: Used to indicate that something proceeds exactly according to the content stated before.
examples: 1. 友達が言ったとおり、日本の物価は高い。
Just as my friend said, prices in Japan are high.
2. 自分の思うとおりに生きることは難しい。
Living exactly as you wish is really hard.
3. 希望どおり
Just as hoped.
4. アドバイスどおり
Following the advice.

571.connection: [what was expected] + ところが + [contrary result]

examples.jp: 早く出れば間に合うと思った。ところが、事故で大渋滞だった。
examples.tr: I thought I'd make it in time if I left early. However, there was a huge traffic jam because of an accident.

examples.jp: 薬を飲めば治るはずだ。ところが、熱が上がった。
examples.tr: Taking the medicine should have cured it. However, the fever went up.

examples.jp: 彼は来ると約束した。ところが、現れなかった。
examples.tr: He promised he would come. However, he never showed up.

examples.jp: テストは簡単だと思った。ところが、平均点は低かった。
examples.tr: I thought the test was easy. However, the average score turned out to be low.

examples.jp: 連絡したつもりだった。ところが、相手に届いていなかった。
examples.tr: I thought I had contacted them. However, the message hadn't reached them.

571.explain:
Used when there is a clear “gap between expectation and reality”; creates a sense of surprise and irony.
Can be used in both spoken and written language; somewhat more formal than でも, close to しかし but with a stronger nuance of “surprise”.
Avoid following it with a command/suggestion/volition: use でも/しかし instead if needed.

• A conjunction meaning “however/who would have thought”: presents an actual result completely contrary to an earlier prediction or plan.
• Carries a nuance of surprise and the unexpected; the degree of reversal is stronger than でも/しかし in many contexts.
• The second clause must be a fact that has occurred, not the speaker's volition/suggestion.

rows: The second clause is a fact that has occurred
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。ところが<ruby>閉<rt>し</rt></ruby>まっていた。
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>した。しかし<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>は<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>ない。
Widely used; can be followed by a suggestion
Well, the thing is… (contrary to the plan)
Conversation; explains a reason that went against the plan
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くつもりが、それが<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けなくて…
ところで<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>議題<rt>ぎだい</rt></ruby>は？

mistakes: Using it with volition/suggestion in the second clause: ×「雨だ。ところが、行きましょう。」→ use でも/しかし.
Confusing it with しかし in sentences without an element of “surprise”: if the question emphasizes surprise → choose ところが.
Using it when the two clauses contrast only slightly: not strong enough → しかし/だが is more natural.
571.notes:
• It often stands at the beginning of a sentence followed by a comma: ところが、… to emphasize the turn.
• Suits narration/storytelling: clause 1 is a “reasonable premise”, clause 2 is “the twist”.
• In emails/when presenting risks, ところが helps make clear that it was an “unavoidable incident”. explain: Often used to negate a conjecture, plan, or thought about a matter or action ⏐ examples: 1. 昨夜はコンサートに行くつもりだった。ところが病気で行けなくなった。
Last night I was planning to go to a concert. However, I got sick and couldn't go.
2. 田中さんは私より若いと思っていた。ところが私より５歳も年上だった。
I thought Tanaka was younger than me. However, Tanaka turned out to be a full 5 years older.

572.connection: V plain form + とすれば としたら とすると / N + だ / Na + だ / Aい

examples.jp: この中から一つ選ぶとしたら、一番右のがいい。
examples.tr: If I had to choose one of these, I'd go with the one on the far right.

examples.jp: 今日で世界が終わるとしたら、最後にステーキを食べるだろう。
examples.tr: If the world were to end today, I'd probably eat a steak as my last meal.

examples.jp: もし彼が来ないとしたら、会議は延期にします。
examples.tr: If he doesn't come, we'll postpone the meeting.

examples.jp: 明日が休みだとしたら、どこへ行きたいですか。
examples.tr: Supposing tomorrow were a day off, where would you want to go?

examples.jp: この計画が失敗するとしたら、原因は何だろう。
examples.tr: If this plan were to fail, what would the cause be?

examples.jp: 地震が起きるとしたら、まず何をすべきですか。
examples.tr: If an earthquake were to happen, what should we do first?

572.explain:
Suitable for discussions, planning, scientific suppositions, and hypothetical-situation questions.
Rarely used for habits/real conditions. For real conditions, use なら/たら.
Comes before the concluding clause and is often accompanied by conjecture: ～だろう／かもしれない／と思う.
More formal than とすれば; softer than とすると (which has a more logical/technical nuance).

• Supposing/if we assume that ~, then…; used to state a consequence or a choice based on a hypothesis.
• Often used for situations that “may not happen”, leaning toward conjecture, planning, or asking for opinions.
• Often accompanied by どうする／どうなる／だろう／でしょう／場合は…など.
• More formal in nuance than なら; rarely used for conditions that already are/have been true.

rows: <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けないとしたら、<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>する
Based on information given by the speaker/listener
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたら<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>して
Concession/emphasizes that the result does not change
<ruby>事実<rt>じじつ</rt></ruby>とすれば<ruby>重大<rt>じゅうだい</rt></ruby>だ

mistakes: Using ～としたら for a certain condition: replace it with なら/たら.
Forgetting だ with N/na: × 学生としたら → 〇 学生だとしたら.
Confusing it with ～としても (concession) in sentences that require the emphasis “even if”: choose ～としても.
～としたら is usually followed by a conjecture/conclusion; avoid abruptly attaching a strong command directly.
572.notes:
• At the beginning of the sentence, もし is often added to make the suppositional nuance clear: もし～としたら.
• In academic writing, the flow is: 前提Aだとしたら→仮説→検証/示唆…
• Avoid using it when the condition has been confirmed, as it sounds roundabout/distant.

examples.jp: 今は留学生だが、以前に一度観光客として来日したことがある。
examples.tr: I'm an international student now, but I once came to Japan before as a tourist.

examples.jp: Aさんは最近歌手としてよりも俳優として活躍している。
examples.tr: Recently, A has been more active as an actor than as a singer.

examples.jp: 私個人としては賛成だが、皆と相談してからでないと結論は出せない。
examples.tr: Personally I'm in favor, but I can't reach a conclusion until I've discussed it with everyone.

examples.jp: 「我が社といたしましては、今月中に契約をまとめたいと思っております」
examples.tr: "Our company would like to finalize the contract within this month."

examples.jp: 赤やピンクは色としては好きだが、私には似合いそうもない。
examples.tr: I like red and pink as colors, but they don't seem to suit me.

examples.jp: 彼はバレーボールの選手としては小柄だ。
examples.tr: He is small for a volleyball player.

573.explain:
Formal-neutral; usable in both spoken and written language.
Often appears in contexts of profession, social status, legal capacity, or a role within a group.
としては emphasizes a standpoint; としての links the following noun to the role.
Not used directly with adjectives; you must go through nominalization or choose another structure.

• Specifying a role/capacity: states a position, title, or status as the basis for speaking/acting.
• Modifier expressing a quality with としての + N: emphasizes characteristics and responsibilities tied to the role.
• Viewpoint/evaluation with としては: “from the standpoint of…, …”.
• Hypothetical concession with としても: “even as…, still…”.

rows: <ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>として<ruby>助言<rt>じょげん</rt></ruby>する

Leaving out の in としての + N when it modifies a noun.
Using として directly with an adjective: incorrect; a noun/role concept is needed.
573.notes:
• The noun before として should be a noun that clearly indicates a role (教師, 専門家, 親, 市民...). Abstract nouns may need further nominalization.
• When the subject is not shown, the context usually implies “the capacity of the sentence's subject”.
• In job applications/self-promotion: 〜としての強み/経験/実績 are frequently occurring phrases. meaning: As/in the position of/ As/in the position of…, then/ Even as/in the position of… ⏐ explain: Used when talking about a thing or person as a representative of, or an individual belonging to, a general group ⏐ examples: 1. 彼は外国人だが、日本代表として試合に出る。
He is a foreigner, but he plays in the match as a representative of Japan.
2. 彼女は女性としても女優としても最高だが、妻としてはどうだろう。
She is wonderful both as a woman and as an actress, but how is she as a wife?

If we suppose that …, in the case of …

examples.jp: 太陽を直径１メートルの球だとします。すると地球は９ミリくらいです。
examples.tr: Let's suppose the sun is a ball 1 meter in diameter. Then the earth would be about 9 millimeters.

examples.tr: “If I were to visit someone in the hospital, around what time would be best?”

examples.tr: If A=B and B=C, then A=C.

examples.jp: あの工場の廃水が病気の原因だとすれば、当然補償問題が出てくるだろう。

574.explain:
Used to suppose a situation or condition that has not happened, and from there draw an inference or state an opinion.

574.notes:
1) The supposition forms are easy to confuse.
→ ～とする means “suppose that…”, often used when setting up an imaginary condition.
2) Your data contains many ct (ghichu=2/3).
→ If you want separate traps for each form (としたら／としても), you need to add updates according to the corresponding ghichu.
3) Do not confuse it with ～とすると (natural result).
→ ～とする means “regard as/suppose”; ～とすると can mean “if so, then” based on inference.

575.meaning: If we suppose…, if we assume…
575.connection: V plain form + とすれば としたら とすると / N + だ / Na + だ / Aい

examples.jp: Aさんが欠席だとすると、人数は9人だ。
examples.tr: If A is absent, there will be nine people.

examples.jp: 出発が1時間遅れるとすると、到着は19時ごろになる。

examples.jp: 明日雨だとすると、試合は中止だ。

575.explain:
Leads an analysis: sets up a supposition and immediately draws a conclusion/consequence.
Avoid using it with a command/strong volition in the second clause; it suits judgments, plans, and calculations better.
In conversation, the contracted form だとすると/とすると at the beginning of a sentence sounds natural for continuing a line of reasoning.

• Sets up a supposition as a premise for reasoning, calculating, or deciding: “if/supposing … then …”.
• Often used when the information is uncertain; the speaker temporarily treats it as true to draw a logical consequence.
• Suitable for quick calculations, “what-if” scenarios, and checking conditions.
• Neutral nuance, usable in both spoken and written language; somewhat argumentative.

rows: <ruby>増税<rt>ぞうぜい</rt></ruby>とすると<ruby>影響<rt>えいきょう</rt></ruby>は…
<ruby>事実<rt>じじつ</rt></ruby>とすれば<ruby>由々<rt>ゆゆ</rt></ruby>しき<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>
More colloquial, closer to the speaker
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>だとしたら…
Takes previously received information as the condition
<ruby>着<rt>ちゃく</rt></ruby>いたら<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して

mistakes: Confusing it with 〜としたところで (concession). 〜とすると is an inferential condition and does not imply “even if … still …”.
Using a command/strong volition in the second clause → unnatural. Use a judgment/plan, not “〜しろ”.
Multiple-choice trap: とすると vs なら. When the information comes from the listener/outside context → なら; when you set up a supposition yourself to infer something → とすると.
575.notes:
• In logic/textbooks, 〜とすると often goes with 証明・仮定・結論. Example: 「仮にAとすると、Bが導かれる。」
• Used in quick estimates: 「一人500円とすると、合計は…」
• Placed at the beginning of a paragraph to shift the line of argument: 「だとすると、次に問題となるのは…」

576.meaning: Together with…, at the same time…

examples.jp: 年を取るとともに、記憶力が弱くなる。
examples.tr: As you get older, your memory gets weaker.

examples.jp: 春の訪れとともに、花が咲き始めた。
examples.tr: With the arrival of spring, the flowers began to bloom.

examples.jp: この町は観光地であるとともに、歴史的な価値も高い。
examples.tr: This town is a tourist destination and, at the same time, has high historical value.

examples.jp: スマホの普及とともに、生活スタイルも変化した。
examples.tr: With the spread of smartphones, lifestyles have also changed.

examples.jp: 彼は医者であるとともに、大学の教授でもある。
examples.tr: He is a doctor and also a university professor.

examples.jp: この地域では、工業の発展とともに、人口も増え続けている。
examples.tr: In this area, along with the development of industry, the population also continues to grow.

576.explain:
Used in written language, speeches, reports, and theses → formal.
Not used much in casual speech (replaced by いっしょに, ～につれて, ～ながら).
When it means “a change that brings along another,” it is close to ～につれて/～にしたがって but more formal.
When it means “at the same time,” it is close to ～だけでなく / ～そして, but the wording is tighter.

•
① Together with, at the same time as: two actions/events happen simultaneously.

•
② As A changes, B also changes: expresses parallel change in a tendency.

•
③ Holding several roles/qualities at the same time: “is … and at the same time also …”.

• The context is usually formal, written language, or logical expression.

rows: Together with / At the same time / Both… and…
Formal, used in written language or speeches.
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>とともに<ruby>経験<rt>けいけん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>える。
The more… the more… / Brings along
Only about change over time, does not mean “accompanying”.
<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>経<rt>た</rt></ruby>つにつれて<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れてきた。
Expresses two parallel actions by the same agent.
<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聞<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する。
Adds another piece of information; does not mean “happening at the same time”.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>だけでなく<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>も<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>せる。

mistakes: Confusing it with につれて → につれて is only about change and is not used to say “together with someone”.
Dropping “である” with nouns/na-adjectives → grammatically incorrect in written language.
Using it in very casual conversation makes the sentence stiff and unnatural.
Not putting a comma “、” after とともに in written language → you should include it to make the flow clear.
576.notes:
1) The three meanings of ～とともに are easy to confuse.
→ It can mean “together with” (accompanying), “at the same time” (simultaneity), and “as A changes, B also changes”.
2) Look at the type of word before the pattern.
→ If it is a person/group: usually “together with”.
→ If it is a simultaneous event: “at the same time”.
→ If it is a change: “changing together”.
3) Easy to confuse with ～につれて／～にしたがって.
→ When emphasizing objective change over a process, ～につれて／～にしたがって is usually clearer. explain: Used when you want to say that things or events progress at the same time.
Together with one change, another change also takes place. ⏐ examples: 1. 家族とともに来日した。
Came to Japan together with my family.
2. 自動車が普及するとともに、事故も増加した。
As cars became widespread, accidents also increased.

examples.jp: 合格の知らせを聞いて、どんなに嬉しかったことか。
examples.tr: I was so happy when I heard I had passed!

examples.jp: 一人で海外にいて、どんなに心細かったことか。
examples.tr: How lonely I felt being alone abroad!

examples.jp: あなたに会える日をどんなに待ったことか。
examples.tr: How long I've waited for the day I could see you!

examples.jp: 親になって初めて、両親の苦労がどんなに大きいことか分かった。
examples.tr: Only after becoming a parent did I understand how great my parents' hardships were.

examples.jp: 事故が起きなくて、どんなにほっとしたことか。
examples.tr: What a relief it was that there was no accident!

examples.jp: 支えてくれた皆さんに、どんなに感謝していることか。
examples.tr: I'm so grateful to all of you who supported me!

577.explain:
The sentence usually stops at ～ことか。 to keep the exclamatory nuance (no following clause needed).
Use equivalent interrogative words: どれほど／どれだけ／なんと to change the level of formality.
Suitable for speeches, moving written texts, diaries, and narration.
In casual speech, many people shorten it to どんなに嬉しかったか (dropping こと), but standard JLPT keeps ことか .

• Exclamation of a high degree: “how … (it was)!”, expressing strong emotion (joy, sadness, hardship, gratitude…).
• Often retrospective: frequently used with the past (～たことか) when looking back on an experience.
• Usage: leans toward written language, speeches, narration; rarely used in very everyday dialogue.
• Does not state a specific figure: it is deliberately vague about “how much/how big”.

rows: どんなに<ruby>大変<rt>たいへん</rt></ruby>だったことか
Concessive condition, with a second clause
どんなに<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>くても<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う
なんて<ruby>美<rt>うつく</rt></ruby>しいんだ
いかに<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>であるか

mistakes: Confusing it with どんなに～ても: that one is a condition, not an exclamation.
Dropping こと in exam style: the JLPT requires the correct pattern ～ことか.
Adding an explanatory clause after ～ことか muddles the structure; the sentence usually stops there.
577.notes:
• Verbs of desire: V-たい/てほしい + ことか expresses “how much I wished/had wished”.
• The negative can also be used: どんなに大変でなかったことか, but the affirmative form is more natural.
• Add 副詞 to intensify the emotion: 本当に／実に／心から＋どんなに～ことか。 meaning_vi: Very, so many times, so much time… ⏐ explain: Used to express a high degree or high frequency of an event or characteristic
Has an exclamatory sense ⏐ examples: 1. 合格できたら、どんなにうれしいことか。
If I pass, how happy I will be!
2. 何度注意したことか。
How many times I've warned you!

578.meaning: It's not that … not, it is possible

examples.jp: 日本語で論文を書くのは難しくないことはないが、時間がかかる。
examples.tr: It's not that writing a thesis in Japanese isn't difficult, but it takes time.

examples.jp: お金がないことはないけど、今は節約したい。
examples.tr: It's not that I don't have money, but I want to save right now.

examples.jp: この店は安くないことはないが、品質は普通だ。
examples.tr: It's not that this store isn't cheap, but the quality is ordinary.

examples.jp: 彼の提案は悪くないことはないと思う。
examples.tr: I think his proposal isn't bad, really.

examples.jp: 週末に手伝えないことはないですが、短時間なら。
examples.tr: It's not that I can't help on the weekend, but only for a short time.

examples.jp: 辛い物は食べないことはないけど、あまり得意じゃない。
examples.tr: It's not that I don't eat spicy food, but I'm not really good with it.

578.explain:
Used when:Acknowledging a possibility but wanting to keep a distance/attach a condition.Responding politely to a request/invitation:検討しないことはありませんが…
Acknowledging a possibility but wanting to keep a distance/attach a condition.
Responding politely to a request/invitation:検討しないことはありませんが…
Not used when:You need a firm affirmation; replace it with ～できる/～だ.You need a definite negative; use ～ない。
You need a firm affirmation; replace it with ～できる/～だ.
You need a definite negative; use ～ない。
Intonation: stress ないことはない to create the feeling “it's OK, but…”.
Formal: use ではないことはありません, ないことはありません。

• Core meaning: double negative → “it's not that … not” = acknowledges that a possibility/degree exists, but weakly, cautiously, with conditions.
• Nuance: vague, avoids direct affirmation; often used to avoid committing 100% (reserved, modest).
• Degree of affirmation: low to medium. It does not mean “certainly” but “it is possible/not completely not”.
• Often goes with degree words: まあ/別に/そんなに/少し/多少… to soften: 別に難しくないことはない。
• Often comes before が/けど/しかし, with the second clause stating a condition, obstacle, or other option.

rows: <ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>わないこともないよ。
Contracted form, colloquial, stresses the negative.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたくないわけではない。
<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>できないでもない。

mistakes: Misreading the meaning: thinking it is a strong negation. It is actually a weak affirmation.
Using it when a commitment is needed: answering a definite “Yes/No” with this pattern → creates ambiguity.
Confusing it with ～ないこともない: difficult JLPT questions test the “open condition” nuance of も.
Missing が/けど in the second clause → the sentence is cut short and lacks explanation.
578.notes:
• When translating into Vietnamese, you can render it as “it is possible”, “not exactly not…”, “it's not that… not… but…”.
• Often combined with a hypothetical condition: 条件次第では、参加できないことはない。
• In the past: 行けないことはなかった (back then it wasn't that I couldn't go) → retrospective nuance, slight regret. | Extension: N/Na じゃなくはない・Aくなくはない

579.meaning: It's not that … not, it is possible

examples.jp: フライパンでできないこともないけど、鍋があれば、鍋のほうがいいよ。
examples.tr: It's not that you can't do it in a frying pan, but if you have a pot, a pot is better.

examples.jp: 明日なら参加しないこともないです。
examples.tr: If it's tomorrow, it's not that I can't take part.

examples.jp: 値段は高くないこともないけど、品質がいいから買う。
examples.tr: It's not that the price isn't high, but I'll buy it because the quality is good.

examples.jp: 辛い料理も食べないこともないよ。
examples.tr: It's not that I don't eat spicy food, you know.

examples.jp: 努力すれば合格できないこともない。
examples.tr: If you work hard, it's not impossible to pass.

examples.jp: この条件なら、契約を延長しないこともないと思います。
examples.tr: Under these conditions, I think it's not out of the question to extend the contract.

579.explain:
Used to:Give an “open” answer with a concessive tone.Prepare for an accompanying condition, making it easy to move into negotiation.
Give an “open” answer with a concessive tone.
Prepare for an accompanying condition, making it easy to move into negotiation.
Politeness: use ありません/です to sound soft at work.
Usage: often followed by が/けど + a condition/concern.

• Meaning: “It's not that … not” similar to ～ないことはない, but often implies “if the conditions are right, it's possible/I don't object”.
• Nuance: slightly more positive than ～ないことはない; “leaves open” the possibility, compromise.
• Often used in negotiations/responding to an invitation: 価格次第では、購入しないこともない。
• Comes with conditions, adverbs: 条件次第で/場合によっては/まあ/別に/そんなに… + ～ないこともない。

rows: Slightly more positive; suited to negotiation.

mistakes: Confusing the degree with ～ないことはない: JLPT questions often ask about the “open condition” nuance of も.
Translating it too positively as “definitely can” → wrong meaning (it is only a possibility).
Forgetting the conditional clause makes the sentence sound unfinished and hard to understand in work conversations.
579.notes:
• Natural translation: “it is possible…”, “it's not that … not… if…”.
• Combined with なら/さえ/ば to emphasize the condition: これさえあれば、できないこともない。
• Past: 行かなかったこともない（it wasn't that I didn't go… → may have gone a little/gone on some occasion). meaning_vi: ～の可能性もある
There is also a possibility that, it's not that it's impossible to… ⏐ examples: 1. 毎日、漢字を４つか５つなら、覚えられないこともない。
If it's four or five kanji a day, it's not impossible to remember them.
2. この会社を辞める人の気持ちがわからないこともない。
It's not that I don't understand how people who quit this company feel.

examples.jp: そろそろ寝ないと。
examples.tr: I'd better get to bed soon.

examples.jp: 提出期限に間に合わせないと。
examples.tr: I have to make the submission deadline.

examples.jp: 早く行かないと、電車に乗り遅れるよ。
examples.tr: If you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.

examples.jp: 薬を飲まないと治らないよ。
examples.tr: If you don't take your medicine, you won't get better.

examples.jp: 明日までに資料を準備しないといけない。
examples.tr: I have to prepare the documents by tomorrow.

examples.jp: 寒いから、窓を閉めないと。
examples.tr: It's cold, so I'd better close the window.

580.explain:
When the contracted form is used (ending in ～ないと。 ), the context implies “いけない/だめ”.
In the conditional meaning, the second clause usually carries a negative/consequence:間に合わない／困る／怒られる…
Formal: prefer ～ないといけない／～なければならない in reports and business emails.

• Obligation meaning (colloquial): V-ないと is usually a contraction of V-ないといけない, the second clause being omitted because it is obvious.
• Conditional meaning: “if not … then …”, the second clause states a bad/undesirable consequence.
• Nuance: natural, everyday; in formal written language use the full form.

rows: <ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>しなければならない。
V-なくてはならない／V-なくちゃ
Must; なくちゃ is colloquial
Always has a result clause after it
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>しないと<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>ちる。

mistakes: Understanding every ～ないと as “must”: some sentences are conditions “if not… then…”; look at the second clause.
Dropping the second clause when it is not the contracted form: with the conditional meaning there should be a result clause.
Using it in formal documents: switch to ～ないといけない/～なければならない.
580.notes:
• ～ないと can express a sense of hurry/urgency: cutting the sentence short shows “reminding oneself”.
• The negative verb must be in the correct ない form: 行く→行かない、とる→とらない、する→しない、来る→こない。
• In casual speech, the variants 〜なきゃ/〜なくちゃ replace 〜ないと with a softer nuance.
meaning_vi: Expresses the meaning “If not ~ then ･･･”, where ･･･ is a bad situation or event. Sometimes ･･･ is omitted.
examples: 1. ①　気をつけないと
I have to be careful.
2. ②　よく見ないと、間違えるよ。
If you don't look carefully, you'll make a mistake.
3. ➂　あの字は小さいから、目がよくないと読めないだろう。
That writing is small, so if your eyes aren't good, you probably won't be able to read it.
4. ➃　時間がないから、急がないと。
There's no time, so I have to hurry.

581.meaning:
「心理的事情があるので、～しなければならない。」規則などで決まっていて～なければならないのではなくて、あまり～したくないが、社会的常識・心理的義務感があってそうする必要があるという意味で使う。主語は普通一人称。
Must do ~ for psychological reasons.
Used to mean that it is not a rule or regulation requiring you to do ~, but that although you don't really want to do it, it is necessary to do so because of social common sense, a psychological sense of obligation, etc.
The subject is usually first person.

examples.jp: 行くと約束したからには、行かないわけにはいかないだろう。
examples.tr: Since I promised to go, I guess I can't not go.

examples.jp: 外国語は必修だから、取らないわけにはいかない。
examples.tr: A foreign language is required, so I have no choice but to take one.

examples.jp: 彼女が初めて作ってくれた料理だったので、おなかはいっぱいだったが、食べないわけにはいかなかった。
examples.tr: It was the first dish she had ever made for me, so even though I was full, I couldn't not eat it.

examples.jp: この町では自転車がないとやはり困る。買わないわけにはいかない。
examples.tr: In this town, it's really inconvenient without a bicycle. I have no choice but to buy one.

examples.jp: 本当に暑いですけど、何も着ないわけにはいきませんよね。
examples.tr: It's really hot, but we can't go around wearing nothing, can we?

examples.jp: このCD、ずっと持っていたいけど、図書館のだから返さないわけにはいかない。
examples.tr: I'd like to keep this CD forever, but it's from the library, so I have to return it.

581.explain: Expresses being obliged to do something, being unable not to do it, even though you don't want to.
581.notes:
1) Easy to confuse with ～わけにはいかない.
→ ～ないわけにはいかない means “cannot not…”, meaning that in the end you still have to do it.
2) Has a nuance of reluctance.
→ You don't really want to do it, but the circumstances force you to.
3) Not used when the speaker acts voluntarily.
→ If you “really want to do it,” use another volition pattern.

examples.jp: 危険だと知りながらも、彼は前に進んだ。
examples.tr: Even though he knew it was dangerous, he pressed on.

examples.jp: 小さいながらも、この店は評判がいい。
examples.tr: Although this shop is small, it has a good reputation.

examples.jp: 彼は学生でありながらも会社を経営している。
examples.tr: Although he is a student, he runs a company.

examples.jp: このツールは便利でありながらも、使い方は簡単だ。
examples.tr: This tool is convenient, yet it is also easy to use.

examples.jp: 不満を感じながらも、彼女は仕事を続けた。
examples.tr: Although she felt dissatisfied, she kept on working.

582.explain:
Used in essays, reports, and objective descriptions to express a mild “paradox”.
The second clause should not be a command or strong volition directed at the listener (avoid giving orders). When you need to give advice, 〜ものの/〜とはいえ is more suitable.
“も” adds emphasis to the contrast; it can be omitted in formal language if the context is clear.

• Meaning: “although… (still)…”. States two contrasting facts that exist simultaneously.
• Nuance: more formal and objective than 〜のに; less reproachful emotion than 〜くせに.
• The first clause usually expresses a condition/limitation/disadvantage; the second clause is an actual fact that overcomes or contrasts with it.
• “でありながら（も）” is used with N/Na to avoid ambiguity and is more natural.

rows: The second clause often runs contrary to expectations, sometimes left hanging
<ruby>危険<rt>きけん</rt></ruby>とはいえ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く

mistakes: Using 〜ながら (simultaneity) instead of 〜ながらも (concession) → wrong meaning.
Na-adj/N attached directly to 〜ながらも: “便利ながらも” is possible, but with nouns you should use “Nでありながら（も）”.
The second clause gives a direct command/request to the listener → unnatural.
582.notes:
• With Adj-i: “狭いながらも工夫がある” is a pattern for praising something that overcomes a limitation.
• “でありながら” can take a contracted form in formal academic writing: AでありながらB（である）。
• To emphasize a clear paradox, add しかし/それでも at the beginning of the second clause for more force.
meaning_vi: ～けれども（逆接(ぎゃくせつ)）
examples: 1. 子どもたちは文句をいながらも、後片付けを手伝ってくれた。
The children complained, but they still helped clean up afterward.
2. 残念ながら曇っていて、初日の出は見られなかった。
Unfortunately it was cloudy, so we couldn't see the first sunrise of the New Year.
3. 「私はもう10年も東京にすんでいながら、まだ一度も東京タワーに行ったことがないんです」
I've lived in Tokyo for 10 years, but I still haven't been to Tokyo Tower even once.
4. 事情はよくわからないながら、何とかして助けてあげたいと思った。
Although I didn't really understand the situation, I wanted to help you somehow.
5. この車は小型ながら乗り心地がいい。
This car is small, but it's comfortable to ride in.
6. 警察官でありながら飲酒運敵をするとは許せない。
Driving after drinking while being a police officer is unforgivable.
7. A氏は若いながらも古い習慣をよく知っている。
Mr. A is young, but he knows old customs well.
8. 初めて作った料理だが、我ながらおいしくできた。
It's the first time I've cooked this dish, but it turned out delicious, if I do say so myself.
9. 何度も練習しているのに、一向に上手にならない。我ながら情けない。
No matter how many times I practice, I don't get any better. I'm hopeless.
10. ・当然のことながら
Naturally.
11. ・いやいあやながら
Reluctantly
12. ・狭いながらも楽しい我が家
My home is small but happy.
13. ・細々ながら
Though only a trickle. meaning_vi: Although, however ⏐ explain: Expresses contrast, something contrary to common thinking or to what one imagined. ⏐ examples: 1. 悪いことと知りながら、盗みを繰り返した。
Although they knew it was wrong, they kept on stealing.
2. 「狭いながらも楽しいわが家」という言葉がある。
There is a saying meaning ‘our home may be small, but it is happy’.

583.connection: [result] + なぜなら(ば)・なぜかというと・どうしてかというと + [reason]

examples.jp: 今日は参加しません。なぜなら体調が悪いからです。
examples.tr: I won't be participating today. That's because I'm not feeling well.

examples.jp: この案には反対です。なぜならばリスクが大きすぎるためです。
examples.tr: I'm against this plan. The reason is that the risks are too great.

examples.jp: 海外へ引っ越します。なぜかというと新しい挑戦をしたいからです。
examples.tr: I'm moving abroad. The reason is that I want to take on a new challenge.

examples.jp: 本日は閉店いたします。というのは停電の可能性があるからです。
examples.tr: We will be closed today. This is because there may be a power outage.

examples.jp: 彼を推薦します。なぜなら最も適任だと考えるからです。
examples.tr: I recommend him. That's because I believe he is the most suitable person.

583.explain:
Position: almost always at the beginning of the sentence giving the reason, right after the conclusion sentence.
At the end of a sentence giving the reason, からだ／ためだ／からである is usually used to complete the flow of reasoning.
More formal than だって; more neutral than というのは; more logical in academic writing.
Works well when answering an implied "Why?" after a statement that raises a question.
Avoid overusing it several times in a row; use it once to introduce the main reason.

• Used to state the reason/explanation for the statement in the sentence just before. Translation: "because; if you ask why...".
• Typical structure: conclusion sentence first → なぜなら＋clause giving the reason＋からだ／ためだ at the end.
• Nuance: coherent, argumentative; often seen in written language, presentations, and reports. Also used in conversation to switch into an explanation.
• Different from から／ので: なぜなら is a conjunction between two independent sentences; から／ので connect within one complex sentence.
• Often goes with nouns indicating cause, basis, or reason: 事情／理由／都合／ため, or a clause ending in からだ.

rows: Connects within one complex sentence; natural conversational nuance.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったから<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だ。
Gives the reason for the previous sentence
Two independent sentences; reasoning flow, more formal.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きません。なぜなら<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからだ。
Soft; used in both conversation and writing; close in meaning to なぜなら.
<ruby>延期<rt>えんき</rt></ruby>です。というのは<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby><ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>だから。
Very colloquial, sometimes used to make excuses.
だってお<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>がないもん。

mistakes: Forgetting the ending that closes the reason: writing "なぜなら時間がない。" is incomplete; correct: "なぜなら時間がないからだ。"
Putting なぜなら in the middle of a complex sentence connected with から/ので → unnatural; split it into two sentences.
Using なぜなら for obvious information that raises no question → redundant.
Confusing it with だって on the JLPT: だって is too colloquial and cannot replace it in written language.
583.notes:
• Often seen in argumentative writing, business emails, and reports: "結論。なぜなら根拠…".
• In formal language, ending with ためである gives a more serious nuance than からだ.
• If the reason spans several clauses, split it into a few short sentences, each still keeping the explanatory flow after なぜなら.
• Do not use なぜなら to state a result; use it only to give the reason for the previous sentence.

examples.jp: 週末はカフェなんか行かない？
examples.tr: Want to go to a café or something this weekend?

examples.jp: 私なんかまだまだ勉強不足です。
examples.tr: Someone like me still has a lot more studying to do.

examples.jp: 勉強もしないで合格できるなんかありえない。
examples.tr: Passing without even studying? No way.

examples.jp: あいつなんかに負けるもんか。
examples.tr: There's no way I'll lose to someone like that!

examples.jp: なんか今日は機嫌がいいね。
examples.tr: Somehow you seem to be in a good mood today.

examples.jp: 渋谷や原宿なんか
examples.tr: Places like Shibuya and Harajuku

584.explain:
Soft suggestion: Nなんかどう？／行かない？ is suggestive, not imposing.
Humble:私なんか… to lower oneself; in written language, 私など is more polite.
Contemptuous:人なんか／あいつなんか shows disdain; be careful with the context.
Emphatic negation: ～なんか…ない／できるわけない, expressing strong emotion.
Filler: なんか＋clause, softens the affirmative nuance; said casually without much thought.

• Expresses examples/suggestions in a suggestive, casual way: "like…, sort of…".
• Softening/contemptuous nuance: placed after a noun to downplay its importance (self-deprecation/contempt).
• Used in negative sentences/exclamations to emphasize rejection: ～なんか…ない／できるわけがない。
• Very colloquial; avoid in formal texts or with superiors (it can easily sound rude).

rows: <ruby>寿司<rt>すし</rt></ruby>や<ruby>天ぷら<rt>てんぷら</rt></ruby>など。
Emphasizes emotion/evaluation more than なんか.
More neutral than なんか, less contemptuous.
<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない？

mistakes: Using なんか in a JLPT essay → lowers the formality score. Prefer など／とか.
Attaching なんか to the listener/a superior → sounds impolite/contemptuous.
Thinking なんか is purely for listing. In fact, it also carries an emotional nuance (belittling, negation).
A long AなんかBなんか chain makes the sentence messy; limit it to 1–2 examples.
584.notes:
• In marketing/sales conversations, avoid なんか because it sounds unprofessional; prefer など／などの.
• Several なんか in a row in one sentence can sound hesitant; use it in moderation to keep the flow clear.
• It can also come before adjectives in spoken language: なんか嬉しい（somehow kind of happy） has a vague nuance. | Comparison: など (more formal, N4) / なんて (dismissive, exclamatory)

examples.jp: 親にうそをつくなんて、できません。
examples.tr: Lie to my parents? I just can't do that.

examples.jp: 私が代表選手になるなんて、信じられない。
examples.tr: Me, becoming a representative athlete? I can't believe it.

585.explain: ◎ 「～なんて」in 「ひとりで登なんて」means "as for ~ / the idea of ~", and leads to a negation or a feeling of surprise.

examples.jp: この問題の研究においては、高橋先生ほど有名な人はいない。
examples.tr: In research on this problem, no one is as famous as Professor Takahashi.

examples.jp: 地方の多くの都市においては、人口の減少が大きな問題になっている。
examples.tr: In many regional cities, population decline has become a serious problem.

examples.jp: 近代工業はヨーロッパにおいて誕生した。
examples.tr: Modern industry was born in Europe.

examples.jp: 災害時においては、冷静になることが何よりも大切だ。
examples.tr: In times of disaster, staying calm is more important than anything.

examples.jp: 卒業式は○○ホールにおきまして１０時より行われます。
examples.tr: The graduation ceremony will be held at ○○ Hall from 10 o'clock.

examples.jp: 我が社の車は、安全性においてはどこにも負けません。
examples.tr: Our company's cars are second to none in terms of safety.

586.explain:
Used to open a paragraph/set the context: N + において(は)、〜。
In ceremonial emails, prefer におきまして for added politeness.
When talking about abstract topics (歴史/社会/教育…), において is more natural than で.
Not used to describe everyday actions: use で instead.

• Establishes the context (place/time/field) for presenting the main information.
• Written/academic style; used in reports, press releases, and theses.
• における used as a modifier makes the sentence concise and formal.
• Different from で: broader in scope, rarely used in everyday conversation.

rows: <ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>において<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby><ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>にて<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>
<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>にあたって<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using it in everyday sentences: × コンビニにおいて弁当を買った → ○ コンビニで買った.
Confusing it with the meaning “regarding”: × 料金において → ○ 料金に関して.
Dropping “における” when a modifier is needed: × 研究において成果 → ○ 研究における成果.
JLPT: Choose において over で for administrative documents/reports.
586.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～で (at/in).
→ ～において is more formal and often used in written language, news, and announcements.
2) Used for contexts “at…, in…, in terms of…”.
→ Not only places but also “within a field/event”.
3) Not suited to casual speech.
→ In conversation, ～で is usually more natural. explain: Used when talking about a time or a place.
A more formal usage than “で” ⏐ examples: 1. 大阪において、国際会議が行われた。
An international conference was held in Osaka
2. 結果はホームページにおいて発表されます。
The results will be announced on the website

587.meaning: In place of, on behalf of

examples.jp: 本日は部長にかわって私がご挨拶申し上げます。
examples.tr: Today I will give the greeting on behalf of the department manager.

examples.jp: 父にかわって兄が式に出る。
examples.tr: My older brother will attend the ceremony in place of my father.

examples.jp: 紙に代わってタブレットが会議で使われている。
examples.tr: Tablets are being used in meetings in place of paper.

examples.jp: 人間に代わってロボットが危険な作業を行う。
examples.tr: Robots carry out dangerous work in place of humans.

examples.jp: 石油にかわり再生可能エネルギーの比率が高まっている。
examples.tr: The share of renewable energy is rising in place of oil.

examples.jp: 社長にかわって
examples.tr: On behalf of the company president

587.explain:
Formal representation at the office: " Nにかわって ご連絡いたします" is very natural.
Noun form " Nにかわり のN":電子契約 にかわり の仕組み.
With replacement trends, the sentence is often passive/general: ～が使われる／注目される／普及している.
Not used simply for "taking temporary turns" (alternating). In that case, use代わりばんこ／交代で.
More formal than のかわりに; suitable for administrative documents and reports.

• Representation/on behalf of: person/thing B performs the action in place of A. Example: 上司にかわって説明する。
• Replacement (trend/innovation): B is replacing/has replaced A in function/use. Example: ガソリンにかわって電気自動車が普及。
• Nuance: formal; often used in announcements, speeches, and business writing.
• The agent is usually the replacing party (after にかわって), while A is the target being replaced.

rows: in place of, on behalf of; replacement
Formal; emphasizes the representative role or a replacement trend.
<ruby>上司<rt>じょうし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>代<rt>か</rt></ruby>わって<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>うかわりにご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>をおごって。
Verb; a concrete act of replacing.
<ruby>紙<rt>かみ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>代<rt>か</rt></ruby>えてメールで<ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>る。
<ruby>代理<rt>だいり</rt></ruby>で／<ruby>代理<rt>だいり</rt></ruby>として
<ruby>代理<rt>だいり</rt></ruby>で<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Using a verb directly before にかわって → incorrect. A noun must come before にかわって.
Confusing it with "in exchange": ～のかわりに also carries the meaning of exchange/compensation; ～にかわって does not have this nuance.
Expressing temporary alternation with にかわって → unnatural; use 交代で／代わりばんこで instead.
Reversing the replacing agent: 人間にかわってロボットが… (correct), not ロボットにかわって人間が… if you mean robots replace humans.
587.notes:
• In the "representation" meaning, it often goes with keigo: ご説明申し上げます／ご連絡いたします.
• In phrases about technological replacement, the kanji 代 is used for formality: ～に代わって.
• The topic being replaced (Nにかわって) is not the subject of the action; the replacing agent comes after it and performs the action. | Variant: ～にかわり; not used for simple replacement of objects

examples.jp: 資料に関して、いくつ質問があります。
examples.tr: I have a few questions regarding the materials.

examples.jp: 彼は大学で、自然エネルギに関する研究をしている。
examples.tr: He is doing research on natural energy at university.

588.explain: ◎ Indicates a target or topic; the meaning is the same as 「～について」. It is a somewhat stiff expression.

rows: <ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>について<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す
<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>する

<ruby>本件<rt>ほんけん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>し、<ruby>通知<rt>つうち</rt></ruby>する

mistakes: Using に関して for an attitude toward a person: ×彼に関して優しい → ○彼に対して優しい.
Overusing it in everyday conversation makes sentences stiff; switch to について in casual conversation.
Wrong modifier form: ×環境に関して対策 → ○環境に関する対策.
588.notes:
explain: Preferred in work/official contexts: emails, announcements, reports, research papers.
Attach it directly before a noun as に関するN for conciseness and formality.
Add は after に関して to make it a topic emphasized for the whole sentence.
examples: 1. この問題に関して、ご意見を伺いたいです。
I would like to ask your opinion on this problem.
2. 日本史に関する本を探しています。
I'm looking for books on Japanese history.
3. 新制度に関しては、来月説明会があります。
Regarding the new system, there will be an information session next month.
4. 安全に関しての注意事項を必ず読んでください。
Be sure to read the notes regarding safety.
5. その件に関しては後ほど連絡します。
Regarding that matter, I will contact you later.
6. 環境政策に関して調査を行った。
A survey was conducted on environmental policy.
──────
1. ➀　事件に関して
Regarding the incident
2. ②　この事件に関して、新しい情報が入りました。
New information has come in regarding this incident.
3. ③　事件に関する情報は、警察に届けてください。
Please report any information regarding the incident to the police.
meaning_vi: About …; regarding … (formal)
explain: Similar in meaning to ～について but more formal. Often used in written language and announcements; has the form ～に関する＋N.
examples: 1. 「申し込み手続きに関してお伺いしたいのですが」
I'd like to ask about the application procedure.
2. パソコンで環境問題に関する記事を検索した。
I searched for articles on environmental issues on my computer.
3. 議長は時間に関して厳しいので、絶対遅刻はできない。
The chairperson is strict about time, so I absolutely can't be late.
4. 「その件に関しましては、後ほどご説明いたします」
I will explain that matter later. explain: Used when talking about some aspect related to an issue ⏐ examples: 1. この問題に関して、ご意見ありませんか。
Do you have any opinions regarding this problem?
2. 農業に関する論文を読む。
Read a paper on agriculture

examples.jp: 北へ行くにしたがって、日照時間が短くなる。
examples.tr: The farther north you go, the shorter the hours of sunshine become.

examples.jp: データが増えるにしたがって、計算量も増大する。
examples.tr: As the amount of data increases, the amount of computation increases as well.

examples.jp: 渋滞が解消されるにしたがって、到着時刻が早まった。
examples.tr: As the traffic jam cleared up, the arrival time moved earlier.

examples.jp: 担当者の連絡に従って、次の工程へ進んでください。
examples.tr: Please proceed to the next step following the message from the person in charge.

examples.jp: 法律に従い適切に処理する。
examples.tr: Handle it appropriately in accordance with the law.

589.explain:
Suited to written language, reports, and textbooks.
Clause A should be an axis of continuous change; if there are two discrete states, consider につれて/一方で.
The form “に従い” is often used in headings/procedure notes because it is concise.

• Expresses a covariant relationship between A and B (gradual, a tendency).
• Expresses doing B based on the framework of A (rules/instructions/plans).
• Clause B is usually a fact/rule; avoid commands in the “covariation” meaning.

rows: <ruby>人口<rt>じんこう</rt></ruby><ruby>増加<rt>ぞうか</rt></ruby>にしたがって<ruby>需要<rt>じゅよう</rt></ruby><ruby>増<rt>ぞう</rt></ruby>
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>につれて<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わる
データに<ruby>基<rt>もと</rt></ruby>づいて<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>
<ruby>方針<rt>ほうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>沿<rt>そ</rt></ruby>って<ruby>実施<rt>じっし</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Confusing it with につれて in terms of formality and naturalness in conversation.
Using it for instantaneous events: × 合図にしたがって走り出した → use と同時に/とたんに.
Mixing the meanings “follow” and “change” in one sentence causes ambiguity; keep them clearly separate.
589.notes:
• In the meaning “follow/obey”, commands/advice can be used because they are instructions: 〜に従って提出してください.
• In the meaning “change”, avoid combining it with volition: × 〜にしたがって、〜しよう.
• The kanji 従 has the nuance “follow/submit to”, suited to legal and regulatory documents. | Formal variant: ～にしたがい

examples.jp: 年を取るにつれて、時間が早く感じられる。
examples.tr: As you get older, time seems to pass more quickly.

examples.jp: 気温が下がるにつれて、紅葉が進む。
examples.tr: As the temperature drops, the autumn leaves turn more and more red.

examples.jp: 都市化が進むにつれて、緑が減っている。
examples.tr: As urbanization advances, green spaces are decreasing.

examples.jp: 経験を積むにつれて、自信がついてきた。
examples.tr: As I gained experience, I gradually became more confident.

examples.jp: 時間の経過につれ、痛みは和らいだ。
examples.tr: As time passed, the pain eased.

examples.jp: 暖かくなるにつれて、公園を訪れる人の数が増えている
examples.tr: As it gets warmer, the number of people visiting the park is increasing

590.explain:
Used for continuous tendencies/developments, usually natural, social or psychological phenomena.
The second clause is the resulting consequence and does not carry a direct command/volition.
Often appears in explanations, reports and data analysis.

- “The more … the more …/Along with … …”: Two phenomena change in the same direction, where a change in A brings about a corresponding change in B.
- Emphasizes a relationship of covariation/gradual change; not used for instantaneous events, and not used with volition/command in the second clause.

rows: Along with A, B also changes
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>につれて<ruby>視力<rt>しりょく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>ちる。
More formal; also carries the nuance of “according to/following”
<ruby>温度<rt>おんど</rt></ruby>の<ruby>上昇<rt>じょうしょう</rt></ruby>にしたがって<ruby>溶<rt>と</rt></ruby>ける。
<ruby>人口<rt>じんこう</rt></ruby><ruby>増加<rt>ぞうか</rt></ruby>にともなって<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>深刻<rt>しんこく</rt></ruby><ruby>化<rt>か</rt></ruby>。
Has both the meaning of simultaneity and of changing together
<ruby>成長<rt>せいちょう</rt></ruby>とともに<ruby>責任<rt>せきにん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>増<rt>ま</rt></ruby>す。

mistakes: Using it with an instantaneous event (×到着するにつれて驚いた) → wrong, as it lacks the “gradual” nuance.
Putting a command/volition in the second clause (×増えるにつれて買いなさい) → unnatural.
Getting the relationship wrong: につれて does not express a direct cause like ので/から.
590.notes:
• Besides changes in the same direction, it can also indicate changes in opposite directions (A increases, B decreases), as long as one follows the other.
• Clause A usually represents the “time basis/point of change”, and clause B is the observed result.
• Often used with words such as: 進む, 高まる, 低下する, 増える, 減る, 深まる,…
meaning_vi: The more … the more …
explain: Expresses two changes taking place in parallel: as A gradually changes, B changes along with it. Continuous and objective in character.
examples: 1. 試験が近づくにつれて、だんだん心配になってきた。
As the exam approached, I gradually became more worried.
2. 日本での生活が長くなるにつれ、友だちもできて楽しくなった。
The longer I lived in Japan, the more friends I made and the more I enjoyed it.
3. 再開発が進むにつれて、駅前の様子がすっかり変わってしまった。
As the redevelopment progressed, the area in front of the station changed completely.
4. 時間の経過につれ、その事件のことは忘れられてしまった。
As time went by, the incident was forgotten.

examples.jp: 東京は若者にとっては刺激のある魅力的な街だ。
examples.tr: Tokyo is an exciting, attractive city for young people.

examples.jp: 百万円は私にとっては大金だが、彼にとってはたいした金額ではないようだ。
examples.tr: A million yen is a lot of money to me, but to him it doesn't seem to be much.

examples.jp: 私にとって日本は、自分の夢を実現するための国だ。
examples.tr: To me, Japan is the country where I can make my dreams come true.

examples.jp: 規制緩和は政府にとっても民間企業にとっても切実な問題だ。
examples.tr: Deregulation is a pressing issue for both the government and private companies.

examples.jp: 私にとっての故郷とは、青春時代を過ごしたあの町しかない。
examples.tr: For me, home can only be that town where I spent my youth.

examples.jp: 留学生にとって奨学金は大きな支えだ。
examples.tr: For international students, scholarships are a great support.

591.explain:
Used to set a frame of evaluation; the predicate that follows is a property/evaluation.
Add は for emphasis/contrast; add も to extend the inclusion.
Do not use “Nにとって + action V” in the sense of “N does …”; use が/は instead.

• States a viewpoint/advantages and disadvantages/value from the standpoint of N: “for N, …”.
• Usually used with subjective judgments, but can also be an objective evaluation (when the target is a group/organization).
• Not used to indicate the agent performing an action.

rows: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>にとって<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>専門<rt>せんもん</rt></ruby><ruby>家<rt>か</rt></ruby>からすると<ruby>危険<rt>きけん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもに<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して<ruby>優<rt>やさ</rt></ruby>しい。
Sets the subject matter, not a viewpoint of advantages and disadvantages
<ruby>政策<rt>せいさく</rt></ruby>について<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Using “にとって” to indicate the agent performing an action (wrong function).
Using a direct action predicate (unnatural): use an adjective/judgment instead.
Confusing it with “に対して/について”: they differ in semantic purpose.
Forgetting “の” when modifying a noun: “NにとってのN2”.
591.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～には.
→ ～にとって means “for (from N's standpoint)” and is used to evaluate/comment from N's point of view.
2) This pattern is usually followed by a judgment.
→ Example: 大切だ, 難しい, 便利だ… (evaluation).
3) Not used to indicate the direct target of an action.
→ If it means “doing something toward someone” (an action directed at them), consider ～に対して.

examples.tr: The meeting was held over three days.

examples.tr: The effects of the typhoon spread throughout the entire Kanto region.

examples.tr: He presented the results of twenty years of research.

examples.tr: The discussion went on until late at night.
