examples.tr: They are active in a wide variety of fields.

examples.jp: 父は２０年にわたってこの研究をしている。
examples.tr: My father has been doing this research for 20 years.

592.explain:
The preceding N must be a unit of “coverage”: time (時間/日/年), space (地域/全域), quantity (回/項目), field (分野).
Formal nuance; used in narration and in describing scale/length.
Not used for very short/trivial spans; for short ones use ずっと/ずいぶん/長い間.

Expresses extending/spanning “throughout/all over” a period of time, scope, quantity or field. It focuses on breadth and duration; it does not necessarily mean nonstop continuity, but the degree of coverage is large.
• Usually used for considerable spans (several days, many years, nationwide...).
• Formal style, common in reports and news.

rows: <ruby>全国<rt>ぜんこく</rt></ruby>にわたって<ruby>影響<rt>えいきょう</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>一年<rt>いちねん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて<ruby>暖<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かい。
Vague limits; does not cover the whole span
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>にかけて<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>滞在<rt>たいざい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>した。

mistakes: Using it with an N that does not indicate coverage: “気持ちにわたって” is wrong; use it with a specific time/scope.
Confusing it with “を通じて”: exams test the difference between “coverage” (にわたって) and “continuously throughout a period” (を通じて).
Forgetting the noun-modifying variant: choose “にわたるN” before a noun.
592.notes:
• The modifier form “多岐にわたる + N” is a very common phrase in academic/PR writing.
• “長期にわたって/長時間にわたって” are set phrases often seen in the news.
• Does not combine directly with verbs (no “V にわたって”); nominalization is needed: “検討にわたって” is unnatural → “長期にわたる検討”. | Variants: ～にわたり・にわたる+N

examples.jp: 予想に反して、試合は大差で終わった。
examples.tr: Contrary to expectations, the match ended in a lopsided score.

examples.jp: 規則に反して教室で飲食してはいけない。
examples.tr: You must not go against the rules by eating or drinking in the classroom.

examples.tr: The proposal goes against the boss's wishes, but there are good grounds for it.

examples.tr: Unfortunately, the result turned out contrary to expectations.

examples.tr: Contrary to the weather forecast, it didn't rain.

examples.jp: 予測に反し（て）
examples.tr: Contrary to predictions

593.explain:
Neutral to formal; can be used in both spoken and written language.
Emphasizes contrast with a norm/general expectation.
In the sense of “violation”, it carries a clear nuance of criticism/norms.

Expresses actions/results that are “contrary to, go against” rules, policies, expectations, forecasts... It can refer both to intentional actions (violations) and to objective results contrary to expectation.
• With normative nouns (規則/法律/方針), the meaning is close to “violate/oppose”.
• With nouns of expectation/prediction (期待/予想), it means “contrary to”.

rows: <ruby>期待<rt>きたい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>反<rt>はん</rt></ruby>して<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>した。
<ruby>兄<rt>あに</rt></ruby>は<ruby>内向<rt>ないこう</rt></ruby><ruby>的<rt>てき</rt></ruby>であるのに<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して、<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>社交<rt>しゃこう</rt></ruby><ruby>的<rt>てき</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>今年<rt>ことし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>と<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>って<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>い。
Opposite in meaning to “に<ruby>反<rt>はん</rt></ruby>して”
<ruby>方針<rt>ほうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>沿<rt>そ</rt></ruby>って<ruby>実行<rt>じっこう</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Using it after a verb clause: “来るに反して” is wrong; a noun is needed: “予想に反して来た”.
Confusing it with “に対して”: exams test “opposition to a norm” (に反して) vs “comparison/contrast” (に対して).
Forgetting the noun-modifying variant: choose the correct “に反するN/に反したN” before a noun.
593.notes:
• “反する” is a Sino-Japanese verb with a formal nuance; its conjugations are “に反するN/に反したN/に反してV”.
• To say contrary to “what actually happened”, use ～のに/～にもかかわらず; “に反して” does not follow a verb clause but goes with nouns.
• Antonym pair: “～に沿って/～に即して” (following/in line with) vs “～に反して”.
explain: Expresses a result that is contrary to predictions, expectations or rules.
examples: 1. Aチームが勝つだろうという予想に反してBチームが勝った。
Contrary to predictions that Team A would win, Team B won.
2. 応募者数は当初の見込みに反し、非常に多かった。
Contrary to initial estimates, the number of applicants was very large.
3. 無断外泊は寮の規則に反する。
Staying out overnight without permission is against the dormitory rules.
4. 自由な言論を許さないのは憲法の精神に反する。
Not allowing free speech goes against the spirit of the constitution.
5. たとえ親の命令でも、自分の意思に反することはしたくない。
Even if my parents order me to, I don't want to do anything against my own will.
6. 予測／予報／教え／法律／意／期待／希望／願い　＋　に反して
Contrary to prediction / forecast / teachings / law / intention / expectation / hope / wish. explain: Expresses something contrary to, or in contrast with, a desire or expectation. N is usually a word such as: 予想、期待、命令、意図など ⏐ examples: 1. 専門家の予想に反して、景気は回復し始めた。
Contrary to the experts' predictions, the economy began to recover.
2. 我々の期待に反して、新商品はあまり売れなかった。
Contrary to our expectations, the new product did not sell very well.

examples.jp: 子どもに対して、もっと優しく話してください。
examples.tr: Please speak more gently to children.

examples.tr: Many objections were raised against his remarks.

examples.jp: 新人に対するサポート体制を強化した。
examples.tr: We strengthened the support system for new employees.

examples.jp: 兄は活動的なのに対して、弟は読書が好きだ。
examples.tr: My older brother is active, whereas my younger brother likes reading.

examples.jp: １人に対して３本ずつ配ります。
examples.tr: We'll hand out three to each person.

examples.jp: 前年同期に対して売上は10％増となった。
examples.tr: Sales rose 10% compared with the same period last year.

594.explain:
Used with a noun referring to a person/organization/specific target when applying a policy, attitude or action.
Used for contrast when the two clauses are clearly parallel; for a simple comparison of degree, ～より/～に比べて is more natural.
In formal written language it can be shortened to に対し; to modify a noun, use に対するN.
Rarely used for a pure topic of discussion; for “about/regarding”, について/に関して is more natural.

• Target: expresses a behavior/attitude/measure directed toward a person/group/thing.
• Evaluation/praise and criticism: used when giving a comment aimed at a specific target (会社に対して厳しい意見, 親に対して失礼だ).
• Contrast: connects two clauses to emphasize a clear difference between A and B. Close in meaning to “while/on the other hand”.
• Ratio/per: states ratios or distribution (１人に対して２個, 男性１人に対して女性２人).
• Nuance: formal and more objective than について; not used for simple casual emotions.

rows: <ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby>について<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す
<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>する
Emphasizes the goal, direction of movement
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>に<ruby>向<rt>む</rt></ruby>けて<ruby>番組<rt>ばんぐみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>る
Comparison of degree; no nuance of “toward”
<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べて<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>い
Connects sentences/paragraphs to present a contrast
Aは<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>だ。それに<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>してBは<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>だ。

mistakes: Mixing it up with について/に関して: when just saying “about a topic”, prefer について; に対して can sound too stiff/formal.
Using に対して for a comparison of degree: for comparison, use ～より/～に比べて.
Forgetting to change to に対する when modifying a noun: ×学生に対して支援制度 → ○学生に対する支援制度.
Wrong order in the contrast structure: it must be “Aに対して、B…”.
594.notes:
• に対して often goes with verbs of evaluation/attitude such as 優しい, 厳しい, 失礼だ, 敬意を払う, 批判する.
• The ratio structure “N1に対してN2” appears often in figures/statistics and reports.
• For contrast, you can write Aは…。それに対して、Bは… to separate the sentences clearly.
meaning_vi: A is…, while B is… (contrast/comparison)
explain: Used to set A and B against each other to highlight the difference: “A is…, while B is…”. Often appears in the form Aのに対してB.
examples: 1. あの二人はふたごなのに、兄はおとなしいのに対して、弟はよくしゃべる。
Although those two are twins, the older one is quiet, while the younger one talks a lot.
2. 近所のスーパーは夜１１時閉店なのに対し、コンビニは２４時間営業だ。
The nearby supermarket closes at 11 p.m., while the convenience store is open 24 hours.
3. この映画は海外では人気があるのに対して、日本国内ではそうでもない。
This movie is popular overseas, whereas in Japan it is not so popular.
4. 一般に、日本の若者は洋食を好む。それに対して、中高年は和食を好む。
In general, young Japanese people prefer Western food. In contrast, middle-aged and older people prefer Japanese food.
──────
1. 目上の人に対しては敬語を使わなければならない。
You must use keigo with your superiors.
2. 先生は学生のどんな質問に対しても、ていねいに答えてくれる。
The teacher answers any question from the students carefully.
3. 厳しい父に対し、私はいつも反抗的な態度をとった。
I always took a rebellious attitude toward my strict father.
4. 長引く不況で、国民の政府に対する不満が高まっている。
Because of the prolonged recession, people's dissatisfaction with the government is growing.
5. 彼女は自分に対して非常に厳しい人だ。
She is very strict with herself. meaning_vi: Toward, toward… (as for…), even toward…, …toward…. ⏐ explain: Used to express an attitude or action toward a matter or issue
Or used when presenting two contrasting things or matters ⏐ examples: 1. 田中先生は、生徒に対して厳しい。
Mr. Tanaka is strict with his students
2. まじめな長男に対して、次男は遊んでばかりで学校もよく休む。
In contrast to the diligent eldest son, the second son does nothing but play and often misses school explain: Used to indicate the target: toward some matter… The second clause usually contains words expressing an opposing relationship (words of resistance, opposition, refutation…) ⏐ examples: 1. 目上の人に対して、そういう言い方は失礼ですよ。
Speaking like that to a superior is rude.
2. 都市で人口が増えているのに対し、農村では減っている。
While the population is increasing in cities, it is decreasing in rural areas. | Modifier form: ～に対する + N

examples.tr: Compared with last year, there has been less rain this year.

examples.tr: Compared with other countries, Japan is safe.

595.explain:
Points out a specific standard in order to show a gap in degree. Suitable for commentary and analysis.
Usable in both spoken and written language; the form に比べ is concise written language.
Avoid comparing incompatible categories; items should be of the same category to sound natural.

• Expresses a comparison of degree against a clear reference point (Aに比べてBは…: B differs in degree from A).
• Emphasizes the criterion/aspect of comparison; often used with ほう, より, ほど to clarify the degree.
• Often used with figures, points in time, places, products, or people/things of the same kind, to avoid mismatched comparisons.

rows: Short, neutral; does not emphasize the criterion
Emphasizes comparison with a standard/aspect; more formal than より
<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べて<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い
Comparison of inferiority; negates the degree
Aほど<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しくない
Not a comparison of degree; indicates direction/contrast
Equivalent to に<ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べて
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>と<ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べて…

mistakes: Confusing it with に対して: ×Aに対してBのほうが高い → ○Aに比べてBのほうが高い.
Leaving out the subject being compared makes it ambiguous: include Bのほうが to make clear which side is greater.
Mismatched comparisons (of different kinds) are unnatural.
Wrong order: it must be “Aに比べて、B…”; do not invert the idea and leave out the subject.
595.notes:
• Often used with figures: 去年に比べて10％増, 昨日より2度高い.
• When B is clearly the subject, “Aに比べて、Bのほうが…” is often used.
• To compare clauses, use の for nominalization: 勉強するのに比べて…
explain: ◎ Expresses the meaning "Compared with ~, ~ is more".
examples: 1. 私の国に比べて、日本は人が多い。
Compared with my country, Japan has more people.
2. 前回に比べて、参加者が少ない。
Compared with last time, there are fewer participants.
meaning_vi: Expresses comparison. Compared with ~
explain: Used to compare A with B. ～に比べて is usually followed by a characteristic, an evaluation or figures that show the difference.
examples: 1. 昼間に比べて深夜は電器料金が安い。
Compared with the daytime, electricity is cheaper late at night.
2. 今年は例年に比べ、寒さが厳しいそうだ。
I hear the cold is more severe this year compared with an average year.
3. 女性のほうが男性に比べ平均寿命の長い国が多い。
In many countries, women have a longer average life expectancy than men.
4. 「私は話すのに比べて、書く力が弱いんです。」
Compared with speaking, my writing is weak.

3. ➂     とり肉は豚肉に比べ、脂が少ない。

The exam questions became easier compared with last year
2. 店で買うのに比べ、通信販売は便利だが、欠点もある。

596.meaning:
Expresses the speaker's strong conviction.
［ふつう］　+　に違いない
［Na：ひまだN：雨だ］

596.explain: Strongly asserts the speaker's conjecture based on evidence: “it must be…”. The speaker believes it is almost certainly true.
596.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～はずだ／～に決まっている.
→ ～に違いない means “certainly” based on inference with evidence, but it is still the speaker's conjecture.
2) Not used for weak conjecture.
→ If you mean only “maybe”, use ～かもしれない／～だろう.
3) Often goes with signs/evidence.
→ There is usually prior information serving as the basis for the conclusion.

597.explain:
Public style: signs, flyers, regulations, event announcements.
Not used with verbs/descriptions of free actions; mainly attaches to nouns indicating a target/time frame.
Usually placed near the beginning of the sentence to set the condition of a special offer/limitation.

• Specifies a special scope of application: "only … can …".
• Tone of announcements, regulations, temporary or permanent offers.
• Often used with words indicating time/target: 本日／女性／会員／学生／初回 など.
• Does not express "the best" like ～に限る, and is different from ～に限って.

A different pattern; states an exception/irony
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>って<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らず。

mistakes: Using it with a verb: "行くに限り" is incorrect; it must attach to a noun.
Confusing it with ～に限る (evaluation "the best"): a different communicative purpose.
Adding は after に限り to make "に限りは" (unnatural); if you need emphasis, use "Nに限っては".
The JLPT often sets traps with the contrasting pair に限り／に限らず; pay attention to the opposite meanings.
597.notes:
• In policy documents: "Aに限り、Bとする" is the standard regulatory formula.
• The predicate can be omitted on signs: "関係者に限り"。
• Combine with "一部店舗に限り" to state an exception in the area of application.

599.connection: V plain form + ばかりでなく… (も) / N / Na + な / Aい + い

examples.jp: スキーができないばかりでなく、日常生活にも影響が出ている。
examples.tr: Not only can I not ski, but it is also affecting my daily life.

examples.jp: この暑さで、人間ばかりでなく、動物も、じっとして動かなくなっている。
examples.tr: Because of this heat, not only people but animals too have stopped moving and are lying still.

examples.jp: 彼女は英語ばかりでなく、フランス語やドイツ語も話せる。
examples.tr: She can speak not only English but also French and German.

examples.jp: この本はただ面白いばかりでなく、仕事にも役立つ。
examples.tr: This book is not just interesting; it is also useful for work.

examples.jp: 「自分のことばかりでなく、人の気持ちも考えなさい」
examples.tr: "Don't think only about yourself; think about other people's feelings too."

examples.jp: あのスーパーは商品が豊富なばかりでなく、値段も安い。
examples.tr: That supermarket not only has a wide range of products, but its prices are also low.

599.explain: ◎ A way of emphasizing something by mentioning not just one thing but several.
599.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～だけでなく／～はもちろん.
→ ～ばかりでなく means "not only… but also…", is often used in written language, and has a slightly formal nuance.
2) The second clause is usually the point you want to emphasize more.
→ Common structure: AばかりでなくBも／まで.
3) Not used when merely giving examples.
→ For giving examples, use ～など…
meaning_vi: 「～だけでなくて、その他にも…。」
Not only ~, but in addition to that also…
examples: 1. 日本人ばかりでなく、世界中の人がエネルギー問題に関心を持っている。
日本人ばかりでなく、世界中の人がエネルギー問題に関心を持っている。=> Not only Japanese people but people all over the world are interested in energy problems.
2. この番組は、面白いばかりでなく、さまざまなことが学べる。
この番組は、面白いばかりでなく、さまざまなことが学べる。=> This program is not only interesting; you can also learn many different things from it.
3. 彼は町を案内してくれたばかりでなく、この地方の料理もご馳走しててくれた。
彼は町を案内してくれたばかりでなく、この地方の料理もご馳走しててくれた。=> He not only showed me around the town but also treated me to the local cuisine.
meaning_vi: Used when you want to say "not only ~ but also ~"
［ふつう］　+　だけでなく／だけじゃなく（て）／ばかりでなく／ばかりじゃなく（て）
［Na：元気な　N：学生だ］
examples: 1. ➀　部屋だけでなく
Not only the room
2. ②　飛行機だけでなく船にも乗った。
I rode not only a plane but also a ship.
3. ③　この製品は、日本ばかりでなく、海外でも使われている。
This product is used not only in Japan but also overseas.
4. ➃　今日は、風が強いばかりでなく、雨も降るらしい。
I hear that today it will not only be windy but also rain.
5. ⑤　考えるだけじゃなくて、実際にやってみなくちゃ。
Don't just think about it; you have to actually try it.

examples.jp: あのとき謝ればよかった。
examples.tr: I should have apologized then.

examples.jp: もっと早く医者に行けばよかった。
examples.tr: I should have gone to the doctor sooner.

examples.jp: 高いカメラを買わなければよかった。
examples.tr: I wish I hadn't bought an expensive camera.

examples.jp: 雨になると知っていたら、傘を持って来ればよかった。
examples.tr: If I had known it would rain, I would have brought an umbrella.

examples.jp: 彼に本当のことを言えばよかったのに。
examples.tr: You should have told him the truth.

examples.jp: 聞けばよかった
examples.tr: I should have asked

600.explain:
A strong nuance of regret or self-blame.
It can be used in a gentle tone, sometimes conveying self-reproach or wistfulness.
A softer form can add: ～ばよかったのに → "If only…, yet…" (with a slight complaint or reproach).

•
Expresses regret about something in the past that you did not do (or did).

•
Natural translations: "If only…", "I should have…", "I wish I had…".

• Usually refers to an action that was not done but should have been, or an action that was done but you wish you hadn't.
• This is an emotional expression, used a lot in conversation, movies, and inner monologues in diaries.

rows: Regret about an action not taken.
Very close in meaning, with a softer or neutral nuance.
Adds a clearer nuance of complaint and regret.
<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれれ ばよかったのに。
It would be good if… (future wish)
Used for future wishes, not regret about the past.
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>える といいね。

mistakes: Using the wrong verb tense: you must use Vば or Vたら.
Confusing it with ～といい／～ばいい (a wish about the future).
Dropping よかった and using only Vば → wrong meaning.
For the negative, you must use なければよかった or なかったらよかった.
600.notes:
• This is an N3–N2 grammar point that appears often in conversation and in the listening and reading sections of exams.
• In casual speech, だ can be omitted: ～ばよかったなぁ, ～ばよかったのに….
• It can be followed by って → ～ばよかったって for emphasis when reporting.
meaning_vi: If only … it would have been good
explain: Used to express regret about something that happened differently from what you wanted
examples: 1. 遅刻してしまった。もっと早く家を出ればよかった。
I was late. I should have left home earlier.
2. 田中さんにあんなことを言わなければよかった。
I wish I hadn't said such things to Tanaka.
meaning_vi: And yet…/ If only…
explain: Used to express regret about something that happened differently from what you wanted
examples: 1. パーテイー、楽しかったよ。君も行けばよかったのに。
The party was fun. You should have come too.
2. 安かったら買うのに。
If it were cheap, I would buy it, but…

examples.jp: スピーチは、練習すればするほどうまくなる。
examples.tr: With speeches, the more you practice, the better you get.

examples.jp: 給料は高ければ高いほどうれしい。
examples.tr: The higher the salary, the happier I am.

examples.jp: 外国語はだれでも、練習すればするほど上手になる。
examples.tr: With foreign languages, anyone gets better the more they practice.

examples.jp: 将来のことを考えれば考えるほど不安になる。
examples.tr: The more I think about the future, the more anxious I become.

examples.jp: 見れば見るほどすばらしい絵だ。
examples.tr: The more I look at it, the more wonderful this painting is.

examples.jp: 夢は大きければ大きいほど良い。
examples.tr: The bigger your dream, the better.

601.explain:
Emphasizes a proportional relationship: increase–increase or decrease–decrease (少なければ少ないほど…).
The second clause can deny absoluteness with ～とは限らない／～わけではない.
With Aな/N, the form であればあるほど is formal/precise in written language.
In conversation, the first clause can be shortened if the context is clear:若ければ若いほど…

- Meaning: "The more A, the more B". Expresses a covariant relationship or an increase/decrease in one direction.
- Form: The same word class is repeated in the two halves before ～ば and ～ほど to create a comparison of degree.
- Scope: Used for general tendencies/relationships; rarely used for a single, one-time event.

rows: Emphasizes change over time/a process; no need to repeat the word
<ruby>温度<rt>おんど</rt></ruby>が<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がるにつれて<ruby>氷<rt>こおり</rt></ruby>が<ruby>溶<rt>と</rt></ruby>ける。
Unlike the proportional "the more… the more…" model, it only indicates degree
<ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>くほど<ruby>美<rt>うつく</rt></ruby>しい。
～と also expresses a regular relationship, but ～ば～ほど emphasizes degree
<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べると<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>になる。

mistakes: Wrong repeated form: using different forms in the two clauses (× 行けば行ったほど) → it must be Vば・Vる.
Using it for a single event rather than a tendency → unnatural.
Incorrect with Aな/N: forgetting な/である before ほど (× 静かほど) → 静かなほど／静かであるほど.
Confusing it with "～ほど～はない" (superlative) → a completely different meaning.
601.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ばいい (simple condition).
→ ～ば～ほど expresses a parallel increase/decrease: "the more… the more…".
2) The two clauses change in the same direction.
→ If there is no sense of "degree increasing accordingly", this pattern does not fit.
3) Pay attention to the conjugation.
→ V/A in the ba-form in the first clause; the second clause usually comes with ほど (can be omitted in some sentences). explain: Used to show that the degree of the result increases as the characteristic of the thing increases ⏐ examples: 1. 彼のことを知れば知るほど好きになる。
The more I get to know him, the more I like him.
2. 荷物は少なければ少ないほどいい。
The less luggage, the better. | Na form: Naなら Naなほど

602.connection: V plain form + ふりをする / N + の / Na + な / Aい

examples.jp: 彼は質問に気づかないふりをした。
examples.tr: He pretended not to notice the question.

examples.jp: 子どもは寝たふりをして、お菓子を待っていた。
examples.tr: The child pretended to be asleep and waited for the sweets.

examples.jp: 彼女は元気なふりをしているが、実はつらい。
examples.tr: She is pretending to be fine, but actually she is having a hard time.

examples.jp: 彼は大人のふりをして背伸びしている。
examples.tr: He is pretending to be an adult and trying to look more grown-up than he is.

examples.jp: 痛くないふりをしたけれど、かなり痛かった。
examples.tr: I pretended it didn't hurt, but it hurt quite a lot.

602.explain:
Used to describe behavior that hides the truth; often carries an implied evaluation (insincere/evasive).
Often combined with して/している to state a purpose or a continuing state.
Not used for natural phenomena/inanimate things (×雨が降らないふりをする).

• Expresses pretending, acting as if in some state/behavior while the reality is different.
• The subject is usually a conscious person/animal; it has a nuance of insincerity, sometimes with a critical meaning.
• Both past and present tense can be used: 知らないふりをした (pretended), している (is pretending).

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>王様<rt>おうさま</rt></ruby>であるかのように<ruby>振<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る<ruby>舞<rt>ま</rt></ruby>う
<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らぬ<ruby>体<rt>からだ</rt></ruby>／<ruby>悲<rt>かな</rt></ruby>しげ

mistakes: Wrong particle with nouns: it must be Nのふりをする, not Nなふりをする.
Using it with an inanimate subject is incorrect: × ドアが壊れたふりをする.
Confusing it with ～かのようだ: that pattern describes outward appearance, not "pretending".
Forgetting to keep 「な」 with na-adjectives: × 元気ふりをする → ◯ 元気なふりをする.
602.notes:
• Negative: ～ふりをしない (not put on an act). Past: ～ふりをした.
• An evaluative adjective can be inserted: わざと～、いかにも～のふり。
• In conversation, add 「なんて」 for criticism: 知らないふりなんてやめて。

examples.jp: 収入があるなら国民として税金を納めるべきだ。
examples.tr: If you have an income, you should pay taxes as a citizen.

examples.jp: 教授に、読むべき本を３０冊も指示された。
examples.tr: The professor told me to read as many as 30 books.

examples.jp: 学生時代、もっとよく勉強するべきだった。
examples.tr: I should have studied harder when I was a student.

examples.jp: 人を傷つけるようなことは言うべきではない。（=～してはならない）
examples.tr: You should not say things that hurt people. (=～してはならない)

examples.jp: *部屋に入るときはノックすべし。
examples.tr: *Knock before entering the room.

examples.jp: 彼女は愛すべき人柄で、がれからも好きかれている。
examples.tr: She has a lovable personality, and is liked by everyone.

603.explain:
More formal than ～たほうがいい, conveying responsibility or moral principle.
It can sound somewhat imposing if used in the wrong context, since it expresses a strong opinion.
It is very suitable in written language, speeches, and social judgments.
When talking about your own actions → softer, expressing self-reproach.

•
Expresses what should be done or must be done based on morality, common sense, or responsibility.

• Has a nuance of the speaker's subjective judgment but with a universal character: "everyone should do this".
• Can be used to criticize, advise, or emphasize moral obligation.
• Natural translations: "should…", "must…", "ought to have…".

rows: <ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らなければならない。

mistakes: Using ～べきだ with older people/superiors may be seen as impolite.
Confusing it with ～たほうがいい – use べきだ when the opinion is about "right/wrong, should/must", not general advice.
Dropping だ at the end when writing the standard formal form is incorrect (it must have だ or です).
The JLPT often tests the distinction from ～はずだ and ～なければならない.
603.notes:
• Polite negative form → ～べきではありません.
• In casual speech, a softer form can be used: ～べきだったなぁ (I should have…).
• Old-fashioned form used a lot in law and official documents: ～すべし (must…).

examples.jp: 約束は破るべきではない。
examples.tr: You should not break a promise.

examples.jp: 他人の個人情報を共有するべきではない。
examples.tr: You should not share other people's personal information.

examples.jp: 感情に任せて決めるべきではない。
examples.tr: You should not make decisions based on your emotions.

examples.jp: こんな夜道を一人で歩くべきではない。
examples.tr: You shouldn't walk alone on a road like this at night.

examples.jp: 軽はずみな発言をするべきではなかった。
examples.tr: I should not have made such a careless remark.

604.explain:
Used for general standards: morality, professional rules, safety, manners.
In casual communication, it can be softened: ～ないほうがいい／やめたほうがいい.
Not used for simple ability/permission; that is the scope of ～てはいけない／～てもいい.

• Expresses "should not/ought not" based on social rules, morality, common sense, professional standards.
• Stronger than "ないほうがいい" (advice), weaker than "てはいけない" (legal/regulatory prohibition).
• Usually an objective judgment; use it according to context to avoid being too imposing.

rows: <ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をつくべきではない。
<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby><ruby>更<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>かしはないほうがいい。
ここで<ruby>喫煙<rt>きつえん</rt></ruby>してはいけない。
Expresses that something is unnecessary, not prohibition/should not
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>することはない。

mistakes: Using it instead of "てはいけない" on signs/strict regulations → the nuance does not fit.
Confusing it with "ことはない": the latter means "there is no need", not "should not".
The JLPT often asks for the conversion: するべきではない ⇄ すべきではない.
Outdated/unnatural: × 行くべきではないと思いますか → better: 行かないほうがいいと思います (when it is just light personal advice).
604.notes:
• "するべきではない" is used in practice, but in proper writing: "すべきではない".
• A passive/vague-topic structure helps make it objective: 個人を特定する発言はすべきではない。
• When speaking within an organization, add grounds to make it less imposing: 安全面から見て、～すべきではない。

605.meaning: To the extent that, the more… the more…
605.connection: V plain form・Aい・N + ほど / Vば Vる + ほど

examples.jp: この論文は難しくて、途中で読むのをやめたくなるほどです。
examples.tr: This paper is so difficult that it makes me want to stop reading halfway through.

examples.jp: 一日中働いたので、疲れて、もう歩けないほどです。
examples.tr: I worked all day, so I'm so tired that I can't walk anymore.

examples.jp: ズボンに100円玉ほどの穴が空いていた。
examples.tr: There was a hole about the size of a 100-yen coin in my pants.

examples.jp: すみません、１０分ほどお待ちください。
examples.tr: I'm sorry, please wait about 10 minutes.

examples.jp: うちから学校まで３０分ほどで行ける。
examples.tr: I can get from home to school in about 30 minutes.

examples.jp: 夜も眠れないほど悩んだ。
examples.tr: I was so troubled that I couldn't even sleep at night.

605.explain:
Used to emphasize degree or a strong comparison.
Can be used with both positive and negative emotions.
In casual speech, people use 「～くらい」 instead of 「～ほど」.
Formal nuance, common in written language, essays, and JLPT exams.

•
① Degree "to the extent that…": Expresses a high degree of a state/action.

•
② Comparison: "Nothing is as…, no one is as…": Often used in the structure「Aほど～はない」＝ "There is nothing as … as A".

•
③ The more… the more…: Shows a directly proportional relationship between the two clauses.

•
Note: Mostly written language / JLPT; it can be used in spoken language but less often.

rows: To the extent…, the more…, nothing is as…
More formal; used in strong comparisons or for degree.
<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>く ほど<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しかった。
Spoken language, lighter than ほど.
<ruby>死<rt>し</rt></ruby>ぬ くらい<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れた。
Expresses the correlation between two actions/states.
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>れば<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る ほど<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きになる。
<ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>ほど<ruby>優<rt>やさ</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>はいない。

mistakes: Using it incorrectly when there is no correlation → you need the logic: however much A changes → B changes that much.
Confusing it with くらい: くらい is more casual and not used in formal writing.
The form "VればVるほど" requires the verb to be repeated.
Often appears in JLPT N3-N2 in the forms "AほどBはない", "Vるほど".
605.notes:
1) ～ほど is easily confused with ～くらい.
→ The meaning "about/approximately" is similar, but ～ほど is usually more formal and often used in written language.
2) Be careful because ～ほど has many uses (degree, extreme…).
→ In the same test, ～ほど may appear with different meanings (to the extent that, ~ is the best), making it easy to fall into a trap when choosing the answer.
3) Look at the accompanying structure to determine the meaning.
→ If it indicates a quantity/estimate: the meaning is "about".
→ If it is used with a comparison/extreme: it probably has a different meaning.

examples.jp: 空気が悪いので、しばらく窓を開けたままにした。
examples.tr: The air was stuffy, so I left the window open for a while.

examples.jp: あとでかたづけますので、そのままにしておいてください。
examples.tr: I'll tidy up later, so please leave it as it is.

examples.jp: 電源を切ったままにする
examples.tr: Leave the power switched off

examples.jp: この鉢植えは、夏の間ずっと外に出したままにしています。
examples.tr: I've kept this potted plant outside the whole summer.

examples.jp: そのままにしておいてください。
examples.tr: Please leave it as it is.

606.explain: ◎ Continuing the same state as it is now.

examples.jp: めったにない機会だから、ぜひ参加してください。
examples.tr: It's a rare opportunity, so please do take part.

examples.jp: 彼が失敗することはめったにない。
examples.tr: He rarely fails.

examples.jp: こんな良い条件はめったにないよ。
examples.tr: Conditions this good are really rare.

examples.jp: この町で事件が起こることはめったにない。
examples.tr: Crimes rarely happen in this town.

examples.jp: これはめったにない名前だ。
examples.tr: This is a rare name.

examples.jp: 今年のような猛暑はめったにない。
examples.tr: A heat wave like this year's is rare.

607.explain:
Used to present rarity as a property of N, not focusing on a repeated action.
In formal language, it can be replaced by まれな／きわめてまれな (very rare).
Polite: ～はめったにありません. Past: ～はめったになかった.

• Expresses that a "thing/event" is rare and hardly ever exists/happens. It is an evaluation of the rarity of the target.
• Unlike めったに～ない (540), which emphasizes "frequency of an action", this pattern emphasizes "the rarity of the opportunity/event itself".
• Often used with nouns such as 機会, チャンス, 例, こと, ケース, 出来事, 名前, 品物.

rows: Modifies N or evaluates an event
めったにない<ruby>機会<rt>きかい</rt></ruby>
まれな／<ruby>希少<rt>きしょう</rt></ruby>な
ほとんど<ruby>例<rt>れい</rt></ruby>がない

mistakes: Confusing it with めったに～ない: めったにない must go with a noun or a nominalized clause.
Misunderstanding "ない" as negating the whole sentence: めったにない has the affirmative meaning "rare", not "not".
JLPT: choose correctly between "めったにない機会" and "めったに行かない" according to the required structure.
Wrong tense: × めったにないでした → ✓ めったにありませんでした / めったになかった.
607.notes:
• An emphatic structure can be used: こんなことは本当にめったにない.
• In terms of nuance, めったにない often conveys a "precious opportunity": 今回はめったにないチャンスだ.
• Avoid using "めったにある": it is unnatural; use the negative "めったにない".

examples.jp: あんな店、二度と行くものか！
examples.tr: A shop like that? I'll never go there again!

examples.jp: 彼が遅刻するものか。とても真面目な人だよ。
examples.tr: There's no way he'd be late. He's a very serious person.

examples.jp: これが簡単なものか。一週間はかかるよ。
examples.tr: This is anything but easy. It'll take at least a week.

examples.jp: また騙されるものか。
examples.tr: I won't be fooled again!

examples.jp: 彼女が嘘をつくものか。
examples.tr: There's no way she would lie.

examples.jp: そんな噂、信じるもんですか。
examples.tr: Believe a rumor like that? Never.

608.explain:
Usually used in spoken language with strong emotion; be careful about politeness when speaking to a superior.
Uses an affirmative form to emphasize negation (rhetorical question): "〜ものか" is equivalent to "No way ~".
In conversation, the subject and the preceding part can be omitted, blurting out just "〜ものか".

• Strong, emotional negation: "No way/Never/Not in a million years…".
• Used to reject the other person's invitation, evaluation, or assertion; can also be said to oneself.
• Sounds harsh if said directly; 〜もんですか/〜ものですか is slightly softer but still strong.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるわけがない
Spoken language; attaches to V-ます with ます removed

mistakes: Incorrect combination with na-adjectives: × 静かなものか → ✓ 静かなものか.
Using it in formal written language → does not fit the style; choose わけがない/はずがない.
Confusing it with a real question: "〜ものか" is a strong negation, not a question asking for information.
608.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～わけがない.
→ ～ものか is a strong negation expressing emotional volition/opposition (no way, definitely not).
2) Usually used in spoken language.
→ Often has a nuance of anger, determination, or rebuttal.
3) Not used for mild negation.
→ For "not exactly" or soft negation, use a different pattern.

examples.jp: 人間は忘れるものだ。だからメモしておくべきだ。
examples.tr: People are bound to forget things. That's why you should write notes.

examples.jp: 約束は守るものだ。
examples.tr: Promises are meant to be kept.

examples.jp: 子どものころは、夏になると川で泳いだものだ。
examples.tr: When I was a child, I would often swim in the river when summer came.

examples.jp: 時間が経つのは早いものだ。
examples.tr: Time really flies.

examples.jp: ここまでよく頑張ったものだ。
examples.tr: You've really done well to get this far.

examples.jp: 危ないことはするものではない。
examples.tr: You shouldn't do dangerous things.

609.explain:
For rules/truths: not tied to a specific point in time; general in nature.
For memories: use V-たものだ; often used with past time expressions (昔/子どものころ…).
For exclamation: carries a strong emotional nuance; usually at the end of a sentence.
“〜ものではない” emphasizes prohibition/advice not to do something, and is more formal than “〜ないほうがいい”.

• Generalization/social or natural law: “it is normal/it is natural that…”.
• Moral norms: “should/of course must” (admonishing in tone).
• Past memories: “used to/would often”, emphasizing a nostalgic feeling.
• Exclamation: expresses a strong impression of a reality (it really goes fast, time flies…).

rows: <ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>くものだ
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をつくものではない
<ruby>昔<rt>むかし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>ったものだ
それは<ruby>無責任<rt>むせきにん</rt></ruby>というものだ

mistakes: Confusing “V-たものだ” with “V-たことがある”: the former emphasizes a remembered habit, while the latter can refer to an experience that happened only once.
Using exclamatory “ものだ” in very formal texts → does not match the style.
Confusing “ものだ” (general rule) with “はずだ/べきだ”: べきだ is a strong obligation; ものだ leans toward a general judgment/moral principle.
609.notes:
• “たいものだ/てほしいものだ” strengthens the exclamatory nuance of desire: 休みたいものだ.
• When “ものだ” is pronounced with a drawn-out “も〜のだ”, it creates a pensive/reminiscent feeling.
• In formal written language, “ものだ” for truths is often followed by a reason/explanation.

examples.jp: 住所も電話も知らないから、彼に連絡しようがない。
examples.tr: I don't know his address or phone number, so there's no way to contact him.

examples.jp: 証拠がなければ、真偽は確かめようがない。
examples.tr: Without evidence, there's no way to verify whether it's true or false.

examples.jp: 説明が丁寧で、間違えようがない。
examples.tr: The explanation is so thorough that you can't possibly get it wrong.

examples.jp: 鍵をなくしてしまって、部屋に入りようがない。
examples.tr: I lost my key, so there's no way to get into the room.

examples.jp: この模様は手作業では再現しようがない。
examples.tr: There's no way to reproduce this pattern by hand.

examples.jp: 地図も標識もないと、ここから先へ進みようがない。
examples.tr: Without a map or signs, there's no way to go any further from here.

610.explain:
Often used with words indicating a lack of information: 手がかりがない,情報がない,手段がない.
Not used for “do not want to/dare not because of social norms” (in that case use ～わけにはいかない or ～かねる).
Can be used in the present or past tense, and is natural in both spoken and written language.
The negative form emphasizes “absolutely no possibility in terms of method”, stronger than 単なる「できない」.

• There is no means/method to carry out action V: “cannot (because there is no way)”.
• Also used in the reverse sense of “no mistake can happen”: 間違えようがない = you can't possibly get it wrong.
• Focuses on “lack of conditions/clues”, not “not wanting to/not daring to”.

rows: <ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようがない
Vる + わけにはいかない
Vえない（<ruby>可能<rt>かのう</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby><ruby>否定<rt>ひてい</rt></ruby>）
Neutral, does not emphasize “there is no way”

mistakes: Using it with V辞書形: × 連絡するようがない → ✔ 連絡しようがない.
Confusing it with わけにはいかない: if the reason is “there are no means”, choose ～ようがない.
Expressing ability in terms of one's own capability: use 可能形/えない; ～ようがない emphasizes “there is no way”.
JLPT: when you see “手がかりがない/情報がない/方法がない”, the answer is usually ～ようがない/～ようもない.
610.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～できない.
→ ～ようがない means “there is no way to…”, emphasizing that no method exists.
2) Often used when information/a solution is lacking.
→ Usually carries a feeling of helplessness.
3) Not used for simply “not wanting/not intending to”.
→ If it is about volition, use another pattern that negates intention.

611.connection: V volitional form + としない

examples.jp: 彼は謝ろうとしない。
examples.tr: He won't apologize.

examples.jp: 子どもが野菜を食べようとしない。
examples.tr: The child won't eat vegetables.

examples.jp: 彼女は話そうとしないで、ずっと黙っている。
examples.tr: She won't say anything and has been silent the whole time.

examples.jp: 雨が止もうとしない。
examples.tr: The rain shows no sign of stopping.

examples.jp: 彼は説明を聞こうともしない。
examples.tr: He won't even listen to the explanation.

examples.jp: 最後まであきらめようとしなかった。
examples.tr: They never tried to give up until the very end.

611.explain:
Usually used with a third-person subject to make an evaluation; can be used in the first person for self-criticism or describing one's own state of mind.
Used with verbs expressing volitional actions: 話す・食べる・手伝う・謝る...
With natural phenomena: ～やむ／晴れる／止まる + ようとしない → “shows no sign of ...”.
“ともしない” strengthens the negation and the nuance of criticism.

• Expresses “has no intention of/won't bother/won't (even try to) do V”, “shows no sign of V-ing”.
• Nuance of the speaker's criticism/dissatisfaction, especially with human agents. Can also be used with natural phenomena (showing no sign of change).
• Unlike simple negation, it emphasizes “lack of effort/lack of intention” rather than the result not happening.

rows: Try to/be about to do V
Subjective statement; does not focus on a specific action at that moment.
Does not want to V (third person)

mistakes: Wrong intention: using it with a non-volitional verb (分かる) → unnatural.
Wrong volitional conjugation: 来る→こよう, する→しよう; Group 1 verbs change u→o + う.
Confusing it with “つもりがない”: JLPT questions often test the nuance of “not trying to do” (ようとしない) vs. “having no intention” (つもりがない).
Forgetting “と”: writing “ようしない” is wrong; it must be “ようとしない”.
611.notes:
• In spoken language, “と” can be dropped for rhythm, but the standard form is “としない”.
• With non-volitional verbs (分かる, 見える...), this pattern is hardly ever used, because the subject has no intention.
• Often used with degree words: 全然・まったく・少しも + ～ようとしない to strengthen the nuance.
meaning_vi: Expresses the will behind the action of some person other than the speaker.
examples: 1. ①　払おうとしない
Has no intention of paying
2. ②　妹はお金を持っていますのに、自分で払おうとしなかった。
Even though my younger sister had money with her, she made no attempt to pay herself.
3. ③　彼は全然、私の話を聞こうとしない。
He won't listen to what I say at all.

612.meaning:
ある目的のためにそう作られている
Something is made that way for a certain purpose

examples.jp: このドアはボタンを押すと開くようになっている。
examples.tr: This door is designed to open when you press the button.

examples.jp: 食事は、肉料理が魚料理か、選べるようになっている。
examples.tr: For the meal, you can choose either a meat dish or a fish dish.

examples.jp: このストーブは大きく傾くと、自動的に火が消えるようになっている。
examples.tr: This heater is designed so that the flame goes out automatically if it tilts too far.

examples.jp: このドアは閉めると、カギがかかるようになっている。
examples.tr: This door locks automatically when you close it.

examples.jp: この自動販売機はレバーを押さないと、おつりが出ないようになっている。
examples.tr: This vending machine won't give change unless you push the lever.

examples.jp: この画面はパスワードを入力しないと、開くことができないようになっている。
examples.tr: This screen is set up so that it can't be opened unless you enter the password.

612.explain: Used to talk about the structure, mechanism, or function of objects, machines, or systems: made so that…, has a mechanism to…. Not used for human volition.
612.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ようになった.
→ ～ようになっている refers to a state that is designed or has a built-in mechanism, not a change over time.
2) Easily confused with ～ようにする.
→ ～ようにする means making an effort or setting a goal; ～ようになっている is an existing structure or function.
3) Usually used with objects, machines, and systems.

examples.jp: よくその店に行くので、顔を覚えられるようになった。
examples.tr: I go to that shop often, so they've come to remember my face.

examples.jp: この商品は、名前を変えたら、売れるようになった。
examples.tr: After we changed its name, this product started selling well.

examples.jp: 机の位置を変えたので、仕事中でも外の景色が見えるようになった。
examples.tr: I moved my desk, so now I can see the scenery outside even while I'm working.

examples.jp: 親が楽しそうに家事をしていれば、子どもも進んで手伝うようになる。
examples.tr: If parents do housework cheerfully, children will also come to help willingly.

examples.jp: ジョギングをするようになる
examples.tr: Start jogging

examples.jp: 今年は、毎朝ジョギングをするようになりました。
examples.tr: This year, I've started jogging every morning.

613.explain:
Expresses “reaching” a state/ability after a process (implies there was a process).
Does not express volition directly; to emphasize effort, use ～ようにする.
Used both for natural changes/practice and for system functions (～ようになっている).

• Expresses a change in state/ability/habit over time: “come to/become able to/start doing”.
• Emphasizes the result/outcome of the change (objective), unlike “making an effort” (～ようにする).
• Negative なくなる: “no longer…”.
• Often used with adverbs: だんだん／少しずつ／やっと／とうとう.

rows: <ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きするようにする。
Decision due to circumstances/rules, not a change in ability.
<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>転勤<rt>てんきん</rt></ruby>することになった。
Adj + くなる／N + になる
Change of an adjective/noun; ～ようになる is for verbs/ability/habit.
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くなる／<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>になる。
Unexpected onset; ～ようになる is not necessarily sudden.

mistakes: Using it for a one-time action: × 今すぐ出発するようになった → this is a decision, so use ことになった。
Confusing it with ～ようにする: × 日本語が話せるようにする (effort) when you want to state the result → ○ 日本語が話せるようになった。
Wrong use with nouns/adjectives: × 静かようになる → ○ 静かになる／静かになるようにする (if emphasizing effort).
Forgetting “なくなる” for natural negation: × 食べないようになった (not wrong, but 食べなくなった is usually more natural).
613.notes:
• With potential verbs: する→できる, 行く→行ける…; 見える・聞こえる already mean “can see/hear”, but ～ようになる is still used to talk about circumstances that make it possible: 眼鏡で黒板が見えるようになった。
• Developmental sequence: 練習する→少しずつできるようになる→うまくなる。
• Cause form: AになってからBようになった（After A, started B）. meaning_vi: To become a certain way ⏐ explain: Used to express a thing or subject changing into a different state.
Often used with intransitive verbs and verbs in the potential form ⏐ examples: 1. 「このDVDプレーヤー、こわれているんだよね。」
「いや、直してもらったから、使えるようになったよ。」
This DVD player is broken, right?
No, I had it fixed, so it can be used now.
2. ここの電気は人が通るとつくようになっています。
The lights here are set up to turn on when someone passes by.

examples.jp: この問題はまだ習っていないのだから、できるわけがない。
examples.tr: We haven't learned this problem yet, so there's no way I can solve it.

examples.jp: あんなにきれいで優しいA子さんに恋人がいないわけはないだろう。
examples.tr: There's no way someone as pretty and kind as A-ko doesn't have a boyfriend.

examples.jp: 「映画見に行かない？」「そんなに暇なわけないでしょ。試験が近いんだから」
examples.tr: “Want to go see a movie?” “There's no way I'm that free. The exam is coming up.”

examples.jp: 「そのバッグ、いくら？１万円ぐらい？」「そんなに安いわけないじゃない。ブランド物なのよ」
examples.tr: “How much was that bag? About 10,000 yen?” “No way it was that cheap. It's a designer brand.”

examples.jp: 「彼はそのとき私といっしょにいました。だから彼が犯人の（／犯人である）わけがありません」
examples.tr: “He was with me at that time. So there's no way he can be the culprit.”

examples.jp: 彼がそんなミスをするわけがない。
examples.tr: There's no way he would make a mistake like that.

614.explain:
Used when the speaker has a strong enough basis; otherwise it sounds dogmatic.
Often used with そんな／だれが／どうして…わけがない for added emphasis.
In conversation, it can sound like a blunt denial; consider politeness by using ～はずがない／考えにくい.

• Asserts “cannot possibly/no way” with a high degree of certainty.
• Based on knowledge, experience, relationships, or common-sense logic.
• Emotionally stronger in nuance than ～はずがない; somewhat subjective/dismissive.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるわけがない
そんなことがあるはずがない
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>むわけにはいかない

mistakes: Wrong combination with Na/N: × 彼は元気わけがない → ✔ 彼は元気なわけがない／元気であるわけがない.
Confusing it with ～わけではない: one is a strong total negation, the other is a partial negation.
Choosing the nuance: if the question calls for politeness/neutrality, prefer ～はずがない over ～わけがない.
JLPT: appearing together with “到底/どうして/常識的に/この状況で” → hints at the answer ～わけがない/～はずがない.
614.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～はずがない.
→ ～わけがない is a strong negation: “cannot possibly”, “no way”.
2) Usually carries strong emotion.
→ Often used when refuting, disbelieving, or asserting strongly.
3) Not used for mild negation.
→ If you only mean “not necessarily”, use ～わけではない.
meaning_vi: Strongly expresses that there is no possibility, no reason.
examples: 1. ①　そんなに安いわけがない
It can't possibly be that cheap
2. ②　お金がないのだから、家を買えるわけがない。
I have no money, so there's no way I can buy a house.
3. ➂　「今日、いま？」「ひまなわけないよ。明日、引っ越しなんだから」
"Are you free today?" "No way I'm free. I'm moving tomorrow"

615.meaning: No wonder, that's why; that means…, in other words… (rephrasing)

examples.jp: 「働く女性は増えてるけど、保育園の数は増えないんです。」「なるほど。入園できない子どもが増えるわけだ。」
examples.tr: “More women are working, but the number of daycare centers isn't increasing.” “I see. So that's why the number of children who can't get into daycare is going up.”

examples.jp: 「田中さんは足をけがしたそうです」「それで、試合に出てないわけだ」
examples.tr: “I heard Tanaka hurt his leg.” “So that's why he isn't playing in the game.”

examples.jp: 消費税は５％だから、１０５０円払ったら、５０円は税金というわけだ。
examples.tr: The consumption tax is 5%, so if you pay 1,050 yen, 50 yen of that is tax.

examples.jp: 私は毎日８時間寝ている。つまり、人生の３分の１をベッドで過ごすわけだ。
examples.tr: I sleep 8 hours every day. In other words, I spend a third of my life in bed.

examples.jp: （テレビが）つかないわけだ。コンセントが抜けている。
examples.tr: No wonder (the TV) won't turn on. It's unplugged.

examples.jp: 足が速いわけだ。彼は元陸上選手だったのだそうだ。
examples.tr: No wonder he's so fast. I heard he used to be a track and field athlete.

615.explain:
Often appears after receiving additional information (どおりで/なるほど/やっぱり) to “settle on” a reasonable conclusion.
Not used for guesses without a basis. For a strong conjecture alone, use ～に違いない/～はずだ.
Spoken language: …ってわけだ has a casual, emphatic nuance.
N + というわけだ is usually more natural than N + なわけだ when the noun stands alone.
Can be used at the end of a sentence or mid-sentence to lead into an explanation: ～から、～わけだ。

• No wonder/that explains it: Based on information just learned, the speaker draws a reasonable conclusion. Example: 日本語が上手なわけだ。
• In other words/so it turns out: Sums up the result inferred from the stated premises. Example: つまり、今日は休講というわけだ。
• Something natural as a matter of course: Because of condition A, B is understandable. Example: 山の上だから涼しいわけだ。
• Nuance of explanation/justification: Used to provide the reason why B is “understandable”. Usually follows a clause containing new information.
• Degree of certainty: High (based on facts), but more of a logical explanation than a strong conjecture like ～に違いない.

rows: Explanation, logical conclusion based on facts
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。<ruby>濡<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>れているわけだ。
Expectation-based inference from common sense; not necessarily an “explanation”
<ruby>犯人<rt>はんにん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない。
The “in other words” meaning is close to ～というわけだ, but more neutral
Partial negation; completely different from the explanatory function

mistakes: Mixing it up with ～はずだ/～に違いない: if the question calls for a “reasonable explanation” → choose ～わけだ, not a strong conjecture.
Attaching a noun directly + わけだ: use Nというわけだ or Nであるわけだ to sound natural.
Confusing it with ～わけではない (partial negation). The two patterns are opposite in function.
Missing ～な before わけだ with na-adjectives: 正: 便利なわけだ; Wrong: 便利わけだ.
615.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～はずだ.
→ ～わけだ is used to conclude/explain “so naturally…”, emphasizing the cause → result relationship.
2) Often used to mean “in short/so that's how it is”.
→ It can confirm a reasonable conclusion, not necessarily a strong judgment.
3) Not used for vague guesses.
→ If you are only guessing “maybe”, use ～だろう／～かもしれない. meaning_vi: Naturally, that means… ⏐ explain: Used to say that something turning out that way is natural because there was a prior cause or reason. Or when you want to say that such a result naturally follows from a certain sequence, direction, fact, or situation. ⏐ examples: 1. 寒いわけだ。雪が降っている。
No wonder it's cold. It's snowing.
2. 定価が１万円で、２割引きだから８千円になるわけだ。
The list price is 10,000 yen, and with a 20 percent discount it comes to 8,000 yen. meaning_vi: No wonder, it's not surprising that, naturally, ⏐ explain: Used when talking about the natural consequence of a result (with an explanation of the cause in the previous/following sentence) ⏐ examples: 1. 暑いわけだ。気温が36度もある。
No wonder it's hot. The temperature is as high as 36 degrees.
2. 「田中さん、彼女にふられたらしいよ。」「なるほど、それで、元気がないわけだ。」
"It seems Tanaka got dumped by his girlfriend" "I see, no wonder he looks so down"
Variant: ～というわけだ

616.meaning: Not necessarily, it is not that

examples.jp: 日本人が皆、日本文化に詳しいわけではない。
examples.tr: Not all Japanese people are familiar with Japanese culture.

examples.jp: お金がたくさんあれば幸せというわけではないだろう。
examples.tr: Having a lot of money probably doesn't necessarily mean you're happy.

examples.jp: 日本料理が嫌いというわけではない。作り方を知らないので作らないだけだ。
examples.tr: It's not that I dislike Japanese food. I just don't make it because I don't know how.

examples.jp: それほど忙しいわけではないが、それでも毎日１～２時間は残業している。
examples.tr: I'm not all that busy, but I still work 1 to 2 hours of overtime every day.

examples.jp: 「あなたの気持ちがわからないわけでもありませんが、ご両親の気持ちも考えたほうがいいですよ」
examples.tr: “It's not that I don't understand how you feel, but you should think about your parents' feelings too.”

examples.jp: 高い料理が好きなわけではない。
examples.tr: It's not that I like expensive food.

616.explain:
Used to reject a misunderstanding/an overstated idea; often follows a clause that the listener may be misunderstanding.
Add からといって/だからといって in the first clause to state a condition that is not enough to lead to the conclusion.
To strongly negate everything, use ～わけがない/～はずがない instead of ～わけではない.
Often combined with adverbs: いつも/全部/誰でも/必ずしも.

• Not necessarily/it does not mean that: Partial negation, rejecting a generalization.
• Not always/not necessarily: Used with 必ずしも, いつも, みんな, 全部 to weaken an absolute judgment.
• Softening a sentence: Used to avoid a blunt denial (to stay polite).
• Nuance: Limitations, exceptions exist. Not a total negation like ～わけがない.

rows: <ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby><ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きなわけではない。
Neutral, leans more toward generalizing facts
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いから<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない。
It is not the case that just because… then…
Written language, criticizes a simplistic notion
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>すれば<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>するというものではない。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるわけがない。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～わけがない (strong). If the question calls for “mild negation/exceptions exist” → choose ～わけではない.
Dropping “では”: Wrong: 好きなわけない (→ different/unclear meaning). Correct: 好きなわけではない.
Attaching “な” to a noun: Wrong: 学生なわけではない. Correct: 学生というわけではない or 学生であるわけではない.
Understanding it as total negation. ～わけではない only negates partially or indicates an insufficient condition.
616.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ない.
→ ～わけではない means “not necessarily/it does not mean that…”, a partial negation.
2) Often used to qualify a statement.
→ For example: 全部が悪いわけではない (not everything is bad).
3) Not used for total negation.
→ For strong negation, use ～わけがない／～はずがない. | Variant: ～(という)わけではない・わけじゃない

examples.jp: あしたは大事な試験があるから休むわけにはいかない。
examples.tr: I have an important exam tomorrow, so I can't take the day off.

examples.jp: 「きょうは車で来たので酒を飲むわけにはいかないんです」
examples.tr: “I came by car today, so I can't drink alcohol.”

examples.jp: ひどい不正を見て、黙っているわけにはいかなかった。
examples.tr: Seeing such terrible injustice, I couldn't stay silent.

examples.jp: ＊「いやなら断ったら」「そういうわけにはいかないよ。先輩の誘いなんだから」
examples.tr: ＊“If you don't want to, why not turn it down?” “I can't do that. It's an invitation from my senior.”

examples.jp: 親友がお金を貸してほしいと言っている。親友の頼みを断るわけにはいかない。

617.explain:
Expresses being unable to do something for social, moral, or psychological reasons, even if you might want to.

「心理的事情があるので、～することはできない。」能力などが原因でできないのではなくて、～したいが、社会的常識に反する・心理的抵抗感があるなどの事情があってできないという意味で使う。主語は普通一人称
Cannot do … for psychological reasons
Used to say that it is not ability etc. that prevents the action; in fact you would very much like to do ~, but you cannot do ~ because of particular circumstances, such as it going against social common sense or causing psychological resistance.
The subject is usually first person.
mistakes: Already explained in detail in block 410.
617.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～できない (cannot in terms of ability).
→ ～わけにはいかない means “cannot (for social/moral/psychological reasons)”: even if you want to, you cannot.
2) Often used in contexts of responsibility, etiquette, or circumstances.
→ Emphasizes “cannot do such a thing”.
3) Not used simply because you have no time.
→ If it is about conditions/ability, another pattern is usually used.

618.explain: Expresses putting a lot of emotion or meaning into an action.

mistakes: Using it with concrete nouns in a grammatical sense → wrong meaning (e.g., “砂糖を込めてコーヒーを入れる” is unnatural; it should be 砂糖を入れて).

618.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ために (purpose).
→ ～をこめて means “to put into / to be filled with”; it emphasizes the feelings/meaning put into an action or object.
2) Often used with words such as 気持ち／愛／感謝.
→ It means “with all…”, “putting all one's … into it”.
3) Not used for practical purposes.
→ If it is a clear purpose of an action, use ～ために／～ように.
meaning_vi: With all…, putting… into
explain: Used for creative/expressive actions: writing, speaking, giving, making, singing, praying…
The noun-modifying form Nを込めたN₂ is often seen in written language/advertising.
Not used with concrete nouns in the sense of “stuffing” unless it is the original meaning of the 動詞「込める」.
Expresses formality and sincerity; suited to positive/ceremonial contexts.
examples: 1. 心を込めて料理を作りました。

619.explain:
Used with a noun that serves as the “axis” around which an activity, scope or target unfolds.
Common in the news: 地域・年齢層・時間帯+ を中心に.
“～を中心として” is more formal than “～を中心に”; “～を中心にして” emphasizes the process of revolving around something.
The noun-modifying variant “Nを中心としたN₂” is very natural in writing.
Not used to express volition/requests; it mainly describes facts/directions.

• Taking N as the center/core/main element: organizations, plans and activities revolve around N.
• Mainly N: the main target group, main area, key content.
• Spatial/temporal scope “around N”: concentrated in/around the area N or the point in time N.
• Nuance: objective, describes distribution/focus; suited to announcements, news and reports.
• Different from “only about N”: emphasizes a center-satellite relationship, not “on the topic of N”.

rows: Taking N as the center/mainly N
<ruby>若者<rt>わかもの</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>売<rt>う</rt></ruby>れている
Around (an issue), revolving around (often with a dispute)
Emphasizes debate/conflict; does not describe a scope of distribution
<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>をめぐって<ruby>対立<rt>たいりつ</rt></ruby>がある
N as a representative example, first and foremost N
<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>をはじめ<ruby>各国<rt>かっこく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>
Emphasizes means or the whole period, not a center
SNSを<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて<ruby>情報<rt>じょうほう</rt></ruby><ruby>発信<rt>はっしん</rt></ruby>
Topic/target; does not imply a “central core”
<ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby><ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Confusing it with ～をめぐって: the latter emphasizes disputes; ～を中心に only indicates distribution/focus.
Using it with verbs: incorrect. This pattern attaches directly to nouns.
Using it to state volition/requests: unnatural (the pattern is descriptive).
Forgetting the noun-modifying variant “Nを中心としたN₂”, which often appears in JLPT reading comprehension.
619.notes:
• Can have a spatial meaning (東京を中心に), refer to a group of people (高齢者を中心に), or to time (夏を中心に).
• In headlines/advertising, を is often omitted: 週末中心にセール開催.
• “中心に据える/据えた” is an advanced expression: placing N as the axis.
• Avoid overusing it with abstract nouns that cannot clearly be a “center”.
meaning_vi: Taking ~ as the center
explain: ◎ Expresses the idea "taking ~ as the central position" or "regarding ~ as the most important".
examples: 1. 彼を中心に新しいバンドができた。
A new band was formed with him at its center.
2. ４月２２日は「地球の日」で、この日を中心に各地でさまざまなイベントが行われます。
April 22 is "Earth Day," so various events will be held in many places before, after and on that day. | Variants: ～を中心として・を中心にして

620.explain:
Used mainly in casual speech. In formal written language, ～ということだ／～そうだ (伝聞) is used.
The intonation rises at the end of the sentence when it is a confirmation question: ～んだって？
～んだって is not used to state a personal opinion; its function is reporting.
Combine it with っていう話／って聞いた to emphasize the source: ～って聞いたんだって (A said they heard…)

- Expresses indirect reporting: “I heard / someone said that…”. The spoken equivalent of ～そうだ／～ということだ when used for reporting.
- Casual, conversational nuance; shows that the speaker is not asserting anything with certainty but only passing on information they heard.
- Can be used as a question to confirm information: ～んだって？

rows: Neutral, can be used in writing
<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>になるということだ。
Contracted form of と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っている
Very colloquial; ～んだって includes the explanatory のだ

mistakes: Confusing it with ～だって (because/even). “雨なんだって” = I heard it's raining; “雨だって” = even rain… a different meaning.
Using it in formal language: switch to ～ということだ／～そうだ.
Forgetting “な” before nouns/な-adjectives: 有名んだって × correct: 有名なんだって。
620.notes:
• Adding the source: ～んだって、ニュースで（友だちが／先生が）。
• Negative/past forms stay as they are: 来ないんだって／行ったんだって。
• Emphasizing doubt: 本当なんだって？／マジなんだって？

examples.jp: この制度は公平な一方、手続きが複雑だ。

examples.jp: 彼は社交的である一方で、一人の時間も大切にする。
examples.tr: He is sociable, but he also values his time alone.

621.explain:
Used to balance information and show a multifaceted view; suits an objective style.
Should be used when the two clauses share the same topic or the same scope of comparison/contrast.
“その一方で” stands at the beginning of the sentence that follows to present the other side, avoiding repetition of the subject.
“一方” is not used for pure listing; there must be some contrast/difference.

• Presents two opposing or different sides/aspects of the same issue/subject: “on the one hand …, on the other hand …”.
• Contrasts two phenomena/groups: “while …, …”. They do not have to contradict each other completely; it just emphasizes the contrast.
• “その一方で” is used as a transition phrase in the following sentence, adding contrary information to balance the argument.
• Formal nuance; often used in journalism, reports and argumentative writing.
• Note the distinction from “一方だ” (one-way progression); “一方” here does NOT mean “more and more”.

rows: Formal; used within the same topic or for two related phenomena
<ruby>都心<rt>としん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby><ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>家賃<rt>やちん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
Stronger “flip side” nuance; usually the same subject
<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>な<ruby>反面<rt>はんめん</rt></ruby>、<ruby>騒音<rt>そうおん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>い。
Emphasizes the symmetry between two different targets
<ruby>兄<rt>あに</rt></ruby>に<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して、<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>無口<rt>むくち</rt></ruby>だ。
More and more, a one-way tendency
Not a contrast; only indicates the degree of increase/decrease
<ruby>物価<rt>ぶっか</rt></ruby>は<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がる<ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>だ。
しかし/その<ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>で
“その<ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>で” is formal and softer than “しかし”
… 。その<ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>で、<ruby>課題<rt>かだい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>残<rt>のこ</rt></ruby>る。

mistakes: Confusing it with “一方だ” when you want to say “more and more”. “一方” (contrast) does not express a tendency.
Dropping “で” after “一方” when connecting: both “一方、” and “一方で、” are correct; choose according to the context.
Using it when the two clauses have no topical connection → the sentence becomes disjointed and loses its logic.
Using it for cause and effect → wrong nuance; “一方” expresses contrast, not cause.
621.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ていく／～てくる.
→ ～一方だ expresses a change in only one direction.
2) Often has a negative meaning or describes something beyond one's control.
→ Example: 悪化する一方だ.
3) Not used for controlled positive changes.
→ For a development plan, another pattern is usually used.

examples.jp: レポートを一晩で書き上げた。
examples.tr: I finished writing the report in a single night.

examples.jp: 職人が何年もかけて作り上げた工芸品だ。

examples.tr: To launch a project.

examples.jp: 原価高騰で価格を引き上げる方針だ。
examples.tr: Due to soaring costs, the plan is to raise prices.

622.explain:
Attaches directly after the continuative form (Vます). Note how the meaning changes depending on the base verb: 書く→書き上げる (completion); 上げる carries the nuance of “up / all the way”.
Many compound words are fixed and need to be memorized as set phrases: 仕上げる／見上げる／立ち上げる／積み上げる。
Do not confuse it with ～てあげる (doing something for someone). ～上げる, written with the kanji “上げる”, indicates result/direction/increase.

- Meaning 1 (result/completion): Expresses doing something to the end, completing a process that produces a tangible product/result. Commonly seen: 仕上げる, 仕上がる (intransitive), 書き上げる, 作り上げる, 立ち上げる.
- Meaning 2 (direction/upward movement): Moving an object/the body upward: 持ち上げる, 立ち上げる（start up, set up）.
- Meaning 3 (raising/pushing up): Raising a level/value: 値段を引き上げる, スピードを上げる.
- Nuance: decisive, strong, sometimes implying effort to produce a result.

rows: Strong sense of direction: “up / all the way”
Neutral, only ending; no nuance of “raising up”
Doing something to the end, thoroughly
Emphasizes thoroughness/ending; a different range of meaning from “up”

mistakes: Confusing it with ～てあげる: 書いてあげる ≠ 書き上げる. The first means “write for (someone)”, the second means “finish writing”.
Mixing up intransitive and transitive verbs: 出来上がる（intransitive） vs 作り上げる（transitive）。
Choosing the wrong nuance compared with ～終える: the JLPT often sets a trap with “読み上げる” (read aloud) vs “読み終える” (finish reading).
622.notes:
• Many IT/business terms: 立ち上げ（launching a project/system）, 立ち上げる（launch）。
• “仕上げる/仕上がる” is a very common pair for “finishing”.
• In economics: 値上げ（price increase）, 引き上げ（raising a level）, 金利を引き上げる。

examples.jp: このカメラは軽い上に、操作も簡単だ。

examples.tr: The location is convenient, and on top of that, the rent is reasonable.

623.explain:
Used to emphasize the “accumulation” of characteristics; avoid using it for a direct cause-and-effect relationship.
Suited to formal language; in casual spoken language it can be replaced with “それに/しかも”.
Avoid combining two clauses pointing in opposite directions (good + bad).

• “Not only … but also …”: adds a characteristic/condition in the same direction (good → better, bad → worse).
• The two clauses must share the same direction of evaluation (both positive or both negative).
• More formal nuance than “それに/しかも/さらに”; used a lot in writing/reports/introductions.

rows: <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>丈夫<rt>じょうぶ</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いだけでなく<ruby>丈夫<rt>じょうぶ</rt></ruby>。
Adverb/conjunction form, at the beginning of a sentence
<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>うえに<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い。

mistakes: Combining opposite directions: “安い上に味が悪い” → contradictory nuance; use “が/けれど” instead.
Dropping “である” with N/na-adjectives in formal language → unnatural: “専門家上に” → incorrect.
Using it to state a direct cause → wrong function; “上に” adds information, it does not mean because/therefore.
623.notes:
• Written language often uses the pair: Aである上に、Bである。This creates a formal, consistent feel.
• In advertising/PR, “A上にB” makes the message more persuasive when both A and B are positive.
• When adding a third clause, use “その上/さらに” to avoid repeating “上に”.
explain: ◎ Means "Not only that".
examples: 1. さくらさんは頭がいいうえに、スポーツもできる。

meaning_vi: States one fact, then states another fact that heightens the positive or negative evaluation.
［ふつう］　+　うえ（に）
ひまな　N：お茶の］

meaning_vi: ～に加(くわ)えて、～だけでなく
Not only, in addition
examples: 1. 彼の妹は美人の上に性格も良い/成績優秀な上、スポーツもよくできる。

On top of that, the print is small, so it is hard for children to read. meaning_vi: Not only… moreover ⏐ explain: Adds something with the idea that it has the same tendency as the preceding fact (besides this good point there is another good point, or a bad point added to a bad thing).
In the second clause, sentences that act on the listener, such as commands, prohibitions, requests, invitations…, cannot be used. ⏐ examples: 1. 彼は仕事ができる上に優しい。
