624.explain:
Used in news, biographies and personal stories.
Often used with ずっと／一度も～ない to emphasize continuity/absoluteness.
The second clause is usually in the present or the present perfect in Japanese (～ている).

• Since … (until now). Emphasizes duration/continuation.
• The second clause describes an ongoing state or a change that has lasted until the present.
• Not used with direct commands/volition.

rows: Only indicates sequence; does not suggest continuity.
<ruby>昼寝<rt>ひるね</rt></ruby>してから、<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>した。
Can be used for the future; drier, more administrative.
<ruby>5月<rt>ごがつ</rt></ruby><ruby>1日<rt>ついたち</rt></ruby><ruby>以降<rt>いこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>有料<rt>ゆうりょう</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>帰国<rt>きこく</rt></ruby>して<ruby>以来<rt>いらい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>っていない。

mistakes: Mixing it up with 以降 in announcements about the future: X 来週以来 → it should be 来週以降.
The second clause expresses an instantaneous event that does not last: X 結婚して以来、昨日パーティーをした。
Wrong vague reference point (repeated action): X 彼に会う以来 → should be: 彼に会って以来.
624.notes:
• Besides people/things, the reference point can be a social event: コロナ禍以来.
• Not used with a repeated action as a vague reference point: X 彼に会う以来.
• The second clause is sometimes a one-time change but implies that it continues: 吸わなくなった（and it is still that way now）. meaning_vi: Since, ever since　～ ⏐ explain: Indicates something that has continued from a point in time in the past up to now, after a certain action.
The second clause does not use sentences expressing things that happen only once. ⏐ examples: 1. 日本に来て以来、母の料理を食べていない。
Since coming to Japan, I haven't eaten my mother's cooking.
2. 入学以来、一度も授業を休んでいない。
Since entering school, I haven't missed a single class.

626.name: ～向き（suitability）

examples.jp: 子ども向きのデザイン / 初心者向きのコース
examples.tr: A design suited to children / A course suited to beginners

examples.jp: 最近、職業に関しては、男性向きとか女性向きとか言えなくなってきた。
examples.tr: These days, when it comes to occupations, you can no longer say that a job is suited to men or suited to women.

examples.jp: 日本の伝統的な家屋は夏向きにできている。
examples.tr: Traditional Japanese houses are built to suit the summer.

examples.jp: このあたりは雨が少ないので、米作りには不向きだ。
examples.tr: This area gets little rain, so it is unsuitable for growing rice.

626.explain: Indicates suitability for a particular purpose or target.
626.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～向け (intended for).
→ ～向き means “suitable for a target/purpose”; it emphasizes suitability.
2) Often used to evaluate suitability.
→ Example: 初心者向き, 子ども向き.
3) It is not necessarily something made specifically for that target.
→ If it means “made to serve a target” (in terms of intended release), ～向け is usually used.

examples.jp: これは子供向けの番組です。
examples.tr: This is a program for children.

examples.jp: 初心者向けに、用語をやさしく説明しました。
examples.tr: I explained the terms simply for beginners.

examples.jp: この製品は法人向けです。
examples.tr: This product is for businesses.

examples.jp: 海外向けの仕様に変更する。
examples.tr: We will change it to the specifications for overseas markets.

examples.jp: 女性向け雑誌の広告を出した。
examples.tr: We placed an ad in a women's magazine.

examples.jp: この工場では主にアメリカ向けの車を造っている。
examples.tr: This factory mainly builds cars for the American market.

627.explain:
Used often in marketing, instruction manuals, and user segmentation.
Neutral/formal; can stand alone as a modifier:学生向け割引.
The target can be broad (海外向け) or narrow (上級者向け).

• Indicates that something is “aimed at” or “designed for” a specific group/target.
• Carries the nuance of the intention of the maker/creator: “directing a product/content toward …”.
• Different from ～向き (suitable): ～向け means “oriented toward, intended specifically for”; ～向き means “suitable in general”.

rows: Naturally suitable in character/strength, not necessarily designed for.
この<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>登山<rt>とざん</rt></ruby><ruby>向<rt>む</rt></ruby>きだ。
For use/ to be used for
States the specific intended use of an item; more physical.
<ruby>業務<rt>ぎょうむ</rt></ruby><ruby>用<rt>よう</rt></ruby><ruby>冷蔵庫<rt>れいぞうこ</rt></ruby>。
Intentionally directed at a group of people/ market.
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby><ruby>向<rt>む</rt></ruby>けの<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>。
A verb of direction of movement, completely different from the nominalization function of ～<ruby>向<rt>む</rt></ruby>け.

mistakes: Confusing it with ～向き: both 子供向き and 子供向け are possible, but 向け emphasizes “aimed at/designed for”.
Confusing it with ～行き: X 東京向けの電車 → it should be 東京行きの電車.
Using 向け for an immediate personal action: X 私向けに席を取って → sounds odd; better: 私のために席を取って.
627.notes:
1) ～向け and ～向き are easily confused.
→ ～向け means “for/aimed at a target”, usually products, information, or services directed at N.
2) There are 2 usages in the data (ghichu=1 and ghichu=2).
→ The meaning “for” differs from “working toward a goal” (～に向けて).
3) Look at what comes after this phrase.
→ If it is “a product/material for someone”: ～向け.
→ If it is “an action toward a goal”: ～に向けて.
explain: ◎ A way of saying what kind of person something is suitable for.
examples: 1. これは女性向けの雑誌です。
This is a magazine for women.
2. このホテルは、旅行者向けのサイトで見つけました。
I found this hotel on a website for travelers.

628.meaning: In the middle of, right while

examples.jp: 会議の最中に電話が鳴った。
examples.tr: The phone rang in the middle of the meeting.

examples.jp: 試験を受けている最中に、停電になった。
examples.tr: The power went out while I was taking the exam.

examples.jp: 食事している最中に席を立たないでください。
examples.tr: Please don't leave your seat in the middle of the meal.

examples.jp: プレゼンの最中に、資料が見つからなくなった。
examples.tr: In the middle of the presentation, I couldn't find the materials.

examples.jp: 工事の最中に雨が降り始めた。
examples.tr: It started raining in the middle of the construction work.

628.explain:
Used in both spoken and written language; slightly more formal than ～間に.
The first clause sets a point in time when something is “in progress”; the second clause is usually an interrupting event.
Unnatural with stative verbs such as知っている・分かっている; actions/activities are preferred.
Often used with activity nouns:会議・授業・試合・手術・面接・作業.

• “Right while… was going on, … (usually an interruption/something unwanted)”
• Emphasizes the peak moment of an action/activity, stronger than ～間に.
• Usually used with short/limited actions (会議・試験・食事), rarely with static, lasting states.
• The second clause is often a mishap, an obstacle, or an unexpected announcement; but it can also be a neutral event.

rows: Midpoint, peak; strong sense of interruption
<ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>最中<rt>さいちゅう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>
Does not focus on the exact midpoint
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みの<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>
Just as about to/in the middle of/just after
Fine-tunes the point in time; neutral nuance
<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけるところに<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>
Focus on the process, not necessarily the peak
<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>る<ruby>途中<rt>とちゅう</rt></ruby>で<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Forgetting “の” with nouns: incorrect “会議最中に” → correct “会議の最中に”.
Using the dictionary form of V: incorrect “食事する最中に” → correct “食事している最中に”.
Applying it to a static state (知っている最中に) is unnatural.
Confusing it with ～間に: exam questions often test the nuance “right at the moment” vs “during the period”.
628.notes:
• The form “最中だ/です” is often used to set the scene: 会議の最中です。
• In polite language: ～最中にございます is rarely used, so keep ～最中に/～最中です.
• To emphasize what should not be done: ～最中に…しないでください／～最中はご遠慮ください。
meaning_vi: While doing that, right at that moment... (Expresses that something unexpected happens.)
examples: 1. ①　シャワーを浴びている最中に
While I was taking a shower...
2. ②　シャワーを浴びている最中に、客が来た。
A guest came while I was taking a shower.
3. ③　引っ越しの最中に雨が降り出した。
It started raining while we were moving. | Sentence-final form: ～最中だ

examples.jp: 最近、仕事が忙し気味で、睡眠不足だ。
examples.tr: Lately work has been a bit busy, and I'm short on sleep.

examples.jp: 雨で試合の開始が遅れ気味だ。
examples.tr: Because of the rain, the start of the game is running a little late.

examples.jp: 会議のとき、彼はいつも緊張気味だ。
examples.tr: He always seems a bit nervous during meetings.

examples.jp: 風邪気味なので、今日は早めに帰ります。
examples.tr: I think I'm coming down with a cold, so I'll go home early today.

examples.jp: 食べ過ぎで太り気味になってきた。
examples.tr: I've been eating too much, and I've started to put on a little weight.

examples.jp: 疲れ気味だ
examples.tr: I'm feeling a bit tired.

629.explain:
Formation: N/ Vます-stem directly +気味; does not attach to i-adjectives or な-adjectives.
Degree: “a little/rather”, not heavy; for a strong degree use ～気がする, ～っぽい, ～過ぎ, ～ぎみでもない.
Context: neutral to polite; can be used at work when describing a situation.
Often used with words that have a somewhat negative tone:疲れ,太り,不足,下降,遅れ; positive ones are less common (上向き気味exists but is rare).

• “A bit, a feeling of”: expresses a mild degree, not yet clear but tending to appear.
• Range of meaning: often used for physical condition (疲れ気味, 太り気味), mental state (緊張気味, 焦り気味), situations (遅れ気味, 下降気味).
• Highly objective: spoken as an observation of oneself/others without strong judgment.
• Different from っぽい: 気味 emphasizes “a slight current tendency”, っぽい emphasizes “resembling/leaning toward a quality, sometimes subjective, colloquial”.

rows: Colloquial, subjective, wide range of combinations
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>っぽい／ミスしがちっぽい(×)
Stronger than <ruby>気味<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>, with a negative nuance
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れがち／<ruby>病気<rt>びょうき</rt></ruby>がち
Emphasizes a subjective feeling, full clause
<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れている<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がする

mistakes: Wrong word class: × 寒い気味 → Correct: 寒気味 is unnatural; use 寒気がする／寒がりだ.
Wrong degree: 気味 only means “a bit”; to say strongly “very tired”, use すごく疲れている, 疲れすぎだ, ぐったりだ.
Confusing it with ～がち: 遅れ気味 (a bit late) ≠ 遅れがち (often late).
JLPT: trick questions ask you to choose between 気味/っぽい/がち based on the nuance “slight – frequent – resembling”.
629.notes:
• Written forms: 忙し気味／忙しぎみ are both seen; the hiragana form ぎみ is common in learning materials.
• With fixed Sino-Japanese words: 目つきが悪い vs 目つき気味(rare) → prefer familiar state nouns.
• In spoken language, it can be used with adverbs for slight exaggeration: ちょっと疲れ気味, 少し太り気味. meaning_vi: Seems, a bit, a feeling that ⏐ explain: Expresses the meaning “to be in such a state, to have such a tendency”. Often used for things with a bad meaning. ⏐ examples: 1. 残業続きで、疲れ気味だ。
I've been working overtime nonstop, so I'm a bit tired.
2. 新入社員は緊張気味の顔をしていた。
The new employee looked a bit nervous.

630.meaning: To be scheduled, to be decided ～

examples.jp: 明日、ここで卒業式が行われることになっている。
examples.tr: The graduation ceremony is scheduled to be held here tomorrow.

examples.jp: ６０点以上が合格ということになっている。
examples.tr: The rule is that 60 points or more is a pass.

examples.jp: 明日、新しい企画についての会議が行われることになっている。
examples.tr: A meeting about the new project is scheduled to be held tomorrow.

examples.jp: 今度、大阪に転勤することになりました。
examples.tr: It has been decided that I will be transferred to Osaka.

630.explain: Used to emphasize that the matter was not decided by the subject themselves but was determined, set, or ordered by other people or other factors

examples.jp: 窓を開けたとたん、強い風が入ってきた。
examples.tr: The moment I opened the window, a strong wind blew in.

examples.jp: お酒を飲んだとたん、顔が赤くなった。
examples.tr: As soon as I drank the alcohol, my face turned red.

631.explain:
Used when something happens right when an action has just been done.
The second clause does not use sentence patterns with an active meaning (transitive verbs), the causative form, or obligation

examples.jp: ご登録の際に、身分証明書をご提示ください。
examples.tr: When registering, please present your ID.

examples.jp: 来社の際は、受付でお名前をお伝えください。
examples.tr: When you visit our office, please give your name at the reception desk.

examples.jp: 日本へ入国する際に、この書類が必要です。
examples.tr: This document is required when entering Japan.

examples.jp: ご利用の際には、必ずパスワードを変更してください。
examples.tr: When using it, please be sure to change your password.

examples.jp: 災害発生の際、エレベーターの使用はお控えください。
examples.tr: In the event of a disaster, please refrain from using the elevators.

632.explain:
“際（に）” takes “は/には” to mark the topic: ～際には (more emphatic than ～際に).
Usually placed in the first clause; the second clause is an instruction, rule, or polite request.
Common nouns: ご利用／ご来場／ご来店／ご乗車／入学／登録／申請／購入／訪問。
Not used for very everyday, momentary feelings; use とき in casual situations.

• Expresses the point in time when an action/event occurs, equivalent to “when/at the time”, but formal; used a lot in instructions, signs, and company emails.
• Often used with expressions of request, caution, or prohibition: ご注意ください／ご連絡ください／持参してください／ご遠慮ください。
• Not used for daily habits or casual conversation; use とき instead.

rows: <ruby>上京<rt>じょうきょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>折<rt>おり</rt></ruby>に～
<ruby>紛失<rt>ふんしつ</rt></ruby>した<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>は～

mistakes: Using it in casual conversation sounds stiff: × 映画を見る際にポップコーン買う？ → とき is more natural.
Forgetting “には” when emphasis is needed: ご利用の際には is better than ご利用の際 when you want to be polite/emphatic.
Confusing it with 場合: for “in case of trouble”, use 場合, not 際.
JLPT: ～折に (very polite) and ～際に are easily confused; pay attention to the context of letters/cards.
632.notes:
• “際” is read さい; do not confuse it with きわ (meaning “edge”). In this grammar point it is read only さい.
• “際は/際には” often appear on forms/signs; adding には makes it more emphatic and formal.
• Common 敬語 pairs: ごV-ます＋の際（に）／V-辞＋際（に）＋お/ご～ください。
• Variant: ～際（に）は

633.meaning:
～の可能性もある
There is also a possibility that…, it's not that one can't…

examples.jp: 食べないことはないが、あまり好きじゃない。
examples.tr: It's not that I don't eat it, but I don't like it very much.

examples.jp: お酒やタバコをやめるのは難しいが、やめられないことはない。
examples.tr: Quitting drinking and smoking is hard, but it's not impossible.

examples.jp: 鶏肉は、食べないことはないですが、あまり好きではありません。
examples.tr: It's not that I don't eat chicken, but I don't like it very much.

examples.jp: 「走れば間に合わないことはないよ。急ごう！」
examples.tr: "If we run, we can still make it. Let's hurry!"

633.explain: Used when you want to say that you are not denying the matter or thing itself, but want to express a reason/ a lower degree compared with a negative

examples.jp: 少しも痛くないから、心配しないで。
examples.tr: It doesn't hurt at all, so don't worry.

examples.jp: 彼の説明は少しも難しくない。
examples.tr: His explanation isn't difficult at all.

examples.jp: この映画は少しも面白くなかった。
examples.tr: This movie wasn't interesting at all.

examples.jp: 疲れているのに、彼は少しも休もうとしない。
examples.tr: Even though he's tired, he won't rest at all.

examples.jp: 彼女は私のことを少しも疑っていないようだ。
examples.tr: She doesn't seem to suspect me at all.

634.explain:
Place 少しも/すこしも before the negated word to emphasize “not even a little”.
Suitable for both written and spoken language; ちっとも〜ない leans toward spoken language and casual speech.
Can be used with the past, potential, and volition:少しもできなかった／少しも行く気がしない.

• “Not … at all/not … one bit”. Emphasizes a degree of zero.
• Used to completely negate a feeling/state/action.
• Compared with 全然〜ない/まったく〜ない: milder than まったく, equal to or milder than 全然 depending on the context.
• Spelling: both 少しも and すこしも are correct; 少しも is common in written language.

rows: Casual, sometimes with a complaining nuance
ちっとも<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>くならない
Strong, common; in modern usage can be used with the affirmative (colloquial)
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない
まったく<ruby>興味<rt>きょうみ</rt></ruby>がない

mistakes: Using it with an affirmative: 少しも must be followed by a negative. 誤）少しも大丈夫 → 正）少しも大丈夫ではない。
Wrong degree: まったく＞全然≧少しも＞ちっとも（relative; depends on the context).
Spelling mistake: すくしも× → すこしも／少しも〇.
Wrong position: it must come before the negated element to have full effect.
634.notes:
• An emphatic word can be inserted between: 少しも全く覚えていない（written language, double emphasis）.
• In polite communication, avoid overusing it toward the listener so as not to sound extreme.
• Rhetorical interrogative form: 少しも悪くない？（Not bad at all, right?）

examples.jp: 天気が悪いです。ですから、今日は出かけません。
examples.tr: The weather is bad. So I'm not going out today.

examples.jp: 私は新人ですから、まだ分からないことが多いです。
examples.tr: I'm new, so there's still a lot I don't know.

examples.jp: 試験は明日ですから、早く寝てください。
examples.tr: The exam is tomorrow, so please go to bed early.

examples.jp: こちらは危険区域です。ですから、立ち入らないでください。
examples.tr: This is a danger zone. Therefore, please do not enter.

examples.jp: 彼は担当者ですから、直接相談したほうがいいですよ。
examples.tr: He's the person in charge, so you should talk to him directly.

examples.jp: 需要が増えています。ですから、増産します。
examples.tr: Demand is increasing. Therefore, we will increase production.

635.explain:
Used when presenting logic, in presentations, and in business emails: “A (information). ですから、B (conclusion/recommendation)”.
In conversation, ですから can begin a response: “ ですから、先ほど申し上げたとおり…”.
Compared with だから: more polite, less direct; suits formal settings.
Not used to express strong emotion; when you need to emphasize firm reasoning, use したがって.
Within a sentence, “Aですから、B” is usually used when A is a noun/na-adj; with verbs/い-adj use ～から/～ので: 「雨が降る から、…」.

• Main meaning: States a conclusion/result based on the information/condition just mentioned: “therefore/so/thus”.
• Politeness: More polite than だから; often used in presentations, news, and refined written language.
• Position: Usually at the start of the result clause, separate from the reason clause (the previous sentence).
• Two usages to distinguish:

Independent conjunction: 「A。ですから、B。」
Linking within a sentence: 「Aですから、B。」 (A is a noun/na-adj + です)

• Independent conjunction: 「A。ですから、B。」
• Linking within a sentence: 「Aですから、B。」 (A is a noun/na-adj + です)
• Nuance: Objective, polite reasoning; avoids strong/overly personal emotion.

rows: Polite; used as a conjunction or as “Aですから、B”.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>です。ですから、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>です。
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れる。だから<ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>って。
Continuative link; more about connected events than logical reason.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。それで、<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>にいた。
<ruby>需要<rt>じゅよう</rt></ruby><ruby>増<rt>ぞう</rt></ruby>。したがって、<ruby>価格<rt>かかく</rt></ruby><ruby>上昇<rt>じょうしょう</rt></ruby>。
Links within a sentence to state a direct reason.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なので<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>します。

mistakes: Using ですから in a casual context among friends → sounds distant; use だから/それで instead.
Confusing “Aです。ですから、B。” with “Aだから、B。” When A is a noun/na-adj, both are possible, but the nuance differs.
Using ですから to state a strongly subjective reason (anger) → not appropriate; use だって/だもん, which carry emotion.
JLPT: a trap distinguishing それで vs ですから (both translated as “so”): それで leans toward a sequence of events; ですから emphasizes a logical conclusion.
635.notes:
• To soften a request: 「危険ですから、こちらへお願いします。」 sounds more polite than 「危ないから…」.
• In a debate, starting a sentence with ですから to lead to the conclusion makes it coherent and avoids an abrupt “change of direction”.
• Instead of repeating ですから in a row, alternate with それで/したがって to make the text natural. explain: Used for a sentence that is the result or consequence of the previous sentence. The preceding sentence usually states a reason, a judgment, or a natural result ⏐ examples: 1. 「天気予報では午後から雨だそうです。ですから、傘を持っていったほうがいいですよ。」
According to the weather forecast, it will rain from the afternoon. So you should take an umbrella.
2. 明日から旅行に行きます。ですから、申し訳ありませんが、来週のパーテイーには出席できません。
I'm going on a trip from tomorrow. So, I'm sorry, but I can't attend the party next week

examples.jp: どんなに疲れていても、約束は守る。
examples.tr: No matter how tired I am, I keep my promises.

examples.jp: どんなに練習しても、なかなか上達しない。
examples.tr: No matter how much I practice, I just don't improve.

examples.jp: どんなに忙しくても、家族との時間は大切だ。
examples.tr: No matter how busy you are, time with your family is important.

examples.jp: どんなに高くても買うつもりだ。
examples.tr: No matter how expensive it is, I intend to buy it.

examples.jp: どんなに説明しても伝わらないことがある。
examples.tr: No matter how much you explain, sometimes it doesn't get across.

examples.jp: どんなに不安でも、挑戦してみたい。
examples.tr: No matter how anxious I am, I want to give it a try.

636.explain:
For emphasis, いくら／どれほど can be used instead of どんなに (similar nuance).
The second clause is usually a clause stating a firm position/volition or a general judgment.
Suitable for both spoken and written language; carries the nuance of “regardless of any degree”.

• Extreme concession: “no matter to what degree… (the result/view does not change)”.
• Emphasis with どんなに: covers every degree, every way.
• The second clause usually expresses an unchanging result/volition/evaluation, or has a nuance of being constant and hard to change.

rows: どんなに<ruby>遅<rt>おそ</rt></ruby>くても<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く
いくら<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っても<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ない
A strong marker of supposition, more formal
たとえ<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>諦<rt>あきら</rt></ruby>めない
Not a supposition; states a contradiction
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>したのに<ruby>伝<rt>つた</rt></ruby>わらない
Different function: exclamation, not a condition
どんなに<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しかったことか

mistakes: Confusing it with ～ことか: one is a condition, the other an exclamation.
Wrong form: Aい→Aくても; Aな→Aでも; N→Nでも; V→Vてでも? (a different pattern, do not confuse).
Dropping も: “ても/でも” is required; without “も” the structure is incorrect.
636.notes:
• It can be repeated: どんなにどんなに… but repetition is usually avoided so it doesn't sound heavy.
• A negative second clause is not required; both affirmative and negative are common depending on the content.
• Combine with potential verbs to emphasize “regardless of effort”: どんなに頑張ってもできない。

637.meaning: Spoken-language form of the structure 「なければならない／なくてはいけない」
637.connection: Vなければならない → Vなきゃ・Vなく(っ)ちゃ / Vないと（spoken language）

examples.jp: 買わなきゃ
examples.tr: I have to buy it.

examples.jp: あしたまでにレポートを書かなきゃ。
examples.tr: I have to write my report by tomorrow.

examples.jp: あ、もう８時だ。そろそろ出かけなく（っ）ちゃ。
examples.tr: Oh, it's already eight. I'd better get going soon.

examples.jp: あしたから新しい教科書を使うから、今日買わないと。
examples.tr: We're using the new textbook from tomorrow, so I have to buy it today.

examples.jp: 私は彼の話がまったく分からない。
examples.tr: I don't understand what he's saying at all.

examples.jp: この問題はまったく難しくない。
examples.tr: This problem isn't difficult at all.

examples.jp: 彼女は約束をまったく守らない。
examples.tr: She never keeps her promises.

examples.jp: 昨日のことはまったく覚えていない。
examples.tr: I don't remember anything about yesterday.

examples.jp: そんなこと、まったく興味がない。
examples.tr: I have absolutely no interest in that kind of thing.

638.explain:
まったく usually comes before the negative part to emphasize the idea “not even a little”.
Can be used at many language levels, from casual speech to written language.
If it is not used with ～ない but with a positive adjective (まったく素晴らしい), the meaning changes to “really…”, “truly…”.
In conversation, when used alone, “まったく！” → expresses a complaint: “I can't stand it!”, “Honestly!”.

•
まったく～ない is used to emphasize a degree of absolute negation: “not … at all”, “never …”, “not even a little …”.

• Usually used with negative verbs, adjectives, or nouns: ～ない・～くない・～ではない.
• Has a strong nuance, sometimes expressing surprise, complaint, or disappointment.

rows: まったく<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない。
More colloquial, used a lot in daily life.
ぜんぜん<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない。
Used to emphasize “not even a little”.
<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しも<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わっていない。
<ruby>全<rt>まった</rt></ruby>く～ない（<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>）
Kanji form of まったく
Used in written language and newspapers.
<ruby>全<rt>まった</rt></ruby>く<ruby>興味<rt>きょうみ</rt></ruby>がない。

mistakes: Confusing it with ぜんぜん → まったく feels stronger, not even a little.
Using まったく with a non-negative word → the meaning changes to “really…” and is no longer negative.
The JLPT often tests the nuance: まったく～ない vs 全然～ない.
638.notes:
• In written language, the kanji 全く can be used instead of まったく.
• With the positive meaning (まったく～だ), you need to distinguish it clearly when translating to avoid misunderstanding.
• Example: まったく君は… → “Honestly, you… (slightly reproachful)”. explain: Used to assert that something does not exist at all or cannot happen at all. ⏐ examples: 1. 私はまったく泳げない。
I can't swim at all
2. 彼が怒っている理由は、私にはまったくわからない。
I have no idea at all why he is angry
3. 前とは違うまったく新しい計画を立てた。
We made a completely new plan, different from before

examples.jp: ここから見る夜景はまるで夢のようだ。
examples.tr: The night view from here is just like a dream.

examples.jp: 彼はまるで子どものように喜んだ。
examples.tr: He was as happy as a child.

examples.jp: 雲がまるで綿みたいだ。
examples.tr: The clouds look just like cotton.

examples.jp: 彼はまるで何もなかったかのように話し続けた。
examples.tr: He kept talking as if nothing had happened.

examples.jp: 専門用語でまるで分からない。
examples.tr: It's all technical terms, so I don't understand it at all.

639.explain:
Emphasizes a vivid, emotional comparison; suited to descriptive writing.
With ～かのようだ: a nuance of "as if", avoiding a claim about reality.
With ～ない: means "not at all", close to まったく/ぜんぜん, but まるで feels more strongly emphatic in written language.
ようだ vs みたいだ: ようだ is formal/written; みたいだ is casual/spoken.

まるで emphasizes a degree of resemblance or strangeness to the point of "just like, exactly like". With ようだ/みたいだ it forms a figurative comparison; with ～ない it means "not at all". かのようだ adds a hypothetical nuance and is written language.
• まるで + N のようだ: describes the whole as "exactly like N".
• まるで + ように/ような: modifies manner/quality.
• まるで + みたい: colloquial, casual, very frequent in conversation.

rows: まるで<ruby>別世界<rt>べっせかい</rt></ruby>のようだ
まったく<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>できない
<ruby>夢<rt>ゆめ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ているかのようだ

mistakes: Using まるで in the affirmative without ようだ/みたいだ: ×まるで綺麗 → 〇まるで綺麗な絵のようだ.
Confusing まるで～ない with まったく～ない: both mean "not at all", but まるで often goes with できない/分からない in emphatic writing.
Confusing formality: みたいだ is colloquial and unsuitable for academic writing; use ようだ/かのようだ.
639.notes:
• The negative structure "まるで～ない" is often used when feeling "helpless / not understanding / having nothing", with a stronger nuance than ぜんぜん in written language.
• For concrete images, まるで + N みたい is the natural choice in everyday conversation.
• Avoid overusing it in formal writing: choose ようだ/かのようだ for balance.

641.connection: もしも + N/Naなら / もしも + V/A plain form + (の)なら

examples.jp: もしも明日雨なら、遠足は中止にします。
examples.tr: If it rains tomorrow, the field trip will be canceled.

examples.jp: もしも時間があるなら、この資料を読んでください。
examples.tr: If you have time, please read this document.

examples.jp: もしも彼が来ないなら、私が行きます。
examples.tr: If he doesn't come, I'll go.

examples.jp: もしも私が鳥なら、空を自由に飛びたい。
examples.tr: If I were a bird, I would want to fly freely in the sky.

examples.jp: もしも間に合わないなら、先に始めてください。
examples.tr: If you can't make it in time, please start first.

examples.jp: もしも危険なら、その計画はやめよう。
examples.tr: If it's dangerous, let's give up that plan.

641.explain:
Used to emphasize "supposing" or "in the worst case".
Suited to warnings, safety instructions and contingency plans: もしも火事 なら、非常口へ。
Creates a polite/gentle feel when asking: もしもご都合が悪い なら、日程を変えます。
Combines flexibly with ～たら／～場合は to express a specific point in time or situation.

• "もしも～なら": If by chance / supposing / if ... then ...; emphasizes supposition, usually an unlikely situation or a contingency scenario.
• More formal in nuance than "もし～なら", with a feel of "if something should happen" or "a strong hypothesis".
• Often used to set a condition before giving advice, an option, or a counter-question.
• Compared with ～たら: なら focuses on a condition that has been stated/is known, while たら suggests the time when the condition actually occurs.

rows: More neutral; "もしも" is more emphatic.
もし<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して。
Tied to the time something actually happens.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったら<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>非常時<rt>ひじょうじ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>階段<rt>かいだん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>う。
Not compatible with volition; leans toward general rules.
<ruby>春<rt>はる</rt></ruby>になると<ruby>暖<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かくなる。
Concession; the result does not change.

mistakes: Confusing "なら" with the time relation of "たら": contingency plans use なら/場合は; events in actual sequence use たら.
Forgetting that "もしも" only adds emphasis and does not change the verb/adjective conjugation: still use 普通形 + なら.
Using "と" with volition/commands is wrong: もしも地震が起こると、逃げてください（wrong） → 起こったら／起こるなら（correct in context).
641.notes:
• "もしも" often appears in guide titles: もしもの時に備える (preparing for emergencies).
• "なら" suits conditions given by or known to the listener; easy to use in interactive conversation.
• In emotional writing, "もしも～なら" opens up imagination: もしも生まれ変われるなら… | Variants: もしも～たら・もしもの場合

examples.jp: もし彼が来ていたなら、直接話せたのに。
examples.tr: If he had come, I could have talked to him directly.

examples.jp: もしあの時もっと勉強していたなら、合格できたかもしれない。
examples.tr: If I had studied harder back then, I might have passed.

examples.jp: もし早く出発していたなら、渋滞に巻き込まれなかっただろう。
examples.tr: If we had left earlier, we probably wouldn't have gotten caught in traffic.

examples.jp: もし君が本当のことを言っていたなら、誤解は起きなかった。
examples.tr: If you had told the truth, there would have been no misunderstanding.

examples.jp: もし彼女が医者だったなら、助けられたのに。
examples.tr: If she had been a doctor, she could have saved them.

examples.jp: もし注意して見ていたなら、ミスに気づけたのに。
examples.tr: If I had been watching carefully, I could have noticed the mistake.

642.explain:
Emphasizes the counterfactual nature of the condition; suited to expressing regret / "if only".
The second clause often comes with のに／だろう／よかった to express emotion and inference.
Spoken language often simplifies it to もし～たら; use ～たなら when you want to emphasize "the condition did not happen".
Avoid using it for real conditions in the present/future (use もし～たら／～なら／～ば instead).

• Counterfactual supposition about the past: "If ... had ... (but in reality it didn't), then ...".
• Often expresses regret or infers a result that could have happened.
• The second clause often uses のに／だろう／よかった（のに）／と思う／かもしれない to show the hypothetical consequence.
• Unlike もし～たら (neutral), ～たなら emphasizes that "the condition did not happen".

rows: もし<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったなら<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>えたのに
もし<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったら<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して
More formal; hard to use for past counterfactuals
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>れば<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>ったのに
Making a supposition based on information
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だ
もっと<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>すればよかった

mistakes: Using it for the future: × もし明日雨が降ったなら、行かない → use もし明日雨が降ったら/降れば.
Not using the past in the conditional clause: × もし行くなら会えたのに → ✓ もし行ったなら会えたのに.
Confusing it with ～ばよかった: ～たなら needs two clauses; ～ばよかった expresses regret on its own.
JLPT: pay attention to the counterfactual nuance and the endings のに／だろう／よかった to choose the correct answer.
642.notes:
• Inversion can be used to emphasize the result first: 会えたのに、もし彼が来ていたなら。 (written language).
• ～ていたなら emphasizes a state continuing at a past point in time: 雨がやんでいたなら…
• "もしも" strengthens the hypothetical/remote nuance, often used in warnings/scenarios: もしも地震が起きていたなら… explain: Used to put forward a hypothesis about something that is not real and the consequence of that unreal thing ⏐ examples: 1. もし試験を受けていたなら、合格していたと思う。
If I had taken the exam, I think I would have passed
2. もし彼が社長でなかったなら、会社はつぶれていたと思う。
If he hadn't been the president, I think the company would have gone under
3. もし、留学しなかったなら、今ごろは国で結婚しているだろう。
If I hadn't studied abroad, I would probably be married in my home country by now

645.connection: 必ずしも + V/A plain form + とは限らない

examples.jp: 高いからといって、必ずしも品質が良いとは限らない。
examples.tr: Just because something is expensive doesn't necessarily mean it's good quality.

examples.jp: 留学すれば、必ずしも日本語が上手になるとは限らない。
examples.tr: Studying abroad doesn't necessarily mean your Japanese will improve.

examples.jp: 噂は必ずしも真実だとは限らない。
examples.tr: Rumors aren't necessarily true.

examples.jp: 仕事が早い人が、必ずしもミスが少ないとは限らない。
examples.tr: People who work fast don't necessarily make fewer mistakes.

examples.jp: データが多いほど良いとは限らないのは、必ずしも量より質が大切だからだ。
examples.tr: The reason more data isn't always better is that quality matters more than quantity.

645.explain:
A cautious, counterargument nuance; neutral to slightly formal, usable in reports and discussions.
Often appears with: ～からといって,一般的に…が、必ずしも…,見た目は…が、必ずしも…
Not used for a definitive 100% negation; implies "it depends on the case".
Position: usually in the middle of the sentence; putting 必ずしも…とは限らない at the beginning of a sentence is also natural in writing.

• "Not necessarily / not always ...": negates a general statement.
• Emphasizes the existence of exceptions or that the degree is not absolute. 必ずしも strengthens the meaning "not absolute".
• Usually follows a general judgment, preconception or conjecture in order to argue against it.
• Logically it is a "negation of necessity", not total negation (it does not say it is completely wrong).

rows: <ruby>必<rt>かなら</rt></ruby>ずしも ～ とは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない
Objective; argues against a general rule
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い＝<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない
<ruby>必<rt>かなら</rt></ruby>ずしも ～ わけではない
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからといって<ruby>暇<rt>ひま</rt></ruby>がないわけではない
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>したとは<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>らないとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない

mistakes: Confusing it with "not at all": 必ずしもAではない ≠ 全くAではない.
Dropping 必ずしも: using ～とは限らない on its own is still correct, but exam questions often require it together for emphasis.
Confusing the direction of meaning with ～ないとは限らない (reversed meaning). Read the position of ない carefully.
Polite form: とは限りません, not とは限られません.
645.notes:
• In casual speech it can be slightly shortened into a contracted form: とは限らない → とは限んない (colloquial).
• Avoid using it with commands/requests; this is a pattern of evaluation, not a request for action.
• Scope negation: 必ずしもAではない differs from "Aは全くない"; do not translate it as "not at all". meaning_vi: Not certain that / not necessarily / not limited to ⏐ explain: Usually used to negate a proposition, saying that a situation does not apply to everything, not to all cases ⏐ examples: 1. （お）金持ちが必ずしも幸福だとは限らない。
Being rich doesn't necessarily mean being happy
2. 高いものが必ずいいものだとは限らない。
Expensive things aren't necessarily good things

examples.jp: 決して諦めません。
examples.tr: I will never give up.

examples.jp: これは決してあなたのせいではありません。
examples.tr: This is by no means your fault.

examples.jp: 秘密は決して誰にも言わないでください。
examples.tr: Please never tell anyone the secret.

examples.jp: 日本の物価は決して安くはない。
examples.tr: Prices in Japan are by no means cheap.

examples.jp: 私は彼を決して疑っているわけではないが、確認は必要だ。
examples.tr: It's not that I doubt him at all, but it still needs to be confirmed.

646.explain:
Used for prohibition, warnings and strong commitments: signs, rules, promises.
"は" in安く は ない creates a contrastive nuance and emphasizes the negative.
Suited to formal written language; in everyday conversation it can sound somewhat harsh.

• "Absolutely not / by no means / never ...".
• Emphasizes will, rules or strong evaluation; a stiff, decisive nuance.
• Can express an oath/promise: 決して忘れない (I will never forget).
• Unlike "not necessarily": 決して expresses strong negation, not partial negation.

rows: <ruby>絶対<rt>ぜったい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない
まったく／<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby>～ない
Focuses on a degree of zero
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない
<ruby>必<rt>かなら</rt></ruby>ずしも<ruby>正<rt>ただ</rt></ruby>しくない

mistakes: Forgetting the negative after 決して: wrong "決して行く" → correct "決して行かない/行きません".
Confusing it with 必ず (definitely): 決して = absolutely not, 必ず = definitely (affirmative).
Overusing it in casual conversation makes the sentence sound harsh.
Distinguish its degree from 全然/絶対に: exam questions often ask about nuance.
646.notes:
• Natural combinations: 決して～してはいけない／忘れてはならない／油断してはならない.
• In strong statements, it often comes at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis: 決して～ない。
• Avoid using it with vague judgments; 決して requires a clear position. meaning_vi: Absolutely not, definitely not, never ⏐ explain: Used to show determination not to do something ⏐ examples: 1. 私は決して夢をあきらめません。
I will never give up on my dream
2. 「うそは決して申しません。」と彼は言った。
He said, "I will never tell a lie"

647.name: Question word～（の）か／～かどうか
647.connection: Question word + V/A plain form + (の)か / [sentence/clause] + かどうか

examples.jp: 何を買うかわからない
examples.tr: I don't know what to buy.

examples.jp: 鈴木さんが明日のパーティーに来るかどうか知りません。
examples.tr: I don't know whether Mr. Suzuki is coming to the party tomorrow.

examples.jp:
「試験はどこで申し込むのか知っていますか」
「いいえ、知(し)りません」
examples.tr:
"Do you know where to apply for the exam?"
"No, I don't."

examples.jp:
「どうすれば漢字をたくさん覚えられるのか教えてください。」
「毎日(まいにち)練習(れんしゅう)すれば、覚(おぼ)えられますよ」
examples.tr:
"Please tell me how I can memorize a lot of kanji."
"If you practice every day, you'll be able to memorize them."

648.name: Contracted form（～ている／～でいる）
648.meaning:
Contracted form: ～ている → てる／～でいる → でる
Contracted form: ～ておく → とく／～でおく → どく
Contracted form: ～なければ → なきゃ
Contracted form: ～なくては/～なければ → なくちゃ/なきゃ
648.connection: Vている → Vてる / Vでいる → Vでる（spoken contraction）

examples.jp: 「あそこに座ってる人、だれ？」
examples.tr: "Who's that person sitting over there?"

examples.jp: 「すぐ行くから、先に行ってて」
examples.tr: "I'll be right there, so go on ahead."

examples.jp: 「どうしたの。泣いてちゃわからないよ。理由を言ってくれなくちゃ。」
examples.tr: "What's wrong? If you just cry, I won't understand. You have to tell me why."

examples.jp: 「来週までにこの本、読んどいてください」
examples.tr: "Please read this book by next week."

examples.jp: 「これ、どこに片付けるんですか」「机のうえに置いといていいよ」
examples.tr: "Where should I put this away?" "You can just leave it on the desk."

examples.jp: 「大切なことはメモしといてください」
examples.tr: "Please make a note of the important things."

648.explain:
Casual contracted form of ～ている／～でいる, commonly used in everyday conversation.
Casual contracted form of ～ておく／～でおく, still keeping the meaning of doing something in advance or preparing.
Casual contracted form of ～なければ, often used in conversation.
Casual contracted form of the obligation patterns "must…", used a lot in spoken language.
648.notes:
1) It is easy to confuse the contracted form with the standard form in written language.
→ てる／でる is colloquial, mainly used in conversation.
2) On the JLPT, pay attention to spoken-language contexts.
→ Choose the contracted form only if the sentence has a casual, quick, conversational nuance.
3) Not used in formal documents, announcements or essays.
→ Written language usually uses ～ている／～でいる.

649.name: Expressions using intransitive verbs
649.connection: Nが/は + V intransitive verb（describing property・function: 入る・開く）

examples.jp: このかばんは軽くてたくさん入るので、旅行に便利だ。
examples.tr: This bag is light and holds a lot, so it's convenient for traveling.

examples.jp: このマンガはよく売れている。人気があるのだろう。
examples.tr: This manga is selling well. It must be popular.

examples.jp: 「壊れやすいものですから、気をつけて運んでください」
examples.tr: "It's fragile, so please carry it carefully."

examples.jp: 私の髪はパーマがかかりにくいんです。
examples.tr: My hair doesn't take a perm easily.

examples.jp: この包丁はよく切れる。
examples.tr: This kitchen knife cuts well.

649.explain: Uses an intransitive verb to express a property, state or ability as a natural condition, without emphasizing the agent.
649.notes:
1) It is easy to confuse intransitive verbs with transitive verbs.
→ This pattern uses intransitive verbs to talk about a property/state (ability, characteristics), without emphasizing the agent who does it.
2) Often used with words meaning "easy/hard" or describing properties.
→ For example: 開きやすい, 壊れやすい… usually properties of things.
3) When there is a clear agent, a transitive verb or another structure is usually used.
→ If you want to say "someone does…", do not use this intransitive-verb style describing a state.

650.meaning:
Expresses a reason. Used to say "... is because of ..."
［ふつう］　+　からだ

examples.jp: よくないと思ったからだ
examples.tr: It's because I thought it wasn't good.

examples.jp: また、朝寝坊をしてしまった。きっと疲れているからだ。（≒疲れているから朝寝坊した）
examples.tr: I overslept again. It must be because I'm tired. (≒ I overslept because I'm tired)

examples.jp: 朝寝坊をしたのは、疲れているからだ。（≒疲れているから朝寝坊した）
examples.tr: The reason I overslept is that I'm tired. (≒ I overslept because I'm tired)

examples.jp:
こんなに渋滞しているのは、何か事故があったからだろう。
（≒何(なに)か事故(じこ)があったから、こんなに滞(とどこおり)している）
examples.tr:
The traffic is probably this bad because there was some kind of accident.
(≒ Because there was some kind of accident, traffic is this backed up)

650.notes:
This form is the reason pattern "X から Y" inverted into "Y のは X からだ". The から in this pattern cannot be replaced with ので.
* (incorrect) 試験に落ちたのは勉強しなかったのでだ。

examples.jp: 教えてくれと頼まれた
examples.tr: I was asked to tell (them)

examples.tr: Mr. Yamashita asked me to give him Mr. Tanaka's email address.

examples.tr: When I told my mother I wanted to study in Japan, she told me not to go.

652.name: （imperative form）と言われる
652.connection: 「V imperative form / Vるな」 + と言われる

examples.jp: 行くなと言われる
examples.tr: To be told not to go

examples.jp: 父に、夏休みに国に帰って来いと言われた。
examples.tr: My father told me to come back home during summer vacation.

examples.jp: 先生に、遅刻するなと注意された。
examples.tr: My teacher warned me not to be late.

examples.jp: 国に帰ると、いつも母に「もっとたくさん食べなさい」と言われる。
examples.tr: Whenever I go back to my home country, my mother always tells me, "Eat more."

examples.jp: 自己紹介は以上です。さて、本題に入りましょう。
examples.tr: That's all for self-introductions. Now, let's get to the main topic.

examples.jp: 前回の復習を終えました。さて、新しい文法に進みます。
examples.tr: We've finished reviewing last lesson. Now, let's move on to new grammar.

examples.jp: 長く待たせてしまいました。さて、結果を発表します。
examples.tr: Sorry to have kept you waiting so long. Now, I'll announce the results.

examples.tr: That completes the preparations. Now, let's set off.

examples.jp: さて、ここで問題です。次のうち正しいのはどれでしょう。

654.explain:
Polite, inviting nuance that guides the listener; often used in presentations, classes and emails.
Position: at the beginning of a sentence/new clause; followed by a comma.
Used to "change direction" or "move forward", not to comment or give an evaluation.
Not used to change abruptly to an unrelated topic (use ところで in that case).
In emails: " さて、早速ですが…" to move on to the main content.

さて: "well/now then/so now…", used to:
• Move on to the next topic or return to the main topic after an introduction.
• Move to the next step in a procedure/instruction/explanation.
• Start a new action and draw the listener's attention.
• Does not express cause-and-effect or same-direction addition; purely a transition.

rows: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>み？ ところで、<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>は？
Concludes/moves to action after closing a part.
それでは、<ruby>発表<rt>はっぴょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めます。
A different grammar point, meaning "leave for later".
<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>はさておき、<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>戻<rt>もど</rt></ruby>ろう。
Moves to a coherently connected step/topic.
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>。さて、<ruby>質疑<rt>しつぎ</rt></ruby><ruby>応答<rt>おうとう</rt></ruby>へ。

mistakes: Confusing it with ところで: exam questions often test the context; if the two sentences are connected/move forward a step → さて; if the topic changes abruptly → ところで.
Using さて for a cause-and-effect relation is wrong: use それで/したがって.
A harsh command after さて sounds forced; use an inviting form instead.
654.notes:
• In spoken language, the intonation often rises slightly after "さて" to draw attention.
• "さてさて" can be repeated in casual spoken language to soften the atmosphere.
• In formal language, "それでは/では" is usually safer when announcing a decision/action. explain: Used when changing to a new topic. ⏐ examples: 1. 「これで授業を終わります。さて来週の予定ですが・・・」
This is the end of the class. Now, about next week's schedule…
2. 「以上、今日のニュースをお伝えしました。さて次に天気予報です。」
That's all for today's news. And now, the weather forecast.

examples.jp: ドアを開けた。すると、猫が飛び出してきた。
examples.tr: I opened the door. Then a cat came running out.

examples.jp: 薬を飲んだ。すると、すぐに頭痛が治った。
examples.tr: I took some medicine. Then my headache went away right away.

examples.jp: 彼に電話した。すると、もう出発したと言われた。
examples.tr: I called him. Then I was told he had already left.

examples.jp: 外に出た。すると、雪が降っていた。
examples.tr: I went outside. Then I saw that it was snowing.

examples.jp: パソコンの電源を入れた。すると、変な音がした。
examples.tr: I turned on the computer. Then it made a strange noise.

655.explain:
Position: Always comes at the beginning of the second clause, after the first clause ends with a period or comma.
Naturalness: Used when the result happens quickly, right after the preceding action.
Emotional nuance: Can carry a sense of surprise or a new discovery.
No command or volition meaning: Not used in sentences giving a command → only narrates events.
Style: Moderately formal, often used in writing – narratives, diaries, JLPT exam texts.

•
Indicates a result that happens right after the preceding action: "Then…", "As soon as… …".

•
Expresses a result that comes as a surprise, not predicted beforehand: The speaker did not expect B to happen after A.

•
Used to create a natural flow in storytelling: suitable for descriptive and narrative writing.

•
Neutral nuance → somewhat written language: Not used in casual speech between friends (where そしたら、するとさ... is often used).

rows: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ってきた。 すると、<ruby>風<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>くなった。
Lists consecutive events, does not emphasize the result.
ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べた。 そして、<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>た。
Emphasizes the time sequence – the next action.
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>した。 それから、<ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>した。
Well then (indicates the speaker's conclusion/next action)
Used in conversation, different from the grammar point “A。するとB。”
「<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がないよ」「 すると、<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>ごう！」

mistakes: Confusing it with そして: そして only connects information and has no element of surprise.
Using it with volition/command: Writing “すると、行きましょう” is incorrect for this grammar point.
Confusing it with the conversational usage "Well then...": For example, “すると、君はどうする？” has a different meaning.
Omitting the comma after すると: In formal writing, there should be a “、”.
Using it when the two events have no cause-and-effect relationship or closeness in time is logically wrong.
655.notes:
•
Appears often in JLPT reading comprehension because of its narrative, descriptive quality.
• Often used to lead to an important discovery in a text: “すると、驚くべき事実が判明した。”
• Never used to introduce an intentional action of the speaker in the second clause. meaning_vi: Immediately, then ～ ⏐ explain: (1) A is the trigger for event B, which happens immediately afterward.
(2) From A, judgment B is drawn. ⏐ examples: 1. 薬を塗った。すると痛みが治まった。
I applied the medicine. Immediately the pain went away.
2. 窓を開けた。すると、蛾が入ってきた。
I was at the door. Immediately a moth flew in.
3. 「私は外出していました。」
「すると、家は誰もいなかったんですね。」
I was out. So there was nobody at home, right?

656.meaning: Speaking of which, that reminds me

examples.jp: 明日は試験だね。そういえば、鉛筆を買わなきゃ。
examples.tr: The exam is tomorrow, right? That reminds me, I have to buy pencils.

examples.jp: 彼、最近見ないね。そういえば、留学に行ったんだっけ。
examples.tr: I haven't seen him lately. Oh, that's right, he went to study abroad, didn't he?

examples.jp: 日本の夏は暑いよね。そういえば、去年は40度になったね。
examples.tr: Summers in Japan are hot, aren't they? Speaking of which, it got up to 40 degrees last year.

examples.jp: 宿題は終わった？そういえば、先生が明日までって言ってたよ。
examples.tr: Have you finished your homework? Oh, that reminds me, the teacher said it's due tomorrow.

examples.jp: 駅前に新しいカフェができたよ。そういえば、まだ行ってないな。
examples.tr: A new café opened in front of the station. Come to think of it, I still haven't been there.

656.explain:
Used at the beginning of the second sentence to bring up a new idea related to the previous sentence.
Casual, natural nuance; often used in everyday communication and spoken language.
Often used when the speaker has just remembered something, expressing a natural thought as it is put into words.
Not used in formal documents or official reports (ところで or それにしても can be used instead at a more neutral level).

•
Used for a topic shift based on association: When hearing, saying, or thinking about A, the speaker suddenly remembers a related B.

•
Implies "That reminds me", "Oh, that's right": B is not the main topic, but something that has just suddenly come to mind.

•
Natural, casual: Often used in conversation or narrative writing; a friendly nuance, not too formal.

•
Does not express a direct cause-and-effect relationship: A is not the cause of B, only a reminder.

rows: Used when you suddenly remember something related.
そういえば、<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby><ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みだ。
A topic shift, but not necessarily based on association.
ところで、<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>は？
Expresses a strong emotion about what came before.
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>いね。それにしても<ruby>今年<rt>ことし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>異常<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>だ。
Expresses a conclusion drawn from the previous information (logic).
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>か。そうすると<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だね。

mistakes: Using it in formal writing: Not suitable in reports or theses → replace with ちなみに or ところで.
Confusing it with そうすると ("if so, then") in logical sentences.
Using it when the two sentences are unrelated: そういえば requires an association or memory triggered by the previous sentence.
Forgetting the comma after そういえば: In written language, write “そういえば、…”.
656.notes:
• Often appears in JLPT listening conversations, giving a natural feel to the speaker's speech.
• In narrative writing, it serves to lead into recalling the past or related information.
• Flexible translations: "That reminds me", "Oh, that's right", "Oh, right"…
• Must be distinguished from “そうすると” (if so, then), since they sound similar but have completely different meanings. meaning_vi: Speaking of which; Oh, wasn't it ～ ⏐ explain: Used to begin a sentence whose topic is related to something you have remembered. ⏐ examples: 1. 「そういえば、田中君、元気かな？」
Speaking of which, I wonder if little Tanaka is doing well.
2. 「いい家ですね。そういえば、お父様は設計士さんでしたよね。」
What a nice family. Oh, your father is a designer, isn't he?

examples.jp: 彼に連絡した。それが、返事がまだ来ないんだ。
examples.tr: I contacted him. But I still haven't gotten a reply.

examples.jp: 明日は行けると思っていた。それが、急に熱が出ちゃって…。
examples.tr: I thought I'd be able to go tomorrow. But then I suddenly came down with a fever…

examples.jp: テストは簡単だったよね。それが、全然できなかったんだ。
examples.tr: The test was easy, wasn't it? Actually, I couldn't do any of it.

examples.jp: 旅行に行く予定だったんだけど、それが、台風でキャンセルになった。
examples.tr: I was planning to go on a trip, but it got canceled because of a typhoon.

examples.jp:
宿題はもう終わった？
―それが、まだ半分も…
examples.tr:
Have you finished your homework yet?
―Well, actually, I haven't even done half…

657.explain:
Position: Comes at the beginning of clause B, after a complete sentence A.
Nuance: Soft, with a slight sense of regret, reluctance, or a reason that is hard to say.
Level of casualness: Used a lot in everyday conversation; rarely used in formal written language.
Trailing off: It can be left hanging after それが to create a sense of hesitation or difficulty saying something directly.

•
Expresses something contrary to expectation: The fact in clause B differs from or is the opposite of what was expected from clause A.

•
Used to shift the idea with gentle emotion: carries the nuance of "you'd think so, but it isn't", "but in reality…".

•
Used to explain a difficult reason / to decline tactfully: When the speaker hesitantly gives a reason why something cannot be done.

• Common in natural conversation; has a justifying, soft-contrast quality, unlike でも (which has a more direct nuance).

rows: Soft; often used to decline or explain.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くつもりだった。 それが、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けなくて。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。でも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けない。
The reality is completely contrary to what was expected, often a strong surprise.
<ruby>勝<rt>か</rt></ruby>つと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>った。ところが<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けた。
Talks about the result that follows; no contrastive meaning.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。 それで<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>した。

mistakes: Confusing it with それで: それで = "so, therefore…", while それが = "and yet…", contrary to expectations.
Using it in overly formal writing: Not suitable; replace with しかし or ただし in argumentative writing.
Using it when B does not contrast with A: それが requires clause B to differ from what is expected from A.
Omitting clause A: Previous context is always needed for それが to make sense.
657.notes:
• Often accompanied by expressions of feeling and hesitation to reduce the degree of negation or refusal.
• Can be used to answer when asked directly about something that is hard to answer straight.
• In spoken language, it can be stretched to “それがね…” to open an explanation. meaning_vi: (1) (As for) that, ～, but ～
(2) But ～ ⏐ explain: (1) Used when talking about an unexpected result.
(2) Expresses a result different from the plan or expectation in the previous sentence. ⏐ examples: 1. 「お嬢さん、もう大学をご卒業されましたでしょう？」
「それが、まだなんですよ。」
Your daughter has already graduated from university, hasn't she? Well, not yet, actually.
2. たばこをやめると誓った。それが、たった三日でまた吸ってしまった。
I swore I would quit smoking. But after only 3 days I ended up smoking again.

examples.jp: 彼は何度も失敗した。それでも、諦めなかった。
examples.tr: He failed many times. Even so, he didn't give up.

examples.jp: 雨は強く降っていた。それでも、観客は帰らなかった。
examples.tr: It was raining hard. Even so, the audience didn't leave.

examples.jp: 注意した。それでも、彼は同じミスをした。
examples.tr: I warned him. Even so, he made the same mistake.

examples.jp: この仕事は大変だよ。それでもやるの？
examples.tr: This job is tough, you know. Are you still going to do it?

examples.jp: 全力を出した。それでも、勝てなかった。
examples.tr: I gave it my all. Even so, I couldn't win.

658.explain:
Position: Comes at the beginning of clause B, after clause A ends with a period or comma.
The two clauses must be in an opposing relationship: A makes us think B will not happen, but in reality B still happens.
Nuance: Emotional – surprise, disappointment, admiration, perseverance.
Style: Used in both conversation and written language; neutral level of formality.

•
Expresses concession + contrast: Even though A is an obstacle, a difficulty, or something that makes B unlikely, result B still happens.

•
Emotional implication: Often carries a nuance of perseverance, surprise, disappointment, or praise (for still doing B despite A).

•
Natural translations: "Even so…", "But…", "Nevertheless…", "Even then…".

•
Different from それが・それで・そこで: それでも emphasizes the strong contrast between expectation (from A) and reality (B).

rows: Emphasizes that B happens in spite of A.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。 それでも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Emphasizes an emotion of surprise or complaint.
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>いね。 それにしても<ruby>今年<rt>ことし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>異常<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>だ。
Colloquial, simple; does not emphasize overcoming an obstacle.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。 でも<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しい。
Used when reality is contrary to expectation; somewhat hesitant.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。 それが<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けなくなった。

mistakes: Confusing it with それで: それで = "so, therefore…", while それでも = "even so…".
No contrasting element: Incorrect if clauses A and B are not opposed, or if A is not an obstacle to B.
Using it in overly formal writing: Not suitable in research or reports → use しかしながら.
Omitting the comma after それでも in written language: write “それでも、…”.
658.notes:
• Often used in narratives, emotional statements, and expressions of volition.
• Often used together with emphatic words such as それでもなお (but still…) and それでもやっぱり.
• Flexible translations: "But", "Nevertheless", "Even then…", "And yet…".
• Appears often in the reading and listening sections of JLPT N3–N2. meaning_vi: However, even so ～ ⏐ explain: Expresses an opinion or result opposite to situation A in the preceding clause. ⏐ examples: 1. 外は大雨だ。それでも出かけないといけない。
It's raining heavily outside. Even so, I have to go out.
2. みんなに反対されている。それでも私は彼と結婚したい。
Everyone is against it. Even so, I want to marry him.

examples.jp: 明日休みだよ。—それなら一緒に出かけよう。
examples.tr: I'm off tomorrow. —Then let's go out together.

examples.jp: もう売り切れです。—それなら予約しておけばよかったね。
examples.tr: It's already sold out. —Then we should have reserved one.

examples.jp: 車がないの？それならバスで行こう。
examples.tr: You don't have a car? Then let's go by bus.

examples.jp: この案はリスクが高い。それなら別案を検討しましょう。
examples.tr: This plan is high-risk. In that case, let's consider an alternative.

examples.jp: 体調が悪い？それなら無理しないで。
examples.tr: You're not feeling well? Then don't push yourself.

659.explain:
Usually comes at the beginning of a reply, together with a suggestion/solution/concession.
Not used simply for contrast; there must be a conditional relationship "if A is true, then B...".
Casual: だったら／じゃ(あ); polite: それならば／それでは.

• Meaning: "If so, then / in that case...", used when you take in information A and then decide on/suggest B.
• Conversational function: responding, moving on to a solution, giving advice or a new condition.
• Formality: neutral in conversation; それならば is more polite; だったら/じゃ(あ) are more casual.

rows: More casual than それなら
If so, then; well then (opening/closing a section)
More polite; also used to move to the next step in a presentation
それでは<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めます。
A grammatical element attached directly to nouns/verbs/adjectives

mistakes: Using それなら for pure contrast (use しかし/だが instead) → wrong function.
Mixing it up with それでは: in natural conversation, それなら is neutral; それでは is formal/used for guiding through procedures.
B lacks the quality of "reacting to A" → the sentence becomes disjointed.
659.notes:
• Suitable in negotiation/problem-solving because it shows a flexible response.
• Can be used with a command/advice: それなら、やめたほうがいい。
• In polite emails, prefer それでは／それならば.

examples.jp: 行きたくない。だって、疲れているんだもん。
examples.tr: I don't want to go. I mean, I'm tired.

examples.jp: 今日は無理。だって、約束があるから。
examples.tr: Today's impossible. Because I have plans.

examples.jp: そんなの知らないよ。だって、誰も教えてくれなかったし。
examples.tr: How would I know that? I mean, nobody told me.

examples.jp: 怒らないで。だって、冗談のつもりだったんだ。
examples.tr: Don't be angry. I only meant it as a joke.

examples.jp: 彼は優しいよ。だって、いつも手伝ってくれるもん。
examples.tr: He's kind, you know. Because he always helps me.

660.explain:
Casual spoken language, usually in conversations between friends/family.
Adding んだもん／もの strengthens the nuance of self-justification/cuteness; から is more neutral.
Avoid using it to open formal texts; if a standard reason is needed, use ので／ため／だから.

• Explains a reason based on emotion/mild excuse-making: "It's because… you know".
• Not meant for strict logical argument, but to show personal feelings and self-justification.
• Usually comes at the beginning of the sentence, followed by a comma; S2 is the reason clause.

rows: だって、<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>いんだもん。
More neutral, can be used in writing
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だ。だから、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいので<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>できません。
Not a conjunction; comes after a noun

mistakes: Using だって in essays/business letters → not suitable; replace with ので／ため／理由は～です.
Confusing the conjunction だって with the particle だって meaning "even": look at the position (beginning of a sentence vs. after a noun).
Combining だって with です／ます creates a style mismatch: avoid “だって、忙しいですから。” in formal situations.
In listening comprehension, だって + んだもん signals emotion, not an objective reason.
660.notes:
• The form “だってさ” is used when quoting rumors/what others said, not to give a reason.
• In polite conversation, you can switch to: 申し訳ありません。忙しいので…。 (avoid だって).
• Children and women often use ～んだもん／もの; adult men tend to use it less to avoid sounding childish. explain: A spoken-language way of saying 「なぜなら」 「なぜかというと」 「どうしてかというと」 ⏐ examples: 1. 「何を怒ってるの？」「だって、約束を破ったじゃないか。」
What are you angry about? Isn't it because you broke your promise?
2. 「テストの点、よかったんだって？」
「うん。だってやさしかったんだもん。」
I heard you got a good score on the test? Yes, that's because it was easy.

examples.jp: この制度は来年から見直される。というのは、現状に合わなくなっているからだ。
examples.tr: This system will be reviewed starting next year. That's because it no longer fits the current situation.

examples.jp: SDGsというのは、持続可能な開発目標のことだ。
examples.tr: SDGs means the Sustainable Development Goals.

examples.jp: 彼は出席しないようだ。というのは、さっき体調が悪いと連絡があったからだ。
examples.tr: It seems he won't attend. That's because we just heard from him that he isn't feeling well.

examples.jp: この薬は保険が効かない。というのは、まだ承認が下りていないためだ。
examples.tr: This medicine isn't covered by insurance. That's because it hasn't been approved yet.

examples.jp: ブラック企業というのは、労働者に過度な負担を強いる企業のことだ。
examples.tr: A "black company" is a company that forces excessive burdens on its workers.

661.explain:
A comma usually follows というのは to separate the explanation.
When explaining a reason, end with からだ／ためだ to make the cause-and-effect relationship clear.
Used for definitions: XというのはYのことだ → concise, formal, often seen in textbooks and articles.
Colloquial: っていうのは → softer, suitable for conversation and blogs.
Not used at the end of a sentence; it is always followed by an explanatory clause.

• Explanation/definition: A way to "clarify" the content just stated in the previous sentence. Often used with のことだ／ということだ.
• Giving a reason: States a cause that serves as a conclusion for the preceding clause. Often accompanied by からだ／ためだ to settle the reason.
• Scope of reference: というのは usually refers directly to the whole previous sentence (A)。この/その＋話/件 can be used to make this clear.
• Nuance: Logical, objective; used a lot in newspapers, discussions, reports, and presentations.

rows: Refers to the previous sentence; often with からだ/ということだ
なぜなら／なぜかというと
Introduces a reason directly; usually ends with からだ
Rephrases the same content; not really giving a reason
B does not explain A but is inferred from A
Usually used right after a term; no previous sentence needed

mistakes: Confusing it with ということは: というのは explains A; ということは infers B from A.
Forgetting からだ/ためだ when giving a reason makes the sentence lack conclusive force.
Putting というのは at the end of a sentence (incorrect); it must be followed by an explanatory clause.
Writing it without a comma: “というのはB…” is still acceptable, but a comma should be used for clarity in reading exams.
661.notes:
• Instead of からだ, わけだ/ためだ/にほかならない can be used to strengthen the nuance of a conclusion.
• If the explanation is long, break up the sentence and use a comma after というのは for readability.
• In spoken language, というのは can take the contracted form つーのは/てのは (very colloquial); avoid using these in the JLPT.

662.meaning: What is called…, the thing named…

examples.jp: 「デジカメ」というのは、デジタルカメラを短くした言い方です。
examples.tr: 「デジカメ」 is a shortened way of saying "digital camera."

examples.jp:
「電車で「カクテイ」っていうのは何のことですか。」
「各駅に停車する電車のことです。」
examples.tr:
What does 「カクテイ」 mean when talking about trains?
It's a train that stops at every station.

662.explain: Used when you want to define or explain a thing or matter (with the phrase to be defined as the subject)

examples.jp: 君があやまることはないよ。
examples.tr: You don't need to apologize.

examples.jp: 来ることはありません。郵送でいいですよ。
examples.tr: There's no need to come. Sending it by mail is fine.

664.explain: Used when you want to tell the other person that they do not necessarily have to do a certain action. It is acceptable even if that action is not done.

665.meaning: Expresses taking ~ as the standard for evaluation. Judging from ~, in terms of ~

examples.jp: 健太の性格から言って
examples.tr: Judging from Kenta's personality, ...

examples.jp: 健太の性格から言って、好きな人にはっきり「好きだ」と言えないだろう。
examples.tr: Judging from Kenta's personality, he probably can't clearly say "I like you" to the person he likes.

examples.jp: あの人の態度から言って、私のことが嫌いに違いない。
examples.tr: Judging from that person's attitude, they must dislike me.

665.notes: Indicates a clue for a judgment. Also expressed as 「からして」 or 「からみて」.（９０）

667.meaning:
「～がいちばん…。」客観的な事実ではなくて、話者が主観的に言うときに使う。
Used when the speaker wants to express their subjective impression rather than an objective fact.
667.connection: N + くらい/ぐらい/ほど + ～はない（～ is the most, subjective）

examples.jp: リーさんぐらい動物好きな人はいない。
examples.tr: Nobody loves animals as much as Lee.

examples.jp: わたしは料理を作ることぐらい楽しいことはないと思っています。
examples.tr: I think there's nothing as enjoyable as cooking.

examples.jp: ああ、あしたも漢字のテストがある。テストほどいやなものはない。
examples.tr: Oh no, there's another kanji test tomorrow. There's nothing I hate more than tests.

examples.jp: 2年前に病気だと分かったときほど不安になったことはない。
examples.tr: I've never felt as anxious as when I found out I was sick two years ago.

667.explain:
Used to elevate the degree of a thing, matter, or person.
Affirms that apart from that thing, matter, or person, there is nothing equivalent that could replace it
667.notes:
meaning_vi: 「ほど．．．はない」expresses the meaning of the structure「～が一番．．．だ」. There is nothing as ~ as ~
examples: 1. ①　ニューヨークほど（は）寒くない
Not as cold as New York
2. ②　A大学の入学試験は、B大学の試験ほど難しくない。
The entrance exam of University A is not as difficult as the exam of University B.
3. ③　ロンドンはニューヨークほどは寒くない。
London is not as cold as New York.
4. ④　今日は思ったほど暑くない。

──────
1. ①　サッカーほどおもしろいスポーツはない

2. ②　健太ほど忘れっぽい人はいない。

3. ③　人の自慢話を聞くことほど退屈なことはない。
There is nothing more boring than listening to other people brag about themselves.
meaning_vi: As … as that, there is none….
examples: 1. 彼女くらい親切な人はいない。
There is no one as kind as her
2. 今年ほど雪の降った年はなかった。
There has never been a year with as much snow as this year

668.meaning: At least, at the very least

examples.jp: 遅れるなら、電話くらいは入れてください。
examples.tr: If you're going to be late, at least give us a call.

examples.jp: 初対面なら、挨拶くらいはちゃんとしよう。
examples.tr: When meeting someone for the first time, let's at least greet them properly.

examples.jp: 忙しくても、メッセージを読むくらいはできるでしょ。
examples.tr: Even if you're busy, you can at least read a message, right?

examples.jp: 試験前は、単語くらいは覚えておけ。
examples.tr: Before the exam, at least memorize the vocabulary.

examples.jp: 財布を忘れても、交通費くらいは持っておきなさい。
examples.tr: Even if you forget your wallet, at least have your fare money on you.

examples.jp: 彼に謝るくらいはしたほうがいい。
examples.tr: You should at least apologize to him.

668.explain:
Often used together with せめて to strengthen the nuance of a "minimum."
What comes before くらいは is something obvious/basic, so use it with subordinates/acquaintances to avoid sounding rude.
Suitable in recommendations/rules:参加する くらいは 義務だ。

• Emphasizes the minimum acceptable level: "at least…".
• Speaker's attitude: often accompanies a reminder, a mild reproach, a minimum request, or a suggestion.
• The target before くらいは is something "easy to do/basic," or a small amount.

rows: <ruby>10分<rt>じゅっぷん</rt></ruby>くらい<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ
Similar in meaning when emphasizing a minimum, but softer
<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>だけでもして
A supporting adverb; くらいは is the core structure
せめて<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して
If it's only to the extent of…
A comparative conditional sentence, not "at least"
<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つくらいなら<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない

mistakes: Confusing it with くらい (degree): くらいは requires the particle は to create the meaning "at least."
Using it with a request that is too strong in a polite context can sound rude; add ください／いただけますか.
Do not use it for something beyond the "minimum"; if you are asking for a lot, use べき/必要がある instead of くらいは.
668.notes:
• After くらいは there is usually a clause expressing an expectation/request (～しなさい／～してほしい／～べきだ…).
• In business emails, use it indirectly to be polite: ご連絡くらいはいただけますと幸いです。
• It can be used with a negative to emphasize the minimum: それくらいは難しくない（at least that isn't difficult）。

669.connection: V/A plain form + からこそ / N・Naだ + からこそ

examples.jp: 明日こそ
examples.tr: Tomorrow, for sure

examples.jp: 今年こそ、頑張ろうと思う。
examples.tr: This year, I'm going to really give it my all.

examples.jp: 頑張ったからこそ、合格できたのです。
examples.tr: It was precisely because I worked hard that I was able to pass.

669.explain:
Expresses emphasis. Precisely ~
N：雨　+　こそ
［ふつう］　+　からこそ

examples.jp: この店はおいしいことはおいしいが、量が少ない。
examples.tr: This restaurant's food is certainly tasty, but the portions are small.

examples.jp: 日本語は話せることは話せるけど、専門用語は苦手だ。
examples.tr: I can speak Japanese well enough, but I'm weak with technical terms.

examples.jp: 便利なことは便利だが、料金が高い。
examples.tr: It is convenient, sure, but the fees are high.

examples.jp: 行くことは行くが、今日は無理かもしれない。
examples.tr: I will go, but today might not be possible.

examples.jp: 必要であることは必要であるが、今すぐではない。
examples.tr: It is necessary, yes, but not right now.

670.explain:
You must repeat the same word/same stem to create the emphasis of concession.
"が/けど" can be swapped; "けれども" is more formal.
Usually used in the general present; the tense can change if the context allows, but keep the two clauses parallel.
The nuance is gently polite and avoids an absolute assertion.

• Partially acknowledges something in the first clause, but gives a limitation/exception/different point in the second clause: "It is … all right, but …".
• The nuance emphasizes reservation, not complete denial.
• The second clause usually states a reason/condition that changes the final evaluation.

rows: <ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いことは<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いが…
Does not emphasize acknowledgment through repetition
A double negative pattern with a different function
<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>とはいえ、<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。

mistakes: Not repeating the same word: ×おいしいことは美味だが… → it must be the same stem: おいしいことはおいしいが…
Confusing it with "Vることはある" (something happens occasionally). That is a pattern with a completely different meaning.
Wrong combination with na-adjectives: ×便利だことは便利だが → correct: 便利なことは便利だが。
Overusing it with nouns in ordinary conversation is unnatural; prefer verbs/adjectives.
670.notes:
• Emphatic form: ～のは～のだが also exists, but it is a different structure.
• You can insert an adverb between the two repetitions to fine-tune the nuance: 少し高いことは高いが…
• In spoken language, が can be omitted, ending the sentence and continuing the idea in the next sentence.
meaning_vi: 「確かに～だが、その事実はあまり重要ではなくて、…。」
It is certainly true that ~, but that fact is not very important, so …
examples: 1. 彼からの手紙は読んだことは読んだんですが、意味がよくわかりませんでした。
I did read his letter, but I didn't really understand what it meant。
2. わたしは泳げることは泳げますが、長い距離はだめなんです。
I can swim, but I can't swim long distances。
3. この本は高いことは高いが、写真が多くて楽しめそうです。
This book is certainly expensive, but it has lots of photos, so it looks like it will be enjoyable。
4. 子どもを育てるのは大変なことは大変だが、成長が楽しみで大変さを忘れる。
Raising children is certainly hard, but the joy of watching them grow makes you forget the hardship。

671.meaning: A negative question; an expression with a meaning like "ですね"

examples.jp: 元気がないじゃない（か）
examples.tr: You don't look well, do you?

examples.jp: 元気がないじゃないか。何かトラブルがあったの？
examples.tr: You don't look well. Did something go wrong?

examples.jp: 「あれ？僕のめがね、どこに置いたっけ？」「さっき、そこにあったじゃない」
examples.tr: "Huh? Where did I put my glasses?" "They were right there a minute ago, weren't they?"

examples.jp: そのスカート、かわいいじゃない。よく似合ってるよ。
examples.tr: That skirt is cute! It really suits you.

671.notes: A casual way of saying 「Ｖ－ようではないか」.

examples.jp: 割引のおかげで、高いバッグを買わずにすんだ。
examples.tr: Thanks to the discount, I didn't have to buy the expensive bag.

examples.jp: 早く病院へ行ったので、手術をせずにすんだ。
examples.tr: Because I went to the hospital early, I managed to avoid surgery.

examples.jp: 雨がやんで、タクシーに乗らずにすんだ。
examples.tr: The rain stopped, so I didn't have to take a taxi.

examples.jp: 上司に説明したら、叱られずにすんだ。
examples.tr: When I explained it to my boss, I got away without being scolded.

examples.jp: 資料を事前に共有しておいたので、会議で長く説明せずにすんだ。
examples.tr: I had shared the materials in advance, so I didn't need to give a long explanation at the meeting.

673.explain:
Has a nuance of relief and luck; to keep it neutral, add the adverb なんとか/うまく.
Used with a result that is positively contrary to expectation: なんとか間に合って謝ら ずにすんだ。
In natural spoken language: ～ないで済んだ; formal/written: ～ずに済んだ.
Used with で済む/で済まない to talk about degree:罰金で済んだ（got off with just a fine）.

～ずにすんだ expresses "did not have to do …; managed to avoid …", usually with a nuance of relief or luck at not needing to carry out an action that was planned or that should have been done.
• Presupposition: the speaker thinks X would normally have to be done, but in reality it was not.
• Often used with costly, troublesome or painful things: 手術, 追加料金, 叱られる, 謝る, 行列する.
• Can be used in the present/potential: ずにすむ（現在）, ずにすんだ（過去）.
• It is not necessarily a good result, but most of the time it carries a feeling of "luckily."

rows: Not having to do (managed/will manage to) avoid
<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>らないで<ruby>済<rt>す</rt></ruby>んだ
～ずに／～ないで + <ruby>済<rt>す</rt></ruby>む（で<ruby>済<rt>す</rt></ruby>む）
<ruby>修理<rt>しゅうり</rt></ruby>は<ruby>千<rt>せん</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>済<rt>す</rt></ruby>んだ
Being in a state of not doing
Does not carry the idea of "avoided"
<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べずにいる

mistakes: Wrong sound change of する: it must be せずにすんだ, not "しずにすんだ".
Confusing the meaning "didn't do" with "didn't need to do": ～ずにすんだ includes the idea of "avoided."
JLPT: a trap is choosing ～なくてもいい instead of ～ずにすんだ; if there is a past result "managed to avoid" → choose ～ずにすんだ.
Combining it with something positive that does not fit the context: "ご飯を食べずにすんだ" usually implies something negative for health; consider the context.
673.notes:
• The classical negative "ずに" = "ないで". With する → せずに; 来る → 来ずに（こずに）.
• In reports, you can add a reason: ～のおかげで／～ために + ずにすんだ.
• Negating the nuance of luck: ～ずにすまず（could not avoid） is rare and written language.

675.connection: Vます(drop ます) + そうにない

examples.jp: このペースでは、締め切りに間に合いそうにない。
examples.tr: At this pace, it doesn't look like we'll make the deadline.

examples.jp: 雨は今夜中には止みそうにない。
examples.tr: The rain doesn't look like it will stop tonight.

examples.jp: 彼は渋滞に巻き込まれているから、時間どおりに来そうにない。
examples.tr: He's stuck in traffic, so he's unlikely to arrive on time.

examples.jp: この問題は子どもには理解できそうにない。
examples.tr: This problem doesn't look like something children could understand.

examples.jp: 価格は当分下がりそうにない。
examples.tr: Prices don't look like they'll come down for the time being.

675.explain:
Used when you want to say "unlikely to happen" while staying polite and avoiding absolute negation.
Often used in reports/forecasts:回復しそうにない,改善しそうにない.
Combine with どうも/この様子では to emphasize that it is based on observation.

• Expresses the prediction "unlikely to/doesn't look like it will …; low possibility."
• Based on the current situation or objective conditions, not on subjective will.
• The nuance is relatively objective and softer than a direct negative; more polite than "V-るのは無理だ".

rows: <ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようがない。
Not a forecast, but inherent difficulty
<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みづらい／<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>しがたい。

mistakes: Using the form ～そうにない with adjectives → incorrect; use ～くなさそうだ／ではなさそうだ.
Confusing the degree with ～そうもない: the JLPT tests the nuance "mild vs very difficult."
Mixing it up with ～なさそうだ of ある; do not say ×ありそうにない.
675.notes:
• In risk reports, use ～そうにない to avoid flatly asserting "no," leaving room for a change of plan.
• Combined with expressions of duration: しばらく／当面／当分＋V-そうにない strengthens the nuance of "not anytime soon."
• Impersonal subjects fit well: 天気・相場・交通・業績・回復.
meaning_vi: Hardly likely to…, very unlikely to…
explain: Emphasizes a stronger degree of pessimism than ～そうにない; often used with adverbs: とても／どう見ても／この調子では.
Used when you want to suggest changing plans: ～そうもないから、Aに切り替えよう.
Suitable in both spoken and written language; not overly formal.
examples: 1. この量では、今日中に終わりそうもない。
With this amount of work, there's no way it will be done today.
2. バスは来そうもないから、歩いたほうがいい。
The bus doesn't look like it's coming, so we'd better walk.
3. 彼はあの件について謝りそうもない。
He doesn't seem at all likely to apologize about that matter.
4. 予算が足りないので、新機種の導入はできそうもない。
The budget is insufficient, so introducing the new model seems impossible.
5. この天気だと、明日の試合は開催されそうもない。
With this weather, tomorrow's game seems unlikely to be held.
comparison: Pattern | Degree of "impossible" | Nuance | Short example
～そうにない | Low possibility | Mild, objective | 帰（かえ）れそうにない。
～そうもない | Very low/hardly any | "も" adds emphasis, somewhat pessimistic | 帰（かえ）れそうもない。
～ようがない | Absolutely impossible | There is no way to do it | 連絡（れんらく）の取（と）りようがない。
～っこない（spoken language） | No way | Casual, strong negation | 今（いま）からじゃ間（ま）に合（あ）いっこない。
common_mistakes: • Confusing the degree with ～そうにない: when choosing an answer in the exam, look for "も" to spot the emphasis.
• Using this form with adjectives → incorrect; switch to the pattern for adjectives.
• Combining it with the potential form can be unnatural: prefer the plain V + そうもない (間に合いそうもない).
meaning_vi: doesn't seem at all able to～
explain: The possibility of an action or event being carried out or happening is very low.
examples: 1. 最近仕事がすごく忙しくて、同窓会に行けそうにないよ。
Work has been really busy lately, so I don't think I can make it to the class reunion.
2. できそうもないことを、できると言ってしまって後悔している。
I regret saying I could do something that I can't possibly do.

examples.jp: この店は安い。その上、サービスもいい。
examples.tr: This restaurant is cheap. On top of that, the service is good too.

examples.jp: 雨が降っている。その上、雷まで鳴ってきた。
examples.tr: It's raining. On top of that, it has even started thundering.

examples.jp: 彼は経験が豊富だ。その上、人望も厚い。
examples.tr: He has a wealth of experience. Moreover, he is highly respected.

examples.jp: 熱が下がらない。その上、咳もひどくなった。
examples.tr: My fever won't go down. On top of that, my cough has gotten worse.

examples.jp: 説明がわかりやすい。その上、例が多くて助かる。
examples.tr: The explanations are easy to understand. Moreover, there are lots of examples, which helps a lot.

676.explain:
Placed at the beginning of the added clause; usually followed by a comma after その上、 to mark a pause.
Tone: used in presentations, written language and evaluations; increases persuasiveness by listing reasons.
Combines well with だけでなく, ばかりか, さらに to build a chain of arguments.

• Adds information in the same direction: one more reason/strength/weakness to reinforce the argument.
• The nuance is somewhat more formal than それに; close to しかも in degree of emphasis but more neutral.
• Works at the sentence level: it stands at the start of the second clause, linking to the preceding clause; その上 is followed by a comma or a sentence break.
• Can be used for both positive and negative things: その上、遅刻してきた (negative), その上、親切だ (positive).

rows: <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い。その<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>きれい。
おいしい。それに<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い。しかも<ruby>無<rt>む</rt></ruby><ruby>添加<rt>てんか</rt></ruby>。
そのうえに<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>売上<rt>うりあげ</rt></ruby>はさらに<ruby>増加<rt>ぞうか</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Confusing it with しかも: しかも has strong emphasis and a sense of surprise; その上 is more neutral.
Using it in a very casual sentence sounds bookish; in conversation, それに is usually chosen.
JLPT: trap questions ask you to choose a conjunction by nuance; for a formal/logical style → その上; for exclamation/surprise → しかも.
676.notes:
• "その上" can also link a negative clause to add weight: 時間がない。その上、予算もない。
• In essays, the structure 第一に…、第二に…、その上… is used to add points.
• Avoid overusing it consecutively; limit it to 1–2 times per paragraph to avoid repetition.
meaning_vi: Moreover, in addition… (adds something in the same direction) explain: Suitable in essays, reports and advertisements: strengthens a point with evidence/additions in the same direction.
