<ruby>迷<rt>まよ</rt></ruby>うことなしに<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めた
Meaning differs by context; not an equivalent pattern
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>することはなく<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>できる

mistakes: Using ことなく in everyday conversation → sounds stiff. The JLPT tests style appropriate to the context.
Confusing it with ずに/ないで: if the sentence is a report/scientific or emphasizes “not at all” → prefer ことなく.
Attaching it directly before a noun: ×「休むことなく人」→ use 「休むことのない人」 instead.
Tense error: ことなく only follows V-る (dictionary form). Do not use V-ない／V-た before ことなく.
921.notes:
• JLPT keywords that often go with it: 最後まで／一度も／延々と／決して／絶えることなく.
• In exclamatory/praising writing: 「休むことなく努力を重ねた」 creates a tone of tribute.
• With mistakes: 「確認することなく送信してしまった」 gives the feel of an objective incident report.

922.meaning: Have no choice but to…, be forced to…

examples.jp: 父は事業に失敗して、借金をせざるを得なかった。
examples.tr: My father failed in business and had no choice but to borrow money.

examples.jp: 休みが取れないので、来月の旅行はあきらめざるを得ない。
examples.tr: I can't get time off, so I have no choice but to give up next month's trip.

examples.jp: 学校の規則なので、髪を切らざるを得ない。
examples.tr: It's a school rule, so I have no choice but to cut my hair.

examples.jp: 未経験者だけで冬山に登るなど、無謀と言わざるを得ない。
examples.tr: Climbing a winter mountain with only inexperienced people has to be called reckless.

examples.jp: 今年は仕事が忙しいので、夏休みの海外旅行はあきらめざるを得ない。
examples.tr: Work is busy this year, so I have no choice but to give up my overseas trip for summer vacation.

examples.jp: 新たな証拠が出てきた以上、彼女が犯人だと断定せざるを得ない。
examples.tr: Now that new evidence has come out, we have no choice but to conclude that she is the culprit.

922.explain:
Formal; used in reports, news, official documents and official statements.
Often carries the speaker's feeling of regret/reluctance.
Not used for actions driven by a sudden emotion; in that case, use ～ずにはいられない.
Does not combine directly with adjectives; convert to a suitable verb (認める、変更する…).

• Expresses reluctance: “have no choice but to / cannot help but…”, due to circumstances, rules or outside pressure.
• Formal, written-language nuance; stronger than ～ないわけにはいかない in its sense of “unavoidability”.
• Unlike ～ずにはいられない (inner urge), ～ざるを得ない emphasizes external pressure.
• Often used with words such as 事情で／状況的に／法律上／やむを得ず／どうしても.

rows: <ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>変更<rt>へんこう</rt></ruby>せざるを<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>ない。
<ruby>招待<rt>しょうたい</rt></ruby>されたら、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないわけにはいかない。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>褒<rt>ほ</rt></ruby>めずにはいられない。
<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>せねばならない。

mistakes: Using it to express a sudden emotion: incorrect. Use ～ずにはいられない.
Wrong form: 食べないざるを得ない × → 食べざるを得ない ✓
Confusing nuances: ～ないわけにはいかない (social obligation) ≠ ～ざるを得ない (strong external pressure).
Using it with adjectives: incorrect. Convert to a verb (変更する、認める…).
922.notes:
• In casual speech, ～しかない can be used instead in conversation, but the nuance is lighter.
• In legal documents/notices, the phrase “やむを得ず” often accompanies it to explain the reason.
• 来る→来ざるを得ない is rarely used in conversation; it is usually seen in written language. explain: Used to express that you do not like or want to do something, but must do it for some reason.
Kanji: ざるを得ない ⏐ examples: 1. いやな仕事でも、生活のためには続けるざるをえない。
Even if it's a job I dislike, I have no choice but to continue it to make a living.
2. この戦争は間違いだったと言わざるをえない。
I cannot help but say that this war was a mistake.

923.meaning: In the end, still did not…

examples.jp: いくつか検査を受けたけど、めまいの原因はわからずじまいだった。
examples.tr: I had several tests, but in the end the cause of my dizziness was never found.

examples.jp: 京都に滞在中に先生に会うつもりだったが、結局、会えずじまいになった。
examples.tr: I had planned to see my teacher while I was staying in Kyoto, but in the end I never got to.

examples.jp: 忙しくて、今年は花見に行かずじまいだった。
examples.tr: I was so busy that I never went cherry-blossom viewing this year.

examples.jp: 彼に本当の気持ちを言えずじまいで別れてしまった。
examples.tr: We broke up without my ever being able to tell him my true feelings.

examples.jp: 映画、評判は聞いたけど見ずじまいだった。
examples.tr: I'd heard good things about the movie, but I never ended up seeing it.

examples.jp: チャンスをつかめずじまいに終わった。
examples.tr: It ended without my ever seizing the chance.

923.explain:
Used for matters that are already closed (the time/opportunity has passed). Not used for the future.
Often accompanied by adverbs of final outcome:結局／とうとう／そのまま.
Fine in both spoken and written language; carries the speaker's subjective emotion.

• Expresses that something planned or that should have been done was in the end “not done” by the time a period/opportunity ended.
• Nuance of regret, a missed chance, something left unfinished; different from a simple negative ～なかった.
• Often used with markers of an ending: 結局・とうとう・そのまま・気づいたら...

rows: In the end, did not V
More neutral, less nuance of regret
<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>さないで<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わった
<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby>しないまま<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めた
<ruby>朝食<rt>ちょうしょく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べずに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた

mistakes: Using it for the future: × 明日は行かずじまいだ → unnatural. It must be used for things that are already over.
Confusing it with ～ずに: ～ずに only means “not V” and does not include regret/final outcome.
Forgetting to change する → せずじまい; “しずじまい” is not used.
923.notes:
• “じまい” means “outcome/closing”. Close to 終わりのニュアンス.
• Often used with opportunity verbs: 見る・言う・行く・会う・聞く・試す.
• Avoid using it for obligatory daily repeated actions (× 歯を磨かずじまいだった — sounds odd, unless talking about a special period).

examples.jp: この映画を見ると、毎回、感動せずにはいられない。
examples.tr: Every time I watch this movie, I can't help being moved.

examples.jp: ケーキを見たら、ダイエット中でも、食べずにはいられない。
examples.tr: When I see cake, I can't help eating it, even though I'm on a diet.

examples.jp: 彼の努力を見て、泣かずにはいられなかった。
examples.tr: Seeing how hard he worked, I couldn't help crying.

examples.jp: あのオチは面白すぎて、笑わずにはいられない。
examples.tr: That punchline is so funny that I can't help laughing.

examples.jp: 不公平だと思うと、言わずにはいられない。
examples.tr: When I think something is unfair, I can't help saying so.

examples.jp: そのニュースを聞いて、彼も喜びの声を上げずにはいられなかった。
examples.tr: When he heard the news, he too couldn't help crying out with joy.

925.explain:
Often used with the adverbs つい／思わず to emphasize spontaneity.
Has an emotional nuance; used a lot in narratives and personal comments.
Not suitable for expressing obligation/rules; in that case use ～ざるを得ない／～ねばならない.
Used in the past tense when talking about a reaction that has already happened: ～ずにはいられなかった.

• Expresses an inner urge/emotion that the speaker cannot hold back, so they end up doing V: "cannot help but…/feel compelled to (out of emotion)".
• Often used with verbs expressing natural reactions: 笑う、泣く、言う、拍手する、謝る、触る、見直す…
• Unlike ～ざるを得ない (forced by external circumstances), this pattern is driven by inner feelings.
• The subject is usually the speaker; if it is someone else, there must be grounds/observation for the conjecture.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>けずにはいられない。
<ruby>笑<rt>わらわ</rt></ruby>わないではいられない。
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>延期<rt>えんき</rt></ruby>せざるを<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>ない。
Neutral, not necessarily due to emotion
つい<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ってしまった。
Strong, usually an influence that brings about a consequence
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>演説<rt>えんぜつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>聴衆<rt>ちょうしゅう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>感動<rt>かんどう</rt></ruby>させずにはおかない。

mistakes: Using it for obligation: incorrect. Use ～ざるを得ない／～ねばならない when it is due to circumstances/rules.
A subject other than the speaker without emotional grounds → sounds arbitrary. Add らしい／ようだ for conjecture.
Wrong form: 行かないずにはいられない × → 行かずにはいられない ✓
Confusing it with ～てしまう: ～てしまう is not necessarily due to an emotion one cannot hold back.
925.notes:
• Formally a double negative, but the meaning is a strong affirmative: "cannot not V" = "will surely V".
• When the subject is someone else, add evidence: ～ようだ／～に違いない to sound less presumptuous.
• Everyday spoken language often uses the variant ～ないではいられない because it is easier to pronounce.
meaning_vi: Cannot help but…, cannot hold back/suppress…
examples: 1. ①　〈映画について〉
A: 泣いてるの？
B: だって、あのラストシーンを見たら、泣かずにはいらないよ。
2. ②　A:　何一人で笑ってるの？
B:　あの時の先生の顔を思い出すと、笑わずにはいられなくて。
explain: Used when emotions/impulses drive an action; it is natural, not intentional.
Formal written language uses ～ずにはいられない; natural spoken language uses ～ないではいられない.
Combines with emphatic adverbs: どうしても/つい/思わず/あまりに… + ～。
Avoid overusing it for actions that require reason/strong will (signing contracts, surgery…).
examples: 1. その話を聞いて、泣かないではいられなかった。
When I heard that story, I couldn't hold back my tears.
2. どうしても気になって、見ないではいられなかった。
I was so curious that I couldn't help looking.
──────
1. その映画は感動的で、涙を流さずにはいられなかった。
The movie was so moving that I couldn't help shedding tears.
2. 彼の冗談を聞くと、笑わないではいられない。
When I hear his jokes, I can't help laughing.
3. 彼女の努力を見ると、応援せずにはいられない。
When I see how hard she works, I can't help cheering her on.
4. この曲を聴くと、昔を思い出さずにはいられない。
When I listen to this song, I can't help remembering the old days.
5. 目の前に限定品があると、買わないではいられない。
When there is a limited-edition item in front of me, I can't help buying it.
6. 彼は困っている人を見ると、声をかけずにはいられないタイプだ。
He is the type who can't help speaking to people when he sees them in trouble.
──────
1. ①　この曲を聴くと、歌わないではいられなくなるんです。
2. ②　親もだいぶ年をとってきたので、私も家事を手伝わないではいられなくなった。
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
～ないではいられない | Cannot help but… (strong urge) | Spoken; spontaneous emotion. | 泣（な）かないではいられない
～ずにはいられない | Cannot help but… | Formal/written; する→せずに | 言（い）わずにはいられない
～てしまう | Accidentally/ended up… | The result happens; milder nuance. | つい買（か）ってしまった
～ずにいられない（文語（ぶんご）） | Cannot help but… | Shorter, more archaic variant. | 帰（かえ）らずにいられない
common_mistakes: • Confusing it with ～てしまう in questions that ask you to distinguish the nuances "could not hold back" vs "ended up".
• Using it for a third-person subject without adding ようだ/らしい → an unfounded conjecture.
• Wrong conjugation of する: ×しずにはいられない → correct: せずにはいられない。
meaning_vi: どうしても～しないでいることができない/自然(しぜん)に～してしまう主語(しゅご)は基本的(きほんてき)には一人称(いちにんしょう)
Cannot not do
examples: 1. もう真夜中だったが、心配で電話をしないではいらなかった。
It was already late at night, but I was so worried that I couldn't help calling.
2. 驚いた彼の顔があまりにおかしかったので、失礼だとは思ったが、笑わないではいられなかった。
His startled face was so funny that, although I knew it was rude, I couldn't help laughing.
3. 隣の家の騒音のひどさに、一言苦情を言わずにはいられないらしい。
It seems they can't help complaining about how terrible the noise from the house next door is.
4. 兄は最近酒を飲みすぎている。ストレスから飲まずにはいられないらしい。
My older brother has been drinking too much lately. It seems that, because of stress, he can't help drinking.
5. 人間は「見てはいけない」と言われると、かえって見てみずにはいられなくなるものらしい。
People, it seems, when told "Don't look," will do the opposite and simply have to look.
meaning_vi: どうしても～してしまう
（どうしても我慢できず、自然にそうなってしまうと言いたい時の表現）
End up doing… no matter what (cannot bear it no matter what; used when you want to say that it happens naturally)
explain: Note: The subject is limited to the first person. If it is the third person, the end of the sentence usually adds
examples: 1. 態度の悪い店員に、一言文句を言わないではいられなかった。
I couldn't help saying a word of complaint to the rude store clerk.
2. 工事の音がうるさくて、耳をふさがないではいられない。
The construction noise is so loud that I can't help covering my ears.
meaning_vi: どうしても～してしまう
（どうしても我慢できず、自然にそうなってしまうと言いたい時の表現）
End up doing… no matter what (cannot bear it no matter what; used when you want to say that it happens naturally)
explain: Note: The subject is limited to the first person. If it is the third person, the end of the sentence usually adds
examples: 1. 職場でいやなことがあると、酒を飲まずにはいられない。
Whenever something unpleasant happens at work, I can't help drinking
2. あの映画を見たら、だれでも感動せずにはいられないだろう。
that movie, probably no one would fail to be moved.

926.connection: V plain form + だけあって だけのことはあって / N / Na + な / Aい

examples.jp: あの店はいつも行列ができているだけあって、何を頼んでもおいしい。
examples.tr: As you'd expect from a shop that always has a line, everything you order there is delicious.

examples.jp: 若いだけあって、彼は何も恐れず、いろいろなことに挑戦した。
examples.tr: Being young, he wasn't afraid of anything and took on all kinds of challenges.

examples.jp: ドイツはビールの本場だけあって、種類が多い。
examples.tr: As you'd expect from the home of beer, Germany has many kinds.

examples.jp: あの店は有名なだけあって、いつもお客さんでいっぱいだ。
examples.tr: As you'd expect from a famous shop, it is always full of customers.

examples.jp: この歌は世界中でヒットしただけあって、歌手もメロディーもすばらしい。
examples.tr: As befits a song that became a hit all over the world, both the singer and the melody are wonderful.

examples.jp: あの子は昆虫博士といわれているだけあって、本当に虫のことには詳しい。
examples.tr: True to being called an insect expert, that child really does know a lot about bugs.

926.explain:
Used to acknowledge a reasonable cause-and-effect relationship with a nuance of "praise that is well deserved".
Often used together with さすが to emphasize the acknowledgment: さすが～だけあって...
Style: natural in both spoken and written language; suits polite contexts.
The second clause is a result that meets expectations; rarely used with commands/intentions.

• States a cause ("worthy of/truly") that leads to a reasonable result, usually praising or acknowledging value.
• Evaluation nuance: mostly positive; sometimes neutral, rarely direct criticism.
• Often used in comments on quality, ability, brands, depth of experience, status.
• Order: [Reason (characteristic)] + だけあって、[a well-deserved result].

rows: <ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いだけあって、<ruby>美味<rt>おい</rt></ruby>しい。
Emphasizes degree; can also be used with negative/contrasting results
<ruby>期待<rt>きたい</rt></ruby>しただけに、がっかりだ。
Usually placed at the end of the sentence as a comment
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>しただけのことはある。
Exclamatory adverb; can be used with だけあって

mistakes: Confusing it with ～だけに: test questions often ask you to distinguish the nuances "well-deserved praise" vs "precisely because... all the more...".
Wrong particle attached to a na-adjective: 有名だだけあって× → 有名なだけあって✓.
A command/intention in the second clause is unnatural: 高いだけあって、買いましょう×.
926.notes:
• When a noun comes before another noun: NのN + だけあって: 彼の出した論文の質は、研究者だけあって高い。
• It can still be used with a mildly negative evaluation if the result is "only natural": 都会だけあって、騒音がひどい。
• Not used for desires: 高いだけあって、買いたい× → Use a comment, not an intention.

927.meaning:
～だからやはり（当然(とうぜん)）、～だからなおさら
Because
927.connection: V plain form + だけに / N / Na + な / Aい

examples.jp: 田中さんは２０年も勤めているだけに、会社のことに詳しい。
examples.tr: Having worked there for 20 years, Mr. Tanaka knows a lot about the company.

examples.jp: 彼は子供のころ、アメリカに住んでいただけに、英語がうまい。
examples.tr: He lived in America as a child, so naturally his English is good.

examples.jp: 彼は１０年も日本にいただけに、日本事情に詳しい。
examples.tr: Having been in Japan for as long as 10 years, he knows a lot about Japanese affairs.

examples.jp: この機種は今一番人気があるだけに、なかなか手に入らないそうだ。
examples.tr: Because this model is the most popular one right now, I hear it's hard to get hold of.

examples.jp: 苦しい試合だっただけいに、、優勝できてうれしい。
examples.tr: Because it was such a tough match, I'm all the happier that we won the championship.

examples.jp: 周囲の期待が大きいだけに、失敗は許されない。
examples.tr: Precisely because everyone's expectations are so high, failure is not allowed.

927.explain: ◎ Has the form 「AだけにB」, expressing that from fact A, the assertion or result B naturally follows. Used in spoken language more than 「～だけあって」.
927.notes: Means that, contrary to the good result that would normally be expected, the opposite happened. Used when a bad result, contrary to what was expected, came about.

928.meaning: As expected…, no wonder… (worthy of the reputation/effort put in)
928.connection: V plain form + だけ(のことは)ある / N / Na + な / Aい

examples.jp: 青木さん、カナダに留学していただけのことはあって、英語がうまいね。
examples.tr: Aoki, your English is good. That's what studying abroad in Canada does for you.

examples.jp:
A: このイタリア製の靴、10万円だって。
B: へー。でも、高いだけのことはあるね。形も色すごくいい。
examples.tr:
A: These Italian shoes are 100,000 yen, apparently.
B: Wow. But they're worth the price. The shape and color are really nice.

928.notes: Means that something is worthy of the effort, status or experience. Expresses a positive evaluation of the corresponding results, ability, features, etc. (193)

929.meaning: At least…, it could be worse…
929.connection: V plain form + だけましだ / N + である / Na + な / Aい

examples.jp: 給料は低いけれど、仕事があるだけましだ。
examples.tr: The pay is low, but at least I have a job.

examples.jp: 雨に降られたが、雷がなかっただけましだ。
examples.tr: I got caught in the rain, but at least there was no thunder.

examples.jp: ミスはあったが、大事故にならなかっただけましだ。
examples.tr: There were mistakes, but at least it didn't turn into a major accident.

examples.jp: 古いアパートだが、駅に近いだけましだ。
examples.tr: It's an old apartment, but at least it's close to the station.

examples.jp: 試合には負けたが、完封されなかっただけましだ。
examples.tr: We lost the game, but at least we weren't shut out.

examples.jp: 遅刻したが、授業に出られただけましだ。
examples.tr: I was late, but at least I was able to attend the class.

929.explain:
Has a nuance of consoling oneself/seeing the minimum positive side; strongly subjective.
Often used in conversation and everyday comments; not very formal.
The first clause can state the bad side; the clause with ～だけましだ states the saving grace.

• Relative evaluation: it falls short of the desired standard, but is still better than a worse situation.
• Often implies consolation, self-consolation, or seeing the minimum positive side.
• Can be accompanied by an explicit comparison with ～だけましだ＋ほう／他と比べて..., but it is usually implicit.

rows: At least..., it could be worse...
Evaluates the current situation against a worse one
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>がやんだだけましだ。
バスより<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>のほうがまだましだ。
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れるくらいなら、<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>むほうがましだ。
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いに<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>したことはない。

mistakes: Using it for absolute praise is incorrect: "最高だ" × → ～だけましだ is relative praise, not absolute.
Wrong attachment to N/Na: Nであるだけましだ／Naなだけましだ. Avoid using Nだ/Naだ before だけましだ in written language.
Confusing it with まだまし／～ほうがましだ: exam questions often ask you to choose between a pattern of direct comparison vs one evaluating the current situation.
929.notes:
• The negative form is rare: ～だけましではない（not even "at least"） is seldom used; restructuring the sentence is preferred.
• Often combined with まあ/さすがに/せめて to strengthen the nuance: せめて無事だっただけましだ。
• In colloquial speech: だけマシ, だけでもマシ have a casual nuance.

examples.jp: 無理です。私なんかにはできっこありません。
examples.tr: It's impossible. Someone like me could never do it.

examples.jp: 相手は前回の優勝校だよ。勝てっこないって。
examples.tr: The other team won the championship last time. There's no way we can win, I'm telling you.

examples.jp: 今日中に漢字を１００字覚えるなんて無理だ。できっこない。
examples.tr: Memorizing 100 kanji by the end of today is impossible. There's no way I can do it.

examples.jp: こんな話、だれも信じてくれっこないと思う。
examples.tr: I don't think anyone would ever believe a story like this.

examples.jp: 「お母さんには私の気持なんか、分かりっこないよ」
examples.tr: "There's no way you could ever understand how I feel, Mom!"

examples.jp: 今からじゃ、間に合いっこないよ。
examples.tr: Starting now, there's no way we'll make it in time.

930.explain:
Casual, decisive tone; can sound a bit "blunt" or impolite depending on the context.
Better suited to expressing personal judgments than objective, proven facts.
Common with the verbs: 間に合う、できる、起きる/起きられる、覚える、わかる、勝つ、治る.
When you need to be polite/in writing: switch to ～はずがない・～わけがない・～可能性は低い.

• Strong negative assertion: "no way, cannot possibly, absolutely not".
• Shows the speaker's subjective conviction (confident conjecture, strong emotion).
• Used in conversation; sometimes sounds rather blunt.
• Often used with potential verbs, result verbs, and verbs expressing possibility/time.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をつくはずがない
Strong, but more neutral in politeness than っこない
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>するわけがない
っこない is stronger than ordinary negation
<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わない ＜ <ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>ごう</rt></ruby>いっこない

mistakes: Using it in formal writing: × っこありません → Use instead: ～はずがありません/～わけがありません.
Attaching to the wrong verb stem: × 覚えるっこない → correct: 覚えられっこない (use the potential).
Confusing the nuance with ～ないだけ: っこない is absolute negation, not "simply not".
JLPT multiple-choice questions often test recognition of "colloquial, strong negation" and the structure Vます＋っこない.
930.notes:
• "っこ" is a colloquial suffix that adds emphasis, also seen in other forms such as "やりっこない (rare)".
• Often appears in drama/manga dialogue to show a straightforward attitude.
• In many cases the potential form is more natural: 覚えられっこない, 起きられっこない.

931.meaning: Looks like, seems; tending toward ~, full of ~ (e.g. 水っぽい)

examples.jp: 彼女は高校生だけど、いつも大人っぽい服を着ている。
examples.tr: She's a high school student, but she always wears grown-up-looking clothes.

examples.jp: その部屋は普段、掃除をしていないみたいで、ほこりっぽかった。
examples.tr: The room didn't seem to get cleaned very often, and it was dusty.

examples.jp: 弟は飽きっぽいから、すぐ新しいものをほしがる。
examples.tr: My younger brother gets bored easily, so he's always wanting something new.

examples.jp: 年のせいか、最近、忘れっぽくなったよ。人の名前とか、ちょっとした用事とか。
examples.tr: Maybe it's my age, but I've become forgetful lately. People's names, little errands, and so on.

examples.jp: ほこりっぽい部屋
examples.tr: a dusty room

examples.jp: 白っぽい服
examples.tr: whitish clothes

931.explain:
"N + っぽい" expresses an outward appearance/general air, without asserting the actual nature.
"Vます + っぽい" turns a tendency into an adjective: 飽きっぽい（easily bored）, 怒りっぽい（quick-tempered）.
When describing people, it easily takes on a critical nuance: 子どもっぽい（childish）. Be careful in formal communication.
Expresses color/substance: 黒っぽい（blackish）, 茶色っぽい（brownish）, 油っぽい（oily/greasy）.

• Meaning 1: "similar to/like N" in appearance or general impression. Example: 子どもっぽい（childish, immature）.
• Meaning 2: "tends to V easily" (forgetful, easily bored…). Usually has a somewhat negative nuance.
• Meaning 3: "has the color/quality of N" (blackish, greasy, watery…).
• Nuance: casual, colloquial; used for impressionistic, subjective descriptions; can carry mild criticism when describing people.

rows: Attaches to emotions/character (<ruby>得意<rt>とくい</rt></ruby>げ/<ruby>寂<rt>さび</rt></ruby>しげ)
Mild, more objective than っぽい

mistakes: Using っぽい about people in formal language can be crude/impolite: ×社長は子どもっぽい → better to avoid.
Confusing it with らしい: 男っぽい（somewhat masculine-looking, may not be the real thing） ≠ 男らしい（truly manly）.
Attaching it at random to Vます is rare: ×走りっぽい（unnatural）. Only a few familiar verbs such as 忘れる/飽きる/怒る…
Misunderstanding the strength: っぽい is subjective, a feeling; it does not assert an objective fact.
931.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～みたい／～よう.
→ ～っぽい has a colloquial nuance, "seems/full of/similar to", and sometimes indicates a tendency.
2) Often carries a subjective feeling or evaluation.
→ Not formal; usually used in conversation.
3) Be careful, as it can mean "easily/often".
→ Cases like 忘れっぽい (forgetful) are tendencies and a trap for mechanical translation. meaning_vi: Overflowing, full of, steeped in ⏐ explain: Usually used in spoken language. Used to describe things, situations, or people that are imbued with a certain quality. ⏐ examples: 1. あの小学生は、大人っぽい。
That elementary school student is so grown-up.
2. この料理は油っぽくていやだ。
This dish is very oily, so I don't like it meaning_vi: Like…, similar to…, seems like… ⏐ explain: Expresses the feeling "it feels like", it seems like… ⏐ examples: 1. 年を取ると、忘れっぽくなる。
As you get older, you become forgetful.
2. このコート、デザインはいいけれど、生地が安っぽいね。
This coat has a nice design, but the fabric looks cheap, doesn't it?

examples.jp: このレポートが示すとあり、地球の人口は限界に近付きつつある。
examples.tr: As this report shows, the earth's population is approaching its limit.

examples.jp: 会社の業績は、少しずつ改善されつつある。
examples.tr: The company's performance is gradually improving.

examples.jp: 都市部で人口が増えつつある。
examples.tr: The population is increasing in urban areas.

examples.jp: オンライン教育の需要は高まりつつある。
examples.tr: Demand for online education is growing.

examples.jp: 絶滅の危機にある種は年々減りつつある。
examples.tr: Endangered species are decreasing year by year.

examples.jp: 働き方は多様化しつつある。
examples.tr: Ways of working are becoming more diverse.

932.explain:
Objective nuance, describes trends; rarely used in casual conversation.
Good with time-series data/charts: 増加しつつある傾向、低下しつつある割合.
Not used with commands, volition, or invitations.
Often accompanied by adverbs and time expressions: ますます、徐々に、次第に、年々、徐々に～しつつある.

• Expresses a trend/change that is ongoing and likely to continue in the present.
• States a transitional state, "in the process of" rather than "having reached".
• Often appears in academic language, newspapers, and reports: objective, formal.
• Often used with verbs of change: 増える、減る、広がる、進む、深まる、弱まる、安定する(しつつある).

rows: General; does not emphasize a trend of change
Doing A while doing B; although
<ruby>徐々<rt>じょじょ</rt></ruby>に/<ruby>次第<rt>しだい</rt></ruby>に + V
Adverb; can be combined with つつある
<ruby>徐々<rt>じょじょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>回復<rt>かいふく</rt></ruby>しつつある
Nothing goes in between; correct is Vます + つつある

mistakes: Wrong structure: × V辞書形＋つつある → correct: Vます(without ます)＋つつある.
Using it with punctual verbs: × 到着しつつある (if you mean "on the way", use instead: 到着に向けて進んでいる).
Confusing it with Vている: つつある emphasizes a trend of change, not just a state that is happening.
The JLPT often asks you to recognize the formal style and the combination with verbs of change.
932.notes:
• Often used with nominalization: ～しつつある＋N (例: 変化しつつある社会, 失われつつある文化).
• Combined with evaluation: ～しつつある一方で、～／～しつつあるが、～ (stating a contrast).
• In newspaper headlines: 「～が広がりつつある」 is concise, neutral, and easy to read.

examples.jp: 健康であってこそ、毎日楽しく生活することができる。
examples.tr: Only when you are healthy can you enjoy life every day.

examples.jp: 技術は使ってこそ価値がある。
examples.tr: Technology has value only when it is used.

examples.jp: 努力してこそ、夢は現実になる。
examples.tr: Only through effort do dreams become reality.

examples.jp: 親になってこそ、親の有り難みがわかる。
examples.tr: Only after becoming a parent do you truly appreciate your parents.

examples.jp: 実際に会ってこそ、相手の人柄が見えてくる。
examples.tr: Only by actually meeting someone do you begin to see their character.

examples.jp: 失敗してこそ、次に活かせる学びがある。
examples.tr: Only by failing do you gain lessons you can use next time.

933.explain:
Used when you want to affirm a “necessary and sufficient” condition in terms of experience/practice.
Carries a nuance of emphasis and persuasion; suited to written language, speeches, and expert commentary.
Unnatural when used to ask permission, give commands, or make direct requests.
The subject is usually generic/unspecified; the following sentence is a general evaluation rather than a single event.

～てこそ expresses “only when one has actually done V does…”. Emphasizes the prerequisite condition for a value/understanding/ability to truly appear.
• Exclusive implication: if V has not happened, what follows cannot yet become reality/hold true in the full sense.
• The second clause is usually: ability (～できる), awareness (～わかる), evaluation of the essence (本当の～だ), discovery (～というものだ).
• Point in time: usually about the present/future; rarely used to refer to a specific past event.
• A nuance of honoring the “true value” that only reveals itself after real experience: 会ってこそ, 苦労してこそ, 失敗してこそ, 親になってこそ…

rows: Only after V, for the first time…
More neutral; marks the “first time” point
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>してはじめて<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>づく
Emphasized reason; not necessarily an experience
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>するからこそ<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>する
～てからでないと/～てからでなければ
Necessary condition for allowing an action
<ruby>許可<rt>きょか</rt></ruby>してからでないと<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れない
Used with nouns; similar honoring nuance
<ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>あってこその<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Used for a specific past event: ×昨日会ってこそ、分かった。→ 昨日会って、初めて分かった。
Confused with ～てはじめて: ～てこそ emphasizes value/prerequisite, not just “the first time”.
Used for direct requests/advice: unnatural.
JLPT N2: often tests the distinction from ～てはじめて, ～からこそ, ～あってこそ.
933.notes:
• After ～てこそ, a specific simple past such as ～た is usually not used (though it can be used for a general truth/awareness one has come to realize: 失敗してこそ学びがあった is less natural).
• Does not combine with direct volition/commands: ×努力してこそ、頑張れ。
• The negative of this form is rare; to express a negative, use a different structure (～だけでは/～なしには…). meaning_vi: Precisely because… ⏐ explain: Means that precisely because there is A, B becomes possible. The following sentence usually has a meaning of possibility. ⏐ examples: 1. お互いに信頼してこそ、悩みも言える。
We can share our worries precisely because we trust each other.
2. 親になってこそ、親の苦労がわかる。
Only when you become a parent do you understand the hardships your parents went through.

examples.jp: 彼に会いたくてたまらない。
examples.tr: I want to see him so badly I can't stand it.

examples.jp: 虫に刺されて、かゆくてたまらない。
examples.tr: I got bitten by a bug, and it itches unbearably.

examples.jp: 結果が心配でたまらない。
examples.tr: I'm terribly worried about the results.

examples.jp: この映画が見たくてたまらない。
examples.tr: I'm dying to see this movie.

examples.jp: 彼の失礼な態度が腹立たしくてたまらない。
examples.tr: His rude attitude makes me unbearably angry.

examples.jp: 会えなくてたまらない日々が続く。
examples.tr: The days go on, unbearable because we can't see each other.

934.explain:
Strong nuance, an outburst of emotion; very natural with physical sensations.
Usable in both spoken and written language; also acceptable in formal written language.
Avoid using it with things that are fully controllable (×勉強してたまらない if you mean “I really like studying”; use 大好きだ instead).

Expresses an emotion/sensation so strong that it is “unbearable”, usually stronger than ～しょうがない, spontaneous and clearly personal.
• Often used with physical sensations: 痛い、かゆい、眠い… and strong emotions: 会いたい、悔しい、恥ずかしい。
• The preferred subject is the speaker; using it for others requires clear grounds (objective signs).
• The content is usually something that is emotionally/physically hard to control.

rows: <ruby>退屈<rt>たいくつ</rt></ruby>で(は)しょうがない
Close to しょうがない
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>くて<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない

mistakes: Wrong form: ×嬉しいでたまらない → 嬉しくてたまらない; ×静かなたまらない → 静かでたまらない.
Used for an objective fact instead of the subject's emotion/sensation → unnatural.
Mistaking it for the positive meaning “really like” can lead to using たまらない in the wrong place; consider 大好きだ/とても～.
JLPT N2: a trap distinguishing it from ～でしょうがない and ～でならない in strength and style.
934.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～てならない.
→ ～てたまらない is usually more colloquial and expresses a strong emotion/desire one cannot bear.
2) Only used for subjective emotions/states.
→ Not used for objective facts.
3) In written/formal language, ～てならない is usually chosen. explain: Extremely ~ (cannot be held back) ⏐ examples: 1. 子どものことが心配でたまらない。
I'm so worried about my child.
2. 家族に会いたくてたまらない。
I miss my family so much.

examples.jp: 熱はあるけど、大事な仕事だから、今日は這ってでも会社に行かないといけない。
examples.tr: I have a fever, but it's important work, so today I have to get to the office even if I have to crawl.

examples.jp: 電車に乗って、わざわざ言ってでも食べたいラーメンです。
examples.tr: This is ramen I want to eat even if it means taking the train and going out of my way.

examples.jp: 「若い時の苦労は買ってでもしろ」ということわざがあるが、当たっていると思う。
examples.tr: There is a proverb, “Take on hardship in your youth, even if you have to buy it,” and I think it's true.

examples.jp:
A: 課長、電車、止まってるみたいです。
B: 大事な打つ合わせだから、歩いてでも行かないと。電車はあきらめて、タクシーを拾おう。
examples.tr:
A: Section chief, it looks like the trains have stopped.
B: It's an important meeting, so we have to get there even if we walk. Let's give up on the train and catch a taxi.

935.explain: ◎ Expresses strong volition: “will do it even if it means using extreme measures”.
935.notes: Indicates forceful means. Followed by an expression of strong volition or desire, it expresses a firm resolve not to hesitate to use such extreme means in order to achieve something. （２５７）

examples.jp: 明日の試験が心配でならない。
examples.tr: I'm terribly worried about tomorrow's exam.

examples.jp: 彼が何か隠しているように思えてならない。
examples.tr: I can't help feeling that he is hiding something.

examples.jp: 今回の失敗が悔やまれてならない。
examples.tr: I deeply regret this failure.

examples.jp: 彼女の才能には不思議でならないほどの魅力がある。
examples.tr: Her talent has a charm so captivating it seems almost a mystery.

examples.jp: そのとき助けられなかったことが残念でならない。
examples.tr: I deeply regret that I couldn't help at that time.

examples.jp: 故郷のことが気になってならない。
examples.tr: I can't stop thinking about my hometown.

936.explain:
Formal nuance, used in essays, academic interviews, and narratives.
Usually expresses lingering emotions or thoughts that won't go away.
Rarely used for direct physical sensations (pain, itching) — in that case たまらない is more natural.

Expresses an emotion/perception that “cannot be avoided, keeps going on and on”, with a formal, written-language nuance. Usually used for inner psychology: worry, regret, strangeness, lingering thoughts.
• Has an “irresistible” quality but is softer than たまらない; leans toward lingering thoughts/impressions.
• Common in phrases such as: 気になってならない, 心配でならない, 残念でならない, 不思議でならない, 悔やまれてならない, ～ように思えてならない.
• The subject is usually the speaker; it can be used for others in written descriptions of someone's psychology.

rows: ～でたまらない/～てたまらない
<ruby>退屈<rt>たいくつ</rt></ruby>で(は)しょうがない
Close to しょうがない, not archaic
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない

mistakes: Wrong form: Aい→くてならない; Aな/N→でならない; V→てならない.
Used for acute physical sensations (itching, pain) → less natural than ～たまらない.
Confusing the level of formality: ～でならない is more formal than ～でしょうがない.
JLPT N2: collocation traps such as 気になってならない／悔やまれてならない.
936.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～てたまらない.
→ ～てならない is more formal and often used in written language, but the meaning is similar: a strong emotion of “cannot help…”.
2) Usually used for strong emotions/worry/regret.
→ Not used for objective facts.
3) Does not emphasize intentional actions.
→ Mainly emotions that arise naturally. meaning_vi: Extremely, very, unbearably. ⏐ explain: Expresses a state in which some emotion or feeling arises naturally and you cannot control it. In most cases, it describes a state where you cannot hold back even if you try, so the degree of emotion is also very high. ⏐ examples: 1. 親友の結婚式に出席できないのが、残念でならない。
I'm so sorry that I can't attend my best friend's wedding.
2. 検査の結果が気になってならない。
I'm terribly anxious about the test results.

examples.jp: 法律を守らねばならない。差別してはならない。
examples.tr: We must obey the law. We must not discriminate.

examples.jp: 試験中、携帯電話を使用してはならない。
examples.tr: Mobile phones must not be used during the exam.

examples.jp: 個人情報を外部に漏らしてはならない。
examples.tr: Personal information must not be leaked to outside parties.

examples.jp: 未成年者に酒類を販売してはなりません。
examples.tr: Alcoholic beverages must not be sold to minors.

examples.jp: 歴史の悲劇を繰り返してはならぬ。
examples.tr: The tragedies of history must not be repeated.

examples.jp: 管理者の許可なく施設に立ち入りてはならない。
examples.tr: You must not enter the facility without the administrator's permission.

937.explain:
Formal/written documents: rules, laws, ethical principles, official statements.
Rarely used in casual conversation; in everyday speech, ～てはいけない／ちゃいけない is used.
Often accompanied by adverbials that emphasize absoluteness: いかなる場合でも, たとえ～でも,決して.

• Absolute prohibition: “must not…”, legal/ethical/rule-based standards.
• Usually expresses general regulations, not aimed at a specific individual; the implied subject is “everyone”.
• Stronger than ～てはいけない (has the character of laws, charters, regulations, speeches).

rows: <ruby>喫煙<rt>きつえん</rt></ruby>してはならない。
ここで<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>てはいけない。
Admonition, morals; not an absolute prohibition
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>責<rt>せ</rt></ruby>めるべきではない。
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>破<rt>やぶ</rt></ruby>るものではない。

mistakes: Used for a casual personal reminder → sounds stiff/arrogant: use てはいけない instead.
Confused with べきではない: べきではない is advice; てはならない is prohibition.
Adding a subject, as in “私は～してはならない”, sounds forced in regulatory texts; the subject is usually omitted.
JLPT nuance trap: choose てはならない when “法律/規則/条約/倫理” are mentioned.
937.notes:
• Affirmative counterpart: ～ねばならない／～なければならない (must). Legal texts often contain both the affirmative and the negative.
• On signs and short texts, the subject and context can be omitted, leaving only the prohibition clause.
• 尊敬/謙譲 forms are rarely used; its normative character gives the sentence an impersonal nuance.

examples.jp: 雨が続くね。先週から降っては止み、降っては止みの繰り返しだね。
examples.tr: The rain just keeps going, doesn't it? Since last week it's been raining and stopping, raining and stopping, over and over.

examples.jp: 手紙を書いているんだけど、書いては消し、書いては消しで、なかなか書けない。
examples.tr: I'm writing a letter, but I keep writing and erasing, writing and erasing, so I can't get it done.

938.explain: ◎ Expresses the same action or state being repeated over and over.
938.notes:
meaning_vi: 行為(こうい)を（/状況(じょうきょう)が）繰(く)り返(かえ)している
Repeated actions
examples: 1. 雨が降ってはやみ、降ってはやみしている。
It rains and stops, rains and stops.
2. 書いては消し、書いては消しで、レポートがなかなか進まない。
I write and erase, write and erase, and the report just isn't making progress.
3. 冬休みは食べっては寝、食べっては寝（→食べっちゃ寝、食べっちゃ寝）で、３キロも太ってしまった。
Over winter break, I kept eating and sleeping, eating and sleeping, and ended up gaining a whole 3 kg.
4. （注）「～ては」一つだけで反復を表すこともある。
5. 彼女は毎年海外旅行に行っては、珍しい織物を買って帰ってくる。
Every year she travels abroad and comes back with rare textiles.
6. 留学のために貯金をしているのだが、なかなかたまらない。貯金通帳を見てはため息をつく毎日だ。
I'm saving money to study abroad, but it just won't build up. Every day I look at my bankbook and sigh.

examples.jp: 夫にはもう少し家事に協力してほしいものだ。
examples.tr: I wish my husband would help a little more with the housework.

examples.jp: 努力をしている人が、ちゃんと認められる社会になってほしいものです。
examples.tr: I hope we become a society where people who work hard are properly recognized.

examples.jp: 〈母親の言葉〉もう高校3年なんだから、サッカーばかりしてないで、少しは勉強してほしいものだよ。
examples.tr: 〈A mother's words〉 You're already a third-year in high school, so I wish you'd stop playing nothing but soccer and study at least a little.

examples.jp:
A: ガソリン、去年からずっと高いね。
B: うん。もう少し安くなってほしいもんだね。
examples.tr:
A: Gas has been expensive ever since last year, hasn't it?
B: Yeah. I wish it would get a little cheaper.

939.explain: ◎ An expression conveying the feeling “not expecting much, but still hoping”.

940.meaning: To the extent of…, even going so far as to…

examples.jp: 整形してまで有名になりたいとは思わない。
examples.tr: I don't want to be famous badly enough to go as far as getting plastic surgery.

examples.jp: 借金してまで旅行に行くものではない。
examples.tr: You shouldn't go so far as to borrow money to go on a trip.

examples.jp: 彼は泣いてまで許しを乞うた。
examples.tr: He even went so far as to cry to beg for forgiveness.

examples.jp: 徹夜までして論文を仕上げた。
examples.tr: I even stayed up all night to finish the paper.

examples.jp: 嘘をついてまで評価を上げたいのか。
examples.tr: Do you want to raise your evaluation so badly that you'd even lie?

examples.jp: 彼女は人脈を使いてまで企画を通した。
examples.tr: She even used her connections to get the project approved.

940.explain:
Usually goes with a negative judgment/dissuasion: ～てまで…ない／～てまでするな.
When praising someone's volition, add a positive context to avoid it being understood as criticism.
N + までして highlights extreme means (徹夜、借金、嘘、中傷…).

• Expresses an extreme degree: “going so far as to… (usually an undesirable/excessive method)”.
• An implication of criticism/disapproval is the default. For praise/strong volition, a clear context is needed.
• The agent is usually the same person for both action A and goal B.

rows: Going so far as to do A
Focuses on a noun as the means
Even if it means doing A, still…
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>までして<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>る<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない。

mistakes: Confused with ～てでも: if the question praises volition → choose てでも; if it criticizes excess → choose てまで.
Used for ordinary (non-extreme) actions → unnatural.
Different subjects for A and B → the sentence becomes vague/nonstandard.
Tests often set traps with Nまでして vs Vてまで: look at whether what follows まで is して or まで to decide.
940.notes:
• Accompanying words often carry a negative nuance: 嘘、借金、徹夜、犠牲、中傷、違法、裏切り.
• In some emotional contexts the nuance can flip to admiration, but ambiguity should be avoided in academic writing.
• Position: Aてまで + main V. Do not use “BてまでA” when A is the goal; the focus easily becomes wrong.

941.meaning: Will do it and show you

examples.jp: 難しくても、必ず合格してみせる。
examples.tr: No matter how hard it is, I'll definitely pass. Just watch.

examples.jp: このマジック、もう一度やってみせます。
examples.tr: I'll perform this magic trick for you once more.

examples.jp: 彼女をもう一度笑わせてみせる。
examples.tr: I'll make her smile again, you'll see.

examples.jp: 医者に症状を再現してみせた。
examples.tr: I demonstrated my symptoms for the doctor.

examples.jp: 誰にもできないと言われたが、やり遂げてみせた。
examples.tr: I was told no one could do it, but I proved them wrong and pulled it off.

examples.jp: サンバって、どういうふうに踊るんですか。ちょっと踊っみせてください。
examples.tr: How do you dance the samba? Please show me a little.

941.explain:
Used when you want to affirm your ability/volition, or when actually “demonstrating something”.
Strong nuance; in formal situations it can be changed to みせます to be polite.
Usually directed at the listener as a declaration/challenge/encouragement.
Not used to ask permission/make suggestions. For the meaning “try”, use ～てみる.

• Meaning 1 (demonstration/proof): “do it and show”, an action that takes place right before one's eyes to prove one's ability.
• Meaning 2 (resolve/commitment): “will definitely … , you'll see”, a promise, vow, or challenge.
• The subject is usually the speaker; strong nuance, sometimes a bit boastful/proud.
• Different from ～てみる (try doing): ～てみせる is not “trying” but “doing it for sure, to prove it”.

rows: Do and show / Resolve to do
No emphasis on certainty; merely experimental.
Intend to do, attempt to do
Describes effort/intention, without the “show you” nuance.
<ruby>必<rt>かなら</rt></ruby>ず<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Confused with ～てみる: choose ～てみせる when you mean “for sure/show you”, not “try”.
Used to ask someone else to do something: unnatural. ～てみせてください is the polite request.
Used for an action that cannot happen right before one's eyes (e.g., something in the distant future) with a concrete “show” nuance: use the resolve meaning, not demonstration.
In JLPT questions, the sentence comes with adverbs of resolve such as 必ず、絶対に, or a context of challenge.
941.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～てやる／～てあげる.
→ ～てみせる emphasizes “I'll do it and show you”, expressing volition/a display of resolve.
2) Usually carries a nuance of resolve or challenge.
→ Often used when you want to prove your ability.
3) Not the “try doing” pattern (～てみる).
→ An easy trap because of the shared “み”.

942.meaning: It's not too much to ~ / it's all right even if ~

examples.jp: 熱が下がれば、お風呂に入ってもさしつかえないですよ。
examples.tr: Once your fever goes down, it's fine to take a bath.

examples.jp: 彼がいなければ、この作品は生まれなかったといってもさしつかえない。
examples.tr: It's no exaggeration to say that without him, this work would never have been created.

examples.jp: この内容なら、そのまま放送してもさしつかえない。
examples.tr: With this content, it's fine to broadcast it as it is.

examples.jp:
A: 検査の前の晩は、何も飲めないんですか。
B: いえ、水やお茶なら、飲んでもさしつかえありません。
examples.tr:
A: Can't I drink anything the night before the test?
B: No, water or tea is fine to drink.

942.explain: ◎ A formal expression meaning that it is not too much to affirm it.
942.notes: Both 「…てもさしつかえない」 and 「…なくてもさしつかえない」 are used. A concessive expression meaning that the condition shown with 「…ても」 is fine and causes no problem. It is also said as 「さしつかえはない」. Close to 「てもいい」 and 「てもかまわない」, but it is normally used in more formal situations than these two. （２８１）

examples.jp: 彼は学校始まって以来の秀才と言われていた。
examples.tr: He was said to be the most brilliant student since the school was founded.

examples.jp: 犬を飼って以来、毎朝の散歩が日課になった。
examples.tr: Ever since I got a dog, a morning walk has become part of my daily routine.

examples.jp: 彼に会ったのは、大学を卒業して以来です。
examples.tr: This is the first time I've seen him since I graduated from university.

examples.jp: 日本へ来て以来、忙しくてまだ一度も帰国していない。
examples.tr: Since coming to Japan, I've been so busy that I haven't gone back home even once.

examples.jp: 子どもが生まれて以来、家の中ではたばこを吸わないようにしている。
examples.tr: Ever since my child was born, I've made a point of not smoking in the house.

examples.jp: この薬を飲みはじめて以来、体の調子がどんどん良くなってきた。
examples.tr: Since I started taking this medicine, my health has been getting better and better.

943.explain: Expresses a state, habit, or event that has continued from a point in time in the past up to the present.
943.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～てから.
→ ～て以来 emphasizes a state/habit that lasts from a point in the past up to the present.
2) The second clause is usually a continuing state.
→ It does not just indicate chronological order.
3) Not used for events that have already ended.
→ If you are only describing a sequence, use ～てから.

examples.jp: 約束を破ったのだから、信用を失って当然だ。
examples.tr: Having broken a promise, it's only natural to lose people's trust.

examples.jp: あれだけ練習したんだ、優勝して当然だ。
examples.tr: After practicing that much, it's only natural to win the championship.

examples.jp: 突然の別れで、悲しくて当然だ。
examples.tr: It was a sudden parting, so it's only natural to feel sad.

examples.jp: 違法行為には厳しい処分が下って当然だ。
examples.tr: It's only natural that illegal acts receive severe punishment.

examples.jp: 台風だったのだから、電車が遅れたのは当然だ。
examples.tr: There was a typhoon, so naturally the trains were late.

examples.jp: そんな態度では、上司に叱られて当然だ。
examples.tr: With an attitude like that, it's no wonder you get scolded by your boss.

944.explain:
Emphasizes a reasonable cause-and-effect relationship. Avoid overusing it in sensitive situations so as not to seem lacking in sympathy.
When praising/giving a positive evaluation: “して当然だ” = “deserves to”.
Compared with 当たり前だ, 当然だ is more formal and leans toward logical reasoning.

• An evaluation of something as “natural/obvious”, based on common sense, rules, or cause-and-effect relationships.
• Often carries a nuance of criticism when the subject suffers an unfavorable result: “deserves to be…”.
• When talking about natural emotions: “it's natural to be sad”, a degree of sympathy, no judgment.

rows: <ruby>批判<rt>ひはん</rt></ruby>されて<ruby>当然<rt>とうぜん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れたのは<ruby>当然<rt>とうぜん</rt></ruby>だ。
～のももっともだ／～も<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>はない
<ruby>怒<rt>おこ</rt></ruby>るのも<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>はない。
A normative recommendation, not a consequence
Colloquial, less formal than <ruby>当然<rt>とうぜん</rt></ruby>だ

mistakes: Using 当然だ for someone else's emotions without context → sounds judgmental; consider using 無理はない.
Confusing the “should” relation (べき) with “consequence” (当然): if the question has a clear cause → choose 当然だ.
Wrong form: なA/N + で当然だ (do not use に/は).
The example sentence “勝って当然だチームだ” needs to be split: 勝って当然だ。強いチームだ。
944.notes:
• Goes with verbs that have social consequences: 評価される／非難される／罰せられる／称賛される.
• Inverting the predicate with a noun: N + で当然だ (彼が優勝して当然だチーム＝sounds forced; it is better to split the sentence to make it natural).
• In essays, 当然だ helps wrap up an argument after sufficient grounds have been presented.

945.meaning: It is not necessarily the case that ~
945.connection: V/A plain form + というものでもない / N・Na + (だ)

examples.jp: 安ければいいと言うものでもありません。もちろん、中身も見ます。
examples.tr: Cheap isn't necessarily good. Of course, I look at the contents too.

examples.jp: 薬を飲めば治るというものでもありません。いろいろな生活改善が必要です。
examples.tr: Taking medicine won't necessarily cure you. Various lifestyle improvements are needed.

examples.jp: 美人だから幸せになれるというものでもない。
examples.tr: Being beautiful doesn't necessarily mean you'll be happy.

examples.jp: 物価が安くなるのはうれしいけど、何でも安くなればいいというものでもない。
examples.tr: I'm glad prices are going down, but it's not as if anything getting cheaper is a good thing.

945.explain: ◎ Expresses the idea “one cannot say for certain that it is so”.

examples.jp: 親というものはいつも子供のことを心配しているものです。
examples.tr: Parents are always worried about their children.

examples.jp: 幸運というものは、追いかけると逃げていくものです。
examples.tr: Good fortune is something that runs away when you chase it.

examples.jp: 子供というものは、親のまねをするものです。
examples.tr: Children imitate their parents.

examples.jp: 人生というものは、思い通りに行かないものです。
examples.tr: Life doesn't go the way you want it to.

946.explain: ◎ An expression that defines something, accompanied by a sense of exclamation.

examples.jp: ここは、黄色やオレンジといった、明るい色の方がいいです。
examples.tr: Here, bright colors such as yellow or orange would be better.

examples.jp: サッカーや野球といったボールを使ったスポーツが得意です。
examples.tr: I'm good at sports that use a ball, such as soccer and baseball.

examples.jp: 今年の夏は青やオレンジといった、鮮やかな色が流行している。
examples.tr: This summer, vivid colors such as blue and orange are in fashion.

examples.jp: この学生寮にはベトナムやインドネシアといった、倒産アジアからの学生大勢住んでいる
examples.tr: Many students from Southeast Asia, such as Vietnam and Indonesia, live in this student dormitory.

examples.jp: この奨学金を申請するためには、成績証明書や教授の推薦書といった書類が必要だ。
examples.tr: To apply for this scholarship, documents such as an academic transcript and a professor's letter of recommendation are required.

examples.jp: オーストラリアにはコアラやカンガルーといった、珍しい動物がたくさんいる。
examples.tr: Australia has many rare animals, such as koalas and kangaroos.

947.explain: ◎ An expression giving concrete examples, meaning “such as ~” “what is called ~”.
947.notes: Used to list examples. It implies that these are not all and that there are others as well.

948.connection: [sentence/clause in plain form] + とか / N + とか

examples.jp: 「あの家を建てるのに１億円以上かかっているとか。」「へー、そうなんだ。」
examples.tr: "I hear it cost over 100 million yen to build that house." "Wow, really?"

examples.jp: 彼女は今度の連休に温泉に行くとか言っていた。
examples.tr: She said something about going to a hot spring over the upcoming long weekend.

examples.jp: 〈手紙〉お元気ですか。こちらは皆元気です。原さんに聞きましたが、幸子さんは来月京都に来られるとか。ぜひ、こちらにもお立ち寄りください。
examples.tr: <Letter> How are you? Everyone here is well. I heard from Mr. Hara that you, Sachiko, are coming to Kyoto next month. Please be sure to stop by and see us too.

examples.jp: 「あしたの英語の授業は休みだとか聞いたけど、本当？」
examples.tr: "I heard tomorrow's English class is canceled or something. Is that true?"

examples.jp: お母様が入院なさったとか。具合はいかがですか。（手紙）
examples.tr: I heard your mother was hospitalized. How is she doing? (letter)

examples.jp: 駅で人身事故があったとかで電車が止まり、遅刻してしまった。
examples.tr: The train stopped because of some accident involving a person at the station, apparently, and I ended up being late.

948.explain:
Non-exhaustive listing, implying "there are many other things too".
Hearsay with sentence-final "とか": reduces the speaker's responsibility for the statement and shows a lack of certainty.
In conversation, "とかさ/とかって" may also appear to emphasize the colloquial tone.
Do not use too many "とか" in a row in written language, as it feels wordy/unclear.

- Listing: Gives a few typical examples without covering everything; suggestive, loose, and casual.
- Hearsay: "とか" at the end of a sentence expresses a vague source of information; the speaker does not assert it with certainty (I hear, apparently).
- With "とかで": indicates a vague cause; the speaker does not know exactly (something like "because of something like…").
- Politeness level: fairly colloquial; avoid it in formal documents where high precision is needed.

rows: <ruby>寿司<rt>すし</rt></ruby>や<ruby>天ぷら<rt>てんぷら</rt></ruby>
More formal than とか in written language
Neutral, more objective than とか
Even more casual than とか
<ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>とかで<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using "とか" in formal writing/academic presentations → sounds unserious. Replace with や/など/によると～そうだ.
Confusing "とか" (listing) with "とかで" (reason). "とかで" needs to be followed by a verb showing a result: 中止になった/遅れた.
Using "とか" for hearsay but then asserting strongly → a contradiction in nuance. If you are certain, use ～と聞いた/～そうだ.
Overusing "とか" in a row makes the sentence choppy; pick 1–2 typical items.
948.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～という／～って.
→ ～とか is usually used to pass on information you heard but are not sure of, or for vague quotation.
2) Common in conversation/letters.
→ A light "I heard that…" nuance, not an assertion.
3) Not used when the source of information is certain.
→ To convey something more certainly, use ～ということだ／～そうだ.

examples.jp: 駅のホームで押されて、あやうく線路に落ちるところだった。
examples.tr: I was pushed on the station platform and almost fell onto the tracks.

examples.jp: 出かけるとき急いでいたので、もう少しでさいふを忘れるところだった。
examples.tr: I was in a hurry when I went out, so I nearly forgot my wallet.

examples.jp: 彼女が注意してくれなかったら、だまされるところだった。
examples.tr: If she hadn't warned me, I would have been tricked.

examples.jp: （試験のとき）あと少しで書き終わるところだったのに、ベルが鳴ってしまった。
examples.tr: (During an exam) I was just about to finish writing, but the bell rang.

examples.jp: 高橋選手はもう少しで正選手になれるところだったのだが、事故でけがをして、引退してしまった。
examples.tr: Takahashi was very close to becoming a regular player, but he was injured in an accident and ended up retiring.

examples.jp: もう少しで電車に乗り遅れるところだった。
examples.tr: I almost missed the train.

949.explain:
Expresses an action that almost happened but was avoided in the end. Usually used for undesirable situations.
Expresses something that was almost achieved or almost happened but did not succeed in the end, with a feeling of regret.

• Expresses something that "almost happened" right at that moment but in the end did NOT happen.
• Two directions:

Vるところだった：almost did X (but avoided it).
Vないところだった：almost did NOT do X (but did it in the end).

• Vるところだった：almost did X (but avoided it).
• Vないところだった：almost did NOT do X (but did it in the end).
• Often used with もう少しで, 危うく, 今にも to emphasize the "almost".
• Different from ～そうになった: ～ところだった emphasizes the critical moment; ～そうになった emphasizes "nearly" changing into a state.

rows: <ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わないところだった
Emphasizes nearly changing state; not necessarily "at the last minute"
In the middle of an action

mistakes: Using it when the event actually happened: wrong for the meaning "almost".
Confusing it with Vるところだ (about to do) and Vたところだ (just did): different tense and meaning.
Confusing it with ～そうになった: if the question asks for "almost" emphasizing the critical moment → prefer ～ところだった.
Forgetting the negative in "almost not": ×間に合うところだった（almost not in time）→ correct: 間に合わないところだった。
949.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～そうになった／～かけた.
→ ～ところだった means "nearly…" and is usually used for undesirable situations.
2) Often carries the nuance "luckily it didn't happen".
→ Emphasizes a close call that nearly had consequences.
3) Note the other meaning in your data (ghichu=2).
→ If you want to record a separate trap for the ghichu=2 meaning, you should add an update for ct ghichu=2.

950.connection: V (plain form) + ところを見ると

examples.jp: 仕事を１週間も休んでいるところを見ると、かなり体調が悪いようだ。
examples.tr: Judging from the fact that he's been off work for a whole week, he must be in pretty bad health.

examples.jp: 何も言わないところをみると、社長も反対ではないみたいだ。
examples.tr: Judging from the fact that he isn't saying anything, the company president doesn't seem to be against it either.

examples.jp: 〈母親が子供に〉宿題はもう済んだの？･･･黙っているところをみると、まだなのね。早くやりなさい。
examples.tr: <Mother to child> Have you finished your homework yet? ... Judging from your silence, you haven't. Hurry up and do it.

examples.jp: いつも行列ができているところをみると、きっとおいしい店に違いない。
examples.tr: Judging from the fact that there's always a line, it must be a good restaurant.

950.explain: ◎ Expresses conjecture, with the sense of "judging from the actual situation ~".
950.notes:
Used when the speaker states a conjecture based on direct experience. 「らしい／ようだ／にちがいない」 and the like are often used at the end of the sentence. The form 「…ところからみて」 is also sometimes used.
* (Example) 高級車に乗っているところからみて、相当の金持ちらしい。

examples.jp: 雨だとしても、試合は予定どおり行います。
examples.tr: Even if it rains, the game will be held as scheduled.

examples.jp: 失敗するとしても、挑戦してみたい。
examples.tr: Even if I fail, I want to give it a try.

examples.jp: 彼が本当のことを言ったとしても、すぐには信じられない。
examples.tr: Even if he did tell the truth, I can't believe him right away.

examples.jp: 値段が高いとしても、品質を選びます。
examples.tr: Even if the price is high, I'll choose quality.

examples.jp: 学生だとしても、責任は負うべきだ。
examples.tr: Even if you're a student, you should take responsibility.

examples.jp: （もし）引っ越すとしても
examples.tr: (Supposing) even if I do move

951.explain:
Emphasizes that "the result/position does not change".
Suitable for argument and rebuttal: "Granted that…, but…".
Can be used with both realistic and far-fetched suppositions; more formal nuance than ～ても.
Often combined with たとえ for emphasis: たとえ～としても.

• Concession: even if supposition X is true, result/opinion Y still does not change.
• Used both for unlikely suppositions and for temporarily granting a point for the sake of argument.
• Often used with expressions of strong determination/opinion: ～買う／～変わらない／～構わない／～挑戦したい.

rows: Formal, argumentative; result does not change
たとえ<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けても<ruby>学<rt>まな</rt></ruby>ぶ
<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>にしても<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>いすぎだ
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けないとしたら<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Confusing it with ～としたら: a sentence that needs the nuance "even if" must use ～としても.
Dropping だ with N/na in written language: × 学生としても (ambiguous) → 〇 学生だとしても.
Using it when the result actually depends on the condition: if the result changes, do not use ～としても.
The JLPT often sets traps with the pairs たとえ/仮に + ～としても/～ても: choose the natural pair.
951.notes:
• With N/na, keep だ in written language: N/na + だとしても.
• Often used in counterarguments: たとえAとしても、B（Aを認めつつB）.
• In speeches, used for a "strategic concession" before asserting an opinion.

examples.jp: 彼の作品は、一つとして容易に理解できるものはない。
examples.tr: Not a single one of his works is easy to understand.

examples.jp: 私が仕事を辞めた本当の理由は、誰一人として知らない。
examples.tr: Not a single person knows the real reason I quit my job.

examples.jp: 事故から10年になりますが、一日として思い出さない日はありません。
examples.tr: It's been ten years since the accident, but not a single day goes by that I don't think of it.

examples.jp: この謎を解こうと多くの研究者が試みたが、誰一人として成功していない。
examples.tr: Many researchers have tried to solve this mystery, but not one of them has succeeded.

952.explain: ◎ Expresses total negation: "not any one at all".
952.notes:
Follows words with 「一」 that express a minimal quantity, such as 「一日」「一時（いっとき）」「（だれ）一人」「（何）一つ」, and is followed by the negative form of the predicate, meaning 「全然…ない」 (not … at all). When it is used with interrogatives such as 「なに」「だれ」, 「として」 can be omitted.
* (Example) だれ一人、私の発言を支持してくれる人はいなかった。It is a somewhat written-language expression; in spoken language, phrasing like 「一人も…ない」 is usual.

953.meaning: If it comes to…, if that's the case…

examples.jp: 来週の月曜日が締め切りとなると、急がないといけない。
examples.tr: If the deadline is next Monday, we have to hurry.

examples.jp: 彼がいけないとなると、じゃ、誰が行くことになるんだろう？
examples.tr: If he can't go, then who's going to end up going?

examples.jp: 引っ越すとなると、かなりお金がかかりますね。
examples.tr: If you're going to move, it'll cost quite a lot of money.

examples.jp: 海外勤務となると、家族のことも考えないといけない。
examples.tr: If it means working overseas, I have to think about my family too.

examples.jp: 試験となると、彼は急に緊張する。
examples.tr: When it comes to exams, he suddenly gets nervous.

examples.jp: 明日出張となると、今日は早めに帰らないと。
examples.tr: If I'm going on a business trip tomorrow, I need to go home early today.

953.explain:
Used when: stating a condition and then immediately discussing the consequences/what needs to be dealt with.
The second clause often contains:費用がかかる、時間が必要だ、手続きが増える、難しい、無理だ、見直しだ.
Topic-shift nuance: "A となると、(話は)～" as a framework for reasoning.
More objective than となったら; carries little personal volition, usually a general judgment/consequence.

• Main meaning: "When it comes to A, B will arise". Focuses on recognizing the situation and discussing the consequences and issues to consider.
• Nuance: more objective than となったら; often used to state difficulties, costs, constraints, requirements, etc. in the second clause.
• Often appears in conversation/negotiations when moving from a premise to analyzing the consequences.
• The second clause is rarely a direct personal desire; usually an evaluation, conjecture, obligation, or inevitability.

rows: <ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>となると、<ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>するとなったら、<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby><ruby>開始<rt>かいし</rt></ruby>だ。
If it were the case/came to A, ...
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>となれば、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>避<rt>さ</rt></ruby>けられない。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くとすると、<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby><ruby>時<rt>じ</rt></ruby>？
Topic association, no emphasis on consequences
<ruby>春<rt>はる</rt></ruby>というと、<ruby>桜<rt>さくら</rt></ruby>だね。

mistakes: Confusing it with というと/といえば (association) – となると talks about consequences to be dealt with, not just calling up an association.
Using となると to express a strong personal desire (～したい) sounds forced; turn it into an obligation/suggestion (～しないと/～すべきだ).
JLPT context trap: when the second clause is "費用・手続き・見直し・困る", the answer is usually となると.
953.notes:
• Emphatic expressions: ～となると、話は別だ／大問題だ／厄介だ.
• Expresses "whenever ..., ..." for habits/traits: N となると～ (試合となると燃えるタイプだ).
• Suitable in work discussions when listing requirements arising from a premise.
• Do not overuse it for direct commands to the listener; an obligation/recommendation form sounds more natural.

954.connection: V/A (plain form) + とはいうものの / N・Na + (だ)

examples.jp: 面接会場がうちから近いとはいうものの、当日は早めに家を出るつもりだ。
examples.tr: Although the interview venue is close to my house, I plan to leave home early on the day.

examples.jp: 時間がなかったからとはいうものの、このレポートはひどすぎる。
examples.tr: Granted you didn't have time, but this report is just too awful.

examples.jp: 3月とはいうものの、まだまだ寒い日が続きますね。
examples.tr: Although it's March, the cold days are still continuing, aren't they?

examples.jp: 工場の火災は、大きな事故にならなかったとはいうものの、周辺住民に大変な不安を与えた。
examples.tr: Although the factory fire did not turn into a major accident, it caused great anxiety among nearby residents.

examples.jp: 勝ち負けは関係ないとはいうものの、負ければ、やっぱり悔しい。
examples.tr: Although winning or losing doesn't matter, it's still frustrating when you lose.

954.explain: ◎ Expresses the feeling "it is ~, but even so ~" or "I acknowledge that fact, but that alone is not enough".

examples.jp: 忙しくて、海外どころか、近くの温泉にも行けない。
examples.tr: I'm so busy I can't even go to a nearby hot spring, let alone abroad.

examples.jp: 彼は謝るどころか、文句を言っていたそうだ。
examples.tr: I heard that, far from apologizing, he was complaining.

examples.jp: 勉強が忙しくて、友達と遊ぶどころか、家でテレビを見る時間もない。
examples.tr: I'm so busy studying that I don't even have time to watch TV at home, let alone hang out with friends.

examples.jp: のどが痛くて、ご飯を食べるどころか水も飲めない。
examples.tr: My throat hurts so much that I can't even drink water, let alone eat.

examples.jp: この絵は１００万円した。しかし私はこの絵には１００万円どころか２００万円の価値があると思う。
examples.tr: This painting cost 1,000,000 yen. But I think it's worth not just 1,000,000 yen but 2,000,000 yen.

examples.jp: 評判の映画を見に行ったのだが、面白いどころか退屈で、途中で帰ってしまった。
examples.tr: I went to see a popular movie, but far from being interesting, it was boring, and I left partway through.

955.explain:
Emphasizes the big gap between expectation (A) and reality (B).
Often has a nuance of dissatisfaction or criticism, but can also be used in the direction of "much better".
Not used with direct commands/volition. Usually description/evaluation.
After N/Aな, keep the correct form: Aな＋な＋どころか.

- Expresses a fact completely contrary to the expectation/assumption A: "Far from A / let alone A, (actually) B…".
- Two basic uses:
1) "Let alone A, even B (a lower/more basic level) is not/was …".
2) "Not only not A, but on the contrary B (opposite)."
- Often used with pairs of antonyms or degree scales to emphasize the gap.

rows: <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かどころかうるさい
About a situation where A is impossible
Even A… (the second clause is a more obvious level)
<ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby>はおろか<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>も…
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>どころか<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>まで

mistakes: Confusing it with どころではない (not the time to do A) → different meaning. Read the context carefully: "not the time" vs "quite the opposite/let alone".
Missing "な" before どころか with Aな: ×便利どころか → ◯便利などころか.
Wrong degree logic: A must be the expected/lighter level compared with B. Example: ×難しいどころか簡単だ (possible, but consider whether the context is a strong flip).
Using it for commands/suggestions → unnatural. Avoid: ×勉強するどころか早くしろ。
955.notes:
- When A is a positive expectation, use どころか to flip it strongly to negative (or the reverse). Example: 安いどころか高い（flip）.
- Often combined with まで/さえ/も to increase the contrast: AどころかBまで～.
- In written speeches, the form Aどころか、むしろBだ may be seen to make the contrast clear.

examples.jp: 母親が入院したので、旅行に行くどころではなくなった。
examples.tr: My mother was hospitalized, so going on a trip was out of the question.

examples.jp: 忙しくて、人の世話をするどころではない。
examples.tr: I'm so busy that I'm in no position to look after other people.

examples.jp: 今日はあまりに忙しくて、食事どころではなかった。
examples.tr: I was so busy today that I had no time to even think about eating.

examples.jp: 母が手術をすることになり、心配で勉強どころではない。
examples.tr: My mother has to have surgery, and I'm too worried to study.

examples.jp: 「今度の土曜日に映画でも見に行かない？」
examples.tr: "Do you want to go see a movie or something this Saturday?"

examples.jp: 「ごめん、試験で、それどころじゃないんだ」
examples.tr: "Sorry, I have exams, so I can't even think about that right now."

956.explain:
Meaning 1 usually goes with Vる/Vている and nouns for activities:遊ぶ、休む、旅行、花見…
Meaning 2 emphasizes seriousness/going far beyond the normal level:痛いどころではない, ミスどころではない…
Strongly colloquial nuance; still usable in formal written language.
Not followed by volition/commands to the listener; mainly an objective judgment about the situation.

• Meaning 1 (common): It is not the time/there are no conditions to do ~ because the situation does not allow it. Carries a nuance of urgency, busyness, or a serious situation.
• Meaning 2: "Far from ~ / not ~ at all", emphasizing a degree far beyond expectations or complete opposition.
• Unlike simple negation, ～どころではない focuses on "the context/situation does not allow it" or "a very different degree".
• Often used with situational nouns: 暇, 冗談, 笑い事, 花見, 旅行, ボーナス…

rows: <ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しくて<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>ぶどころではない
Not only not ~, but on the contrary…
Strong contrastive comparison; presents two opposite clauses
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>がやむどころか、<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>くなった
～ている<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>ではない
Close to Meaning 1; a warning, blunt nuance
<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>んでいる<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>ではない
Partial negation; no focus on the situation
～どころの<ruby>騒<rt>さわ</rt></ruby>ぎではない
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいどころの<ruby>騒<rt>さわ</rt></ruby>ぎではない

mistakes: Confusing it with ～どころか: if there are two clearly contrasting clauses, use どころか; if you only mean "not the time/far from ~", use どころではない.
Attaching the wrong verb form: both Vる/Vている are possible, but for the situation "in the middle of doing ~, it's not the time" Vている is usually used.
Using it for the listener's volition is incorrect: × 遊ぶどころではないから、遊びなさい.
Overusing it with na-adjectives: it is more natural with nouns/situational expressions.
956.notes:
• To emphasize an urgent point in time, use the past: ～どころではなかった.
• With abstract nouns: 笑い事どころではない, 人手不足どころではない… very natural in the news.
• In casual conversation the contracted form can be used: ～どころじゃない.

957.meaning:
～なければ・・・ない
Unless... cannot

examples.jp: 議長が来ないことには懐疑は始められない。
examples.tr: Unless the chairperson comes, the meeting can't begin.

examples.jp: 実際に会ってみないことには、どんな人かわからないと思う。
examples.tr: I don't think you can tell what kind of person someone is unless you actually meet them.

examples.jp: 「テストを受けてもらわないことには、あなたのレベルがわかりません」
examples.tr: "Unless you take the test, we can't tell your level."

examples.jp: 「どんなに具合が悪くても、私が家事をしないことには家の中がめちゃめちゃになってしまうんです」
examples.tr: "No matter how sick I am, if I don't do the housework, the house becomes a complete mess."

examples.jp: あの二人が来ないことには、パーティーを始められない。
examples.tr: Unless those two come, we can't start the party.

examples.jp:
A: どう？直せそう？
B: うーん、やってないことには、わからないなあ。
examples.tr:
A: How is it? Can you fix it?
B: Hmm, I can't tell unless I try.

957.notes: In the form 「ＸないことにはＹない」, it means that Y will not happen unless X happens. X expresses a necessary condition for Y. It can be paraphrased as 「なければ」「なくては」.（１２２）

958.meaning: Somehow manage to; I wish…, isn't there any way to…

examples.jp: なんとかそのツアーに参加できないものか、旅行会社に相談した。
examples.tr: I consulted a travel agency to see if there was any way I could join that tour.

examples.jp: もっといい方法がないものかと色々調べていたら、あった。
examples.tr: I was looking into various things, wondering if there wasn't a better way, and I found one.

examples.jp:
A: カレーライス、もっと簡単に作れないものかなあ。
B: すぐ楽をしようとする。
examples.tr:
A: I wish there were an easier way to make curry rice.
B: You always want to take the easy way out.

examples.jp:
A: ここはいつも混雑してるね。
B: うん。もうちょっと何とかならないものかね。
examples.tr:
A: It's always crowded here, isn't it?
B: Yeah. I wish something could be done about it.

958.explain: ◎ Expresses the feeling of searching for some way to accomplish something difficult.
958.notes:
meaning_vi: isn't there any way to ～, I wish ～ ⏐ explain: Expresses the desire to accomplish something or find some solution in a difficult situation.
Formal sentence. ⏐ examples: 1. 最近、変なメールがたくさん来る。どうにかならないものか。
Lately I've been getting a lot of strange emails. I wish I could do something about it.
2. デジカメが壊れた。（なんとか） 直らないものだろうか。
My digital camera broke. I wish I could fix it.

examples.jp: 彼の言うことが正しいと思いながら、つい反対してしまった。
examples.tr: Even though I thought what he said was right, I ended up opposing it.

examples.jp: 弟は、食事の後に勉強すると言いながら、まだテレビを見ている。
examples.tr: My younger brother said he would study after dinner, but he's still watching TV.

examples.jp: スマホをいじりながら歩くのは危ない。
examples.tr: Walking while fiddling with your smartphone is dangerous.

examples.jp: 彼は歌いながら料理を作る。
examples.tr: He cooks while singing.

examples.jp: 知りながら、何も言わなかった。
examples.tr: Although I knew, I didn't say anything.

examples.jp: 残念ながら、今回は見送らせてください。
examples.tr: Unfortunately, please allow me to decline this time.

959.explain:
The following action is the main action, the focus of the sentence. Example: "音楽を聞きながら勉強する" → the main action is "studying".
Often used in daily life, casual conversation, or simple written language.
Used only when the two actions are performed by the same person/same agent.
Not used with opposing actions or actions that cannot happen at the same time (✕泳ぎながら寝る).

• Simultaneity: Expresses two actions happening at the same time by the same agent. The action in the main clause is the focus; the ～ながら clause is the background.
• Concession: "Although …, …". Emphasizes the contradiction between the two clauses, usually knowing but not doing/being unable to.
• Restriction: Not used for two different subjects; avoid using it in the sense of simultaneity with momentary actions (一回性) that are hard to do in parallel, such as 立つ・着く.

rows: Fairly neutral; used in both spoken and written language.
<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聴<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する
More formal/written; rarely used in spoken language.
<ruby>反省<rt>はんせい</rt></ruby>しつつ<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>ける
<ruby>不十分<rt>ふじゅうぶん</rt></ruby>ながらも<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>した
No implication of simultaneity; purely contradiction.
<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っているのに<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>わない

mistakes: Wrong subject: using ながら when the two actions are done by two different people is incorrect.
Confusing it with ～ながらも (a pattern expressing contradiction, not simultaneity).
Not dropping ます: the correct form is Vます → V(drop ます) + ながら (✕ 食べますながら → ○ 食べながら).
The JLPT often tests: which action is main/secondary and whether they have the same agent.
959.notes:
• Natural order: background first – main after. Example: "走りながら考える" is more natural than "考えながら走る" depending on the focus.
• With verbs of perception (聞く・見る・考える) it is very natural for the background: 考えながら運転する。
• Noun + ながらに/ながらの: old/fixed forms (生まれながらに, 昔ながらの味).

960.meaning: On the occasion of…, when starting… (an important, formal matter)

examples.jp: 奨学金を申し込むにあたっては、いくつかの条件がありますので、詳しくは事務所までお問い合わせください。
examples.tr: There are several conditions for applying for the scholarship, so please contact the office for details.

examples.jp: 論文を書くにあたって大切なことの一つは、書き方のルールを守るということです。
examples.tr: One of the important things when writing a thesis is to follow the rules of writing.

960.notes: Variants: ～にあたり・にあたっては

examples.jp: 次に、社会における企業の役割について述べます。
examples.tr: Next, I will discuss the role of companies in society.

examples.jp: あなたにとって、人生において最も大切にしていることは何ですか。
examples.tr: What is the most important thing to you in life?

961.explain: ◎ A usage in written language expressing "Y in (the scope or place of) X".

examples.jp: 経験にかかわらず、応募可能です。
examples.tr: Anyone can apply, regardless of experience.

examples.jp: 雨天にかかわらず、試合を行います。
examples.tr: The match will be held regardless of rain.

examples.jp: 参加するかどうかにかかわらず、連絡してください。
examples.tr: Please let us know whether or not you will attend.

examples.jp: 賛否にかかわらず、結果を尊重する。
examples.tr: We will respect the result, regardless of whether people are for or against it.

examples.jp: 昼夜にかかわらず、救急は受け付けています。
examples.tr: The emergency department accepts patients day or night.

examples.jp: 金額の多少にかかわらず、感謝いたします。
examples.tr: We are grateful regardless of the amount.

962.explain:
Ideal for the language of regulations / general application; highly universal.
The second clause is usually an impersonal clause:実施する・受け付ける・可能だ…
In ordinary conversation, with nouns it can be replaced by 〜を問わず.

• “Regardless of / not depending on …” → the second clause does not change according to the preceding condition.
• Used in rules/policies/announcements; formal/all-encompassing nuance.
• Goes well with familiar categories (年齢/性別/経験/国籍/天候/有無…).

rows: Used with N or かどうか
<ruby>国籍<rt>こくせき</rt></ruby>にかかわらず
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かか</rt></ruby>わりなく

mistakes: Confusing it with “にもかかわらず” (although): the function is completely different.
Dropping かどうか after a verb/adjective: × 行くにかかわらず → ○ 行くかどうかにかかわらず.
Using it with a clause of strong personal volition does not suit the style (except in official announcements).
962.notes:
• Colloquial shortened form with a pair of opposites: 行く行かないにかかわらず (still correct but formal).
• Adding は for contrast: Nにかかわらずは (rarely used) → it is better to avoid 〜かどうかにかかわらずは.
• In designing forms/signs: “〜の如何を問わず” is a very formal equivalent expression. | Variant: ～にかかわりなく

963.meaning: When it comes to…, in the field of…

examples.jp: 私は足の速さにかけてはだれにも負けない自信がある。
examples.tr: When it comes to running fast, I'm confident I won't lose to anyone.

examples.jp: B社のブランドはデザインにかけては定評がある。
examples.tr: Company B's brand has a good reputation when it comes to design.

examples.jp: 歴史の知識にかけては、クラスで佐藤さんにかなう人はいない。
examples.tr: When it comes to knowledge of history, no one in the class can match Sato.

examples.jp: 彼女は分析力にかけては群を抜いている。
examples.tr: When it comes to analytical skills, she is head and shoulders above the rest.

examples.jp: この選手は持久力にかけては世界トップクラスだ。
examples.tr: When it comes to endurance, this athlete is among the best in the world.

examples.jp: うちの会社は品質管理にかけては妥協しない。
examples.tr: Our company does not compromise when it comes to quality control.

963.explain:
It is a sentence of praise; used when introducing abilities, in PR, sports commentary, and personnel evaluations.
The noun must be a measurable area of skill/quality.
Combines with set phrases of praise: 〜は一番だ／随一だ／ピカイチだ／右に出るものはいない.

• Highlights a strength in a specific area; used to compare relative/absolute superiority.
• The second clause usually goes with expressions of not being inferior / being the best / being impressive.
• Not suitable for direct complaints; for criticism, use 苦手だ/下手だ.

rows: <ruby>営業<rt>えいぎょう</rt></ruby>にかけては<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けない
<ruby>制度<rt>せいど</rt></ruby>については<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>する
Formal, no implication of being good at something
<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しては<ruby>厳格<rt>げんかく</rt></ruby>だ
<ruby>晩秋<rt>ばんしゅう</rt></ruby>にかけて<ruby>冷<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>え<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む

mistakes: Using it with a noun that is not a “field”: × 天気にかけては → use については instead.
Using it for direct criticism: × 彼は時間管理にかけては下手だ → unnatural; use 彼は時間管理が下手だ.
Confusing it with 〜にかけて (until/spanning); exam questions often set traps with the two meanings.
963.notes:
• Can be used for groups: 日本チームにかけては守備が堅い.
• Implies a relative comparison with the rest of the set (社内/リーグ/地域など).
• The order of elements can be reversed for emphasis: 守備にかけてはこのチームが最強だ.
explain: After ［～にかけては］comes a sentence expressing a positive evaluation.
examples: 1. 足の速さにかけては、彼は町で一番だ。
When it comes to running fast, he is the best in town.
2. 歌のうまさにかけては、彼に勝てる人はいない。
When it comes to singing well, no one can beat him.

964.meaning:
（もちろん）～のほうがいい
Naturally… would be better

examples.jp: 「その仕事は経験がなくてもできますか」
examples.tr: "Can I do that job even without experience?"

examples.jp: 「はい、経験はあるに越したことはありませんが、なくても大丈夫です」
examples.tr: "Yes, it's better if you have experience, but it's fine if you don't."

examples.jp: 家賃は安いにこしたことはないが、だからと言って、駅から遠いのは困る。
examples.tr: Cheap rent is of course best, but that said, being far from the station is a problem.

examples.jp: アルバイトではなく正社員になれるのなら、それに越したことはない。
examples.tr: If you can become a full-time employee rather than a part-timer, nothing could be better.

examples.jp: インタネットでの買い物は、用心するに越したことはない。
examples.tr: When shopping online, you can never be too careful.

examples.jp: 何もないにこしたことはないけど、用心のため、海外旅行に行くときは必ず保険に入ります。
examples.tr: Of course it's best if nothing happens, but just in case, I always take out insurance when I travel abroad.

964.explain:
Used in recommendations and principles of life/experience:保険は入っておくに越したことはない。
It is not a command; it implies “if possible, …”.
In conversation it can be shortened:早いに越したことないよ。
With Aな/N, the standard form is である + に越したことはない (formal).

rows: <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いに<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>したことはない
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>むのが<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby>だ
Specific advice; less of an “obvious” sense
<ruby>薬<rt>くすり</rt></ruby>を<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>んだほうがいい
～なら<ruby>尚更<rt>なおさら</rt></ruby>だ／なおさらだ
Emphasizes a condition that raises the priority
<ruby>冬<rt>ふゆ</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>めに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>るべきだ

mistakes: Forgetting “である” with Aな/N in written language: ×安全に越したことはない（acceptable in conversation; in written language use: 安全であるに～）。
Taking it as a firm command → wrong nuance; this is gentle advice.
Overusing it for something already decided → sounds redundant: ×会場はここに決めた。広いに越したことはない。
JLPT N2–N1: Recognize it when it appears with できれば／やはり; it carries the sense of “something everyone agrees on”.
964.notes:
examples: 1. 早めに出発するに越したことはない。
Nothing beats leaving early.
2. 安全であるに越したことはないが、過剰な警戒は不要だ。
Being safe is best, but excessive caution is unnecessary.
3. 初めてなら、説明書を読んでから始めるに越したことはない。
If it's your first time, it's best to read the manual before starting.
4. 無理をしないに越したことはない。
It's better not to overdo it.
5. 経験があるに越したことはないが、必須ではない。
Having experience is better, but it's not required.

examples.jp: 日曜日の夜にしては、電車が込んでいる。
examples.tr: For a Sunday night, the train is crowded.

examples.jp: 彼は、ずっとスポーツをしていたにしては、よく風邪をひいて休む。
examples.tr: For someone who has always played sports, he often catches colds and stays home.

examples.jp: 父は50歳にしては若く見える。
examples.tr: My father looks young for 50.

examples.jp: 「彼女、バレーボールの選手なんだって」「それにしては背が低いね」
examples.tr: "I hear she's a volleyball player." "She's short for that, isn't she?"

examples.jp: 2年アメリカに住んでいたにしては、彼女は英語が下手だ。
examples.tr: For someone who lived in America for two years, her English is poor.
