examples.tr: Several safety issues can be observed at the site.

examples.jp: データの偏りが懸念される。
examples.tr: There are concerns about bias in the data.

examples.jp: 今回の結果は偶然とも考えられる。
examples.tr: This result could also be considered a coincidence.

1058.explain:
The speaker as subject is usually omitted; emphasizes a “natural/objective” quality.
The person who perceives can be added with に/には:彼には誠意が感じられた (less common than the impersonal form).
Suits a report style: ～が観察される／～が指摘される／～が確認される .

• Spontaneous passive: feelings/thoughts arise naturally, with no agent mentioned. Example verbs: 思われる・感じられる・思い出される・偲ばれる・うかがわれる・懸念される.
• Observation/recognition: describes phenomena that are seen/noticed objectively: 見られる・見受けられる・観察される・確認される.
• Nuance: objective, neutral; written language, reports, academic writing, news.

rows: <ruby>温<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かみが<ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じられる
Subjective; the speaker is the agent
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>温<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かみを<ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じる
<ruby>増加<rt>ぞうか</rt></ruby><ruby>傾向<rt>けいこう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>られる
～ように<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>える/<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえる
<ruby>受身<rt>うけみ</rt></ruby> ordinary: NはXにVられる
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>笑<rt>わらわ</rt></ruby>われた

mistakes: Confusing it with the potential form: 見られる does not always mean “can see”; it can mean “is observed”.
Adding an agent with に to the spontaneous form distorts the meaning: 誠意が彼に感じられる is unnatural; say 彼の発言には誠意が感じられる instead.
Confusing it with the subjective ～ように感じる/思う; exam questions often ask you to choose the more objective form over the subjective one.
1058.notes:
• Typical spontaneous verbs: 思われる・考えられる・感じられる・思い出される・偲ばれる・うかがわれる・期待される・懸念される.
• 見られる has two meanings: “can see” (ability) and “is observed” (objective passive); distinguish them by context.
• Avoid “ら抜き言葉” in exams/writing: use the correct 考えられる, not 考えれる.

1059.connection: Vます(drop ます) + きれる（negative: きれない）

examples.jp: 書くことがたくさんあるから、これ一枚では書ききれない。
examples.tr: There's so much to write that I can't fit it all on this one sheet.

examples.jp: B: すみません、売りきれてしまったんです。明日、また入ります。
examples.tr: B: I'm sorry, it's sold out. More will come in tomorrow.

1061.meaning: Since… (giving one of several reasons); seeing as…, so…

examples.jp: 〈父が息子に〉今日はお母さんもマキもいないことだし、夕飯は二人で外に食べに行こうか。
examples.tr: 〈A father to his son〉 Since Mom and Maki are both out today, shall we two go out for dinner?

examples.jp:
A: どうしよう、レポートが間に合わない。体調もよくないことだし、明日、バイトを休ませてもらおうかなあ。
B: そうしたら。
examples.tr:
A: What should I do? I won't finish my report in time. And since I'm not feeling well either, maybe I'll ask for tomorrow off from my part-time job.
B: Why don't you?

1061.notes: Attaches to a clause. With the structure 「ことだ＋し」, it is used to state the circumstances or situation that serve as the reason or grounds for some judgment, decision, or wish. 「ことですし」, as in ②, is a more polite form. It can be used to state two reasons, as in ③, or just one, as in ②, or tacked on at the end like an afterthought, as in ①. It is spoken language, but a more formal expression than 「し」 alone. （１１７）

1062.meaning: When it comes to… (attitude/state changes completely)

examples.jp: 彼は普段は無口だけど、山登りのこととなると、急におしゃべりになる。
examples.tr: He's usually quiet, but when it comes to mountain climbing, he suddenly becomes talkative.

examples.jp: お弁当を作るほうが経済的だし、体にもいいけど、毎日のこことなると、大変かもしれない。
examples.tr: Making a packed lunch is more economical and better for your health, but when it comes to doing it every day, it might be hard.

examples.jp: この薬の主成分、すなわちビタミンCが不足している。
examples.tr: The main ingredient of this medicine, namely vitamin C, is lacking.

examples.jp: 彼は三言語話者、すなわちトリリンガルだ。
examples.tr: He is a speaker of three languages, that is, trilingual.

examples.jp: A社とB社は同一法人、すなわち法的には同じ組織だ。
examples.tr: Company A and Company B are the same corporation; in other words, legally they are the same organization.

examples.jp: この数字は売上高、すなわち純粋な収入ではない。
examples.tr: This figure is sales revenue, that is, not net income.

1064.explain:
Used in definitions, explanations of terms, and to state a relationship of identity.
Formal/academic style; つまり is more of an everyday summarizing word.
Usually accompanied by commas before/after to set off the explanatory clause.
Not used to state a result, a command, or an exclamation.

すなわち: “that is/namely/in other words (in the sense of identity)”. Used to give a definition, an exact explanation, or to restate something with an equivalent expression.
• Emphasizes a relationship of identity/equality: S2 ≒ a different expression of S1.
• More formal than つまり; leans toward precision and objectivity.
• Not used for inferring a result or for emotional summarizing.

rows: Summarizes/implies a general conclusion; less formal.
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れる。つまり、<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わない。
Sums up the main point, with a subjective nuance.
<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>長<rt>なが</rt></ruby>い。<ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに、<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>だ。
Implies inference, not an identity definition.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>？ ということは、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だね。

mistakes: Confusing it with つまり: if the question requires an “identity definition” → すなわち; if it requires “summarizing/inferring” → つまり.
Using it for a result/cause and effect is incorrect: ×「雨だ。すなわち、行かない」→ use それで/だから instead.
Making S2 not equivalent to S1 makes the sentence imprecise; make sure there is a relationship of identity.
1064.notes:
• Tip: if you could put “= (equals)” between S1 and S2, すなわち is the correct choice.
• In scientific writing it often appears in definitions: Xとは、すなわちYである。
• The kanji 即ち is rarely used today; the kana すなわち is preferred for readability. meaning_vi: In other words, that is ⏐ explain: Used when expressing something in a different way.
Similar to　「つまり」 but cannot be used when talking about a result.
財布をなくした。すなわちお金がない。（X)
→財布をなくした。つまりお金がない。（O)
Stiff sentence. ⏐ examples: 1. 「母の兄、すなわち僕のおじですが・・・・・・」
My mother's older brother, in other words my uncle…
2. このペットボトルには１０００ミリリットル、すなわち１リットルの水が入っています。
This bottle holds 1000 ml, that is, 1 liter of water.

examples.jp: この小説は読む者を感動させずにはおかない。
examples.tr: This novel cannot fail to move its readers.

examples.jp: 不正は必ず暴かずにはおかない。
examples.tr: Wrongdoing will without fail be exposed.

examples.jp: 彼の真摯な言葉は、聞く人の心に響かずにはおかない。
examples.tr: His sincere words are bound to touch the hearts of those who hear them.

examples.jp: この問題は今日中に解決せずにはおかない。
examples.tr: This problem will be solved today, no matter what.

examples.jp: あの映像は世論を揺り動かさずにはおかないだろう。
examples.tr: That footage will surely stir up public opinion.

1065.explain:
States a strong cause-and-effect relationship or determination: a sense of “will surely happen/will definitely do”.
Formal; suitable for commentary, speeches, and news; rarely used in everyday conversation.
Meaning A usually goes with N/人を + V-使役: “to make/drive … into state X”.
Meaning B suits contexts expressing the volition, responsibility, or determination of the speaker/organization.
Usually not used for ordinary actions with no inevitability/decisiveness.

• Meaning A (inevitable result): “Will surely/cannot fail to cause …” — a powerful agent inevitably leads to a reaction/result. Example: その演説は聴衆を魅了せずにはおかない。
• Meaning B (strong volition/determination): “Will definitely do …; will not let it go” — the speaker expresses the will to carry it through no matter what. Example: この件は必ず突き止めずにはおかない。
• Nuance: stiff, written language, journalism/commentary/speeches; decisive, close to a confident prediction or unshakable determination.
• The subject is usually a thing/event that has an impact (Meaning A) or “I/we” with determination (Meaning B).

rows: Formal, decisive; emphasizes inevitability or firm volition
<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>は<ruby>観客<rt>かんきゃく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>かせずにはおかない。
Sense of duty/morality; must do it to do the proper thing
<ruby>迷惑<rt>めいわく</rt></ruby>をかけたから<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>らずにはすまない。
Spontaneous emotion; more colloquial; no decisive or inevitable nuance
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>曲<rt>きょく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聴<rt>き</rt></ruby>くと<ruby>踊<rt>おど</rt></ruby>らずにはいられない。
A slightly more colloquial variant; same meaning
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>感心<rt>かんしん</rt></ruby>させないではおかない。

mistakes: Mixing it up with ～ずにはすまない: this one means “will surely cause/will definitely do”, the other means “it won't do not to (a sense of duty)”.
Using it in casual conversation → sounds forced; choose ～ずにはいられない in everyday conversation.
Unsuitable subject: for Meaning A, use a thing/work/statement as the subject to sound more natural.
1065.notes:
• In commentary, this pattern helps “upgrade” the certainty of a prediction, almost asserting the result.
• With Meaning A, avoid making “I” the subject unless it is a strategic statement (PR, declaration, resolution).
• A double negative is not used with this pattern; to negate it, rephrase the whole sentence with a different expression.

examples.jp: 約束を破った以上、謝らずにはすまない。
examples.tr: Since I broke my promise, I have no choice but to apologize.

examples.jp: 顧客にご迷惑をかけたから、会社として説明せずにはすまないだろう。
examples.tr: Since we caused trouble for our customers, as a company we will probably have to give an explanation.

examples.jp: 重要書類を紛失したので、上司に報告せずにはすまない。
examples.tr: I lost an important document, so I have to report it to my boss.

examples.jp: 法令に違反したとなれば、処分を下さずにはすまない。
examples.tr: If it turns out laws were violated, disciplinary action will have to be taken.

examples.jp: こんなに助けてもらったから、何かお礼をせずにはすまない気がする。
examples.tr: After all this help, I feel I have to do something to thank them.

1066.explain:
Emphasizes a “social/moral obligation”, not a burst of emotion.
To soften it, ～だろう／と思う is often used; at work it is used to affirm the responsibility to deal with something.
Not used for fun or hobbies; suits situations that call for apologizing, explaining, compensating, or handling something.

• Meaning: “It won't do/It's not right not to do it” because of moral principles, etiquette, rules, or responsibility.
• Not strong volition but the pressure of norms/circumstances that make you do it in order to settle things properly.
• Often goes with verbs such as 謝る, 連絡する, 説明する, 報告する, 対応する, 補償する, etc.
• Formal nuance; written language, work, official announcements.

rows: <ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>したら<ruby>一言<rt>ひとこと</rt></ruby><ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>せずにはすまない。
Have no choice but to, reluctantly
Due to objective circumstances; more neutral morally
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>せざるを<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>ない。
<ruby>招待<rt>しょうたい</rt></ruby>されたから<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないわけにはいかない。
Burst of emotion; no sense of “the proper thing to do”
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>には<ruby>笑<rt>わらわ</rt></ruby>わずにはいられない。
その<ruby>発言<rt>はつげん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>波紋<rt>はもん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>広<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>げずにはおかない。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～ずにはいられない: the JLPT often sets a trap between emotion (いられない) and duty (すまない).
Choosing the wrong subject/action: use it with “handling” actions involving responsibility (謝る, 説明する, 対応する...).
Not softening it in polite writing: add だろう／と思う to sound natural.
1066.notes:
• Besides apologizing/explaining, this pattern suits statements of managerial responsibility: 対応せずにはすまない, 再発防止策を講じずにはすまない.
• In business emails, combine it with ものと存じます/と考えております to be polite.
• Do not overuse it in casual conversation, as it sounds “heavy with responsibility”.

1067.connection: [topic A]。 + それはそうと、 + [topic B]

examples.jp: 企画は順調だね。それはそうと、来週の出張、誰が行く？
examples.tr: The project's going well, huh. By the way, who's going on next week's business trip?

examples.jp: 今日はここまでにしよう。それはそうと、この資料見た？
examples.tr: Let's stop here for today. By the way, have you seen this document?

examples.jp: ありがとう。それはそうと、駅への行き方を教えて。
examples.tr: Thanks. By the way, can you tell me how to get to the station?

examples.jp: 新製品の話は面白い。それはそうと、予算は足りる？
examples.tr: The story about the new product is interesting. By the way, is the budget enough?

examples.jp: その映画よかったよ。それはそうと、宿題終わった？
examples.tr: That movie was good. By the way, did you finish your homework?

1067.explain:
Often used in everyday conversation to steer over to another topic.
Avoid using it too abruptly with a superior in a formal context; consider ところで/さて.
Placed at the beginning of a sentence: a new sentence, right after the period of the previous one.

• Meaning: a connecting phrase for shifting the topic, often rather sudden but gentle.
• Nuance: casual, somewhat everyday; carries the feeling of “suddenly remembering something else”.
• Link: may be loosely related or unrelated to A.

rows: Sudden topic shift, not necessarily related
<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わり。それはそうと、<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>は？
ところで、<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>件<rt>けん</rt></ruby>。
Implies “skip A to get to the main point B”
それはさておき、<ruby>本題<rt>ほんだい</rt></ruby>へ。
Very colloquial, announces a change of topic
<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わるけど、さ...

mistakes: Choosing それはそうと for a sentence that needs “cause-result” → incorrect (use だから/そのため/それで).
Using it mid-sentence or after a comma within the same long sentence → unnatural; the standard position is after the period of the previous sentence.
Confusing it with それでは (opening the next step in a presentation) → different function.
1067.notes:
• Often used to slip in a “reminder” you have just remembered during a conversation.
• For a more coherent flow in a formal presentation, use さて/次に/では instead of それはそうと.
• It carries no cause-and-effect or contrast relation; it is only a signal of a topic shift. explain: Used when changing the topic. ⏐ examples: 1. 「今日の授業、おもしろかったね。」
「うん、すごくためになった。それはそうと、今度の試験いつだっけ？」
Today's class was interesting, wasn't it? Yeah, I learned a lot. By the way, when is the next exam again?
2. 「春になりましたね。それはそうと、田中さんの息子さん、大学受かったでしょうか。」
It's spring now, isn't it? By the way, I wonder if Mr. Tanaka's son got into university.

1068.meaning: I really want…, if only… (earnest wish)

examples.jp: 一度はこういう高級ホテルに泊ってみたいものです。
examples.tr: I'd like to stay at a luxury hotel like this at least once.

examples.jp: こんなに働いているんだから、もう少し給料を上げてもらいたいものだね。
examples.tr: I work this hard, so I really wish they'd raise my salary a little.

1068.notes: Used together with expressions of desire such as 「たい」 and 「ほしい」 to emphasize that feeling.

examples.jp: 雨が降ったかと思ったら、もう晴れてきた。
examples.tr: No sooner had it rained than it cleared up.

examples.jp: 赤ちゃんは泣いたかと思うと、すぐに笑い出した。
examples.tr: The baby cried and then immediately burst out laughing.

examples.jp: 店が開いたかと思ったら、行列があっという間にできた。
examples.tr: The moment the store opened, a line formed in no time.

examples.jp: 彼は戻ってきたかと思えば、またどこかへ出かけてしまった。
examples.tr: Just when I thought he'd come back, he went off somewhere again.

examples.jp: この季節は寒くなったかと思ったら、急に暑くなる。
examples.tr: In this season, just when it gets cold, it suddenly turns hot.

examples.jp: ベルが鳴ったかと思ったら、停電でまた静かになった。
examples.tr: Just as the bell rang, a power outage made everything quiet again.

1069.explain:
Point in time: used for two events that follow each other very closely.
Person: usually objective observation; avoid using the speaker's intentional action in the second clause.
Nuance: emphasizes surprise/speed; can be used to complain about erratic changes.
Style: common in spoken language, also appears in written language describing phenomena.

• Expresses that B happens almost immediately after A, giving the speaker a “flash-like”, surprising feeling.
• Usually used for objective observation (the subject is usually a third party/thing); the speaker does not intentionally intervene.
• The second clause is usually a surprising fact/phenomenon; not suitable for commands, intentions, or direct invitations.
• Can express repeated, opposite changes: A, then immediately the opposite B.
• Emotional nuance: surprise, annoyance, mild complaint, or describing a fast pace of change.

rows: ～たかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>ったら/～たかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと
Emphasizes surprise; second clause is not a command/intention
<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと、また<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た。
B is usually an unintended incident; the subjects of both clauses are usually the same
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたん、<ruby>倒<rt>たお</rt></ruby>れた。
Expresses an even closer degree; more neutral nuance
<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わるか<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わらないかのうちに<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>る。
As soon as A, immediately B
Formal/old written style; not used with commands
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>まった。
I thought A, but unexpectedly B
Not necessarily “immediate”; emphasizes contrary to expectation
<ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いきや、<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。

mistakes: Using a command/volition in the second clause: 読んだかと思ったら、勉強しよう× → Use a fact/observation.
Using it for the speaker's own intentional action: 私は家に着いたかと思ったら、寝ます× → Unnatural.
Confusing it with ～と思いきや (contrary to expectation) or ～たとたん (an unintended incident). Read the nuance of the question carefully.
The time between the two clauses must be very short; if it is long, use ～てから or ～その後.
1069.notes:
• The second clause uses a factual/objective form (～た／～ている／～たところだ...). Avoid ～ましょう、～てください.
• Often used with natural phenomena, other people's behavior, and changes of state.
• For repeated opposite changes, the pattern helps describe a “sunny in the morning, rainy in the afternoon” character.

examples.jp: 彼は去年家を出たきり、一度も戻っていない。
examples.tr: He left home last year and hasn't come back even once since.

examples.jp: 一度会ったきりで、あの人とは連絡を取っていない。
examples.tr: I met that person only once, and I haven't been in touch with them since.

examples.jp: この本は買ったきり、読まずに棚に置いてある。
examples.tr: I bought this book and just left it on the shelf without reading it.

examples.jp: 電話をもらったっきり、その後音沙汰がない。
examples.tr: I got a phone call, and after that I haven't heard a thing.

examples.jp: 祖父は病気以来、ほとんど寝たきりの生活だ。
examples.tr: Since his illness, my grandfather has been almost entirely bedridden.

examples.jp: 彼女は卒業してそれっきり、街で見かけない。
examples.tr: She graduated, and since then I haven't seen her around town.

1070.explain:
Often used with personal events as a reference point (contact, returning, meeting, studying...).
Nuance: slightly negative/regretful, or the objective sense “from then on, that was it”.
Time: lasts up to the observed present; equivalent to “ever since A, still...”.

• “Since A, (the expected thing) has not happened again” → emphasizes a prolonged interruption.
• Usually accompanied by a negative (～ない／～ていない) in the second clause. Without a negative, the nuance is still “only that once” → less natural in this meaning.
• Focuses on the “only, once” nature of a past action and its consequences lasting until now.
• Often used in spoken language describing the state of contact, meeting, returning, and changes.

rows: Emphasizes the interruption and the expectation that it should have happened again
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>ったきり、<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しない。
More neutral, just a point in time; no expectation necessarily
<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby>して<ruby>以来<rt>いらい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>にいる。
Emphasizes a big change, more formal
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>生<rt>う</rt></ruby>まれてからというもの、<ruby>外食<rt>がいしょく</rt></ruby>しない。
Different meaning; just leaving/neglecting things as they are
<ruby>電気<rt>でんき</rt></ruby>をつけっぱなし。
Does not mean “ever since”; do not confuse with っきり (only)

mistakes: Dropping ない in the second clause distorts the main meaning: 連絡したきり。× → 連絡したきり（連絡が）来ない。/ 連絡していない。
Confusing it with ～て以来: if there is an implication of “should have... but didn't”, prefer ～たきり.
Using it for naturally repeating events (the sun rising/setting) is unnatural.
Confusing it with ～っきり meaning “only”: 会ったっきり＝会って以来（not met again), which is different from 一回だけ会った.
1070.notes:
• In conversation, っきり is more common than きり after a verb.
• 寝たきり is a fixed phrase meaning “bedridden”, used descriptively in a medical/social sense.
• In written language you may see ～たきりだ／～たきりで (subject-predicate shortened) to emphasize a lasting state.

1071.meaning: Although…, still…; even though (I) know…, still…
1071.connection: Vます(drop ます) + つつも

examples.jp: もう間に合わないと半分諦めつつも、必死で走った。
examples.tr: Although I had half given up, thinking I wouldn't make it in time, I ran desperately.

examples.jp: 勉強しようと思いつつも、彼女のとこが気になって、できない。
examples.tr: Although I mean to study, I keep thinking about my girlfriend and can't.

examples.jp: 足の状態は少しずつよくなりつつも、走れるようになるには、あと半年はかかる。
examples.tr: Although my leg is gradually getting better, it will take another half a year before I can run.

1071.notes:
meaning_vi: (1) Although …
(2) While/at the same time … ⏐ explain: (1) Often used when the speaker confesses, regrets, reconsiders… ⏐ examples: 1. 彼女は忙しいと言いつつ、長電話をしている。
She says she's busy, yet she's chatting away on the phone.
2. 今日こそがんばろうと思いつつ、また勉強しなかった。
Although I thought I'd really work hard starting today, I didn't study again.
3. 先生と相談しつつ、進路を決めたいと思う。
I want to decide my future path while consulting with my teacher.

1072.meaning: Cannot keep on…, cannot just go on…

examples.jp: 結果を待っていられないから、直接問い合わせる。
examples.tr: I can't just keep waiting for the results, so I'll inquire directly.

examples.jp: いつまでも落ち込んではいられない。前に進もう。
examples.tr: I can't stay down forever. Let's move forward.

examples.jp: のんびりしてられない。締め切りが近いんだ。
examples.tr: I can't take it easy. The deadline is close.

examples.jp: 泣いてばかりはいられないよ。
examples.tr: You can't just keep crying, you know.

examples.jp: ここでぐずぐずしてちゃいられない。早く避難しよう。
examples.tr: We can't dawdle here. Let's evacuate quickly.

1072.explain:
Often used with stative verbs: 待つ／落ち込む／のんびりする／迷っている…
Nuance of urgency, determinedly pushing yourself; mostly spoken language, but fine in ordinary written language too.
Polite negative form: ～いられません. The contracted forms sound stronger: ～てられない／～ちゃいられない.

• Expresses a situation where you cannot continue a state/action any longer because of time pressure, responsibility, or circumstances.
• Implies the speaker realizes they must change their action right away: “I can't just keep … forever”.
• Unlike “cannot in terms of ability” (できない), this pattern means “cannot because of the situation/urgency”.

rows: Full form; same meaning as Vていられない
Vている<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>じゃない
This is no time to V
<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>んでいる<ruby>場合<rt>ばあい</rt></ruby>じゃない
Moral/social reason, not because of being busy
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないわけにはいかない
Strongly expressive, does not mean “cannot continue”

mistakes: Confusing “cannot in terms of ability” with “cannot because of the situation”: ×疲れて走っていられない（may be correct if it means “cannot keep running” because of tiredness; do not confuse it with 走れない）.
Leaving out the reason makes the sentence sound abrupt: state the circumstance/urgency to sound more natural.
Wrong subject: the pattern usually expresses the speaker's own feeling; avoid imposing it on a third party unless it is a clear conjecture.
1072.notes:
• Often accompanied by a reason/circumstance right after or before the sentence: 締め切りがあるから、待っていられない。
• Emphasizes switching actions: the following sentence is often an alternative (直接問い合わせる／行動に移す…).
• The てられない form is common in conversation, stressing urgency.
meaning_vi: Cannot keep on … forever
explain: Nuance of determination: acknowledging the current situation but emphasizing “things must change”.
Often appears with a pressing reason/circumstance: 時間がない／責任がある／状況が厳しい…
Suitable for both spoken and written language; in speeches/meetings it shows a spirit of change.
examples: 1. 締め切りが近いから、遊んでばかりはいられない。
The deadline is close, so I can't just keep playing.
2. 失敗したけど、いつまでも泣いてばかりはいられない。
I failed, but I can't keep crying forever.
3. もう社会人だ。親に甘えてばかりはいられない。
I'm a working adult now. I can't keep depending on my parents.
4. いつまでも学生でばかりはいられない。自立しなければ。
I can't stay a student forever. I have to become independent.
5. 危機の今、守りに回ってばかりはいられない。
Now, in a crisis, we can't just stay on the defensive.
6. わからないからといって、人に聞いてばかりはいられない。
Just because you don't understand, you can't keep asking other people all the time.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
Vてばかりはいられない | Cannot keep doing V forever | Emphasizes changing actions | 寝（ね）てばかりはいられない
N/なでばかりはいられない | Cannot stay in state N/な forever | Uses “で” to connect N/Aな | 学生（がくせい）でばかりはいられない
～てばかりだ | Doing nothing but V | Describes the current situation, no implication of needing to change | 遊（あそ）んでばかりだ
～てはいられない | Cannot keep V-ing | Without “ばかり” → emphasizes being unable to continue the behavior | 悠長（ゆうちょう）にしてはいられない
～ばかりではない | Not only… | Negates “only”; different meaning | 彼（かれ）は遊（あそ）びばかりではない
common_mistakes: • Wrong form with N/Aな: ×学生ばかりはいられない → 学生でばかりはいられない.
• Using the dictionary form: ×遊ぶばかりはいられない → 遊んでばかりはいられない.
• Confusing it with ～てばかりだ (describing a habit) → it lacks the nuance of “must change”.
• JLPT N2: a trap distinguishing ～てはいられない and ～てばかりはいられない; note the core meaning “cannot just do one thing”.
meaning_vi: Cannot keep on…, have no time to… (てはいられない)
meaning_vi: Cannot keep on… forever (てばかりはいられない)
meaning_vi: Cannot continue …, cannot keep on …
examples: 1. 田中君、遅いなあ。もう待ってられないから先に行こう。
Tanaka's so late. We can't wait any longer, so let's go on ahead.
2. 忙しくてテレビなんか見てらんない。
I'm so busy I can't sit around watching TV.
meaning_vi: Cannot keep … forever
examples: 1. 連休だけれど、もうすぐ試験があるから、遊んでばかりはいられない。
It's a long holiday, but I have an exam soon, so I can't just play.
2. もう親に頼ってばかりはいられない。
I can't keep relying on my parents anymore.

1074.connection: Vて + はかなわない / V passive form て + はかなわない (来られてはかなわない)

examples.jp: お客さんが自分で間違えただけなのに、こっちのせいにされてはかなわないよ。
examples.tr: The customer simply made a mistake on their own, so I can't stand being blamed for it.

examples.jp: 休みの度に遊びに来られちゃかなわないよ。
examples.tr: It's too much having people come over to hang out every time I have a day off.

1075.meaning: Is it…?, could you call it…?
1075.connection: V/A plain form + というのか / N/Na(だ) + というのか

examples.jp: これが愛というのか、ただの憧れなのか、まだわからない。
examples.tr: I still don't know whether this is what you call love or just admiration.

examples.jp: 彼の態度は失礼というのか、無神経というのか、とにかく腹が立つ。
examples.tr: Whether you call his attitude rude or insensitive, anyway, it makes me angry.

examples.jp: あんなに努力したのに、結果はこれというのか。
examples.tr: After all that effort, is this what the result is?

examples.jp: 幸せというのか、不安というのか、複雑な気分だ。
examples.tr: I don't know whether to call it happiness or anxiety; it's a complicated feeling.

examples.jp: これを奇跡というのか、偶然というのか、とにかく信じられない。
examples.tr: Whether you call this a miracle or a coincidence, anyway, it's unbelievable.

1075.explain:
Usually at the end of the sentence or mid-sentence, expressing inner thoughts or hesitant feelings that are hard to put into words.
Used in spoken language or in written language describing emotions, not in formal written language such as reports or theses.
The intonation is usually that of a light question or exclamation, but it is not a question that requires an answer.

• Expresses hesitation when you want to name, evaluate or express something: “Can you say it is…?”, “What should I call it?”.
• Often contains emotions such as surprise, irony, disbelief, or difficulty expressing oneself.
• Can be used to make a gentle judgment or express doubt: “Is it right to call it…?”.
• Often used in conversation or in writing that describes a character's inner state.

rows: Hesitation, hard to express, complicated feelings.
<ruby>才能<rt>さいのう</rt></ruby>というのか、<ruby>運<rt>うん</rt></ruby>というのか。
<ruby>民主<rt>みんしゅ</rt></ruby><ruby>主義<rt>しゅぎ</rt></ruby>というのは…
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だというのに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>怒<rt>おこ</rt></ruby>っているのではないか。

mistakes: Confusing it with というのに/ということだ → look at the nuance: an exclamatory question or a paradox.
Using it in a formal context: this pattern is emotional and not used in academic texts.
Missing the first clause/second clause: information to compare is needed; otherwise the sentence will be vague.
1075.notes:
• This pattern is often used to describe a state of indecision in literature, anime, and movies.
• It can be repeated twice to present two options: ～というのか、～というのか.
• Unlike an ordinary question, this is a rhetorical question that does not need an answer from the listener.

examples.jp: こんなに寒いというのに、彼はコートも着ていない。
examples.tr: Even though it's this cold, he isn't even wearing a coat.

examples.jp: 早く帰ってきてほしいというのに、まだ連絡もない。
examples.tr: I want them to come home soon, and yet I haven't even heard from them.

examples.jp: 大雨だというのに、試合は中止にならなかった。
examples.tr: Even though it was pouring, the game wasn't canceled.

examples.jp: 給料が安いというのに、残業ばかりさせられる。
examples.tr: Even though the pay is low, I'm constantly made to work overtime.

examples.jp: 彼女は忙しいというのに、手伝ってくれた。
examples.tr: Even though she was busy, she helped me.

1076.explain:
Position: between two clauses A and B. A is a fact, B is an opposite, unwanted result.
Usually carries negative emotions: reproach, disappointment, complaint.
Can be used in spoken language, but has a strong nuance → use it when you want to emphasize something unreasonable.
Not suitable for scientific writing or overly formal situations such as political speeches.

• A sentence pattern expressing a strong contrast between reality and expectation: although A is a fact, the result is B, which is surprising, frustrating or blameworthy.
• Strong emotional nuance: expresses anger, complaint, disappointment, even sarcasm.
• Natural translations: “Even though… still…”, “And yet…”, “Despite… nevertheless…”.
• Differs from (ordinary) 〜のに in that というのに is stronger emotionally and is used a lot in written language and expressive conversation.

rows: Strong emotion, indignation, contrary to expectation.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>というのに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた。
Formal, more common in written language.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>にもかかわらず<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われた。
<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っているくせに<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくれない。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～というのに？ (question) → the question uses intonation, while the grammar point expresses contrast.
Confusing it with ～のに: remember that というのに is stronger and emotional.
Using it in the wrong context when the sentence contains no emotion or no clear contrast.
The JLPT N2 often tests the difference from ～にもかかわらず and ～のに.
1076.notes:
• Often used in novels and emotionally charged dialogue such as in movies, anime, and essays.
• The polite form 「というのです／というのにです」 is rarely used; the plain form is usual.
• Be careful to distinguish its pronunciation from 「というのに？」 (asking back: “you mean…, right?”).

1077.connection: [sentence A]。というのも、[sentence B](からだ)

examples.jp: 彼とはあまり話さない。というのも、性格が合わないからだ。
examples.tr: I don't talk with him much. That's because our personalities don't match.

examples.jp: 来週は忙しくなる。というのも、新しいプロジェクトが始まるからだ。
examples.tr: I'll be busy next week. The reason is that a new project is starting.

examples.jp: 今日は外出できない。というのも、雨がひどいからだ。
examples.tr: I can't go out today. That's because the rain is terrible.

examples.jp: 試合は中止になった。というのも、台風が近づいているためだ。
examples.tr: The game was canceled. That's because a typhoon is approaching.

examples.jp: 彼は会社を辞めた。というのも、自分の店を開くつもりだからだ。
examples.tr: He quit his company. That's because he plans to open his own shop.

1077.explain:
Placed at the beginning of clause b to explain clause a.
More formal than だって or なんでかというと.
Often used when explaining in polite conversation, newspapers, essays, and argumentative writing.
It differs from というのは in that というのは introduces a reason, while というのも emphasizes “this is the reason for what was just said”.

• Used to give a reason or explanation for the preceding clause.
• Equivalent to “The reason… is that…”, “The reason is…”.
• Clause A is a conclusion or fact. Clause B (after というのも) is the cause or reason.
• Often used in written language and formal spoken language, especially in argumentative, explanatory, or persuasive writing.

rows: Explains the cause of the previous sentence; written language, formal.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。というのも、<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからだ。
Introduces a reason or defines a word/concept.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。というのは、<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからだ。
Emphasizes the reason part, often used with ～からだ.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない。なぜかというと、<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいからだ。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないよ。だって<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいもん。

mistakes: Confusing it with ということだ (hearsay / conclusion) – a completely different function.
Not used in simple casual speech – it sounds stiff; use だって/なんでかというと.
What follows というのも must be a reasonable reason; do not use it for unrelated information.
The JLPT N2~N1 often asks you to distinguish it from というのは/なぜかというと.
1077.notes:
• よく used in essays and argumentative writing, when you want to present things coherently.
• Can be combined with the polite form: ～ということです・～というのです.
• If the reason is long, it can be inverted: というのも、～からだ。

examples.jp: 留学するとなったら、早めに準備を始めるべきだ。
examples.tr: If you decide to study abroad, you should start preparing early.

examples.jp: いざ出発となったら、急に不安になってきた。
examples.tr: When the moment to depart finally came, I suddenly started to feel anxious.

examples.jp: 引っ越しとなったら、粗大ごみの処分が大変だ。
examples.tr: If you're moving, getting rid of bulky garbage is a lot of work.

examples.jp: もし大会が中止となったら、参加費は返金されます。
examples.tr: If the tournament is canceled, the entry fee will be refunded.

examples.jp: 来週となったら、もう間に合わないかもしれない。
examples.tr: Once it gets to next week, it may already be too late.

1078.explain:
Used when: referring to the point in time when a decision is made or an event begins (本番、締め切り、出発、中止...), or when an action has already been decided on (V-辞書形).
The second clause often goes with: 準備する、手配する、覚悟する、～べきだ、～つもりだ、～ないと（いけない）.
The nuance is more decisive/personal than となると; more familiar and colloquial than となれば.
Unnatural if the second clause is a direct command to the listener in a formal context; a suggestion or mild volition is preferable.

• Main meaning: “If/when (something) becomes or is decided to be A, then B”. Emphasizes the point in time when the change of state or the decision is established.
• Nuance: leans toward the speaker's standpoint, often followed by the speaker's volition/suggestion/planned action in the second clause. A feeling of “now that the time has come, I have to…”.
• Scope of use: both hypothetical situations (もし～) and situations that are almost certain or already decided (いざ/いよいよ～). The second clause is usually a plan, a preparation, or a predicted consequence.
• Difference from ～となると/～となれば: となったら is casual and practical, often used with personal preparations; となると leans toward “when it comes to that…” with an evaluation/difficulty; となれば leans toward a general supposition and is more written.

rows: <ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>すとなったら、<ruby>段取<rt>だんど</rt></ruby>りを<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めよう。
When it comes to A, then...
Raises an objective issue/consequence; shifts the direction of the conversation
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>となると、<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>見直<rt>みなお</rt></ruby>しだ。
If it were to be / come to A, then...
General supposition, written language, strong sense of inevitability
<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>となれば、<ruby>損失<rt>そんしつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きい。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くとしたら、いつにする？

mistakes: Confusion with となると: a sentence emphasizing an objective issue is better with となると (例: お金がかかる“となると”が自然).
Use with adjectives: Aい/na + となったら is less natural; prefer event-like N/V.
Direct commands: 避ける with となったら in formal writing; replace with ～べきだ／～ほうがいい.
JLPT: Identify the personal nuance (となったら) vs objective (となると) vs general supposition (となれば).
1078.notes:
• “いざ～となったら/となると” is a very natural phrase to emphasize “when the time actually comes”.
• With time expressions: 今日・明日・来週・年度末 + となったら expresses “once it gets to…”.
• Intonation: となった「ら」 makes the sentence softer than となると; a post-decision feeling.
• When the content of A is an official announcement (会社の方針、中止等)、となったら shows “how to respond” from the speaker's side.

1079.meaning: I hear that…, it is said that…
1079.connection: V/A plain form + とのことだ / N/Naだ + とのことだ

examples.jp: 田中さんは本日お休みとのことです。
examples.tr: I'm told that Mr. Tanaka is off today.

examples.jp: 気象庁によると、明日は大雪になるとのことだ。
examples.tr: According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, there will be heavy snow tomorrow.

examples.jp: 会議は中止とのことですので、ご注意ください。
examples.tr: We have been informed that the meeting has been canceled, so please take note.

examples.jp: 担当者から、資料は明日送付するようにとのことだ。
examples.tr: The person in charge has asked that the documents be sent tomorrow.

examples.jp: 彼は来週は来られないとのことだ。
examples.tr: I hear he won't be able to come next week.

1079.explain:
Used to pass on objective information while keeping a polite distance from the source.
When conveying an indirect command/request: 「～するようにとのことです」 sounds polite and avoids direct pressure.
Sentences often end in ～とのことです (polite) in business writing.
Not used to state the speaker's own opinion or subjective evaluation; it only reports.

• A hearsay pattern (伝聞): conveys information indirectly from another source in a polite, neutral way.
• Often used in company announcements, emails, and the news: “～とのことです” is more polite than “～そうです”.
• The source can be added: ～によると／～から／関係者によれば + ～とのことだ.
• Difference from ～ということだ: ということだ is somewhat more direct and is also used when explaining rules; とのことだ is polite/diplomatic and emphasizes the source of information.

rows: I hear / I've been informed that...
Polite, with a sense of “passing on information”
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みとのことです。
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みだそうだ。
<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>ということだ。
Conjecture based on rumors/impressions, less certain

mistakes: Using it for your own opinion → incorrect: 「おいしいとのことだ」 (when it is your own impression). Use 「おいしいと思う」 instead.
Leaving out the source in formal writing can be vague; add ～によると／～から.
Confusion with ～そうだ（様態） “looks like”: とのことだ is only used to convey information, not to describe sensory impressions.
JLPT: When the answer requires the nuance of “a work announcement/polite passing on of information”, choose とのことだ over そうだ/らしい.
1079.notes:
• Negative/past structures stay in the plain form: 来ないとのことだ／終わったとのことだ.
• The source can be omitted when it is clear from context: （上司から）明日は在宅勤務とのことです。
• For long quotations, 「～ということだ」 can be used to emphasize an explanation, while 「～とのことだ」 is used to wrap up the information.
• Very polite variant: ～とのことでした（polite past, softens the sentence in reports).

1080.meaning: It is believed that…, it seems…
1080.connection: V/A plain form + とみられる / N/Na(である) + とみられる

examples.jp: 死者は10人とみられるが、詳細は確認中だ。
examples.tr: The death toll is believed to be 10, but the details are still being confirmed.

examples.jp: 原因は配線の劣化が主因だとみられる。
examples.tr: The main cause is believed to be deterioration of the wiring.

examples.jp: 同社の来期売上は回復に向かうとみられる。
examples.tr: The company's sales for the next fiscal year are expected to head toward recovery.

examples.jp: 犯人とみられる男が近所で目撃された。
examples.tr: A man believed to be the culprit was seen in the neighborhood.

examples.jp: 参加者は約300人とみられる。
examples.tr: The number of participants is estimated at about 300.

examples.jp: 彼は既に国外へ出国したとみられる。
examples.tr: He is believed to have already left the country.

1080.explain:
Neutral, objective nuance: often used in headlines/news reports to avoid absolute assertions before a final conclusion is reached.
Natural combinations: 数字＋とみられる／原因は～とみられる／～に関与したとみられる .
Position: used as the predicate (at the end of the sentence) or as a noun modifier.
Avoid subjectivity: do not add personal emotions; if a softer nuance is needed, use ～とみられている／～とみられます .
Tense and aspect: present to state an evaluation that is currently accepted; past when stating an evaluation of a past event.

～とみられる expresses the idea “ is believed to be / is considered to be / is likely to be…”, showing an objective judgment, usually based on facts, figures, or expert assessment. It is a typical nuance of news and report style, reducing the speaker's subjective imprint.

•
Source of conjecture: indirect or combined evidence (figures, investigations, observations, experts).

•
Objectivity: uses an impersonal subject, often combined with 警察・専門家・当局・気象庁 in another clause.

•
Scope of meaning: estimates ( 約N＋とみられる), causes ( 原因は～とみられる), states ( ～にあるとみられる).

•
Reference JLPT level: N2–N1 (appears often in newspaper reading comprehension).

rows: It is believed that (a grounded judgment, news style).
<ruby>死因<rt>しいん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>心不全<rt>しんふぜん</rt></ruby>とみられる。
Is regarded as (a judgment currently in circulation).
<ruby>被害<rt>ひがい</rt></ruby><ruby>総額<rt>そうがく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>数<rt>すう</rt></ruby><ruby>億<rt>おく</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>と<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>られている。
これは<ruby>世界<rt>せかい</rt></ruby><ruby>最古<rt>さいこ</rt></ruby>とされる<ruby>文書<rt>ぶんしょ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>原因<rt>げんいん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>複合<rt>ふくごう</rt></ruby><ruby>要因<rt>よういん</rt></ruby>と<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えられる。
I hear / it seems (based on sources, rumors).
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休職<rt>きゅうしょく</rt></ruby><ruby>中<rt>ちゅう</rt></ruby>らしい。
More personal/colloquial than とみられる.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>お</rt></ruby>りそう みたいだ。

mistakes: Confusion with ～らしい: exam questions often set traps around the source of information. とみられる = objective evaluation; らしい = hearsay/rumor.
Confusion with ～とされる:
とされる has a stronger “normative/academic” character; it is not a temporary estimate.
Forgetting 「だ」 with N/na-adj: N/na＋ だ＋とみられる is the standard form in written language.
Overuse in everyday spoken language: everyday speech is better suited to ～ようだ／～みたいだ.
Using it for commands/volition: unnatural. Avoid combining it with a direct command in the second clause.
Not appropriate when the evidence is already certain: once the result has been confirmed, use a direct assertion instead of とみられる.
1080.notes:
•
Implied responsibility for information:
～とみられる allows reporting without absolute assertion, suitable during the investigation stage.
•
Quantity expressions:
約N＋とみられる／N超とみられる are common in statistics, economics, and natural disasters.
•
Cause-and-result clauses:
～が原因だとみられる／～に起因するとみられる are used when there is no forensic/technical conclusion yet.
•
Switching style: when writing academic reports, you can mix in と考えられる／と推定される to vary the nuance.

examples.jp: 身分証の提示がないことには、貸し出しはできません。
examples.tr: We cannot lend anything out unless you present your ID.

examples.jp: 事前連絡がないことには、キャンセル料は発生します。
examples.tr: Unless you contact us in advance, a cancellation fee will be charged.

examples.jp: 契約書を確認しないことには、納品は進められません。
examples.tr: We cannot proceed with the delivery unless we check the contract.

1081.explain:
Increase objectivity with ～ます／です; avoid direct commands.
Suitable for signs/regulations: 入室不可,立入禁止…

- Used to state a mandatory condition in instructions/procedures: if it is not met, the next step cannot be carried out.
- Highly normative; often appears in official notices, procedures, and safety control.

rows: <ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>しないことには<ruby>閲覧<rt>えつらん</rt></ruby>できない
<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>がないと<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わない

mistakes: Mistaking it for a sufficient condition: in fact it is only a necessary condition; even with A, it may not be enough for B to happen.
Forgetting で after N/A-na: Nでないことには／静かでないことには.
1081.notes:
• Conversational contracted form: ～なきゃ（い）けない/～ないと, but the formality nuance differs.
• In reading comprehension, headings such as 〜手続きの流れ・注意事項 often come with this pattern. meaning_vi: Unless ～, not ⏐ explain: Expresses the idea that if the first clause is not ～, the following action cannot be carried out.
The second clause is a sentence with a negative meaning. It often expresses the speaker's negative feelings. ⏐ examples: 1. やってみないことには、できるかどうかわからない。
You won't know whether you can do it unless you try.
2. 実物を見ないことには、買う気にはなれない。
I can't bring myself to buy it unless I see the actual item.

examples.jp: 今の会社をやめない限り、こういう生活は変わらないと思ったんです。
examples.tr: I thought that as long as I didn't quit my current company, this kind of life would never change.

examples.jp: がんはかなり進行していて、手術をしない限り、助からないと言われたそうです。
examples.tr: Apparently the cancer was quite advanced, and they were told there would be no chance of survival unless there was surgery.

examples.jp: 行けなくはないけど、今日は準備が必要だ。
examples.tr: It's not that I can't go, but I need to prepare today.

examples.jp: この価格なら、買わなくはない。
examples.tr: At this price, it's not that I wouldn't buy it.

examples.jp: 彼の気持ちは分からなくはない。
examples.tr: It's not that I don't understand how he feels.

examples.jp: この問題は難しくなくはない。
examples.tr: It's not that this problem isn't difficult.

examples.jp: 日本酒は嫌いでなくはないが、弱いんだ。
examples.tr: It's not that I dislike sake, but I can't hold my alcohol.

1083.explain:
Often accompanied by conjunctions/modifiers that express a condition: けど／が／なら／とはいえ.
Often used to politely decline or to accept with reservation: “可能だが積極的ではない”.
With i-adjectives, the long form “〜くなくはない” is fine for the JLPT, but spoken language tends to use まあ/別に to express something similar.

• “It's not that… not…”, i.e., a partial/reluctant/conditional acknowledgment.
• An ambivalent nuance that avoids a definite assertion; it often implies “it's OK, but…/there is some, but…”.
• The meaning depends heavily on intonation and the clause that follows (concession, condition, limitation).

rows: Emphasizes logic, slightly stronger than “なくはない”
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いから<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない

mistakes: Forgetting “で” with Na/N: “静かでなくはない”.
Confusing “〜くはない” (only emphasizes the contrasting part) with “〜くなくはない” (double negative). Example: 高くはない ≠ 高くなくはない.
Using it for a strong affirmation → wrong nuance (this pattern is not definite).
JLPT trick questions: choosing among なくはない／ないことはない／なくもない; pay attention to the degree of certainty and the style.
1083.notes:
• Rising intonation at the end strengthens the sense of “quite possibly”, while falling intonation strengthens “reluctance”.
• Combine with conditions such as “〜次第で／〜条件なら” to clarify the limits: 手伝わなくはないが、時間次第だ。
• Na/N require “でなくはない”; dropping で is grammatically incorrect.

examples.jp: 辛い料理は食べなくもないが、得意ではない。
examples.tr: It's not that I can't eat spicy food, but I'm not good with it.

examples.jp: 彼の気持ちもわからなくもない。
examples.tr: I can also understand how he feels, to some extent.

examples.jp: 無理をすれば間に合わなくもない。
examples.tr: If I push myself, it's not impossible to make it in time.

examples.jp: 静かな所が嫌いではなくもないが、都会のほうが好きだ。
examples.tr: It's not that I dislike quiet places, but I prefer the city.

examples.jp: 値段次第では買わなくもないよ。
examples.tr: Depending on the price, I might buy it.

1084.explain:
Politeness level: Neutral; usable both in conversation and in light written language.
Building a soft argument: Often used to make a partial concession before stating a contrasting condition/main point.
Common combinations: ～なくもないが／けど, ～なくもないと思う, ～なくもないかな.
Pragmatics: Avoids giving the impression of a definite assertion; suitable when you don't want to make a firm promise or want to save face.

• Main meaning: A double negative with a mildly affirmative sense: “it's not exactly that… not…”, “it's possible that…”, “it's not that bad…”.
• Nuance of hesitation/concession: The speaker does not assert strongly but acknowledges only to a certain degree, usually to leave a possibility open or to avoid saying it directly.
• Implied condition/context: Often used with “が／けど／なら” to state a condition or exception: ～なくもないが…
• Intensity: The degree of affirmation is weaker than “できる/ある/いい” and stronger than “わけではない”.

rows: Colloquial, concise; nuance close to ～なくもない.
Negates exceptions; weaker affirmation than the three patterns above.
Direct negation, without the mild affirmation of ～なくもない.

mistakes: Confusion with ～わけではない: a sentence with ～なくもない carries a mild affirmation, not just a negation of exceptions.
Leaving out the condition that follows: ～なくもない usually needs a following clause to clarify the limits.
Using it where a clear commitment is needed can give a “half-hearted” impression.
Wrong form with i-adjectives: 高くない→高くなくもない (not 高いなくもない).
1084.notes:
• With な-adjectives and nouns, ではなくもない is more polite than じゃなくもない.
• Often used with adverbs of degree: 少し/まあ/わりと/条件次第で + ～なくもない.
• Rising intonation on “ない” helps emphasize “it's still possible/it's not that… not”.

1085.meaning:
～というのは→驚(おどろ)き、意外(いがい)等(など)の感情(かんじょう)
Expresses a feeling of surprise at something beyond what one imagined
1085.connection: N / V/A plain form + なんて/とは（だ can be omitted after present-tense Na）

examples.jp: 日本での生活はこんなに忙しいとは（夢にも思わなかった）。
examples.tr: I never dreamed that life in Japan would be this busy.

examples.jp: セミットの警備がこんなに厳重とは（知らなかった）。
examples.tr: I didn't know that security at the summit would be this tight.

examples.jp: ３億円の宝くじが当たったとは（うらやまし）！
examples.tr: To think they won a 300-million-yen lottery! (I'm so jealous!)

examples.jp: 「あの二人が離婚するなんて！あんなに仲が良かったのに」
examples.tr: “Those two are getting divorced?! They got along so well.”

examples.jp: この商品がどれだけ売れるのか、社長にしたところで実際のところは分からない。
examples.tr: Even the company president doesn't really know how well this product will sell.

examples.jp: 携帯の使用を禁止にしたところで、どのくらいの生徒が従うかわからない。
examples.tr: Even if we ban the use of cell phones, there's no telling how many students will actually comply.

1087.name: ～にしたら・にすれば（standpoint）
1087.meaning:
～の立場(たちば)からいえば/いっても→気持(きも)ち、考(かんが)え方(かた)
Contrast, from the standpoint of

examples.jp: 会社の経営が苦しいことがわかっているので、組合側にしても大幅な賃金アップは要求できないだろう。
examples.tr: Since they know the company's business is struggling, even the union probably can't demand a big wage increase.

examples.jp: 夫は転勤が多い。夫自身は好きで選んだ仕事だからいいだろうが、子どもにしたら、２年ごとに転校させられて嫌だと思っているだろう。私にしても、やむを得ないことと理解はしているが、引っ越しのたびに気が重い。
examples.tr: My husband is transferred often. It's probably fine for him, since he chose the job because he likes it, but the children probably hate being made to change schools every two years. As for me, I understand that it can't be helped, but I feel down every time we move.

1088.meaning:
基準(きじゅん)になるもの、相手(あいて)の希望(きぼう)等(など)から離(はな)れないようにする
In line with

examples.jp: 線路に沿って5分ほど歩くと、右側に公園があります。
examples.tr: If you walk along the train tracks for about 5 minutes, there's a park on the right.

examples.jp: 受験まであと3か月だ。この計画に沿って勉強しよう。

examples.jp: A高校は個性尊重という教育方針に沿い、受験でも面接を重視している。

examples.jp: 当旅行社では多くのプランの中から、お客様のご希望に沿ったツアーをお選びいただけます。
examples.tr: At our travel agency, you can choose a tour that matches your wishes from among many plans.

examples.jp: 「ご期待に沿えなくて申し訳ありません」
examples.tr: “We are sorry that we could not live up to your expectations.”

examples.jp: 海沿いの道にはしゃれたレストランが並んでいた。
examples.tr: Stylish restaurants lined the road along the sea.

examples.jp: このミスは会社の信用に関わる問題だ。
examples.tr: This mistake is a matter that affects the company's credibility.

examples.jp: 個人の命に関わっている以上、最優先で対応してください。
examples.tr: Since a person's life is at stake, please deal with this as the top priority.

examples.jp: 彼は新規事業に関わって、市場調査を担当している。

examples.jp: プライバシーに関わる情報は社外に出してはならない。

1089.explain:
Used in regulations/notices to emphasize seriousness: 安全に関わる、生命に関わる等.
The connecting form ～に関わって… helps introduce a related reason/consequence.
In conversation, to say “take part in (something)”: プロジェクトに関わる/関わっている.
Avoid overusing it when it only means “about/on the topic of”: in that case ～に関する／～について is more natural.

• Related to, having an influence on a field/target (broad, covering both good and bad effects).
• Implies a deep degree of involvement, sometimes with a nuance of “being mixed up in” (negative) depending on context.
• Often used with serious matters: 命・安全・名誉・権利・プライバシー・信用・成否.
• Difference from 関する: 関わる implies intertwining/influence, not merely a topic.

rows: <ruby>名誉<rt>めいよ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かか</rt></ruby>わる<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>について<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す。
A pattern with a different meaning, easily confused
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かか</rt></ruby>わらず。
Different spelling; often seen in official documents
<ruby>当社<rt>とうしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>係<rt>かか</rt></ruby>る<ruby>案件<rt>あんけん</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Confusion with ～に関する/～について when only stating a topic.
Confusion with ～に関わらず (regardless of) because they share the same root verb 関わる.
Machine-translating it as “mixed up in” everywhere → easily gives an unnecessary negative nuance; consider the context.
1089.notes:
• “命に関わる” is almost a fixed warning phrase (medicine, occupational safety).
• In investigations: “事件に関わる（人物・証拠）” = “involved/implicated”.
• To emphasize an active participating role: 関与する/携わる may also be suitable (with different nuances).

1090.meaning:
～を除(のぞ)いて/入(い)れないで
Excluding, without

examples.jp: 朝食ぬきは体に悪い。
examples.tr: Skipping breakfast is bad for your health.

examples.jp: あの映画は理屈ぬきに面白い。
examples.tr: That movie is simply entertaining, no explanation needed.

examples.jp: お世辞ぬきの批評が聞きたい
examples.tr: I want to hear criticism without flattery

examples.jp: このビルが地震で壊れたのは、手抜き工事のせいだ。
examples.tr: This building collapsed in the earthquake because of shoddy construction.

examples.jp: 「冗談はぬきにして、本当のことを教えてください」
examples.tr: “Joking aside, please tell me the truth.”

examples.jp: 「忘年会では仕事の話はぬきにしましょう」
examples.tr: “Let's leave work talk out of the year-end party.”

examples.jp: この制度は都市部のみならず、地方でも広く受け入れられている。
examples.tr: This system has been widely accepted not only in urban areas but also in rural regions.

examples.jp: 彼は英語のみならず、中国語も流暢に話す。
examples.tr: He speaks not only English but also Chinese fluently.

examples.jp: 環境問題は一国のみならず、国際社会においても重要だ。
examples.tr: Environmental problems matter not only to a single country but also to the international community.

examples.jp: この薬は症状を抑えるのみならず、原因治療にも有効だ。
examples.tr: This medicine not only suppresses the symptoms but is also effective in treating the cause.

examples.jp: オンライン教育は学生のみならず、社会人にも需要がある。
