1091.explain:
Used in reports, academic writing, press releases, and formal speeches.
Part B should match A in word class/aspect (parallelism); avoid combining A and B of very different types unless it is a deliberate rhetorical choice.
「も」 usually attaches to the noun/particle of B: でも/にも/も.
Can be used with scope: A（範囲）＋のみならず、B（範囲）＋も to widen it.

～のみならず～も expresses “not only A but also B”, with a formal, written-language nuance. B usually widens the scope compared with A, or adds an equally important aspect. The form A＋のみならず、B＋も/まで/さえ… is common.
• Formal listing: emphasizes that A is only one example, and B (and possibly more) is also true.
• 「も」 is placed in the second clause to emphasize B; sometimes 「まで」「さえ」 are used instead of 「も」 to heighten the surprise.
• Close in meaning to ～だけでなく・～ばかりか, but 「のみならず」 is formal and has the nuance of argumentative writing.

rows: Not only A but also B
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>だけでなく<ruby>中国語<rt>ちゅうごくご</rt></ruby>も
Not only A, but B as well
Emphatic, often with a stronger nuance of surprise than 「のみならず」
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったばかりか<ruby>風<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>も
A goes without saying, and B too
Assumes A is obvious; lighter nuance
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>はもちろん<ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby><ruby>人<rt>じん</rt></ruby>も
Similar in terms of scope; less formal
<ruby>若者<rt>わかもの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らず<ruby>高齢<rt>こうれい</rt></ruby><ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby>も

mistakes: Forgetting 「も」 in the second clause: use B＋も/にも/でも to follow the pattern correctly.
Using it in casual speech sounds stiff; in everyday conversation, 「だけでなく」 is used.
Mixing non-parallel word classes between A and B makes the sentence unnatural.
Joining a very long A without a comma after 「のみならず」 makes it hard to read; add a break.
1091.notes:
• In very formal writing, you may see「A のみならず、B に至るまで」 to emphasize an extremely wide scope.
• If B is very surprising, you can use「も」→「まで/さえ」: 彼は英語のみならず、中国語さえ独学した。
• Keep grammatical parallelism between A and B so the sentence is coherent: N with N, V with V (nominalized form when needed).

examples.jp: 有名な教授の下で研究ができて幸せだ。
examples.tr: I'm happy to be able to do research under a famous professor.

examples.jp: 両親の下で、愛情いっぱいに育てられた。
examples.tr: I was raised by my parents with plenty of love.

examples.jp: このプロジェクトは市長の下で進められている。
examples.tr: This project is being carried out under the direction of the mayor.

examples.jp: 日本では、すべての人が法律のもとで平等である。
examples.tr: In Japan, everyone is equal under the law.

examples.jp: 平和のもとで暮らせることに感謝している。
examples.tr: I'm grateful to be able to live in peace.

1093.explain:
の下で is mostly used for specific people or direct guidance: “under the teaching of…”, “under the leadership of…”.
のもとで is used for abstract, broad things such as laws, policies, and conditions: “under the law”, “under peaceful skies…”.
Style: Formal, common in written language, speeches, and newspapers, JLPT N2~N1.
Not used in casual conversation when simply saying “under a tree” → in that case use ～の下に (物理).

•
Expresses the environment, conditions, or influence under which an action/event takes place.

•
Means “under”, “under the management/influence of…” – often used with nouns referring to people, organizations, the law, or protection.

•
の下で (のもとで): Emphasizes the direct direction, guidance, or influence of a person (teacher, doctor, coach…).

•
のもとで (のもとで): More formal; emphasizes scope, conditions, or principles (the law, peace, government…).

rows: Direct influence from an individual or organization.
<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>下<rt>した</rt></ruby>で<ruby>学<rt>まな</rt></ruby>ぶ。
<ruby>法律<rt>ほうりつ</rt></ruby>のもとで<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>られている。
Emphasizes following rules/a process of change.
<ruby>指示<rt>しじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>従<rt>したが</rt></ruby>って<ruby>動<rt>うご</rt></ruby>く。
Based on…, in the name of…
Close to のもとで but means “on the grounds of”.
<ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>のもとに<ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>した。

mistakes: Confusing it with the physical meaning (under a table, under a tree…) → this pattern is not used for that.
Using it in ordinary spoken language sounds unnatural; use it in written language, newspapers, and essays.
Dropping の after the preceding noun → grammatically incorrect (の is required).
1093.notes:
• Remember: の下で＝direct influence, のもとで＝broad environment/rules.
• In legal contexts it expresses “everyone is equal under…”, so it appears often on the JLPT.
• In everyday conversation with the physical meaning “under a tree, under a table”, this pattern is not used.
meaning_vi: Under the (direction/guidance/influence) of…
examples: 1. ①　〈感謝を述べる〉先生のもとで勉強できて、本当によかったです。
2. ②　人の性格は、どういう親のもとで育ってかで、全く異なってくる。
meaning_vi: 条件(じょうけん)、指導(しどう)、支配(しはい)等(など)の下(もと)で
Under (management, direction, etc.)
examples: 1. 晴れた空のもとで運動会が盛大に行われた。
Under clear skies, the sports day was held on a grand scale.
2. 女の子は両親の温かい愛情のもとですっくすくと育った。
The girl grew up quickly in the warm love of her parents.
3. 選挙は国連の管理のもとで行われた。
The election was held under the supervision of the United Nations.
4. 「ぜひ鈴木先生の下で研究させていただきたいと思っております」
I would very much like to do research under the guidance of Professor Suzuki.
5. ～を表面上の理由にして（-）の行為が行われている
6. 開発の名のもとに自然破壊が進み、さまざまな問題が生じている。
In the name of development, the destruction of nature is advancing, causing many problems.
7. 一部の学校では、教育の名のもとに体罰が行われているそうだ。
It is reported that in some schools, corporal punishment is carried out in the name of education.
explain: A formal expression typical of written language.
examples: 1. 子どもたちが青空の下で元気に遊んでいる。
The children are playing energetically under the blue sky.
2. 田中先生のご指導の下、研究論文を書いています。
I am writing a research paper under the guidance of Professor Tanaka.

1094.meaning:
～か（どうか）わからない
No idea whether
1094.connection: V/Aい plain form + のやら/ものやら / N・Naな + のやら/ものやら

examples.jp: リさんは授業がわかっているのやらいないのやら、無表情なのでわからない。
examples.tr: Lee has no expression on his face, so I can't tell whether he understands the class or not.

examples.jp: 最近は、男なのやら女なやらわからないかっこうの若者がいる。
examples.tr: These days there are young people dressed so that you can't tell whether they're men or women.

examples.jp: コートに洗濯物の札がついている。本人に言っていいものやら悪いものやら。
examples.tr: There's a dry-cleaning tag on his coat. Should I tell him, or would it be better not to?

examples.jp: 子どもが帰ってこない・どこで何をしているのやら。
examples.tr: The kids haven't come home. Where on earth are they, and what are they doing?

examples.jp: 「あれ、めがねがない。どこに置いたものやら」
examples.tr: "Huh, my glasses are gone. Where did I put them?"

examples.jp: * ・いつのことやら ・何のことやら
examples.tr: * ・Who knows when that was ・What on earth is that about

1095.meaning:
～かどうかは…しだいだ
Depends on, rests on

examples.jp: 合格できるかどうかは、これから１か月のがんばりにかかっている
examples.tr: Whether I pass or not depends on how hard I work over the next month.

examples.jp: 契約の成否は、取り引き先がこの条件をどう考えるかにかかっている。
examples.tr: Whether the contract succeeds depends on how our business partner views these conditions.

examples.jp: 「ぼくが幸せになれるかどうかは君の返事にかかっているんだ」
examples.tr: "Whether I can be happy depends on your answer."

examples.jp: 目的が達成できるかどうかは、事前準備がどれだけしっかりできたかにかかっている。
examples.tr: Whether we can achieve our goal depends on how thoroughly we've prepared in advance.

examples.jp: * 「このプロジェクトが成功するかどうかは、あなたの肩にかかっているんです」
examples.tr: * "Whether this project succeeds or not rests on your shoulders."

examples.jp: 見た目はともかく、味は最高だ。
examples.tr: It may not look great, but the taste is excellent.

examples.jp: 費用はともかく、期限は守ってください。
examples.tr: Never mind the cost; please keep to the deadline.

examples.jp: 結果はともかく、挑戦することは意味がある。
examples.tr: Whatever the result, taking on the challenge is meaningful.

examples.jp: 日本語はともかく、英語は問題なく話せる。
examples.tr: My Japanese aside, I can speak English without any problems.

examples.jp: 安全かどうかはともかく、話題性はある。
examples.tr: Whether it's safe or not, it's certainly getting attention.

1096.explain:
N₂, which comes after, is usually the point the speaker wants to affirm/evaluate.
Soft, polite nuance; it does not deny the value of N₁.
Often used in discussions, negotiations, and evaluations of products/services.

• Setting A aside to discuss B: The speaker intentionally skips/does not consider A for now and shifts the focus to B.
• Soft contrast: Does not completely negate A; only gives priority to B in the context.
• Scope: Most common with nouns; with a clause, you must nominalize it with の/こと/かどうか.

rows: <ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>はさておき、<ruby>本題<rt>ほんだい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>る。
Stronger sense of exclusion than “はともかく”.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>別<rt>べつ</rt></ruby>として<ruby>真面目<rt>まじめ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いどころか<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>外見<rt>がいけん</rt></ruby>はともかくとして…

mistakes: Forgetting the particle “は” after N₂: it must be “N₁はともかく N₂は…”.
Using it with a bare adjective/verb: you need to nominalize it (～の/こと/かどうか).
Confusing it with “どころか”: exam traps test the degree of contrast. “はともかく” is not a strong negation.
1096.notes:
• Easily paired with noun pairs: 見た目／中身、価格／品質、量／質、形式／内容、結果／過程.
• When N₁ is long, use “～という点はともかく” to keep the sentence compact.
• In presentations, “前置きはともかく、本題は…” is very natural.

examples.jp: 冗談はまだしも、人を傷つける発言は許されない。
examples.tr: Jokes are one thing, but hurtful remarks are unacceptable.

examples.jp: 立っているのはまだしも、長時間歩くのは無理だ。
examples.tr: Standing is still OK, but walking for a long time is impossible.

examples.jp: 初心者はまだしも、プロはそんなミスをしないはずだ。
examples.tr: A beginner might, but a professional shouldn't make a mistake like that.

examples.jp: 文字での連絡はまだしも、電話は苦手だ。
examples.tr: Contacting people in writing is fine, but I'm not good on the phone.

examples.jp: 雨はまだしも、雪は交通に大きな影響が出る。
examples.tr: Rain is one thing, but snow has a major impact on traffic.

1097.explain:
The second clause is mostly negative/expresses difficulty, to highlight the limit of what is acceptable.
A mild nuance of criticism; it sets a social/personal standard.
In debates, it is used to reduce conflict: acknowledge part of it (A) and then reject (B).

• “A is still acceptable, but B is not”: Sets a minimum acceptable level (A). B goes beyond that threshold, so it is rejected/hard to accept.
• Evaluation nuance: Usually followed by a negative/difficulty in the second clause (～ない／無理だ／困る／許せない).
• Scope of use: Natural with nouns; with a verb/adjective, nominalize it with の.

rows: If it were A, it would still be OK
Emphasizes supposition/condition; about as common as “はまだしも”.
Shifts the focus; does not compare levels of acceptance.
<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>はともかく<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>は…
Stronger, harsh negation; “まだしも” only indicates a minimum level of tolerance.
<ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>どころか<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。
General concessive supposition; “まだしも” leans toward comparing degree.
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもにしても<ruby>言<rt>いいすぎ</rt></ruby>い<ruby>過<rt></rt></ruby>ぎだ。

mistakes: Dropping the particle “は” after part B: it must be “Aはまだしも、Bは…”.
The second clause is not negative/unpleasant: this weakens the meaning. Use 無理だ／問題だ／ダメだ…
Confusing it with “はともかく”: an exam trap contrasting shifting the focus vs. setting a level of acceptance.
1097.notes:
• Common noun pairs: 冗談／嘘、雨／雪、初心者／プロ、遅刻／無断欠勤、立つ／走る、挨拶／説教.
• With verbs, a symmetrical structure with のは…のは… keeps the sentence coherent: V₁のはまだしも、V₂のは…
• Avoid it when A and B are not on the same level of criteria (hard to compare).

examples.jp: 冗談は抜きにして、真面目に話そう。
examples.tr: Joking aside, let's talk seriously.

examples.jp: 今日は仕事の話は抜きにして、楽しみましょう。
examples.tr: Let's leave work talk out of it today and just enjoy ourselves.

examples.jp: お世辞抜きで、本当においしい。
examples.tr: No flattery, it's really delicious.

examples.jp: アレルギーがあるので、ナッツ抜きのメニューはありますか。
examples.tr: I have an allergy, so do you have a menu without nuts?

examples.jp: この町の発展は、彼を抜きにしては語れない。
examples.tr: You can't talk about this town's development without mentioning him.

1098.explain:
“N は抜きにして” steers the topic: used when you want to ask someone to focus/change the topic.
“N抜きで/抜きに/抜きの” describes the state of “without A” (food, services…).
In formal contexts, it can be replaced with “～はさておき／～はともかく”.
Avoid using it as a blunt command to a superior; add a polite softener:失礼ですが、冗談は抜きにして…

• “Setting aside…, leaving out…, no talk of…”: removes an element A from the conversation/situation to focus on the main point.
• With things/ingredients: means “without A/with no A added”.
• Often used to change direction in a conversation or meeting: cut off joking/beating around the bush to get to the point.
• Direct, sometimes strong nuance; consider politeness depending on the listener.

rows: Leave A aside to discuss B
<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>抜<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>きにして…
<ruby>詳細<rt>しょうさい</rt></ruby>はさておき、<ruby>結論<rt>けつろん</rt></ruby>を。
Neutral, less of a “cutting off” nuance
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>た<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>はともかく、<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>い。
Common vocabulary, no implication of changing the topic

mistakes: Confusing it with “～なしで”: the JLPT tests the difference in nuance between changing the topic (抜きにして) and the state of not having something (なしで).
Using “は抜きにして” about sensitive matters (someone else's contribution) can sound rude; mind your politeness.
Wrong position of は: × 抜きには冗談して → ○ 冗談は抜きにして
1098.notes:
• “お世辞抜きで/冗談抜きで” are set phrases, shortened without は.
• With food: “～抜きでお願いします” is very natural when ordering (氷抜きで/ネギ抜きで…).
• “N を抜きにしては” is a different pattern: a necessary condition; do not confuse it with “N は抜きにして”. meaning_vi: Leave… out, stop… ⏐ explain: Used to say that something is no longer to be done.
It means ｢…は除いて｣(remove that),「は止めて」(stop that) ⏐ examples: 1. 皆さん、仕事の話は抜きにして楽しく飲みましょう。
Everyone, let's drop the work talk and enjoy our drinks together.
2. お世辞抜きに、君の日本語は本当にうまいよ。
I'm not just flattering you, your Japanese is really good.
3. 田中さん抜きで（は）パーティーは始められません。
We can't start the party without Mr. Tanaka.

1100.meaning: It's not as if just… is enough

examples.jp: 値段が安ければ良いというものでもない。品質も大事だ。
examples.tr: Being cheap isn't everything. Quality matters too.

examples.jp: 速ければいいというものでもない。安全性が最優先だ。
examples.tr: Being fast isn't enough. Safety comes first.

examples.jp: 説明すれば分かるというものでもない。体験してこそ理解できる。
examples.tr: Explaining something doesn't necessarily make people understand. You only really understand through experience.

examples.jp: 学歴が高ければ成功できるというものでもない。
examples.tr: Having a good education doesn't guarantee success.

examples.jp: 練習量が多ければ上達するというものでもない。質も重要だ。
examples.tr: Practicing a lot doesn't automatically make you improve. Quality matters too.

1100.explain:
Placed after a conditional clause “～ば/～であれば/～なら”. What comes before is usually a single criterion.
A rebutting tone, gentle but instructive/normative.
Often followed by a contrasting element in the second clause to state the right criterion: ～も必要だ／～こそ重要だ。

• “It's not as if just… means…”: Rebuts an oversimplified view (cheap, fast, a lot… is good).
• Pragmatics: Used in argumentation, explanation, and criticism. Often used with evaluative words such as いい／十分／大丈夫／完璧.
• Normative: Implies “condition A is only one part; other factors are needed”.

rows: ～からといって～とは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない
Just because A doesn't mean B
More conversational; negates a possibility in general, does not emphasize a norm.
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いからといって<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない。
Partial negation; does not need the ば condition.
Affirms a rule; the pattern being studied negates a “simple” rule.
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>報<rt>むく</rt></ruby>われるものだ。

mistakes: Dropping the ば condition: “安いというものでもない” is not wrong but lacks the contrast; exam questions usually require “安ければ”.
Using it with obvious facts: “酸素がなければ生きられるというものでもない” is logically wrong.
Mixing it up with “とは限らない”: Both are general negations, but the JLPT requires the right nuance of “a norm/a single criterion”.
1100.notes:
• Easily combined with pairs of contrasting adjectives: 速い・安全、安い・品質、高い・価値、量・質.
• In written language, a nominalized structure often comes before this pattern: ～であるからといって… but keep “～というものでもない” to conclude the argument.

examples.jp: 彼の仕事ぶりには誰もが感心した。
examples.tr: Everyone was impressed by the way he works.

examples.jp: 彼女の話しぶりは落ち着いていて、説得力がある。
examples.tr: She speaks calmly and persuasively.

examples.jp: 今日は一週間ぶりに晴れた。
examples.tr: Today the sun came out for the first time in a week.

examples.jp: 十年ぶりの再会に、思わず涙がこぼれた。
examples.tr: Meeting again after ten years, I couldn't hold back my tears.

examples.jp: 彼の飲みっぷりを見て、相当疲れていると感じた。
examples.tr: Seeing the way he drank, I felt he must be very tired.

1101.explain:
N + ぶり emphasizes “the way/appearance” and implies an evaluation (can be praise or criticism).
Time + ぶり（に）: used to say “for the first time in…”; it can come before a noun (～ぶりのN) or serve as the predicate (～ぶりだ).
Vます + っぷり is the natural choice when attaching to a verb to say “the way of …”.
In formal writing, ～ぶり meaning “way/manner” suits reports/evaluations:仕事ぶりの改善,指導ぶり,経営ぶり.

• Means “way/manner/appearance” when attached to a noun referring to a behavior: 話しぶり（way of speaking）、働きぶり（way of working）. Often implies an evaluation.
• Expresses “a period of time that has passed” when attached to a time expression: 十年ぶりに（for the first time in 10 years）、三日ぶりの雨（the first rain in 3 days).
• With verbs, the more natural form is Vます + っぷり: 食べっぷり（way of eating）, 飲みっぷり（way of drinking）. The form ～ぶり after Vます exists but is limited and sounds old-fashioned/less natural.
• Nuance: descriptive and objective, but often accompanied by the speaker's impression/evaluation (good/bad).

rows: Attaches to a behavior noun; more formal than っぷり
Talks about a gap in time
<ruby>三年<rt>さんねん</rt></ruby>ぶりに<ruby>帰国<rt>きこく</rt></ruby>した
<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>／<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>しよう

mistakes: Confusing Vます + ぶり with っぷり: with verbs, use っぷり to sound more natural.
Forgetting に when used as a time adverbial: 十年ぶり会った（incorrect）→ 十年ぶりに会った（correct）.
Thinking ～ぶり only has a time meaning: in fact it also means “way/appearance”.
Using ～ぶり too subjectively to judge people in a formal context can be impolite; use it neutrally: 仕事ぶりを評価する.
1101.notes:
• “～ぶり” comes from 振り (to swing/wave), which shifted to mean “look, appearance, manner”.
• In newspaper headlines: ～ぶり often emphasizes a strong impression: 迫力の演技ぶり（a powerful performance）.
• Time + ぶり can combine with inexact amounts: 久しぶり（it's been a long time）, しばらくぶり（after a while）.

1102.meaning: Going so far as to…, even…

examples.jp: 彼は借金までしてギャンブルを続けた。
examples.tr: He went so far as to borrow money to keep gambling.

examples.jp: 彼女は徹夜してまでこのゲームをやった。
examples.tr: She stayed up all night just to play this game.

examples.jp: 親に嘘までついて金を集めるなんて。
examples.tr: To think someone would even lie to their parents to raise money!

examples.jp: 手術してまで延命したくない。
examples.tr: I don't want to prolong my life if it means having surgery.

examples.jp: 泣いてまで謝る必要はないよ。
examples.tr: There's no need to cry when you apologize.

examples.jp: そこまでしてまで勝ちたいのか。
examples.tr: Do you want to win so badly that you'd go that far?

1102.explain:
Emphasizes the “excessive/far-reaching” degree of the means/action used to reach a goal.
Often accompanied by an attitude of criticism or surprise, or advice not to go that far.
Best used with content that is negative/difficult/involves sacrifice; if positive, it needs a suitable context so it does not sound sarcastic.

• Expresses an extreme degree: “going so far as to even do … in order to …”. Often implies a negative or excessive evaluation.
• Two forms with the same meaning: Nまでして (even resorting to N) and Vてまで (going so far as to do V).
• Often followed by an evaluation of “unnecessary/not worth it”: ～までして／～てまで…する必要はない／そこまでして…？

rows: Going so far as to … in order to …
<ruby>借金<rt>しゃっきん</rt></ruby>までして<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う。
Only indicates inclusion, without the sense of “going far to reach a goal”
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>名<rt>な</rt></ruby>さえ<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れた。
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>。
No need to go as far as
Negates necessity; no sense of “going far”
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>するまでもない。

mistakes: Confusing it with “までに” (deadline): × 明日までして提出 → ○ 明日までに提出.
Wrong connection: “Nまでして” goes with nouns; “Vてまで” goes with the te-form of verbs.
Using it in a purely positive context makes the sentence sound sarcastic; the JLPT often tests the negative nuance.
Redundant “してまでして”: use “して” only once: × 借金してまでして → ○ 借金までして.
1102.notes:
• Nまでして emphasizes “extreme means” (borrowing money, lying…); Vてまで emphasizes “extreme actions” (staying up all night, surgery…).
• Often appears in critical questions: そこまでして～たいの？／Vてまで～たいの？
• When used with a positive goal, add a reason to avoid sounding critical: 家族のために徹夜してまで働いた。

1103.meaning:
～も・・・だし、～もまた・・・だ
Both... and...

examples.jp: 会場に独身者もいれば既婚者もいた。
examples.tr: At the venue, there were both single people and married people.

examples.jp: あのレストランは味も良ければ雰囲気も良く、その上値段も手ごろだ。
examples.tr: That restaurant has good food and a nice atmosphere, and on top of that, the prices are reasonable.

examples.jp: 彼はスポーツも得意ならピアノもプロ並みだ。
examples.tr: He is good at sports, and he also plays the piano like a pro.

examples.jp: 私は勉強も嫌いなら運動も苦手で、徒然成績も悪かった。
examples.tr: I disliked studying and was bad at sports, so naturally my grades were poor too.

examples.jp: うちにはクーラーもなければ電子レンジもありません。
examples.tr: At home, we have neither an air conditioner nor a microwave.

examples.jp: *あの親は子どもが迷惑をかけていても注意しようとしない。まったく、親も親なら子どもだ。
examples.tr: *That parent doesn't even try to correct their child when the child is bothering others. Honestly, like parent, like child.

1104.meaning: Not… at all, not the least bit…

examples.jp: 心配しないで。病気でもなんでもないよ。
examples.tr: Don't worry. I'm not sick or anything.

examples.jp: この店、安くもなんでもないのに、いつも混んでいる。
examples.tr: This shop isn't cheap or anything, yet it's always crowded.

examples.jp: それは愛でもなんでもない。ただの執着だ。
examples.tr: That's not love or anything of the sort. It's just obsession.

examples.jp: 彼はヒーローもなんでもない。普通の人だ。
examples.tr: He's no hero or anything. He's an ordinary person.

examples.jp: 別に特別でもなんでもない結果だ。
examples.tr: It's a result that isn't particularly special at all.

1104.explain:
Spoken language, direct; it can feel like a strong, rather blunt denial. Use with care in formal writing.
“でも” means “or something similar,” widening the coverage of the negation; “も” emphasizes “not even …”.
Often used to reassure, clear up a misunderstanding, or rebut an opinion.

• Emphatic negative phrase: “not … or anything,” “not … at all.”
• The form “Nでもなんでもない” is very common; “Nもなんでもない” also occurs but is less common, with a blunt, outspoken nuance.
• With adjectives, the structure emphasizes the degree “not at all”: 高くもなんでもない（not expensive at all）, 怖くもなんでもない（not scary in the least）.

rows: <ruby>病気<rt>びょうき</rt></ruby>でもなんでもない
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby>～ない／まったく～ない
<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>くない
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>すればいいというものでもない

mistakes: Using “Nもなんでもない” in formal settings sounds blunt; switch to “Nではない／Nとは言えない”.
Confusing it with standalone “なんでもない” meaning “it's nothing / it's fine”: 痛くもなんでもない（doesn't hurt at all） is different from なんでもない（it's fine）。
The JLPT often tests recognizing the broad scope of negation created by “でも”: compared with 全然～ない, it is a negation that lists multiple options.
1104.notes:
• The double emphatic form “XでもYでもなんでもない” negates all options: 若さでも実力でもなんでもない.
• With i-adjectives, there is a variant that sounds more natural in some regions: ～くもなんともない (～なんともない means “it's nothing / no problem at all”).
• In conversation, a strong fall in intonation at the end strengthens the nuance of rebuttal.

examples.jp: 人生には失敗もあれば成功もある。
examples.tr: Life has both failures and successes.

examples.jp: この仕事は楽しい時もあれば、大変な時もある。
examples.tr: This job has its fun times and its tough times.

examples.jp: 日本には伝統もあれば革新もある。
examples.tr: Japan has both tradition and innovation.

examples.jp: 安い店もあれば、高い店もある。
examples.tr: Some shops are cheap, and some are expensive.

examples.jp: 親も親なら子も子だ。
examples.tr: Like parent, like child.

1105.explain:
Often used with ある/いる/起こる/見られる to state that two sides exist.
To emphasize strong criticism, use the frame “NもNならNもNだ”.
N can be replaced by a noun phrase: ～こともあれば～こともある.

• Lists two parallel sides: there is both A and B; sometimes with the nuance “there is this, and there is also that.”
• The “NもNならNもNだ” type usually carries an evaluation (often negative): “as A is, so is B.”
• Often used to state general characteristics or give a balanced comment (pros/cons) about a target.

rows: Lists actions/points in time; focuses on activities
<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>いたり<ruby>笑<rt>わら</rt></ruby>ったりする。
Lists causes/characteristics; does not use the conditional ば
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いし<ruby>近<rt>ちか</rt></ruby>いし<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>。
There is A and there is also B
<ruby>長所<rt>ちょうしょ</rt></ruby>もあるし<ruby>短所<rt>たんしょ</rt></ruby>もある。
<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby>も<ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby>だ。

mistakes: Using an い形容詞 with ければ in this frame: × 安ければ高いも → say 安い店もあれば高い店もある instead.
Confusing it with ～たり～たり: when saying “sometimes… sometimes…”, both are correct, but ～も～ば～も～ leans toward existence/general characteristics.
Forgetting to repeat “も”: × 山もあれば海ある → ○ 山もあれば海もある.
1105.notes:
• The “Vば” form in this pattern appears mostly as “ある/いる/起こる…”; with other verbs, it usually switches to a nominalization: ～こともあれば～こともある.
• The phrase “NもNならNもNだ” can occasionally be used positively, but it usually expresses criticism.
• Flexible translations: “also… also…”, “sometimes… sometimes…”, “both… and…”. meaning_vi: not only ～ but also ～ ⏐ explain: Adds a matter in the same direction as the preceding one. (good – good, bad – bad) ⏐ examples: 1. 彼は勉強もできればスポーツもできる。
He is good at studying and good at sports too.
2. 私は歌も下手ならダンスも下手だ。
I'm bad at singing and bad at dancing too.

1106.meaning: Even if one wants to…, still…
1106.connection: V volitional form + にも + [cannot] (行こうにも時間がない)

examples.jp: 連絡しようにも、電話番号がわからない。
examples.tr: Even if I wanted to contact them, I don't know the phone number.

examples.jp: 会場に行こうにも、交通機関が止まっている。
examples.tr: Even if I wanted to go to the venue, public transportation has stopped.

examples.jp: 謝ろうにも、彼に会う機会がない。
examples.tr: Even if I wanted to apologize, I have no chance to see him.

examples.jp: 忘れようにも、そう簡単には忘れられない。
examples.tr: Even if I want to forget it, I can't forget it that easily.

examples.jp: 応募しようにも、締め切りが過ぎてしまった。
examples.tr: Even if I wanted to apply, the deadline has already passed.

1106.explain:
Used when tools/information are lacking: 連絡先がない／手段がない／時間がない.
Moderately formal; can be used in both written and spoken language.
The second clause is usually: 〜ない／難しい／無理だ／困難だ.

～ようにも expresses the situation “even if you want/intend to do V, you cannot, or it is very difficult” because of a lack of conditions or means, or an objective obstacle. “にも” emphasizes a hypothetical effort that is impossible.
• Usually accompanied by a second clause that is negative or describes an obstacle.
• Creates a feeling of “helplessness” in the face of circumstances rather than subjective unwillingness.

rows: Want to do it but cannot
Full form with the verb repeated; emphasizes ability
<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようがない。
Emphasizes the desire (wanting to do it)
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたくても<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けない。
Try to do it but fail
<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ようとしても<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>られない。

mistakes: Using “ようにも” with an affirmative second clause → logically wrong (行こうにも時間がある → contradictory).
Confusing it with “ようと”: “ようにも” means “even if you want to…”, while “ようと〜まいと” means “whether or not”.
Dropping “にも”: 連絡しように… → incorrect; it must be 連絡しようにも…
1106.notes:
• The second clause can be omitted if the context is clear: 金がなくて、行こうにも…。 (spoken language)
• Often used with verbs of perception/emotion: 忘れる／笑う／泣く.
• In formal writing, the second clause uses an abstract noun: 〜に障害がある／〜に支障を来す.

1107.meaning: Cannot… even if one wants to…
1107.connection: V volitional form + にも + V potential form ない (読もうにも読めない)

examples.jp: 忘れようにも忘れられない思い出がある。
examples.tr: There are memories I can't forget even if I try to.

examples.jp: 会場が満員で、入ろうにも入れない。
examples.tr: The venue is packed, so I can't get in even if I want to.

examples.jp: 眠気はあるのに、寝ようにも寝られない。
examples.tr: I'm sleepy, yet even if I try to sleep, I can't.

examples.jp: 彼に連絡しようにもできない。番号を失くしてしまったからだ。
examples.tr: I can't contact him even if I want to. That's because I lost his number.

examples.jp: 笑おうにも笑えない雰囲気だった。
examples.tr: The atmosphere was such that you couldn't laugh even if you wanted to.

1107.explain:
Used for difficulties that are objective rather than subjective.
More formal than “VたくてもVない”.
Suitable for written language, journalism, and theses when you need to emphasize impossibility.

Expresses “even if you want/intend to do V, you cannot do V.” The reason is an objective limitation (lack of conditions, prohibition, health, distance, etc.). Emphasizes helplessness in the face of circumstances.
• Form that repeats the same verb: Vようにも V-可能形-ない.
• The second clause is always the negative potential form of that same verb.

rows: <ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いたくても<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>えない。
Try to do it but fail
<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ようとしても<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>られない。
<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようがない。
Contracted form; the verb need not be repeated
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こうにも<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。

mistakes: Not repeating the same verb: 忘れようにも考えられない → incorrect; it must be 忘れようにも忘れられない.
Using the affirmative in the second clause → incorrect: 会おうにも会える.
Using the wrong potential form of する/来る: しようにもしれない → incorrect; it must be しようにもできない. 来ようにも来れない (colloquial) → use 来られない in standard language.
1107.notes:
• Avoid “ら抜き言葉” in standard language: 見れない → use 見られない instead.
• Often used with verbs of perception/emotion: 忘れる／笑う／泣く／動く.
• The second clause can also use the passive-potential structure: 〜られない.

1108.connection: Vます(drop ます) + ようもない (連絡しようもない)

examples.jp: 住所も電話番号も知らないから、彼に連絡しようもない。
examples.tr: I don't know his address or phone number, so there's no way to contact him.

examples.jp: 手がかりがなくて、事件を調べようもない。
examples.tr: There are no clues, so there's no way to investigate the case.

examples.jp: この汚れは古すぎて、落としようもない。
examples.tr: This stain is too old; there's no way to get it out.

examples.jp: 説明が曖昧で、理解しようもない。
examples.tr: The explanation is vague, so there's no way to understand it.

examples.jp: 暗号化されていて、データを復元しようもない。
examples.tr: It's encrypted, so there's no way to recover the data.

1108.explain:
Used when something is objectively impossible, not because the speaker doesn't want to.
Decisive, strong nuance; suitable for written language and reports.
With emotions: 「言いようもない」= not knowing how to put it properly (a literary aura).

～ようもない expresses “there is no way / it is impossible to do V” because of a lack of information, tools, or conditions. The degree of impossibility is stronger than “〜にくい/づらい”.
• The focus is on “there is no method.”
• Often used with nouns giving the reason: 連絡先／手がかり／手段／方法／証拠.

rows: Almost synonymous with ようもない
Want to do it but cannot
V<ruby>不可能<rt>ふかのう</rt></ruby>（できない）
Neutral, no implication of “there is no way”

mistakes: Wrong verb form: using V辞書形 + ようもない → incorrect; it must be V-ます with ます dropped.
Using it when other options still remain → a semantic contradiction.
Confusing it with “〜にくい”: “ようもない” means impossible due to a lack of method, not just “difficult”.
1108.notes:
• “どうしようもない” is a common set phrase: to be at a loss / to have no options left.
• Often used in investigation reports, QA, and IT: 再現しようもない／検証しようもない.
• Do not confuse it with “〜しかない” (the only option left) — the meanings are opposite.

examples.jp: 彼は誰にも相談することなしに、会社を辞めた。
examples.tr: He quit the company without consulting anyone.

examples.jp: 彼女は一言も言うことなしに、部屋を出ていった。
examples.tr: She left the room without saying a single word.

examples.jp: 休むことなしに働き続けた。
examples.tr: They kept working without resting.

examples.jp: 許可を得ることなしにデータを閲覧してはいけない。
examples.tr: You must not view the data without obtaining permission.

examples.jp: 彼はミスをすることなしに、プロジェクトを終えた。
examples.tr: He finished the project without making any mistakes.

examples.jp: 何の準備をすることなしに、発表に臨むのは無謀だ。
examples.tr: Going into a presentation without any preparation is reckless.

1109.explain:
Suitable for formal documents, reports, and academic writing.
Emphasizes that action A “absolutely did not happen”; stronger than ～ないで／～ずに.
Often used when A is something one would normally do, but the speaker emphasizes that it was not done.

• Expresses doing action B while not doing action A (V-る) at all.
• Highly formal; often used in reports, articles, and narratives.
• Often used with frequency-emphasizing words “一度も／少しも／まったく”.
• V-る must be a normally expected action that here “did not happen.”

rows: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べないで<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた。
<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>もせずに<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>った。
<ruby>途中<rt>とちゅう</rt></ruby>で<ruby>止<rt>と</rt></ruby>まることなく<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>った。
<ruby>断<rt>ことわ</rt></ruby>りなしに<ruby>欠席<rt>けっせき</rt></ruby>した。

mistakes: Using it for an action that is not clearly “habitual/expected” → the sentence sounds less natural (the pattern emphasizes “A should have been done”).
Confusing it with ～ないで: exams often test the formal nuance; choose ～ことなしに/ことなく for written language.
Using the wrong form: V-ない + ことなしに（×）; the correct form is V-る + ことなしに.
Overusing it in everyday conversation -> sounds stiff; switch to ～ないで／～ずに.
1109.notes:
• In policy/regulation texts, ことなしに creates a serious tone: 許可を得ることなしに～は禁止する。
• Combined with evaluative expressions: ～ことなしに済む（get by without having to do A）.
• When you want to sound gentle, consider ～ないで／～ずに; when you need formality/emphasis, use ～ことなしに／～ことなく.

1110.meaning: So as not to…, to avoid…

examples.jp: ミスをすることのないように、提出前に再確認してください。
examples.tr: Please double-check before submitting so that you don't make any mistakes.

examples.jp: 事故が起きることのないように、安全基準を徹底する。
examples.tr: We will strictly enforce safety standards so that no accidents occur.

examples.jp: 誤解を招くことのないように、表現に気をつけてください。
examples.tr: Please be careful with your wording so as not to cause misunderstandings.

examples.jp: 子どもが迷子になることのないように、連絡先を書いた札を持たせた。
examples.tr: I had my child carry a tag with our contact information so that they wouldn't get lost.

examples.jp: 二度と同じ過ちを犯すことのないように、仕組みを見直す。
examples.tr: We will review the system so that we never make the same mistake again.

examples.jp: 風邪をひくことのないように、マフラーをして出かけなさい。
examples.tr: Put on a scarf before you go out so you don't catch a cold.

1110.explain:
Formal; often used in instructions, internal notices, and signs.
Focuses on the preventive goal; the second clause states a clear measure/suggestion.
Can be used as a modifier: ～ことのないよう注意書き（a notice so that … does not happen）

• “So as not to …”, “in order to avoid …”: expresses a goal/prevention so that something bad does not happen.
• Ceremonious, formal nuance; suited to notices/instructions/policies.
• Often accompanied by a request, suggestion, or concrete measure in the second clause.

rows: General, less formal; common in everyday conversation.
<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れないようにメモする。
More formal/archaic; equivalent to ～ないように.
<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えぬように<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>をつける。
Emphasizes a clear purpose-reason relationship; more rational nuance.
<ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>こさないために<ruby>速度<rt>そくど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>とす。
Try to make sure not to…
<ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>することのないようにする。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～ことがない (almost never) → a completely different meaning.
Putting an adjective/noun directly before ことのないように → incorrect; it must be a verb in the V-る form.
Omitting the measure/suggestion in the second clause makes the sentence unnatural in instructions.
1110.notes:
• The phrase “二度と～ことのないように” is very common in letters of apology and corrective-action reports.
• On signs: 火事の起きることのないように → 火事を起こさないように (shorter), depending on the level of formality.
• Can stand at the beginning of a sentence as a subordinate clause: ～ことのないように、関係各所に周知した。

1111.meaning: The more you…, the more endless it gets

examples.jp: 彼の欠点を挙げるときりがない。
examples.tr: If you start listing his faults, there's no end to them.

examples.jp: 欲しいものを数え上げるときりがない。
examples.tr: If I start counting up the things I want, there's no end to it.

examples.jp: この話題は語り出すときりがないから、このへんでやめよう。
examples.tr: Once I start talking about this topic, there's no end to it, so let's stop here.

examples.jp: メニューの良さを挙げればきりがないが、まずは定番を紹介する。
examples.tr: If I listed all the good points of the menu, there would be no end to it, but first, let me introduce the standard dishes.

examples.jp: 今の不満を言い始めるときりがないので、解決策に集中しよう。
examples.tr: If we start voicing our current complaints, there'll be no end to it, so let's focus on solutions.

examples.jp: 改善点を探し始めるときりがないが、優先順位を決めよう。
examples.tr: Once you start looking for areas to improve, there's no end to it, but let's set priorities.

1111.explain:
A rhetorical nuance used to switch topics, wrap up an issue, and avoid rambling.
Often accompanied by から／ので to give the reason for stopping: ～ときりがないから／ので.
Suitable for both spoken and written language; in writing, it often appears with 挙げる・数える.

• If you start doing/mentioning V, it is “endless / there is no stopping point.”
• Used to cut things short or sum up: “there's a lot more to say, but let's stop here.”
• Often used when listing examples, complaints, wishes, pros/cons…

rows: Once you…, (bad consequence, hard to stop)
<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めたら<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>、<ruby>止<rt>と</rt></ruby>まらない。
Once you start, you can't stop
Colloquial, emotionally strong; close in meaning.
<ruby>文句<rt>もんく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>したら<ruby>止<rt>と</rt></ruby>まらない。
<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りがない／<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りない
Adjective/noun; differs from the set phrase きりがない.
<ruby>人間<rt>にんげん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>欲望<rt>よくぼう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りない。
If you start talking about it, it's endless
<ruby>欠点<rt>けってん</rt></ruby>と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えばきりがない。

mistakes: Confusing “きり” with “切り/限り” in writing → note that きりがない is written in ひらがな in this pattern.
Using it with an unsuitable verb (one without a sense of listing/starting) makes the sentence unnatural.
Forgetting the conditional と／ば/たら → there must be a conditional clause before きりがない.
1111.notes:
• “きり” in きりがない = 切り（limit/boundary）; literal meaning: “there is no line marking the end.”
• Precede it with a listing phrase so the sentence sounds natural: 例を挙げるときりがない／数え上げればきりがない。
• Very handy for ending a rambling passage: ～ときりがないので、このあたりで切り上げます。

examples.jp: この結果を見れば、原因は説明するまでもない。
examples.tr: Looking at this result, there's no need to explain the cause.

examples.jp: 小雨だから、タクシーに乗るまでもない。歩いて行こう。
examples.tr: It's only drizzling, so there's no need to take a taxi. Let's walk.

examples.jp: 彼が最適任者なのは言うまでもない。
examples.tr: It goes without saying that he is the best person for the job.

examples.jp: 少し見れば分かることだ。検査するまでもない。
examples.tr: It's obvious at a glance. There's no need to run a test.

examples.jp: 会議はメールで済むから、わざわざ来社するまでもない。
examples.tr: The meeting can be handled by email, so there's no need to go to the trouble of coming to the office.

1112.explain:
When emphasizing that something is “obvious”: often used with 当然・明らか・見れば分かる.
When emphasizing “not worth the effort”: used with わざわざ・わずか・この程度なら.
In formal written language, ～までもなく flows more smoothly mid-sentence.
After ～るまでもない, strong commands are not used; it suits mild recommendations/evaluations.

• Judges an action to be unnecessary: because it is too obvious, too simple, or not worth the cost/effort.
• Objective, polite nuance; used in both spoken and written language. 言うまでもない often comes at the beginning of a sentence that states something obvious.
• Different from なくてもいい: ～るまでもない usually implies “superfluous / no need because it is too obvious.”

rows: Neutral, gives permission; no implication of “obvious”.
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>はやらなくてもいい。
Polite/formal; means “no need to trouble anyone”.
ご<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>には<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>びません。
To the point of (going too far)
Different meaning: emphasizes an excessive degree.
<ruby>借金<rt>しゃっきん</rt></ruby>までして<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない。
Set phrase, used flexibly at the beginning of a sentence.
<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うまでもないが、<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>第<rt>だい</rt></ruby><ruby>一<rt>いち</rt></ruby>だ。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～なくてもいい: exams often ask you to choose the “obvious/superfluous” nuance → choose ～るまでもない.
Wrong form: it must be V-る + までもない; V-ない is not used.
“来なくてもいい” vs “来るまでもない”: the first gives permission not to come; the second implies “no need to come because it isn't worth it”.
Placing it after a noun is incorrect: ×予約までもない → 予約するまでもない.
1112.notes:
• “までも” originally means “to the extent that…”; combined with the negative “ない”, it creates the meaning “not to the point of having to…”.
• In reports, use “検討するまでもなく” when the conclusion is clear from the data.
• Avoid overusing it so as not to sound condescending in communication.

1114.meaning: Relying on…, with the help of…

examples.jp: 地図を頼りに目的地へ向かった。
examples.tr: I headed for my destination, relying on a map.

examples.jp: 懐中電灯の明かりを頼りに山道を歩いた。
examples.tr: I walked along the mountain path by the light of a flashlight.

examples.jp: 記憶を頼りに昔の友人を探す。
examples.tr: Relying on my memory, I'm looking for an old friend.

examples.jp: 友人を頼りにして就職先を紹介してもらった。
examples.tr: I relied on a friend and had them introduce me to a job.

examples.jp: 父の言葉を頼りとしてここまで頑張ってきた。
examples.tr: I have worked hard up to now, relying on my father's words.

examples.jp: 伝手を頼りに取引先を見つけた。
examples.tr: I found a business partner by relying on my connections.

1114.explain:
Emphasizes “relying/leaning on” rather than an objective rule; a personal, situational nuance.
Often used with verbs of motion/searching/resolving actions:行く,探す,見つける,進む.
“～を頼りとして” is formal, with a written-language style; “～を頼りにして” emphasizes an ongoing state.

• Relying on N as a clue, means, or support to carry out an action.
• Often implies that N is not perfect but is something you can cling to in a difficult situation.
• Used for both concrete things (杖, 地図, 明かり) and abstract ones (記憶, 縁, 伝手, 言葉).

<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>をもとに<ruby>分析<rt>ぶんせき</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Confusing it with ～をもとに/～に基づいて: these two patterns emphasize a firm basis and do not carry the nuance of “clinging to”.
Using it with a subject that cannot be a “support”: a noun that is too abstract cannot serve as a concrete clue → the sentence becomes vague.
Wrong particle direction: it must be を頼りに (not に頼りに).
1114.notes:
• Often used with vague “clues”: 手がかり, 記憶, 伝手, 当て.
• Can imply a feeling of weakness/needing something to cling to, creating a literary nuance.
• In polite communication, “ご縁を頼りに” sounds humble. | Variant: ～を頼りにして

1115.explain:
Emphasizes role/function rather than essential nature. When you want to define the essential nature, consider ～という.
In expository writing: often used with abstract nouns such as目的/手段/基準/対象/材料/資源/代表.
Polite style, suitable for reports and plans: ～を～として活用/位置づける/採用/設定.

• N1をN2として: regard/place/position N1 in the capacity/role/purpose of N2.
• Used to indicate: a role (代表/責任者), a function (材料/手段/目的), a standard/basis (根拠/基準).
• Nuance: somewhat formal, often found in written language, presentations, and descriptions of function.
• Different from にとって: ～として means “in the capacity of/role”, not “for (a viewpoint, benefit)”.

rows: Using N in the role of N
<ruby>紙<rt>かみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>材料<rt>ざいりょう</rt></ruby>として<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>う。
No “を” needed; the subject itself has the role
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>として<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>にとって<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>だ。
A verb of deciding; usually written language
Aを<ruby>目標<rt>もくひょう</rt></ruby>とする。
Taking N as a cutoff point/means
<ruby>本日<rt>ほんじつ</rt></ruby>をもって<ruby>終了<rt>しゅうりょう</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Dropping “を” in the double pattern: Incorrect: AとしてB. Correct: AをBとして when you mean “take A as B”.
Confusing it with にとって: “for (a viewpoint)” → にとって; ～として is not used.
Using an N2 that does not fit a role: choose a noun meaning “role/function”; do not use an adjective.
Wrong order: put N1 (the target) first and N2 (the role) after: N1をN2として.
1115.notes:
• N2 is usually an abstract noun indicating a role: 目的/基準/根拠/立場/象徴/題材/条件/前提.
• In advertising/PR: ～を強みとして/特徴としてアピールする is a very common pattern.
• Inversion to emphasize N2: N2としてN1を活用する is also found in written language.
meaning_vi: ～を・・・にする/と考(かんが)える/と決(き)める
Take... as..., decide

a TV program with environmental problems as its theme.

1124.explain:
More formal than構わない,大丈夫; suited to office contexts and regulations.

- Meaning: “there is no obstacle/problem”, “it is fine/OK” in contexts of rules, regulations, and polite communication.
• Used to give permission/agree formally, or to describe that something has no effect.
• Often seen in notices, business emails, instructions, and customer service.
• The question form “差し支えなければ …” is used as a polite opener when asking for private information.

mistakes: Used in a casual context, it sounds stiff; choose 構わない/大丈夫 instead.
Confusing who gives permission: only a person with authority should use it to give permission in a notice.

Confusing the nuance of 問題ない (judgment) vs 差し支えない (a matter of rules).

examples.jp: 果たしてこの計画は成功するのだろうか。
examples.tr: Will this plan really succeed, I wonder?

examples.jp: 実験してみると、果たして仮説は正しかった。
examples.tr: When we ran the experiment, sure enough, the hypothesis was correct.

1147.meaning: For the time being, roughly, briefly… (一応)

examples.jp: 一応説明を読みましたが、まだよく分かりません。
examples.tr: I did read the explanation, but I still don't really understand it.

examples.jp: 明日は晴れるそうですが、一応傘を持って行きます。
examples.tr: I hear it'll be sunny tomorrow, but I'll take an umbrella just in case.

examples.jp: 一応大学は出ています。
examples.tr: I did graduate from university, for what it's worth.

examples.jp: 関係者以外は入れません。
examples.tr: No one other than authorized personnel may enter.

examples.jp: 日曜日以外は毎日営業しています。
examples.tr: We're open every day except Sunday.

examples.jp: 彼以外にこの仕事ができる人はいない。
examples.tr: There's no one other than him who can do this job.

examples.jp: 犬がいきなり飛び出してきた。
examples.tr: A dog suddenly darted out.

examples.jp: いきなり質問されて、答えられなかった。
examples.tr: I was suddenly asked a question and couldn't answer.

examples.jp: 彼はいきなり会社を辞めると言い出した。
examples.tr: He suddenly announced that he was quitting the company.

1150.meaning: In one go, in one gulp, all at once… (一気に)

examples.jp: 彼は水を一気に飲み干した。
examples.tr: He drank the water down in one gulp.

examples.jp: 階段を一気に駆け上がった。
examples.tr: I ran up the stairs in one go.

examples.jp: 春になって、桜が一気に咲いた。
examples.tr: Spring came, and the cherry blossoms bloomed all at once.

examples.jp: 彼はいわゆる天才というタイプではない。
examples.tr: He's not the so-called genius type.

examples.jp: これがいわゆる「おもてなし」の心です。
examples.tr: This is what is known as the spirit of 「おもてなし」.

examples.jp: いわゆるエリートだけが成功するわけではない。
examples.tr: It's not only the so-called elite who succeed.

1153.meaning: …doesn't mean that… (ことにはならない)
1153.connection: V plain form（including past） + (という) + ことにはならない / Naだ + という / Aい + という

examples.jp: 謝ったからといって、許されたことにはならない。
examples.tr: Just because you apologized doesn't mean you've been forgiven.

examples.jp: お金を払えば済むということにはならない。
examples.tr: It doesn't mean that paying money settles everything.

examples.jp: 参加しただけでは、頑張ったことにはならない。
examples.tr: Just participating doesn't mean you've made an effort.

1154.connection: V plain form + の + も当然だ / Vて

examples.jp: あんなに練習したのだから、優勝するのも当然だ。
examples.tr: After practicing that hard, it's only natural that they would win the championship.

examples.jp: 彼が怒るのも当然だ。
examples.tr: It's only natural that he gets angry.

examples.jp: 毎日遅刻していれば、注意されるのも当然だ。
examples.tr: If you're late every day, it's only natural that you get warned.

1155.meaning: No way…, there's no way that… (ものか/もんか)

examples.jp: あんな店、二度と行くものか。
examples.tr: That shop? I'll never go there again.

examples.jp: 彼に負けるものか。
examples.tr: There's no way I'll lose to him.

examples.jp: これが偶然なものですか。
examples.tr: There's no way this is a coincidence.

1155.notes:
meaning_vi: absolutely not ～, not at all ～ ⏐ explain: Expresses strong negation.
「～もんか」、「～もんですか」 are used in spoken language or casual speech. ⏐ examples: 1. あんな店、二度と行くものか。
I will never go to a shop like that again.
2. 元気なもんか。くたくただよ。
Fine? Not at all. I'm exhausted.
3. うれしいもんですか。困っているんです。
How could I be happy? I'm in trouble.

1156.meaning: In the midst of…, while… (雨の中を)
1156.connection: V plain form + 中を 中では / N + の / A

examples.jp: 雨の中を、わざわざ来てくれてありがとう。
examples.tr: Thank you for taking the trouble to come in the rain.

examples.jp: お忙しい中を、お集まりいただき感謝します。
examples.tr: Thank you for gathering here despite your busy schedules.

examples.jp: 暗い中では、細かい字が読めない。
examples.tr: You can't read small print in the dark.

1157.meaning: Not having to…, getting by without… (なくて済む)

examples.jp: 友だちが車で送ってくれたので、タクシーに乗らなくて済んだ。
examples.tr: My friend gave me a ride, so I didn't have to take a taxi.

examples.jp: 説明書を読めば、人に聞かなくて済みますよ。
examples.tr: If you read the manual, you won't have to ask anyone.

examples.jp: 保険のおかげで、手術代を払わずに済んだ。
examples.tr: Thanks to my insurance, I didn't have to pay for the surgery.

examples.jp: 船は港に向かって進んでいる。
examples.tr: The ship is heading toward the port.

examples.jp: 目標に向かって努力し続けます。
examples.tr: I will keep working hard toward my goal.

examples.jp: 台風は北に向かって動いている。
examples.tr: The typhoon is moving north.

1159.meaning: Please…, kindly… (お願う/～ようお願いします)

examples.jp: 少々お待ち願います。
examples.tr: Please wait a moment.

examples.jp: 詳しくは受付までお問い合わせ願います。
examples.tr: For details, please inquire at the reception desk.

examples.jp: こちらの用紙にご記入願います。
examples.tr: Please fill out this form.

examples.jp: 恐らく明日は雪になるだろう。
examples.tr: It will probably snow tomorrow.

examples.jp: 彼は恐らく来ないと思う。
examples.tr: I think he probably won't come.

examples.jp: 工事は恐らく来月まで続くでしょう。
examples.tr: The construction will probably continue until next month.

1161.meaning: And, together with… (formal written language: 及び)

examples.jp: 会議には社長及び部長が出席します。
examples.tr: The president and the department managers will attend the meeting.

examples.jp: 氏名及び住所をご記入ください。
examples.tr: Please fill in your name and address.

examples.jp: 館内での飲食及び喫煙は禁止です。
examples.tr: Eating, drinking and smoking are prohibited inside the building.

1162.connection: 幸いなことに 幸い + [sentence/clause]

examples.jp: 幸いなことに、けが人は一人もいなかった。
examples.tr: Fortunately, not a single person was injured.

examples.jp: 幸いなことに、旅行中は天気に恵まれた。
examples.tr: Fortunately, we were blessed with good weather throughout the trip.

examples.jp: 幸い、終電に間に合った。
examples.tr: Luckily, I made the last train.

examples.jp: 空が次第に明るくなってきた。
examples.tr: The sky has gradually grown brighter.

examples.jp: 痛みは次第に消えていった。
examples.tr: The pain gradually went away.

examples.jp: 新しい生活にも次第に慣れてきました。
examples.tr: I have gradually gotten used to my new life, too.

1164.meaning: Even so…, even taking that into account… (それにしても)

examples.jp: 遅れると言っていたが、それにしても遅すぎる。
examples.tr: They said they'd be late, but even so, this is far too late.

examples.jp: それにしても、今日は暑いですね。
examples.tr: Anyway, it's really hot today, isn't it?

examples.jp: 難しい試験だとは聞いていたが、それにしてもこんなに難しいとは。
examples.tr: I'd heard it was a difficult exam, but even so, I never expected it to be this hard.

1165.meaning: If you do that…, in that case… (そうすると)

examples.jp: このボタンを押してください。そうすると、切符が出ます。
examples.tr: Please press this button. When you do, the ticket will come out.

examples.jp: 毎日30分歩いてみた。そうすると、体の調子がよくなった。
examples.tr: I tried walking for 30 minutes every day. As a result, I started feeling better.

examples.jp:
A: 出発は朝6時です。
B: そうすると、5時に起きなければなりませんね。
examples.tr:
A: We leave at 6 a.m.
B: In that case, we'll have to get up at 5, won't we?

1166.meaning: At least…, at a minimum… (少なくとも)

examples.jp: 完成までに少なくとも1か月はかかる。
examples.tr: It will take at least a month to complete.

examples.jp: 少なくとも私は彼を信じている。
examples.tr: I, at least, believe him.

examples.jp: 参加者は少なくとも100人はいた。
examples.tr: There were at least 100 participants.

examples.jp: 火事のときは直ちに避難してください。
examples.tr: In case of fire, please evacuate immediately.

examples.jp: 問題が見つかり次第、直ちに報告します。
examples.tr: As soon as a problem is found, I will report it immediately.

examples.jp: 工場は直ちに生産を停止した。
examples.tr: The factory immediately stopped production.

1168.meaning: Do… (command from a superior, male speech in spoken language: たまえ)

examples.jp: まあ、座りたまえ。
examples.tr: Come now, have a seat.

examples.jp: 遠慮しないで言いたまえ。
examples.tr: Don't hold back, say it.

examples.jp: 君も一緒に来たまえ。
examples.tr: You come along with us too.

1169.meaning: If you keep… (it will lead to a bad result: ていては)

examples.jp: 毎晩遊んでいては、試験に合格できないよ。
examples.tr: If you go out and play every night, you won't pass the exam.

examples.jp: 失敗を恐れていては、何もできない。
examples.tr: If you're afraid of failure, you can't do anything.

examples.jp: そんなにお金を使っていては、貯金できませんよ。
examples.tr: If you keep spending money like that, you won't be able to save any.

1170.meaning: Repeatedly… and… (repeated over and over: ては)

examples.jp: 食べては寝て、食べては寝ての生活だった。
examples.tr: It was a life of eating and sleeping, eating and sleeping.

examples.jp: 書いては消し、書いては消しして、手紙を仕上げた。
examples.tr: Writing and erasing, writing and erasing, I finally finished the letter.

examples.jp: 波が寄せては返している。
examples.tr: The waves keep rolling in and drawing back.

1171.meaning: At the same time as…, simultaneous with… (と同時に)
1171.connection: V plain form + と同時に / N・Naである + と同時に

examples.jp: ドアが開くと同時に、客が入ってきた。
examples.tr: The moment the door opened, the customers came in.

examples.jp: 彼は学生であると同時に、経営者でもある。
examples.tr: He is a student and, at the same time, a business owner.

examples.jp: ベルが鳴ると同時に、試験が始まった。
examples.tr: The exam began the moment the bell rang.

1172.meaning: In such a way as…, in the manner of… (というふうに)
1172.connection: [sentence/clause] + という風に というふうに

examples.jp: 月曜は掃除、火曜は洗濯というふうに、予定を決めている。
examples.tr: I've set my schedule like this: cleaning on Mondays, laundry on Tuesdays, and so on.

examples.jp: 「体調が悪い」というふうに言えば、休めますよ。
examples.tr: If you say something like 「体調が悪い」, you can take the day off.

examples.jp: 誰でも参加できるというふうに、ルールを変えた。
examples.tr: They changed the rules so that anyone can take part.

1174.meaning: I hear that…, apparently because… (とかで)
1174.connection: V plain form + とか(で) / N + だ / Na + だ / Aい

examples.jp: 彼は用事があるとかで、先に帰った。
examples.tr: He went home early, apparently because he had something to do.

examples.jp: 事故があったとかで、電車が止まっている。
examples.tr: The trains have stopped, apparently because there was an accident or something.

examples.jp: 体にいいとかで、母は毎朝酢を飲んでいる。
examples.tr: My mother drinks vinegar every morning because she heard it's good for your health.

examples.jp: 優勝までわずかに2点足りなかった。
examples.tr: We fell a mere 2 points short of winning the championship.

examples.jp: その村には今、わずかに10人しか住んでいない。
examples.tr: Only a mere 10 people live in that village now.

examples.jp: 部屋にはわずかに光が差し込んでいた。
examples.tr: A faint light was coming into the room.

examples.jp: 雨はやがて雪に変わった。
examples.tr: Before long, the rain turned to snow.

examples.jp: 子どもたちもやがて大人になる。
examples.tr: Children, too, will eventually become adults.

examples.jp: やがて春が来て、花が咲くだろう。
examples.tr: Before long, spring will come and the flowers will bloom.

1177.meaning: If… (then it's no good: ようでは)
1177.connection: V plain form + ようでは + bad result

examples.jp: こんな簡単な問題ができないようでは、合格は無理だ。
examples.tr: If you can't solve a problem this simple, there's no way you'll pass.

examples.jp: 少し注意されたぐらいで泣くようでは、社会でやっていけない。
examples.tr: If you cry just because you were warned a little, you won't make it in the working world.

examples.jp: 約束を守れないようでは、信用を失うよ。
examples.tr: If you can't keep your promises, you'll lose people's trust.

1178.meaning: Not… at all (ちっとも～ない)

examples.jp: 薬を飲んでも、ちっともよくならない。
examples.tr: Even though I took the medicine, I'm not getting any better at all.

examples.jp: 彼の話はちっともおもしろくない。
examples.tr: His stories aren't interesting at all.

examples.jp: 弟はちっとも勉強しない。
examples.tr: My younger brother doesn't study at all.

examples.jp: どうやら明日は雨らしい。
examples.tr: It looks like it's going to rain tomorrow.

examples.jp: どうやら彼は本気のようだ。
examples.tr: It seems he is serious.

examples.jp: 足音がする。どうやら誰か来たようだ。
examples.tr: I hear footsteps. It seems someone has come.

1180.meaning: Either way…, in any case… (どうせ)

examples.jp: どうせやるなら、楽しくやろう。
examples.tr: If we're going to do it anyway, let's have fun doing it.

examples.jp: どうせ間に合わないから、次の電車にしよう。
examples.tr: We won't make it anyway, so let's take the next train.

examples.jp: どうせ私には無理だと思っていた。
examples.tr: I had assumed it would be impossible for me anyway.

1181.meaning: At last…, the time has finally come… (いよいよ)

examples.jp: いよいよ明日は試験の日だ。
examples.tr: Tomorrow is finally the day of the exam.

examples.jp: いよいよ夏休みが始まる。
examples.tr: Summer vacation is finally starting.

examples.jp: 雨はいよいよ強くなってきた。
examples.tr: The rain has grown heavier and heavier.

1182.meaning: Not… properly, not… decently (ろくに～ない)

examples.jp: 忙しくて、ろくに寝ていない。
examples.tr: I've been so busy that I haven't slept properly.

examples.jp: 彼はろくにあいさつもしないで帰った。
examples.tr: He left without even properly saying hello.

examples.jp: ろくに調べもしないで文句を言うな。
examples.tr: Don't complain when you haven't even looked into it properly.

1183.meaning: After going to the trouble of…, a rare chance to… (せっかく)
1183.connection: せっかく + [sentence/clause] ( + のに / のだから)

examples.jp: せっかく作ったのに、誰も食べてくれなかった。
examples.tr: I went to the trouble of cooking, but nobody ate it.

examples.jp: せっかくの休みだから、どこかへ出かけよう。
examples.tr: It's a rare day off, so let's go out somewhere.

examples.jp: せっかく日本にいるのだから、富士山に登ってみたい。
examples.tr: Since I'm here in Japan, I'd like to try climbing Mt. Fuji.

1184.meaning: At least…, at the very least… (せめて)

examples.jp: せめてあと1時間あれば、終わったのに。
examples.tr: If only I'd had at least one more hour, I would have finished.

examples.jp: 全部は無理でも、せめて半分はやりなさい。
examples.tr: Even if you can't do all of it, at least do half.

examples.jp: せめて一言、連絡してほしかった。
examples.tr: I wish you had at least sent me a word.

1185.meaning: Long ago, already… a long time ago (とっくに)

examples.jp: 映画はとっくに始まっていますよ。
examples.tr: The movie started ages ago, you know.

examples.jp: そのニュースならとっくに知っている。
examples.tr: If it's that news, I've known about it for a long time.

examples.jp: 彼はとっくに帰りました。
examples.tr: He went home a long time ago.

1186.meaning: Very…, much more than usual (よほど/よっぽど)

examples.jp: よほど疲れていたのか、彼はすぐ眠ってしまった。
examples.tr: He must have been really tired, because he fell asleep right away.

examples.jp: この店のほうがよっぽど安い。
examples.tr: This shop is much cheaper.

examples.jp: よほど言おうかと思ったが、やめておいた。
examples.tr: I seriously thought about saying it, but I held back.

1187.meaning: More and more… (only changing in one direction, usually for the worse)

examples.jp: 物価は上がるばかりだ。
examples.tr: Prices just keep going up.

examples.jp: 状況は悪化するばかりだ。
examples.tr: The situation is only getting worse.

examples.jp: 事故がないようにとただ祈るばかりだ。
examples.tr: All we can do is pray that there are no accidents.

examples.jp: 解決策はない。ただ忍耐あるのみだ。
examples.tr: There is no solution. All we can do is be patient.

1187.notes:
meaning_vi: (1) more and more
(2)(3) only
used in written language.

1188.meaning: That's what… is, truly… (affirmation of a general feeling)
1188.connection: V plain form/N + というものだ

examples.jp: 人の手紙を勝手に読むのは、プライバシーの侵害というものだ。
examples.tr: Reading someone else's letters without permission is an invasion of privacy.

examples.jp: 困ったときに助け合うのが友情というものだ。
examples.tr: Helping each other in hard times is what friendship is all about.

examples.jp: 一人だけ働かされるなんて、不公平というものだ。
examples.tr: Making only one person do the work is simply unfair.

1189.meaning: Even though…, despite… (criticism, like くせに)
1189.connection: V/A plain form + くせして / Nの + くせして

examples.jp: 知らないくせして、知っているふりをするな。
examples.tr: Don't pretend to know when you don't.

examples.jp: 自分は遅刻するくせして、人には厳しい。
examples.tr: He's late himself, yet he's strict with others.

examples.jp: 子どものくせして、生意気なことを言う。
examples.tr: Just a child, yet saying such cheeky things.

1190.meaning: All of them…, every one of them…

examples.jp: 三つの案は、いずれもすばらしかった。
examples.tr: All three proposals were excellent.

examples.jp: 参加者はいずれも20代の若者だった。
examples.tr: The participants were all young people in their twenties.

examples.jp: 彼の作品はいずれも高く評価されている。
examples.tr: Every one of his works is highly regarded.

examples.jp: 計画は素晴らしい。しかしながら、費用がかかりすぎる。
examples.tr: The plan is excellent. However, it costs too much.

examples.jp: 多くの人が反対した。しかしながら、工事は進められた。
examples.tr: Many people opposed it. Nevertheless, the construction went ahead.

examples.jp: 技術は進歩した。しかしながら、新しい問題も増えている。
examples.tr: Technology has advanced. However, new problems are also increasing.

examples.jp: 今日は昨日よりやや暖かい。
examples.tr: Today is slightly warmer than yesterday.

examples.jp: 値段はやや高めだが、品質はいい。
examples.tr: The price is somewhat on the high side, but the quality is good.

examples.jp: 会議はやや長引いた。
examples.tr: The meeting ran somewhat long.

1193.meaning: There is no choice but to…, have no option but to…

examples.jp: 終電が出てしまったので、歩いて帰るよりしかたがない。
examples.tr: The last train has already left, so I have no choice but to walk home.

examples.jp: 雨だから、試合は中止するよりしかたがない。
examples.tr: It's raining, so we have no choice but to cancel the game.

examples.jp: 材料がないので、あきらめるよりしかたがない。
examples.tr: We don't have the ingredients, so there's no choice but to give up.

examples.jp: いったん約束したら、必ず守るべきだ。
examples.tr: Once you have made a promise, you should be sure to keep it.

examples.jp: いったん始めると、途中でやめられない。
examples.tr: Once you start, you can't stop halfway.

examples.jp: いったん引き受けたら、最後まで責任を持ちなさい。
examples.tr: Once you have taken something on, take responsibility for it to the end.

1195.meaning: In the unlikely event…, if by any chance…

examples.jp: 万が一火事になったら、この階段から逃げてください。
examples.tr: If by any chance there is a fire, please escape by these stairs.

examples.jp: 万が一の場合は、この番号に電話してください。
examples.tr: In an emergency, please call this number.

examples.jp: 万が一失敗しても、もう一度挑戦すればいい。
examples.tr: Even if by some chance you fail, you can just try again.

examples.jp: 何から何までお世話になりました。
examples.tr: Thank you for everything you have done for me.

examples.jp: 彼は何から何まで私と正反対だ。
examples.tr: He is the complete opposite of me in every way.

examples.jp: 旅行の準備は何から何まで妻がやってくれた。
examples.tr: My wife took care of every single part of the trip preparations.

1197.meaning: As one wishes… (思うようにいかない)
1197.connection: 思うように + V（usually negative: 思うようにいかない）

examples.jp: 体が思うように動かない。
examples.tr: My body won't move the way I want it to.

examples.jp: 仕事が思うように進まなくて、いらいらする。
examples.tr: My work isn't progressing as I'd like, and it's frustrating.

examples.jp: 思うように話せなくても、あきらめないでください。
examples.tr: Even if you can't speak as well as you'd like, please don't give up.

1198.meaning: Still… even now (has not changed for a long time)

examples.jp: 彼の名前がいまだに思い出せない。
examples.tr: I still can't remember his name.

examples.jp: 事故の原因はいまだに分かっていない。
examples.tr: The cause of the accident is still unknown.

examples.jp: 卒業して10年たつが、いまだに先生と連絡を取っている。
examples.tr: It's been 10 years since I graduated, but I'm still in touch with my teacher.

1199.connection: V plain form + というか + V plain form + というか / N + N / Na + Na / Aい + Aい

examples.jp: 彼は優しいというか甘いというか、人に厳しくできない。
examples.tr: He's kind, or rather soft, and can't be strict with people.

examples.jp: 驚いたというか呆れたというか、言葉が出なかった。
examples.tr: Surprised, or maybe appalled, I was at a loss for words.

examples.jp: これは仕事というか趣味というか、やっていて楽しい。
examples.tr: Call it work or call it a hobby, it's fun to do.

examples.jp: 日本の夏は暑いというか蒸し暑い。
examples.tr: Summer in Japan is hot, or rather, muggy.

examples.jp: 今日は忙しいというかバタバタしてて、連絡が遅れました。
examples.tr: Today was busy, or rather hectic, so I'm late getting in touch.

examples.jp: 彼の発言は正直というか失礼というか、聞いていてハラハラする。
examples.tr: His remarks are honest, or maybe rude; listening to him makes me nervous.

1199.explain:
Suited to conversation, blogs and social media; rarely used in formal documents.
Usually pairs two expressions of the same part of speech (N with N, A with A…) to keep the rhythm natural.
Can be used once to correct yourself: A、 というか、B（正確にはB）.
Expresses a modest/softened attitude, avoiding a strong assertion.
The variant っていうか has a more casual nuance.

• Expresses hesitation/rephrasing: “you could say it this way, or you could say it that way”, “or rather…”.
• Usually presents two expressions with similar meanings or two sides of the same thing, showing a vague evaluation that is hard to state definitively.
• Can be used to correct the statement just made: “A… no, more accurately, B”.
• Has a conversational, soft nuance, more narrative/exclamatory than a normative judgment.
mistakes: Mixing parts of speech: A is a noun and B is a verb, which sounds forced. Keep the same part of speech when possible.
Using it in formal documents (reports, theses) makes them less serious; the JLPT often sets traps with a formal context → choose というより/すなわち.
Confusing it with というより: if the sentence needs to “negate A to choose B”, you must use というより, not というか.
Repeating というか too many times in one sentence makes it wordy and incoherent.
JLPT level: というか usually appears at N2 (also seen at N3 in conversational contexts); questions often test the nuance of “adjusting what was said”.
1199.notes:
• Put “AというかB” right after the previous statement to adjust it naturally: A（大雑把）→ というかB（精確/婉曲）.
• Don't overuse it with too many long pairs; two phrases at most is most natural.
• In formal presentations, prefer というより/すなわち/つまり, which are clearer than というか.
meaning_vi: I don't know whether to call it ~ or ~
explain: ◎ An expression used when you want to explain something with several different expressions, avoiding asserting it with just one.
examples: 1. この靴は、おしゃれというか、派手というか、デザインが変わっている。
These shoes have an unusual design; I don't know whether to call them stylish or flashy.
2. こういう会は、面倒というか、疲れるというか、あまり行きたくない。
I don't really want to go to gatherings like this; they feel like a hassle, or tiring.
meaning_vi: 思(おも)いつくままに評価(ひょうか)の言葉(ことば)を並(なら)べる
examples: 1. 彼女はかわいいというか子どもっぽいというか、とにかく年よりはずいぶん若く見える。
Whether you call her cute or childish, anyway, she looks much younger than her age.
2. 「父は曲がったことが大嫌いな人です。くそまじめと言うか融通が利かないと言うか・・・・・」
My father is someone who hates anything crooked. He's extremely serious, and also inflexible.
3. 「山本のやつ、会社を辞めて自転車で世界一周旅行をするんだって。勇気があると言うか無謀と言うか。でも、ちょっとうらやましいなあ」
That guy Yamamoto, I hear he's quitting his job to travel around the world by bicycle. He's brave and reckless at the same time. Still, I'm a bit jealous!

examples.jp: 帰りがけに牛乳を買ってきて。

examples.tr: The new product sold out in no time.

examples.jp: うわさはたちまち学校中に広がった。
examples.tr: The rumor instantly spread throughout the school.

examples.jp: 空が暗くなり、たちまち雨が降り出した。
examples.tr: The sky grew dark, and in an instant it started to rain.

examples.jp: 二人はなにやら小さい声で話している。
examples.tr: The two of them are talking about something in low voices.

examples.jp: 台所からなにやらいいにおいがする。
examples.tr: Something smells good from the kitchen.

examples.tr: He seems to be troubled about something.

examples.tr: She is about the only one who would grant such an unreasonable request.

examples.jp: 夜中に呼び出されて文句も言わないのは彼ぐらいのものだ。

examples.jp: この難問を時間内に解けるのは田中さんぐらいのものだ。

examples.jp: 彼の冗談に本気で怒るのは新入社員ぐらいのものだ。
examples.tr: Only new employees would get genuinely angry at his jokes.

examples.jp: 親の前で弱音を吐けるのは子どもぐらいのものだ。

1204.explain:
Emphatic structure: [clause] + のは + [the only target] + ぐらいのものだ。
“ぐらいのものだ” strengthens the nuance of “only… and no one else”, with a slight exaggeration.
Often used in conversation/narration, and also found in descriptive writing.

• Emphasizes an extremely narrow scope: “only … can / it really is …”.
• Nuance of exaggeration/emphasis on the speaker's emotion (may overstate a little).
• Often used to praise/criticize, or to emphasize something special or exceptional.

rows: ～のは N ぐらいのものだ
できるのは<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>くらいのものだ
<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かるのは<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>だけだ
<ruby>頼<rt>たよ</rt></ruby>れるのは<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>くらいしかない

mistakes: Wrong position of のは: ×彼くらいのものだ助けてくれる → correct: 助けてくれるのは彼ぐらいのものだ。
Overuse in formal writing; in reports, use だけだ to be more neutral.
Understanding it as an absolute fact → in fact it has a nuance of exaggeration/personal emphasis.
JLPT N2–N1: Distinguish it from ～しかない (lack of choices) and ～だけだ (neutral).
1204.notes:
• “ぐらいのものだ” > “くらいだ” in degree of emphasis; both are natural.
• Can be used with time/place: こんな景色が見られるのはここぐらいのものだ。
• Often used with special/exceptional topics for a rhetorical effect.
meaning_vi: Only… and nothing else (emphasis: くらいのものだ)

examples.jp: ラジオを聞くともなく聞いていたら、いつの間にか寝ていた。
examples.tr: I was half-listening to the radio and before I knew it I had fallen asleep.

examples.jp: 公園で空を眺めるともなく眺めていた。
examples.tr: I was idly gazing at the sky in the park.

examples.jp: どこからともなく花の香りが漂ってきた。
examples.tr: The scent of flowers drifted in from somewhere.

examples.jp: いつからともなくこの町に外国人が増えた。
examples.tr: At some point, the number of foreigners in this town increased.

examples.jp: 道を歩くともなく歩いていたら、海に出た。
examples.tr: I was walking aimlessly along the road and came out at the sea.

1205.explain:
Used when the speaker has no clear purpose (looking, listening, thinking, strolling…).
The form question word＋ともなく emphasizes that the origin, place or point in time is “unspecified”.
Not used for strongly intentional acts, commands or clear volition.
Often used in descriptive writing, diaries and novels to create a hazy atmosphere.

• Meaning 1 (unconscious action): Describes doing an action idly, unintentionally, without a clear goal. Example: 聞くともなく聞く (listen absentmindedly).
• Meaning 2 (unknown origin/time): Used with question words such as いつ／どこ／誰 to say “no one knows since when/from where/by whom”. Example: どこからともなく (from somewhere unknown).
• Nuance: Written language, neutral; descriptive, sometimes creating a vague, hazy feeling.
• Grammar: Vるともなく can stand alone or be repeated as VるともなくVる; the subject is usually the speaker/the person observed, in a “relaxed” state.

rows: Used with V or question word＋ともなく
テレビを<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るともなく…
Emphasizes “without intention”; used less with question words
<ruby>空<rt>そら</rt></ruby>を<ruby>眺<rt>なが</rt></ruby>めるともなしに…
Intentional “while at it”; opposite of unconscious
<ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>がてら<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>する
<ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>のついでに<ruby>観光<rt>かんこう</rt></ruby>した

mistakes: Using it for an action with a clear goal: incorrect. Incorrect example: × 目的地へ行くともなく行く (use どこへともなく for going aimlessly).
Confusing it with ～がてら/～ついでに: ～ともなく is unconscious; the other two patterns are intentional.
Dropping から/へ in a phrase with a question word: どこともなく (has a different meaning, “anywhere”); for the meaning “from somewhere unknown” you need どこからともなく.
1205.notes:
• The repeated form VるともなくVる balances the rhythm of the sentence and highlights the “absentminded” quality.
• With question words, から/へ are usually used: どこからともなく, どこへともなく.
• Often seen with verbs of perception: 見る, 聞く, 眺める, 考える, 歩く.
meaning_vi: Unintentionally…, without intention
explain: Describes a “relaxed” state: doing something halfheartedly, without concentrating.
Often used with the repeated form to sound more natural in spoken/written language.
Not used when the speaker wants to show a clear goal or give a command/express volition.
examples: 1. ラジオを聞くともなしに聞いていたら、懐かしい曲が流れてきた。
I was half-listening to the radio when a nostalgic song came on.
2. 通勤電車で外を眺めるともなしに眺めていた。
On the commuter train, I was idly gazing outside.
3. 公園を歩くともなしに歩いていたら、友達に会った。
I was wandering aimlessly in the park when I ran into a friend.
4. SNSを見るともなしに見て時間をつぶす。
Killing time idly scrolling through social media.
5. どこからともなしに拍手が起こった。
Applause broke out from somewhere.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Key difference | Short example
～るともなしに | Doing something absentmindedly | Gentle, rich in everyday nuance | 外（そと）を 眺（なが）めるともなしに …
～るともなく | Doing something absentmindedly; question word＋ともなく is common | Wide use; many set phrases with question words | どこ からともなく …
～ながら | Doing A while doing B | Expresses simultaneity, does not emphasize “absentmindedness” | 音楽（おんがく）を聞（きき）き ながら 勉強（べんきょう）する
～つい | Doing by mistake, unintentionally | Expresses “slipping”/carelessness, unlike prolonged idleness | つい 食（た）べ過（す）ぎた
common_mistakes: • Using it with a command/volition: × 見るともなしに見てください → unnatural.
• Using it for a clear purpose: × 情報を集めるともなしに集める (this action usually has a goal).
• Confusing it with ～つい: ～ともなしに is a prolonged idle state; ～つい is a momentary “slip”.
meaning_vi: Idly…, without intention… (ともなく/ともなしに)

1206.connection: どうにか + V (managing to do something): Somehow, finally manage to do it / どうにか + Aい / Na / Adv (just enough degree): A state of just getting by, so-so / どうにかなる: Everything will be fine, it will work out

examples.tr: Before computers became widespread, letters were the main means.

1209.meaning: The situation is that…, that is how… (formal explanation)

examples.jp: ご報告が遅れたのは、確認に時間がかかった次第です。
examples.tr: The reason my report was late is that the confirmation took time.

examples.jp: 皆様のご協力をお願いしたく、ご連絡した次第です。
examples.tr: I am contacting you because I would like to ask for everyone's cooperation.

examples.jp: 以上のような経緯で、本日の会議となった次第です。
examples.tr: Due to the circumstances described above, we are holding today's meeting.

1210.meaning: At the same time… / While at it…

examples.jp: 新年のご挨拶かたがた、本日伺いました。
examples.tr: I have come today to offer my New Year's greetings as well.

examples.jp: お礼かたがた、成果をご報告申し上げます。
examples.tr: I would like to express my thanks and, at the same time, report the results.

examples.jp: 資料送付かたがた、近況をご連絡いたします。
examples.tr: Along with sending the materials, I would like to update you on recent developments.

examples.jp: 見学かたがた、ご挨拶に参りました。
examples.tr: I have come to see the facility and to pay my respects as well.

examples.jp: お詫びかたがたご訪問いたしました。
examples.tr: I visited to offer my apologies as well.

1210.explain:
Formal, polite; suitable for company documents, invitations and speeches.
Often used with keigo: 伺う, 参る, 申し上げる, 拝見する, 致します.
Used for actions such as moving/visiting/exchanging that have a social, courtesy character.

• Meaning: “while at it, at the same time with the purpose N”, in a ceremonial, very polite way of speaking.
• Context: letters, speeches, formal announcements; when visiting someone politely.
• The subject is usually the speaker/the speaker's group. Rarely used to talk about a distant third party.
• The preceding noun is usually a courtesy noun: ご挨拶, お礼, お詫び, ご報告, ご連絡, 見学.

rows: Courtesy N; mainly the speaker; keigo verbs
ご<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>かたがた<ruby>伺<rt>うかがう</rt></ruby>う
Going out, doing A and B while at it
<ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>がてら<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く
<ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>のついでに<ruby>観光<rt>かんこう</rt></ruby>する

mistakes: Using it with casual verbs, without keigo: unnatural in the style of 「かたがた」.
Using it to talk about a distant third party: not typical; keep the speaker as the agent.
Confusing it with 「がてら」: 「かたがた」 is formal and social; 「がてら」 is everyday.
Attaching it to an unsuitable N (an everyday N): something like 「ゲームかたがた」 sounds odd.
1210.notes:
• Place an N with a “polite purpose” in front to show good manners and a legitimate reason for the visit/contact.
• Effective in business emails: 「ご報告かたがた資料を送付いたします」。
• Avoid overusing it in everyday conversation so as not to sound overly stiff.

1211.connection: V plain form + (か)と思いきや / N + (だ) / Na + (だ) / Aい

examples.jp: 雨がやんだかと思いきや、すぐまた降り出した。
examples.tr: Just when I thought the rain had stopped, it started again right away.

examples.jp: 今日は楽かと思いきや、むしろ忙しかった。
examples.tr: I thought today would be easy, but it was actually busy.

examples.jp: 値下げかと思いきや、実は内容量が減っていた。
examples.tr: I thought it was a price cut, but in fact the contents had been reduced.

examples.jp: 彼が優勝かと思いきや、最後に逆転された。
examples.tr: Everyone thought he had won, but he was overtaken at the very end.

examples.jp: 静かかと思いきや、隣の工事が始まった。
examples.tr: Just when I thought it would be quiet, construction next door started.

1211.explain:
A formal/lightly humorous style in narration; suitable for headlines: 順調かと思いきや… .
Not used when Y is not contrary but just a normal sequence.
X can be a subjective feeling or an objective sign; Y negates that expectation.

～かと思いきや expresses “I thought/assumed … but (in reality) …”, emphasizing a contrast with a prediction or initial sign. Written-language nuance, newspaper headlines, storytelling.
• X is usually the basis for the prediction; Y is the contrary, surprising result.
• Not used for the speaker's intentional actions such as commands/intentions.
• Often used with adverbials of time/context: ところが・しかし.

rows: <ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いきや<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>いた
～かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと／～かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>えば
<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うとやむ
Spoken language, does not emphasize unexpected contrast
<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>ったらまた<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た
Only states the expectation, does not necessarily state a contrary result
<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>った

mistakes: Using it for an ordinary time relation → incorrect; this pattern requires a “contrary result”.
Dropping である before nouns/na-adjectives: you must say N/na + である + かと思いきや.
Attaching a request/command after ～かと思いきや is unnatural on the JLPT.
1211.notes:
• “きや” in 思いきや is a fixed form; 思う is not conjugated here.
• Often used with Vた to suggest “just when I thought…”.
• Rhetorical effect: creates a “twist” in the story; suitable for essays and leading into newspaper articles.

examples.jp: 古さこそあれ、性能は十分だ。
examples.tr: It may be old, but its performance is sufficient.

examples.jp: 不便さこそあれ、住めば都だ。
examples.tr: It may be inconvenient, but home is where you make it.

examples.jp: 多少のリスクこそあれ、挑戦する価値はある。
examples.tr: There is some risk, but it is worth trying.

examples.jp: 欠点こそあれ、彼の誠実さは本物だ。
examples.tr: He may have his faults, but his sincerity is genuine.

examples.jp: 初期費用の高さこそあれ、長期的には割安だ。
examples.tr: The initial cost may be high, but in the long run it is cheaper.

examples.jp: 苦労こそあれ、学びは大きい。
examples.tr: There are hardships, but you learn a lot.

1212.explain:
Style of speeches/reports/light academic writing; polite, formal.
The first clause is usually short and concise; the second clause develops the main argument.
Suitable when you want to “acknowledge a drawback but still be supportive”.

• A formal concession structure: admits a shortcoming/disadvantage, but affirms the latter part.
• Typically used with nouns of quality (古さ/不便さ/欠点/リスク/難点/苦労).
• Focuses emphasis on the second clause, usually expressing a positive evaluation/affirmation.

rows: <ruby>古<rt>ふる</rt></ruby>さこそあれ<ruby>快適<rt>かいてき</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いものの<ruby>満足<rt>まんぞく</rt></ruby>。
Even though it is said… still…
Used in both conversation and writing; flexible.
<ruby>不便<rt>ふべん</rt></ruby>とはいえ<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>める。
Used with Vます/いA/なA; quite colloquial.
<ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さいながら<ruby>機能<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>的<rt>てき</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Using it directly with verbs or adjectives that are not nominalized: ×高いこそあれ → ○高さこそあれ.
