The second clause must not totally negate the topic: “古さこそあれ、全然価値がない” clashes in style; use ものの instead.
JLPT: recognize the formal flavor and the combination limits (N/〜さ) to choose こそあれ correctly.
1212.notes:
• こそ creates strong emphasis; あれ is a verb form of ある (classical continuative form) giving a written-language nuance.
• Nominalization of adjectives with 〜さ makes it natural: 高さこそあれ／弱さこそあれ.
• Often used with quantifiers 多少の／わずかな to play down the shortcoming.

1213.connection: N + こそすれ + [second clause] / Vます

examples.jp: 疑問こそすれ、賛成はできない。
examples.tr: I may have doubts, but I cannot agree.

examples.jp: 彼の誠実さは疑いこそすれ、非難する点はない。
examples.tr: One may have doubts about his sincerity, but there is nothing to criticize.

examples.jp: 時間が経てば愛情は深まりこそすれ、薄れることはない。
examples.tr: As time passes, affection only deepens; it never fades.

examples.jp: 新制度は戸惑いを生みこそすれ、混乱を招くものではない。
examples.tr: The new system may cause confusion at first, but it is not something that leads to chaos.

examples.jp: 努力は評価こそすれ、笑いものにはしない。
examples.tr: We would praise effort, but never make fun of it.

1213.explain:
Form: with verbs, use Vます without ます + こそすれ; with nouns, use N + こそすれ directly.
Semantic link: the second clause is usually followed by ～ない／～はしない／～できない／～ことはない to clearly negate.
Nuance: formal, decisive, “closing off the proposition”; suitable for written language, speeches and serious commentary.
Pragmatics: emphasizes the “upper limit” of A (the most that can be admitted) and denies any other interpretation.

～こそすれ emphasizes one-sidedness: it admits possibility/phenomenon A while firmly rejecting possibility B. It can be understood as: “if anything, only A, and absolutely not B.”
• Strong degree of affirmation/negation, with a formal, argumentative flavor.
• Often used to counter the listener's or public's prediction: “You think B? No. At most it's A.”
• The second clause takes a negative: ～ない／～はしない／～できない… to close off the meaning completely.

rows: Strongly negates B; written language, decisive
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れこそすれ、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>はしない。
Concedes A (usually negative) but result B still holds
<ruby>不便<rt>ふべん</rt></ruby>こそあれ、<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>みやすい。
Softer, without the “only A, not B” constraint
<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>とはいえ<ruby>油断<rt>ゆだん</rt></ruby>できない。
It is said to be A, but actually B
<ruby>得意<rt>とくい</rt></ruby>といっても<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しだけ。

mistakes: Wrong form: with verbs, use the Vます form (without ます); do not use the dictionary form directly.
Missing negation in the second clause: the pattern requires the relation “only A, not B”, so a clear negative marker is needed.
Confusing it with ～こそあれ: both are formal, but こそすれ negates B; こそあれ means “although A, (still) B”.
Nuance: used in a serious style; in casual speech it can sound “stiff”.
1213.notes:
• こそ here is a strongly emphatic particle, giving a literary tone when combined with すれ (the continuative form of する in its classical form).
• Part A is usually the “highest/furthest” thing the speaker is willing to admit; part B is the remaining possibilities, which are negated.
• Often used with abstract nouns or mental actions: 疑問・不満・期待・評価・尊敬・戸惑い…

examples.jp: 子どものこととて、どうか大目に見てください。
examples.tr: Since they're only children, please be lenient with them.

examples.jp: 初めてのこととて、手際が悪く失礼いたしました。
examples.tr: As it was my first time, I handled things clumsily. Please forgive me.

examples.jp: 事情も知らぬこととて、余計なことを申し上げました。
examples.tr: Not knowing the circumstances, I said something I should not have.

examples.jp: 急な出張のこととて、ご挨拶もできず失礼しました。
examples.tr: Because of a sudden business trip, I was unable even to say goodbye. My apologies.

examples.jp: 不慣れなこととて、少々お時間をいただきます。
examples.tr: As I am not used to this yet, I will need a little time.

1214.explain:
Nuance: humble, asking for forgiveness, explaining an unavoidable cause.
Position: usually at the beginning of a sentence to state the reason, followed by an apology/request.
Suitable for business emails, official notices, and speeches.
Combinations: often used with apologetic keigo phrases such as 失礼いたしました,申し訳ございません.

～こととて means “because/since it is … ”, used to state a circumstantial reason and ask for understanding/forgiveness. It is a classical, formal expression, often seen in written language, apologies, and notices.
• Usually follows N denoting a situation: 子ども, 初めて, 不慣れ, 急用, 留守, 多忙.
• What follows ～こととて is usually a clause asking for understanding, expressing an unavoidable result.
• Rarely used in everyday conversation; replaced by ～ものですから, ～もので, ～ため.
• Not used directly with commands/strong resolutions; suitable for asking permission, apologizing, and explaining.

rows: <ruby>渋滞<rt>じゅうたい</rt></ruby>なもので<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れました
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>のため<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>
Set phrase for notices; no personal request for forgiveness
<ruby>臨時<rt>りんじ</rt></ruby><ruby>休業<rt>きゅうぎょう</rt></ruby>につき

mistakes: Using it in casual conversation sounds stiff and affected; use ～もので instead.
Attaching it directly to the dictionary form of a verb is sometimes awkward; prefer Nのこととて or a shortened clause.
JLPT: a trap distinguishing the nuance of asking forgiveness (～こととて) from the neutral one (～ため). If the sentence has 失礼/ご容赦ください → choose ～こととて.
Not used for commands/strong volition: ～こととて, 行け is unnatural.
1214.notes:
• “こととて” comes from “こと（事）+とて（と言って）”, with a nuance like “saying that it is …, so”.
• Formulaic: 子どものこととて, 初めてのこととて are almost fixed phrases.
• Often accompanied by keigo/humble language to keep the style consistent.
• In literature/parallel prose, used to create an old-fashioned, polite tone.

examples.jp: 子どもが生まれてからというもの、外で飲むことがほとんどなくなった。
examples.tr: Ever since my child was born, I've hardly gone out drinking.

examples.jp: この町に引っ越してからというもの、車を使う頻度がぐっと増えた。
examples.tr: Ever since I moved to this town, I've been using the car much more often.

examples.jp: あの事故を目撃してからというもの、夜道を一人で歩けなくなった。
examples.tr: Ever since I witnessed that accident, I haven't been able to walk alone at night.

examples.jp: 新しい上司になってからというもの、残業が当たり前になった。
examples.tr: Ever since we got a new boss, overtime has become the norm.

examples.jp: スマホを替えてからというもの、写真を撮るのが楽しくて仕方がない。
examples.tr: Ever since I changed my smartphone, I can't get enough of taking photos.

1215.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize a change that has lasted since a certain point.
The subject is usually the speaker or a close group, since it involves subjective perception.
Rarely used with a direct command/intention in the second clause.
Often used with the negative to emphasize “no longer doing X”: ～なくなった／とんと～ない.

～てからというもの emphasizes that, from a certain point in time/action that serves as a marker, the situation in the following clause changed markedly and continues to the present.
• Often accompanied by words of duration: ずっと／めっきり／とんと～ない／まったく～ない.
• The second clause is usually a habit/state, rarely a single action that ends immediately.
• Has a stronger emotional/subjective nuance than ～て以来, suggesting “from then on, everything was different”.
• Not used for very short time spans or trivial everyday events.

rows: Neutral, shows order only; no emphasis on duration
<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ご<ruby>飯<rt>はん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べてから<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた
Similar meaning but more neutral; widely used
<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby>して<ruby>以来<rt>いらい</rt></ruby><ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>っていない
Since X, the situation has changed markedly and lasted
Emphasizes a change to “something completely different”
<ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>してからというもの～

mistakes: Using it for a brief, one-time event in the second clause → wrong nuance (it must be a lasting state).
Confusing it with ～てから: that lacks the sense of “completely changed and lasting”.
Using it with a trivial reference point (e.g., 昨日～) → unnatural.
Attaching a direct command/volition in the second clause → inappropriate.
1215.notes:
• The second clause is often in the present/present perfect in the Japanese sense (～ている／～なくなる).
• Works well in written language, narratives about life, and essays about turning points.
• Can follow social events: 震災／コロナ禍／不況 からというもの、～

examples.jp: 皆様のご健康とご多幸を願ってやまない。
examples.tr: I sincerely wish you all good health and happiness.

examples.jp: 被災地の一日も早い復興を祈ってやまない。
examples.tr: I pray with all my heart for the swift recovery of the disaster-stricken areas.

examples.jp: 私は故郷を愛してやまない。
examples.tr: I love my hometown dearly.

examples.jp: 新しい時代の到来を期待してやまない。
examples.tr: I have the highest hopes for the arrival of a new era.

examples.jp: 亡き友の安らかな眠りを願ってやみません。
examples.tr: I pray earnestly that my late friend may rest in peace.

1216.explain:
Suitable for well-wishes, formal speeches, and reflective writing.
Rarely used with concrete action verbs; mainly with verbs of mental state.
Can be used as a modifier:私の 愛してやまない 家族.
Not used for momentary emotions like驚く,怒る in an outburst sense.

• Expresses feelings, wishes, or inner attitudes that are “unceasing, never fading” and enduring.
• Usually used with psychological/emotional verbs: 願う, 期待する, 愛する, 慕う, 祈る, 尊敬する.
• Formal nuance, often used in written language, speeches, eulogies, and well-wishes.
• The subject is usually the speaker or a representative speaker; rarely used for strong, sudden negative emotions.

rows: Formal, often used with <ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>う, <ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>する.
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>ってやまない。
Different, spontaneous nuance; often with <ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じる/<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>える/<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>だ.
Strong, leaning toward physical sensations/sudden emotions.
Neutral in nuance; describes duration, not formal.

mistakes: Using it with concrete action verbs (行く, 食べる): unnatural.
Using it for sudden emotions: wrong nuance; use ～てたまらない/～てならない instead.
Dropping を before a psychological verb: you need Nを願ってやまない/期待してやまない.
Wrong tense: ～てやまない is usually in the present to express lasting feelings; the past is rare.
1216.notes:
• The pattern often appears with formal nouns: ご健康, ご多幸, 平和, 復興.
• 愛してやまない can be used as a modifier to emphasize a special degree of affection.
• The polite form ～てやみません suits business correspondence and eulogies.

1217.meaning: If not…, then what is it?

examples.jp: 家族みんなが無事に帰ってきた。これが幸せでなくてなんだろう。
examples.tr: The whole family came home safely. If this isn't happiness, what is?

examples.jp: 三十年の研究が実を結んだ。まさに努力の結晶でなくてなんだろう。
examples.tr: Thirty years of research have borne fruit. If this isn't truly the fruit of hard work, what is?

examples.jp: 荒野に湧いた一筋の泉、それは奇跡でなくてなんだろう。
examples.tr: A single spring welling up in the wilderness: if that isn't a miracle, what is?

examples.jp: この静けさと調和は芸術でなくてなんだろう。
examples.tr: If this tranquility and harmony isn't art, what is?

examples.jp: 彼が命がけで守った行為は勇気でなくてなんだろう。
examples.tr: What he did, protecting it at the risk of his life: if that isn't courage, what is?

examples.jp: 厳しい状況を乗り越えた仲間との絆、これが愛でなくてなんだろう。
examples.tr: The bond with friends who overcame hard times together: if this isn't love, what is?

1217.explain:
Used in emotional writing, speeches, and editorials; rarely used in ordinary conversation.
Usually placed after “これが／それは／まさに／こそ”.
Not used to ask for real information; it is a rhetorical question meant to affirm.

• A rhetorical question for strong affirmation: “if it is not …, then what else is it?”.
• Expresses deep emotion toward something rare/precious/moving.
• Usually used with abstract nouns: 幸せ・愛・奇跡・努力の結晶・芸術・誇り…

rows: If not …, then what is it
これが<ruby>愛<rt>め</rt></ruby>でなくてなんだろう
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>にほかならない
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るに<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>こそ<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>鍵<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>だ

mistakes: Using it with an i-adjective in the dictionary form: × 嬉しくなくてなんだろう → use 名詞化 instead: 喜びでなくてなんだろう.
Understanding it as a real question awaiting an answer; it is actually a rhetorical affirmation.
Using it in everyday situations makes the sentence overly dramatic and unnatural.
1217.notes:
• With i-adjectives, nominalize them: 美しい → 美しさ／美 → 美でなくてなんだろう.
• Often combined with まさに／こそ to increase expressive force.
• Sometimes “か” is added at the end of the sentence: ～でなくてなんだろうか (softer).

examples.jp: 子供ではあるまいし、そんなことで泣くな。
examples.tr: You're not a child, so don't cry over something like that.

examples.jp: 冗談ではあるまいし、そんな大金は払えないよ。
examples.tr: It's not as if this is a joke. I can't pay that kind of money!

examples.jp: 素人ではあるまいし、基本的なミスは避けてほしい。
examples.tr: You're not an amateur, so I'd like you to avoid basic mistakes.

examples.jp: 学生じゃあるまいし、徹夜でゲームなんてやめなさい。
examples.tr: You're not a student anymore, so stop staying up all night playing games.

examples.jp: 休日ではあるまいし、そんなラフな格好で会社に来るな。
examples.tr: It's not a day off, so don't come to the office dressed so casually.

1218.explain:
Used when the speaker thinks that, “since it is not N”, the behavior/demand in the second clause is inappropriate.
The second clause is usually: a command (～しろ/するな), a request (～してくれ), a critical evaluation (～のはおかしい/だめだ), or advice (～ほうがいい).
The style is somewhat stiff and can sound reproachful; avoid using it with superiors or in very polite contexts.
The variant じゃあるまいし is colloquial and natural in conversation.

- Meaning: “It's not as if it's N, so…”, “It's not N, so (don't/no need to) …”. Used to gently reproach, admonish, or reject excessive behavior/standards by giving the reason “it is not N”.
- Nuance: Fairly strong, critical/admonishing. Usually followed by a command, prohibition, or advice in the second clause. Sounds somewhat old-fashioned, with a masculine/mature tone.
- Range of combination: Mainly attaches to nouns denoting a status/state used for contrast (子供、素人、学生、冗談…). Use with a clause is an extended variant, so use it with care.

rows: <ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>ではあるまいし、<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>くな。
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>ではないんだから、<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いて。
It's not as if… (negating a reason)
<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby><ruby>君<rt>くん</rt></ruby>のせいというわけではあるまいし…
それは<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>ではあるまいか。
It's not as if it's to the point of N
Similar meaning, but emphasizes “to the extent of / it's not as if”
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>でもあるまいし…

mistakes: Using it directly with verbs/adjectives: Incorrect; this pattern attaches to nouns. With a clause, switch to ～というわけではあるまいし.
Confusing it with ～ではあるまいか (conjecture). The two patterns have different meanings.
Using it in polite contexts with superiors can be rude because of its reproachful nuance.
JLPT: a trap of choosing between “～ではないんだから” and “～ではあるまいし” based on formality/nuance.
1218.notes:
• Often appears in written language, speeches, or “mature” criticism. In casual conversation, consider the softer version: ～ではないんだから.
• The preceding noun should be a category whose opposite everyone understands (子供/大人, 冗談/本気, 素人/プロ…).
• Not used to describe a purely objective fact; it must carry an evaluation/implication of correcting behavior.

1219.meaning: Cannot be let go with just…
1219.connection: V (plain form) + (の) + ではすまない ではすまされない / N

examples.jp: 機密を漏らしたとなれば、謝罪ではすまない。
examples.tr: If it turns out you leaked confidential information, an apology won't be enough.

examples.jp: この事故は注意だけではすまない重大な問題だ。
examples.tr: This accident is a serious problem that can't be settled with just a warning.

examples.jp: 修理費は数万円ではすまないだろう。
examples.tr: The repairs will probably cost more than a few tens of thousands of yen.

examples.jp: 公共物を壊したら、弁償では済まされない場合もある。
examples.tr: If you damage public property, compensation alone may not be enough to settle it.

examples.jp: これだけ遅刻したら、口頭注意ではすまないかもしれない。
examples.tr: If you are this late, you may get more than just a verbal warning.

1219.explain:
Follows N denoting a mild measure/form of handling, to say it is “not enough”.
A critical, stern tone; suits written language or firm statements.
The passive variant ～では済まされない emphasizes that it cannot be overlooked.

• Expresses seriousness: something cannot be resolved/ended with just measure N (an apology, a warning, a small fine…).
• An objective/somewhat formal evaluation; often used in the news, written language, and serious criticism.
• Often used with nouns such as: 謝罪, 弁償, 注意, 罰金, 処分, 数量表現, この程度.

rows: N is a mild measure, which is negated
<ruby>謝罪<rt>しゃざい</rt></ruby>ではすまない
Different grammar; says “it won't do unless you do it”
<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>らないではすまない
Not about handling something, but about circumstances not allowing it
<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>だけで<ruby>済<rt>す</rt></ruby>む

mistakes: Using it directly with a verb: “謝ってではすまない” × → “謝罪ではすまない” ○ (nominalization).
Confusing it with “Vないではすまない” (meaning you must do it), which is completely different in structure and meaning.
Without context showing the seriousness, the sentence sounds exaggerated; state the consequence/measure.
Mixing up 済む/住む (different kanji with different meanings).
1219.notes:
• N1–N2. The JLPT often sets traps with “Vないではすまない/ずにはすまない”.
• Kanji variant: 済む/済まない is common in written language.
• Used with counters to exaggerate the extent of damage/cost.

1220.connection: V (plain form) + とあれば / N / Na / Aい

examples.jp: 子どものためとあれば、私はどんな苦労もいとわない。
examples.tr: If it's for my children, I'm willing to endure any hardship.

examples.jp: あなたの頼みとあれば、喜んでお受けします。
examples.tr: If it's a request from you, I'll gladly accept.

examples.jp: 必要とあれば、夜中でも駆けつけます。
examples.tr: If necessary, I'll rush over even in the middle of the night.

examples.jp: 会社の将来のためとあれば、改革もやむを得ない。
examples.tr: If it's for the future of the company, reform is unavoidable.

examples.jp: 彼のこととあれば、みんな協力するだろう。
examples.tr: If it's about him, everyone will probably cooperate.

1220.explain:
The second clause usually expresses volition/determination/an evaluation of high likelihood.
Used when the condition has special value:子ども、恩人、緊急、必要、国益…
More formal than ～なら; a rhetorical/resolute nuance.

• If (it really is) …, then (I/we) will …; the condition is special or worth making sacrifices for.
• Emphasizes determination/readiness to do something difficult/unusual for a great purpose.
• Often used in formal spoken language/advertising/declarations.

rows: Strong volition/determination in the second clause
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>とあれば<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く
<ruby>休日<rt>きゅうじつ</rt></ruby>とあって<ruby>混<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む
Neutral, no emphasis on anything special
<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>があるなら<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して

mistakes: In natural writing, the second clause cannot be a direct command to the listener; use the speaker's volitional/declarative form instead.
Confusing it with ～とあって: one is a condition (volition), the other a cause (narration).
Applying it to an ordinary condition makes the sentence sound exaggerated; choose a “special” condition.
1220.notes:
• N2–N1. Often seen in slogans/internal rules of a declarative nature.
• Readily used in fixed phrases: 必要とあれば／あなたの頼みとあれば／子どものためとあれば.
• The second clause sometimes uses the passive/natural form: ～だろう for strong conjecture.

1221.connection: N (unit of time) + というもの

examples.jp: ここ一ヶ月というもの、まともに休めていない。
examples.tr: For this past month, I haven't been able to get any proper rest.

examples.jp: 試験前の三日というもの、毎日図書館にこもっていた。
examples.tr: For the three days before the exam, I shut myself up in the library every day.

examples.jp: 礼儀というものをわきまえなさい。
examples.tr: Learn some manners.

examples.jp: これというものの特技もないが、粘り強さには自信がある。
examples.tr: I don't have any special talent to speak of, but I'm confident in my perseverance.

examples.jp: 社会人というもの、時間を守るのは当然だ。
examples.tr: As a working adult, it goes without saying that you should be punctual.

examples.jp: この二年というもの、彼から便りがない。
examples.tr: For these two years, I haven't heard a word from him.

1221.explain:
Duration meaning: Usually used with negative/difficult expressions (～ない、～できない、～ばかりだ…). Used for a period of time that has lasted up to the present.
Defining meaning: Emphasizes a standard, with a generalizing nuance, sometimes critical.
Formality: Fairly formal; often found in written language/essays.

• Meaning 1 (duration): “For the whole … (just past)”, emphasizing continuity up to the present, often with a nuance of complaint/difficulty/absence.
• Meaning 2 (definition/emphasis): “What is called …/the thing known as …”, used to state the essence, a standard, or something worthy of being called X.
• Pragmatics: Meaning 1 leans toward written language/description; meaning 2 is used in explanations, criticism, or stating general standards.

rows: Neutral; does not necessarily last up to the “present moment of speaking”.
<ruby>休暇<rt>きゅうか</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>よく<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>った。
A past reference point → the present; no default nuance of complaint.
<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby><ruby>以来<rt>いらい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>っていない。
A different pattern: judgment/moral principle, not “duration”.
<ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>というものだ。
Negative form of judgment; easily confused with “というもの”.
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>すれば<ruby>必<rt>かなら</rt></ruby>ず<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>するというものではない。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～というものだ: one is “definition/judgment”, the other is “duration”. Look at the following verb to tell them apart.
Using it with a future time span is incorrect: you cannot say ×来月というもの. It is used only for a period that “has passed” up to the present.
Dropping the negative nuance in the duration meaning: a neutral sentence tends to sound awkward. Use it with a negative/difficulty.
1221.notes:
• “Time span + というもの” is often linked with negative emotions or an unusual state that has continued.
• With “これというもの”: usually used with the negative to say “there is nothing decent/worth mentioning”.
• Put “というもの” after an abstract noun (礼儀、常識、誠意…) to emphasize a social standard.

1222.connection: V (plain form) + といえ(ども) / N + (だ) / Na + (だ) / Aい + い

examples.jp: 子どもといえども、他人に危害を加えてはならない。
examples.tr: Even a child must not harm others.

examples.jp: いかに忙しいといえども、健康管理を怠ってはならない。
examples.tr: No matter how busy you are, you must not neglect your health.

examples.jp: プロといえども、ミスはある。
examples.tr: Even professionals make mistakes.

examples.jp: 学生であるといえども、社会の一員である自覚が必要だ。
examples.tr: Even though you are a student, you need to be aware that you are a member of society.

examples.jp: 何歳といえども、学ぶ姿勢さえあれば成長できる。
examples.tr: No matter how old you are, you can grow as long as you are willing to learn.

examples.jp: 戦時中といえども、人権は守られるべきだ。
examples.tr: Even in wartime, human rights should be protected.

1222.explain:
A stiff, rational nuance; avoid it in everyday casual conversation (use とはいえ/といっても instead).
Suitable for stating principles/standards, legal rules, morals, and public statements.
The following clause usually means “no exceptions/must not/cannot/naturally…”.
Emphasis with いかに/たとえ ⇒ strong concession.

- A formal concession pattern: “Even if/even though … (still) …”. It presents a strong fact/condition, but the following clause negates the expectation or affirms an unchanging principle.
• Highly formal (written language, speeches, essays, news).
• Often used with N denoting a status or general attribute: 天才・プロ・子ども・政府・法律… to say “even … is no exception”.
• Common accompanying adverbs: たとえ, いかに, どれほど, 誰・何・いつ + といえども (whoever/whatever/whenever…).
• The following clause usually contains a normative judgment, a firm command, or something that does not change.

rows: <ruby>専門<rt>せんもん</rt></ruby><ruby>家<rt>か</rt></ruby>といえども<ruby>誤<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>る。
<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>だとはいえ、<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>といっても、<ruby>日帰<rt>ひがえ</rt></ruby>りだ。
Neutral; とはいうものの is fairly formal
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>したものの<ruby>不安<rt>ふあん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>貧<rt>まず</rt></ruby>しいながら<ruby>幸<rt>しあわ</rt></ruby>せだ。

mistakes: Using it in casual conversation → sounds awkward: switch to とはいえ/といっても.
Wrongly attaching “だ”: with N/na, だ is usually dropped before といえども; use である for formality: 正) 学生であるといえども; 子どもといえども.
The following clause should not be an unrelated, incidental event: it needs to be a conclusion/standard that goes against expectations.
Confusing its meaning with とはいえ: exam questions often test the degree of formality and the range of combination.
1222.notes:
• Common emphatic phrases: 誰といえども (anyone at all), 何人といえども (whoever it may be), いかに/どれほど + Adj/Adv + といえども.
• Old-fashioned/legal/speech style: appears often in policy documents and speeches.
• Strongly negates expectations: often used to create a “no exceptions” stance, suitable for argumentation.

examples.jp: 合格の知らせを聞いて、嬉しいといったらない。
examples.tr: When I heard the news that I had passed, I was happier than words can say.

examples.jp: 彼の配慮の細やかさといったらない。
examples.tr: His attentiveness to others is beyond words.

examples.jp: この道の暗さといったらない。危なくて歩けない。
examples.tr: This road is unbelievably dark. It's too dangerous to walk on.

examples.jp: 渋滞のひどさといったらない。
examples.tr: The traffic jam is terrible beyond words.

examples.jp: 手伝ってくれたことがありがたいといったらない。
examples.tr: I am more grateful than I can say that you helped me.

1223.explain:
Can be used in polite contexts and in writing that describes emotions/impressions.
To emphasize a strong subjective emotion, it can stand as an independent sentence: きれい といったらない。
With nouns, prefer Nの/Aさ for naturalness: 美しさ といったらない rather than 美しい といったらない in some contexts.

- Expresses an extremely high degree, “very / beyond description”; more neutral than ありはしない/ありゃしない. Can be used for both praise and criticism; suits written language and polite speech.
• Focuses on describing intensity, with little nuance of crude complaint.
• Often used with emotions/abstract qualities: 嬉しさ・ありがたさ・美しさ・恥ずかしさ・迷惑…
• ほど/くらい can be added to express the degree more softly.

rows: <ruby>美<rt>うつく</rt></ruby>しさといったらない。
といったらありはしない
<ruby>面倒<rt>めんどう</rt></ruby>といったらありはしない。
といったらありゃしない
Strong complaint; avoid in polite contexts
<ruby>最悪<rt>さいあく</rt></ruby>といったらありゃしない。
〜<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まりない／〜の<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>み
<ruby>不遜<rt>ふそん</rt></ruby><ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まりない。

mistakes: Using it directly with the dictionary form of a verb → unnatural. Use a nominalization instead: 驚きといったらない／疲れといったらない.
Confusing its nuance with ありはしない/ありゃしない: exam questions test politeness/neutrality.
Using it for objective facts that require absolute objectivity (scientific writing) → avoid; choose “非常に/極めて”.
Repeating the adjective: “とても嬉しいといったらない” is redundant emphasis; the JLPT often sets an “over-emphasis” trap.
1223.notes:
• Literal meaning “there is nothing more to say (describe)” → figurative “indescribable”.
• When it follows a long clause, nominalize it for coherence: 〜という事実の重大さといったらない。
• Often appears in descriptive writing, reportage and accounts of emotions.

examples.jp: うちの上司ときたら、会議にいつも遅れてくるんだ。
examples.tr: When it comes to my boss, he always shows up late to meetings.

examples.jp: 隣の犬ときたら、夜中に吠えてばかりで困る。
examples.tr: That dog next door does nothing but bark in the middle of the night. It's a real nuisance.

examples.jp: 最近の天気ときたら、晴れたと思ったらすぐ雨だ。
examples.tr: The weather lately — just when you think it's cleared up, it starts raining again.

examples.jp: あの店ときたら、味はいいのに接客が最悪だ。
examples.tr: That restaurant — the food is good, but the service is terrible.

examples.jp: 弟ときたら、約束をすぐ忘れる。
examples.tr: My little brother forgets his promises in no time.

1224.explain:
Used like “speaking of …”, but leans toward criticism/blame; avoid using it about superiors in formal situations.
Often paired with casual sentence endings: ～んだ、～ったらない、～こと！
Not used for formal praise; to praise, use another pattern.

• Introduces a topic in order to criticize, complain about, or express surprise in a negative direction about the target N.
• Used often in conversation; not suitable in formal documents or when talking about the listener (it can sound rude).
• Usually followed by concrete examples of bad habits, shortcomings or repeated trouble.

rows: Strongly colloquial, very casual; ときたら is slightly more formal.
<ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>ってば、また<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れたの？
Neutral, for information/explanation; implies no criticism.
<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>については<ruby>後<rt>のち</rt></ruby>ほど。
A pattern of degree, often used with ～ない/～たらない; a different function.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>食欲<rt>しょくよく</rt></ruby>といったらすごい。

mistakes: Using it in a formal style/academic paper → inappropriate.
It can be used about yourself as self-criticism, but avoid being rude to the listener/superiors.
Confusing it with といったら（degree） in JLPT questions: check whether the second clause is a “complaint” → choose ときたら.
1224.notes:
• Can be used to open a story of complaint and catch the listener's attention.
• Talking directly about the listener can easily seem impolite; replacing it with ね or やっぱり… sounds softer.
• To further emphasize the degree of the complaint, continue with ～ったらない／～ことだ。

1225.connection: V plain form + ときている / N / Na / Aい + い

examples.jp: 安くておいしいときているから、行列ができないわけがない。
examples.tr: It's cheap and delicious on top of that, so there's no way it wouldn't draw a line.

examples.jp: 彼は頭がよくて努力家ときているので、結果を出すのも当然だ。
examples.tr: He's smart and a hard worker as well, so it's only natural that he gets results.

examples.jp: 締め切り間近なうえに人手不足ときている。残業は避けられない。
examples.tr: The deadline is close, and on top of that we're short-staffed. Overtime is unavoidable.

examples.jp: 便利ときているのに、家賃は意外と安い。
examples.tr: It's convenient, and yet the rent is surprisingly cheap.

examples.jp: 初日から雨ときているから、計画を練り直さないと。
examples.tr: It's raining from the very first day, so we'll have to rework our plans.

1225.explain:
Has the nuance “no wonder / and on top of that” → exclamation with evaluation.
Suited to presenting an obvious reason that leads to a consequence: …わけだ／当然だ／無理はない／〜に決まっている.
Can be used for both praise and criticism; often used when piling up several favorable/unfavorable conditions.

- Presents a feature/circumstance as “and on top of that…”, indicating that it is a very favorable/unfavorable condition leading to an understandable consequence. Carries an exclamatory nuance, sometimes sarcasm, complaint or admiration.
• Often lists 2+ strengths/weaknesses and then concludes “no wonder…”.
• Used with から/ので/ものだから/のに to connect to the consequence.
• Mainly with N/Adj or state phrases (Aくて/Bで/Cも… + ときている).

rows: … and on top of that … → an obvious consequence
<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いときているから<ruby>売<rt>う</rt></ruby>れる。
If it's / speaking of …, then (usually a familiar result)
Leans toward supposition, evokes a reflex
Makes something the topic in order to complain; a different function
うちの<ruby>息子<rt>むすこ</rt></ruby>ときたら…。
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いだけあって<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>がいい。

mistakes: Attaching it directly to a pure action clause that does not express a “quality”: use a quality/state instead. Incorrect) 彼が来るときている → Correct) 彼が有名人ときている／忙しいときている.
Confusing it with “ときたら” (a pattern for criticizing a topic) → a different function; the JLPT often tests this pair.
Leaving out the concluding consequence → the sentence feels incomplete. This pattern usually leads to a conclusion like “no wonder / naturally…”.
Mistaking its nuance for objective: the pattern is exclamatory; in strictly serious writing, switch to “ため/ので”.
1225.notes:
• The form “Xときているから/ので” is the typical frame: state X (a striking condition) → an obvious conclusion.
• Easily combined with listing: AくてBでCときている (piling up conditions).
• Often used in commentary on daily life/consumption/the economy: 値段・立地・性能・人手・天候…

examples.jp: 「お忙しいところをわざわざ来ていただき、ありがとうございました」
examples.tr: 「Thank you very much for taking the trouble to come when you are so busy.」

examples.jp: 「お話し中ところをちょっと失礼します」
examples.tr: 「Excuse me for interrupting your conversation.」

examples.jp: 「お休みのところを、朝早くからお電話して申し訳ありません」
examples.tr: 「I'm very sorry to call you so early in the morning while you're resting.」

examples.jp: お忙しいところを恐れ入りますが、こちらにご署名ください。
examples.tr: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but please sign here.

examples.jp: 会議を始めようとするところを、社長から電話が入った。
examples.tr: Just as we were about to start the meeting, a call came in from the company president.

examples.jp: 寝ているところを起こしてしまって、本当に申し訳ありません。
examples.tr: I'm truly sorry for waking you up while you were sleeping.

1226.explain:
When used to apologize/make a request: it comes at the beginning of the sentence, followed by a short, polite request. Often accompanied by 恐れ入ります／失礼します／申し訳ありません.
In the meaning of “concession”: the preceding clause (before ところを) states an unfavorable condition / what should have happened, and the second clause shows a result contrary to expectations (leniency, letting it go, helping anyway...)
Used with verbs of perception/control: 見る／見つける／撮る／捕まえる to emphasize the exact point in time of being discovered/caught.
More formal than 〜のに. Avoid overusing it in casual conversation (it can sound affected).

• Meaning 1: Indicates the exact point in time when an action takes place. Emphasizes “right at that moment” (in progress / just done / about to). It depends on the form of ところ:

- V-るところ: about to, getting ready to

- V-ているところ: in the middle of

- V-たところ: have just

• Meaning 2: Politeness/apology when intruding on the other person's situation. Pattern: お忙しいところを／お休みのところを／夜分のところを + 失礼します など.
• Meaning 3: Formal concession “although / should have”. Used when handing down a lenient decision, thanking, or apologizing:

例: 厳しく叱るべきところを、温かい言葉をいただいた。
• Nuance: More formal than ところで/のに. In the concessive meaning, it is often seen in official documents, minutes and speeches.

rows: <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけるところに<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>った。
Right in the middle of doing
Emphasizes being midway; rarely used in set phrases of apology
<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>最中<rt>さいちゅう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>鳴<rt>な</rt></ruby>る。
More casual, not a ceremonial set formula
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいのに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくれた。
（お）〜ところを〜<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>します
Fixed formula in the workplace/on the phone
お<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みのところを<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>します。

mistakes: Confusing it with ところで: ところを carries a nuance of apology/concession or indicates the point in time of being affected; ところで usually means “by the way, even if”.
Wrong tense/form: when apologizing while the other person “is” doing something → use V-ているところを, not V-るところを.
Too casual a use: in conversation with friends, ところを can sound a bit stiff; replace it with のに／ときは…など.

JLPT: trick questions often use inversion of the clauses to test your understanding of the concession “should have … but …”. Note that the preceding clause (before ところを) states “what should/ought to happen”.
1226.notes:
• The “place – point in time” sense of ところ frames the situation, making an apology/request softer and showing awareness of the inconvenience caused.
• In minutes/decisions, ところを often goes with the passive form/honorific language to increase formality.
• V-たところを in the time sense is often equivalent to “had just … when”, creating a sense of surprise.

1227.connection: V plain form + とはいえ / N + (だ) / Na + (だ) / Aい + い

examples.jp: 春とはいえ、まだ夜は冷える。
examples.tr: It may be spring, but the nights are still cold.

examples.jp: 新人とはいえ、基本は守ってもらう。
examples.tr: You may be new, but you will still have to follow the basics.

examples.jp: 日本に長く住んだとはいえ、敬語は今も難しい。
examples.tr: Although I've lived in Japan for a long time, keigo is still difficult for me.

examples.jp: 安いとはいえ、無駄な買い物はしたくない。
examples.tr: It may be cheap, but I don't want to buy things I don't need.

examples.jp: 専門家とはいえ、ミスをゼロにはできない。
examples.tr: They may be experts, but even they can't reduce mistakes to zero.

1227.explain:
Used to “soften, then counter”: acknowledges A but emphasizes that B is the main point.
Serious style, suited to reports, arguments and news.
Often used with words that limit the degree: まだ、やはり、必ずしも、それでも.
Different from にしては: とはいえ does not compare against a specific standard, but simply concedes and then counters.

• A pattern of concession/acceptance of fact A, while the second clause B gives a judgment contrary to expectations: “although… still…”.
• Formal nuance, written language; stronger than けど/が; close to とはいえ＝とは言え.
• The second clause is usually an evaluation, a limitation or a counterargument: with the feel of しかし/それでも/とはいっても.
• Not followed directly by an opposing command/volition; usually by a judgment or an objective fact.

rows: <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いとはいえ、<ruby>質<rt>しつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だ。
Plays down the degree of A, more colloquial
<ruby>金持<rt>かねも</rt></ruby>ちといっても、<ruby>普通<rt>ふつう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>だ。
Compared with the standard of A...
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもにしては、<ruby>字<rt>じ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>だ。
Written language, formal, similar meaning; とはいうものの is stronger
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>したものの、<ruby>不安<rt>ふあん</rt></ruby>だ。

mistakes: Confusing it with にしては: とはいえ has no specific standard of comparison; if there is a clear standard (年齢のわりに), use にしては.
Following とはいえ with a direct command sounds harsh; use a judgment/comment instead.
Nuance trap: といっても leans toward the colloquial; とはいえ is formal. Choose according to the context.
JLPT: when a sentence needs “acknowledge A but hold position B”, the answer is usually とはいえ/とはいうものの.
1227.notes:
• Both the full form とは言え (kanji) and とはいえ (kana) are used; kana is more common today.
• Often combined with nouns of time/season: 春・子どもの日・連休 とはいえ,...
• Can stand in the middle of a sentence or at the beginning of a sentence to open a counterargument: とはいえ、～。
• With the past: ～たとはいえ emphasizes “although … already …, still …”.

examples.jp: 今のスマホは、十年前とは比べものにならない。
examples.tr: There's no comparison between today's smartphones and those of ten years ago.

examples.jp: 彼の今回の演奏は、前回とは比べものにならないほど素晴らしかった。
examples.tr: His performance this time was so superb that there's no comparing it with last time.

examples.jp: この店のサービスは他店とは比べものにならない。
examples.tr: This shop's service is in a completely different class from other shops.

examples.jp: 都会の物価は、地方とは比べものにならないくらい高い。
examples.tr: Prices in the city are incomparably higher than in the countryside.

examples.jp: 素人の作品は、プロとは比べものにならない。
examples.tr: Amateur work can't compare with that of professionals.

1228.explain:
Typical structure: AはBとは比べものにならない（A far surpasses/falls far short of B）. The topic is usually A.
Often combined with ほど／くらい to emphasize the degree: ～ほど速い／～くらい高い.
Decisive tone; suited to commentary, evaluation, and comparing products/performance.

• Expresses a gap so large that comparison becomes meaningless: “cannot be compared with …”.
• Usually used for praise/superiority (A is better than B), but can also criticize (A is far worse than B) depending on the context.
• More formal than くらいじゃない/桁違いだ; usable in writing and presentations.

rows: Usually means “not at that level”; a different function from direct comparison.
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しくて<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>どころではない。
Strongly colloquial; less formal than <ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べものにならない.
<ruby>性能<rt>せいのう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>桁違<rt>けたちが</rt></ruby>いだ。
Means being equal (positive); pragmatically the opposite of “cannot compare”.
<ruby>世界<rt>せかい</rt></ruby><ruby>記録<rt>きろく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>匹敵<rt>ひってき</rt></ruby>する。
Short and colloquial; similar nuance but abbreviated.

mistakes: Reversing A/B causes misunderstanding: topic A is what is evaluated against B.
Using it in contexts that call for objectivity or an indirect expression: avoid it, as it is too absolute.
Confusing it with ～に匹敵する (equivalent) in trick questions: watch for keywords like “surpass / far different”.
1228.notes:
• “とは” marks the point of comparison. In colloquial speech it can be replaced with “と(は)”: ～とは／～と(は)比べものにならない.
• Easy to use in headlines/commentary: コスパは前機種とは比べものにならない.
• To stay neutral, ～より（も） is better than this absolute negation.

examples.jp: 高い物が必ずしも良いとは限らない。
examples.tr: Expensive things are not necessarily good.

examples.jp: 日本人がみんな寿司好きとは限らない。
examples.tr: Not all Japanese people like sushi.

examples.jp: 雨だからといって、試合が中止とは限らない。
examples.tr: Just because it's raining doesn't mean the match will be canceled.

examples.jp: オンラインの情報が正確だとは限らない。
examples.tr: Information online is not always accurate.

examples.jp: 経験が長いからといって、結果を出せるとは限らない。
examples.tr: Having long experience doesn't necessarily mean you can get results.

examples.jp: この駅は古くから歌われているが、日本人だみんな知っているとは限らない。
examples.tr: This station has been sung about for a long time, but that doesn't mean every Japanese person knows it.

1229.explain:
Objective, polite nuance; often used in debate, academic writing and news.
Placed after a clause regarded as a common assumption/stereotype to negate its absoluteness.
Add 必ずしも to emphasize “not necessarily”.
The combination “Aからといって、Bとは限らない” is a very natural frame.

• Not necessarily / not always ~; negates inevitability/generality.
• Often used with 必ずしも for emphasis: 必ずしも～とは限らない.
• Used to refute stereotypes/generalizations: “if A, then B” is not always true.

rows: <ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>とは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない
<ruby>嫌<rt>きら</rt></ruby>いというわけではない
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいわけではない
～とは<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない／<ruby>言<rt>いい</rt></ruby>い<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>れない
<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>とは<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない
<ruby>必<rt>かなら</rt></ruby>ずしも～とは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない
<ruby>必<rt>かなら</rt></ruby>ずしも<ruby>正<rt>ただ</rt></ruby>しいとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない

mistakes: Dropping は in とは限らない: × という限らない → 〇 とは限らない.
Confusing it with absolute negation: ～とは限らない only allows for exceptions; it does not negate completely.
Forgetting だ with N/na in written language: 学生だとは限らない.
JLPT trap: choose the correct pair “必ずしも～とは限らない” rather than “必ず～ない”.
1229.notes:
• Often appears in counterarguments: AからといってBとは限らない.
• To soften the negation, いつも/必ずしも/必然的に + ～とは限らない can be added.
• Suitable when you want to allow for exceptions and avoid absolute assertions. meaning_vi: not necessarily ～, not certain that ～ ⏐ explain: Used for partial negation of things and events. ⏐ examples: 1. 相手が弱いチームであっても、必ず勝つとは限らない。
Even if the opponent is a weak team, you can't necessarily win easily.
2. あまり使わない表現だが、必ずしもテストに出ないとは限らない。
It's a rarely used expression, but that doesn't mean it won't appear on the test.

1230.connection: V plain form + とみると

examples.jp: 兄はセールとみると、大量に買い込む。
examples.tr: Whenever my older brother sees a sale, he buys things in bulk.

examples.jp: 子どもは先生がいないとみると、途端に騒ぎ出した。
examples.tr: As soon as the children saw that the teacher wasn't there, they started making a racket.

examples.jp: 猫はドアが少し開いたとみると、さっと外へ出た。
examples.tr: The moment the cat saw the door open slightly, it darted outside.

examples.jp: 敵は我々が疲れているとみると、一気に攻めてきた。
examples.tr: As soon as the enemy saw that we were tired, they attacked all at once.

examples.jp: 彼はチャンスとみると、すぐ連絡してくる。
examples.tr: Whenever he sees an opportunity, he gets in touch right away.

1230.explain:
Has a narrative nuance, describing a quick reaction, with a touch of surprise or establishing a habit.
Unnatural if followed by a command/the speaker's direct volition (let's / go on…). Suited to description, not to making requests.
Often used with words that suggest a “signal”: チャンス、セール、隙、警官の姿、雨雲…

• Used when, “having just noticed/judged that it is X”, action Y occurs “immediately/regularly”. Emphasizes a quick reflex or a habit.
• The subject of the second clause is usually someone else/the target being described; the speaker narrates the situation.
• Can express a regular pattern: “Whenever X is seen, Y” (habit). Also used for one specific instance (causing surprise).

rows: As soon as X is noticed, Y
Formal, means an instant point in time
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>した。
Narrates a quick sequence of actions, often surprising
<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>したかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと<ruby>止<rt>や</rt></ruby>んだ。
Emphasizes the point in time; no nuance of “evaluation”
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたん、<ruby>倒<rt>たお</rt></ruby>れた。
Written language/more stylized than ～とみると
<ruby>好機<rt>こうき</rt></ruby>と<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るや<ruby>動<rt>うご</rt></ruby>いた。

mistakes: Using it to give a direct command/advice in the second clause → unnatural: × 安いとみると、買いましょう！
Confusing it with ～たとたん: ～とみると has a nuance of “judging, then reacting”, not just a point in time.
Using it for purely internal emotions that are hard to observe → inappropriate: × 悲しいとみると、泣いた (use ～とたん if it is about a point in time).
1230.notes:
• Use the past to narrate a one-time event: ～たとみると、～た。
• The first clause can be the subjective evaluation of the subject in the sentence: 敵は我々が弱いとみると…
• Easily used with adverbials of immediacy: すぐ／途端に／一気に／さっと…

examples.jp: 条件次第では、受け入れないものでもない。
examples.tr: Depending on the conditions, it's not out of the question that we would accept.

examples.jp: 少しなら手伝えないものでもない。
examples.tr: If it's just a little, I could possibly help.

examples.jp: 努力すれば合格できないものでもない。
examples.tr: If you make an effort, it's not impossible to pass.

examples.jp: このデザインも、見慣れれば悪くないものでもない。
examples.tr: Once you get used to it, this design might not be so bad after all.

examples.jp: 値段次第で買わないものでもない。
examples.tr: Depending on the price, I might buy it.

1231.explain:
Nuance of an “indirect expression”: no strong commitment; shows openness, but with conditions.
Often accompanied by conditions: ～ば／～なら／条件次第で／工夫すれば／少しなら.
Suited to negotiations, discussions, and polite answers that do not bind you.

• “It's not that … not…”, “It is possible…/it's not entirely impossible…”.
• Weak, reserved affirmation, often with conditions or exceptions.
• Used to open the way to negotiation, expressing possible acceptance under certain conditions.

rows: <ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>しないでもない

mistakes: Using it as a firm promise → wrong nuance: this is only weak, conditional acceptance.
Confusing it with ～ないものだろうか (wish). Here it is about “possibility/conditional agreement”, not “wishing”.
Leaving out the condition makes the sentence vague: adding “～ば／～なら／次第で” makes the meaning clear.
The JLPT often asks you to distinguish ないことはない／なくはない／ないものでもない by their degree of reserve.
1231.notes:
• Suitable when you want to keep a “safety margin” in what you say and avoid absolute commitment.
• In work emails: 前向きに検討しないものでもない（considering it positively but not promising yet).
• Apart from verbs, with adjectives it is usually the fixed phrase “悪くないものでもない”.

examples.jp: 京都ならではの風情がある。
examples.tr: Kyoto has a charm all its own.

examples.jp: 当店ならではのサービスをご提供します。
examples.tr: We offer service you can only get at our store.

examples.jp: 彼ならではの発想にいつも驚かされる。
examples.tr: I'm always amazed by ideas that only he could come up with.

examples.jp: ここならではの体験をぜひお楽しみください。
examples.tr: Please be sure to enjoy an experience you can only have here.

examples.jp: 日本ならではの四季の移ろいを感じられる。
examples.tr: You can feel the changing of the four seasons that is unique to Japan.

examples.jp: 小規模企業ならではの機動力が強みだ。
examples.tr: Agility that only a small business can have is our strength.

1232.explain:
Used to praise and emphasize “the quality found only in/belonging only to” N.
Avoid using it with strongly negative content; if used, it becomes sarcastic and needs a clear context.
Suitable for headlines, brochures, reviews and PR articles.
The form “N ならではだ” is concise and gives strong emphasis.

• “～ならでは” emphasizes the uniqueness/distinctive character found only in N; it praises and highlights.
• Usually used in a positive context: strengths, identity, competitive advantages.
• N is usually a place name, an organization, a store, a person with their own style, regional culture or a special material.
• It has a strong advertising/promotional nuance, but is also used in everyday conversation to give praise.

rows: <ruby>職人<rt>しょくにん</rt></ruby>ならではの<ruby>技<rt>わざ</rt></ruby>
N だけの／N ならではの vs N <ruby>固有<rt>こゆう</rt></ruby>の・<ruby>特有<rt>とくゆう</rt></ruby>の
<ruby>固有<rt>こゆう</rt></ruby>の/<ruby>特有<rt>とくゆう</rt></ruby>の are more neutral descriptive vocabulary
<ruby>地域<rt>ちいき</rt></ruby><ruby>特有<rt>とくゆう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>文化<rt>ぶんか</rt></ruby>
Does not imply “only N has it”
これこそ<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ
ここにしかない<ruby>景色<rt>けしき</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using it for a directly negative meaning → the nuance is off; if you must, there should be a clear sarcastic/metaphorical context.
Confusing it with “だけの”: “ならでは” stresses “uniqueness/distinctiveness”; “だけの” indicates quantity/limitation.
Dropping “の” when modifying a noun: you need “ならではの N”.
Wrong order: “N のならでは” is incorrect; the correct form is “N ならでは（の）”.
1232.notes:
• Can imply a comparison with other places/targets without stating the comparison directly.
• In PR, it often appears with positive vocabulary: 体験・魅力・景観・味・香り・強み・こだわり・サービス.
• Sarcastic use: 文句ならではの多さ (the “characteristic” amount of complaints of ~), but context is needed so the listener understands it as sarcasm.

examples.jp: 一言なりともご感想をいただけますか。
examples.tr: Could you give us your impressions, even in just a word?

examples.jp: 少しなりとも力になれれば幸いです。
examples.tr: I would be glad if I could be of help, even a little.

examples.jp: 一円なりとも無駄にしてはいけない。
examples.tr: You must not waste even a single yen.

examples.jp: 手伝いなりともさせてください。
examples.tr: Please let me help, even if it's just a little.

examples.jp: お気持ちなりとも受け取ってください。
examples.tr: Please accept this, even if it is only a small token of my feelings.

examples.jp: ご不明点はなんなりともお申し付けください。
examples.tr: If anything is unclear, please do not hesitate to ask.

1233.explain:
Polite/courteous; used a lot in letters and formal conversation when making a suggestion or request.
Implies that the speaker lowers the level of expectation so that the listener can accept easily.
Not used directly after the dictionary form of a verb; nominalize it instead: 参加→参加、手伝う→手伝い.
With quantities, it is usually a small amount; avoid using it with large amounts, as that goes against the “minimum” nuance.

• States a minimum: “even just … ”, expressing a minimal concession or the hope that at least the smallest amount will be accepted.
• A humble offer/suggestion: offering to help “at least …”, avoiding a sense of pressure.
• Emphasizes smallness and limitation: often used with words for small amounts (一言・一円・少し・気持ちなど).
• The phrase なんなりとも has the broader meaning “anything at all”, different from the “minimum” meaning.

rows: Neutral; does not stress the “minimum” as strongly as なりとも.
<ruby>一言<rt>ひとこと</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>して。
Close in meaning; せめて expresses the feeling “at least”.
せめて<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>いだけでもしたい。
なんなりと/なんなりとも
Set phrase meaning “as you wish”, not “minimum”.
なんなりとお<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>付<rt>つ</rt></ruby>けください。
わずかでも/<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しでも
Purely adverbial; lacks the stylized nuance of なりとも.
<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しでも<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>けたい。

mistakes: Using it after an ordinary verb: × 手伝うなりとも → ○ 手伝いなりとも.
Using it with a large amount gives the wrong nuance: × 一万円なりともあげる → use it with a small amount such as 一円/少し.
Confusing なんなりとも with “minimum”: なんなりとも = “any”, different from “at least”.
Confusing it with ～でも: the JLPT often tests the polite nuance and the “minimum level”.
1233.notes:
• In formal written language, なりとも sounds more courteous than ～でも/だけでも.
• Often used with abstract nouns: 気持ち・援助・情報・意見・協力.
• Business set phrases: なんなりとも＋お申し付けください／お尋ねください.
• Goes well with せめて for emphasis: せめて一言なりとも.

examples.jp: 五十歳にして初めて海を見た。
examples.tr: I saw the sea for the first time at the age of fifty.

examples.jp: 三度目にしてようやく合格した。
examples.tr: I finally passed on my third try.

examples.jp: 専門家にして初めて理解できる理論だ。
examples.tr: It is a theory that only an expert can understand.

examples.jp: 彼は医師にして作家でもある。
examples.tr: He is a doctor and also a writer.

examples.jp: 今日にしてなお解決すべき課題が山積している。
examples.tr: Even today, there are still countless problems that must be solved.

examples.jp: 親にして初めて分かる気持ちがある。
examples.tr: There are feelings you only understand once you become a parent.

1234.explain:
Formal/written language; creates an emphatic, slightly dramatic impression.
With “age/number of times”: expresses that something was achieved late or after many tries; often used with ようやく/初めて.
With “limitation”: usually has初めて to emphasize “only when… ”.
With “AにしてB”: the two nouns should be of equal/impressive status.

• Point in time/age: emphasizes lateness, rarity or surprise (五十歳にして, 三度目にして).
• Limitation of ability: emphasizes “only at that level/position is it possible” (専門家にして初めて～).
• Two roles at once: formal written language describing a person/institution with two roles (医師にして作家).
• The form にしてなお adds a concessive meaning = “even now, still…”.

rows: Spoken language; lacks the formal/emphatic nuance of にして.
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>になって<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かった。
Neutral expression; にして is formal and concise.
<ruby>医師<rt>いし</rt></ruby>で<ruby>作家<rt>さっか</rt></ruby>でもある。
Emphasizes the subject; does not mean “only when/not until”.
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>こそ<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>鍵<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>だ。
Indicates place/setting; lacks the three versatile meanings of にして.
<ruby>歴史<rt>れきし</rt></ruby>において<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Confusing it with になって: にして has a formal nuance and a sense of surprise; になって is neutral.
Using “AにしてB” for two nouns that do not match → sounds forced: × 学生にして社長 (except in special cases).
Dropping “初めて” in the limitation pattern weakens the meaning: 専門家にして理解できる → still correct, but exams usually prefer “初めて”.
Using it directly with a verb: にして attaches to nouns; nominalize when needed.
1234.notes:
• “AにしてB” is often used in titles/introductions: 世界的ピアニストにして作曲家のX氏.
• “Nにして初めて” is an almost fixed formula in academic books and essays.
• “今日にしてなお/今にしてなお” is used in newspapers to emphasize “still… even now”.
• Avoid overusing it in everyday conversation, as it sounds stilted.

examples.jp: 学生にしろ社会人にしろ、時間管理は大切だ。
examples.tr: Whether you are a student or a working adult, time management is important.

examples.jp: 行くにしろ行かないにしろ、早めに連絡してください。
examples.tr: Whether you go or not, please let us know early.

examples.jp: 高いにしろ安いにしろ、品質は確認すべきだ。
examples.tr: Whether it is expensive or cheap, you should check the quality.

examples.jp: 雨にしろ雪にしろ、試合は予定どおり行う。
examples.tr: Rain or snow, the game will be held as scheduled.

examples.jp: 経験があるにしろないにしろ、応募は歓迎します。
examples.tr: Whether or not you have experience, we welcome your application.

examples.jp: たとえ冗談にしろ、言っていいことと悪いことがある。
examples.tr: Even if it's a joke, there are things you can say and things you can't.

1235.explain:
A and B should be the same part of speech and play the same grammatical role. After AにしろBにしろ there is usually a comma, followed by a general concluding clause.
Suffix particles: は/も/など are often attached after the whole phrase to make it the topic/for emphasis. Example:時間にしろお金にしろは大切だ。
Nuance: neutral → slightly colloquial; used in stating rules, advice and judgments. For a more formal tone, use ～にせよ／～であれ.
Used with question words to cover a wide scope:誰にしろ、どこにしろ、いつにしろ…
Single form “～にしろ”: has the concessive meaning “even if… still…”. Example:少し無理 にしろ、挑戦する価値はある。 (Even if it is a bit too much, it is worth trying.)
Often used with connecting words that add emphasis: たとえ、いずれ、結局など.

Meaning: “Whether it is A or B, (the conclusion) is the same”, “Regardless of A or B…”. Emphasizes that both options (usually of the same category or opposite in meaning) lead to the same evaluation/decision in the second clause.
• Character: has a generalizing nuance, close to neutral spoken language. Compared with ～にせよ／～であれ, ～にしろ is softer and more everyday.
• The following structure is usually an evaluation, position, request or rule: ～べきだ／～なければならない／～たい／～は変わらない…
• Combines naturally with pairs of opposites (高い/安い、賛成/反対、有無、有/無、行く/行かない…).
• Can be used with question words: 誰にしろ／どこにしろ／いつにしろ… meaning “no matter who/where/when”.
• たとえ can be added to strengthen the concessive nuance: たとえAにしろBにしろ…
• The single form “～にしろ” is also used like “even if... ”, close to ～にしても/～ても.

rows: Whether A or B, the conclusion is the same
Neutral spoken language; often used with opposites/items of the same category.
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>にしろ<ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby><ruby>人<rt>じん</rt></ruby>にしろ、<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るべきだ。
More formal, leaning toward written language/speeches.
<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>にせよ<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>にせよ、<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>してください。
Similar to “regardless of A or B”
Most formal; usually used with nouns/technical terms.
<ruby>貧富<rt>ひんぷ</rt></ruby>であれ、<ruby>法<rt>ほう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>下<rt>した</rt></ruby>では<ruby>平等<rt>びょうどう</rt></ruby>だ。
A single concession; AにしてもBにしても also exists but is less common and weaker in the “regardless” sense.
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いにしても、<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ。
Does not list contrasting items; used for a single condition.
Formal; usually used with nouns/range expressions (<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>性別<rt>せいべつ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>天候<rt>てんこう</rt></ruby>…).
<ruby>天候<rt>てんこう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず、<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Confusing it with the command “～にしろ!”: 静かにしろ (Be quiet!) is not the listing pattern, but the command “しろ” of する + the state marker “に”. Do not confuse it with AにしろBにしろ.
Mixing parts of speech: both parts must be the same type. Incorrect: 学生にしろ来ないにしろ…; Correct: 学生にしろ社会人にしろ… or 行くにしろ行かないにしろ…
Inappropriate suffix particle: avoid inserting を right after each element. Place the particle after the whole phrase: 時間にしろお金にしろは大切だ。 (Instead of ×時間にしろお金にしろを…)
Choosing a second clause that does not cover both: the conclusion must be true for both A and B. If it is true for only one side, use a different structure.
Register: formal writing (reports, JLPT reading essays) should prefer ～にせよ／～であれ to suit the context.
Negative forms: with verbs use V-ないにしろ; with i-adjectives use A-くないにしろ. Example: 参加しないにしろ、連絡して。/ 寒くないにしろ、上着を持っていけ。
Past tense: V-たにしろ／V-なかったにしろ can be used to cover the past. Example: 行ったにしろ行かなかったにしろ、報告して。

Distinction trap with ～にかかわらず／～を問わず: these two patterns do not require listing contrasting items; they are used to cover an entire range (年齢、性別…). ～にしろ～にしろ leans toward giving representative/opposite examples.
1235.notes:
• Form: ～にせよ is the original formal form; ～にしろ is the colloquialized form (the command form “しろ” of する), but in this pattern it has no command meaning.
• Naturalness: with na-adjectives, spoken language usually uses them directly: 便利にしろ不便にしろ; in serious written language, である can be used.
• Particle position: は/も/など can be placed after the whole phrase to mark the topic/for emphasis. Avoid inserting case particles after each element unless the structure clearly allows it.
• Three or more items can be listed: AにしろBにしろCにしろ…, but keep it short to avoid confusion.
• The second clause should be a general clause that applies to all options; avoid information that is true for only one side.
• Common combinations: 賛成にしろ反対にしろ／有利にしろ不利にしろ／行くにしろ行かないにしろ／多いにしろ少ないにしろ.

examples.jp: 問題は教育現場にとどまらず、家庭にも波及している。
examples.tr: The problem is not limited to schools; it is also spreading to families.

examples.jp: 彼の研究は学術界にとどまらず、産業界にも影響を与えた。
examples.tr: His research influenced not only academia but also industry.

examples.jp: 人気は首都圏にとどまらず、地方にも広がった。
examples.tr: Its popularity was not limited to the capital region; it also spread to the provinces.

examples.jp: 温暖化の影響は環境問題にとどまらず、経済にも打撃を与える。
examples.tr: The effects of global warming are not limited to environmental problems; they also deal a blow to the economy.

examples.jp: この手法は理論にとどまらず、実務にも応用されている。
examples.tr: This method does not stop at theory; it is also applied in practice.

examples.jp: 熱帯雨林の減少の影響は周辺地域にとどまらず、地球全体に及んでいる。
examples.tr: The effects of the loss of tropical rainforests are not limited to the surrounding areas; they extend to the entire planet.

1236.explain:
Formal; used in reports and presentations; adds weight to an argument.
Suitable when A is a subset and B is a larger set on the same classification axis.
Avoid using it for everyday listing or for targets that have no inclusive relationship.

Expresses that something is not confined to the scope of A but extends to B (a wider one). It highlights the quality of “going beyond the boundary”, so it suits contexts of scale/impact.
• The second clause often has words of breadth/spread: 全体に・広く・多方面に・世界に.
• Common content: damage, influence, popularity, fields of application, significance.
• Can be combined with figures/levels to emphasize the degree of expansion.

rows: Not only A but also B
Does not stress “going beyond the scope”; widely used
AだけでなくBも<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だ。
Stresses universality across the whole category; not “spreading”
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らず<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>も<ruby>学<rt>まな</rt></ruby>ぶ。
Close in meaning, but lacks the “not stopping at” nuance
<ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby>のみならず<ruby>経済<rt>けいざい</rt></ruby>も～。
Written variant with an active nuance
<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>理論<rt>りろん</rt></ruby>にとどめず<ruby>実践<rt>じっせん</rt></ruby>へ。

mistakes: The second clause does not expand → the “going beyond the scope” logic is lost.
Using it for two items of the same level with no inclusion (A and B are siblings, not “outside A”).
Confusing it with “に限らず”: a distinction trap between “inclusion/spreading” vs “universality”.
1236.notes:
• Effective when combined with a corresponding phrase: Aにとどまらず、Bにまで～／Bにも～。
• Strong as a modifier: ～にとどまらない影響／意味／範囲／成果.
• In headlines: “～、国内にとどまらず” quickly conveys the wide spread.

1237.meaning: No need to…, not necessary to…

examples.jp: その件は心配するには及ばない。
examples.tr: There is no need to worry about that matter.

examples.jp: わざわざ来ていただくには及びません。
examples.tr: There is no need for you to go to the trouble of coming.

examples.jp: 実力では彼には及ばないが、努力で補う。
examples.tr: I'm no match for him in ability, but I make up for it with effort.

examples.jp: 詳しい説明には及びません。要点だけ申し上げます。
examples.tr: A detailed explanation is unnecessary. I will just state the main points.

examples.jp: 時間が十分あるから、急ぐには及ばない。
examples.tr: There is plenty of time, so there is no need to hurry.

examples.jp:
A: 先日お借りした傘を今日お返しに参りたいのですが、ご都合はいかがでしょうか。
B: それには及びませんよ。また、いらっしゃるときにお持ちください。
examples.tr:
A: I'd like to come and return the umbrella I borrowed the other day. Would today be convenient for you?
B: Oh, there's no need for that. Please bring it the next time you come.

1237.explain:
Often used in notices/messages/polite refusals: お礼には及びません.
The meaning “cannot compare with” has a modest nuance or expresses an objective evaluation.
Suitable for written language and formal speeches; also used in polite conversation.

• No need/not necessary to: used when an action is superfluous or unnecessary. Example: 連絡するには及ばない.
• Cannot compare with: expresses inferiority in ability or degree. Example: 経験では彼には及ばない.
• Nuance: more formal and polite than ～までもない/～なくてもいい.

rows: Close to the meaning “no need”; ～には<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ばない is more formal.
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>するまでもない。
Close to “cannot compare with”, leaning toward rivalry/competition.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>速<rt>はや</rt></ruby>さにかなわない。
Completely different meaning; be careful not to confuse it with ～には<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ばない.
<ruby>被害<rt>ひがい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>広範囲<rt>こうはんい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ぶ。

mistakes: Confusing the meaning with ～に及ぶ (extend/reach) because of the similar form.
Missing “に”: incorrect “心配するは及ばない” (correct: 心配するには及ばない).
Using it for something already done in the past: ×もう説明したから説明するには及ばない (a time contradiction).
Confusing it with ～には当たらない: “not worth …” (evaluation) is different from “no need to …” (necessity).
1237.notes:
• Fixed keigo expressions: ご心配には及びません／お礼には及びません.
• In the “no need” meaning, the subject is usually a future/proposed action; avoid using it for something that has already happened.
• The “cannot compare with” meaning is often used with nouns referring to people/abilities: 速度・経験・実力＋には及ばない.

examples.jp: 無口な父にひきかえ、母はよくしゃべる。
examples.tr: Unlike my quiet father, my mother talks a lot.

examples.jp: 落ち着いた前半のにひきかえ、後半は波乱続きだった。
examples.tr: In contrast to the calm first half, the second half was full of upheaval.

examples.jp: 温暖な南側にひきかえ、北側は風が冷たい。
examples.tr: Compared with the mild south side, the wind is cold on the north side.

examples.jp: 先輩の発表が明快なのにひきかえ、私は要点がぼやけていた。
examples.tr: In contrast to my senior's clear presentation, my main points were vague.

examples.jp: 好調だった昨年のにひきかえ、今年は伸び悩んでいる。
examples.tr: In contrast to last year, which went well, this year growth has stalled.

1238.explain:
Has a strong evaluative nuance; used in criticism/comments.
Not used to compare objective figures; when you need to be neutral, switch to “に比べて/に対して”.
The second clause usually states a clear contrast and is the focus of the statement.

“～にひきかえ” states a clear contrast between A and B, together with the speaker's evaluation. Often used to emphasize opposition in quality/personality/situation between two sides that can be placed on the same axis of comparison.
• The two parts should be naturally comparable: weather on one day vs another, one person vs another, the previous part vs this part.
• Works well when you want to express a subjective impression, not just numerical information.
• Easily combined with contrastive evaluation phrases: ～のに対し／一方で (when you need to be more neutral).

rows: Neutral, can be used for figures
<ruby>昨年<rt>さくねん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>比<rt>くら</rt></ruby>べて5％<ruby>増<rt>ぞう</rt></ruby>。
Aは<ruby>増<rt>ぞう</rt></ruby>、Bは<ruby>減<rt>げん</rt></ruby>なのに<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して。
Same subject, not two different targets
<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かな<ruby>反面<rt>はんめん</rt></ruby>、<ruby>不便<rt>ふべん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>需要<rt>じゅよう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>える<ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>で～。

mistakes: Missing “の” when A is a clause/adjective: × 暑かったにひきかえ → 〇 暑かったのにひきかえ.
Using it for comparing figures → unsuitable; use “に比べて”.
The two parts are not on the same axis of comparison → the sentence is forced/hard to understand.
1238.notes:
• Rhetorically effective when A is positive and B negative (or vice versa) to create a sharp contrast.
• Use inversion of A/B to change the focus of emphasis.
• In writing, placing a comma after “にひきかえ” helps separate the argument: ～にひきかえ、～。

examples.jp: 今年は例年にもまして台風が多い。
examples.tr: This year there are even more typhoons than usual.

examples.jp: 今日はいつにもまして落ち着いている。
examples.tr: Today I'm calmer than ever.

examples.jp: 彼女は以前にもまして仕事に情熱を注いでいる。
examples.tr: She is putting even more passion into her work than before.

examples.jp: 何にもまして命が大切だ。
examples.tr: Life is more important than anything else.

examples.jp: 円安で、輸出の追い風はこれまでにもまして強い。
examples.tr: With the weak yen, the tailwind for exports is stronger than ever.

1239.explain:
Formal/rhetorical; expresses a strong increase, an appeal, or emphasis on a topic.
Used adverbially before adjectives/verbs; rarely used directly before a noun (needs の to act as a modifier).
Choose a natural reference point:去年/以前/例年/従来/他人/いつも.

Expresses that the current degree is higher than a reference point (the past, other people, a standard). Has an emphatic/rhetorical tone and often appears in speeches, commentary and news headlines.
• Suitable for: degrees of emotion/qualities (重要/深刻/厳しい/高い/強い/多い).
• Suggests a “significant increase”, not just a small measurable difference.
• Can be combined with intensifying adverbs: さらに/一層/ますます (avoid excessive redundancy).

rows: Neutral; lacks the “more than ever” nuance
<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>より<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>予想<rt>よそう</rt></ruby><ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。
ますます／<ruby>一段<rt>いちだん</rt></ruby>と
No specific reference point for comparison
ますます<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>になる。
<ruby>以前<rt>いぜん</rt></ruby>にも<ruby>増<rt>ま</rt></ruby>して<ruby>厳<rt>きび</rt></ruby>しい。

mistakes: Using it for purely numerical differences → use “より/以上に”.
No clear reference point (when not using a question word) → the sentence is vague.
Confusing it with “にも劣らず” (no less than) → the meaning goes in the opposite direction.
1239.notes:
• Used with question words for very strong emphasis: 何/誰/いつにもまして.
• In corporate speeches: 「安心・安全を何にもまして最優先します」。
• Rare as a modifier: 例年にもましての猛暑（written language/headlines).

examples.jp: 年齢によらず、誰でも応募できます。
examples.tr: Anyone can apply, regardless of age.

examples.jp: 国籍によらず、平等に扱われるべきだ。
examples.tr: People should be treated equally regardless of nationality.

examples.jp: 天候のいかんによらず、大会は予定通り実施します。
examples.tr: The tournament will be held as scheduled, whatever the weather.

examples.jp: 経験の有無によらず、研修を受けてもらいます。
examples.tr: Everyone will undergo training, regardless of whether they have experience.

examples.jp: 支払い方法によらず、手数料はかかりません。
examples.tr: There is no fee, regardless of the payment method.

examples.jp: 事情のいかんによらず、遅刻は減点対象です。
examples.tr: Whatever the circumstances, being late results in a point deduction.

1240.explain:
A normative/policy nuance, leaning toward written language, announcements, guidelines and regulations.
The second clause usually states something that holds for every case: “～できる/～とする/～は同じだ”.
Nのいかんによらず is more formal than Nによらず ; used in business/official contexts.
Not used when the result really does “depend” on N. When it depends, use ～によって/～次第で.

• Meaning: “Regardless of/not depending on/without regard to N, the result/condition stays the same”.
• Scope of N: age, gender, nationality, experience, weather, method, reason…
• Used to state general principles, policies, regulations, or general statements.
• The form Nのいかんによらず emphasizes all-inclusiveness and is very formal (announcements, contracts).
• Usually accompanied by a main clause meaning “allowed/not allowed/unchanged/applies to all/free of charge…”.

rows: More common in spoken language; wide scope, less formal than “いかんによらず”.
<ruby>性別<rt>せいべつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>できる。
Close in meaning; also used with opposites (<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い/<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い)。Very widely used.
<ruby>雨天<rt>うてん</rt></ruby>にかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>学歴<rt>がくれき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby>なく<ruby>評価<rt>ひょうか</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>理由<rt>りゆう</rt></ruby>のいかんによらず<ruby>返金<rt>へんきん</rt></ruby><ruby>不可<rt>ふか</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>によって<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>が<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>う。

mistakes: Confusing “～によらず” with “～によって”. Incorrect example: 年齢によって誰でも応募できる (wrong meaning). Correct: 年齢によらず誰でも応募できる.
Using “によらず” when the actual result does depend on something → unnatural. When there is dependence, use “によって/次第で”.
Writing “いかん” incorrectly as “如何に” in this structure. Correct: Nのいかんによらず.
JLPT: trick questions often compare it with “～を問わず/～にかかわらず”. All three mean “regardless of”, but the formal nuance and the combination with “いかん” belong to “によらず”.
1240.notes:
• “によらず” is the negative form of “～による” (based on/depending on), meaning “not based on/not depending on”.
• “いかん” = 如何 (state/how things turn out). Fixed phrases:「天候のいかん」「成績のいかん」.
• Works well in regulatory texts: “～は、理由のいかんによらず、～とする”.

examples.jp: 工事開始に先立ち、近隣への説明会を行います。
examples.tr: Prior to the start of construction, we will hold a briefing session for the neighborhood.

examples.jp: 入学式に先立って、オリエンテーションがあります。
examples.tr: Prior to the entrance ceremony, there will be an orientation.

examples.jp: 発表に先立つ最終チェックを済ませた。
examples.tr: I completed the final check prior to the presentation.

examples.jp: システム移行を実施するに先立ち、バックアップを取得してください。
examples.tr: Before carrying out the system migration, please make a backup.

examples.jp: 上映開始に先立ち、注意事項をご案内いたします。
examples.tr: Before the screening begins, we would like to inform you of some important notes.

1241.explain:
Formal; used in official documents, announcements and ceremonies.
Emphasizes the “preparation” for an important event/activity.
Not used for everyday chores: “食事に先立ち手を洗う” sounds too formal; 前に is more natural.

Expresses “before (an important matter) takes place, carrying out the preparation/related step”. Formal usage, suited to ceremonial, business and official-announcement settings. Implies necessary preparation, unlike “前に”, which simply indicates a point in time.

rows: Used for important events, ceremonial style
<ruby>開会<rt>かいかい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>先立<rt>さきだ</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>する。
Widely used, including for everyday matters
<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>歯<rt>は</rt></ruby>を<ruby>磨<rt>みが</rt></ruby>く。
On the occasion of/when (starting something important)
Emphasizes the “important occasion”, not necessarily preparation
<ruby>開業<rt>かいぎょう</rt></ruby>にあたって<ruby>決意<rt>けつい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>述<rt>の</rt></ruby>べる。
Close in meaning to にあたって; highly formal
<ruby>契約<rt>けいやく</rt></ruby><ruby>締結<rt>ていけつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>際<rt>さい</rt></ruby>して<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Using it for everyday matters makes the sentence too stiff → choose “前に”.
Forgetting to switch to the modifier form before N: “に先立つN”.
Confusing it with “にあたって”: exam questions often test the nuance of “preparing beforehand” (に先立ち) vs “on the occasion of starting” (にあたって).
1241.notes:
• With verbs, the dictionary form (V辞書形) is usually used to nominalize the intended event: “発表するに先立ち”.
• Suitable for company templates: “導入に先立ち、～をご案内いたします”.
• In speeches, the fixed pair “に先立ち、簡単ではございますが…” is very natural.
meaning_vi: Before (carrying out a major undertaking)…, on the eve of…
examples: 1. ①　会議に先立って、メンバーの紹介が行われます。
2. ②　試合を始めるのに先立って、ルールの説明が行われます。
examples: 1. 選手団の出発に先立って、激励会が開かれた。
Before the team of athletes departed, a send-off rally was held to encourage them.
2. 記者会見に先立ち、講演要旨が配られた。
Before the press conference, a summary of the lecture was handed out.
3. 「試合開始に先立ち、国歌を演奏いたします」
“Before the start of the match, the national anthem will be performed”
4. 今回のケースでは、噴火に先立つ地震が４８時間続いた。
In this case, before the volcano erupted, earthquakes continued for 48 hours.
5. 駅前の再開発を進めるに先だって、住民の意見を聞く会が開かれた。
Before proceeding with the redevelopment in front of the station, a meeting to hear residents' opinions was held.
explain: Has the meaning of preparing in advance before ～. N is a word for an important event.
examples: 1. 開店に先立ち、関係者だけのパーティーが行われた。
Before the restaurant opened, a party for those involved only was held.
2. 新製品の開発に先立って、アンケート調査を行った。
Before developing the new product, a questionnaire survey was conducted.

examples.jp: 新製品の発売に先駆けて、試用イベントを開催する。
examples.tr: Ahead of the release of the new product, we will hold a trial event.

examples.jp: 開幕に先駆けて、記者会見が行われた。
examples.tr: A press conference was held ahead of the opening.

examples.jp: オープンに先駆け、関係者向けの内覧会を実施した。
examples.tr: Ahead of the opening, we held a preview for people involved.

examples.jp: 同社は業界に先駆けてAIを導入した。
examples.tr: That company introduced AI ahead of the rest of the industry.

examples.jp: 来年度の制度改正に先駆けて、説明会が開かれる。
examples.tr: An information session will be held ahead of next fiscal year's system reform.

examples.jp: 東京公演に先駆けたプレイベントが全国で行われる。
examples.tr: Pre-events leading up to the Tokyo performance will be held nationwide.

1242.explain:
Placed before nouns denoting a point in time/major event:開幕・発売・公開・導入・実施・改正…
A promotional/official nuance; often seen in news headlines, plans and press releases.
Used for preparatory actions, announcements, trial runs, introductions… that take place before the main milestone.
If you simply mean “before” without emphasizing “pioneering”, use ～に先立って or ～前に.

• Meaning 1: Doing something “before” an important event/point in time (preparation/launch/introduction/opening…).
• Meaning 2: “Pioneering” ahead of rivals/other organizations in the same field.
• Often appears in news, press releases and slogans: emphasizes being in the lead.
• The subject is usually an organization/company/government; rarely used for an individual's everyday actions.

rows: <ruby>開会<rt>かいかい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>先立<rt>さきだ</rt></ruby>って<ruby>黙祷<rt>もくとう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>捧<rt>ささ</rt></ruby>げる。
Going ahead of, getting ahead of
<ruby>他社<rt>たしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>んじて<ruby>新<rt>しん</rt></ruby><ruby>機能<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>提供<rt>ていきょう</rt></ruby>。
Spoken language, neutral, no PR nuance.
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>する<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>。
Emphasizes a series of events beginning from a milestone.
<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>皮切<rt>かわき</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>全国<rt>ぜんこく</rt></ruby>ツアー。

mistakes: Using it for small everyday actions (e.g. 朝食に先駆けて歯を磨く) → sounds exaggerated, unnatural.
Confusing it with ～に先立って: exam questions often ask you to pick the “pioneering/PR” nuance → choose “に先駆けて”.
It does not attach directly to a time clause (Vる＋前に) → it needs an event noun: ×出発に先駆けて vs 〇出発に先立って.
1242.notes:
• “先駆ける” = to go ahead, to pave the way; news reports like to use it to create a sense of leadership.
• The modifier form “Nに先駆けたN’” is very common in headlines: 「世界に先駆けた発表」.
• Does not combine directly with verbs; it must go through an event noun: “発売に先駆けて発表する”.

examples.jp: 彼に言わせれば、これは単なる偶然だ。
examples.tr: If you ask him, this is just a coincidence.

examples.jp: 専門家に言わせれば、原因は別にあるという。
examples.tr: According to experts, the cause apparently lies elsewhere.

examples.jp: 親に言わせれば、私はまだ子どもらしい。
examples.tr: In my parents' view, I'm apparently still a child.

examples.jp: 私に言わせれば、その案は非現実的だ。
examples.tr: If you ask me, that plan is unrealistic.

examples.jp: 世間に言わせれば、彼は天才だが、私はそうは思わない。
examples.tr: In the eyes of the public he is a genius, but I don't think so.

examples.jp: 当事者に言わせると、手続きが複雑すぎるらしい。
examples.tr: According to the people involved, the procedures seem to be far too complicated.

1244.explain:
Used when quoting/presenting a point of view; often accompanied by a subjective evaluation (good/bad/unrealistic…).
The nuance can be slightly “snarky/distancing”: “according to them… (but it may not be true)”.
In everyday spoken language, “～に言わせると” is more natural; “～に言わせれば” is more formal/emphatic.

• Gives an evaluation/judgment “from N's point of view”. May imply “that is just how N sees it”.
• Often carries a distancing nuance, sometimes with a sense of rebuttal/skepticism/light mockery.
• Can be used with “私”: 私に言わせれば～ to emphasize a strong personal opinion.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>わせれば<ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>わせると<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>ない。
Nからすると／からすれば
Based on grounds/a viewpoint (not necessarily something said).
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>からすると<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>だ。
Nにしてみれば／にしてみると
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>にしてみれば<ruby>複雑<rt>ふくざつ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>にとって<ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby>。
Topicalization, not someone's point of view.

mistakes: Confusing it with “にとって”: “彼に言わせれば大切だ” ≠ “彼にとって大切だ”. One is an “opinion”, the other is “value for someone”.
Missing the distancing nuance: exam questions may build in a sense of skepticism → choose “に言わせれば/に言わせると” instead of “によると”.
Using it with inanimate things (×会社に言わせれば) → if it is an organization understood as “the representatives/the company side”, it is acceptable: 会社側に言わせれば…
1244.notes:
• Translate flexibly: “according to N”, “if you ask N”, “as far as N is concerned”. Depending on the context, keep a distancing or neutral nuance.
• Goes well with nouns for agents who make evaluations: 専門家・医者・教師・親・世間・当事者・本人…
• When the subject is “I”, use “私に言わせれば” to make it more subjective and emphasize a personal stance.

examples.jp: この病気は高齢者に限ったことではない。
examples.tr: This disease is not limited to the elderly.

examples.jp: SNSでの誹謗中傷は芸能人に限ったことではない。
