examples.tr: Online slander on social media is not something that only happens to celebrities.

examples.jp: ミスは新人に限ったことではない。
examples.tr: Mistakes are not limited to newcomers.

examples.jp: 地震は日本だけに限ったことではない。
examples.tr: Earthquakes are not unique to Japan.

examples.jp: 都会のストレスは大人に限ったことではない。
examples.tr: Urban stress is not limited to adults.

examples.jp: 長時間労働の問題はIT業界に限ったことではない。
examples.tr: The problem of long working hours is not limited to the IT industry.

1245.explain:
Placed after a noun to deny that something is “exclusive to/occurs only in N”.
Often accompanied by words of limitation such as だけ, ばかり to emphasize and then negate: Nだけに限ったことではない.
An objective nuance, used when making a general statement or broadening the scope of the discussion.
Not used directly with adjectives/verbs; if needed, nominalize the subject: 〜する人/〜な傾向/〜という現象+ に限ったことではない.

• “It is not something limited to N” → the phenomenon/matter does not only happen with N but is more widespread.
• Structure: 限る (to limit) → 限った (limited) + ことではない (is not a matter) → “not a matter limited to N”.
• Often used to counter the idea that “only N…”, broadening the scope to other targets.
• Neutral nuance, usable in both spoken and written language. Commonly seen in news/editorials.

rows: Nに<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>ったことではない
Formal, nominalized structure “a matter not limited to N”
<ruby>過労<rt>かろう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>ったことではない。
<ruby>原因<rt>げんいん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>一<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>つだけではない。
More concise; almost the same meaning
<ruby>差別<rt>さべつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>一<rt>いち</rt></ruby><ruby>国<rt>こく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない。
Nに<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>ったことでもない
でもない → softer/more open, often used in conversation
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>ったことでもない。

mistakes: Using it directly with verbs/adjectives: × 忙しいに限ったことではない → ✔ 忙しい人に限ったことではない.
Confusing it with Nに限る (N is best/limited to N). The meaning is completely different.
Dropping “こと”: × Nに限ったではない → ✔ Nに限ったことではない.
Confusing its nuance with だけではない: exam questions may ask you to choose the more formal pattern → prefer に限ったことではない in serious written language.
1245.notes:
• When the subject is a person/group of people, use a noun phrase: 都市に住む人に限ったことではない.
• Often used with social topics: 少子化、物価高、ハラスメント、気候変動 など.
• Corresponding positive expression: Nに限った話ではない (not a story only about N).

examples.jp: このような賞を頂き、光栄の極みです。
examples.tr: Receiving an award like this is the greatest honor.

examples.jp: お忙しいところを煩わせてしまい、失礼の極みでございます。
examples.tr: I am terribly sorry to have troubled you when you are so busy; it was the height of rudeness.

examples.jp: せっかくの機会を逃すとは、残念の極みだ。
examples.tr: To miss such a precious opportunity is extremely regrettable.

examples.jp: この応接室は贅沢の極みだ。
examples.tr: This reception room is the height of luxury.

examples.jp: 多大なご迷惑をおかけし、遺憾の極みでございます。
examples.tr: We deeply regret having caused you such great inconvenience.

1246.explain:
Used to emphasize the highest degree through formal exaggeration.
Often appears in thanks/apologies, speeches and press releases:光栄の極み,遺憾の極み.
Not used in everyday conversation unless deliberately creating a “dramatic/rhetorical” nuance.
What follows can be だ/です/でございます to adjust the level of politeness.

• Expresses the “utmost/extreme” degree of a state or emotion: “N is at its peak”.
• Formal nuance with a strong rhetorical character; usually used in speeches and official documents.
• Limited combinations: tends toward abstract nouns or evaluations. Does not attach directly to adjectives; nominalization is needed.
• Different from 極まる/極まりない: の極み leans toward “naming something at its extreme” and is highly lexically fixed.

rows: Attaches to abstract N; extremely formal
<ruby>光栄<rt>こうえい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>みだ
Attaches to ナ<ruby>形<rt>がた</rt></ruby>/<ruby>一部<rt>いちぶ</rt></ruby>N; written language
<ruby>無礼<rt>ぶれい</rt></ruby><ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まる<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>
（ナ<ruby>形<rt>がた</rt></ruby>/イ<ruby>形<rt>がた</rt></ruby>）<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まりない
<ruby>危険<rt>きけん</rt></ruby><ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まりない
Often used for the speaker's feelings (<ruby>光栄<rt>こうえい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>り)
<ruby>感激<rt>かんげき</rt></ruby>の<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>りです

mistakes: Using it directly with adjectives: incorrect. You do not say “嬉しいの極み” → correct: “感激の極み”.
Using it in casual speech sounds “over the top”. Choose 極まりない/とても… in everyday conversation.
Confusing it with の至り: “迷惑の至り” sounds forced; for negative things use “迷惑の極み”.
1246.notes:
• The phrase “遺憾の極み” is often seen in political statements/hearings.
• “贅沢の極み” can carry a nuance of praise or of sarcasm depending on the context.
• If you want a strong critical tone, consider “極まりない”: その発言は無責任極まりない。

examples.jp: このような場にお招きいただき、光栄の至りです。
examples.tr: It is the greatest honor to be invited to an occasion like this.

examples.jp: 多くの方に支えられ、感激の至りでございます。
examples.tr: I am deeply moved by the support of so many people.

examples.jp: 先日の無礼は、若気の至りでございました。
examples.tr: My rudeness the other day was the result of youthful folly.

examples.jp: この受賞は身に余る評価で、恐縮の至りです。
examples.tr: This award is more recognition than I deserve, and I am truly humbled.

examples.jp: ご迷惑をおかけし、痛恨の至りに存じます。
examples.tr: I most deeply regret having caused you trouble.

1247.explain:
A humble/ceremonial nuance, suitable for official speeches, letters and congratulatory speeches.
Usually comes at the end of a sentence with です／でございます／に存じます to increase politeness.
“若気の至り” is also used in spoken language, but still carries a slight sense of excuse-making.

• Expresses an “utmost/extreme” degree, but leans toward the speaker's humble, polite expression.
• Common in formal thanks/congratulations/apologies; has a more classical tone than の極み.
• “若気の至り” gives youth as the reason excusing immature behavior.
• The range of nouns it combines with is limited; emotion/ceremonial nouns are preferred.

rows: Used for both positive and negative; broader in nuance
Strongly critical tone, little ceremonial character
<ruby>無責任<rt>むせきにん</rt></ruby><ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>まりない

mistakes: Using it with everyday negative nouns sounds unnatural: “迷惑の至り” → prefer “迷惑の極み”.
Using it in casual conversation sounds “overly solemn”.
Getting the keigo wrong: “至りに思います” is unnatural → “至りに存じます”.
1247.notes:
• In formal letters, the fixed pattern まことに光栄の至りに存じます。 can be used.
• “恐悦至極/至りに存じます” is an archaic, highly formal form used in ceremonies.
• Do not overuse “若気の至り” to dodge responsibility in serious contexts.

examples.jp: 結果はどうであれ、プロセスを大切にしたい。
examples.tr: Whatever the result, I want to value the process.

examples.jp: 彼が誰であれ、規則は守ってもらう。
examples.tr: Whoever he is, he will have to follow the rules.

examples.jp: 契約が取れるかどうかはどうであれ、見積もりは出しておこう。
examples.tr: Whether or not we win the contract, let's submit a quote anyway.

examples.jp: 成否がどうであれ、挑戦した価値はある。
examples.tr: Whether it succeeds or fails, the attempt was worth it.

examples.jp: 会場がどこであれ、時間厳守でお願いします。
examples.tr: Wherever the venue is, please be punctual.

examples.jp: 評価はどうであれ、事実を淡々と報告する。
examples.tr: Whatever the evaluation, report the facts calmly.

1248.explain:
Used to affirm a stance/standard that does not change.
Often used with commands/suggestions/volition: ～してください／～べきだ／～つもりだ.
More formal than ～にかかわらず／～を問わず, with a declarative character.

• “No matter how A turns out, B (stays the same).” Emphasizes that B is not affected by A.
• Formal style, used when stating principles/views/directions.
• The scope of A can be a result, circumstances, identity, place,...

rows: <ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>はどうであれ、<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>せよ
<ruby>天候<rt>てんこう</rt></ruby>にかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず<ruby>応募<rt>おうぼ</rt></ruby><ruby>可<rt>か</rt></ruby>
No matter what it may be
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>がどうであろうと<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>ける

mistakes: Using it for matters without multiple possible “hows” → unnatural. This pattern presupposes that A has several possibilities.
Attaching it to a purely descriptive clause (with no stance) → the meaning becomes weak: it should be followed by a clear request/view.
Confusing it with ～ても: ～はどうであれ is more formal and general, not used for momentary emotions.
1248.notes:
• An equivalent expression with a legal/regulatory nuance: ～のいかんにかかわらず.
• “は/が” before どうであれ: は for contrast/emphasis, が is more objective.
• Often used with pairs of opposites: 成功/失敗, 賛成/反対, 高い/安い.

examples.jp: 泥まみれになっても、最後まで走り抜いた。
examples.tr: Even though I got covered in mud, I ran all the way to the end.

examples.jp: 彼は汗まみれのシャツを着替えた。
examples.tr: He changed out of his sweat-soaked shirt.

examples.jp: 血まみれの手で触らないでください。
examples.tr: Please do not touch it with blood-covered hands.

examples.jp: 嘘まみれの報告書では信頼を失う。
examples.tr: A report riddled with lies will lose people's trust.

examples.jp: 借金まみれの生活から抜け出したい。
examples.tr: I want to escape from a life buried in debt.

examples.jp: 油まみれの機械を丁寧に拭き取る。
examples.tr: Carefully wipe down the oil-covered machine.

1249.explain:
Preferably used with substances that “stick/spread/run”; in metaphorical use, it carries a strongly negative implication.
In polite speech or journalistic description, まみれ creates a vivid, sometimes heavy impression.
Not used with positive/lovely things (×花まみれ → use花だらけ/花いっぱい).

• “Full of / smeared with / covered in N”, usually dirt or something unpleasant (泥, 砂, 血, 汗, 油, ほこり...).
• Can be used metaphorically for a state of being steeped in something negative: 嘘まみれ, 噂まみれ, 借金まみれ.
• Difference from だらけ: まみれ emphasizes “covering the surface/the whole body”; だらけ emphasizes “many mistakes/flaws scattered about”.

rows: Emphasizes the surface/being stuck on; negative
<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>いだらけの<ruby>作文<rt>さくぶん</rt></ruby>
<ruby>白<rt>しろ</rt></ruby>づくめの<ruby>服装<rt>ふくそう</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using it with positive nouns → unnatural: × 褒め言葉まみれ → use 褒め言葉だらけ instead.
Using it for “mistakes/errors” → choose ～だらけ: × 間違いまみれ → ◯ 間違いだらけ.
Forgetting the negative nuance → the sentence sounds too heavy in a light context.
1249.notes:
• The image of “まみれる” suggests unpleasantness/dirtiness → metaphorical use creates a strong nuance of criticism.
• With absorbent things (紙, 布), it describes being soaked: 血まみれ/汗まみれ sounds stronger than 濡れた.
• Can be combined with adjectives: 汗まみれで臭う (covered in sweat and smelly).

1250.meaning: … goes without saying, but … even more

examples.jp: 彼の歌唱力もさることながら、表現力が圧倒的だ。
examples.tr: His singing ability is impressive, of course, but his expressiveness is truly overwhelming.

examples.jp: 立地もさることながら、アフターサービスの良さが評判だ。
examples.tr: The location is one thing, but it is the excellent after-sales service that has earned it a good reputation.

examples.jp: スピードもさることながら、安定性で他社を上回る。
examples.tr: Its speed is impressive, but it outperforms other companies even more in stability.

examples.jp: デザインもさることながら、機能が秀逸だ。
examples.tr: The design is great, but the functionality is truly outstanding.

examples.jp: 経験もさることながら、倫理観の高さを重視する。
examples.tr: Experience matters, but we place even greater value on a strong sense of ethics.

examples.jp: 被害の大きさもさることながら、風評の影響が深刻だ。
examples.tr: The scale of the damage is serious enough, but the impact of harmful rumors is even more serious.

1250.explain:
Used in praise/professional evaluations, PR texts, and presentations.
N1 and the following part should be on the same axis of evaluation (quality, service, people...).
Difference from “だけでなく”: it emphasizes the move of raising A and then pushing B forward as “even more”.

• “Not only is A significant, but B is even more so.” A is raised first, then the focus shifts to B.
• Polite nuance; used in advertising/introductions/formal evaluations; usually positive, but can also be used with negatives.
• The following part is the informational focus; avoid putting important content in A.

rows: Not only A, B even more
Formal; B is the focus; elevating nuance
<ruby>外見<rt>がいけん</rt></ruby>もさることながら、<ruby>中身<rt>なかみ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>大事<rt>だいじ</rt></ruby>
A goes without saying, B too
Neutral; not necessarily “B more than A”
<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>はもちろん、<ruby>価格<rt>かかく</rt></ruby>も<ruby>魅力<rt>みりょく</rt></ruby>
Not only A but also B
<ruby>機能<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>だけでなく、デザインも<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>い
Not to mention A, even B
<ruby>基本<rt>きほん</rt></ruby>はおろか、<ruby>応用<rt>おうよう</rt></ruby>もできない

mistakes: Placing a verb/adjective directly before it → unnatural; use nominalization if needed.
Putting important information in A → loses its effect; B is the focus to be emphasized.
Confusing it with ～はおろか (negative) or ～だけでなく (neutral) → wrong nuance on the exam.
1250.notes:
• Has a refined, literary quality; in copywriting it makes the sentence sound more “classy”.
• Often paired with contrasting/supporting words: まして／なおさら／とりわけ in part B to add emphasis.
• It is fine to set more than one criterion as A, but take care not to blur the focus on B.

examples.jp: 彼は人の話を聞きもしないで結論を出す。
examples.tr: He jumps to conclusions without even listening to what others say.

examples.jp: 彼女は資料を読みもしないで批判した。
examples.tr: She criticized it without even reading the materials.

examples.jp: 挨拶をしもしないで部屋に入ってきた。
examples.tr: They came into the room without so much as a greeting.

examples.jp: 何も調べもしないで噂を信じるな。
examples.tr: Don't believe rumors without even looking into anything.

examples.jp: 子どもは手伝いもしないでゲームばかりしている。
examples.tr: The kids don't even help out; they just play video games all the time.

examples.jp: 約束の時間を確認もしないで出かけた。
examples.tr: They went out without even checking the time of the appointment.

1251.explain:
Used when the speaker is annoyed and makes a negative evaluation of behavior that lacks the bare minimum.
Usually placed before a main clause that brings a bad consequence: ～もしないで＋(reaction/consequence).
Can be used for self-criticism:私は説明書を 読みもしないで 壊してしまった。
Natural in spoken language; in written language it can be replaced with ～もせずに to sound less harsh.

- Expresses “not doing V at all / not even bothering to do V (not even a little)” and then doing the next action. Implies reproach, criticism, annoyance.
- “も” means “even…” → combined with the negative “しない” it creates strong emphasis.
- Often used when talking about others, for behavior seen as lacking the bare minimum/common sense: “挨拶もしないで…”.
- Difference from ～ないで/～ずに (neutral): ～もしないで has an emotional nuance and emphasis.

rows: <ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>まないで<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めた。
Close in meaning to ～もしないで, less emotional
<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>もせずに<ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>った。
Does not connect to a following clause with “で”; reproachful nuance
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>なんて<ruby>聞<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きもしない。
Coarser, strongly expressive; does not mean “without doing… and then”

mistakes: Wrong position of “も”: ×「聞くもしないで」 → correct: 「聞きもしないで」.
Confusing it with ～ないで/～ずに (which have no critical nuance). The JLPT often asks you to choose the pattern that expresses “not even bothering to…”.
Using it in a polite context with a superior can easily sound rude because of its reproachful nuance.
Forgetting to change to Vます: ×「行くもしないで」 → correct: 「行きもしないで」.
1251.notes:
• “も” is placed right before “しない/せずに” or right after the noun of a する verb: 挨拶もしないで; 聞きもせずに.
• Putting “も” in the wrong place easily blurs the emphatic meaning: ×「も聞かないで」 (should be: 聞きもしないで).
• In polite language, the whole sentence can be shifted to です／ます, but the “～もしないで” part keeps its form.

examples.jp: 期日までに提出がない場合、辞退したものとして扱います。
examples.tr: If nothing is submitted by the deadline, it will be treated as a withdrawal.

examples.jp: 参加費の入金を確認できたものとして、座席を確保いたします。
examples.tr: We will reserve your seat on the understanding that payment of the participation fee has been confirmed.

examples.jp: 本規約に同意したものとして、サービスを提供します。
examples.tr: The service is provided on the understanding that you have agreed to these Terms.

examples.jp: 未成年であるものとして、保護者の同意が必要です。
examples.tr: As you are regarded as a minor, parental consent is required.

examples.jp: 無断欠席は放棄したものとして処理する。
examples.tr: An unexcused absence will be processed as a forfeiture.

1252.explain:
Formal; often appears in regulations, contracts, official notices, and business procedures.
Stiff nuance; establishes in advance a rule for handling situations that occur.
In everyday conversation, とみなす／として is more natural.

• Used to establish an assumption/convention: “regard as / be considered as / be treated as …”. Highly regulatory in nature.
• “Vた + ものとして” is very common: 合格したものとして手続きを進める（proceed with the procedures as if having passed）.
• “N + ものとして” is close to “N として” but emphasizes identification/definition within a framework of rules rather than a simple role.

rows: <ruby>欠席<rt>けっせき</rt></ruby>したものとして
Standard verb, easy to use in both spoken and written language; formal
Indicates only a role/function; no implied handling convention
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>として<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>
～<ruby>扱<rt>あつか</rt></ruby>い（として<ruby>扱<rt>あつか</rt></ruby>う）
Emphasizes the actual act of handling
<ruby>不在<rt>ふざい</rt></ruby><ruby>扱<rt>あつか</rt></ruby>いにする

mistakes: Using it in casual conversation sounds stiff: switch to とみなす／として when it is not a written document.
Confusing “Nとして” (role) with “Nであるものとして” (identification by convention): the legal meanings differ.
The JLPT often asks about the regulatory nuance and the form Vたものとして (regarded as having V-ed) in rule sentences.
1252.notes:
• Often follows a conditional clause: ～ない場合、…したものとして…. A set structure in regulations.
• “であるものとして” keeps the formal tone when attached to academic/legal nouns: 自然人であるものとして.
• In service notices, a polite variant: ～したものとして取り扱わせていただきます.

examples.jp: あいつは約束の時間に来やしない。
examples.tr: That one never shows up at the agreed time.

examples.jp: 何度説明しても、彼は分かりゃしない。
examples.tr: No matter how many times I explain, he just doesn't get it.

examples.jp: 子どもは片付けなんてしやしないくせに、文句ばかり言う。
examples.tr: The kids never bother tidying up, yet all they do is complain.

examples.jp: そんな高い店、誰も行きやしないよ。
examples.tr: Nobody's going to go to such an expensive place.

examples.jp: こんな量、食べきれやしない。
examples.tr: There's no way I can finish this much.

1253.explain:
Strong, coarse, leaning toward spoken language; avoid using it with superiors/in formal situations.
Often accompanied by evaluative words: どうせ／全然／まったく…＋Vやしない.
Used to refute expectations: 「頼んでも 来やしない よ」.
At the end of the sentence, nothing usually needs to be added after ～やしない.

- Emphasizes negation: “absolutely not / never ever / not even if it kills me…”. Expresses annoyance, sarcasm, criticism.
- Usually used in spoken language, with strong emotion. The subject is usually a person/target being criticized.
- Difference from ～もしないで: ～やしない does not have the sense “without doing… and then” to connect clauses; it only strongly negates the action.

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>りはしない。
Similar in meaning, but not as coarse as ～やしない
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聞<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きもしない。
No way / extremely unlikely to happen
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>からじゃ<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いっこない。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>断<rt>ことわ</rt></ruby>るわけがない。

mistakes: Confusing its clause-connecting function: ～やしない is not used like ～ないで to connect “not doing A but doing B”.
Using it with superiors in formal writing → rude nuance.
Forgetting to change to Vます: ×「行くやしない」 → correct: 「行きやしない」.
Confusing it with ～っこない (possibility) in JLPT questions on nuance.
1253.notes:
• “やしない” comes from “はしない” (a colloquial sound change). “りゃしない” is a contraction of “りはしない”.
• Combines widely with potential forms/forms of potential completion: 分かりゃしない／できやしない／終わりゃしない.
• In serious written language, prefer ～はしない or switch to another, more polite structure.

examples.jp: 彼は悪天候をものともせずに、山頂を目指した。
examples.tr: Undaunted by the bad weather, he headed for the summit.

examples.jp: 多くの批判をものともせずに、彼女は改革を進めた。
examples.tr: Undeterred by heavy criticism, she pushed ahead with the reforms.

examples.jp: 病気をものともせず、研究を続けた。
examples.tr: Undeterred by illness, they carried on with their research.

examples.jp: 強風と高波をものともせずに、漁師たちは出航した。
examples.tr: Braving strong winds and high waves, the fishermen set sail.

examples.jp: 子どもたちは寒さをものともせず、外で遊んでいる。
examples.tr: Undaunted by the cold, the children are playing outside.

1254.explain:
Used to praise someone's spirit/determination; a narrative tone, describing heroism.
Avoid using it about yourself in humble contexts; if needed, soften the nuance: ～にもめげず／～に負けず.
Not used directly with clauses/verbs; it requires a noun denoting adversity.

• “In defiance of / think nothing of” – expresses an undaunted attitude in the face of adversity.
• Strong, literary nuance; used to give a high evaluation of the spirit of overcoming difficulties.
• Not applied to positive factors; combines only with negative/unfavorable agents.

rows: In defiance of, thinking nothing of
<ruby>困難<rt>こんなん</rt></ruby>をものともせず<ruby>挑<rt>いど</rt></ruby>む
Neutral; states a fact without implying praise
<ruby>大雨<rt>おおあめ</rt></ruby>にもかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>
～に<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けず／～にも<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けない
Not losing to, not giving in
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>さに<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けず<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>る
Usually has a nuance of criticism
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>の<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>をよそに<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>び<ruby>回<rt>まわ</rt></ruby>る

mistakes: Using it with positive factors (例: 応援をものともせず ×) → wrong scope of meaning.
Using it to praise yourself in a formal context → sounds boastful.
Confusing it with ～をよそに: the JLPT tests the nuance of praise vs. criticism.
1254.notes:
• Often accompanied by challenging vocabulary: 逆境、障害、重圧、痛み、非難、逆風.
• Useful in descriptive writing, encouraging speeches, and sports news.
• Usual word order: N（adversity）+ をものともせずに + V (toward a goal).

examples.jp: 親の心配をよそに、彼は海外へ一人旅に出た。
examples.tr: Despite his parents' worries, he set off on a solo trip abroad.

examples.jp: 世間の非難をよそに、その企業は事業を拡大し続けた。
examples.tr: Ignoring public criticism, the company continued to expand its business.

examples.jp: 医者の忠告をよそに、彼は無理なトレーニングを続けている。
examples.tr: Ignoring the doctor's advice, he keeps on training excessively.

examples.jp: 家族の反対をよそに、二人は同棲を始めた。
examples.tr: Disregarding their families' opposition, the two began living together.

examples.jp: 台風接近の警報をよそに、一部の登山者は入山を強行した。
examples.tr: Despite warnings of an approaching typhoon, some climbers went ahead and set out up the mountain.

examples.jp: 周囲の期待をよそに、彼女は大企業への就職ではなく起業を選んだ。
examples.tr: Contrary to the expectations of those around her, she chose to start her own business rather than join a large company.

1255.explain:
Common nouns:親の心配・家族の反対・周囲の期待・世間の批判/非難・医者の忠告・危険/リスク・規則/ルール.
What follows: after ～をよそに comes a clause of intentional action (～する/～続ける/～強行する...).
Nuance of criticism/detachment: the speaker stands in the position of an observer who evaluates.
Strongly written in style; suits essays, newspapers, and news.

• In defiance of / ignoring / paying no heed to N: the person/group acts as if N (opposition, worry, expectations, warnings, public opinion...) did not exist.
• Evaluative nuance: implies criticism or surprise at “turning a deaf ear” to something that should have been heeded.
• Scope of use: mainly describes the actions of others/third parties; limit using it about yourself in formal contexts (used about yourself, it easily sounds like bragging about “defying everything”).
• Not used for spontaneous natural phenomena: it must be a volitional act. Avoid sentences like “天気をよそに雨が降った”.
• Formal/written; close in meaning to ～もかまわず but emphasizes “ignoring the reactions of those around” rather than “not minding the inconvenience”.

rows: Emphasizes “ignoring the voices around”; nuance of criticism.
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>の<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>をよそに<ruby>進学<rt>しんがく</rt></ruby>。
More neutral; the target is not necessarily “the voices around”.
<ruby>人目<rt>ひとめ</rt></ruby>もかまわず<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>く。
<ruby>困難<rt>こんなん</rt></ruby>をものともせず<ruby>挑戦<rt>ちょうせん</rt></ruby>する。
A structure linking clauses; no implication of “deliberately ignoring”.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>にもかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Used with natural phenomena: Incorrect. It must be a volitional act. × 雨をよそに降った → √ 雨にもかかわらず試合を行った。
Unsuitable N: Avoid neutral N such as 気温, 数字 unless they imply a “voice/warning”.
Using it about yourself in a formal context may be seen as self-aggrandizing; consider the point of view.
Confusing it with ～もかまわず: the latter emphasizes “not minding inconvenience”, not “ignoring other people's opinions”.
1255.notes:
• “よそ” originally means “elsewhere/outsider”, from which it came to mean “set aside, treat as unrelated”.
• In journalism, it often goes with 強行する・続行する・押し切る, creating a sense of criticism.
• When you want to praise the spirit of overcoming difficulties, choose ～をものともせず instead of ～をよそに to avoid a negative nuance.

examples.jp: 大雨のため、野外コンサートは中止を余儀なくされた。
examples.tr: Because of heavy rain, the outdoor concert had to be canceled.

examples.jp: 彼は病気で引退を余儀なくされた。
examples.tr: He was forced to retire due to illness.

examples.jp: パンデミックにより、多くの学校がオンライン授業への移行を余儀なくされた。
examples.tr: Because of the pandemic, many schools were forced to switch to online classes.

examples.jp: 原材料価格の高騰が、事業計画の見直しを余儀なくした。
examples.tr: Soaring raw material prices forced a review of the business plan.

examples.jp: 地震の影響で、二次試験は延期を余儀なくされた。
examples.tr: Due to the earthquake, the second-round exam had to be postponed.

examples.jp: 需要低迷が人員削減を余儀なくした。
examples.tr: Sluggish demand forced job cuts.

1256.explain:
The passive subject is the party that “has to accept” it (人/組織/イベント…), not the cause.
The cause (natural disasters, epidemics, the market…) usually becomes the subject in the active form ～を余儀なくする.
Not used for trivial everyday matters; preferred for decisions/scales of a social/official nature.
Stiff, objective nuance; avoid using it when you want to assign blame subjectively.

• “Be forced to / have no choice but N”: expresses reluctance due to circumstances/objective pressure.
• N must be a noun that can form a サ変 verb (an act/measure): 中止・延期・変更・撤退・縮小・移行・辞任・閉鎖・解散・見直し…
• Often preceded by a cause phrase with により・ため・せいで.
• Literary nuance; often used in news, reports, and press releases.

rows: N を<ruby>余儀<rt>よぎ</rt></ruby>なくされる
Be forced to N (サ<ruby>変<rt>へん</rt></ruby> noun)
<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>余儀<rt>よぎ</rt></ruby>なくされる
Have no choice but to V
Goes with verbs; more personal nuance.
<ruby>延期<rt>えんき</rt></ruby>せざるを<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>ない
The only option is to V
N を<ruby>余儀<rt>よぎ</rt></ruby>なくする
<ruby>台風<rt>たいふう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>余儀<rt>よぎ</rt></ruby>なくした

mistakes: Attaching it directly to a verb: Incorrect. × 行くを余儀なくされる → √ 出席を余儀なくされる.
Confusing the subject: the “party that is forced” is the subject of ～を余儀なくされる.
Confusing it with せざるを得ない: that one goes with verbs and has a personal nuance; exams often ask you to distinguish the type of word it attaches to.
Using it in small personal contexts (shopping, errands) sounds too formal and unnatural.
1256.notes:
• “余儀ない” = “there is no other way”. This structure is fixed; avoid altering it arbitrarily.
• Avoid overusing it with N that is not an act (× 景気を余儀なくされる); change it to a related act (縮小・撤退 etc.).
• In administrative writing, combine it with により/に伴い/の影響で to state an objective cause.

examples.jp: この計画は全員の参加を前提として進められている。
examples.tr: This plan is being carried out on the premise that everyone will participate.

examples.jp: 契約は信頼関係の継続を前提として結ばれている。
examples.tr: The contract is concluded on the premise that the relationship of trust will continue.

examples.jp: データが正確であることを前提としてモデルを評価した。
examples.tr: The model was evaluated on the premise that the data were accurate.

examples.jp: 十分な予算確保を前提としたスケジュールは現実的ではない。
examples.tr: A schedule that presupposes securing a sufficient budget is not realistic.

examples.jp: 第三者の合意を前提として、公開は来月に行う。
examples.tr: On the premise that third-party consent is obtained, the release will take place next month.

1257.explain:
Common combinations:参加・合意・継続・確保・存在・達成・安定・正常稼働など + を前提として.
Used to state policy/design assumptions; state them clearly to avoid misunderstanding the scope of application.
Compared with ～を前提にして, ～を前提として is more formal, leaning toward statements of principles/definitions.

• Establishes a “premise/something taken for granted as true” in order to proceed with a plan, discussion, or design.
• Unlike a condition “if… then…”, 前提 is a foundational assumption: one proceeds as if it were already true.
• Often used in policy, business, academic, and technical contexts; formal nuance.
• When the premise is off, the conclusion/design may become invalid; therefore it often goes with verification/見直し.

rows: Used in documents and normative statements.
<ruby>全員<rt>ぜんいん</rt></ruby><ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>を<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>として
Leans toward operation/practice; natural in on-site settings.
スマホ<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>にして
Does not imply “assumed true” but “a source of reference”.
データに<ruby>基<rt>もと</rt></ruby>づいて<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>
More natural when the subject is a clause.
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>するという<ruby>前提<rt>ぜんてい</rt></ruby>で

mistakes: Confusing it with the condition “if… then…”. 前提 is something taken for granted that already exists, not a future condition.
Attaching a long clause directly to を前提として makes the sentence heavy; という前提で is more natural.
Confusing it with ～を前提にして when choosing the nuance; exams often test your feel for formality/implementation.
1257.notes:
• If you want to emphasize that “the assumption may change”, add a word meaning temporary: 当面/暫定的に + ～を前提として.
• In research, it is often accompanied by a scope condition: 本研究はXの環境を前提として評価を行う。
• To avoid ambiguity, when the premise is a long clause, prefer という前提で.

examples.jp: 彼の勇気ある行動には感動を禁じ得ない。
examples.tr: I cannot help being moved by his courageous act.

examples.jp: 相次ぐ不祥事に、怒りを禁じ得ない。
examples.tr: I cannot contain my anger at the string of scandals.

examples.jp: 被災地の惨状を目の当たりにし、言葉にならない悲しみを禁じ得ない。
examples.tr: Witnessing the devastation in the disaster area firsthand, I cannot hold back a sorrow beyond words.

examples.jp: 彼の無責任な発言には驚きを禁じ得ない。
examples.tr: I cannot help being astonished by his irresponsible remarks.

examples.jp: この判決は妥当であり、同時に安堵を禁じ得ない。
examples.tr: This ruling is fair, and at the same time I cannot help feeling relieved.

1258.explain:
Attaches only to emotion nouns; does not go directly with verbs/adjectives.
Usually placed at the end of a sentence; what comes before states the situation that causes the emotion.
Stronger and more formal than ないではいられない／ずにはいられない (which are used with verbs).

• Cannot hold back / cannot help feeling N (a strong emotion) in the face of some situation.
• Written, formal nuance; often used in commentary, newspaper articles, and speeches.
• The subject is a person or group acting as the speaker/observer; rarely used with an inanimate subject.

rows: <ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>き/<ruby>怒<rt>いか</rt></ruby>り/<ruby>失望<rt>しつぼう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>禁<rt>きん</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>ない。
<ruby>笑<rt>わらわ</rt></ruby>わないではいられない。
Slightly more formal than ～ないではいられない
<ruby>涙<rt>なみだ</rt></ruby>せずにはいられない。
Not an emotion; circumstances force it
<ruby>撤退<rt>てったい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>余儀<rt>よぎ</rt></ruby>なくされる。

mistakes: Using it with a verb: incorrect. It must be an emotion noun.
Inanimate subject (会社、この結果など) + を禁じ得ない: unnatural. The subject should be a person/group of people.
Confusing it with ～ずにはいられない: exam questions ask about the difference in the type of word it attaches to and the level of formality.
1258.notes:
• Sino-Japanese emotion nouns give a serious feel: 憤り、憤怒、落胆、羞恥、感嘆、悲嘆...
• To emphasize the degree, you can add 割り切れない思い/やりきれない思いなど and then use ～を禁じ得ない.
• In critiques/editorials, this phrase helps make the writing more objective and coherent.

examples.jp: 度重なる試作を経て、ついに製品化にこぎ着けた。
examples.tr: After repeated prototyping, we finally managed to bring it to market.

examples.jp: 厳格な審査を経て、認証を取得した。
examples.tr: After a rigorous review, the certification was obtained.

examples.jp: 長い交渉を経て、双方は和解に至った。
examples.tr: After long negotiations, the two parties reached a settlement.

examples.jp: 先行研究を経て、新しい仮説が提示された。
examples.tr: Building on previous research, a new hypothesis was presented.

examples.jp: SNSを経て、情報が瞬時に拡散した。
examples.tr: Via social media, the information spread instantly.

1259.explain:
Usually attaches to time nouns/nouns of stages (年月、期間、準備、交渉、審査、試験運用...).
Formal, objective style; suited to administrative/technical documents.
To emphasize "throughout a period of time," consider ～を通じて/～を通して; to emphasize "through a channel," you can use ～を経由して, but ～を経て is more formal.

• Expresses "going through" a period of time/process/stage/intermediate channel, which then leads to a later result.
• Official nuance; used in reports, press releases, histories of development, and descriptions of procedures.
• Emphasizes accumulation/sequential progress through several steps before reaching a result.

rows: <ruby>交渉<rt>こうしょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>経<rt>へ</rt></ruby>て<ruby>合意<rt>ごうい</rt></ruby>。
～を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて／を<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して
<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて leans toward “throughout,” <ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して toward “by means of” (less formal)
<ruby>一年<rt>いちねん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて<ruby>温暖<rt>おんだん</rt></ruby>だ。メディアを<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して<ruby>発信<rt>はっしん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>香港<rt>ほんこん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>経由<rt>けいゆ</rt></ruby>して<ruby>出荷<rt>しゅっか</rt></ruby>。
Emphasizes the outcome after a lot of effort; emotional nuance
<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>末<rt>すえ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>結論<rt>けつろん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>達<rt>たっ</rt></ruby>した。

mistakes: Misreading “へて” as “えて”: incorrect. The kanji 経 is read へ(る).
Using it for an instantaneous event with no process: inappropriate. Choose ～を通じて／経由して depending on the context.
Confusing it with ～の末（に）: “の末” has an emotional coloring of a final outcome, while “を経て” is neutral and procedural.
1259.notes:
• “経る(へる)” suggests a verified process/intermediate step: 試験運用→本格運用, パイロット→ローンチ.
• Goes well with 至る・実現する・承認される・完成する to emphasize the result achieved.
• In histories/summaries of events, a sequence like “創業→拡大→再編→上場” is often described with ～を経て.

examples.jp: 最新の統計を踏まえて、販売戦略を見直す。
examples.tr: We will review our sales strategy based on the latest statistics.

examples.jp: 先行研究を踏まえた仮説を提示する。
examples.tr: Present a hypothesis that builds on previous research.

examples.jp: 皆様からのご意見を踏まえまして、サービスを改善いたします。
examples.tr: Taking all of your feedback into account, we will improve our service.

examples.jp: 判例を踏まえ、和解案を提示した。
examples.tr: Taking legal precedents into account, a settlement proposal was presented.

examples.jp: 現地調査の結果を踏まえて、計画を修正した。
examples.tr: The plan was revised based on the results of the field survey.

1260.explain:
Serious and objective; often appears in reports, proposals, research papers, and official statements.
Often combines with verbs meaning adjust/decide:見直す,決定する,設計する,立案する,判断する,改善する,策定する.
Can come at the beginning of a sentence to state the basis, followed by the main action.
Not used for purely emotional opinions; there should be a concrete/objective "basis" involved.

• Based on, taking … as the basis for deciding/evaluating/proposing.
• Implies "having carefully considered" data/facts/precedents before acting; formal nuance, common in academic, business, and administrative contexts.
• Different from "rough reference": ～を踏まえて implies a firm foundation (a basis that carries weight).
• Often used with nouns such as: データ, 結果, 実績, 事実, 判例, ご意見, 先行研究, 反省, 需要動向, 市況, ガイドライン.

rows: <ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>を<ruby>踏<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>まえて<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>する
In accordance with (rules/data) in a standard way
<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>基<rt>もと</rt></ruby>づいて<ruby>処理<rt>しょり</rt></ruby>する
Using … as "material" to create something new
<ruby>実話<rt>じつわ</rt></ruby>をもとに<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby><ruby>化<rt>か</rt></ruby>
<ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>鑑<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>みて<ruby>見直<rt>みなお</rt></ruby>す

mistakes: Use it for an objective basis; avoid using it with vague personal feelings (× 気分を踏まえて決める).
Confusing it with ～をもとに when you mean "adapt/create" (films, stories) → use ～をもとに.
The JLPT often asks you to distinguish を踏まえて vs に基づいて vs をもとに; note the "careful consideration" nuance of を踏まえて.
1260.notes:
• “踏まえる” originally means "to step on" → metaphor of "standing on a foundation (basis)."
• In emails/minutes: “ご指摘を踏まえまして～” is very natural and polite.
• When the basis is highly quantitative, you can use ～に基づいて instead to emphasize standardization.
meaning_vi: ～を前提(ぜんてい)、根拠(こんきょ)として→考(かんが)える、作成(さくせい)する
Based on
力(ちから)を入(い)れて踏(ふ)む
examples: 1. 先行研究を踏まえて論文を書く。
Write a thesis based on previous research.
2. 「今回の失敗を踏まえて、次はどうすべきかを考えてみます」
Based on this failure, let's think about what we should do next time.
3. 会議では前回までの議論を踏まえて、さらに内容を深めた話し合いが行われた。
At the meeting, a discussion was held that deepened the content further, building on the discussions up to the previous meeting.
4. 両足で大地を踏まえて立つ。
Step firmly on the ground with both feet.

examples.jp: 今日を限りに甘い物を断ちます。
examples.tr: As of today, I'm giving up sweets.

examples.jp: この連載は次号を限りに終了いたします。
examples.tr: This series will end with the next issue.

examples.jp: 当店は今月を限りに閉店します。
examples.tr: Our store will close at the end of this month.

examples.jp: 彼は今季を限りに引退を表明した。
examples.tr: He announced that he would retire after this season.

examples.jp: 本企画への応募は本日を限りに締め切ります。
examples.tr: Applications for this project close today.

1261.explain:
Formal; suited to notices and official statements.
Often used with verbs such as: やめる,終了する,閉店する,打ち切る,引退する,打ち切り,打ち止め.
The emphasis is on the "final point in time," unlike a plain "from now on."

• "With … as the last time / at the end of …, something stops/no longer continues."
• Emphasizes that a point in time is the boundary at which an action/state ends.
• Often used in declarations, press releases, personal resolutions, or organizational announcements.
• Typical accompanying words: 今日, 今回, 今月, 今季, 今年, 本日, 今号, 次回, 〇月末, 〇年度 など.

rows: With N as the last time/the end
Emphasizes the point in time when something ends
<ruby>本日<rt>ほんじつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>販売<rt>はんばい</rt></ruby><ruby>終了<rt>しゅうりょう</rt></ruby>
Often seen on signs/in press releases
<ruby>今季<rt>こんき</rt></ruby><ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りで<ruby>退団<rt>たいだん</rt></ruby>
Does not state a "last time" point
タバコをやめることにする
<ruby>今月<rt>こんげつ</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Use it with nouns of "time/period"; avoid nouns that are not about time (× 気分を限りにやめる).
Confusing it with “N までに” (deadline) → ～を限りに means "last time/ending," not "deadline for completion."
The JLPT often asks about the set ～を限りに vs 限りで vs をもちまして in the context of announcements.
1261.notes:
• In everyday spoken language, speakers often use 今日で/今月で instead of ～を限りに to sound softer.
• Notice boards/posters prefer “N 限りで” or “N をもちまして” (very formal).

1262.connection: Vない(drop ない) + んがため(に)・んがための + N (exception: しない→せん)

examples.jp: 彼は名声を得んがために、無謀な挑戦を繰り返した。
examples.tr: He repeatedly took on reckless challenges in order to gain fame.

examples.jp: 会社は生き残りんがために、大規模なリストラを断行した。
examples.tr: In order to survive, the company pushed through large-scale restructuring.

examples.jp: 真実を明らかにせんがために、彼女は内部告発をした。
examples.tr: She blew the whistle in order to bring the truth to light.

examples.jp: 彼は勝たんがための戦略を練りに練った。
examples.tr: He worked out a strategy for winning down to the last detail.

examples.jp: 難民は戦火を逃れんがため、国境へと向かった。
examples.tr: The refugees headed for the border in order to escape the war.

1262.explain:
Has a determined, "at all costs" nuance. Used to emphasize a strong motive or the legitimacy (or reprehensibility) of an action.
Often appears with heavy vocabulary:無謀,極端,決行,犠牲,断行…
Not used for natural/objective purposes (e.g., "so as not to miss the train" usually takes ～ように/ために).
Placed before a noun as ～んがための + N to highlight "for the purpose of X."

- Meaning: "in order to (achieve at all costs) …"; expresses a purpose with extremely strong volition, sometimes with a "regardless of anything" nuance.
• Emphasizes an intense, determined motive, much stronger than ～ために, ～ように.
• Often used with purposes of great value (victory, fame, survival…), sometimes leading to excessive actions.
• The subject of the purpose clause and the main clause is usually the same intentional agent.
• Style: formal, written language, speeches, history; not used for daily life or small purposes.
• Not used with direct command/request sentences.

rows: Neutral, widely used; does not necessarily imply strong volition
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>するために<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する
Does not emphasize volition; used with ability, machines, phenomena
<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れないように<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>る
Formal but milder than ～んがために
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>すべく<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>した
Same form, but means "because" when it is a reason clause
<ruby>貧<rt>まず</rt></ruby>しいがために<ruby>進学<rt>しんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>断念<rt>だんねん</rt></ruby>した

mistakes: Wrong subject: the purpose clause and the main clause must have the same intentional agent.
Using it for trivial matters: × 時間を節約せんがために早起きする → use ～ために/～ように.
Mistaking “せん” for a negative: “せんがため” ≠ “しないため”.
Attaching it to a request sentence: × 合格せんがために手伝ってください → clash of nuance.
Confusing it with “～がために” (cause): distinguish the meaning "purpose" vs "because of (negative)."
1262.notes:
• “せんがため” is the classical form of “する” used in this structure; it is not the negative “しない.”
• For 来る, the classical form “こんがため” exists but is rare; avoid it in exam prep and use a substitute verb (来訪す, 訪れる…).
• In literature/speeches, this pattern is often placed at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize the purpose.

1263.connection: Vない(drop ない) + んばかり(に)・んばかりの + N (exception: しない→せん)

examples.jp: 彼は涙を流さんばかりに喜んだ。
examples.tr: He was so happy he was almost in tears.

examples.jp: 頭を床に擦りつけんばかりに謝った。
examples.tr: He apologized, practically pressing his head to the floor.

examples.jp: 会場は割れんばかりの拍手に包まれた。
examples.tr: The hall was filled with thunderous applause.

examples.jp: 胸が張り裂けんばかりだ。
examples.tr: My heart feels as if it is about to burst.

examples.jp: コップから水が溢れんばかりに注がれている。
examples.tr: The water has been poured so full that the glass is about to overflow.

1263.explain:
Used when the speaker judges that something is "about to" happen, though in reality it usually has not happened; leans toward exaggerating an impression.
Suited to literary descriptions, newspaper articles, and storytelling; rarely used in ordinary conversation.
Not used for ordinary objective events (×早起き んばかりに 起きた).

- Meaning: "to the point of being about to …," "as if … at any moment"; emphasizes an extremely high degree, though it usually has not actually happened.
• Describes an outward state/image that makes the speaker "feel as if" something is about to happen.
• Often used with strong emotions and gestures: 泣く, 叫ぶ, 壊れる, 溢れる, 飛び出す…
• Slightly more literary/formal style than ～ほど/～くらい.

rows: Neutral, widely used; no literary nuance
<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>きたいほど<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しい
Hypothetical comparison; not necessarily "about to" happen
<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>砂糖<rt>さとう</rt></ruby>であるかのように<ruby>白<rt>しろ</rt></ruby>い
Emphasizes a gesture/action as if wanting to say something
<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていたとばかりに<ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す
Different meaning: shows only an upward/downward trend
<ruby>物価<rt>ぶっか</rt></ruby>は<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がるばかりだ

mistakes: Describing something that actually happened: × 泣いんばかりに泣いた → redundant; use ほど/くらい.
Attaching it to everyday objective actions → does not fit the nuance.
Confusing it with ばかりだ (tendency) in JLPT questions; note the different semantic field.
Choosing the wrong verb: prefer vivid verbs/phrases with strong emotion.
1263.notes:
• Very common set phrases: 割れんばかりの拍手, 溢れんばかりの笑顔／花, 飛び出さんばかりの勢い.
• “せんばかり” for する is a classical form; do not confuse it with the negative.
• Often used with a noun + の as a modifier: ～んばかりのN makes the sentence more natural.

examples.jp: 彼はアマチュアだが、プロ並みの知識を持っている。
examples.tr: He's an amateur, but he has the knowledge of a professional.

examples.jp: 今年の寒さは例年並みだ。
examples.tr: This year's cold is about the same as usual.

examples.jp: このスマホはカメラが一眼レフ並みによく撮れる。
examples.tr: This smartphone's camera takes pictures as good as a DSLR's.

examples.jp: 人並みの生活がしたいだけです。
examples.tr: I just want to live a normal life like everyone else.

examples.jp: 東京並みの家賃では地方では借りられない。
examples.tr: At Tokyo-level rents, you can't rent anything in the provinces.

1264.explain:
Usually placed before a noun to state the "standard of comparison."
“人並み” is used to mean the "ordinary level, like other people," sometimes implying modesty.
With “例年並み/平年並み”: expresses an average level over many years.

• "A degree equivalent to/like N"; emphasizes "being on a par with the standard/object of comparison."
• Can have a positive meaning (reaching a high standard: プロ並み) or a neutral one (例年並み), depending on the context.
• Unlike ほど/くらい (estimation), 並み leans toward "a truly equal standard."
• Often used with standards such as: プロ, 大人, 人, 世界, 一流, 例年, 平年, 都会, 東京, 外資, 欧米, 最新.

rows: On a par with, at the same level
<ruby>世界<rt>せかい</rt></ruby><ruby>記録<rt>きろく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>匹敵<rt>ひってき</rt></ruby>する
プロ<ruby>級<rt>きゅう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>選手<rt>せんしゅ</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Confusing it with ほど/くらい: ～並み emphasizes an "equivalent standard," not just a vague estimate.
Do not use ～並み for comparisons of more/less (× A は B 並みより上). Rephrase as: “A は B 並みかそれ以上”.
The JLPT often tests swapping: プロ並みの vs プロほど（に）は～ない → different nuances.
1264.notes:
• “A 並みの B” → B reaches the standard of A; “A 並みに C” → C happens at a level like A.
• “世界並み” is sometimes translated as "meeting international standards."
• In business, “大手並みの待遇/福利厚生” is a very common phrase.

examples.jp: 東京にお越しの折には、ぜひ弊社へお立ち寄りください。
examples.tr: When you come to Tokyo, please be sure to stop by our office.

examples.jp: 先日はご多忙の折に、ご参加いただきありがとうございました。
examples.tr: Thank you for attending the other day despite your busy schedule.

examples.jp: 来日の折に、古い友人たちと再会した。
examples.tr: When I came to Japan, I met up with some old friends again.

examples.jp: 大阪へ出張した折に、本社にも顔を出した。
examples.tr: When I went on a business trip to Osaka, I also stopped by the head office.

examples.jp: この折に、皆様のご支援に深く感謝申し上げます。
examples.tr: On this occasion, I would like to express my deep gratitude for everyone's support.

examples.jp: 森先生とは、先日のパーティーの折に少し話をしました。
examples.tr: I talked a little with Professor Mori at the party the other day.

1265.explain:
More formal than とき/際に; often found in emails, company notices, and speeches.
Used with “には” when inserting an invitation/suggestion: ～折には、ぜひ…
Works with both the past (Vた) and a planned future (Vる), as long as the "occasion" is fairly specific.

- Meaning: "on the occasion of/when …"; equivalent to ～とき but formal, often used in letters, invitations, and announcements.
• Often used with keigo/refined expressions: お越しの折に, お忙しい折に恐れ入りますが…
• Used for a specific occasion (past/expected), not a hypothetical condition.
• Suited to invitations/politeness: ～折には、ぜひ…ください.

rows: <ruby>暇<rt>ひま</rt></ruby>なとき<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>してください
Formal; a bit stiffer than <ruby>折<rt>おり</rt></ruby>に, used in rules/instructions
ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>際<rt>さい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>身分<rt>みぶん</rt></ruby><ruby>証<rt>しょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>提示<rt>ていじ</rt></ruby>
Emphasizes the opportunity "while still…"; a different nuance from the polite "occasion"
<ruby>若<rt>わか</rt></ruby>いうちに<ruby>挑戦<rt>ちょうせん</rt></ruby>する
Emphasizes the immediate point in time; rarely used in formal letters
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけるところだ

mistakes: Using it in casual conversation sounds "too stiff"; use とき.
Using it for a vague hypothetical condition: × 雨なら折に → wrong semantic field.
Confusing it with 際に in regulations: 際に leans toward rules/clauses; 折に toward letters/speeches.
Dropping “には” in invitations: ～折には is more natural than ～折に in an invitation.
1265.notes:
• “折（おり）” originally means "point in time/opportunity"; mainly written language, and in speech it is usually replaced with とき.
• Common email openers: お忙しい折に恐縮ですが／恐れ入りますが…
• “この折” is used to sum up/thank/change the topic in speeches. meaning_vi: On the occasion of, when, at the time ～ ⏐ explain: Since it means "on some good occasion," the following clause usually does not mention bad things. ⏐ examples: 1. 来日の折には、ぜひこちらにお立ち寄りください。
When you come to Japan, be sure to drop by and see me.
2. 次にお目にかかった折に、お借りしていた本をお返しします。
I'll return the book I borrowed when we meet next time.

examples.jp: ご支援いただき、ありがたい限りです。
examples.tr: I am truly grateful for your support.

examples.jp: 結果が期待外れで、残念な限りだ。
examples.tr: The results fell short of expectations, which is extremely disappointing.

examples.jp: 友人の活躍を聞いて、うれしい限りだ。
examples.tr: I'm so happy to hear about my friend's success.

examples.jp: 災害の被害状況は痛ましい限りだ。
examples.tr: The extent of the damage from the disaster is truly heartbreaking.

examples.jp: 海外で無事だと知って、ほっとする限りだ。
examples.tr: I am so relieved to know they are safe overseas.

1266.explain:
Expresses a strong, polite emotional evaluation; suited to formal contexts.
Not used for purely objective descriptions (temperature, figures...).
Avoid applying it directly to other people's emotions when not making a conjecture.

- Used to emphasize a subjective emotion at its peak: "extremely/very/… utterly."
- More formal than とても/本当に; common in speeches, letters, and formal news.
- Mainly used for the speaker's current emotion or after hearing news/an event.

rows: Formal; the subject is the speaker
<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>めて/<ruby>非常<rt>ひじょう</rt></ruby>に
<ruby>極<rt>きわ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>
Noun form; often used in ceremonial language

mistakes: Confusing it with “～限り” (as long as/the more ~): the two patterns have different functions.
Using it with non-emotional content: (x) 売上は高い限りだ → (o) 非常に高い.
Applying it to other people: (x) 彼は嬉しい限りだ → replace with 彼は嬉しそうだ／嬉しいに違いない when making a conjecture.
1266.notes:
• Common in business style: 嬉しい限り／ありがたい限り carry a humble, polite tone.
• To sound more casual, switch to とても/本当に + Adj to be natural in conversation.
• In the news, it is used to express emotion about a sad event: 痛ましい限りだ／悲しい限りだ.

1267.connection: どんなに + V volitional form + が

examples.jp: どんなに批判されようが、信念は曲げない。
examples.tr: No matter how much I am criticized, I will not bend my convictions.

examples.jp: どんなに忙しかろうが、家族との時間は大切にする。
examples.tr: No matter how busy I am, I make time with my family a priority.

examples.jp: どんなに不利であろうが、挑戦を続ける。
examples.tr: No matter how disadvantaged we are, we will keep taking on the challenge.

examples.jp: どんなに遠くであろうとも、必ず会いに行く。
examples.tr: No matter how far away it is, I will definitely go to see you.

examples.jp: どんなに雨が激しかろうが、試合は予定通り行う。
examples.tr: No matter how hard it rains, the match will be held as scheduled.

1267.explain:
Formal, rhetorical nuance; used to emphasize an unchanging position.
Usually not used for things that have already happened or to describe past facts; to describe actual facts, use ～ても/～たって.
が and とも are interchangeable; とも is more formal and suits written language and speeches.

• Meaning: “No matter how (much)…, (still)…”; emphasizes determination or an unchanging assertion in the face of a high degree of a condition.
• Has a strong nuance; often used in declarations, slogans, formal written language, or firm assertions.
• Usually followed by a main clause expressing volition, determination, or an unchanging evaluation.

rows: どんなに<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>われようが<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Neutral, common; less of a “declaration” nuance
いかに<ruby>困難<rt>こんなん</rt></ruby>であろうが。
Highlights the supposition with たとえ
たとえ<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>ける。

mistakes: Wrong conjugation of Aい: × 忙しいようが → correct: 忙しかろうが.
Wrong with Aな/N: × 不利だようが → correct: 不利であろうが/だろうが.
Used for something already completed → sounds forced: use ～ても instead. Example: × どんなに雨が強かろうが、昨日行った。
1267.notes:
• With Aい it is rare in modern spoken language; choose A-くても if you want everyday naturalness.
• N + であろうが/とも is common with nouns such as 誰・相手・天候・逆境.
• Can be emphasized with たとえ: たとえどんなに～うが/とも、…

1268.meaning: Only thanks to… can there be…

examples.jp: お客様あっての私たちの会社です。
examples.tr: Our company exists only thanks to our customers.

examples.jp: 家族あっての幸せだと実感している。
examples.tr: I truly feel that my happiness is possible only because of my family.

examples.jp: 信頼あっての取引だ。
examples.tr: Business deals depend on trust.

examples.jp: この受賞は、チームあっての成果です。
examples.tr: This award is an achievement made possible by the team.

examples.jp: 命あっての仕事だ。無理はしないで。
examples.tr: Without your health, there is no work. Don't overdo it.

examples.jp: 彼の成功は努力あってのものだ。
examples.tr: His success came only through his hard work.

1268.explain:
Formal, positive; often appears in speeches, announcements, and words of thanks.
Often used with nouns such as: お客様,皆様,家族,仲間,支援,努力,信頼,健康,命.
Asserts a strong cause-and-effect relationship and emphasizes the foundation.

• Expresses the relationship “only with N1 can there be N2”; N1 is the prerequisite and foundation of N2.
• Nuance of gratitude and respect, acknowledging an indispensable role.
• Scope: attaches only to nouns; used often in speeches, words of thanks, and corporate slogans.
• Rhetorical structure: N1 is placed first to emphasize “thanks to…”.

rows: Modifies a noun; nuance of gratitude
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>あっての<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>
Used with V or N; emphasizes the condition necessary for the action to happen
<ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>があってこそ<ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>く。
Usually expresses a concrete result; less formal
<ruby>皆<rt>みな</rt></ruby>さんのおかげで<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>した。
Implies a negative condition; strongly hypothetical
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>なくして<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>なし。

mistakes: Using it directly with a verb: incorrect. It must be N + あっての + N.
Understanding it as “probably thanks to”: incorrect. 「あっての」 is a strong assertion of an essential condition.
Confusing it with 「おかげで」: 「あっての」 modifies a noun, has a formal nuance, and is a fixed structure.
Not keeping the correct order of N1 (foundation) → N2 (result): reversing them makes the meaning wrong.
1268.notes:
• This pattern is effective in slogans: 「安全あっての生産」「健康あっての挑戦」.
• Can be repeated in parallel: 「家族あっての私、仲間あってのチーム」。
• To make it less formal, it can be replaced with 「〜のおかげで」; to emphasize an essential condition, use 「〜なくして」.

1269.connection: V volitional form + が + V volitional form + が

examples.jp: 雨が降ろうが風が吹こうが、マラソンは決行する。
examples.tr: Whether it rains or the wind blows, the marathon will go ahead.

examples.jp: 高かろうが低かろうが、この基準は変えない。
examples.tr: Whether it is high or low, we will not change this standard.

examples.jp: 学生だろうが社会人だろうが、守るべきルールは同じだ。
examples.tr: Whether you are a student or a working adult, the rules you must follow are the same.

examples.jp: 晴れであろうが雨であろうが、毎朝ジョギングする。
examples.tr: Whether it is sunny or rainy, I go jogging every morning.

examples.jp: 好きだろうが嫌いだろうが、与えられた仕事はやり切るべきだ。
examples.tr: Whether you like it or not, you should see the work you are given through to the end.

examples.jp: 合格しようが落ちようが、挑戦した価値はある。
examples.tr: Whether you pass or fail, it was worth taking on the challenge.

1269.explain:
Position: The phrase AうがBうが comes at the beginning of a sentence or in the middle, followed by a concluding clause (often expressing firmness or being unaffected).
Typical collocations after the pattern: 関係ない・問題ない・問わない・構わない・同じだ・変わらない・やり抜く・続ける・実施する など.
Formality: であろうが (formal/written language) > だろうが (spoken language). With Aい, use かろうが (a literary form).
Nuance: Strong; emphasizes determination or rules. Often used in announcements, speeches, policy documents, or statements expressing a position.
Parallel forms: Keep the word class and logic parallel: if A is N, B is also N; if A is V意向, B is also V意向.

• Main meaning: Presents two possibilities or opposites and asserts that the result or position does not change. “Whether A or B, (still)…”, “Regardless of A or B, …”.
• Pragmatic value: Emphasizes determination, disregard of conditions, or the consistency of a rule or judgment. Strong nuance, more formal than ordinary conversational patterns.
• Information structure: Clause Aうが Bうが (concessive–listing clause) + main clause (conclusion/view: 関係ない・問わない・変わらない・続ける・行う…).
• Restriction: A and B should be the same word class and correspond to or contrast with each other (高い↔低い, 晴れ↔雨, 行く↔やめる).
mistakes: Wrong form: using the dictionary form instead of the volitional/conjectural form. Incorrect: 高いが 安いが. Correct: 高かろうが 安かろうが.
Mixing word classes: A is V意向 and B is N + だろう (not parallel), which makes the sentence awkward. Keep the same word class or a clearly corresponding pair.
Confusing it with ～うが～まいが: the JLPT often sets traps with the pair “行こうが 行くまいが” (one verb, two possibilities) vs “晴れだろうが 雨だろうが” (two contrasting nouns). Distinguish their functions clearly.
いい → よかろう: Test takers often write “いいかろうが” (incorrect). Correct: よかろうが.
Nuance too strong: using it in casual conversation can sound stiff. In the exam, choose the pattern that fits the context: であれ/にしろ may be more natural.
Missing the concluding clause: the pattern usually needs a following clause to complete the concession–conclusion meaning. Avoid ending with “AうがBうが、…(left hanging)”.
Answer-choice traps: wrong answers often replace が with は/も/を or use “静かろうが” (wrong word class). Check the endings かろう/だろう/であろう and the 意向形.
1269.notes:
• Rhythm: The repeated pattern “A…が B…が” creates a rhetorical rhythm, suitable for speeches, headlines, and slogans.
• Implicit negation: Often implies “not affected by condition A/B”. Therefore, the second clause rarely expresses an easily changing state.
• Combining with interrogative words: Can be extended to “誰であろうが・いつであろうが・どこであろうが…”, and can also be placed in parallel: “誰であろうが 何であろうが…”.
• Style: For a lighter or more conversational tone, consider 〜にしろ〜にしろ or 〜でも〜でも.
• Note the irregular i-adjective: いい → よい → よかろうが. Example: よかろうが 悪かろうが.

1270.connection: V volitional form + と + V volitional form + と

examples.jp: 雨が降ろうと風が吹こうと、マラソンは予定通り行う。
examples.tr: Whether it rains or the wind blows, the marathon will be held as planned.

examples.jp: 泣こうと笑おうと、時間は待ってくれない。
examples.tr: Whether you cry or laugh, time will not wait for you.

examples.jp: 値段が高かろうと安かろうと、品質が第一だ。
examples.tr: Whether the price is high or low, quality comes first.

examples.jp: 子どもだろうと大人だろうと、ルールは同じだ。
examples.tr: Whether you are a child or an adult, the rules are the same.

examples.jp: どれだけ反対意見が多かろうと、方針は変えない。
examples.tr: No matter how many objections there are, we will not change our policy.

examples.jp: 彼が来ようと来まいと、私は準備を続ける。
examples.tr: Whether he comes or not, I will keep preparing.

1270.explain:
Emphasizes volition or determination: Often used to show a firm position that is not affected.
Formal/rhetorical: Suits speeches and written language; in everyday conversation it can be replaced with ～ても/～に関わらず.
Binary listing: The two possibilities should match in word class and degree (verb with verb, adjective with adjective...).
The second part rarely takes commands or requests: It is seldom used with direct requests; if it is, the tone is strong.

• Meaning: Emphasizes that “whether it is possibility A or possibility B, the result, determination, or judgment in the second clause does not change”.
• Character: Emphatic style, somewhat formal or oratorical; stronger than ～ても.
• Grammar: A and B are usually an opposing pair, two extremes, or two typical options. The following clause often goes with phrases such as 「関係ない」「影響されない」「同じだ」「構わない」「～してみせる」.
• Tense agreement: The second part is usually in the general present, expressing a general judgment or strong volition; it is rarely used for a small, momentary event.

rows: “Whether A or B, still …” Emphatic, rhetorical.
<ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れようと<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だろうと、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Replaces と with が, equivalent nuance; slightly more colloquial.
<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>こうが<ruby>笑<rt>わら</rt></ruby>おうが、<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じだ。
“Whether or not you do …” emphasizes the contrast of doing/not doing the same verb.
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こうと<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くまいと、<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>は<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わらない。
～に<ruby>関<rt>かか</rt></ruby>わらず/～を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず
“Regardless of …” used with nouns or general categories.
<ruby>性別<rt>せいべつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず<ruby>応募<rt>おうぼ</rt></ruby><ruby>可<rt>か</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Conjugation error: using “高いだろうと” instead of “高かろうと”; using “学生だと” instead of “学生だろうと/であろうと”.
Not parallel: combining different word classes or degrees: “雨が降ろうと高かろうと” (logically wrong).
Confusing it with ～うと～まいと: that pattern requires the contrast of doing/not doing the same verb; it cannot be replaced with a pair of other word classes.
Using it for trivial situations: avoid using it with momentary actions; choose ～ても instead.
JLPT: Often tests the conjugations “～かろうと/～であろうと” and comparison with “～に関わらず/～ても”.
1270.notes:
• Group 1 verbs into the volitional form: 書く→書こう, 行く→行こう, 読む→読もう; Group 2: 食べる→食べよう; 来る→来よう; する→しよう.
• i-adjectives: 高い→高かろう, 低い→低かろう. Nouns/na-adjectives: 学生だろう/学生であろう, 便利だろう/便利であろう (であろう is used in formal style).
• Often combined with emphatic words: たとえ～うと, いかに～うと, どれほど～うと.
• The second clause is usually a general judgment, a rule, a fact, or strong volition; avoid describing small, momentary events.

examples.jp: 手術のかいもなく、患者は助からなかった。
examples.tr: Despite the surgery, the patient could not be saved.

examples.jp: 徹夜で勉強したかいもなく、試験に落ちてしまった。
examples.tr: Even though I stayed up all night studying, I failed the exam.

examples.jp: 探し回ったかいもなく、財布は見つからなかった。
examples.tr: Even though I searched everywhere, I couldn't find my wallet.

examples.jp: 長時間並んだかいもなく、チケットは売り切れだった。
examples.tr: Even though we waited in line for a long time, the tickets were sold out.

examples.jp: 親の努力のかいもなく、計画は中止になった。
examples.tr: Despite the parents' efforts, the plan was canceled.

1271.explain:
Placed in the cause clause indicating effort, followed by a negative or unwanted result.
Can be used in both formal and everyday contexts; “甲斐もなく/甲斐なく” is formal.
Has a strong emotional nuance; avoid it when you might hurt the listener in a sensitive situation.
Not combined with a command or suggestion in the second clause.
If you want to say “not worth doing”, 〜がいがない/〜甲斐がない is more natural when talking about potential value.

• Meaning: “Even though… was done, it was in vain / brought no result”, “despite the effort, the outcome was futile”.
• Nuance: Regret, disappointment, sadness; usually goes with a negative result.
• Pragmatics: Used to recount facts that did not turn out as hoped; avoid using it with commands or volition.
• Grammar: “かい” is a noun; it is preceded by Nの or Vた.
• Different from “むだに”: ～かいもなく is specifically tied to “effort/hard work”, not simply waste.

rows: Emphasizes the effort that was made
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>したかいもなく、<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>。
Even if you do it, it is useless
A prediction or judgment before acting
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>から<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>ってもむだだ。
<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>ったところで、<ruby>許<rt>ゆる</rt></ruby>されない。
<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ったかいがあって、<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>えた。
Not worth it, of no value
Speaks of general value, not necessarily an actual result
<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>む<ruby>甲斐<rt>かい</rt></ruby>がない<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Used with a positive result: incorrect. ～かいもなく is used only when the result is bad or not as hoped.
Confusing it with ～てもむだ: one is a fact that has already happened; the other is a hypothetical judgment.
Dropping “の” after a noun: it must be Nのかいもなく, not Nかいもなく.
Spelling mistake: 甲斐 → miswritten as 貝/皆.
Combining it with a command or volition in the second clause: unnatural.
1271.notes:
• “甲斐” is a Sino-Japanese noun; adding “も” emphasizes total negation.
• Appears often in news and medical reports: 〜治療の甲斐もなく.
• Avoid overusing it in polite communication about sad news; you can switch to a more neutral expression.
• It can come at the beginning of a sentence or in the middle of one; it is usually followed by a comma and then the result clause. meaning_vi: Even though you tried, the result was regrettable ⏐ explain: Expresses the meaning that even if you try and make an effort, there is no result as hoped or expected…
1
手術 のかいもなく、愛犬が死んでしまった。 Despite the surgery, my beloved dog died.
2
予選で落ちてしまい、一生懸命 練習した かいがなかった。 I was eliminated in the preliminaries; all that hard practice was in vain.

examples.jp: 彼は教師のかたわら、小説も書いている。
examples.tr: Besides working as a teacher, he also writes novels.

examples.jp: 大学で経営を学ぶかたわら、父の店を手伝っている。
examples.tr: While studying management at university, I help out at my father's shop.

examples.jp: 研究のかたわら、地域のボランティア活動にも参加している。
examples.tr: Alongside my research, I also take part in local volunteer activities.

examples.jp: 子育てのかたわら、在宅で翻訳の仕事をしている。
examples.tr: While raising my children, I work as a translator from home.

examples.jp: 本業のかたわら、週末にポッドキャストを配信している。
examples.tr: Alongside my main job, I put out a podcast on weekends.

1272.explain:
Emphasizes main/secondary roles: A (before かたわら) is usually the main occupation, and B is an accompanying activity.
Duration: Suits activities that continue over a period; not used for two actions performed simultaneously in a brief moment.
Written language/introductions: Natural in résumés, articles, and career interviews; more polite and formal than ～ながら.

• Meaning: “Besides (the job/duty/activity) A, (in parallel) also does B.” Emphasizes that A is the main one and B is a secondary one over a period of time.
• Scope: Expresses an ongoing situation that is regular or periodic rather than a momentary action.
• Pragmatics: Often used in written language, profile introductions, biographies, and career descriptions: 仕事のかたわら, 研究するかたわら…

rows: Parallel over a long period; A is main, B is secondary.
<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby><ruby>員<rt>いん</rt></ruby>のかたわら、<ruby>作家<rt>さっか</rt></ruby><ruby>活動<rt>かつどう</rt></ruby>。
Two actions at the same time (immediate simultaneity) in one moment; neutral nuance, more colloquial.
<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聞<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する。
Presents two contrasting or parallel aspects; does not emphasize “main/secondary”.
<ruby>都市<rt>とし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>な<ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>で、<ruby>物価<rt>ぶっか</rt></ruby>が<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
Doing B while taking the opportunity of doing A; “secondary” by opportunity, not ongoing.
<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>のついでに<ruby>切手<rt>きって</rt></ruby>を<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う。

mistakes: Using it for momentary actions: ×「歩くかたわら、電話に出た」→ use ～ながら instead.
No main/secondary relationship: if A and B are equal, consider using ～一方で or ～ながら.
Wrong word class: used only with N の / V-る; not used with an adjective directly before かたわら.
Confusing it with the positional meaning: 「かたわらに」 (beside) ≠ the grammar point “besides doing…, also…”.
JLPT: Often asks you to distinguish ～かたわら from ～ながら/～ついでに in terms of duration and the main/secondary relationship.
1272.notes:
• Part B can be a habit or regular activity: 「～もしている」「～も行っている」「～も続けている」.
• Not used with direct commands or volition: ×「勉強するかたわら、来なさい」.
• With the noun meaning “beside (physically)”: 「かたわらに」= “beside”: 「机のかたわらに鞄を置く」 (not the grammar point for parallel occupations).
• Often used with words for work or positions: 仕事／研究／育児／学業／本業 のかたわら.

examples.jp: この荷物は20キロからある。
examples.tr: This package weighs a good 20 kilos.

examples.jp: ここから駅までは5キロからあるよ。
examples.tr: It's a good 5 kilometers from here to the station, you know.

examples.jp: あの絵は数千万からする価値がある。
examples.tr: That painting is worth tens of millions or more.

examples.jp: 会場には千人からの観客が集まった。
examples.tr: As many as a thousand spectators gathered at the venue.

examples.jp: 全長3メートルからある大蛇が見つかった。
examples.tr: A huge snake as long as 3 meters was found.

1273.explain:
Emphasizes “larger than one thinks”; can carry a positive exaggerating nuance in advertising and headlines.
Usually not used with small numbers, because the emphasis is lost.
Can be used both as a predicate and as a noun modifier: 〜からある／〜からのN.

• Emphasizes a large degree, beyond the usual: “as much as, about, at least”.
• Used with a specific number + unit; often carries a nuance of surprise or emphasis.
• Choose the right suffix: からある (size/weight/length), からする (price), からの (modifying a large quantity).
• Often used in descriptions, advertising, and the press to emphasize scale.

rows: <ruby>数<rt>すう</rt></ruby><ruby>十<rt>じゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>万<rt>まん</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>からする<ruby>時計<rt>とけい</rt></ruby>
<ruby>百人<rt>ひゃくにん</rt></ruby>からの<ruby>応募<rt>おうぼ</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Used with a small number (1キロからある): sounds forced. Use it when the number feels “large”.
Confusing the scope: for prices you must use 「からする」, not 「からある」.
Forgetting to add a noun when using 「からの」: you need 「数百人からの応募」; it does not stand alone.
Misunderstanding it as “at least”: although the meaning is close, the focus is on emphasizing size/significance, not a purely mathematical lower bound.
1273.notes:
• When modifying a noun, use 「〜からのN」 so that the sentence flows more naturally.
• In the media, this phrase often comes with estimated numbers: 数百、数千、数十万… to heighten the effect.
• For area/volume, 「からある」 can also be used if the focus is on “large scale”.

examples.jp: 改装には数百万円からする費用がかかる。
examples.tr: The renovation will cost several million yen or more.

examples.jp: あの絵は何百万円からするそうだ。
examples.tr: I hear that painting costs several million yen or more.

examples.jp: 最新モデルは千ドルからするという。
examples.tr: They say the latest model costs a thousand dollars or more.

examples.jp: 数十万円からするレンズを大事に使う。
examples.tr: I take good care of my lens, which cost several hundred thousand yen.

examples.jp: 入会金と設備費で数万円からするらしい。
examples.tr: The membership fee and facility fee apparently come to tens of thousands of yen or more.

examples.jp: 彼は何十万円からするスーツを着ている。
examples.tr: He wears suits that cost hundreds of thousands of yen.

1274.explain:
Common in advertising, news, and product or project evaluations; conveys an impression of how expensive something is.
Placed before a noun for emphasis: 〜からするN; placed at the end of a sentence to conclude about the price.
Used with vague numbers:数十／数百／何＋単位to make it more evocative.

• Used to indicate “a price/cost of at least about …”, creating a sense of large/expensive.
• When used as a modifier, からする attaches after the counter to emphasize how “huge” the following N is.
• Typical scope: money, costs, financial value; rarely used for physical size.

rows: 50<ruby>万<rt>まん</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>からするワイン
<ruby>1万人<rt>いちまんにん</rt></ruby>からの<ruby>観客<rt>かんきゃく</rt></ruby>
