mistakes: Used for size instead of money: ×5キロからする道 → ○5キロからある道.
Confusing it with からの when modifying a number of people: ×100人からする観客 → ○100人からの観客.
Using it with a small amount of money makes the sentence sound odd or conveys the wrong emotion.
JLPT: recognize “a large price / at least” → choose からする rather than 以上/からの/からある.
1274.notes:
• In PR writing, からする heightens the sense of “luxury/expensiveness”.
• Used with nouns for cost items: 予算／費用／投資／被害額.
• In headlines: 「〜からする被害」 emphasizes the scale of the damage.

examples.jp: 私から言わせれば、その説明は不十分だ。
examples.tr: If you ask me, that explanation is inadequate.

examples.jp: 被害者から言わせれば、判決は軽すぎる。
examples.tr: From the victims' point of view, the sentence is far too light.

examples.jp: 教師から言わせれば、基礎が大事だ。
examples.tr: If you ask a teacher, the basics are what matter.

examples.jp: 親から言わせれば、夜遊びは心配だ。
examples.tr: From the parents' point of view, staying out late at night is worrying.

examples.jp: 専門家から言わせると、リスクは低くない。
examples.tr: If you ask an expert, the risk is not low.

examples.jp: 正直に言わせれば、賛成できない。
examples.tr: To be honest, I can't agree.

1275.explain:
Placed at the beginning of the sentence, optionally followed by a comma to mark a pause: 〜から言わせれば、…
Used to signal one's own opinion in advance, preparing for a contrary statement.
In casual speech: 〜から言わせりゃ (colloquial, masculine).

• States the subjective opinion of the agent N, often to open a rebuttal or to "speak frankly".
• Implies "if you make me (say it), then…", adding emphasis.
• Usually used with a person/group as the agent: 私／親／教師／専門家／被害者.

rows: You want to "speak frankly" or rebut
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>から<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>わせれば<ruby>高<rt>こう</rt></ruby>すぎ。
<ruby>法律<rt>ほうりつ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えばOK。
Nの<ruby>立場<rt>たちば</rt></ruby>からすると
Viewing from a position or role
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>立場<rt>たちば</rt></ruby>からすると<ruby>不安<rt>ふあん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>としては<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Used with an inanimate noun: ×結果から言わせれば → use から言えば/から見ると.
Confusing the nuance with から言えば: if the question calls for "criticism" → choose から言わせれば.
Omitting the agent N makes the sentence vague: state clearly who is speaking if the context does not make it clear.
1275.notes:
• Can be combined with emphatic adverbs: 正直に／率直に／あくまで個人的には + から言わせれば.
• Avoid overusing it in academic writing because of its strong subjective nuance.

examples.jp: 多かれ少なかれ、誰でも失敗はする。
examples.tr: Everyone makes mistakes to some extent.

examples.jp: 良かれ悪しかれ、その決定は会社に大きな影響を与える。
examples.tr: For better or worse, that decision will have a major impact on the company.

examples.jp: 遅かれ早かれ、真実は明らかになる。
examples.tr: Sooner or later, the truth will come out.

examples.jp: 高かれ安かれ、品質を優先したい。
examples.tr: Whether it's expensive or cheap, I want to put quality first.

examples.jp: 遠かれ近かれ、彼の責任は問われるだろう。
examples.tr: Sooner or later, he will probably be held responsible.

examples.jp: 多かれ少なかれ、皆ストレスを抱えている。
examples.tr: Everyone is under some degree of stress.

1276.explain:
Usage: Used as an adverbial expressing a condition that covers both extremes: 多かれ少なかれ、～ Expresses a general or inevitable result/judgment.Mainly used with i-adjectives; some phrases use nouns/nominalized qualities: 若かれ老いかれ .
Used as an adverbial expressing a condition that covers both extremes: 多かれ少なかれ、～
Expresses a general or inevitable result/judgment.
Mainly used with i-adjectives; some phrases use nouns/nominalized qualities: 若かれ老いかれ .
Nuance: Formal, idiomatic; often found in articles, speeches and the press.Implies "no matter where on the scale it falls, the conclusion still holds".
Formal, idiomatic; often found in articles, speeches and the press.
Implies "no matter where on the scale it falls, the conclusion still holds".
Note: Do not freely create new pairs if they are not natural in Japanese. Prefer the familiar phrases.Some words have an almost fixed order: 多かれ少なかれ , 遅かれ早かれ , 良かれ悪しかれ .
Do not freely create new pairs if they are not natural in Japanese. Prefer the familiar phrases.
Some words have an almost fixed order: 多かれ少なかれ , 遅かれ早かれ , 良かれ悪しかれ .

• Meaning 1: "Whether A or B, … / No matter whether at level A or B, …"

- Emphasizes that the conclusion does not change at either of two opposite extremes of a scale.

- The paired adjectives are usually antonyms or the two ends of a scale of degree, time or quality.

• Meaning 2: "more or less / sooner or later / near or far / expensive or cheap"

- Expresses universality or inevitability: it will happen or be true within a certain scope.

• Nuance: Somewhat formal, written language; idiomatic. Some very common phrases: 多かれ少なかれ (more or less), 遅かれ早かれ (sooner or later), 良かれ悪しかれ (for better or worse).

rows: Fixed, written; emphasizes covering both extremes
<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>かれ<ruby>少<rt>すく</rt></ruby>なかれ、<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>はある。
～にしろ～にしろ / ～にせよ～にせよ
Whether A or B (N/Adj/V all possible)
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いにしろ<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いにしろ、<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>うつもりだ。
～だろうが～だろうが / ～であろうが～であろうが
Even if it is A or B (strong, emphatic)
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だろうが<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>だろうが、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Softer than "<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>かれ<ruby>少<rt>すく</rt></ruby>なかれ"
<ruby>多少<rt>たしょう</rt></ruby>なりとも<ruby>役<rt>やく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>てば<ruby>幸<rt>さ</rt></ruby>いです。
Not a little, quite a lot
<ruby>少<rt>すく</rt></ruby>なからず<ruby>影響<rt>えいきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>けた。
Neutral, no contrast of two extremes
いずれ<ruby>真実<rt>しんじつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>明<rt>あき</rt></ruby>らかになる。

mistakes: Wrong form:
Incorrect: 良いかれ悪いかれ → Correct: 良かれ悪しかれ
Incorrect: 悪かれ in the phrase above → Correct: 悪しかれ
Making up unnatural pairs:
Incorrect: 美しかれ綺麗かれ (unnatural)
Prefer familiar phrases such as 多かれ少なかれ, 遅かれ早かれ.
Confusing it with "AかBか" (choice/question sentences):
行くか行かないか ≠ 遅かれ早かれ. The pattern "～かれ～かれ" is not a question or choice pattern but an idiom covering both extremes.
Fixed word order:
Usually: 多かれ少なかれ, 遅かれ早かれ. Reversing the order tends to sound odd in exams.
JLPT answer-choice traps:
Choosing between 多かれ少なかれ and 多少なりとも: both mean "more or less", but if a formal idiomatic nuance is required → prefer 多かれ少なかれ.
Choosing between 遅かれ早かれ and いずれ: if you need an opposing pair/emphasis on both extremes → 遅かれ早かれ.
1276.notes:
• Origin of the form: "～かれ" is a remnant of an old i-adjective form in Japanese, preserved in some idioms such as 良かれ悪しかれ, 遅かれ早かれ. Because of this history, many phrases are fixed and hard to create freely.
• "悪しかれ": This form is fixed in the phrase 良かれ悪しかれ; learners often mistake it for "悪かれ". Memorize it as the standard phrase.
• Comma: A comma usually follows the phrase when it comes at the beginning of a sentence: 多かれ少なかれ、～ to set off the adverbial.
• Pragmatics: Suited to formal written language, the press and presentations. In everyday conversation, it can be replaced with 多少, いずれ, どっちにしても depending on the context.

1277.connection: V/A plain form + (が)ゆえに / N・Na + (である)

examples.jp: 彼は若さゆえに無謀な挑戦をした。
examples.tr: Because he was young, he took on a reckless challenge.

examples.jp: 彼女は真面目であるがゆえに周囲から誤解されることがある。
examples.tr: Precisely because she is so serious, she is sometimes misunderstood by the people around her.

examples.jp: 知名度がゆえに、些細な発言も大きく取り沙汰される。
examples.tr: Because of their fame, even trivial remarks become a big topic.

examples.jp: 無知ゆえのミスは、教育で減らせる。
examples.tr: Mistakes that come from ignorance can be reduced through education.

examples.jp: 手続きを怠ったがゆえに、支給が遅れた。
examples.tr: Because the paperwork was neglected, the payment was delayed.

1277.explain:
Used when you want to state a reason formally or emphasize that something is inevitable/unavoidable.
Can imply "it can't be helped/it was unavoidable" or "precisely because of that, it is deserved".
In spoken language it is usually replaced with ～ため(に) or ～せいで depending on the nuance.

～がゆえに = "precisely because/owing to (an inherent reason)", formal nuance, sometimes with a feeling of justification or inevitability (can be positive or negative).
• Emphasizes a cause-effect relationship based on an inherent attribute/circumstance: 若さ・貧しさ・有名であること, etc.
• Often used in essays, the press, regulations and formal speeches.
• The form ～がゆえのN turns the cause into a quality that modifies a noun.

rows: Emphasizes a reason based on an attribute
Blaming, attributing fault to the cause
Expresses degree: "precisely because…, all the more…"

mistakes: Omitting である before na-adjectives/N: incorrect. Correct: 不便であるがゆえに, not 不便だがゆえに.
Confusing the nuance with ～せいで: がゆえに is not necessarily negative; it is formal/academic.
Choosing between ～ために and ～がゆえに in answer choices: when the context is formal/an inherent attribute → choose がゆえに.
1277.notes:
• Before がゆえに, na-adjectives/N require である; this is a point often tested in JLPT N1.
• ～がゆえのN is very useful for condensing a cause into a quality that modifies a noun.
• Do not overuse it in everyday conversation, as it sounds affected.

1278.connection: V/A plain form + (が)ゆえの + N / N・Na + (である)

examples.jp: 経験不足がゆえの失敗。
examples.tr: A failure due to lack of experience.

examples.jp: 若さがゆえの無謀さを責めるのは酷だ。
examples.tr: It is harsh to blame someone for the recklessness that comes with youth.

examples.jp: 彼が外国人であるがゆえの誤解が生じた。
examples.tr: A misunderstanding arose because he is a foreigner.

examples.jp: 貧しさがゆえの選択だった。
examples.tr: It was a choice born of poverty.

examples.jp: 責任者であるがゆえの重圧に耐える。
examples.tr: I endure the pressure that comes with being the person in charge.

examples.jp: 急ぐがゆえの判断ミス。
examples.tr: A misjudgment caused by haste.

1278.explain:
Formal nuance; written language, theses, the press, official speeches.
Emphasizes the "unavoidable" nature arising from essence/circumstances: "precisely because ..., ...".
Often used with general abstract nouns:過ち,誤解,苦労,重圧,決断,行動.
Position: ～がゆえの + N (directly before the noun it modifies).
With ナ形/N: であるが望ましい. Avoid "だがゆえの" in formal writing; use "である".
Not used for overly light everyday expressions; replace with ～せいでの, ～ための in casual contexts.

～がゆえの means "precisely because/owing to ..., ..." and modifies the following noun, emphasizing an inherent cause, with a formal, written nuance.
• Implies "because of that nature/circumstance, ... inevitably arises".
• Often used with words denoting attributes such as 若さ, 未熟, 無知, 立場, 事情, 責任.
• Compared with ～ための, ～がゆえの is more formal, with the nuance of "for that reason/because of that very thing".
• It has a parallel sentence form: ～がゆえに (adverbial). The form discussed here modifies a noun: ～がゆえの + N.

rows: Neutral, more colloquial; not necessarily formal
<ruby>経験<rt>けいけん</rt></ruby><ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>のための<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>
<ruby>不<rt>ふ</rt></ruby><ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>のせいでの<ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>
<ruby>病気<rt>びょうき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>理由<rt>りゆう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>欠席<rt>けっせき</rt></ruby>
Used before a clause, does not modify a noun
<ruby>若<rt>わか</rt></ruby>いがゆえに<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>もある

mistakes: Using "だがゆえの" with N/ナ形 in formal writing: use "であるがゆえの" instead.
Confusing it with ～せいでの: if you do not want a strong nuance of blame, choose ～がゆえの.
Wrong modifier position: it must be "X がゆえの N"; do not separate the "の".
JLPT: trap choices between ～ための and ～がゆえの; if the answer requires a formal nuance → choose ～がゆえの.
Confusing its function with ～がゆえに: one modifies a noun, the other is an adverbial for a clause.
1278.notes:
• "ゆえ" is the Sino-Japanese "故", meaning "cause/reason", so it has a classical, solemn nuance.
• The long form "～であるがゆえの" gives the sentence a firm rhythm and is accurate with N/ナ形.
• In media/PR, it is used to soften the nuance of blame: "誤解がゆえの発言".
• Be careful when the agent is a person: it may sound like an excuse. Weigh the context.

1279.meaning: If… is like that, then… is too

examples.jp: 親が親なら、子も子だ。
examples.tr: Like parent, like child.

examples.jp: 上司が上司なら、部下も部下だ。
examples.tr: The boss is no better than the staff, and the staff are no better than the boss.

examples.jp: 客が客なら、店も店だ。
examples.tr: The customers are bad, but the shop is just as bad.

examples.jp: 監督が監督なら、選手も選手だ。
examples.tr: The manager is hopeless, and so are the players.

examples.jp: 先生も先生なら、生徒も生徒だ。
examples.tr: The teacher is no good, and neither are the students.

examples.jp: 親が親なら、子も子だよ、まったく。
examples.tr: Like parent, like child, honestly.

1279.explain:
Often used to criticize, to be sarcastic or to express irritation; avoid using it directly toward a superior so as not to be rude.
The two nouns should be a related pair (parent–child, teacher–student, boss–staff, customer–shop...).
It does not express a real condition (if A, then B). The meaning is "given that A is the kind of A it is, B is the same kind of B".
The sentence usually ends with だ; よ/ね/な can be added to adjust the nuance in spoken language.

The pattern ～が～なら、～も～だ (as well as the variant ～も～なら、～も～だ) judges that both A and B are "just what you'd expect of A/B" and tend to be similar (usually negative). That is, if A is like that, B is no better; both match each other in how good/bad they are (mostly criticism).
• "なら" here is not a real condition but means "in terms of capacity/character".
• It combines almost only with nouns (roles, capacities, groups of people/things).
• Used as a comment/exclamation, often with a sarcastic nuance.

rows: Both A and B are "just what you'd expect of A/B", usually criticism
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>が<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>なら、<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>だ
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>も<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>なら、<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>だ
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>が<ruby>有名人<rt>ゆうめいじん</rt></ruby>だけあって、<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>有名<rt>ゆうめい</rt></ruby>だ
Going too far, there are limits
Criticizes only one side, not a "pair"
<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>にもほどがある
Each side has its own reasons/difficulties
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>は<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>で、<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>大変<rt>たいへん</rt></ruby>だ

mistakes: Using it with verbs/adjectives: this pattern goes almost only with nouns. Incorrect: 忙しいが忙しいなら… → Avoid.
Understanding "なら" as an ordinary condition; here it is an evaluation of capacity/character, not "if…, then…".
Wrong core particle: using は instead of が/も loses the formulaic nuance. Prefer "NがNなら、NもNだ／NもNなら、NもNだ".
Using it in formal situations with the people directly involved can be rude because of its critical nuance.
JLPT: choose the correct order of the related noun pair (親–子, 師–弟…), and choose the ending だ (do not change it to ～ている...).
1279.notes:
• The actual subject can be omitted; it is highly formulaic and common in the press/commentary.
• Exclamatory adverbs can be added: まったく／本当に／やれやれ, but consider politeness.
• Symmetry: keep the same kind of noun (role/capacity) in both clauses so it sounds natural.
• In spoken language, "だ" can be replaced with "だよ／だね／だな" depending on attitude. | Distinguish: ～が～なら、～も～だ (like parent, like child) vs ～も～なら、～も～だ (both sides are at fault) — two separate points; keep both

examples.jp: 愛こそ力だが、表現するのは難しい。
examples.tr: Love is the true source of strength, but it is hard to express.

examples.jp: 努力こそ成功への鍵だが、継続はさらに難しい。
examples.tr: Effort is the very key to success, but keeping it up is even harder.

examples.jp: 対話こそ解決の道だが、感情の整理には時間が要る。
examples.tr: Dialogue is the real way to a solution, but sorting out one's feelings takes time.

examples.jp: 今こそ変革だが、準備なしでは混乱を招く。
examples.tr: Now is the time for change, but without preparation it will lead to chaos.

examples.jp: 信頼こそ協力の基盤だが、一度失えば取り戻しにくい。
examples.tr: Trust is the very foundation of cooperation, but once lost, it is hard to regain.

1280.explain:
Position: こそ comes right after the noun to be emphasized; then an affirmation with Nだ, followed by the conjunction が .
Nuance: strong emphasis in the first clause; the second clause is realistic, cautious, or a warning.
Pragmatics: suitable when balancing ideals and reality, or praising with a condition attached.
Formality: usable in both spoken and written language; add です／ます for politeness.

The pattern NこそNだが、～ puts absolute focus on the first clause (affirming "it is precisely…"), then uses が to present a reality, limitation or difficulty in the second clause. Natural reading: "It is true that N is indeed N, but…".
• こそ creates a strong "spotlight", affirming the target in the first clause unmistakably.
• …だが、 signals a contrastive turn: it acknowledges the value of A but points out B as an obstacle/exception.
• Often used in commentary, speeches and argumentative slogans: emphasis → turn to reality.

rows: It is N that is N (absolute affirmation)
No contrastive clause; ends at the affirmation.
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>こそ<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>だ。 Effort is what success truly is.
Adds a second clause stating a difficulty/condition/exception.
<ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>こそ<ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>だが、<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。 Love is strength, but it is difficult.
Argumentative concession, without the spotlight emphasis of こそ.
<ruby>重要<rt>じゅうよう</rt></ruby>だとはいえ、<ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>だ。 Although it is important, cost is the problem.
Formal written language; close to が but more refined.
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だものの、<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby><ruby>不足<rt>ふそく</rt></ruby>だ。 Although it is necessary, the preparation is insufficient.

mistakes: Mistaking が for the subject particle → here が is a contrastive conjunction that comes after だ.
Putting こそ in the wrong place (after a verb/adjective) → this pattern needs a noun as the core of emphasis.
A second clause that contradicts too strongly "completely negates" the first clause → the meaning becomes unbalanced; it should be a reasonable exception/difficulty.
Dropping だ before が in standard written language → with nouns, use Nだが、 for coherence.
1280.notes:
• This pattern often appears in arguments that "praise a core value" but stress "the conditions for realizing it".
• The first clause can use abstract nouns: 愛・努力・信頼・自由・責任… to add weight.
• If the second clause only gives a mild warning, が can be replaced with けれど(も) to soften it.

examples.jp: 彼は風のごとく走り去った。
examples.tr: He dashed off like the wind.

examples.jp: 春の雪のごときはかなさ。
examples.tr: A fragility like that of spring snow.

examples.jp: まるで夢の中にいるかのごとく感じた。
examples.tr: I felt as if I were in a dream.

examples.jp: 私ごときがこの大役を務めるわけにはいきません。
examples.tr: Someone as humble as I cannot possibly take on such an important role.

examples.jp: 彼ごときにできる仕事ではない。
examples.tr: This is not a job that the likes of him can do.

examples.jp: 炎が燃え広がる（か）のごとく、噂は町中に伝わった。
examples.tr: The rumor spread throughout the town like a spreading fire.

1281.explain:
Written language, speeches, literature; in speech ～ように／～みたいに is usually used.
When modifying a noun: prefer NのごときN. With pronouns/personal references it can be used directly:私ごとき.
"Xごときが/に" can easily sound insulting when said about others; consider the context.

• Comparison/metaphor: "like/similar to/as if". Has a literary, formal nuance.
• ごとき: modifies nouns; ごとく: modifies verbs/adjectives/whole clauses as an adverbial.
• Social nuance: "Xごときが/に" can be contemptuous when said about others; "私ごとき" is humble self-reference.
• かのごとく emphasizes "just as if" (even though it is not actually so).

rows: Close in meaning to "かのごとく", more commonly used
<ruby>氷<rt>こおり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>にいるかのようだ。
Formal, with a rhetorical, contemptuous or self-deprecating nuance

mistakes: Dropping "の" carelessly: most cases need NのごときN; exceptions such as 私ごとき do not need の.
Using it about others causes offense: ×君ごときが口を出すな（strong, easily impolite).
Confusing it with spoken ように in exam questions: choose ごとく／ごとき when the context is formal/rhetorical.
1281.notes:
• "がごとく" has a classical flavor, often seen in titles/novels: ～するがごとく.
• Fixed rhetorical sequence: まるで／さながら＋V（か）のごとく.
• Function: ごとき（連体） ~ like an attributive adjective; ごとく (連用) ~ like an adverb.

examples.jp: 多くを語らずとも、彼の覚悟は伝わってくる。
examples.tr: Even without saying much, his resolve comes across.

examples.jp: 説明せずとも分かるように、図を大きくした。
examples.tr: I enlarged the diagram so that it can be understood without explanation.

examples.jp: 実物を見ずとも、品質の良さは想像できる。
examples.tr: Even without seeing the actual item, you can imagine how good the quality is.

examples.jp: 努力せずとも成功できるほど甘くない。
examples.tr: Life is not so easy that you can succeed without making an effort.

examples.jp: 会わずとも、メールで十分だ。
examples.tr: There's no need to meet; email is enough.

1283.explain:
Often used to emphasize that something is obvious/sufficient, or to negate the expectation that one "must V".
More formal than ～なくても; suited to written language, headlines and declarations.
Can be combined with emphatic adverbs: わざわざ・いちいち + V-ずとも.

• "Even without V-ing / Even if you don't need to V, ... still ..."; emphasizes that condition A is not needed for B to happen.
• Used in arguments, written language and slogans; has a stiff, formal or rhetorical nuance.
• Often used with verbs of perception/ability: 分かる・伝わる・見える・言える・足りる.

rows: <ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>でなくてはならないわけではずともよい
Does not mean "even without V-ing, still ..."
<ruby>昼食<rt>ちゅうしょく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べずに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた

mistakes: Confusing it with ～ずに: ～ずに describes a sequence of actions and does not mean "even without ..., still ...".
Forgetting to change する → せずとも; writing "しずとも" is incorrect.
Using it in casual conversation can sound affected; the JLPT often tests its formal nuance compared with ～なくても.
1283.notes:
• ～とも here has the concessive meaning "even if ..., ...". Combined with "ず" (written negative), it gives a formal feel.
• Common in newspaper headlines/advertising: "登録せずとも使える".
• With verbs of perception, the subject is usually omitted: "言わずとも伝わる".

examples.jp: 教えるそばから、生徒が忘れてしまう。
examples.tr: No sooner do I teach something than the students forget it.

examples.jp: 片付けるそばから、子どもが部屋を散らかす。
examples.tr: No sooner do I tidy up than the kids mess up the room again.

examples.jp: メールを消すそばから、新しい通知が来る。
examples.tr: As soon as I delete an email, a new notification comes in.

examples.jp: 読むそばから、内容を忘れる自分が情けない。
examples.tr: I feel pathetic forgetting the content as soon as I read it.

examples.jp: 給料をもらったそばから、出費で消えていく。
examples.tr: As soon as I get my paycheck, it disappears into expenses.

1284.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize an annoying repetition, not simply "right after."
The second clause is usually something undesirable/negative; the speaker is in a complaining mood.
Not used for natural changes that happen once, such as:春になると桜が咲く（does not fit ～そばから）.

• "No sooner has … been done than … (again)", and this happens over and over.
• Emphasizes a feeling of helplessness/frustration because the action in the first clause is immediately "undone" by the second clause.
• Not used for one-time, ordinary natural events (non-repeating); it is usually a situation that keeps repeating.

rows: As soon as you do it, … (again); repeated
Emphasizes recurrence, a nuance of dissatisfaction
<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うそばから<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れる。
Emphasizes immediacy, once; no repetition required
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたん、めまいがした。
Overlapping moments; repeated or not, either is fine
<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くか<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>かないかのうちに<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>した。
Formal, immediate; no implication of repetition
ベルが<ruby>鳴<rt>な</rt></ruby>るや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や、<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>した。

mistakes: Using it for a one-off event → incorrect; the JLPT often sets traps with non-repeating situations.
Choosing the wrong tense: many materials prefer V-るそばから; V-た also exists but is less "textbook."
If the second clause does not have the sense of "happening again right away" → it does not fit; you need the feeling of being immediately "overridden."
1284.notes:
• In everyday expression, ～たそばから appears quite often (給料をもらったそばから). However, V-るそばから is the standard form.
• Fits pairs of verbs of "getting something done" vs "having it undone again": 片付ける⇔散らかす, 入力する⇔エラーが出る, 修理する⇔壊れる.
• The emphasis is stronger when combined with adverbs: 次から次へと／どんどん／また.

examples.jp: 彼にお金を貸したが最後、二度と戻ってこない。
examples.tr: Once you lend him money, it will never come back.

examples.jp: ギャンブルに手を出したが最後、人生が転落してしまう人もいる。
examples.tr: Some people, once they get involved in gambling, see their lives go downhill.

examples.jp: その噂を信じたが最後、彼を正しく評価できなくなる。
examples.tr: Once you believe that rumor, you can no longer judge him fairly.

examples.jp: 甘えを許したが最後、子どもは際限なくわがままになる。
examples.tr: Once you allow them to be spoiled, children become endlessly selfish.

examples.jp: 一口飲み始めたが最後、止まらなくなる。
examples.tr: Once I start drinking, even a sip, I can't stop.

examples.jp: この業界に足を踏み入れたが最後、簡単には抜け出せない。
examples.tr: Once you set foot in this industry, you can't easily get out.

1285.explain:
Strong, formal nuance; used for warnings/serious consequences.
The second clause is usually an inevitable reality beyond one's control; avoid using it with volition/direct commands.
Often accompanied by emphatic adverbs: いったん,一度, ひとたび.
Rarely used in casual everyday conversation; replaced by ～たら最後in spoken language.
Does not combine well with clearly positive content (sounds forced).

The pattern ～たが最後 expresses: "Once you have done V, the (consequence) is an unavoidable/irreversible outcome that drags on." Strong nuance, written language/speeches, often used to warn or to emphasize irreversibility.
• Meaning frame: trigger point -> one-way road -> fixed consequence (usually bad).
• The second clause often goes with expressions that close off the possibility of reversal: 二度と～ない, ～っぱなし, ～きり, もはや～ない.
• Often used with addictive/risky behavior: 手を出す, 足を踏み入れる, 口を出す, 付き合う, 借りる.
• Compared with ～たら最後: ～たが最後 is more formal and literary; the emphasis is usually stronger.

rows: Once you have…, there is no way back
More colloquial than ～たが<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>; the emphasis may be lighter
<ruby>借<rt>か</rt></ruby>りたら<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>、<ruby>返<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ってこない。
Meaning of obligation/rule; not an inevitable outcome
<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>き<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>けた<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>までやる。
やるからには<ruby>全力<rt>ぜんりょく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>尽<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くす。
Closeness in time; no sense of "no going back"
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたん、めまいがした。
Succession in time, not a fixed outcome
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと、やんだ。

mistakes: Using it for a clearly positive result → unnatural. Use it with negative/hard-to-reverse consequences.
Using volition/a direct command in the second clause (～なさい/～してください) → wrong nuance.
Mistaking the time label for ～たとたん: ～たが最後 does not mean "right after" but "there is no going back."
Confusing it with ～以上(は)/～からには: those two patterns express obligation/a rule and do not imply "a point of no return."
JLPT trap: an answer choice with keywords like 二度と/～っぱなし/～きり alongside ～たが最後 is a sign it is correct.
1285.notes:
• Often used in argumentative writing, news, and descriptions of risk: 依存・中毒・借金・噂・暴力など.
• Verb choices suggest "slipping into" something: 足を踏み入れる, 手を出す, 首を突っ込む, 甘える.
• The second clause often takes a lasting-state form: ～続ける, ～っぱなし, ～きり, ～まま.
• In journalism/headlines, the subject can be omitted to make it more general.

examples.jp: 先ほどの失言は聞かなかったことにしてください。
examples.tr: Please pretend you didn't hear my slip of the tongue a moment ago.

examples.jp: 本日の出席はあったことにしてください。後で欠席理由を説明します。
examples.tr: Please count me as present today. I'll explain the reason for my absence later.

examples.jp: このメールは届かなかったことにしてください。誤送信でした。
examples.tr: Please treat this email as if it never arrived. It was sent by mistake.

examples.jp: 詳細は非公開ということにしてください。
examples.tr: Please treat the details as undisclosed.

examples.jp: 今日は会議がなかったことにしてください。資料が間に合いません。
examples.tr: Please consider today's meeting as not having happened. The materials won't be ready in time.

examples.jp: この件、私が言ったことにしてください。責任は私が取ります。
examples.tr: Please make it so that I was the one who said this. I'll take responsibility.

1286.explain:
Polite, softens a request; implies hoping the listener will be understanding/cover for you.
Often used with verbs of perception:聞く,見る,受け取る,連絡する,報告する.
In official documents, it can be replaced with ～ということにお願いいたします (keigo).
Avoid overusing it in situations that call for transparency; it can give the impression of "covering something up."

The pattern ～たことにしてください expresses a polite request/suggestion: "Please treat (X) as having happened/not having happened." It is the polite imperative variant of ～たことにする (deciding for oneself to treat something as…), used to ask the listener to join in a "hypothetical agreement."
• Social function: soothing, avoiding conflict, saving face.
• Used a lot in the workplace, polite emails, and internal notices.
• Two main directions: overlooking a mistake (～なかったことにしてください) and provisional acknowledgment (～たことにしてください).
• Different from "～てください": it does not request an actual action, but a way of "viewing/recording" something.

rows: Deciding for yourself to treat it as having…
The agent is the speaker; not a request to someone else
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>んだことにする。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>とは<ruby>他人<rt>たにん</rt></ruby>ということにしている。
<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休業<rt>きゅうぎょう</rt></ruby>とする。
Acting as if you had… (in order to do something)
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったつもりで<ruby>貯金<rt>ちょきん</rt></ruby>する。
～ということにしてください
Form that assigns a nominalized clause
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>ということにしてください。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～てください: that one requests an "action," while ～たことにしてください requests a "way of viewing/recording."
Using it for things that cannot be supposed (legal facts, mandatory figures) → pragmatically incorrect.
Missing agent/target: the context must make clear who is doing the "treating as."
JLPT trap: the correct answer often goes with 聞く/見る/連絡する/報告する and the negative なかったことにしてください.
1286.notes:
• In business emails: 〜いただけますと幸いです/〜お願いできますでしょうか to increase politeness.
• With sensitive content (コンプラ), avoid revealing an intent to "conceal"; use procedural wording instead.
• Pragmatics: reflects the "negative politeness" strategy (reducing pressure on the other party).
• To emphasize that "there is agreement," add: ご承知おきください/ご了承のほど.

1287.meaning: There would be no end to it

examples.jp: 欠点を挙げたらきりがないから、このくらいでやめよう。
examples.tr: There'd be no end to it if I listed all the flaws, so let's stop here.

examples.jp: 心配し始めたらきりがないよ。まずやってみよう。
examples.tr: Once you start worrying, there's no end to it. Let's just try it first.

examples.jp: 欲を言い出したらきりがない。
examples.tr: If you start wanting more, there's no end to it.

examples.jp: 例を挙げたらきりがないほど、同じ失敗が起きている。
examples.tr: The same mistakes keep happening, so many that there'd be no end to listing examples.

examples.jp: 細かいことにこだわりだしたらきりがない。
examples.tr: If you start fussing over small details, there's no end to it.

examples.jp: 不満を数え上げたらきりがないが、感謝すべき点も多い。
examples.tr: There'd be no end to it if I counted up my complaints, but there is also a lot to be grateful for.

1287.explain:
Used to "wrap up" a topic and avoid going on too long: ～から、このへんで/やめよう/切り上げよう.
The tone is usually casual to neutral; suitable for conversation and commentary.
The first clause often uses Vます語幹 + 出す/始める to suggest a beginning:言い 出す ,数え 上げる .
Combines well with degree complements: ～ほど/～くらい.

The pattern ～たらきりがない expresses: "If you (say/list/worry/demand…), it will be endless, with no end in sight." Often used to close a topic, stop getting carried away, or emphasize how endless a problem is.
• "きりがない" = "there is no boundary/stopping point."
• Emphasizes endlessness in listing, worrying, or wanting.
• Often appears after verbs that open up a series: 言い出す, 挙げる, 数え上げる, こだわる, 心配する.

rows: If you do it, there is no stopping point
Has a nuance of concluding/wrapping up
<ruby>言<rt>いいだし</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt></rt></ruby>したらきりがない。
If you do it, it is limitless
<ruby>要求<rt>ようきゅう</rt></ruby>しだしたら<ruby>際限<rt>さいげん</rt></ruby>がない。
いくら～てもきりがない
No matter how much, it is never enough
いくら<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>してもきりがない。
<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>には<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りがある。

mistakes: Using it with verbs that do not suggest an "endless series" (such as 着く, 終える) → sounds forced.
Confusing "きり" with "切り" meaning "ending" → here it means "限り/boundary."
Dropping "たら" to make "たらない" → wrong meaning. It must be "Vたら + きりがない."
JLPT trap: set phrases like 挙げたら/言い出したら/数え上げたら with きりがない are a strong hint.
1287.notes:
• In presentations, used as a time-management strategy: 例を挙げたらきりがないので要点だけにします。
• In counseling/psychology, effective for stopping an endless cycle of anxiety: 心配し始めたらきりがないから、今できることに集中しよう。
• For it to sound natural, the verb before たら should be an action that "opens a list/process."

examples.jp: スマホゲームを始めたら最後、課金が止まらなくなるよ。
examples.tr: Once you start playing smartphone games, you won't be able to stop spending money on them.

examples.jp: 彼に秘密を話したら最後、すぐ広まってしまう。
examples.tr: If you tell him a secret, it'll spread right away.

examples.jp: 一度サボり始めたら最後、癖になる。
examples.tr: Once you start slacking off, it becomes a habit.

examples.jp: あの店でツケにしたら最後、二度と返済できないぞ。
examples.tr: Once you run a tab at that place, you'll never be able to pay it back.

examples.jp: 甘いものを食べだしたら最後、止まらない。
examples.tr: Once I start eating sweets, I can't stop.

examples.jp: 安易な噂に乗っかったら最後、信用を失う。
examples.tr: Once you jump on a careless rumor, you lose people's trust.

1288.explain:
Colloquial, natural in conversation; the emphasis is still strong.
The second clause should be a negative, lasting, hard-to-fix consequence.
Combines well with emphatic complements: いったん/一度/ひとたび.
Avoid using it with clearly positive content (sounds contradictory).

～たら最後 expresses "once you have done…, it's all over; a bad consequence is inevitable and hard to reverse." It is the colloquial variant of ～たが最後. Used a lot in conversation to warn or to complain.
• Emphasizes the "point of no return."
• Often used with bad habits/addiction/danger: 飲みだす, 手を出す, さぼる, 嘘をつく.
• The second clause carries a nuance of helplessness/fate: もう～ない, もはや～ない, ずっと～まま.

rows: Once you have…, there is no way back
Colloquial; equivalent to ~たが<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>
<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みだしたら<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>、<ruby>止<rt>と</rt></ruby>まらない。
Once you have…, the outcome is inevitable
<ruby>手<rt>て</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>したが<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>、<ruby>破滅<rt>はめつ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>き<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>けた<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>、やり<ruby>遂<rt>と</rt></ruby>げる。

mistakes: Using it with a positive result → unnatural. Tie it to a bad/hard-to-reverse outcome.
A command/direct volition in the second clause → wrong nuance (it should describe an inevitable reality).
Confusing it with ～たとたん (only immediacy, without the meaning of a "point of no return").
JLPT trap: look for signs like 二度と/もう～ない/～っぱなし/～きり together with ～たら最後.
1288.notes:
• Effective in admonishing advice: ～したら最後だよ (a casual warning).
• In health/education campaigns: 依存の怖さを強調するフレーズとして有効.
• Co-occurs with もう/二度と/もはや/ずっと to reinforce "no going back."

1289.explain:
Creates a rhythm by repeating the word, expressing a "deal with it as it comes" attitude or that "either way has its difficulties."
Often used in contrasting pairs:行ったら…行かなかったら…, あるならあるで…ないならないで…
Does not emphasize a condition leading to a necessity; it is everyday commentary/remarks.
Casual to neutral; can be used in spoken language and light written language.

The pattern ～たら～たで states that even if A happens, "in situation A" there are also its own ways of dealing with it/difficulties. Used to express an attitude: not worrying too much, or that each option has its corresponding problems.
• Two common nuances:

Neutral/accepting: "it's fine either way; it will be handled in its own way."
Pointing out that both sides have drawbacks: "either way has its own hardship."

• Neutral/accepting: "it's fine either way; it will be handled in its own way."
• Pointing out that both sides have drawbacks: "either way has its own hardship."
• The second clause often contains a description of a specific consequence: "～なりの問題/メリット・デメリット".
• With Na/N, use なら～で; do not use だったら～だったで in standard written language.

rows: X たら X たで
Situation X also has its own ways/problems
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>かったら<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>かったで<ruby>安心<rt>あんしん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>楽<rt>たの</rt></ruby>しむ。
General concessive condition, no repetitive rhythm
No matter how much you…, still…
Emphasizes repeating an action; different purpose
<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>つからない。
<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいわ<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいで<ruby>大変<rt>たいへん</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Using だったら～だったで with Na/N in standard written language → use なら～で instead.
Mistaking it for a necessary condition like ～ならば → wrong nuance; this is a comment on "in that situation."
Dropping the repeated stem in the second part → incorrect pattern. Keep the same word: 高かったら高かったで.
JLPT trap: the correct answer often has the matching pair "あるならあるで／ないならないで".
1289.notes:
• A rhythmic pattern that is easy to use in advertising/sales: 高かったら高かったで価値がある.
• Can be chained to emphasize that "either way is hard": ～したらしたで…, しなかったらしなかったで…
• For the negative, ないならないで/なかったらなかったで is more natural than じゃないならじゃないで.

1290.explain:
Placed after the smallest quantity (一 + counter, e.g. 一秒たりとも) to emphasize "absolutely not."
Combines naturally with:一秒・一分・一瞬・一滴・一円・一人・一言・一日…
Often used with a prohibition clause (～てはならない／いけない) or a negative of ability (～できない／ない).

• Emphasizes an absolute degree: "not even a single … / must not even one …."
• Usually combined with the smallest number, expressing strictness, discipline, vigilance.
• Stiff, formal style; often used in regulations and official speeches.

rows: Strong, formal, tied to a minimal unit
<ruby>一<rt>いち</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>たりとも<ruby>無駄<rt>むだ</rt></ruby>にしない
Lower degree of emphasis; no minimal unit required
General negation, no reference unit stated
まったく<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えていない

mistakes: Forgetting the negative at the end of the sentence: × 一円たりとも無駄に → it must have 無駄にしない.
Using it with an abstract noun that is not a minimal unit: × 勇気たりともない (unnatural).
Wrong word order: × たりとも一秒 → it must be 一秒たりとも.
1290.notes:
• After たりとも comes the scope being negated; a negative form is needed at the end of the sentence.
• Not used with large or indefinite quantities (× 何人たりとも in the sense of "anyone" is incorrect in this pattern).
• In everyday spoken language, it can be replaced with "一秒も/一円も～ない".

1291.explain:
Used to emphasize standards of conduct appropriate to one's role/position.
Formal style: speeches, rules, writing on professional ethics.
Rarely used with ordinary/overly specific roles; avoid in casual conversation.

• States a role/position and the corresponding requirements, qualities, and responsibilities: "if you are …, then …."
• Formal, didactic nuance; often used with roles that carry status/moral weight (指導者・医師・社会人・親・教師…).
• Close in meaning to "としての/にふさわしい" but more archaic and stronger.

rows: <ruby>医師<rt>いし</rt></ruby>としての<ruby>責任<rt>せきにん</rt></ruby>
An evaluation of suitability, not admonishing
<ruby>指導<rt>しどう</rt></ruby><ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby>にふさわしい<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>らしい<ruby>行動<rt>こうどう</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using it for inanimate objects/things: × 高級車たるエンジン (unnatural).
Using it in casual conversation makes the sentence sound pompous and overly archaic.
Wrong order: × たる指導者者 → it must be 指導者たる者.
1291.notes:
• "者/もの/身/責任/使命/役割" are nouns that often go with "たる".
• "社会人たるもの" is a very common set phrase in company instructions.
• "たる" is not used before verbs; it attaches to a noun to form a noun phrase.
Do not merge with ～足る～ (): a different point (N+たる+N "as a" vs Vる+に足る "worthy of") — homophones once written in kana.

1292.explain:
Used when judging that the consequences/measures required must go beyond the level of "just …".
Often seen in legal, administrative, business and news contexts; serious nuance.
The one making the judgment can be the speaker or society/general norms.
Used with nouns for actions/measures:謝罪・注意・反省・説明・弁償・処分…

• Doing just … won't settle it; the problem cannot be overlooked or solved only by …; stricter measures/sanctions are needed.
• Implies seriousness, legal/social/moral responsibility; often used with "謝る・注意・弁償・説明" etc.
• Strong, normative judgment: "that is not enough/not acceptable".
• "～だけでは済まされない" is formal and objective; "～だけではすまない" is more neutral.

rows: Just … is not enough/won't settle it
<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>るだけではすまない
Additional listing; no implication of punishment
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>だけではない、<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>もできる
Implies "society/the law will not let it pass"
<ruby>処分<rt>しょぶん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>だけでは<ruby>済<rt>す</rt></ruby>まされない
Does not stop at the scope of …
Focuses on expanding the scope; not necessarily a sanction
<ruby>影響<rt>えいきょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>国内<rt>こくない</rt></ruby>にとどまらない

mistakes: Confusing it with "～だけではない" (completely different meaning: listing, no judgment).
Using it with light, everyday content makes the sentence sound too heavy: × 宿題を忘れて、謝るだけではすまない (may be excessive in an ordinary student situation).
Dropping "だけ": × 謝るではすまない → it must be 謝るだけではすまない.
1292.notes:
• In kanji it is usually written 済む→済まない; both すまない／済まない are used.
• The implied subject is social norms: "by common sense/by the rules, it cannot be just…".
• In formal texts and the news, the passive variant "～済まされない" appears often.

examples.jp: 彼は給料が安いだの、上司が厳しいだのと、いつも文句ばかり言っている。
examples.tr: He's always complaining, saying his pay is low, his boss is strict, and so on.

1293.explain:
Usually used when the speaker wants to show annoyance, criticism or weariness; it can also be fairly neutral, but a mild negative nuance is common.
The listed phrase is often followed by と言う／と騒ぐ／として…／で…／して… to state the next action/evaluation.
It does not list everything; it gives only a few typical examples, implying "there are many more".
Do not use です/ます directly before だの. Use the plain form: N/na-adjective + だ; i-adjectives/verbs stay as they are.
Can be used with the past tense/aspect:行った だの 買った だの と言う（went, bought…）.
Formality: natural spoken language, suited to conversation, diaries and social media; be careful in formal documents.

• Meaning: Lists a few typical examples, "… and …, and so on", often with a nuance of annoyance, criticism, complaint, or a negative/bothersome evaluation. Non-exhaustive: these are only examples, not a complete list.
• Speaker's attitude: Usually shows mild to moderate negative emotion (annoyed, fed up, tired), or judges something as messy and confusing.
• Grammar: Attaches to the plain form. Nouns/na-adjectives need "だ". I-adjectives/verbs keep their plain form, then add "だの".
• Position: The phrase "AだのBだの" can come before the particle と to link to 言う/騒ぐ…, or before で/して to state a cause/manner.
• Formality: Leans toward spoken language; rarely used in formal written language, or requires care with style.
• Number: Usually 2 items; 3 or more are possible; the last item usually also takes "だの".
mistakes: Wrong style: Using ～です／～ます before だの. Incorrect: 高いですだの安いですだの. Correct: 高いだの安いだの.
Giving only 1 item. Incorrect: 物価が高いだの. Correct: 物価が高いだの税金が上がるだの.
Using it in neutral formal documents. If you don't want a complaining nuance, switch to ～や～など or ～とか.
Misunderstanding it as a complete list like "and". In fact it means "for example…", with many other items implied.
Wrong word type: Forgetting "だ" with nouns/na-adjectives. Incorrect: 不便だの危険だの（ok because it is already na-adjective + だ? Note that だ is required）; with na-adjectives it must be 不便だだの危険だだの.
JLPT nuance trap: Sentences with ～だの are usually followed by verbs such as 言う／騒ぐ／して…, and the whole sentence has a complaining nuance. Choosing a neutral answer is wrong.
Logical order: The items should belong to the same category. Avoid combining items that are too far apart unless you intend to emphasize the messiness.
Punctuation: Separate long items with commas for readability: Aだの、Bだのと…
1293.notes:
• Grammatically, だの is a listing particle that follows the "plain form"; with N/na-adjectives, "だ" is part of the plain form, so it appears before "の".
• Style-switching tip: AだのBだの → AやBなど (reduces the critical nuance); or AとかBとか (neutral spoken language).
• "Aだの何だの" means "A and all sorts of other stuff", emphasizing "there are many other things not worth listing".
• In quoted speech you may see: 「…」だの「…」だのと言う（quoting word for word to emphasize that the person complains about all sorts of things）.
• Intonation: When read aloud, there is usually a slight pause before/after each item, creating a rapid-fire listing feel that strengthens the complaining nuance.
meaning_vi: ～や・・・など、～とか・・・とか
Equivalent to the expression toka... toka
examples: 1. 私の部屋には漫画だの服だのが散らかっていて、寝る場所さえないほどだ。
My room is so cluttered with manga, clothes and so on that there isn't even room to sleep.

He's always talking about dreamy things like becoming a star or making movies.

1294.explain:
The second clause expresses an unchanging position/condition:関係ない,影響されない,変わらない.
Firm, formal style; in spoken language it is often replaced by ～かどうかに関わらず or ～ても～なくても.
With N/ナ: であろうとなかろうと is preferred in argumentative writing.
Do not repeat the same phrase twice; state it once in the first clause, then give the conclusion.

～だろうとなかろうと expresses "whether or not it is/is said to be …", "regardless of whether … or not". It emphasizes that the decision/view in the second clause does not change, whatever the situation in the first clause.
• Stiff, rhetorical nuance; used to assert a position.
• "なかろう" is the archaic negative form of "ない" with the copula だ/である.
• Often used with contrasting pairs: 必要だろうとなかろうと, 重要だろうとなかろうと, 本物だろうとなかろうと.
• With i-adjectives: the "かろうとなかろうと" form is very written; in spoken language you can use "～くても～なくても".

rows: <ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>であろうとなかろうと
Whether one does it or not
<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>するかどうかに<ruby>関<rt>かか</rt></ruby>わらず
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>なくても

mistakes: Applying it directly to verbs: "行くだろうとなかろうと" is unnatural; use "行こうが行くまいが/行くかどうかに関わらず".
Wrong i-adjective form: you must use "高かろうとなかろうと", not "高いだろうとなかろうと".
Mistaking だろう for conjecture: in this pattern it is a formal counterpart, not "probably".
JLPT: a trap is choosing ～ても～なくても; if the style is stiff and argumentative → choose ～であろうとなかろうと／～だろうとなかろうと.
1294.notes:
• With i-adjectives, "高かろうとなかろうと/多かろうとなかろうと/難しかろうとなかろうと" are patterns with a pleasing rhythm.
• "だろう" here is not real conjecture; it is a formal counterpart to "なかろう".
• In forceful statements, the structure can be repeated in parallel: Aだろうとなかろうと、Bであろうとなかろうと、結論…

1295.explain:
Formal, written language; rare in everyday conversation except in fixed phrases.
Emphasizes balanced, prolonged repetition.
Usually comes before する or modifies a noun (～のN).
If you create your own verb pair, choose verbs with opposite meanings or two sides of the same activity.

The pattern ～つ～つ expresses two actions/states that alternate back and forth many times, creating a rhythmic, wave-like feel. Usually used in written language, with a literary/classical flavor.
• Focuses on the balanced alternation between the two parts (push-pull, go-return, float-sink...).
• Usually used with pairs of opposite or naturally corresponding verbs.
• Can describe both intentional actions and natural phenomena.
• Many cases are fixed phrases; the verbs cannot be swapped freely.

rows: Repeating over and over (doing, then doing again...)
More colloquial; no classical, rhythmic nuance
Lists two opposite actions that happen sometimes... sometimes...
Does not emphasize balanced alternation; neutral
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったり<ruby>戻<rt>もど</rt></ruby>ったりする
Uses the continuative form; usually a fixed phrase

mistakes: Using the dictionary form instead of the continuative form (incorrect: 行くつ戻るつ → correct: 行きつ戻りつ).
Arbitrarily combining verbs that do not form a natural pair → sounds forced.
Using it in casual spoken language → unnatural (except in fixed phrases).
Confusing it with VてはV: both express repetition, but the nuance and form are different.
1295.notes:
• Phrases such as 持ちつ持たれつ and 抜きつ抜かれつ are very common in the press/sports.
• It can be followed by している／していた to indicate a continuing situation.
• Avoid attaching it to adjectives; this pattern is for verbs.
• Stylistic effect: creates rhythm and is rich in imagery. Suits explanatory and descriptive writing.

examples.tr: The construction work next door is unbearably noisy.

1296.explain:
A strong spoken complaint; avoid it in polite speech toward superiors unless adjusted: ～てかないません（rare, archaic). In practice かなわない is used.
The subject is the speaker or someone close whose feelings can be inferred; do not attribute it to others without signs of their feelings.
It is often accompanied by a clear cause, which makes the sentence more natural:風が強くてかなわない／匂いがきつくてかなわない.

• Expresses the speaker's feeling of "can't stand it/extremely unpleasant/bothersome" in response to some cause.
• Used only with a negative/complaining meaning. Stronger than ～てしょうがない/～てたまらない when complaining.
• Often used with adjectives such as うるさい／暑い／迷惑だ／不便だ／くさい…, or a specific cause: 人が多くてかなわない.

rows: Used with both positive and negative
～てしょうがない／～て<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない
More formal: しょうがない = <ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない; a milder complaint than かなわない
Different meaning group; not a complaint
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>むわけにはいかない

mistakes: Using it with positive adjectives: ×楽しくてかなわない → wrong nuance.
Not stating a clear cause makes the sentence vague: add the agent/situation, e.g. "隣の犬が…"
Directly attributing someone else's feelings: ×彼は暑くてかなわないと思う → if guessing, add ようだ／らしい.
1296.notes:
• "かなわない" originally means "cannot match/cannot bear", and is usually written in kana.
• The form "～てはかなわない" is also found in written language: そんなことをされてはかなわない（it would be unbearable if that were done to me).
• Avoid using it with a positive sense: ×嬉しくてかなわない（use たまらない/しょうがない instead). meaning_vi: Cannot stand~ ⏐ explain: Limited to words that express emotions, sensations and desires.
Expresses the meaning of being unable to bear something, ~ very much. And it is often used for a bad impression. Adding は makes the sentence express a stronger degree of being unbearable. ⏐ examples: 1. 隣の工事がうるさくてかなわない。
The construction next door is so noisy that I can't stand it.
2. 私の家は、駅から遠くて不便でかなわない。
My house is far from the station, and it's terribly inconvenient.

examples.jp: 勉強しては寝て、寝ては勉強する日々です。
examples.tr: My days are spent studying and then sleeping, sleeping and then studying.

examples.jp: 運動しては食べ、食べては運動する生活が続いている。
examples.tr: My life goes on like this: exercising and then eating, eating and then exercising.

examples.jp: この部屋は掃除しては乱雑になり、片づけては散らかる。
examples.tr: This room gets messy as soon as I clean it, and cluttered again as soon as I tidy it.

examples.jp: 雨が降っては止み、降っては止む天気が一週間も続いた。
examples.tr: The weather kept raining and stopping, raining and stopping, for a whole week.

examples.jp: 書いては消し、消しては書くうちに、もう夜になった。
examples.tr: While I kept writing and erasing, erasing and writing, it had already become night.

examples.jp: 彼女に会っては、いつも緊張してしまいます。
examples.tr: Whenever I meet her, I always get nervous.

1297.explain:
Form: Verb in the te-form + は. Often preceded by a phrase marking the target/trigger with N＋に (彼女に会っては…).
Characteristics of the second clause: B is usually a psychological/emotional/reflexive response (緊張する・懐かしくなる・考え込む…). Avoid using B for a strongly intentional action.
Style: Natural in both spoken and written language when describing a habit; polite/gentle.
Timing: Often used when there are multiple observations in the past/present; not suited to a single event.

Meaning: Expresses the situation "whenever/every time A happens, B", where A is the trigger and B is a repeated reaction/result, usually an emotion or a natural state beyond one's control.

•
Repetition: Action/situation A repeats many times in reality; each repetition brings reaction B.

•
Nuance: Natural, habitual; often used for psychological states ("get nervous every time I meet", "get homesick every time I hear"). Different from the "alternating A then B" type, which is a symmetrical cycle.

•
Pragmatics: Used when the speaker wants to emphasize that the reaction certainly occurs every time there is a trigger.

rows: Emphasizes trigger → repeated reaction. B is usually an emotion/natural state.
Every time A, B (neutral, broad meaning). Does not strongly suggest the psychological nuance of "being drawn into it" like ては.
Whenever A (an obvious condition), B (an inevitable result). Stronger sense of objective rule/cause and effect than ては.
たびに is purely "every time" and widely used; ては leans toward "every time… again" (a familiar emotion/response).
Different meaning: "A then B again, B then A again" (symmetrical/cyclical). Not trigger → reaction.

mistakes: Confusing it with "Vては〜V（alternation）": That pattern describes a symmetrical cycle (A then B, B then A). The present one is "every time A, B" and does not need a symmetrical part.
Choosing an unnatural second clause B: B should be a reaction/emotion or a result that follows; avoid strong commands/prohibitions.
Overusing it for a single event: ては implies repetition many times; using it for a single occurrence does not make sense.
Confusing it with "Vると": Vると emphasizes an inevitable rule, while ては leans toward a psychological habit each time a trigger occurs.
1297.notes:
•
Scope of the subject: Usually the speaker/a person mentioned who has emotions; if the subject is a thing/nature, B should be a natural state (落ち着く・懐かしくなる… are also fine if the implied subject is a person).
•
Word combinations: Often used with verbs of perception/emotion: 見る・聞く・読む・会う・思い出す・緊張する・安心する・考え込む…
•
Emphatic nuance: 副詞 such as つい・いつも・決まって can be added to emphasize the regular repetition.
•
Turning it into a noun phrase: Use ～ては…ことがある/ことが多い to generalize a habit.

examples.jp: 彼は借金してまでも店を続けた。
examples.tr: He kept the shop going, even going into debt to do so.

examples.jp: 親に嘘をついてまでも彼女に会いに行った。
examples.tr: He went to see her, even lying to his parents to do it.

examples.jp: 徹夜してまでもこのプロジェクトを終わらせる。
examples.tr: I'll finish this project even if it means staying up all night.

examples.jp: 命を危険にさらしてまでも人を助ける彼の姿に感動した。
examples.tr: I was moved by the sight of him saving people even at the risk of his own life.

examples.jp: そんなことをしてまで成功したくはない。
examples.tr: I don't want to succeed if it means doing something like that.

1298.explain:
Usually used when stating a strong goal or criticizing excessive actions.
The preceding V is an "extreme" action (burdensome, sacrificial, unethical):嘘をつく,徹夜する,借金する,犯罪に手を染める…
The following part expresses a result/volition/evaluation: ～やる/～続ける/～行く/～価値はない.
Rarely used with trivial, ordinary actions; avoid using it with adjectives.
In rhetorical questions: そこまでする てまで ？ means "to that extent?".

• Expresses determination: "even if it means doing V (usually something excessive, undesirable or unreasonable), still …", "even going as far as V, …".
• Evaluative nuance: usually implies the judgment that this is an extreme, abnormal measure; it can be criticism (negative) or praise of determination (positive) depending on the context.
• The focus is the "limit point" まで: the speaker sets V as the maximum boundary that one still accepts crossing to reach the goal.
• ～てまでも emphasizes "even … ", and is more written than ～てまで. In spoken language, ～てまで is more common.

rows: Even if it means doing V (extreme), still …
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をついてまでも<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>する。
Going as far as doing V, …
Spoken, more neutral; often used in critical sentences too.
<ruby>借金<rt>しゃっきん</rt></ruby>してまで<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>うなんて。
Uses a noun as the extreme measure.
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>のコネまでして<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>る。
Does not imply "crossing a moral limit/difficulty".
Emphasizes determination; does not name a specific extreme action.
<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>が<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Using it with adjectives: incorrect. It must be a verb in the te-form.
Using it for small everyday things: unnatural. Reserve it for situations that "cross a limit".
Confusing it with ～ても: ～てまでも implies an extreme nuance and an evaluation; ～ても does not.
Getting the direction of meaning wrong: Vてまでも means "accepting doing V in order to …", not "because one did V, …".
In JLPT questions, the correct answer usually goes with verbs with a heavy nuance such as 嘘をつく, 犯罪に手を染める, 無理をする.
1298.notes:
• The pattern often appears in argumentative writing to criticize excessive trade-offs: 名誉を汚してまで…
• To praise a positive spirit of sacrifice, choose a verb with high value: 命をかけてまでも守る.
• Negative orientation: ～してまで…する価値はない states the view "it is not worth it".

examples.jp: 学歴が高いであれ低いであれ、努力は欠かせない。
examples.tr: Whether your education is high or low, effort is indispensable.

examples.jp: 雨であれ雪であれ、大会は予定どおり開催する。
examples.tr: Rain or snow, the tournament will be held as scheduled.

examples.jp: 金持ちであれ貧乏であれ、法の下では皆平等だ。
examples.tr: Rich or poor, everyone is equal under the law.

examples.jp: 何であれ、まずは相談してください。
examples.tr: Whatever it is, please consult me first.

examples.jp: どこであれ、彼女はすぐ友達ができる。
examples.tr: Wherever she goes, she makes friends right away.

examples.jp: どんな結果であれ、私は受け入れるつもりだ。
examples.tr: Whatever the result, I intend to accept it.

1299.explain:
Placed after a noun; does not attach directly to an adjective/verb (nominalize if needed).
Formal style, used in essays, speeches, regulations, and official announcements.
であれ is usually repeated twice with a pair N1・N2; with a question word, only one であれ is needed.
The second clause is usually a general judgment, a policy, a principle, or a strong volition.
Can be combined with たとえ to add the nuance of "even if".

• Expresses "whether it is A or B, the conclusion/position does not change". Emphasizes that the stance is unchanging.
• With 疑問詞 + であれ, it means "no matter …", with a broad scope (covering every possibility).
• Often pairs two nouns that are opposites/extremes to create a strong contrast: 高い⇔低い, 雨⇔雪, 金持ち⇔貧乏…
• The nuance is stiff and rule-like or principled; the second clause is often a general judgment/direction, and it is rarely used for private, casual matters.
• Morphologically, であれ comes from the imperative form of である, but in this pattern it carries no meaning of command; it expresses the supposition "even if it is".
mistakes: Wrong part of speech: attaching it directly to an i-adj/na-adj/verb. You need to nominalize: 忙しいときであれ / 重要な案件であれ.
Lack of parallelism when using a pair: N1 and N2 must belong to the same category and be balanced: 正しいであれ間違いであれ (correct), 正しいであれ急ぐであれ (incorrect).
Using it in an overly casual context makes the sentence sound forced. JLPT N1 often tests the formal nuance of であれ compared with でも.
Confusion with にせよ: both are correct in many sentences, but exam questions often ask you to choose the pattern that fits the style; in normative texts, であれ is preferred.
Trap with question words: 何であれ (correct), 何でもであれ (incorrect because the functions overlap).
1299.notes:
• When you need to attach it to an adjective/verb, use a noun denoting a type/matter: 忙しい人であれ (busy person); 必要であれ is incorrect; instead: 必要な場合であれ.
• In spoken language, it is often replaced with でも/にせよ to sound more natural.
• In tone, であれ carries a sense of "no exceptions", which suits expressing policies and rules.

examples.jp: この説明は子どもですら理解できる。
examples.tr: Even a child can understand this explanation.

examples.jp: 彼は忙しすぎて、昼食の時間すらない。
examples.tr: He is so busy that he doesn't even have time for lunch.

examples.jp: 専門家ですら頭を抱える問題だ。
examples.tr: It is a problem that even experts are at a loss over.

examples.jp: 彼女の歌声は、批評家でさえ称賛した。
examples.tr: Even the critics praised her singing voice.

examples.jp: 疲れすぎて、昨夜は夢にすら見なかった。
examples.tr: I was so tired that I didn't even dream last night.

examples.jp: そんな基本も知らないなんて、彼は自分の名前ですら正しく書けないのか。
examples.tr: He doesn't even know something that basic? Can't he even write his own name correctly?

1300.explain:
Used to heighten the sense of surprise/the unexpected; it can be used in both affirmative and negative sentences.
In written language/speeches, "ですら" is more formal than "さえ/でさえ".
If you need to keep a case particle, use "N＋助詞＋すら" (夢にすら,彼とすら…).

• Emphasizes the degree of surprise: even the target at the lower edge/beyond expectations does (not) …
• "ですら" has a formal nuance; "すら/でさえ/さえ" are more commonly used.
• When a case particle (に/と/から…) is needed, "ですら" cannot be inserted; use "N＋助詞＋すら".

rows: Most common; has many structural variants
<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>さえあれば<ruby>生<rt>い</rt></ruby>きられる
Used when "に/と/から…" is needed

mistakes: Wrong particle position: × 彼ですらに → correct: 彼にすら.
Using "ですら" right after a case particle: × 学校にですら → use 学校にすら or 学校ですら (depending on the meaning).
Confusing the nuance with "まで": "まで" means to the extent of/even, but does not always carry the sense of surprise that "すら" does.
1300.notes:
• In strong negation, it can go with まったく／全然: 彼は挨拶すらしない.
• Avoid doubling particles: × 子どもにですら → either 子どもですら (no need for に), or 子どもにすら.

examples.jp: 連休初日とあって、空港はどこも混雑している。
examples.tr: Because it is the first day of the long holiday, the airport is crowded everywhere.

examples.jp: 有名店の閉店とあって、朝から長い列ができた。
examples.tr: With a famous shop closing down, a long line had formed since morning.

examples.jp: 久しぶりの晴天とあって、公園は家族連れで賑わった。
examples.tr: Since it was the first sunny day in a long time, the park was bustling with families.

examples.jp: セール最終日とあって、店内は熱気に包まれている。
examples.tr: Because it is the last day of the sale, the store is filled with excitement.

examples.jp: 人気俳優の来日とあって、会場周辺は警備が強化された。
examples.tr: With a popular actor visiting Japan, security around the venue was tightened.

1301.explain:
The second clause is an objective result/phenomenon; avoid using the speaker's command/volition.
Presents the "special/rare" nature of the cause:連休、初雪、有名人来訪…
Usually used with the present tense or the past progressive (～ている/～ていた).

• A "special/noteworthy" reason leads to a natural, observed result.
• A narrative/objective tone; not suitable for stating the speaker's volition/request.
• Often used in news, articles, and commentary on social phenomena.

rows: <ruby>休日<rt>きゅうじつ</rt></ruby>とあって<ruby>混<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む
<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>とあれば<ruby>協力<rt>きょうりょく</rt></ruby>する
Praise/evaluation; does not state a result caused by circumstances
<ruby>一流<rt>いちりゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>店<rt>てん</rt></ruby>だけあって<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い
Neutral; does not need to be "special"
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>のため<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using it for the speaker's volition: × とあって、早く帰ろうと思う → use ので/ため instead.
Confusion with ～だけあって (evaluation) or ～とあれば (condition). Pay attention to the second clause.
A cause that is not "special" makes the sentence awkward; choose a cause that stands out.
1301.notes:
• N2. Very common in newspaper reading passages; recognize it by a "special" noun + とあって.
• Placed at the beginning of a sentence; rarely comes after another subordinate clause.
• Not used with the speaker's direct request/desire: × とあって、手伝ってください。

examples.jp: 景色といい空気といい、ここは本当に素晴らしい。
examples.tr: Both the scenery and the air here are truly wonderful.

examples.jp: この店は味といい値段といい、申し分ない。
examples.tr: This restaurant leaves nothing to be desired, in both taste and price.

examples.jp: 彼は顔といい性格といい、非の打ちどころがない。
examples.tr: In both looks and personality, he is flawless.

examples.jp: あの選手はスピードといいスタミナといい、一流だ。
examples.tr: That athlete is first-class in both speed and stamina.

examples.jp: このパソコンは性能といいデザインといい、コスパが高い。
examples.tr: In both performance and design, this computer is great value for money.

examples.jp: 態度といい言い方といい、彼はちょっと失礼だ。
examples.tr: Both his attitude and the way he talks are a bit rude.

1302.explain:
Used to give an "overall evaluation" based on two representative points.
Not used with commands, invitations, or intentions. It mainly ends in descriptive/evaluative narrative sentences.
Usually used with nouns; rarely used directly with adjectives/verbs. Do not confuse it with "Vるといい" (the wish "if only").
Suitable for written language, commentary, reviews, and concise praise/criticism.

- Meaning: "Both N1 and N2 (from whichever aspect you look at it)…". Used to sum up the value/impression of a target based on two representative features.
- Nuance: Describes a subjective evaluation, usually positive (praise), sometimes negative (criticism). Not used for the speaker's requests/volition.
- The subject is usually the target being evaluated; N1 and N2 are "representative aspects" of that target.

rows: Whether you look at A or B, both…
<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>といい<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>といい、<ruby>最高<rt>さいこう</rt></ruby>
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>にしても<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>にしても<ruby>楽<rt>たの</rt></ruby>しめる
<ruby>和食<rt>わしょく</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>洋食<rt>ようしょく</rt></ruby>とか、<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>き
<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>や<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>大事<rt>だいじ</rt></ruby>
Completely different in meaning and usage
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>くなるといいね

mistakes: Confusion with "Vるといい(ね)": completely different meaning.
Using it to make a request/suggestion: Not appropriate.
Attaching it directly to a verb/adjective without nominalization: Unnatural.
JLPT: the trap of choosing "AやB" (simple listing) instead of "AといいBといい" (overall evaluation).
1302.notes:
• When listing more than 2 aspects, the sentence may become heavy; usually only 2 representative ones are chosen.
• Suitable for opening the first sentence of an evaluative paragraph: "立地といい設備といい、…"
• Can be used for criticism: "雨といい風といい、最悪の天気だ"。

1303.connection: Vる / N / Quantity + というところだ

examples.jp: 準備は８割というところだ。
examples.tr: The preparations are about 80% done.

examples.jp: 到着は午後３時というところでしょう。
examples.tr: We'll probably arrive at around 3 p.m.

examples.jp: 今年の成長率は５％増というところだ。
examples.tr: This year's growth rate is roughly a 5% increase.

examples.jp: 私の日本語力は中級というところだ。
examples.tr: My Japanese is at about an intermediate level.

examples.jp: 今のところ、被害は軽微というところだ。
examples.tr: For now, the damage can be said to be minor.

examples.jp: 今日終わるとしても、半分というところだ。
examples.tr: Even if we finish today, it will only be about half.

1303.explain:
Used when summing up/estimating after weighing the facts; it has a sense of "putting it briefly".
Often accompanied by だろう／でしょう to soften the statement.
Not used for commands/suggestions; it is a narrative sentence of evaluation.

- Meaning: "About…, roughly…, around … at most". Expresses an estimate/evaluation that sums things up at the point in time of speaking.
- Nuance: Objective, somewhat formal; often used in reports, news, and expert assessments. Depending on the context, it may imply "at most/not very high".
- Often accompanied by quantifying expressions (割, パーセント, 時間, 人, 点…) or levels (初級/中級/平均的…).

rows: せいぜい<ruby>半分<rt>はんぶん</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using it as an absolutely exact figure: Incorrect; it is an estimate.
Confusion with ところ (in the middle of, about to, just did): というところだ is completely different.
Using it in a command/suggestion: Does not fit its function.
JLPT: the trap of choosing せいぜい when the context is neutral (せいぜい has the nuance of "at most").
1303.notes:
• Suitable when you need to "anchor" a representative number/level of evaluation, so that it is not taken as an exact value.
• To reduce the nuance of certainty, preferably end with でしょう/だろう or add おそらく/たぶん.
• When assessing your own ability/level, it gives a modest, polite tone in self-introductions.

examples.jp: 売上は回復したが、まだコロナ前の七割といったところだ。
examples.tr: Sales have recovered, but they are still only about 70% of pre-COVID levels.

examples.jp: 休みは多くても月に二日といったところだ。
examples.tr: At most, I get about two days off a month.

examples.jp: 準備期間は一週間といったところで、十分とは言えない。
examples.tr: The preparation period is only about a week, which can hardly be called enough.

examples.jp: 合格ラインは60点といったところだ。
examples.tr: The passing line is around 60 points.

examples.jp: 登山経験は、体験ツアーに一度参加したといったところだ。
examples.tr: As for my mountain-climbing experience, I've only joined a trial tour once.

1304.explain:
Suitable for cautious statements that avoid absolutes; fits written language/presentations.
Not used for boasting/emphasizing superiority; the main nuance is "modest, limited".
Often used to end a sentence giving an assessment of figures, degree, or scope.

• Expresses an approximate degree or an upper limit, "at most, only this much", with a modest/limiting nuance.
• Often accompanied by limiting words such as せいぜい、多くても、せめて to emphasize the ceiling.
• Pragmatics: More formal than くらい/ぐらい; often used in reports and objective assessments.

rows: Neutral, more spoken; does not imply "at most".
<ruby>30人<rt>さんじゅうにん</rt></ruby>ぐらい<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る。
Strong on degree; can be used to exaggerate.
<ruby>息<rt>いき</rt></ruby>ができないほど<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>い。
Spoken; can be combined: せいぜい<ruby>三回<rt>さんかい</rt></ruby>といったところだ。
せいぜい<ruby>二<rt>に</rt></ruby><ruby>千<rt>せん</rt></ruby><ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Using it to exaggerate has the wrong nuance: ×最高で100人も来るといったところだ.
Confusion with くらい: JLPT often asks you to choose the "modest" pattern → prefer といったところだ.
Missing the "upper limit" context: if the meaning is "at least", do not use といったところだ.
1304.notes:
• Works well in academic writing/reports: an open conclusion that leaves a margin of error.
• When talking about your personal experience/qualifications, it helps avoid boasting: "勉強したといったところだ"。
• Placed at the end of a sentence to keep the tone soft and polite while still precise.

examples.jp: この寒さといったらありはしない。暖房なしでは無理だ。
examples.tr: It's unbearably cold. I can't manage without heating.

examples.jp: 彼の部屋の汚さといったらありはしない。
examples.tr: His room is filthy beyond words.

examples.jp: 通勤ラッシュの混雑といったらありはしない。
examples.tr: The rush-hour commuter crowds are indescribable.

examples.jp: 上司の気まぐれといったらありはしない。
examples.tr: My boss is unbelievably fickle.

examples.jp: 料金の高さといったらありはしない。
examples.tr: The fees are outrageously high.

1305.explain:
Leans toward complaint/irritation more than praise.
Spoken language; sounds rather strong and can be crude if used with strangers/in polite situations.
Placed before a concluding/justifying clause: …ので/から/も無理はない…
Goes easily with nouns of states:混みよう・暑さ・痛み・迷惑・恥ずかしさ…

- Expresses an extremely high degree, "very/beyond words", usually with negative emotions (irritation, weariness). "ありはしない" is the emphatic negation of ある → a colloquial nuance, somewhat stiff/strong and full of emotion.
• Focuses on the speaker's subjective impression.
• Suitable for complaining, criticizing, and lamenting; rarely used in formal, objective writing.
• Hyperbolic: it does not mean "there is none", but "too much to put into words".

rows: といったらありはしない
<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>さといったらありはしない。
といったらありゃしない
<ruby>腹<rt>はら</rt></ruby>が<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>つといったらありゃしない。
Can be used for both praise and criticism
<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しさといったらない。
〜のなんのって／〜ことこの<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>ない
のなんのって is very colloquial; ことこの<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>ない is written language
<ruby>迷惑<rt>めいわく</rt></ruby>のなんのって。
〜てしょうがない／たまらない

mistakes: Using it directly with the dictionary form of a verb: unnatural. You should nominalize the phenomenon. Incorrect) 驚くといったらありはしない → Correct) 驚きといったらありはしない.
Confusing the nuance: exam questions often ask you to distinguish といったらない (neutral) vs ありはしない (negative/colloquial).
Using it in formal writing: not appropriate; choose といったらない/極めて/非常に.
Meaningless double negation: "〜ないといったらありはしない" easily muddles the meaning → avoid it.
1305.notes:
• "ありはしない" = "ありはしない(=全くないわけではない, emphasizes negation)" is used to exaggerate the degree.
• Often stands as an independent sentence of exclamation, followed by a sentence of explanation.
• Rarely used for praise, but possible: ありがたさといったらありはしない (still sounds exaggerated/unusual).

examples.jp: 昼といわず夜といわず、救急車のサイレンが鳴りやまない。
examples.tr: Day and night alike, the ambulance sirens never stop.

examples.jp: 教室は床といわず机といわず、埃だらけだ。
examples.tr: The classroom is covered in dust, the floor and the desks alike.

examples.jp: 子どもといわず大人といわず、このアニメに夢中だ。
examples.tr: Children and adults alike are hooked on this anime.

examples.jp: 顔といわず手といわず、泥だらけになった。
examples.tr: I got mud all over, my face and hands alike.

examples.jp: 平日といわず週末といわず、図書館は混んでいる。
examples.tr: Weekdays and weekends alike, the library is crowded.

1306.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize "no exclusions" over a broad scope, with repetition or simultaneity.
The second clause is not a direct volition/command. Avoid: ×子どもといわず大人といわず、集まりなさい。
Most natural with concrete nouns/opposing pairs; be careful with abstract nouns.

• Emphasizes a broad scope: "without excluding/distinguishing … or …, everything is …".
• Often used with natural pairs: 昼／夜, 老人／子供, 左／右, 内／外, 表／裏…
• Strong nuance, somewhat written; the second clause is usually a lasting state, universality, or a pervasive degree (～だらけ、～まみれ、～が続く…).

rows: Formal; does not emphasize pervasiveness like といわず～といわず.
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby><ruby>可<rt>か</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>天候<rt>てんこう</rt></ruby>にかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>。
Only lists illustrations; does not cover the whole.
<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby>ない。

mistakes: Using it with a command/volition → unnatural.
Confusion with ～を問わず in the context of signs/regulations: JLPT usually requires choosing the formal pattern → use ～を問わず.
Listing nouns that are asymmetrical/not in the same semantic field makes the sentence awkward.
1306.notes:
• Rhetorically effective when describing "everywhere/all at once": it easily creates rhythm and emphasis.
• Combines well with degree words "だらけ／まみれ／いっぱい／あふれる／鳴りやまない／絶えない".
• Three items can be used for intensification (rare): 昼といわず夜といわず朝といわず… but avoid being long-winded.

1307.meaning: To be considered…, to be regarded as…
1307.connection: [sentence/clause] + とされる とされている / N

examples.jp: この地域は地震の危険度が高いとされる。
examples.tr: This region is said to have a high risk of earthquakes.

examples.jp: 彼はAI分野の第一人者とされている。
examples.tr: He is regarded as the leading authority in the field of AI.

examples.jp: この寺は日本最古とされる。
examples.tr: This temple is considered the oldest in Japan.

examples.jp: ビタミンDは骨の健康に重要とされている。
examples.tr: Vitamin D is considered important for bone health.

examples.jp: 報道によると、犯人とされる男が逮捕された。
examples.tr: According to reports, a man believed to be the culprit has been arrested.

examples.jp: この慣習は江戸時代から続くとされてきた。
examples.tr: This custom has been said to date back to the Edo period.

1307.explain:
Used when you want to stay neutral and not make an absolute claim; suitable for reports, theses, and news.
Add a source/criterion to clarify the basis:一般には／法律上は／統計的には／専門家の間では + 〜とされる.
Not used for very personal opinions; when subjective, と思う／と考える is more appropriate.

• Expresses an evaluation/standard/view accepted by many people or by experts: "is considered/is said to be".
• Objective nuance with no clear agent; the speaker takes no personal responsibility for the evaluation.
• Difference in degree:

- とされる: a common conclusion/designation (usually in written, academic, legal, and journalistic language).

- とされている: a general assessment that currently holds, slightly softer.

• Can be accompanied by a source: 専門家によって／法律上／一般には + 〜とされる.

rows: <ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>とされる<ruby>基準<rt>きじゅん</rt></ruby>
<ruby>不在<rt>ふざい</rt></ruby>と<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>なされる
Is thought to be (based on reasoning)
<ruby>起源<rt>きげん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>古代<rt>こだい</rt></ruby>と<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えられている
Based more on rumor/word of mouth
おいしいと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>われている
<ruby>政府<rt>せいふ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>目標<rt>もくひょう</rt></ruby>を2％としている

mistakes: Confusing the nuance: とされる ≠ と言われている. JLPT questions often test objectivity; choose とされる when the style is formal/academic.
Forgetting ている: When emphasizing a lasting general state → prefer とされている.
Using it for a personal opinion → wrong style. For personal views, use と思う／と考える.
Modifier: N + とされる + N is a journalistic structure; do not insert だ before とされる in a modifier.
1307.notes:
• In newspaper headlines, the subject is often omitted: 「世界最古とされる洞窟を発見」 → "Cave considered the oldest in the world discovered".
• In academic writing, combine with 出典/調査名 to increase credibility: 「〜とされる（Smith, 2021）」.
• The negative form is rare: 〜とはされない（"is not considered"） when excluding something in legal contexts/regulations.

1308.connection: V (plain form) / N + としたところで

examples.jp: 仮に予算が増えたとしたところで、納期は変わらない。
examples.tr: Even if the budget were increased, the deadline would not change.

examples.jp: 彼が謝罪したとしたところで、被害者の怒りは収まらないだろう。
examples.tr: Even if he apologized, the victims' anger would probably not subside.

examples.jp: 子どもにしたところで、あの映像はショックだ。
examples.tr: Even for children, that footage is shocking.

examples.jp: たとえ天才としたところで、努力なしでは成果は出ない。
examples.tr: Even a genius cannot achieve results without effort.

examples.jp: 今からやり直したとしたところで、間に合うとは限らない。
examples.tr: Even if we started over now, there is no guarantee we would make it in time.

examples.jp: 私にしたところで、決して彼を擁護するつもりはない。
examples.tr: Even I have absolutely no intention of defending him.

1308.explain:
Used to acknowledge a possibility while asserting that the conclusion does not change (limited/ineffective).
The style is somewhat more formal/academic than 〜たところで and 〜としても.
The second clause usually avoids commands/strong volition; it focuses on objective evaluation.

• Meaning: strong hypothetical concession, “even if/suppose that … (still) … the result does not change (usually negative/limited)”.
• Mild nuance of criticism/pessimism, emphasizing futility or the difficulty of changing the situation.
• Goes with negative and limiting expressions: 〜ない／たいした〜ない／所詮〜／わけではない often appear in the second clause.
• にしたところで emphasizes “even for (that person/group)”. としたところで is more neutral and applies to clauses.

rows: Formal; applies to clauses or N
<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>だとしたところで…
Even if (to the point of having done it)
Attaches directly to V-た; more colloquial
<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けるとしても<ruby>学<rt>まな</rt></ruby>びはある
にしたって is colloquial; close in meaning to にしたところで

mistakes: Confusing it with 〜とすると (inferential condition). 〜としたところで is a concession; the result is usually negative/limited.
Lacking a negative nuance in the second clause → the sentence sounds forced. Use 〜ない／限らない／たいした〜ない…
Changing “にしたところで” to “をしたところで” with a noun → wrong particle. It must be に.
Trap: choosing between 〜としても and 〜としたところで. If the style is formal and the result is strongly negative → prefer 〜としたところで.
1308.notes:
• Add たとえ／仮に to emphasize a supposition far from reality.
• In argumentation, this pattern helps “block” a counterargument: it acknowledges the other side's point but preserves the conclusion.
• Should not be used with a direct desire (〜たい) in the second clause; keep the nuance of evaluation/judgment.

examples.jp: 雨となれば、試合は中止だ。
examples.tr: If it rains, the match will be canceled.

examples.jp: 社長が来るとなれば、万全の準備を整えないと。
examples.tr: If the company president is coming, we have to make thorough preparations.

examples.jp: 命に関わるとなれば、迷っている場合ではない。
