examples.tr: If a life is at stake, this is no time to hesitate.

examples.jp: 彼が担当するとなれば、安心できる。
examples.tr: If he is in charge, we can rest easy.

examples.jp: 海外展開となれば、法規制の確認は欠かせない。
examples.tr: If we are expanding overseas, checking legal regulations is essential.

1309.explain:
Used when: stating a major/important condition and then drawing a principled conclusion.
Often appears in written language, reports, and presentations of opinions/policy.
The second clause feels like “something inevitable/something that should be done” rather than a light personal suggestion.
Combines well with emphatic words: いざ、いよいよ、本当に、万一.

• Main meaning: “If (in the case that) A, then B is natural/inevitable/worth doing”.
• Nuance: reasoned, general; used to state principles, general tendencies, or a firm decision when the condition is significant enough.
• Compared with となると: less about “discussing a specific matter”, leaning toward general judgments/opinions. Compared with となったら: more formal and less personal.
• The second clause is often a firm conclusion/strong opinion: ～に違いない、～は避けられない、～べきだ、～ことになる.

rows: General, formal, strong sense of inevitability
<ruby>非常<rt>ひじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>事態<rt>じたい</rt></ruby>となれば、<ruby>避難<rt>ひなん</rt></ruby>だ。
If it comes to/speaking of A, then...
<ruby>海外<rt>かいがい</rt></ruby><ruby>勤務<rt>きんむ</rt></ruby>となると、<ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>がかかる。
If/when the time comes for A, then...
<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>すとなったら、<ruby>片<rt>かた</rt></ruby>づけよう。
やる<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>全力<rt>ぜんりょく</rt></ruby>で。

mistakes: Using となれば in light everyday conversation can sound stiff; consider となると/となったら.
A weak desire (～たい/～ませんか) in the second clause is less natural; replace it with a judgment/obligation.
JLPT: When the question calls for a nuance of “principle/inevitability/broad supposition”, choose となれば; when it calls for “a specific problem arising”, choose となると.
1309.notes:
• Often used to state a “standard of action”: A となれば B すべきだ/不可避だ/当然だ.
• Suitable for opening a paragraph in argumentative writing: “X となれば、Y は避けられないだろう”。
• The tone is more formal than となると; avoid using it for momentary emotions unless emphasizing “いざ”.
• Often combined with abstract nouns: 例外、危機、非常事態、国家レベル、法的問題.

examples.jp: 子どもたちは疲れたとみえて、帰りの電車でぐっすり寝ている。
examples.tr: The children must have been tired; they are sound asleep on the train home.

examples.jp: 空が急に暗くなってきた。雨になるとみえて、風も強くなってきた。
examples.tr: The sky has suddenly grown dark. It looks like it is going to rain, and the wind has picked up too.

examples.jp: 彼は何か悩んでいるとみえて、ここ数日元気がない。
examples.tr: He seems to be worried about something; he has been down for the past few days.

examples.jp: 新製品は好評だとみえて、発売初日から在庫が少ない。
examples.tr: The new product seems to be popular; stock has been low since the first day of sale.

examples.jp: 徹夜したとみえて、目の下にくまができている。
examples.tr: They seem to have stayed up all night; there are dark circles under their eyes.

examples.jp: 彼女は返事を急いでいないとみえて、既読のままだ。
examples.tr: She seems to be in no hurry to reply; the message is still just marked as read.

1310.explain:
Framework: A is evidence → the speaker infers B (a judgment). Not used when there is no concrete sign.
Objective nuance: the speaker steps back slightly to observe, avoiding a sense of imposing a subjective view.
Often accompanied by words indicating signs: 見たところ／様子から／どうやら／最近～／数字を見ると… → increases reliability.
Restriction: usually does not combine with a direct command/volition in clause B.
Written style: in news/reports, the sentence-final form ～とみえる may be used.

～とみえて expresses a judgment, “ it seems that…/apparently…”, based on observable signs (behavior, state, a specific situation). The speaker does not assert absolutely but infers from the facts at hand.

•
Objectivity: there is visible evidence (facial expressions, weather, crowds, figures…).

•
Position: usually in the middle of the sentence: Clause A (observed basis) ＋ とみえて ＋ Clause B (judgment).

•
Degree of certainty: higher than ～ようだ/～みたいだ when A is “strong evidence”. Lower than 断定.

•
Style: often used in written language, reports, and commentary; also natural in formal conversation.

rows: A judgment based on observable signs.
Emphasizes “concrete evidence”. Usually in the middle of the sentence.
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>い とみえて、<ruby>入口<rt>いりぐち</rt></ruby>で<ruby>混雑<rt>こんざつ</rt></ruby>している。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しい とみえる。
Less emphasis on concrete evidence; more colloquial (～みたいだ).
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る みたいだ。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby><ruby>中<rt>ちゅう</rt></ruby>らしい。
Emphasizes outward appearance, without deep inference.
<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>がない ように<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>える。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～らしい:
～らしい is based on an information source; ～とみえて is based on observation. Exam questions often set traps around the source of information.
Confusing it with ～ようだ／～みたいだ: when the question has “concrete evidence” (figures, a clear phenomenon), prefer ～とみえて.
Omitting 「だ」 with nouns/na-adjectives: N/Aな＋ だ＋とみえて → in spoken language it is sometimes omitted, but exam questions usually require the standard form.
Using it with a command/volition: unnatural. Avoid sentences like「遅れるとみえて、急ぎなさい」。Separate the judgment and the command.
Missing the observation clause A:
～とみえて needs A as its basis. If there is no sign, use a different pattern.
Getting the direction of cause and effect wrong: A is the sign and B is the judgment, not an explanation of a definite reason.
1310.notes:
•
Implicit inference chart:
Sign A → Hypothesis H → Soft judgment B. ～とみえて sits between observation and conclusion, helping the sentence “stay soft”.
•
Suitable for academic/journalistic style: used to describe social phenomena or market tendencies when there are no conclusive figures yet.
•
Reliability: increases when A is figures, weather, or repeated behavior; decreases when A is only a passing feeling.
•
Shifting to a polite tone: in clause B, use ～ようです／～でしょう to increase objectivity.

1311.meaning: For someone in the position of… to…

examples.jp: 医者ともあろう人が、喫煙の危険性を軽視するなんて。
examples.tr: To think that a doctor, of all people, would downplay the dangers of smoking.

examples.jp: 教師ともあろう者が、生徒に暴言を吐くとは信じ難い。
examples.tr: It is hard to believe that a teacher, of all people, would verbally abuse students.

examples.jp: 国の指導者ともあろう人が、根拠のない発言を繰り返すべきではない。
examples.tr: Someone who is a national leader should not keep making baseless statements.

examples.jp: 研究者ともあろう立場の人が、データを改ざんするなど許されない。
examples.tr: Tampering with data is unacceptable for someone in the position of a researcher.

examples.jp: 一流企業の社長ともあろう者が、会議に遅刻するとは。
examples.tr: To think that the president of a leading company, of all people, would be late for a meeting.

1311.explain:
The agent is usually a noun carrying prestige: 医者,教師,研究者,社長,公務員, プロ,一流企業など.
The second clause usually contains a negative evaluation or unmet expectations; it is rarely used for praise.
Combines naturally with the topic particle/subject particle: ～が／は; followed by ～とは/～なんて to emphasize exclamation.
Avoid using it about yourself unless you intend strong self-criticism.
Style: formal, rhetorical; suited to editorials, news, and disciplinary reports.

• Expresses surprise, criticism, or high expectations toward a person/organization with high status, prestige, or expertise who nonetheless does something unbecoming.
• Implies that being “someone like X”, one “should not/cannot” do such a thing, or “ought to have…”.
• Formal nuance, often seen in news, commentary, and written language; also used in spoken language but feels heavy.
• Often followed by a second clause carrying emotion: ～とは、～なんて、～べきだ、～あるまじき.

rows: <ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>ともあろう<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>がミスを？
Normative; does not necessarily criticize an action that has occurred
<ruby>指導<rt>しどう</rt></ruby><ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby>たる<ruby>者<rt>しゃ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>誠実<rt>せいじつ</rt></ruby>であるべきだ。
<ruby>教師<rt>きょうし</rt></ruby>にあるまじき<ruby>行為<rt>こうい</rt></ruby>。
An N of the caliber of… and yet…
プロほどの<ruby>選手<rt>せんしゅ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>凡<rt>凡</rt></ruby>ミスをするとは。

mistakes: Using it for a target without clear “status” → wrong nuance. Choose a noun with standing.
Using direct praise in the second clause → goes against the typical feeling. It is mainly used for criticism/surprise.
Confusing it with ～たる者: ～ともあろう expresses something blameworthy that “has happened”; ～たる者 states a recommended standard.
Omitting the exclamatory particle (とは/なんて) makes the sentence less natural when you want to emphasize emotion.
1311.notes:
• The form ものが after ともあろう strengthens the nuance of criticism: ～ともあろう者が.
• Usually comes before a noun referring to a person; rarely used for things/concepts unless personified (例: 国家ともあろう存在).
• Combine with まさか/まことに to raise the degree of exclamation: まさか医者ともあろう人が…

examples.jp: 社会人ともなると、時間の使い方が問われる。
examples.tr: Once you are a working adult, how you use your time is put to the test.

examples.jp: 年末ともなると、どこの店も混み合う。
examples.tr: When the end of the year comes around, every store gets crowded.

examples.jp: 子どもも高校生ともなると、親の言うことを聞かなくなるものだ。
examples.tr: Once children reach high school, they tend to stop listening to their parents.

examples.jp: いざ本番ともなると、普段の力が出せないこともある。
examples.tr: When it comes to the real thing, you sometimes cannot perform as well as usual.

examples.jp: 海外勤務ともなると、家族のサポートが不可欠だ。
examples.tr: When it comes to working overseas, family support is indispensable.

1312.explain:
First clause: a noun expressing a milestone/status:社会人,管理職,年末,本番,受験シーズン.
Second clause: a new consequence/condition, usually a rule/natural consequence rather than personal volition.
Not used to state a single chance event; suited to describing general tendencies.
Different from ともなれば: ～ともなると sounds more colloquial and has more direct emphasis.

• Once the stage/status/situation X is reached, the situation/standards/needs change significantly.
• Nuance of “whenever/once… then”, with a sense of moving up a level. The second clause usually describes a natural consequence or higher demands.
• Often used in explanations and commentary; natural in both spoken and written language.

rows: <ruby>管理<rt>かんり</rt></ruby><ruby>職<rt>しょく</rt></ruby>ともなると<ruby>責任<rt>せきにん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>年末<rt>ねんまつ</rt></ruby>ともなれば<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ。
If speaking of/when it comes to… then…
Topicalization; does not necessarily mean “reaching a stage”
<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>となると<ruby>張<rt>は</rt></ruby>り<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>る。
On the occasion of/when carrying out
<ruby>入学<rt>にゅうがく</rt></ruby>にあたっての<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Using it directly with verbs: this pattern prefers a noun as the milestone, not V＋ともなると.
A single personal volition in the second clause → less natural. State a general/inevitable consequence.
Confusing it with となると (topicalization). ～ともなると means “reaching a stage”, not “speaking of”.
1312.notes:
• Often goes with “threshold” milestones: 本番, 期末, 繁忙期, 子育て, 老後.
• Combine with いざ to emphasize the gap between preparation and the real thing: いざ～ともなると…
• Can be used at the beginning of a sentence as an adverbial phrase: 夏休みともなると、…

examples.jp: 年度末ともなれば、各部署の残業が増える。
examples.tr: When the end of the fiscal year comes, overtime increases in every department.

examples.jp: 管理職ともなれば、意思決定の責任が重くなる。
examples.tr: Once you become a manager, the responsibility for decision-making grows heavier.

examples.jp: 子育て期ともなれば、出費も時間もかさむものだ。
examples.tr: Once you are in the child-rearing years, both expenses and time add up.

examples.jp: 大都市ともなれば、防災計画の整備が欠かせない。
examples.tr: For a big city, developing disaster prevention plans is essential.

examples.jp: いざ災害ともなれば、正確な情報発信が最優先だ。
examples.tr: Should a disaster actually strike, sending out accurate information is the top priority.

1313.explain:
The first clause is a noun as a milestone; the second clause states an inevitable consequence or a normative requirement.
Works well in guidance documents, regulations, and internal notices.
Compared with ～ともなると, it feels more “argumentative” and less colloquial.

• Similar to ～ともなると: once the milestone/status X is reached, certain conditions/standards/consequences follow.
• Sounds formal; often used in official announcements, guidance, and news.
• Often combined with rule-like/procedural content: 必要となる／求められる／増える／避けられない.

rows: <ruby>年度<rt>ねんど</rt></ruby><ruby>末<rt>まつ</rt></ruby>ともなれば<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby><ruby>物<rt>ぶつ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby><ruby>人<rt>じん</rt></ruby>ともなると<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。
To the point of/reaching the stage of
Emphasizes the “extreme point”; not necessarily a social milestone
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>き、<ruby>撤退<rt>てったい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>っては…
A procedural condition rather than a social milestone
<ruby>申請<rt>しんせい</rt></ruby>する<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>すべき<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Using a direct verb clause in the first clause → unnatural. It must be a noun as the milestone.
A single specific personal action in the second clause → less natural; state a general tendency/consequence.
Confusing the nuance with となると (speaking of): ともなれば means “reaching a stage”, a turning point.
1313.notes:
• Combines easily with passive verbs/intransitive stative verbs: 増える・求められる・必要となる.
• Often appears in administrative documents, corporate materials, and political/social news.
• Can open a paragraph to set the context before laying out regulations.

1314.connection: V (plain form) + とも + V (plain form) + とも / N + N / A + A

examples.jp: 彼は行くとも行かないとも言わなかった。
examples.tr: He didn't say whether he would go or not.

examples.jp: この計画は成功とも失敗とも断定できない。
examples.tr: This plan cannot be definitively called either a success or a failure.

examples.jp: 景気は良いとも悪いとも言えない状況だ。
examples.tr: The economy is in a state that can be called neither good nor bad.

examples.jp: この薬の効果は高いとも低いとも言えない。
examples.tr: The effectiveness of this medicine cannot be called either high or low.

examples.jp: 彼の表情は喜びとも怒りともつかない。
examples.tr: His expression is hard to read: it could be joy or it could be anger.

examples.jp: この文は皮肉とも冗談とも取れる。
examples.tr: This sentence can be taken as either sarcasm or a joke.

1314.explain:
Used when a conclusion has not been or cannot be reached, or when deliberately avoiding commitment; suited to written language, reports, and commentary.
What follows is usually a negative/hard-to-determine expression: ～言えない／決められない／断定できない／わからない／はっきりしない.
With verbs, the common contrast is: VるともVないとも…; with -い adjectives: AいともAくないとも…; with -な adjectives and nouns: だ is usually omitted before とも.
If the focus is on “saying/answering”: ～とも～とも言わない／返事しない → “not say (out loud) A or B”.
The form “～とも～ともつかない／取れる” emphasizes ambiguity/multiple meanings in expressions, texts, and attitudes.
Usually exactly two options are listed; if there are more than two, consider other patterns such as ～やら～やら.

• Presents two possibilities/options A and B and then denies that a decision can be made: “cannot say whether it is A or B”, “cannot yet decide whether it is A or B”.
• Used to describe the speaker/other party “not saying clearly whether A or B”: AともBとも言わない.
• Emphasizes ambiguity and two-way possibility: AともBともつかない／取れる → “can be understood as A or B”, “hard to tell”.
• Formal nuance, leaning toward writing or careful statements; avoids definitive assertions.
• Often accompanied by verbs/expressions: 言えない, 言わない, 決められない, 分からない, 断定できない, 判断がつかない, はっきりしない, つかない, 取れる.
• Often combined with antonym pairs: 賛成/反対, 成功/失敗, 良い/悪い, 高い/安い, 有罪/無罪… to highlight “not leaning to either side”.

rows: Cannot/does not say clearly whether A or B; ambiguous
Emphasizes “not deciding”; often goes with <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない・<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>わない・つかない・<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>れる
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>とも<ruby>不<rt>ふ</rt></ruby><ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>とも<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない
Neutral, no implied ambiguity; used in questions/choices
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないか<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めて
どちらとも<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない
Similar content but general; does not list a specific pair
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>はどちらとも<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない
～にせよ／にしろ～にせよ／にしろ
Expresses “regardless”, unlike the “not deciding” of ～とも～とも
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>にせよ<ruby>不<rt>ふ</rt></ruby><ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>にせよ<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>する
Whether A or B (it is all the same)
Inclusive reasoning/condition; no nuance of ambiguity
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>であれ<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>であれ<ruby>歓迎<rt>かんげい</rt></ruby>だ
Gives more than 2 examples; not “cannot conclude A/B”
<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>やらノートやらで<ruby>鞄<rt>かばん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い
Describes repetition/contrast; no meaning of “not deciding”
<ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れたり<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だったりする
AともBともつかない／<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>れる
Cannot be determined; can be understood in 2 ways
A sub-variant of ～とも～とも, leaning toward “ambiguity of interpretation”
<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>とも<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>とも<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>れる

mistakes: Using more than 2 options: ～とも～とも is natural only with exactly two possibilities; for more than two, use ～やら～やら or another kind of listing.
Confusing it with ～にせよ／であれ: these two patterns mean “whether A or B” (regardless), not “cannot say whether A or B”.
Attaching a strongly affirmative predicate: ～とも～とも is usually followed by a negative/hard-to-determine expression; avoid attaching a definitive judgment.
Wrong -な form: writing 便利だとも不便だとも… is not absolutely wrong, but だ is usually omitted to sound more natural: 便利とも不便とも…
Not grammatically parallel: 高いとも安くないとも… sounds forced; use a balanced pair: 高いとも安いとも… or 高いとも高くないとも…
Confusing it with AかBか in questions: AかBか asks for a choice; AともBとも言えない is a comment that no conclusion can be drawn.
JLPT reading trap: the phrase ～とも～ともつかない/取れる expresses “ambiguity”; do not translate it as “both A and B” (and) but as “hard to say whether A or B / can be understood either way”.
1314.notes:
• In terms of form, with -な words and nouns, だ is usually omitted before とも: 便利とも不便とも; 成功とも失敗とも.
• The two parts before とも should be grammatically parallel (same part of speech/same level of negation, or a clear antonym pair) for the sentence to be natural.
• In spoken language, a shortened form is often used: どっちとも言えない instead of listing both in full.
• Do not confuse it with とも meaning “even if” (たとえ～とも); it also differs from 何とも (not… at all) and ～ともなく (unconscious/vague about the agent).
• Often appears in legal documents, research reports, and financial commentary, where cautious language that avoids strong assertions is needed.

examples.jp: 好天と相まって、売り上げが大きく伸びた。
examples.tr: Combined with the good weather, sales rose sharply.

examples.jp: 円安と相まって、海外からの観光客が増加している。
examples.tr: Coupled with the weak yen, the number of tourists from overseas is increasing.

examples.jp: 彼の経験と相まって、チームの努力が成功を導いた。
examples.tr: Combined with his experience, the team's efforts led to success.

examples.jp: 在宅勤務が進むのと相まって、郊外の住宅需要が高まった。
examples.tr: Together with the spread of working from home, demand for suburban housing has grown.

examples.jp: SNSの拡散力と相まって、口コミが一気に広がった。
examples.tr: Combined with the reach of social media, word of mouth spread in no time.

1315.explain:
Emphasizes a relationship of "combined force" rather than simply "and / together with". For plain listing, use と/や.
The things combined are usually objective phenomena/conditions; it is rarely used with specific volitional actions.
Suited to headlines/reports: ～と相まって、～が／を…
It is not used with a negative first clause to express the "absence" of a combined force; in that case use ～ないことも手伝って (which has a different meaning).

• X combines with Y, and the two factors "reinforce" each other to produce result Z. Meaning: "together with", "combined with", "coupled with".
• Formal nuance; written language, reports, news. Expresses a simultaneous, combined-force relationship.
• Often used to describe market, social and natural trends: 景気悪化と相まって／円安と相まって／少子化と相まって.

rows: <ruby>需要<rt>じゅよう</rt></ruby><ruby>増<rt>ぞう</rt></ruby>と<ruby>相<rt>あい</rt></ruby>まって<ruby>価格<rt>かかく</rt></ruby><ruby>高騰<rt>こうとう</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>天気<rt>てんき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いのも<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>って<ruby>完売<rt>かんばい</rt></ruby>。
The more… the more… (change in step)
Proportional change over time; not necessarily a combined force
<ruby>気温<rt>きおん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>下<rt>さ</rt></ruby>がるにつれて<ruby>売上<rt>うりあげ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>伸<rt>の</rt></ruby>びる。
Written entirely in kana, same meaning
<ruby>円<rt>えん</rt></ruby><ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>とあいまって…

mistakes: Using it to join two personal volitional actions → unnatural. Use it for conditions/phenomena.
Confusing it with a simple "and": ～と相まって implies a "combined effect" that causes a result.
Wrong nominalization with a clause: you need ～のと相まって or ～ことと相まって.
1315.notes:
• The verb 相まつ (あいまつ) is archaic; in modern Japanese 相まって is fixed in the te-form.
• It usually comes at the beginning of a sentence as an adverbial phrase, followed by a comma in written language.
• It combines easily with abstract nouns: 相乗効果, 影響, 要因, 需要, 供給, 政策.

examples.jp: 彼は「早くしろ」と言わんばかりに、腕時計を何度も見た。
examples.tr: He kept looking at his watch as if to say, "Hurry up."

examples.jp: 子どもは待ってましたと言わんばかりに、お菓子に飛びついた。
examples.tr: The child pounced on the sweets as if to say, "I've been waiting for this!"

examples.jp: 上司は「質問はするな」と言わんばかりに手で制した。
examples.tr: My boss held up a hand as if to say, "Don't ask questions."

examples.jp: 彼女は「別に興味ない」と言わんばかりの態度で、視線を外した。
examples.tr: She looked away with an attitude that seemed to say, "I'm not really interested."

examples.jp: 猫が餌の皿の前で、くれと言わんばかりに鳴いている。
examples.tr: The cat is meowing in front of its food bowl as if to say, "Feed me."

1316.explain:
Used when a nonverbal signal is strong enough that a spoken message can be inferred from it.
Suited to literary description or vivid reporting; it creates a metaphorical, "personifying" nuance.
Often used with verbs of gesture:見る・にらむ・手で制す・肩をすくめる・うなずく…

• Expresses an attitude/action as if "saying" sentence X, even though it is not said directly. Emphasizes a clear implication conveyed through gestures and facial expressions.
• Often used when the speaker infers a hidden message from another person/thing (even animals).
• Descriptive style; written language or mildly formal conversation; rhetorical.

rows: 「<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>れ」と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>わんばかりに<ruby>睨<rt>にら</rt></ruby>む。
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>だとばかりに<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す。
<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っているかのように<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す。
<ruby>断<rt>ことわ</rt></ruby>れという<ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じで<ruby>首<rt>くび</rt></ruby>を<ruby>振<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る。

mistakes: Using it when there is no clear nonverbal sign → unnatural. A concrete gesture/situation is needed.
Mistaking it for the negative of 言う → incorrect. This is an archaic form meaning “about to say / as if to say”.
Omitting の when modifying a noun: × と言わんばかり態度 → correct: と言わんばかりの態度。
1316.notes:
• “言わん” in modern Japanese is understood as “言おうとする” (about to say). It is not a negative.
• The quoted part can be a short phrase/onomatopoeia: ふんと言わんばかりに肩をすくめた。
• When modifying a noun, use の: ～と言わんばかりの態度／目つき。
explain: Used when describing expressions/gestures that suggest the meaning of words; suited to descriptive and narrative texts.
Common combinations:顔/目/態度/様子/沈黙/仕草/笑み + と言わんばかりの + N.
Compared with “〜ように/〜かのように”: と言わんばかり emphasizes the aspect of “as if saying”.
Not used for objective situations unrelated to “saying” or expressing (e.g. weather, machines) unless personified.
examples: 1. 彼は「もう帰れ」と言わんばかりの顔をした。
He made a face as if to say, “Go home now.”
2. 子どもは助けてほしいと言わんばかりの目でこちらを見上げた。
The child looked up at me with eyes that seemed to beg for help.
3. 彼女は勝ち誇ったと言わんばかりの笑みを浮かべた。
She smiled as if to say she had won.
4. 部長は「早く出せ」と言わんばかりに書類を指さした。
The department manager pointed at the documents as if to say, “Hand it in quickly.”
5. 彼は何も言わず、了解したと言わんばかりのうなずきをした。
He said nothing, just nodded as if to say he understood.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Key difference | Short example
〜と 言（い）わんばかりに/の | As if “saying that …” | Emphasizes implied words through expressions/gestures | 黙（だま）っていろ と言（い）わんばかりに 睨（にら）む
〜とばかりに | As if “it were …” | Broader; not necessarily tied to “saying” | 今（いま）だ とばかりに 走（はし）り出（だ）す
〜かのように | As if, seemingly | Imaginative comparison; more neutral | 何（なに）も知（し）らない かのように 振（ふ）る舞（ま）う
〜と言（い）わんばかりだ | Sentence-final description | Overall evaluation of the whole sentence | 挑発（ちょうはつ）的（てき）だ と言（い）わんばかりだ
common_mistakes: • Using it with direct speech: if something was said outright, と言わんばかり is not used. Incorrect: 「帰れ」と言ってと言わんばかりに… → Redundant.
• Using it for inanimate things without personification → awkward.
• Confusing it with 〜とばかりに: the latter does not emphasize “saying” and has a broader scope.
• Mistaking “言わない” for a negative: in this pattern it is not a negative.

examples.jp: 出張と観光を兼ねてロンドンへ行く。
examples.tr: I'm going to London for both business and sightseeing.

examples.jp: 挨拶とお礼を兼ねてご連絡いたしました。
examples.tr: I am contacting you both to say hello and to express my thanks.

examples.jp: 運動と気分転換を兼ねて歩いて通勤している。
examples.tr: I walk to work, both for exercise and for a change of pace.

examples.jp: 勉強と情報収集を兼ねてセミナーに参加した。
examples.tr: I attended the seminar both to study and to gather information.

examples.jp: 土産と挨拶を兼ねて実家に立ち寄った。
examples.tr: I stopped by my parents' house both to bring a souvenir and to say hello.

1317.explain:
N1 and N2 are both legitimate purposes/functions; there is no clear main-versus-secondary relationship as with “while I'm at it”.
Often attached to purposeful actions (going, coming, attending, sending, giving…).
In formal language, it is often used with keigo:伺う・差し上げる・いたす…
It is not used directly with a clause/verb as a noun unless nominalized (N + の).

- Meaning: “combining both N1 and N2”, “both … and …”, “while at it (doubling as)”. Expresses one action that serves two purposes/functions at the same time.
- Nuance: objective, neutral; often used in written language and business. Compared with ～ついでに, 兼ねて emphasizes “serving two clear purposes”.
- The structure that follows is usually a verb of motion/doing: 行く・訪ねる・参加する・書く・贈る・使う…

rows: <ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>と<ruby>観光<rt>かんこう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>兼<rt>か</rt></ruby>ねて<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く
While doing A, also do B
<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くついでに<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す
Attaches to a limited set of nouns: <ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>/<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>/お<ruby>礼<rt>れい</rt></ruby>…
ご<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>かたがた<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>いました
<ruby>視察<rt>しさつ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>兼<rt>か</rt></ruby>ねて<ruby>訪問<rt>ほうもん</rt></ruby>する

mistakes: Writing “N1とN2に兼ねて”: incorrect. It must be “N1とN2を兼ねて”.
Using it with a verb that has not been nominalized: incorrect. You need N + の to nominalize it.
Confusing it with ついでに: 兼ねて does not imply a “secondary, while-at-it” action but “serving two purposes”.
JLPT exam: a trap is choosing “Nかたがた” for an ordinary context (too formal).
1317.notes:
• Because the N goes with 兼ねる, keep を before 兼ねて. When listing with と, only the noun after と takes を.
• Choose nouns with a “purpose/function” sense; avoid abstract nouns that are hard to “combine” (e.g. 幸せ・愛… are unnatural).
• In titles/brochures you often see the noun-modifying form: 「観光を兼ねた出張プラン」.

examples.jp: この映画は観る者を涙させないではおかない。
examples.tr: This movie is bound to move its viewers to tears.

examples.jp: 彼の無責任な発言は批判を招かないではおかない。
examples.tr: His irresponsible remarks are bound to draw criticism.

examples.jp: その記事は社会に大きな議論を巻き起こさないではおかない。
examples.tr: That article is bound to stir up a major debate in society.

examples.jp: 彼女の真摯な姿勢は周囲を感心させずにはおかない。
examples.tr: Her sincere attitude cannot fail to impress those around her.

examples.jp: この事実の暴露は政府を動かさないではおかない。
examples.tr: The exposure of this fact is bound to force the government to act.

1318.explain:
Used to make a confident prediction/inference about a consequence that has an effect on others.
Not used to talk about the speaker's own personal obligation (use ～ないではすまない for obligation).
The subject is usually an event/product/action, not the speaker.
Formal style; journalism, literary criticism.

• Asserts inevitability: “will certainly lead to / that action or change cannot fail to happen”.
• Often used when a thing/event has such a strong impact that others “cannot help but” react.
• Written-language nuance; the speaker's objective/strong judgment; it does not mean “I am forced to do it”.
• Often used with verbs of psychological or behavioral reaction: 驚かせる, 考えさせる, 批判を招く, 物議を醸す.

rows: <ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>かせないではおかない。
<ruby>笑<rt>わらわ</rt></ruby>わずにはいられない。
Cannot be settled without doing it (obligation)
<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>らないではすまない。
General statement; does not imply a mechanism of “causing an effect”.

mistakes: Using it to say “I am forced to …”: wrong function. Use ～ないではすまない/～なければならない.
Combining it with verbs that have no sense of impact: less natural. Choose 招く, 促す, 驚かせる, 影響を与える.
Confusing the agent: the agent is usually an event/product, not “I”.
JLPT questions often test the variant pair ～ずにはおかない ⇄ ～ないではおかない: they are equivalent in meaning.
1318.notes:
• The pattern often goes with the causative structure ～をV-させる to highlight “making people …”.
• In analytical texts, it combines with abstract nouns: 波紋、影響、議論、批判、共感.
• The ずにはおかない form usually sounds more formal and academic.

examples.jp: これだけ騒ぎを起こしたのだから、責任者は記者会見で説明しないではすまない。
examples.tr: After causing this much of a stir, the person in charge will have to explain at a press conference.

examples.jp: みんなに迷惑をかけたのだから、謝らないではすまない。
examples.tr: Since I caused everyone trouble, I have to apologize.

examples.jp: ルールに違反した以上、処分しないではすまない。
examples.tr: Since the rules were broken, disciplinary action has to be taken.

examples.jp: 重大なミスをしたから、上司に報告せずにはすまない。
examples.tr: I made a serious mistake, so I have no choice but to report it to my boss.

examples.jp: 期限を二度も破ったのだから、今回は契約を見直さないではすまない。
examples.tr: Since the deadline has been missed twice, this time the contract will have to be reviewed.

1319.explain:
Serious, formal nuance; used in documents, official statements, and legal/moral judgments.
The one with the obligation is the responsible individual/organization.
Often combined with phrases stating a binding condition: ～以上、～からには、～手前.
Not used to talk about habits or light personal plans.

• Expresses an obligation/norm arising from circumstances, morality, rules or social relationships: “not doing V would not be acceptable / would not end things”.
• Unlike a general “must”, this pattern emphasizes external pressure or social norms.
• Often used in the context “since A happened, B is necessary”: ～以上、～からには、～以上は.

rows: Cannot be settled without doing it (obligation)
<ruby>賠償<rt>ばいしょう</rt></ruby>しないではすまない。
Inevitable effect, not the subject's obligation.
<ruby>物議<rt>ぶつぎ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>醸<rt>かも</rt></ruby>さないではおかない。
Neutral; not necessarily due to a specific social norm.
Cannot not do (because of the situation)
Similar in meaning, but leans toward common sense/circumstances rather than strict norms.
<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>しないわけにはいかない。
<ruby>笑<rt>わらわ</rt></ruby>わずにはいられない。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～ないではおかない: the latter means “will inevitably cause”, not obligation.
Using it for small matters with no social constraint (今日、掃除しないではすまない): unnatural unless there is a compelling reason.
Wrong negative form: it must be Vない + では + すまない or Vずにはすまない.
In JLPT multiple-choice questions, the correct answer usually involves apologizing/compensating/explaining: 謝る, 弁償する, 説明する, 報告する.
1319.notes:
• Often appears in legal/business documents: ～措置を講じないではすまない, ～対応せずにはすまない.
• The past form すまなかった is used when looking back on a situation in which the obligation arose and was carried out.
• Besides apologizing/compensating, it can be used with any corrective action: 説明する, 公表する, 是正する, 返金する.

examples.jp: 優勝はできないまでも、ベスト４には入りたい。
examples.tr: Even if I can't win the championship, I want to make it into the top four.

examples.jp: 毎日とはいかないまでも、週数回は練習する。
examples.tr: Even if not every day, I practice several times a week.

examples.jp: 理想とまではいかないが、現実的な案だ。
examples.tr: It's not quite ideal, but it's a realistic plan.

1320.explain:
Sets “A = the standard”, then lowers expectations to accept “B”.
The style is more polite than ～ほどではないが.
Not used when the second clause is a total negation.

• Does not reach level A, but still reaches an acceptable level B.
• Modest and realistic; works well in reports/evaluations.
• A is usually a high standard: 完璧・理想・一流・満点・優勝.

rows: Not as far as A, but B
プロにはなれないまでも
<ruby>痛<rt>いたい</rt></ruby>いほどではないが
<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby>でないにしても

mistakes: Attaching a noun directly to ないまでも → you need と(は)いかない: ×完璧ないまでも.
Using a strongly negative clause after ～ないまでも → does not fit the idea of “still achieving something”.
Distinguish it from ～ないことはない (weak possibility) in multiple-choice questions.
1320.notes:
• Typical pairs: 完璧とはいかないまでも／理想とはいかないまでも.
• Suitable for progress reports, product evaluations, and realistic goals.

examples.jp: 事故をこれ以上増やさないものだろうか。
examples.tr: Isn't there some way to keep accidents from increasing any further?

examples.jp: もう少し締め切りを延ばせないものだろうか。
examples.tr: Couldn't the deadline be extended a little longer?

1321.explain:
Not used as a direct command to the listener.
Suitable for writing, speeches, and work discussions.

• Hoping that something difficult can be achieved: “I wonder if it might be possible to…?”.
• Used with problems that are difficult, wide-ranging, or beyond the speaker's control.

rows: <ruby>改善<rt>かいぜん</rt></ruby>できないものだろうか
<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれないだろうか

mistakes: Using it to give a direct command → wrong nuance.
Confusing it with ～ないものでもない (weak, conditional affirmative).

examples.jp: 彼は生まれながらに優れた音感を持っている。
examples.tr: He was born with an excellent ear for music.

examples.jp: 家にいながらにして世界の講義を受けられる時代だ。
examples.tr: We live in an age when you can take lectures from around the world without leaving home.

examples.jp: 彼女は涙ながらに真実を語った。
examples.tr: She told the truth in tears.

examples.jp: この町は昔ながらに石畳の道が残っている。
examples.tr: This town still has its stone-paved streets, just as in the old days.

examples.jp: 都会にいながらにして自然の恵みを感じられる。
examples.tr: Even while living in the city, you can feel the blessings of nature.

1322.explain:
〜ながらに emphasizes “remaining in a state” rather than simultaneous actions like ordinary 〜ながら.
“〜ながらにして” is used to say “even while in that state/condition, one can still…”.
Suited to formal expression; describing tradition, innate qualities, or modern means that let you do something “right where you are”.

• “While still” keeping the original state/condition.
• Expresses doing/achieving something while keeping an existing state (innate, inherent, or through present-day means).
• Formal style; often found in written language, advertising, and explanatory texts.
• Limited use: mainly in set phrases such as 生まれながらに, 涙ながらに, 昔ながらに, 居ながらにして.

rows: <ruby>涙<rt>なみだ</rt></ruby>ながらに<ruby>訴<rt>うった</rt></ruby>える
Broad, colloquial; does not emphasize an “inherent state”
<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聴<rt>きき</rt></ruby>きながら<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>する
Used as an adjective: “having the inherent (look of)…”
ドアを<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けたままにする

mistakes: Using 〜ながらに for any simultaneous actions → incorrect; use ordinary 〜ながら for “while doing… also…”.
Confusing 〜ながらに with 〜ながらの: に = adverbial; の = noun modifier.
Omitting “して” when you need to emphasize the means: 家にいながら〜 and 家にいながらにして〜 are not completely synonymous in nuance.
1322.notes:
• Typical phrases: 生まれながらに（して）, 昔ながらに, 涙ながらに, 居ながらにして, 家にいながらにして.
• The subject is usually a person/thing with an “innate/inherent” quality, or the context is “right where you are”.
• Do not overuse it with every verb, as it will sound awkward; prefer established phrases.

1323.meaning: Inherent… / as it has always been

examples.jp: この店は昔ながらの製法にこだわっている。
examples.tr: This shop is committed to traditional production methods.

examples.jp: 彼は生まれながらのリーダーだ。
examples.tr: He is a born leader.

examples.jp: 彼女はいつもながらの穏やかな口調で話した。
examples.tr: She spoke in her usual calm tone.

examples.jp: 昔ながらの街並みが観光客を惹きつける。
examples.tr: The old-fashioned streetscape attracts tourists.

examples.jp: 彼の演奏には職人ながらの繊細さがある。
examples.tr: His performance has the delicacy of a true craftsman.

1323.explain:
Directly modifies a noun to state a quality that is “the way it has always been / innate”.
Often seen with:昔ながらの +味／家／街並み／製法／店,生まれながらの +才能／天分／素質, いつもながらの +笑顔／優しさ.
Formal; suited to explanatory texts and advertising for traditional products.

• Noun modifier: “having the inherent look/state of…”, “true to… as it has always been”.
• Emphasizes tradition, innate qualities, and unchanging characteristics.
• Formal/descriptive nuance; often used with nouns for flavors, scenery, style, personality, and innate abilities.

rows: Noun modifier: having an inherent look
Adverbial: while remaining in a state…
<ruby>昔<rt>むかし</rt></ruby>ながらに<ruby>暮<rt>く</rt></ruby>らす
<ruby>伝統<rt>でんとう</rt></ruby><ruby>的<rt>てき</rt></ruby>な N
Similar meaning but with less of the “unchanged since long ago” nuance of ながらの
<ruby>伝統<rt>でんとう</rt></ruby><ruby>的<rt>てき</rt></ruby>な<ruby>製法<rt>せいほう</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Wrong position: using 〜ながらに to modify a noun. Correct: 〜ながらの N.
Overusing it with modern nouns that do not fit the context (e.g. “最新ながらのデザイン” → awkward).
Using it with unstable (temporary) qualities → contradicts the “inherent/unchanging” nuance.
1323.notes:
• “Vます-stem + ながらの” is in fact a nominalization of the verb stem: 生まれ（る）→ 生まれながらの.
• “いつもながらの” is a very common set phrase for praising stability/consistency.
• “〜ながらの” evokes more emotional/nostalgic value than neutral adjectives.

examples.jp: 努力なくしては、目標は達成できない。
examples.tr: Without effort, you cannot achieve your goals.

examples.jp: 市民の理解と協力なくしては、改革は前に進まない。
examples.tr: Without the understanding and cooperation of citizens, reform cannot move forward.

examples.jp: 十分な資金なくして、事業は成り立たない。
examples.tr: Without sufficient funds, a business cannot be viable.

examples.jp: データに基づく検証なくしては、結論は出せない。
examples.tr: Without verification based on data, no conclusion can be drawn.

examples.jp: 信頼関係なくしては、チームは機能しない。
examples.tr: Without relationships of trust, a team cannot function.

1324.explain:
Always used with a negative second clause: ～ない／ありえない／成り立たない／不可能だ.
Suitable for headlines/slogans: 「安全なくして生産なし」.
More formal than ～なしには～ない; used to emphasize something absolute.
Not used for trivial/overly obvious conditions in everyday spoken language.

• Without having/doing X, Y is impossible. Emphasizes that X is “absolutely necessary”.
• Strong, formal nuance; used in speeches, slogans, and commentary.
• Often used with positive abstract nouns: 努力, 協力, 理解, 支援, 規律, 資金, 計画, 信頼.

rows: <ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>なくしては<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>はない。
More neutral; often used in spoken language
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>なしには<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>できない。
States an obligation rather than a condition and its consequence
<ruby>資金<rt>しきん</rt></ruby>がなくてはならない。
Y exists only thanks to X
お<ruby>客<rt>きゃくさま</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt></rt></ruby>あっての<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Dropping the negative in the second clause → grammatically incorrect. This pattern must end in a negative.
Using it for small everyday matters → too heavy. Choose a formal/serious context.
Confusing it with ～なくてはならない (obligation) → a different function.
Forgetting to nominalize when using a clause: you need ～こと／～の＋なくしては.
1324.notes:
• Some fixed combinations in the second clause: ～はありえない／～は実現しない／～は語れない／～は成り立たない.
• In slogans/short sentences, は after なくして is often omitted: 努力なくして成功なし。
• The first clause can be a series of nouns joined with と: 努力と工夫なくしては…

examples.jp: インターネットなしでは、現代社会は成り立たない。
examples.tr: Without the internet, modern society could not function.

examples.jp: 彼の助けなしでは、このプロジェクトは成功しないだろう。
examples.tr: Without his help, this project probably won't succeed.

examples.jp: 証拠なしでは、彼を有罪にすることはできない。
examples.tr: Without evidence, we cannot find him guilty.

examples.jp: 練習なしでは、上達はありえない。
examples.tr: Without practice, improvement is impossible.

examples.jp: 資金なしでは、研究は続けられない。
examples.tr: Without funding, the research cannot continue.

examples.jp: 予約なしでは、入場できません。
examples.tr: Admission is not possible without a reservation.

1325.explain:
Used when you want to affirm that N is “indispensable” to an action/result.
Suitable for presentations, reports, and descriptions of systems and procedures (expresses a condition-consequence relationship).
The second clause is usually a verb of ability/possibility of existence: できない・ありえない・成り立たない・難しい.
Not used to express a deliberate act of “doing something without N” (in that case use “N なしで V”).
The subject can be general/subjective; however, the nuance leans toward an objective judgment.

• The pattern “～なしでは～ない” expresses a necessary condition: without N, the following action/result cannot happen, is very unlikely to happen, or does not exist.
• Objective nuance, a general evaluation of how necessary N is (a foundation, condition, means, or resource).
• The second clause is usually a negation of ability/possibility: できない・ありえない・成り立たない・進まない・語れない・理解できない.
• Formality: usable in both written and spoken language; often used in written language, scientific explanations, and journalism to state a necessity.
• Unlike “N なしで”, which simply means “without having/using N”, “N なしでは” implies “because N is missing, it is impossible”.

rows: <ruby>証拠<rt>しょうこ</rt></ruby>なしでは<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>できない
Stiffer nuance; often goes with abstract action nouns (<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>・<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>)
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>なしには<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>しない
Written language; emphasizes that without N it cannot happen
<ruby>信頼<rt>しんらい</rt></ruby>なくしてはチームは<ruby>成<rt>な</rt></ruby>り<ruby>立<rt>たた</rt></ruby>たない
<ruby>朝食<rt>ちょうしょく</rt></ruby>なしで<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけた
If not A, then not B
General condition pattern, not limited to nouns
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>てみないことには<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない

mistakes: Confusing it with “N なしで”: “なしで” only means “without N” and does not imply “cannot”. The JLPT often sets traps with these two patterns.
Using an affirmative second clause: you need ない／できない／難しい… If the second clause is affirmative, the nuance is wrong.
Choosing an unsuitable noun: with something that is not a necessary condition, “なしでは” sounds forced.
Confusing it with “なしには”: the meanings are close, but “なしには” is slightly more formal/stiff and often goes with abstract action nouns (努力・説明).
1325.notes:
• N is usually a fundamental element: 資金・計画・説明・理解・協力・技術・データ・証拠・準備・許可.
• In policy/regulation sentences, this pattern makes the statement more decisive and is common in notices: 許可なしでは入れません.
• Emphatic variants: ～なしではやっていけない (cannot get by), ～なしでは語れない (cannot be discussed or mentioned without).

examples.jp: 努力なしには、夢は叶わない。
examples.tr: Without effort, dreams do not come true.

examples.jp: 許可なしには、入室できません。
examples.tr: You may not enter the room without permission.

examples.jp: 十分な説明なしには、顧客は納得しない。
examples.tr: Without a thorough explanation, customers won't be satisfied.

examples.jp: 合意なしには、計画は前に進まない。
examples.tr: Without agreement, the plan cannot move forward.

examples.jp: データなしには、議論は始まらない。
examples.tr: Without data, the discussion cannot even begin.

examples.jp: 予習なしには、授業についていけない。
examples.tr: Without preparing in advance, you can't keep up with the class.

1326.explain:
Choose an N that is a required condition/procedure, something “procedural” or “fundamental” (許可・同意・説明・検証・準備).
Normative, decisive nuance; suitable for notices, procedures, and business work.
Can be used as “～ことなしには” to make written language more formal.
Not used if you only want to say “did it without N” (use “N なしで”).

• “～なしには～ない” = “unless there is N / without N, cannot/does not happen”.
• Stronger and more formal nuance than “～なしでは”; often used when N is a necessary action/procedure (努力・説明・合意・準備・許可).
• The second clause is a negative form of ability/progress: できない・ありえない・進まない・始まらない・成立しない.
• Often appears in regulations, theses, and business guidelines to emphasize a mandatory condition.

rows: Formal/stiff; often used with action/procedure nouns
<ruby>合意<rt>ごうい</rt></ruby>なしには<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>めない
More neutral; widely used for conditions/resources
<ruby>資金<rt>しきん</rt></ruby>なしでは<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>められない
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>なくしては<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>なし
<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>なしで<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めた
If not A, then not B
Extends to clauses, not limited to nouns
<ruby>試<rt>ため</rt></ruby>してみないことには<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からない

mistakes: Mixing it up with “なしで”: the JLPT often sets the pair 許可なしで/許可なしには as a trap. Choose “なしには” when the second clause means “cannot/may not”.
Using an affirmative second clause: a negative is required (ない・できない・進まない…).
Choosing an unsuitable N (not a condition/procedure) makes the sentence sound forced. Example: “花なしには勉強できない” is usually unnatural.
Confusing the nuance with “なしでは”: both are correct in meaning, but when an exam asks about a formal/normative nuance, “なしには” is preferred.
1326.notes:
• The form “Vることなしには” emphasizes the procedural nature: 確認することなしには出荷しない.
• In advertising/PR, it may be used to emphasize a standard: 身分証なしには購入できません.
• To sound softer in conversation, you can replace it with “N がないと～ない”.

1327.connection: N + ならいざ知らず / V/A plain form + (の)なら

examples.jp: 子どもならいざ知らず、大人がそんなことをするのは恥ずかしい。
examples.tr: It might be different for a child, but it is shameful for an adult to do such a thing.

examples.jp: 冗談ならいざ知らず、本気でそんな要求は飲めない。
examples.tr: If it were a joke, that would be one thing, but I cannot seriously accept such a demand.

examples.jp: 昔ならいざ知らず、今はそんなやり方は通用しない。
examples.tr: That may have worked in the old days, but that approach no longer works today.

examples.jp: 専門家ならいざ知らず、素人には判断できないだろう。
examples.tr: An expert might be able to, but an amateur probably cannot judge it.

examples.jp: 少人数ならいざ知らず、百人規模ではこの方法は無理だ。
examples.tr: It might work with a small group, but this method is impossible on the scale of 100 people.

examples.jp: 旅行ならいざ知らず、出張では観光する時間はない。
examples.tr: On a vacation it would be different, but on a business trip there is no time for sightseeing.

1327.explain:
Used to present an “acceptable hypothetical exception” and then reject the actual situation.
Stays polite but has a nuance of criticism; avoid using it directly with superiors/customers if possible.
Often combined with evaluation words: 恥ずかしい・受け入れられない・無理だ・通用しない・難しい・すべきではない.
The first clause is usually a noun: 冗談・子ども・昔・専門家・少人数・試作品など.

• “～ならいざ知らず” = “if it were ~, it would be somewhat acceptable/understandable, but … (is unsuitable/hard to accept/impossible)”.
• Expresses a hypothetical contrast: sets up an understandable case in order to emphasize that the current reality is unacceptable.
• Nuance of criticism/polite argument, somewhat archaic/written language; used when you want to keep distance and stay objective.
• The second clause is usually a negative judgment, a prohibition, a criticism, or “does not apply/is not accepted”.

rows: If it were ~, it would be less bad, but…
Formal, somewhat written; presents a hypothetical exception
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>ならいざ<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らず、<ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby><ruby>人<rt>じん</rt></ruby>は…
If it were ~, it would be acceptable, but…
<ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>はまだしも、<ruby>無断<rt>むだん</rt></ruby><ruby>欠勤<rt>けっきん</rt></ruby>はだめだ
The second clause is not necessarily negative
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>た<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>はともかく、<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>はいい
Comparison against expectations, no hypothetical exception
<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもにしては<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>だ

mistakes: Using it with an affirmative/positive second clause: wrong nuance. The second clause should be negative/hard to accept.
Using it with the subject “I/we” to talk about yourself sounds unnatural, because the nuance criticizes other people/general matters.
Confusing it with “ならまだしも”: exams set traps with these two patterns; “ならいざ知らず” is more formal and carries the meaning “I cannot say about ~”.
Placing it after a long, complex verb: prefer a short, concise noun in the first clause so the sentence sounds more natural.
1327.notes:
• “いざ知らず” originally means “I cannot say about ~” and developed into a hypothetical concession that emphasizes the negation in the second clause.
• Often found in essays/expert opinions to avoid direct criticism while still keeping a position.
• A similar inversion can be made by using “～ならともかく”: its nuance is lighter than “ならいざ知らず”.

examples.jp: 子どもなら子どもなりに考えている。
examples.tr: Children think about things in their own way, as children.

examples.jp: 行くなら行くなりに準備をしなさい。
examples.tr: If you're going, then prepare properly for it.

examples.jp: 安いなら安いなりに使い道がある。
examples.tr: Even if it's cheap, it has its uses as a cheap item.

examples.jp: できないならできないなりにベストを尽くす。
examples.tr: If I can't do it, I'll still do my best within my limits.

examples.jp: 彼は忙しいなら忙しいなりの工夫をしている。
examples.tr: He is busy, so he finds ways of coping that suit his busy schedule.

1328.explain:
Emphasizes appropriateness, without comparing beyond one's level; avoids excessive complaining.
Can be used in polite criticism: ～なら～なりにしなさい/考えなさい.
“～なりの N” is used to make it concrete: 自分なりの答え, 会社なりの方針.
The tone can be admonishing, sometimes a little stern.

• Appropriateness/propriety: “If …, then (do/can) … in the way/at the level of …”.
• Adapting to conditions: adjusting expectations/actions to suit the circumstances and level.
• Implied limitation: acknowledges limits but still has its own value/way (according to ability, budget, age, level...).
• Advisory usage: used to give gentle advice or indirect criticism.

rows: Neutral, objective; does not imply “if you're going to …, do … properly”.
<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>応<rt>おう</rt></ruby>じて<ruby>選<rt>えら</rt></ruby>ぶ。
Focuses on quantity/limitation; lacks the nuance of “appropriateness”.
できるだけ<ruby>頑張<rt>がんば</rt></ruby>る。
A common branch of this pattern; emphasizes the agent doing it “by oneself”.
<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>なりに<ruby>工夫<rt>くふう</rt></ruby>する。
Carries an evaluation; does not form a repeated pair like ～なら～なりに.

mistakes: Dropping the repetition: “子どもなら自分なりに” is incorrect when the matching “子どもなら子どもなりに” is needed.
Using it for extreme praise or criticism: the pattern accepts limitations; it does not make absolute statements.
Confusing it with ～に応じて: the JLPT often asks you to distinguish the nuance of “appropriate/befitting”.
Wrong form “Adj-ななら Adj-ななりに” (the correct form keeps “な” only once: 静かなら静かなりに).
1328.notes:
• Repeating the same element before and after “なら/なりに” is the characteristic feature of the structure.
• Often combined with a contrast to expectations: 安いなら安いなりに（それ相応の）品質だ.
• In formal writing, “～なりの + N” appears more often, to nominalize the criterion of appropriateness.

examples.jp: コーヒーなり紅茶なり、何か飲みませんか。
examples.tr: Would you like something to drink, like coffee or tea?

examples.jp: 困ったら、先生に聞くなり、図書館で調べるなりしなさい。
examples.tr: If you're stuck, either ask the teacher or look it up in the library.

examples.jp: 休みの日は映画を見るなり、散歩するなりして気分転換しよう。
examples.tr: On days off, let's refresh ourselves by watching a movie or taking a walk.

examples.jp: 暇ならゲームをするなり、本を読むなりすればいい。
examples.tr: If you're free, you could play a game or read a book.

examples.jp: 資料はメールなりFAXなりで送ってください。
examples.tr: Please send the documents by email or fax.

examples.jp: 何かあれば、電話するなりメッセージを送るなりしてください。
examples.tr: If anything comes up, please call or send a message.

1329.explain:
The two listed items should be of the same type (both nouns or both verbs in the dictionary form).
Emphasizes “a concrete action” rather than just listing information.
The nuance can be a bit pushy; use it with equals/acquaintances. With customers/superiors, choose a softer way.
Usually accompanied by an ending that expresses a suggestion/mild command.

• Presents two (or more) choices, “for example A or B”, implying “any way is fine, choose one and do it”.
• Nuance of a mild to moderate suggestion/request; sometimes it feels like urging “do something”.
• Used in instructions, advice, or polite suggestions; not neutral like とか/や, and stronger in terms of “action”.
• The sentence often ends with してください／したらどうですか／しなさい／しよう／すればいい.

rows: For example A or B, doing either is fine
Suggests an action, mild nuance of urging
<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くなり<ruby>薬<rt>くすり</rt></ruby>を<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>むなりしなさい
Neutral, does not push for action
<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>雑誌<rt>ざっし</rt></ruby>とかを<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>む
A different grammar point, not a listing
<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>るなり<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>てしまった

mistakes: Mixing word classes: “N なり Vる なり” is unnatural; they must be of the same type (N-N, V-V).
Using it to describe a one-time past event with no sense of suggestion → とか/や is a better choice.
Confusing it with “Vるなり” meaning “as soon as…”; exams often set traps with this pair.
Using the bare command form as is with superiors/customers sounds rude; switch to a polite form of suggestion.
1329.notes:
• In polite language, the ending can be changed to ～してはいかがでしょうか／～されてはどうでしょうか to reduce the pressure.
• “A なり B なりして” is a very natural frame for advising the listener to “do something”.
• When listing more than two, three items can be used, but keep the rhythm concise and avoid wordiness.

examples.jp: 非常時にあっては、デマに惑わされないこと。
examples.tr: In an emergency, do not be misled by false rumors.

examples.jp: 不況下にあっては、資金繰りの確保が最優先だ。
examples.tr: In a recession, securing cash flow is the top priority.

examples.jp: 江戸後期にあって、商業が発展した。
examples.tr: In the late Edo period, commerce developed.

examples.jp: 彼の立場にあっては、発言には最大限の注意が求められる。
examples.tr: In his position, the utmost care is required in what he says.

examples.jp: 厳しい状況にあっても、挑戦をやめなかった。
examples.tr: Even in a harsh situation, they did not stop trying.

1330.explain:
Placed at the beginning of a sentence to set the context for an argument/recommendation.
Combines with nouns such as: 非常時／緊急時／不況下／戦時／現場／立場／制度下.
Avoid it in casual speech because it sounds too formal.

• Indicates an era, circumstance, or position; used to state what should be done/what is characteristic within that framework.
• Serious nuance, suitable for regulations, reports, and research papers.
• The form ～にあっても adds a contrasting clause to emphasize will/persistence.

rows: Spoken language; does not emphasize norms.
<ruby>緊急<rt>きんきゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>時<rt>とき</rt></ruby>では<ruby>冷静<rt>れいせい</rt></ruby>に。
Formal but neutral; puts little emphasis on a “special condition”.
<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>において<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>する。
A theoretical/regulatory viewpoint; differs from the actual context.
<ruby>制度<rt>せいど</rt></ruby><ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby><ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>はない。

mistakes: Applying it to a noun that is not a context: × 公園にあっては → use 公園では.
Confusing the particles: にあっては ≠ においては; exams often test choosing the right nuance.
Using it in ordinary conversation makes the sentence heavy and unnatural.
1330.notes:
• In legal/administrative language, ～にあっては often goes with a command/condition: ～しなければならない／～こと.
• “不況下にあっては” is a model phrase in economic commentary.
• The past form is rarely used; it is mainly used in the present to describe general norms.

examples.jp: 教師にあるまじき発言だ。
examples.tr: That is a remark unbecoming of a teacher.

examples.jp: 医者にあるまじきミスが起きた。
examples.tr: A mistake unworthy of a doctor occurred.

examples.jp: 公務員にあるまじき不正で、厳しく処分された。
examples.tr: They were severely punished for misconduct unbecoming of a civil servant.

examples.jp: 親としてあるまじき態度だ。
examples.tr: That is an attitude unbecoming of a parent.

examples.jp: 彼の暴言は、リーダーにあるまじきものだ。
examples.tr: His abusive language is unbecoming of a leader.

1331.explain:
Extremely formal and critical; avoid it in casual communication unless emphasizing morality.
Often combined with nouns for “behavior”: 行為・発言・態度・振る舞い・不祥事・ミス.
Usually placed right before the noun being evaluated: N1にあるまじきN2.
The classical feel (あるまじき) creates a strong normative impression and sometimes sounds “harsh”.

• Expresses behavior/an attitude that is “unacceptable, unworthy” of a position, profession, or moral standard.
• Strong criticism, often seen in the news, codes of ethics, and official statements.
• N1 is a role: 教師・医者・公務員・親・学生・政治家・社会人… N2 is 発言・行為・態度・ミス・不祥事, etc.

rows: Milder and more neutral than あるまじき.
<ruby>教師<rt>きょうし</rt></ruby>にふさわしくない<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>。
Expresses a personal opinion, less normative.
<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>とは<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>えない<ruby>振<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る<ruby>舞<rt>ま</rt></ruby>い。
General admonition; あるまじき is stronger and morally critical.
そんな<ruby>発言<rt>はつげん</rt></ruby>をすべきではない。
Emphasizes the emotion of “shame”; strong in degree, but not as classical as あるまじき.
<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>として<ruby>恥<rt>は</rt></ruby>ずべき<ruby>行為<rt>こうい</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Wrong word order: × あるまじき教師の発言 → ○ 教師にあるまじき発言.
Using it with a target that is not a “role/status”: × 天気にあるまじき → not appropriate.
Confusing the degree with ～にふさわしくない: あるまじき is stronger and carries moral condemnation.
Leaving out the noun after あるまじき makes the sentence incomplete: an N2 such as 行為・発言 is needed to complete it.
1331.notes:
• From the archaic “あるまじき” = あるべからざる; belongs to the same semantic field of moral taboos.
• Favored in newspaper headlines to emphasize the degree of seriousness.
• Can be used for self-criticism, but easily gives a dramatic impression: 私も教師にあるまじき言動をしてしまった。

1332.meaning: Only when… for the first time…

examples.jp: 教師にして初めて、生徒の気持ちの複雑さが分かった。
examples.tr: Only after becoming a teacher did I understand how complex students' feelings are.

examples.jp: 現場責任者にして初めて、判断の重さを痛感する。
examples.tr: Only as the person in charge on site do you truly feel the weight of decisions.

examples.jp: 30歳にして初めて、自分の進む道が見えた。
examples.tr: Only at 30 did I see the path I should take.

examples.jp: 社会人にして初めて、時間管理の大切さが身に染みた。
examples.tr: Only after starting work did the importance of time management really sink in.

examples.jp: 親にして初めて、親のありがたみが分かるものだ。
examples.tr: Only when you become a parent yourself do you understand how much you owe your parents.

1332.explain:
Formal, with a depth of experience; suitable for reflective or inspirational writing.
Avoid using it with a trivial/meaningless milestone; it should be a “turning point”.
Often goes with idioms of strong feeling: 身に染みる・痛感する・骨身にこたえる.

Meaning: “Only when (reaching) N does … happen for the first time”. Emphasizes an important/noteworthy milestone, suggesting that it came late, was hard to reach, or that experience/strict conditions were needed to obtain the result/realization.
• N: a point in time (40歳, 入社三年目), a status (親, 社会人, プロ), a setting (現場, 海外).
• Second clause: achieving/realizing something for the first time (～ようになる／分かる／悟る／実感する／達成する).
• Used a lot in written language, essays, memoirs, and interviews about experiences.

rows: Only after doing V, for the first time…
Common, conversational; emphasizes the action V
<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>いて<ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>税金<rt>ぜいきん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>さを<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>った。
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>になって<ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かった。
It is precisely by V that there is value
Usually states a general truth/value, not only “the first time”
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>してこそ<ruby>成長<rt>せいちょう</rt></ruby>できる。
A negative condition, not a “first-time turning point”
<ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>してからでないと<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>できない。

mistakes: Using it with an N that is not a “milestone” → the meaning becomes vague.
Confusing it with Vて初めて when the milestone is a concrete action → Vて初めて is more natural.
Using it for a random, one-time event with no “accumulation” → not suitable.
1332.notes:
• Repetitive structure that adds weight: ～にして初めて、～と分かった／～ことに気づいた.
• Can be combined with ordinal numbers to emphasize lateness: 三度目にして初めて合格した。
• In headlines/interviews: “現場にして初めて見えた真実”.

examples.jp: 彼の理論は、専門家にすら理解が難しい。
examples.tr: His theory is difficult to understand even for experts.

examples.jp: 財布を忘れて、水も買うお金すらない。
examples.tr: I forgot my wallet, so I don't even have money to buy water.

examples.jp: 多忙で、家族と話す時間すら取れない。
examples.tr: I'm so busy that I can't even find time to talk with my family.

examples.jp: 古いPCでは、メールの送受信にすら手間取る。
examples.tr: With an old PC, even sending and receiving email is a struggle.

examples.jp: その事実は当事者にすら知られていなかった。
examples.tr: That fact was not known even to the people involved.

1333.explain:
Often used with ～ない/難しい/不足する to strengthen the negative nuance.
Emphatic and formal; also common in ads and headlines that aim for a strong impression.
Avoid overusing it in casual conversation, as it sounds stiff.

“～にすら/～すら” = “even …”. Stronger than “～さえ”; usually used with negative sentences or difficulties to emphasize surprise, or a degree of badness/harshness beyond expectations.
• Choose “にすら” when the function of “に” must be kept: recipient, place, point in time.
• It emphasizes a minimal example, from which it follows that the other cases are naturally true as well.
• Used a lot in written language, newspapers and speeches; in spoken language, “さえ” is more natural.

rows: <ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>どころか、<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。
More polite; usually in serious writing
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>ですら<ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>いた。

mistakes: Using “にすら” in the wrong place: × 水にすらない → 〇 水すらない.
Confusing it with “さえ”: exam questions test the nuance; “すら” = more formal/stronger.
Forgetting to nominalize when attaching it to a verb: × 行くすらできない → 〇 行くことすらできない.
1333.notes:
• The closer “すら” is placed to the element being emphasized, the stronger the effect: 「彼にすらできない」 vs 「彼はすらできない」.
• With abstract verbs: 想像すらしなかった／予想すらしなかった → “did not even imagine”.
• In polite style: 説明は専門家ですら難解です。

1335.meaning: Whenever… / every time…; both when ~ and when ~

examples.jp: 見るにつけ聞くにつけ、彼の努力に頭が下がる。
examples.tr: Whatever I see or hear of it, I can only bow my head to his hard work.

examples.jp: うれしいにつけ悲しいにつけ、彼女は日記に書き留める。
examples.tr: Whether happy or sad, she writes it down in her diary.

examples.jp: 写真を見るにつけ、子どもの頃を思い出す。
examples.tr: Whenever I look at photos, I remember my childhood.

examples.jp: 雨につけ風につけ、文句を言うのはやめなさい。
examples.tr: Stop complaining about every little thing, rain or wind.

examples.jp: 外国のニュースを聞くにつけ、平和の尊さを考えさせられる。
examples.tr: Every time I hear foreign news, it makes me think about how precious peace is.

examples.jp: 何かにつけ彼に頼りがちだ。
examples.tr: I tend to rely on him for everything.

1335.explain:
When using the paired form, the two elements before につけ should be balanced (verbs/adjectives of the same type, or an opposing pair).
The second clause usually expresses emotions, evaluations or general habits; avoid using it with commands or intentions.
The single form Vる + につけ emphasizes that “each time/on every occasion one meets that situation” an emotional reaction arises.
Somewhat formal style; used a lot in writing, speeches and essays.

• Paired form: “whenever A …, whenever B …” → the result/emotion in the second clause is the same.
• Single form: “every time V, …”, close to ～たびに but usually tied to emotions, recollections and evaluations.
• The nuance leans toward emotion, lament and reflection; it does not suit concrete commands/intentions.
• Often combines with verbs of emotion/recollection: 思い出す, 感心する, 心が痛む, 考えさせられる, 胸が熱くなる.

rows: Broader meaning, also used for intentional actions; ～につけ leans toward emotion/evaluation.
<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るたびに<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す。
Almost synonymous with the single form of ～につけ; につけて has a written-language nuance.
<ruby>故郷<rt>こきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>すことがあるにつけて…
Expresses gradual change; does not mean “every time”.
<ruby>年<rt>とし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>るにつれて<ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きになる。
Refers to a special, one-time point in time; differs from the repetitive nature of ～につけ.
<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>にあたって<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Using a command/volition after ～につけ: unnatural. Incorrect example: “見るにつけ、来てください”。
Combining two unbalanced parts: “見るにつけ悲しいにつけ” (verb + adjective) is incorrect; they should be of the same type.
Confusing it with ～につれて: ～につけ does not express gradual change over time.
Using it for a single event: “明日会うにつけ、報告する” does not fit; use ～たら/～とき instead.
1335.notes:
• Typical pairs: 見るにつけ聞くにつけ／読むにつけ書くにつけ／うれしいにつけ悲しいにつけ.
• “何事につけ” means “in everything …” and is very common in written language.
• This pattern suits general, repeated topics; avoid using it for single events that happen only once in the future.

examples.jp: 実情に即した支援策が求められている。
examples.tr: Support measures that match the actual situation are needed.

examples.jp: 現場に即したマニュアルを作成した。
examples.tr: We created a manual suited to the actual worksite.

examples.jp: 実態に即した見直しを行う。
examples.tr: We will carry out a review in line with the actual conditions.

examples.jp: 事実に即した説明でなければならない。
examples.tr: The explanation must be faithful to the facts.

examples.jp: 地域のニーズに即したサービスを提供する。
examples.tr: We provide services that meet local needs.

examples.jp: 法令に則した手続きを踏む。
examples.tr: We follow procedures in accordance with laws and regulations.

1336.explain:
Used with nouns of circumstance: 実情・現場・実態・事実・ニーズ・状況・要件…
Context of work/policy/documents: emphasizes practical suitability.
Note the difference between the two kanji: 即 (suited to the situation) vs 則 (following rules).

• “～に即した” describes the following noun as suited to, matching the context/circumstances/needs stated in N.
• The focus is on being “practical/realistic/timely” rather than merely “following rules”.
• “～に則した” emphasizes compliance with rules, laws and standards (norms).

rows: Practical, according to the specific circumstances.
<ruby>現場<rt>げんば</rt></ruby>に<ruby>即<rt>そく</rt></ruby>した<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>規定<rt>きてい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>則<rt>そく</rt></ruby>した<ruby>運用<rt>うんよう</rt></ruby>。
Follows a guideline/plan already laid out.
<ruby>方針<rt>ほうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>沿<rt>そ</rt></ruby>った<ruby>対策<rt>たいさく</rt></ruby>。
Used when there is clear data/reasons.
データに<ruby>基<rt>もと</rt></ruby>づいた<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>。
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>を<ruby>踏<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>まえた<ruby>改善<rt>かいぜん</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Wrong kanji: writing “法令に即した” when the meaning is “in accordance with the law” → it should be “法令に則した”.
Using “に基づく” when you want to say “suited to the situation” → use “に即した”.
Confusing it with “に沿った”: “現場に沿った” is unnatural; it should be “現場に即した”.
JLPT: choose between 即/則 based on the context, “actual circumstances” vs “norms”.
1336.notes:
• Base verbs: 即する（そくする）/ 則する（そくする）. They are pronounced the same, so the kanji are easily confused.
• In legal/normative documents, prefer “則”. In practical/situational contexts, use “即”.
• “即した” is a fixed attributive form (even though it is past), functioning like an adjective to modify the following noun.

examples.jp: 事故の映像は惨惨しくて、見るに堪えない。
examples.tr: The footage of the accident is so gruesome that it's unbearable to watch.

examples.jp: 低俗な発言で、聞くに堪えない言葉が続いた。
examples.tr: The vulgar remarks went on, with words too offensive to listen to.

examples.jp: この小説は稚拙で、読むに堪えない。
examples.tr: This novel is so clumsily written that it isn't worth reading.

examples.jp: ご厚情に感謝に堪えません。
examples.tr: I am deeply grateful for your kindness.

examples.jp: 今回の不祥事は誠に遺憾に堪えない。
examples.tr: This scandal is truly most regrettable.

1337.explain:
V of the senses/perception: 見る・聞く・読む・鑑賞する・直視する + に堪えない.
Nouns of emotion: 感謝・喜び・同情・憤り・遺憾 + に堪えない (a standard expression in official documents).
The tone is strong, so consider the level of politeness and your relationship with the listener when using it.

• Unbearable/heartbreaking: so terrible, miserable or vulgar that one “cannot bear to watch/listen/read”.
• Not worth V-ing: quality so poor that it is not worth watching/reading… (a harsh evaluation).
• Emphasizes strong emotion: with nouns of emotion: 感謝/喜び/同情/遺憾 + に堪えない = “extremely …”.
• Style: written language, formal; in the negative sense with V, it is often seen in commentary/criticism.

rows: Worth/good enough to V; able to withstand
Positive opposite; used for works/performance that “meet the standard”.
<ruby>鑑賞<rt>かんしょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える<ruby>作品<rt>さくひん</rt></ruby>。
Similar meaning; “<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>える/<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える” are almost interchangeable in this pattern.
～に<ruby>値<rt>あたい</rt></ruby>しない／<ruby>足<rt>た</rt></ruby>りない
A more rational evaluation; less strong emotional nuance.
<ruby>一読<rt>いちどく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>値<rt>あたい</rt></ruby>しない。

mistakes: Using it with an unsuitable verb (e.g. 操作するに堪えない sounds odd). Prefer verbs of perception/reception.
Confusing the positive nuance of “感謝に堪えない” with the negative one of “見るに堪えない”. Same form, but opposite nuances.
Confusing “に堪えない” with “に足りない/に値しない” (different emotional degree and scope of use).
1337.notes:
• In terms of form, with V it is usually V-る + に堪えない (unlike some materials that give V-ます語幹 + に堪えない; the common usage is V-る, as in 見るに堪えない).
• “に堪えない” with nouns of emotion has a formal, official-document nuance and is often found in speeches and press statements.
• In art criticism, “鑑賞に堪えない” emphasizes poor aesthetic value.

examples.jp: この映画は十分に見るに堪える出来だ。
examples.tr: This movie is well made enough to be worth watching.

examples.jp: 新人の論文だが、読みに堪える内容になっている。
examples.tr: Although it's a paper by a newcomer, its content is worth reading.

examples.jp: このデータは厳しい検証に堪える。
examples.tr: This data can withstand rigorous verification.

examples.jp: 屋外での連続使用に堪える設計だ。
examples.tr: It is designed to withstand continuous outdoor use.

examples.jp: 批判に堪える理論へと練り上げた。
examples.tr: We refined it into a theory that can stand up to criticism.

1338.explain:
Used a lot in professional evaluations: art, academia, engineering.
The point is “meeting the standard/having value”, not excessive praise.
Unlike “いい/素晴らしい”, this pattern evaluates whether objective criteria are met.

• Worth/good enough to V: a work/product is of sufficient quality to be watched/read/listened to/evaluated.
• Able to withstand/meet: can withstand continuous use, verification, criticism…
• Style: written language, formal, often a professional/technical evaluation.

rows: Negative opposite; used when quality is bad or something is painful.
Close synonym, leans toward rational evaluation; more widely used.
<ruby>一見<rt>いっけん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>値<rt>あたい</rt></ruby>する。
“<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>える” and “<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える” are close in meaning; “<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える” is more formal/written.
<ruby>長時間<rt>ちょうじかん</rt></ruby><ruby>使用<rt>しよう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>える。

mistakes: Wrong verb form: V-ます語幹 is needed (読みに堪える); avoid 読むに堪える in technical evaluations; however, with 見る・聞く in art commentary, “見るに堪える” is still natural.
Confusing the nuance of “meeting an objective standard” with emotional praise; the JLPT often tests this difference.
Confusing “堪える” with “耐える”: both are correct in many cases, but “堪える” leans toward evaluation/value, while “耐える” leans toward physical endurance.
1338.notes:
• V-ます語幹 + に堪える is the natural form: 読む→読みに堪える, 見る→見るに堪える (both 読み/見る are found; with 見る/聞く, the V-る form is also common in set phrases).
• In technical standards, common combinations: 実用・耐久・検証・批判 + に堪える.
• In art criticism: 鑑賞に堪える作品／名品.

examples.jp: 幼なじみで、彼は私にとって家族も同然だ。
examples.tr: We're childhood friends, so he's practically family to me.

examples.jp: この値段なら、タダも同然だよ。
examples.tr: At this price, it's practically free.

examples.jp: 前半で3点差をつけられて、もう負けたも同然だ。
examples.tr: They're three points behind after the first half, so they've as good as lost.

examples.jp: 彼女から一週間も返事がない。振られたも同然だ。
examples.tr: I haven't heard back from her for a whole week. I've as good as been dumped.

examples.jp: 手入れされていないから、あの家は廃墟も同然だ。
examples.tr: Since nobody takes care of it, that house is practically a ruin.

examples.jp: このミスは会社にとって致命傷も同然だ。
examples.tr: This mistake is as good as a fatal blow for the company.

1339.explain:
Used to emphasize a degree of near equivalence, often with emotion (surprise, lament, confident judgment).
Often appears with nouns expressing extremes: 無一文, タダ, 死, 廃墟, 失業, 致命傷, … to add weight.
In formal writing, it can be replaced with ～に等しい (more serious and objective).
Before “も同然だ” there is usually N or Vた; adjectives are rare and are usually converted to N (例:貧乏も同然だ).
Not used when the equivalence is weak; in that case choose 「ようなものだ／と言ってもいい」.

• States near-complete equivalence between A and B: AはBも同然だ = A is practically B.
• With Vた: emphasizes that “the result can be considered to have happened”, even if in reality it has not fully happened (e.g. 負けたも同然だ = a sure loss/as good as lost).
• Highly subjective: the speaker judges based on common sense, experience or emotion.
• Can carry an exaggerating nuance to persuade or complain (死んだも同然だ = as good as dead).

rows: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>も<ruby>同然<rt>どうぜん</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>等<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>しないのと<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じようなものだ。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>天才<rt>てんさい</rt></ruby>と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってもいい。
それは<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>と<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じだ。

mistakes: Wrong combination with adjectives: × 寒いも同然だ → should be changed to 名詞化: × 寒さも同然だ → use another pattern, “寒いようなものだ”.
Confusing it with ～に違いない: “も同然だ” is a comparison of degree, not a confident conjecture.
Using it when the equivalence is weak → unnatural. Choose ～ようなものだ/～と言ってもいい instead.
JLPT: easily confused with ～に等しい (formal) and ～同様だ (emphasizes general similarity). Distinguish the strong subjective nuance of “も同然”.
1339.notes:
• “同然” is a Sino-Japanese noun meaning “exactly the same/natural”; it can also be used on its own in written language: 同然の扱い.
• With Vた, the sense “as good as already…” easily sounds pessimistic or like a premature verdict; mind the context so it does not sound blunt.
• Combines with exaggerating quantity words: ゼロも同然, 無意味も同然, 無駄も同然 for stronger emphasis.
• In newspaper headlines: 「値上げは増税も同然」 is used to make a strong argument. explain: Means that although it is not actually the case, the state is almost like that. Expressive and subjective. ⏐ examples: 1. この車は中古車といっても新品（も）同然だ。
This car may be used, but it's just like new.
2. 彼の財産はないも同然だ。
He has practically no assets.

examples.jp: この橋は大地震に耐える設計だ。
examples.tr: This bridge is designed to withstand major earthquakes.

examples.jp: 彼は長年の痛みに耐えて研究を続けた。
examples.tr: He endured pain for many years and continued his research.

examples.jp: この小説は今読み直しても読むに耐える名作だ。
examples.tr: Even reread today, this novel is a masterpiece well worth reading.

examples.jp: 雑音がひどく、到底聴くに耐えない録音だ。
examples.tr: The noise is so bad that this recording is simply not worth listening to.

examples.jp: 戦時中の証言は歴史資料として引用に耐える価値がある。
examples.tr: Wartime testimonies are valuable enough to be cited as historical sources.

1340.explain:
Meaning 1 has a nuance of resilience/endurance; the subject is usually a person/thing subjected to an impact.
Meaning 2 has a nuance of evaluating quality/value. Used in criticism, reports and formal written language.
「～に耐えるN」 usually comes before a noun: 読むに耐える内容・使用に耐える強度。
The negative 「～に耐えない」 emphasizes “unacceptable/not worth…”, with a strong nuance.

• Meaning 1: To endure/resist an unpleasant or harsh impact (physical/mental): 痛み・寒さ・重圧・地震 など。
• Meaning 2: Valuable enough for an act of appreciation/evaluation: 見る・読む・鑑賞・批判・使用 など。「～に耐えるN」 = N good enough to …
• Formality: neutral → formal (when written with 堪). Meaning 2 is often used in written language/academic evaluation and criticism.
• Verb restrictions for meaning 2: usually used with verbs of perception/evaluation (見る・読む・鑑賞する・使用する…). With ordinary verbs it can sound forced.

rows: <ruby>鑑賞<rt>かんしょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>堪<rt>こた</rt></ruby>える<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>
<ruby>直視<rt>ちょくし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>えない<ruby>光景<rt>こうけい</rt></ruby>
Emphasizes going beyond the limit of endurance
<ruby>屈辱<rt>くつじょく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>えかねて<ruby>退職<rt>たいしょく</rt></ruby>した
Describes general properties, little evaluative “worth” nuance
<ruby>熱<rt>ねつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>い<ruby>素材<rt>そざい</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Mixing up meanings: using ～に耐える to say “easy to do” → incorrect. It means “can withstand/worth”, not “easy”.
Using it with an unsuitable verb: 食べるに耐える sounds unnatural. Prefer verbs of appreciation/evaluation.
Forgetting the strong nuance of ～に耐えない: using it in casual speech can be too harsh.
JLPT N1: Distinguish ～に耐える vs ～に耐えかねる vs ～に堪えない in contexts of evaluation/criticism.
1340.notes:
• Kanji: 耐える・堪える. For the meaning “worth…”, 堪える is usually used in formal writing.
• Typical collocations (meaning 2): 観賞/鑑賞・見る・読む・批判・引用・使用 + に耐える。
• Avoid overusing it with everyday action verbs (食べるに耐える…): it sounds forced. Use it with activities of evaluation/appreciation.
• In engineering: 耐震・耐熱・耐水 are common prefixes meaning “resistant to …”.

examples.jp: 数度の交渉を経て、ようやく合意に至った。
examples.tr: After several rounds of negotiations, an agreement was finally reached.

examples.jp: 感染が全身に広がり、残念ながら死亡に至った。
examples.tr: The infection spread throughout the body and, sadly, resulted in death.

examples.jp: 不具合が相次ぎ、製品の出荷は中止に至った。
examples.tr: After a series of defects, shipments of the product ended up being halted.

examples.jp: 長年の研究が実を結び、技術は実用化に至った。
examples.tr: Years of research bore fruit, and the technology reached practical use.

examples.jp: 問題を放置したことが、信頼喪失に至った最大の要因だ。
examples.tr: Leaving the problem unaddressed was the biggest factor that led to the loss of trust.

1341.explain:
Used to emphasize the final result while implying a process that led there.
Formal/objective style: reports, administrative documents, news.
The subject is usually an organization/event; the speaker keeps their own feelings at a distance.
With personal actions, it is used when one wants to sound objective: 私的な事情により辞職 に至った。

• Expresses a process of accumulation/developments and the final outcome “reached/arrived at”.
• Often used in written language, news and reports. Often goes with negative results (死亡・中止・破綻) but can also be neutral/positive (合意・実用化・採用)。
• Objective nuance, describing a result after many factors/developments; avoid using it for the speaker's direct emotions.

rows: Emphasizes the outcome after a process
<ruby>解散<rt>かいさん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>った
Not a “result”, but an extension of scope
<ruby>末端<rt>まったん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>るまで<ruby>検査<rt>けんさ</rt></ruby>
When it came to… / only when…
States the point in time when something arose
<ruby>被害<rt>ひがい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>拡大<rt>かくだい</rt></ruby>するに<ruby>至<rt>いた</rt></ruby>って<ruby>対策<rt>たいさく</rt></ruby>
Focuses on a chain of efforts→result; more emotional
<ruby>協議<rt>きょうぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>末<rt>すえ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>合意<rt>ごうい</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Using it for direct personal emotions → unnatural: ×うれしくて笑うに至った → just use: 笑うようになった。
Confusing it with 「～に至るまで」 (scope) → it does not express a result.
Losing the formal nuance: in casual conversation, 「結局～になった」 is more natural.
JLPT N1: Recognize it when used with nouns of serious outcomes (死亡・破綻) and in report style.
1341.notes:
