• 「至る」 is a formal verb meaning “to arrive at, to reach”. The past form 「至った」 confirms a result that has already happened.
• Often accompanied by a nominalized cause phrase: ～が原因で／～の結果、～に至った。
• Newspaper headlines often shorten it to the present: 死亡に至る、合意に至る（a reporting sense, not future).

examples.jp: 被災者の不安は想像に難くない。
examples.tr: It is not hard to imagine the anxiety of the disaster victims.

examples.jp: 突然の解雇が彼に与えた衝撃は察するに難くない。
examples.tr: It is not difficult to sense the shock that the sudden dismissal gave him.

examples.jp: この決断がいかに困難だったかは理解に難くない。
examples.tr: It is not hard to understand how difficult this decision was.

examples.jp: 彼女が受賞した理由は想像に難くない。
examples.tr: The reason she won the award is not hard to imagine.

examples.jp: データ改ざんが信頼を損なうのは推測に難くない。
examples.tr: It is not hard to guess that falsifying data damages trust.

1343.explain:
Placed after an abstract noun: 想像・理解・推測・察知+ に難くない。
Often used at the end of a sentence / in the assessment part of analytical writing and reports.
Implies empathy or a rational evaluation, without expressing emotion too directly.

• Affirms that something is "not difficult" in the sense of conjecture/empathy: it is easy to imagine/understand/see.
• Not used for concrete physical actions ("not difficult to lift 50kg") → unsuitable.
• Written-language, polite nuance; often shows understanding or evaluation.

rows: <ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>難<rt>かた</rt></ruby>くない
～ても<ruby>不思議<rt>ふしぎ</rt></ruby>ではない
It would not be strange if…
Allows that something may happen; not "easy to understand"
<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>不思議<rt>ふしぎ</rt></ruby>ではない
Strong certainty; does not express "easy to imagine"
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るに<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない
Describes how easy an action is; different scope of use

mistakes: Used for a concrete physical action → unsuitable: ×50kgを持ち上げるに難くない。
Confused with ～に違いない (strong certainty) → wrong nuance of mild inference.
Dropping the perception noun in front → awkward sentence: ×彼の気持ちはに難くない → it should be 彼の気持ちは想像に難くない。
JLPT N1: Recognize the collocation “想像/理解/察する + に難くない”.
1343.notes:
• Common structure: 「N（抽象）＋は／が＋N（perception）＋に難くない」.
• Avoid it in everyday casual conversation; it can be replaced with すぐ分かる／容易に想像できる.
• Emphasizing empathy: adding 前置きに とても／大いに を is usually unnecessary, since it is already formal.

1344.connection: N + に + N + を重ねて (same noun repeated: 苦労に苦労を)

examples.jp: 会議に会議を重ねて、ようやく合意に達した。
examples.tr: After meeting upon meeting, we finally reached an agreement.

examples.jp: 実験に実験を重ねて、安全性を確かめた。
examples.tr: Through experiment after experiment, we confirmed its safety.

examples.jp: 検討に検討を重ねて、計画を改訂した。
examples.tr: After careful deliberation over and over, we revised the plan.

examples.jp: 失敗に失敗を重ねて、学びを得た。
examples.tr: Through failure after failure, I learned my lessons.

examples.jp: 試行に試行を重ねて、最適化に成功した。
examples.tr: After trial upon trial, we succeeded in optimizing it.

1344.explain:
The two nouns should be processes that can be repeated: 実験・検討・会議・調整・試行・努力・苦労.
The clause “～に～を重ねて” is usually followed by a result in the past tense or by ついに／ようやく.
Rarely used in everyday spoken language; it sounds "journalistic/academic".

• Emphasizes a process accumulated by repeating an action/procedure many times.
• Formal nuance, suited to written language, reports and argumentative essays.
• Suggests persistent effort or a chain of successive incidents (positive/negative).

rows: <ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby><ruby>度<rt>ど</rt></ruby>も<ruby>実験<rt>じっけん</rt></ruby>した。
Basic pattern; lacks the emphatic “NにNを”.
<ruby>台風<rt>たいふう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>次<rt>つ</rt></ruby>ぐ<ruby>台風<rt>たいふう</rt></ruby>。

mistakes: Used with a noun that cannot be repeated (× 喜びに喜びを重ねて) → choose a noun of process/action.
Missing a result after the clause makes the sentence less natural in written language.
Confused with 何度も: exams favor the formal pattern with the repeated noun.
Wrong particle: it must be “NにNを重ねて”.
1344.notes:
• N2 can be varied to avoid monotonous repetition: 協議に会議を重ねて (though this is less common).
• Combine with words indicating the outcome: ついに／ようやく／その結果／～に至った to complete the logical flow.
• In white papers/policy documents: 検討に検討を重ねて、～を策定した is a familiar formula.

examples.jp: 試験の結果のいかんでは、補講を受けていただく場合があります。
examples.tr: Depending on your exam results, you may be required to take supplementary lessons.

examples.jp: 交渉の進展のいかんでは、提携を見送ることも検討する。
examples.tr: Depending on how the negotiations progress, we will also consider putting off the partnership.

examples.jp: 天候のいかんでは、イベントを屋内に切り替えます。
examples.tr: Depending on the weather, the event will be moved indoors.

examples.jp: 今後の状況のいかんでは、体制を再編する可能性がある。
examples.tr: Depending on how the situation develops, the organization may be restructured.

1345.explain:
Suitable when presenting a policy or contingency plan based on objective conditions.
The second clause avoids overly subjective/enthusiastic statements; it leans toward the tone of rules and announcements.
Not used for simple everyday personal wishes (use 〜によっては in conversation instead).

• Used to state a condition that depends on the state/degree of N; the result or measure in the second clause changes accordingly.
• Formal nuance, often in announcements, regulations and minutes: “〜のいかんでは、〜もありうる/〜とする”.
• The second clause often contains a possibility, measure or ruling: 〜可能性がある／〜場合がある／〜とする／〜を検討する.

rows: <ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>のいかんでは<ruby>処分<rt>しょぶん</rt></ruby>も
Neutral, conversational, wide range of N
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>によっては<ruby>好<rt>この</rt></ruby>みが<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かれる
N のいかんによっては
Close in meaning, slightly less formal than “では”
<ruby>成績<rt>せいせき</rt></ruby>のいかんによっては<ruby>留年<rt>りゅうねん</rt></ruby>も
N のいかんにかかわらず
<ruby>理由<rt>りゆう</rt></ruby>のいかんにかかわらず<ruby>不可<rt>ふか</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Used with an unsuitable concrete N: ×太郎のいかんでは行きます → 太郎の都合によっては.
A command/request in the second clause sounds forced: ×結果のいかんでは、来てください → use a different structure.
Confused with “によっては”: exams often test the level of formality and the type of noun used.
1345.notes:
• The noun before “のいかん” should be something variable/evaluable: 結果・成績・状況・答申・審査 等.
• In minutes: “〜のいかんでは、〜もありうる/〜とする/〜を認めない” is a set formula.
• “結果のいかんで” is a colloquial contracted form, less formal than “では”.

examples.jp: 天候のいかんにかかわらず、大会は決行します。
examples.tr: The tournament will go ahead regardless of the weather.

examples.jp: 経験のいかんにかかわらず、やる気のある方を募集します。
examples.tr: We are looking for motivated people, regardless of experience.

examples.jp: 理由のいかんにかかわらず、締め切り後の申請は受け付けません。
examples.tr: Regardless of the reason, applications submitted after the deadline will not be accepted.

examples.jp: 成否のいかんにかかわらず、調査結果を公開する。
examples.tr: We will publish the findings of the investigation whether it succeeds or fails.

1346.explain:
Used to declare a clear rule/policy with no exceptions.
Avoid it in casual conversation; use the ordinary “〜に関係なく/にかかわらず” instead.
Best used with an N that is common/variable (理由・天候・状況…).

• Expresses a policy/condition that does NOT change whatever N is: "regardless of / irrespective of".
• Formal tone, often found in regulations, announcements, contracts and job postings.
• Emphasizes fairness/consistency: no exceptions depending on N.

rows: N のいかんにかかわらず
<ruby>年齢<rt>ねんれい</rt></ruby>のいかんにかかわらず
N に<ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby>なく
<ruby>事情<rt>じじょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby>なく
N のいかんでは/によっては
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>のいかんでは<ruby>処分<rt>しょぶん</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Used with a concrete personal N → sounds forced: ×太郎のいかんにかかわらず → 太郎の都合に関係なく.
Confused with “によっては/では”: exams often test the distinction between "regardless of" and "depending on".
The second clause must state a rule/policy; avoid sentences expressing personal emotion.
1346.notes:
• In formal documents: “理由のいかんにかかわらず、〜しない/認めない/不可とする” is a commonly used formula.
• “いかんによらず” is somewhat archaic/written, but is still found in laws and regulations.
• To emphasize "no exceptions" even more strongly, you can add “一切”: 理由のいかんにかかわらず、一切返金いたしません。

examples.jp: 天候のいかんによっては、イベントを中止することがあります。
examples.tr: Depending on the weather, the event may be canceled.

examples.jp: 面談の評価のいかんによっては、配属先が変更される場合があります。
examples.tr: Depending on the evaluation at the interview, your assignment may be changed.

examples.jp: 提出物の品質のいかんによっては、再提出をお願いすることがあります。
examples.tr: Depending on the quality of the submitted work, we may ask you to resubmit it.

examples.jp: 今後の状況のいかんによっては、計画を見直す必要がある。
examples.tr: Depending on how the situation develops, we may need to review the plan.

1347.explain:
Often accompanies open-ended announcements: it leaves room for special cases that may arise.
It has a slight "warning/attached condition" nuance: the listener should be prepared for possible changes.
In conversation, it can be used instead of plain “によっては” to make the statement more formal and binding.

• Expresses that a result/measure may change depending on the state/degree of N; it especially implies that "an exception/special measure may arise".
• The second clause often uses: 〜場合がある／〜こともある／〜可能性がある／〜となりうる／〜も検討する.
• Common in service announcements, school regulations and business instructions.

rows: N のいかんによっては
Depending on N, in some cases…
<ruby>内容<rt>ないよう</rt></ruby>のいかんによっては<ruby>拒否<rt>きょひ</rt></ruby>
<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>のいかんでは<ruby>処分<rt>しょぶん</rt></ruby>
<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>によっては<ruby>辛<rt>つら</rt></ruby>く<ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じる
N のいかんにかかわらず
<ruby>理由<rt>りゆう</rt></ruby>のいかんにかかわらず<ruby>不可<rt>ふか</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Used with an overly concrete personal N → sounds awkward: ×太郎のいかんによっては → 太郎の状況によっては.
Confused with “にかかわらず”: one means "depending on", the other "regardless of".
Missing the "in some cases/possibly" nuance in the second clause; the JLPT often asks you to choose the appropriate clause (〜場合がある／〜可能性がある).
1347.notes:
• Used a lot in business emails: “ご回答のいかんによっては、日程を再調整いたします”。
• The noun before “のいかん” should be something measurable/evaluable: 結果・状況・内容・評価・回答 等.
• “〜のいかんで” is a contracted form; “〜のいかんによっては” keeps a stronger "in some cases" nuance.

examples.jp: 天候のいかんによらず、大会は予定どおり実施します。
examples.tr: Whatever the weather, the tournament will be held as scheduled.

examples.jp: 参加のいかんによらず、納入済みの会費は返金いたしません。
examples.tr: Membership fees already paid will not be refunded, regardless of attendance.

examples.jp: 理由のいかんによらず、遅刻は認められません。
examples.tr: Whatever the reason, lateness will not be accepted.

examples.jp: 結果のいかんによらず、本プロジェクトは来期も継続します。
examples.tr: Regardless of the results, this project will continue into the next term.

examples.jp: 国籍のいかんによらず、応募できます。
examples.tr: Anyone may apply, regardless of nationality.

examples.jp: 合否のいかんによらず、メールにてご連絡いたします。
examples.tr: Whether you pass or fail, we will notify you by email.

1348.explain:
Used when the speaker wants to emphasize the consistency of a rule/policy.
More formal than ～にかかわらず／～を問わず; the range of nouns is narrower (leaning toward "situation/condition").
Not used to describe everyday personal behavior casually.
The second clause is usually an objective command/decision; rarely a personal emotion.

• Meaning: "regardless of / not depending on N", "no matter what N is like…".
• Very formal nuance, used in written language, legal documents/regulations, announcements and speeches.
• N “のいかん” = "the situation/condition of N" (如何). Not used directly with verbs/adjectives.
• The second clause is usually a decisive/general rule: ～します／～いたしません／許可しません／同様に扱います…
• Often used with category nouns: 成否（success or failure）, 合否（pass or fail）, 理由（reason）, 事情（circumstances）, 結果（result）, 天候（weather）, 出欠（attendance or absence）, 国籍（nationality）…

rows: N + のいかんによらず
Regardless of the situation of N
<ruby>理由<rt>りゆう</rt></ruby>のいかんによらず、<ruby>禁止<rt>きんし</rt></ruby>
<ruby>天候<rt>てんこう</rt></ruby>にかかわらず<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>
Close in meaning; leans toward listing a range
<ruby>性別<rt>せいべつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>わず<ruby>募集<rt>ぼしゅう</rt></ruby>
Contrasting concession, a different kind of meaning
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>にもかかわらず<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>た

mistakes: Used directly with a verb/adjective: Incorrect. It must be noun + のいかん.
Used in a casual context: Unnatural. This pattern is formal.
Confused with ～にもかかわらず (although): Completely different in meaning.
A strong personal emotion in the second clause: Unsuitable. It should be an objective decision/rule.
1348.notes:
• “如何” is originally a Sino-Japanese word meaning "how". This phrase is a set phrase in official documents.
• If the noun is too concrete (a person's name, a specific object), it is usually not used with のいかん.
• Suitable for regulations, terms and conditions, job postings and event guidelines.

examples.jp: 彼は鬼のごとき形相で怒鳴った。
examples.tr: He shouted with a face like a demon's.

examples.jp: 春の雪は綿のごとく降り積もった。
examples.tr: The spring snow piled up like cotton.

examples.jp: 夢のごとき一夜だった。
examples.tr: It was a night like a dream.

examples.jp: 彼女は風のごとく去っていった。
examples.tr: She left like the wind.

examples.jp: 砂漠は海のごとく果てしない。
examples.tr: The desert is as endless as the sea.

examples.jp: 彼ごとき者に任せられない。
examples.tr: I can't leave it to the likes of him.

1349.explain:
Used when you want a formal, vivid style (literature, speeches, titles).
In everyday conversation, ～ような／～ように is preferred for naturalness.
Avoid using ごとき for the person you are talking to, as it can carry a contemptuous nuance.
Combines well with abstract nouns:夢・幻・稲妻・雷・光・神…

• Meaning: "like/as…", equivalent to ～のような／～のように but more literary and classical.
• Used for metaphors and conventional comparisons, adding imagery and formality.
• “ごとき” comes before a noun; “ごとく” comes before a verb/adjective or a whole sentence.
• Note the contemptuous nuance when used for people: N + ごとき（者） can mean "the likes of…".

rows: <ruby>光<rt>ひかり</rt></ruby>のごとく<ruby>速<rt>はや</rt></ruby>い
<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るかのような<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>けさ

mistakes: Used carelessly in everyday conversation → awkward style.
Confusing “ごとき” (modifies N) with “ごとく” (adverb) → wrong position.
Not recognizing the contemptuous nuance of Nごとき（者） → impolite.
Confused with ～ほど (degree) → “ごとき” is a figurative comparison, not degree.
1349.notes:
• Originates from “如（ごと）し” in classical Japanese; “夢のごとし” is a classical sentence-final form.
• “～するがごとく” is often seen in classical texts/speeches to create rhythm.
• When you need a neutral tone, replace it with ～ような／～ように to avoid sounding too affected.

1350.connection: [A]のやら + [B]のやら / V plain form + のやら / Na + な / Aい

examples.jp: 彼は怒っているのやら冗談を言っているのやら、さっぱりわからない。
examples.tr: I can't tell at all whether he's angry or joking.

examples.jp: 合格して、うれしいのやらほっとしたのやら、言葉が出なかった。
examples.tr: When I passed, I didn't know whether I was happy or relieved, and I was at a loss for words.

examples.jp: 本当なのやら嘘なのやら、その噂の出どころが不明だ。
examples.tr: Whether it's true or a lie, nobody knows where that rumor came from.

examples.jp: 泣いているのやら笑っているのやら分からない顔をしていた。
examples.tr: He had a look on his face that made it hard to tell whether he was crying or laughing.

examples.jp: この結果が成功なのやら失敗なのやら、判断がつきかねる。
examples.tr: It is hard to judge whether this result is a success or a failure.

examples.jp: 引っ越すとしても、どこへ行けばいいのやら。
examples.tr: Even if I move, where on earth should I go?

1350.explain:
Used when the speaker lacks information and is uncertain; carries a nuance of confusion or mild doubt.
Often followed at the end by a verb of perception/judgment: わからない／見分けがつかない／迷う／困る.
Not used when the speaker already knows the answer; to confirm, use ～かどうか/～か.
Intonation: stress falls on のやら to show confusion.
More formal than ～のか～のか; in written language or explanations, ～のやら gives a more objective feel.

The pattern ～のやら～のやら expresses confusion/difficulty in determining between two possibilities or two states A and B ("not knowing whether it is A or B"). It is often used when the speaker only observes the outward appearance or is in a state of confusion and cannot judge clearly.
• The pair ～のやら～のやら is usually followed by a summarizing clause such as: ～か（どうか）わからない／見当がつかない／判断がつかない／困る.
• With Na-adjectives and nouns, なのやら must be used to connect to “の”.
• The nuance leans toward written language or serious expression; in everyday spoken language it can be replaced with ～のか～のか／～のかどうか.
• A and B are usually opposite or mutually exclusive, emphasizing the "unclear" nature.

rows: Not knowing whether A or B
Nuance of confusion, written language; often with わからない
<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>なのやら<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>なのやらわからない
Not knowing whether A or B
Close equivalent; somewhat stiff, leans toward written language
<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>なのだか<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>なのだか<ruby>不明<rt>ふめい</rt></ruby>だ
A and B and so on (listing)
<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>やらバイトやらで<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しい
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないか<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めて
<ruby>合格<rt>ごうかく</rt></ruby>するかどうか<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>だ

mistakes: Forgetting “な” with Na-adjectives/N: incorrect 本当のやら → correct 本当なのやら.
Using ～やら～やら instead of ～のやら～のやら to express "not knowing": the two patterns have different functions.
Omitting the summarizing clause: many sentences need “～わからない／判断がつかない”; without it, the meaning is incomplete.
Choosing the wrong tense in the following clause: in a past context → わからなかった, not わからない.
Mixing it up with ～かどうか: when there are two specific possibilities A/B → prefer ～のやら～のやら or ～のだか～のだか.
1350.notes:
• With question words: 何・どこ・いつ・だれ… + のやら emphasizes "who knows…". Example: 何を考えているのやら。
• Tense/aspect: ～のやら itself has no tense; tense is expressed in the following clause (わからなかった／困っているなど).
• Avoid overusing it in casual speech if you want to sound natural: prefer ～のか／～かな when the written-language nuance is not needed.
• In literature, ～のやら can stand at the end of a sentence to create a trailing-off effect: どこへ行ったのやら。

examples.jp: 彼は物事を先延ばしにするきらいがある。
examples.tr: He has a tendency to put things off.

examples.jp: この会社は短期的な利益を重視するきらいがある。
examples.tr: This company tends to put too much weight on short-term profits.

examples.jp: 私は人の話を最後まで聞かないきらいがある。
examples.tr: I have a bad habit of not listening to people until they finish.

examples.jp: 彼は形式にこだわるきらいがある。
examples.tr: He tends to be overly concerned with formalities.

examples.jp: 若者は自己主張が強いきらいがある。
examples.tr: Young people tend to be too assertive.

examples.jp: 部内は内向き思考のきらいがある。
examples.tr: The department has a tendency toward inward-looking thinking.

1351.explain:
Suitable in formal writing/comments, reports and analyses.
It has a mild critical nuance; avoid using it bluntly in a way that causes offense, and add 総じて／やや to soften it.
The subject can be an individual, an organization or a social trend.

• Meaning: "have a (bad) tendency to…", "be a bit too…", "have a habit of…".
• Mild critical nuance, more formal than ～がちだ／～気味だ.
• Often used with undesirable behavior: 先延ばしにする／形式にこだわる／短絡的に考える…
• Not used for positive tendencies (praise), because “嫌い” originally means "something bad/disagreeable".

rows: V<ruby>辞書<rt>じしょ</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby> + きらいがある
<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えすぎるきらいがある
Nの/ Vます + <ruby>気味<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>だ
<ruby>消費<rt>しょうひ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>える<ruby>傾向<rt>けいこう</rt></ruby>がある

mistakes: Used to praise → does not fit the meaning (because “嫌い” carries a negative nuance).
Confused with ～がちだ: “がち” is not necessarily critical, while “きらいがある” leans toward criticism.
Unsuitable subject (a specific inanimate object) → unnatural; it should be used for people/organizations/trends.
1351.notes:
• “嫌い” here is a noun meaning "a flaw/something to criticize", not "to dislike".
• Suitable when you need a gentle but weighty criticism (HR reports, performance evaluations…).
• Can be combined with 副詞: どうも／やや／少々／しばしば + V + きらいがある to adjust the degree.

examples.jp: 子どもの手前、弱音は吐けない。
examples.tr: I can't complain in front of my children.

examples.jp: 約束した手前、断るわけにはいかない。
examples.tr: Since I promised, I can't very well refuse.

examples.jp: 先生の手前、スマホをいじるわけにはいかない。
examples.tr: With the teacher right there, I can't fiddle with my phone.

examples.jp: 皆の前で強く言った手前、今さら引き下がれない。
examples.tr: Having spoken so forcefully in front of everyone, I can't back down now.

examples.jp: 親の手前、派手な服は着にくい。
examples.tr: With my parents watching, it's hard to wear flashy clothes.

examples.jp: 一度やると言った手前、最後まで責任を持つ。
examples.tr: Since I once said I would do it, I'll take responsibility to the end.

1352.explain:
Gives the reason why it is “hard to do X” because of a barrier of face or social pressure; often used with ～わけにはいかない／にくい／しかない／ざるを得ない.
The tone is inward and self-imposed; usually used in the first person or about someone close.
Neutral to slightly formal; can be used in both spoken and written language.

• Meaning: because you are in front of someone / to save face / because you have already said or done something, it is hard to do the opposite, so you must keep up appearances or keep your word.
• Nuance: self-imposed restraint, social pressure or concern for face; usually tied to the speaker or someone on the speaker's side.
• N + の手前 emphasizes “in front of …, so it is awkward”; V + 手前 emphasizes “having already …, I cannot take it back”.

rows: Nの<ruby>手前<rt>てまえ</rt></ruby>／Vた<ruby>手前<rt>てまえ</rt></ruby>
Emphasizes social constraint / feeling of awkwardness
<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>の<ruby>手前<rt>てまえ</rt></ruby>、やめた
A more logical/objective reason, not really about face
<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>した<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>るべきだ
Strong sense of obligation/volition, little nuance of “awkwardness”
やるからには、<ruby>勝<rt>か</rt></ruby>ちたい
Different meaning: この<ruby>川<rt>かわ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>手前<rt>てまえ</rt></ruby>（this side of the river）
<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>の<ruby>手前<rt>てまえ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>降<rt>お</rt></ruby>りる

mistakes: Confusing the spatial meaning of “手前” with the grammar point meaning “face” → wrong context.
The second clause does not express a constraint (e.g. a sentence describing a scene) → unnatural.
Using it to carelessly justify negative behavior → sounds like an excuse and is not polite.
1352.notes:
• Derives from the original meaning “the front / the near side”; from there it developed the meaning “in front of others → saving face”.
• Often combined with structures of impossibility: ～わけにはいかない／にくい／づらい／しかない／ざるを得ない to emphasize the obligation.
• Can be used indirectly to decline or explain politely: “上司の手前、今回は見送ります”.

examples.jp: 昔はいざ知らず、今はSNSで情報がすぐ広まる。
examples.tr: The old days may have been different, but now information spreads instantly on social media.

examples.jp: 子どもならいざ知らず、大人がそんな言い訳は通らない。
examples.tr: A child might get away with it, but an adult can't use an excuse like that.

examples.jp: 内情の真偽はいざ知らず、噂に踊らされるべきではない。
examples.tr: Whatever the truth of the inside story, we shouldn't be swayed by rumors.

examples.jp: 日本語の発音はいざ知らず、文法は体系的だ。
examples.tr: Japanese pronunciation is another matter, but the grammar is systematic.

examples.jp: 専門家ならいざ知らず、素人が独断で判断すべきではない。
examples.tr: An expert would be one thing, but a layperson shouldn't make judgments on their own.

1353.explain:
Used to “set aside” one item from the scope of discussion in order to emphasize the main argument.
Part A is usually something remote from the speaker (他人、昔、子ども…), emphasizing “I can't say for sure”.
Part B is usually a standard, a rule, the current situation, a criticism or a suggestion.
The tone is formal; in casual conversation it can be replaced with “〜はともかく”.

• Presents an exception, “unknown / not discussed”, about A in order to emphasize a firm judgment about B.
• “ならいざ知らず”: grants that A might be acceptable (a supposition) in order to deny B more strongly.
• Nuance: polite, a little old-fashioned; strongly associated with written language, speeches and commentaries.
• The second clause often comes with structures of evaluation/difficulty/unacceptability.

rows: Nuance of “can't say for sure”; formal
<ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>はさておき…
Reverses expectations; no sense of “don't know”

mistakes: Attaching it directly to a verb without nominalizing it: incorrect. You need の/こと: 彼が来るのはいざ知らず…
The second clause should not be purely objective information; it should be an evaluation or a rule.
Confusing it with ともかく: いざ知らず has the nuance “unknown, can't say for sure” and is more formal.
1353.notes:
• “いざ” originally means “at the crucial moment”; in this pattern it creates the nuance “hard to say for sure”.
• With a complex clause: 結果がどうなるかはいざ知らず、準備だけは万全に。 (acceptable, but written language)
• Not used for direct questions; this pattern affirms the argument in the second clause.

examples.jp: 漢字はおろか、ひらがなすら読めない。
examples.tr: I can't read even hiragana, let alone kanji.

examples.jp: 海外旅行はおろか、県外に出ることすらなかった。
examples.tr: I never even left the prefecture, let alone traveled abroad.

examples.jp: 休みはおろか、昼休憩すら取れない日が続いた。
examples.tr: Day after day, I couldn't even take a lunch break, let alone a day off.

examples.jp: 礼儀はおろか、挨拶すらできないのか。
examples.tr: Forget manners — can't you even say hello?

examples.jp: 彼は日本語はおろか、英語すら話せる。
examples.tr: He can speak not only Japanese but even English.

1354.explain:
Used to “lower” the point of comparison in order to highlight how serious or surprising the situation is.
Suitable for written language, commentary and complaints; carries a strong nuance of criticism when used with negatives.
In conversation, さえ is more natural than すら; but with はおろか, both すら and さえ are acceptable.

• Emphasizes the degree of surprise: not only N1, but even N2 (a lower level) is not/hardly/…
• Order: N1 is the larger or obvious scope; N2 is the smallest, minimal example.
• “すら” has a more formal nuance than “さえ”; both emphasize the extreme case.
• Usually used with negatives: ない／できない／むずかしい…, but can also be affirmative in some contexts.

rows: N はおろか、N2 すら/さえ…
<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>はおろか<ruby>氷<rt>こおり</rt></ruby>すらない
<ruby>上達<rt>じょうたつ</rt></ruby>どころか<ruby>悪化<rt>あっか</rt></ruby>した
N1 of course, and also N2
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>はもちろん<ruby>中国<rt>ちゅうごく</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>も
Uses a small criterion to evaluate the whole
<ruby>服装<rt>ふくそう</rt></ruby>からしてだらしない

mistakes: Reversing the order of degree: making N2 bigger than N1 makes the sentence illogical. Make N2 the minimum.
Putting a verb directly after はおろか without nominalizing it → incorrect: “食べるはおろか” → correct: “食べることはおろか”.
Confusing it with はもちろん: はおろか usually goes with negative statements and has stronger emphasis.
1354.notes:
• For a softer tone, use “〜はもちろん/〜はもとより”; for a stronger one, keep “はおろか”.
• N2 should be the smallest example, clearly “minimal”, so the sentence is logical and sharp.
• When emphasizing something positive, choose carefully to avoid sounding sarcastic.

examples.jp: 業務管理はおろか、メール対応まで遅れている。
examples.tr: Not just business management — even replying to emails is behind.

examples.jp: 彼は日本語はおろか、英語まで独学で身につけた。
examples.tr: He taught himself not only Japanese but even English.

examples.jp: 住所はおろか、自分の電話番号まで忘れたのか。
examples.tr: You forgot your own phone number, never mind your address?

examples.jp: 雨で試合はおろか、セレモニーまで中止になった。
examples.tr: Because of the rain, not only the match but even the ceremony was canceled.

examples.jp: 彼女は資料作成はおろか、会議準備まで一人でこなした。
examples.tr: She handled not only preparing the documents but even the meeting preparations all by herself.

1355.explain:
Used when you want to highlight that the scope extends to something unexpected (N2).
More neutral in formality than “すら”; suits a wide range of contexts.
N2 should still be a “minimal/peripheral” example to keep the logic of the emphasis.

• Similar to “はおろか〜すら/さえ”, but “まで” highlights the extended scope: “even … too”.
• Less old-fashioned in nuance than “すら”; natural in conversation and writing.
• The second clause can be affirmative (it happens even to N2) or negative (not even N2).

rows: N はおろか、N2 まで…
<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>はおろか<ruby>氷<rt>こおり</rt></ruby>までない
N はおろか、N2 すら/さえ…
“すら” is more formal/old-fashioned; “さえ” is colloquial
<ruby>基礎<rt>きそ</rt></ruby>はおろか<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby>すらできない
Not only N1 but also N2
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>はもちろん<ruby>中国語<rt>ちゅうごくご</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す
No “まで/すら”; strong negative nuance
<ruby>改善<rt>かいぜん</rt></ruby>どころか<ruby>悪化<rt>あっか</rt></ruby>した

mistakes: Making N2 bigger than N1 breaks the logic of the emphasis. Make N2 lower/more peripheral than N1.
Dropping は after N1: an easy mistake in writing. The standard structure is: N1はおろか、N2まで…
Confusing it with はもちろん: はおろか is strong and usually implies something unexpected; はもちろん is neutral/affirmative listing.
1355.notes:
• “まで” is flexible: it can be used with verbs, quantities and time ranges to broaden the statement.
• To emphasize the “surprising minimum”, “すら/さえ” is more effective. To emphasize all-encompassing scope, choose “まで”.

examples.jp: 彼は敬語はおろか、普通の挨拶もできない。
examples.tr: He can't even give an ordinary greeting, let alone use keigo.

examples.jp: 忙しくて旅行はおろか、外食すらしていない。
examples.tr: I've been so busy that I haven't even eaten out, let alone traveled.

examples.jp: 漢字はおろか、ひらがなも読めないなんて信じられない。
examples.tr: I can't believe they can't even read hiragana, let alone kanji.

examples.jp: 予算はおろか、人手まで足りない状況だ。
examples.tr: We're short not only on budget but even on staff.

examples.jp: 彼女は英語はおろか、フランス語まで話せる。
examples.tr: She can speak not only English but even French.

examples.jp: 健康管理は運動はおろか、十分な睡眠も取れていないところから見直すべきだ。
examples.tr: For your health, you should start by reconsidering the fact that you're not even getting enough sleep, let alone exercise.

1356.explain:
Used to emphasize that N2 “goes beyond the expected level”; N1 serves as the stronger standard of comparison.
Often carries a nuance of criticism or negative evaluation; it can be used in affirmative sentences, but then sounds showy or literary.
N1 is mostly a noun. With verbs/adjectives, nominalize with の/こと to sound natural.
Not used in very casual everyday situations; suited to written language, presentations and essays.

• Core meaning: “N1 goes without saying; even N2…”, expressing that N2 is beyond expectations; N1 is the higher or more obvious level.
• Often used with a negative clause to emphasize a lack or impossibility: ～も/すらできない, ～すらない.
• Order of degree: N1 (stronger/harder/more important) ＞ N2 (weaker/more basic). If N2 isn't achieved, N1 is “out of the question”.
• Slightly stiff nuance, leaning toward written language/speeches; can carry criticism or exaggeration.
• Variants with まで/すら make “even/to the extent of” stronger than も.

rows: N1 is stronger than N2; emphatic nuance, slightly stiff
<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>はおろか、ひらがなも<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>めない
Contrastive comparison; does not require an N1/N2 pair on the same scale
<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>むどころか、<ruby>徹夜<rt>てつや</rt></ruby>した
More neutral; not necessarily strongly emotional
<ruby>英語<rt>えいご</rt></ruby>はもちろん、フランス<ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>も<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>せる
No N1 needed; focuses emphasis on the item marked with すら/さえ
<ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>ですら<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っている

mistakes: Reversing the degree: choosing an N1 weaker than N2 → breaks the logic of the emphasis.
Using it carelessly in affirmative sentences → the nuance is off; in affirmative sentences, prefer まで/すら.
Attaching it directly to a verb without nominalizing → unnatural: × 食べるはおろか → ◯ 食べることはおろか.
Confusing it with ～どころか: ～はおろか means “going further in the same direction”, not “the opposite”.
1356.notes:
• Choose an N1 that is “stronger” than N2 in difficulty/importance: 漢字(難) ＞ ひらがな(易).
• In affirmative sentences, まで/すら are more natural than も and add emphasis.
• Avoid overusing it in casual speech; in conversation use ～はもちろん, ～だって/～すら instead.

examples.jp: 欠点を言い出せばきりがない。
examples.tr: Once you start listing the flaws, there's no end to it.

examples.jp: 心配しだせばきりがないから、今できることに集中しよう。
examples.tr: If you start worrying, there's no end to it, so let's focus on what we can do now.

examples.jp: 例を挙げればきりがないが、代表的なものだけ述べる。
examples.tr: I could give endless examples, but I'll mention only the typical ones.

examples.jp: 欲を言い出したらきりがないよ。
examples.tr: If you start wanting more, there'll be no end to it.

examples.jp: 不満を挙げればきりがないので、この辺でやめよう。
examples.tr: There's no end to the complaints we could list, so let's stop here.

1357.explain:
Often used with verbs meaning “to start bringing up”: 言い出す,挙げる,数え上げる,心配する,文句を言う.
Used in discussions to cut a long list short and bring the conversation back to the main point.
In spoken language ～たら／～ときりがない can be used, but in standard JLPT usage ～ばきりがない is common.

• “If … there is no end/no limit”; once you start doing/listing/demanding, it goes on forever.
• Often used for complaints, examples, desires, worries… that could go on endlessly.
• Nuance of warning and restraint: implies “don't go down that path any further”.

rows: If you do it, it's endless
<ruby>例<rt>れい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>挙<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げればきりがない
<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>したら/ときりがない
Adjective / describes a state, unlike the conditional “if…, then”
<ruby>宇宙<rt>うちゅう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>りがない
Used on its own as a comment

mistakes: Confusing it with “限りがない”: that one describes the property of being “unlimited”, not the conditional structure “if…, it's endless”.
Missing “ば/たら/と”: ×言い出すきりがない → correct: 言い出せばきりがない.
Using it for a one-time action that ends immediately → not suitable (this pattern implies going on endlessly).
The JLPT often tests fixed phrases: 欠点を言い出せばきりがない／例を挙げればきりがない.
1357.notes:
• “きり/切り” originally means “limit, stopping point”. “きりがない” = “there is no stopping point”.
• Often placed before a concluding clause to cut a list short: ～ばきりがないが、要点だけ述べる。
• “欲を言えば/言い出せば” has a self-reflective nuance, advising restraint.

examples.jp: 一言相談してくれば助けられたものを。
examples.tr: If you had just asked me, I could have helped you.

examples.jp: もっと早く病院に行けば治ったものを。
examples.tr: If I had gone to the hospital sooner, it would have healed.

examples.jp: 黙っていればいいものを、余計なことを言ったせいで問題になった。
examples.tr: Keeping quiet would have been fine, but saying something unnecessary caused a problem.

examples.jp: 彼に謝れば済むものを、意地を張って関係が悪くなった。
examples.tr: An apology to him would have settled it, but being stubborn made the relationship worse.

examples.jp: 雨が降らなければ出かけられたものを。
examples.tr: If it hadn't rained, we could have gone out.

1358.explain:
Usually used when the speaker feels regret or dissatisfaction about the current result.
Can carry a hint of gentle reproach toward the other person: “if only…”, “you should have…”.
Not used in cheerful, everyday contexts.
Often goes with emotional expressions: のに, くせに, ったら, but with a stronger nuance.

～ば～ものを expresses regret, dissatisfaction or reproach: “if only…, then it would have…, and yet…”. The speaker thinks that if the condition in the first clause had happened, the result would have been better, but in reality it did not.

•
Nuance: regret + mild reproach, or dissatisfaction.

•
Context: written language, serious conversation, emotional.

•
Logical structure:

(If A had happened) → (B would have been better), but in reality it wasn't.

•
Logical example:
If you had spoken up sooner, we could have avoided this… (but you didn't).

rows: <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えばよかった のに。
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>え ばよかった。

mistakes: Confusing it with ～のに in JLPT questions – note that if the sentence contains regret or reproach, choose ～ば～ものを.
Forgetting to conjugate the verb into the ba-form (conditional) before using ものを.
Not used in cheerful or very polite conversation – it easily sounds unnatural.
ものを is usually not followed by a command or request.
1358.notes:
• This pattern has the feel of “if only… it would have…”, but also implies “and yet it wasn't done”.
• Often appears in written language, stories, films, or emotionally charged dialogue.
• Not used for simple advice, because the emotional nuance is quite strong.

examples.jp: 古びた本が棚に並んでいる。
examples.tr: Old, worn books are lined up on the shelf.

examples.jp: 田舎びた服装だが、彼の個性に合っている。
examples.tr: His clothes look a bit countrified, but they suit his personality.

examples.jp: 娘は年のわりに大人びた話し方をする。
examples.tr: My daughter speaks in a grown-up way for her age.

examples.jp: 昔びた言い回しがこの小説の魅力だ。
examples.tr: The old-fashioned turns of phrase are what make this novel appealing.

examples.jp: この通りは少し場末びた雰囲気がある。
examples.tr: This street has a slightly shabby, run-down atmosphere.

1359.explain:
Mostly used to modify nouns:古びた町並み／大人びた顔立ち／田舎びた店。
To describe a current state: ～びている (このホテルは古びている)。
Written-language nuance, evocative; often used in literature, criticism and description.
Expresses a subjective evaluation based on outward impressions.

• Expresses “having the look of / a touch of / a hint of …”, focusing on outward impressions or flavor.
• The nuance can be positive (大人びた = mature), neutral (昔びた = with an old-time feel) or negative (田舎びた = countrified, 古びた = worn and old).
• Usually used as a noun modifier. As a predicate, use “～びている”.
• Limited productivity: only certain combinations are natural; it cannot be attached to just any noun.

rows: A look/air of “having the feel of …”
Usually modifies N; derived from ～びる
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>びた<ruby>雰囲気<rt>ふんいき</rt></ruby>
Colloquial, broad scope, sometimes means “prone to …”
Literary; often used in the form ～めいた
<ruby>皮肉<rt>ひにく</rt></ruby>めいた<ruby>言<rt>いいかた</rt></ruby>い<ruby>方<rt></rt></ruby>
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>ぶった<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Misunderstanding “～びた” as past tense: it is not. It is the modifying form of ～びる.
Attaching “～びた” to any noun: many combinations are unnatural (×ITびたパソコン).
Using bare “～びた” as a predicate: use “～びている/～びていた” at the end of a sentence.
Confusing it with ～っぽい: ～っぽい is colloquial and broader in meaning; they are not interchangeable in every case.
1359.notes:
• Many combinations are set or customary: 古びた／田舎びた／大人びた／昔びた／場末びた／芝居びた。
• “～びた” is a past-form noun modifier but does not indicate past time; it is just a modifying form. To express past tense, use “～びていた”。
• With neutral/positive words: 大人びた (praise); with words of negative evaluation: 田舎びた (slightly disparaging).

examples.jp: 娘は急に大人びてきた。
examples.tr: My daughter has suddenly become very grown-up.

examples.jp: この椅子は年数がたって古びている。
examples.tr: Over the years, this chair has become old and worn.

examples.jp: 長く都会に住んでいるのに、どこか田舎びている。
examples.tr: Even though they've lived in the city for a long time, there's still something countrified about them.

examples.jp: その文章は意図的に昔びて見える。
examples.tr: That text looks deliberately old-fashioned.

examples.jp: 彼の話し方は年齢のわりに落ち着いて大人びている。
examples.tr: For his age, he speaks in a calm, mature way.

1360.explain:
Describes a change in, or a characteristic of, appearance or atmosphere: ～びてくる／～びている.
Written/descriptive in nature; in spoken language it is often replaced with ～っぽくなる in some contexts.
Nuance of “looks like / seems”, without the strong sense of “pretending” that ～ぶる has.

• Expresses “becoming like / taking on a quality of …” in appearance, flavor or feel.
• Usually an intransitive verb, with no direct object.
• Evaluative value: can be positive (大人びる = mature), or slightly negative (田舎びる = countrified; 古びる = to become old and worn).
• Not every noun combines naturally with ～びる; most are customary combinations.

rows: To become/take on the look of …
Stative verb / verb of change; neutral
Literary; often used in the form ～めいた

mistakes: Confusing “～びる” with “～ぶる”: ～ぶる means “to pretend / put on airs”, with a nuance of criticism; ～びる means “to have the look of / become”.
Using it with a direct object: it is mostly an intransitive verb and does not take を.
Making up unnatural combinations (×都会びる言い方 → use instead: 都会的な言い方/洗練された言い方).
1360.notes:
• Some bases come from i-adjectives: 古い→古びる; others are nouns: 大人→大人びる, 田舎→田舎びる.
• Usually written in kana; “びる” rarely has its own kanji.
• Not used with every noun: choose natural, customary combinations.

examples.jp: 上品ぶった物言いは鼻につく。
examples.tr: That affectedly refined way of talking is grating.

1361.explain:
Often comes before:態度／口調／顔／発言。

“Acting/pretending to be …” when modifying a noun, with a sarcastic nuance.
mistakes: Misunderstanding it as past tense.
1361.notes: Stress it with intonation to make it more sarcastic.

examples.jp: 先輩ぶってあれこれ命令するな。
examples.tr: Don't go acting like a senior and ordering people around.

examples.jp: 大人ぶっていても、内心は不安なんだろう。
examples.tr: Even if they act grown-up, they're probably anxious inside.

examples.jp: 知ったかぶって答えたが、間違いだらけだった。
examples.tr: I answered as if I knew it all, but my answer was full of mistakes.

examples.jp: 先生ぶって講釈を垂れる彼にうんざりだ。
examples.tr: I'm fed up with him lecturing everyone as if he were a teacher.

examples.jp: 有名人ぶってサインを断るのは感じが悪い。
examples.tr: Acting like a celebrity and refusing to sign autographs makes a bad impression.

1362.explain:
Placed before the verb / subject of the next action: N + ぶって + V.
“～ぶっている” emphasizes an ongoing state or a habit of putting on airs.
Carries a critical nuance; consider politeness and social relationships when using it directly.

• The te-form of ～ぶる, used to connect clauses: “acting like / pretending to be … and (then) …”.
• Implies criticism or sarcasm toward someone “playing a role”. Stronger than ～ふりをして in its critical nuance.
• Often appears in conversation, describing the other person's behavior or tone.

rows: <ruby>先輩<rt>せんぱい</rt></ruby>ぶって<ruby>説教<rt>せっきょう</rt></ruby>する
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>のふりをして<ruby>黙<rt>だま</rt></ruby>る
<ruby>大人<rt>おとな</rt></ruby>っぽくしてみる

mistakes: Confusing it with ～ふりをして: JLPT questions often test the critical nuance of ～ぶって.
Using “～ぶって” with an i-adjective that has not been nominalized (×賢いぶって → 賢いふりをして/賢そうぶって).
Forgetting to conjugate ～ぶる for the context and tense: when describing a current state, use ～ぶっている; it is not always ～ぶって.
1362.notes:
• “知ったかぶって” comes from “知ったかぶる” (acting as if one knows when one actually doesn't); a common phrase with a mocking nuance.
• Often used with nouns for roles or status: 先生／専門家／先輩／上司／有名人／被害者 など。
• In spoken language, “～ぶってさ…” is used to open a complaint, with a casual nuance.

examples.jp: 彼はすぐ大人ぶるけど、中身は子どものままだ。
examples.tr: He's always acting grown-up, but inside he's still a child.

examples.jp: 彼女は何でも知ったかぶって説明するから、時々困る。
examples.tr: She explains everything as if she knows it all, so it's sometimes a problem.

examples.jp: 紳士ぶった態度で人を見下すのはよくない。
examples.tr: It's not good to look down on people with a gentlemanly air.

examples.jp: 彼、貧乏ぶってるくせに、高い時計をしている。
examples.tr: He acts like he's poor, yet he wears an expensive watch.

examples.jp: 彼は先輩ぶって指示ばかり出す。
examples.tr: He acts like a senior and does nothing but give orders.

1363.explain:
Usually colloquial; the critical/sarcastic nuance is quite clear. Be careful in polite situations.
Progressive/connecting forms: ～ぶって（て形）and ～ぶった（past/modifier）are very common when criticizing someone's attitude.
It combines naturally with relatively few words; it often appears in fixed phrases:大人ぶる,知ったかぶる,先生ぶる, いい子ぶる, かわいこぶる.

• “～ぶる” expresses superficial behavior of “acting like / putting on airs / pretending”, usually with a critical or sarcastic nuance.
• Attaches to nouns for roles or qualities: 大人ぶる（act grown-up）, 先生ぶる（act like a teacher）, 知ったかぶる（act like a know-it-all）.
• Unlike ～がる (showing a real feeling) and ～げ (seeming), ～ぶる implies “trying to look like”, with a strong sense of fakeness.
mistakes: Attaching it to the dictionary form of an i-adjective: 高いぶる（incorrect）→ use a noun/語幹: 上品ぶる, プロぶる.
Using it in formal writing is rude: avoid direct criticism of customers or business partners.
Confusing it with ～がる: ～ぶる means “pretend / act like”, not “feel”.
1363.notes:
• “知ったかぶる” is a shortened form of “知ったかぶりをする”. The noun form “～ぶり” here (different from the ～ぶり in 仕事ぶり) means “the habit of putting on airs”.
• In ads and headlines, it is sometimes used for wordplay: プロぶった素人（an amateur acting like a pro）.
• For a stronger degree, ～気取り (きどり) can be used: 貴族気取り（putting on airs like an aristocrat）, with a highly contemptuous nuance.

examples.jp: 誰も手伝ってくれないなら、自分でやるまでだ。
examples.tr: If nobody will help me, I'll just do it myself.

examples.jp: 落ちたら、また受け直すまでのことだ。
examples.tr: If I fail, I'll simply take the exam again.

examples.jp: 聞かれたから答えたまでだ。
examples.tr: I only answered because I was asked.

examples.jp: 当然のことをしたまでです。
examples.tr: I only did what was natural.

examples.jp: 最善を尽くしてダメなら、諦めるまでだ。
examples.tr: If I do my best and it still doesn't work, I'll just give up.

1364.explain:
Formal; often seen in written language and serious speeches. It is also used in spoken language, but sounds calm and decisive.
Vた + までだ is humble, downplaying one's own contribution to be polite.
Vる + までだ usually comes with a context of “no other way / no one to help / no other choice”.

• Vる + までだ: said when there is no better option, with a nuance of “I'll have to”. It can also express resolve or self-reassurance.
• Vた + までだ: downplays the merit or significance of one's own action: “I only did what was natural”. Often used when praised or misunderstood.
• “～までのことだ” is equivalent, more polite/softer than “～までだ”.

rows: Have to / the only option is
Vる + しかない／ほかない

mistakes: Confusing Vた + までだ (I only … ) with Vる + までだ (I'll have to …): their functions are different.
Using the humble meaning “したまでだ” with someone else as the subject is pragmatically wrong; it is usually the speaker talking about themselves.
Mixing it up with ～しかない: both are grammatically correct, but the JLPT tests the formal/resolute nuance of ～までだ.
1364.notes:
• “まで” originally means “up to / as far as”; in this pattern it shifts to “to the point where the only option is …”.
• Often used with condition/supposition structures: もし～なら／万一～なら … ～までだ.
• Vた + までだ is often used when praised, to avoid boasting: お役に立てて何よりです。したまでです。

examples.jp: 挨拶も兼ねて、課長のところへ伺いました。
examples.tr: I went to see the section chief, partly to say hello as well.

examples.jp: 見学も兼ねて、新工場を回りました。
examples.tr: I went around the new factory, also as a tour of inspection.

examples.jp: 観光も兼ねて北海道へ出張する。
examples.tr: I'm going on a business trip to Hokkaido that will double as sightseeing.

examples.jp: 勉強も兼ねて日本のドラマを見ている。
examples.tr: I watch Japanese dramas partly for study as well.

examples.jp: 報告も兼ねて、結果をメールで共有します。
examples.tr: I will share the results by email, which will also serve as my report.

examples.jp: 名刺交換も兼ねて、ご挨拶申し上げます。
examples.tr: Allow me to greet you, and to exchange business cards at the same time.

1365.explain:
Use it when there are two purposes at the same time that are both reasonable and do not conflict.
Works well with verbs of motion:行く・伺う・訪問する・回る・参加する; and with verbs of sending/exchanging:送る・連絡する。
More formal than ～ついでに; more neutral than ～がてら (relaxed) and less formal than ～かたがた.
In business, it helps you speak politely and indirectly:挨拶も兼ねて伺いました (instead of “I came just to say hello”).

• Expresses “also serving as, at the same time as / in order to” – doing one thing for purpose A while also achieving purpose B.
• Focus: intentionally combining purposes. Slightly more formal than ～ついでに, friendlier than ～かたがた.
• The preceding noun is usually the secondary/accompanying purpose: 挨拶, 見学, 視察, 連絡, 報告, 観光, 勉強, PR…
• Often used in business and social courtesy contexts, politely; also used in everyday life.
• Not used with immoral or reluctant actions.

rows: <ruby>視察<rt>しさつ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>兼<rt>か</rt></ruby>ねて<ruby>訪問<rt>ほうもん</rt></ruby>する
<ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>がてら<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く
<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くついでに<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す
On the occasion of, at the same time
Very formal, mainly in letters and ceremonial speech
ご<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>かたがたご<ruby>挨拶<rt>あいさつ</rt></ruby><ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げます

mistakes: Mixing it up with ～ついでに: the JLPT often asks about nuance; ～も兼ねて is more formal and emphasizes “serving a double purpose”.
Using it directly with an adjective or verb is incorrect: it needs a noun (or a nominalization).
Choosing an unnatural noun: avoid abstract nouns that are not activities (例: 幸せも兼ねて ×).
1365.notes:
• Nouns that express an “activity / purpose” sound more natural: 見学・挨拶・報告・観光・勉強・応援.
• It does not combine directly with a clause; if needed, nominalize it: 安全確認も兼ねて点検する.
• A polite pattern in business emails: 「ご挨拶も兼ねてご連絡申し上げます」。

examples.jp: 好天も相まって、来場者数は過去最多となった。
examples.tr: Helped by the good weather, the number of visitors reached a record high.

examples.jp: 彼の努力も相まって、プロジェクトは成功した。
examples.tr: Combined with his efforts, the project was a success.

examples.jp: 円安傾向であることも相まって、輸出企業の利益が伸びている。
examples.tr: Combined with the trend of a weak yen, exporters' profits are growing.

examples.jp: SNSでの拡散力も相まって、瞬く間に話題になった。
examples.tr: Combined with how quickly it spread on social media, it became a hot topic in no time.

examples.jp: 立地の良さも相まって、この店はいつも混んでいる。
examples.tr: Combined with its good location, this shop is always crowded.

1366.explain:
Used when you want to emphasize a “combination of causes” rather than attributing the result to a single factor.
Often used in narration and reports; a more formal style than everyday conversation.
Suitable for both positive and negative results:人手不足も相まって納期が遅れた。

• “Working together with, combined with” – several factors act at the same time to produce a stronger result.
• An objective tone explaining combined causes; often seen in reports and news.
• Position: between the cause part and the result part; mainly about good/bad results caused by several factors.
• The factor before ～も相まって is usually an additional factor, not the only cause.

rows: <ruby>宣伝<rt>せんでん</rt></ruby><ruby>力<rt>りょく</rt></ruby>も<ruby>相<rt>あい</rt></ruby>まって<ruby>売<rt>う</rt></ruby>れた
Simple listing, no emphasis on “working together”
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>加<rt>くわ</rt></ruby>えて<ruby>風<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>い
<ruby>有名<rt>ゆうめい</rt></ruby><ruby>店<rt>てん</rt></ruby>だけに<ruby>行列<rt>ぎょうれつ</rt></ruby>だ
Colloquial, lighter than ～も<ruby>相<rt>あい</rt></ruby>まって
<ruby>天気<rt>てんき</rt></ruby>がいいもあって<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>い
<ruby>努力<rt>どりょく</rt></ruby>と<ruby>相<rt>あい</rt></ruby>まって<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>が<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た

mistakes: Using it for a single cause → not appropriate; use ～だけに or ～ので.
Using it in very casual spoken language → sounds stiff; consider ～もあって.
Confusing it with ～に加えて: the JLPT tests the nuance of “working together” vs. “in addition”.
1366.notes:
• Often used for social/economic/market phenomena: 物価高、円安、好景気、不況…
• Avoid repeating ～も相まって several times in one sentence; list them as Aに、Bも相まって…
• The subject is usually the result/situation, not the agent of an action.

examples.jp: 親も親なら、子も子だ。
examples.tr: The parents are bad, and so is the child.

examples.jp: 店員も店員なら、客も客だ。
examples.tr: The staff are bad, and the customers are just as bad.

examples.jp: 上司も上司なら、部下も部下だ。
examples.tr: The boss is bad, and the subordinates are no better.

examples.jp: 雨も雨なら、風も風だ、今日は最悪だ。
examples.tr: The rain is bad, and so is the wind; today is the worst.

examples.jp: 学校も学校なら、保護者も保護者だね。
examples.tr: The school is bad, and so are the parents, aren't they?

examples.jp: 対応も対応なら、説明も説明だ。これでは納得できない。
examples.tr: The response is bad, and so is the explanation. I can't accept this.

1367.explain:
Often used in spoken language, on social media, and in sensational headlines, with a sarcastic nuance.
The two nouns are usually two related or corresponding “sides” (parent–child, shop–customer, team–fans).
Not appropriate in extremely formal contexts or when emotional neutrality is needed.
Often accompanied by evaluative words: ひどい,最低, いい加減,雑, ずさん …
Can stand alone as a comment:親も親なら、子も子だ。

• Meaning: “A is just like A, and B is just like B” → emphasizes that both sides have problems / are worth remarking on, usually with a nuance of criticism, sarcasm or complaint.
• Speaker's emotion: a strongly subjective evaluation; often used when disappointed, frustrated, or “too fed up to say more”.
• Pragmatics: usually used with nouns referring to people, organizations or targets of the same kind, compared in parallel: 親−子, 店−客, 上司−部下, 学校−生徒.
• Syntax: the N before and after も is usually the same noun repeated (emphasizing “that's just how … is”). The second clause uses だ/だった to conclude the evaluation.
• Tense: both present and past are possible; future is rare. The polite form です can be used, but the sarcastic nuance remains.

rows: <ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>も<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>なら、<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>だ。
<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いし、<ruby>質<rt>しつ</rt></ruby>もいい。
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>速<rt>はや</rt></ruby>いが、<ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>安定<rt>あんてい</rt></ruby>している。
“there is this, and there is also that”
いい<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>もいれば、<ruby>悪<rt>わる</rt></ruby>い<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>もいる。

mistakes: Using an adjective/verb instead of a repeated noun: incorrect. The standard pattern is a noun repeated before も.
Using it in formal documents such as official reports: inappropriate because of its strong emotional nuance.
Misunderstanding it as praising both: it almost always has a negative/complaining meaning.
Forgetting tense/negation: the second clause needs to end with だ/です/だった according to the appropriate tense.
1367.notes:
• This structure usually has parallel syllables, creating a sarcastic “rhythm”; so the noun is repeated exactly.
• The order of the two clauses can be reversed depending on which side you want to emphasize.
• To soften it, you can add ね or なあ at the end of the sentence, or use です/ます.

1368.meaning: Not sure whether to… or not…
1368.connection: V volitional form + か + Vる + まいか

examples.jp: 行こうか行くまいか、直前まで迷っていた。
examples.tr: I couldn't decide whether to go or not until the last minute.

examples.jp: 彼に本当のことを言おうか言うまいか、何度も考えた。
examples.tr: I thought many times about whether or not to tell him the truth.

examples.jp: 参加しようかすまいか、締め切りまで悩んだ。
examples.tr: I agonized over whether to take part or not until the deadline.

examples.jp: 留学しようかするまいか、家族と相談している。
examples.tr: I'm talking with my family about whether or not to study abroad.

examples.jp: ここに残ろうか残るまいか、彼らは話し合った。
examples.tr: They discussed whether or not to stay here.

1368.explain:
Used when describing a process of deliberation; usually not used for commands or requests.
Can be followed by a nominalization: ～ようか～まいか＋迷い／悩み.
More formal in style than ～かどうか (neutral).

- Expresses hesitation: “whether to do it or not…”. Usually expresses an inner monologue, weighing up a decision.
- The subject is usually the speaker (first person) or a group deliberating; often accompanied by 迷う／悩む／決めかねる／考える.
- Has a formal/slightly literary nuance; “まい” is the classical negative volitional form.

rows: <ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>するかどうか<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>える。
Emphasizes “should / should not” rather than pure hesitation
<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うべきか<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うべきでないか。
Whether or not one does it, still…
<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ようが<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るまいが<ruby>続行<rt>ぞっこう</rt></ruby>する。
～たほうがいいか～ないほうがいいか
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったほうがいいか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないほうがいいか。

mistakes: Choosing ～ようが～るまいが (regardless) by mistake when the context is “hesitating”.
Using it with adjectives/nouns: ×「高いようか高くあるまいか」 (only used with verbs).
Wrong form: ×「食べまいか食べようか」 (the standard order is 食べようか食べるまいか).
1368.notes:
• Standard: Vる＋まい; with 一段 verbs, Vまい is sometimes seen in spoken language, but exams prefer Vるまい.
• With する: both するまい/すまい are correct; すまい is more natural.
• With 来る: 来るまい／来まい (来まい leans toward written language).

1369.connection: V volitional form + が + Vる + まいが

examples.jp: 雨が降ろうが降るまいが、試合は予定どおり行う。
examples.tr: Whether it rains or not, the match will be held as scheduled.

examples.jp: 彼が賛成しようがするまいが、計画は進める。
examples.tr: Whether he agrees or not, we will go ahead with the plan.

examples.jp: 誰が来ようが来るまいが、私はやるべきことをやる。
examples.tr: Whoever comes or doesn't come, I'll do what I have to do.

examples.jp: 成功しようがすまいが、挑戦した事実に意味がある。
examples.tr: Whether you succeed or not, the fact that you tried has meaning.

examples.jp: 景気が良かろうが悪かろうが、投資は続ける。
examples.tr: Whether the economy is good or bad, we will keep investing.

1369.explain:
Emphasizes resolve / a stance that does not change in the face of opposite conditions.
The second clause usually affirms a position; it is not used for questions or requests.
Formal style, used in speeches and essays.

- Expresses a firm stance: “whether one does it or not … (still) …”. The second clause shows an action/decision that is not affected.
- Formal nuance, used in speeches, arguments and declarations of resolve.
- Usually appears with a tight parallel correspondence between the two preceding clauses.

rows: Whether to do it or not (hesitation)
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こうか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くまいか<ruby>迷<rt>まよ</rt></ruby>う。
～ても～なくても／～にかかわらず
Regardless of A or not A
More neutral, less formal than ～ようが～るまいが
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>でなくても<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。
Nuance of denying effectiveness, unlike a declaration of resolve
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>から<ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>ったところで<ruby>遅<rt>おそ</rt></ruby>い。
<ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れであれ<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>であれ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く。

mistakes: Not keeping the same verb in both parts: ×「行こうが 来るまいが」 → correct: 「行こうが 行くまいが」.
Using it to ask a question or make a request → does not fit its declarative nuance.
Confusing it with ～ようか～るまいか in pattern-choice questions: look at the second clause; if it is “still… / continue…”, choose ～ようが～るまいが.
1369.notes:
• Keep the forms parallel: V-ようが ↔ V-るまいが with the same verb.
• Extending it to adjectives/nouns allows more varied expression in argumentative writing.
• Formal style; in everyday conversation it can be replaced with ～ても～なくても.

1370.connection: V volitional form + と + Vる + まいと

examples.jp: 彼が来ようと来るまいと、会議は予定どおり始める。
examples.tr: Whether he comes or not, the meeting will start as scheduled.

examples.jp: 雨が降ろうと降るまいと、試合は続行する。
examples.tr: Whether it rains or not, the match will continue.

examples.jp: 彼女が賛成しようとするまいと、方針は変わらない。
examples.tr: Whether she agrees or not, the policy will not change.

examples.jp: 誰に何を言われようと言われるまいと、自分の道を行く。
examples.tr: Whatever people say to me, or don't say, I'll go my own way.

examples.jp: 会社が支援しようとするまいと、彼は独力でやり抜くつもりだ。
examples.tr: Whether the company supports him or not, he intends to see it through on his own.

1370.explain:
Used when you want to affirm a stance or principle: the second clause usually has a decisive meaning.
Formal; appears in speeches, written language and news reports.
The two preceding clauses should correspond, using the same verb, to create rhythm and symmetry.
Not used for invitations or direct requests.

The pattern ～ようと～るまいと expresses “whether one does (V) or not, the conclusion/judgment that follows does not change”. Equivalent to “whether … or not …”. Formal nuance, in a written/speech style.
• Emphasizes that the second clause is “unchanging” in the face of every opposing possibility (doing / not doing).
• Often talks about resolve, policies, general tendencies, or the irrelevance of the preceding condition to the result.
• The preceding clauses usually use the same verb in two forms: volitional (Vよう) and negative volitional (Vるまい).

rows: <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こうが<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くまいが<ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby>ない。
<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>っても<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくても<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じだ。
Does not require the same verb
<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るにせよ<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ないにせよ<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>を。
Whether it is A or B
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>であれ<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>であれ<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Using different verbs in the two parts: the same verb is required (行こうと来るまいと → incorrect).
Confusing “Vないと” with “Vるまいと”: “まい” is the negative volitional, not “ない”.
Using it in everyday conversation sounds stiff; for the JLPT you need to recognize its formal nuance.
Confusing it with “〜ようにも〜れない” (expressing “even if one wants to, one cannot”), whereas this pattern means “whether one does it or not, the result that follows does not change”.
1370.notes:
• “まい” is a negative volitional form with an archaic/written nuance; in conversation “〜ても〜なくても” is usually used.
• With 来る: 来るまい（くるまい）；with する: するまい. Avoid “来まい/すまい” in standard modern Japanese (except in a very archaic style).
• Different subjects can be inserted in the two preceding clauses, but the same subject is usually kept for coherence.

1371.connection: Vる / V passive form (る) + がままに (言われるがままに)

examples.jp: 彼は営業マンの言われるがままに高い契約を結んでしまった。
examples.tr: He ended up signing an expensive contract, doing just as the salesman told him.

examples.jp: 週末は心の赴くがままに旅に出た。
examples.tr: On the weekend, I set off on a trip wherever my heart led me.

examples.jp: 流れに任せ、成り行きのがままに生きてみる。
examples.tr: I'll try living by going with the flow, letting things take their course.

examples.jp: 上司に指示されるがままに、資料を修正した。
examples.tr: I revised the documents just as my boss instructed.

examples.jp: 涙が流れるがままに、彼女は何も言わなかった。
examples.tr: She said nothing, letting her tears flow.

examples.jp: 思うがままに意見を述べてください。
examples.tr: Please state your opinions just as you think.

1371.explain:
With the passive: tends to carry a passive nuance, a lack of initiative, sometimes criticism (“doing whatever one is told”).
With the active: carries a free, poetic/literary nuance (心の赴くがままに／思うがままに).
More formal/literary than “〜ままに”.

～るがままに expresses “leaving it to…; just as…; exactly in line with that state/wish”. It has two directions:
• Active and free: acting on one's own will/feelings (思うがままに＝as one pleases).
• Passive and resigned: being led/pushed along by what others say/what happens (言われるがままに＝doing whatever one is told).

rows: Being led by the nose/letting others do as they like
<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>われるがままに<ruby>従<rt>したが</rt></ruby>う。
<ruby>指示<rt>しじ</rt></ruby>どおりに<ruby>作業<rt>さぎょう</rt></ruby>する。
<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>従<rt>したが</rt></ruby>って<ruby>行動<rt>こうどう</rt></ruby>する。

mistakes: Not using the passive form: “言うがままに” → lacks the nuance of “being made to”; “言われるがままに” is more natural.
Confusing the meaning with “〜のとおりに”: “がままに” carries a nuance of letting things be/exactly as the state is, not simply “following instructions”.
Dropping “に” when an object follows: 思うがまま意見を… → use 思うがままに意見を…
Used in formal contexts; in casual conversation it may sound too literary.
1371.notes:
• Often used in fixed phrases: 言われるがままに／流されるがままに／心の赴くがままに／思うがままに.
• The “が” in “がままに” adds emphasis to the sense of “just as…/leaving it to…”.
• Suited to expository writing, literature and reportage; in conversation, “ままに/とおりに” sounds more natural.

examples.jp: ベルが鳴るが早いか、学生たちは教室を飛び出した。
examples.tr: No sooner had the bell rung than the students rushed out of the classroom.

examples.jp: 彼は席に座るが早いか、すぐ眠り込んだ。
examples.tr: No sooner had he sat down than he fell fast asleep.

examples.jp: ドアが開くが早いか、子どもたちが外へ駆け出した。
examples.tr: The moment the door opened, the children dashed outside.

examples.jp: 彼女は彼の顔を見るが早いか、涙をこぼした。
examples.tr: The moment she saw his face, tears spilled from her eyes.

examples.jp: 父は家に帰るが早いか、テレビをつけた。
examples.tr: No sooner had my father come home than he turned on the TV.

examples.jp: 警報が鳴るが早いか、みんなが避難を始めた。
examples.tr: The moment the alarm went off, everyone started to evacuate.

1372.explain:
Has a narrative nuance, more formal than ordinary conversation; creates a sense of decisiveness and surprise.
Not used for predicted future events; almost always in the past when recounting things that have happened.
Avoid using it with durative verbs (続く、待つ…) because they lack “immediacy”.
The second clause does not use the speaker's command/volition/suggestion (～なさい、～ましょう、～てください…)

• Main translation: “As soon as/The moment V, …”, emphasizing an extremely quick succession of two actions/events.
• Faster than ～とたん(に); has a written/narrative nuance, creating a sense of an “instant reflex”.
• The second clause describes an actual event, usually a behavior/change that happens immediately, sometimes surprisingly.
• The subject of the first clause and the second clause is usually the same person/thing; if different, a clear context is needed to avoid ambiguity.
• Not used for the speaker's volition, commands, invitations or desires.
• Often used with verbs marking a starting point: 見る、聞く、開く、立つ、座る、鳴る…

rows: More formal; almost never used for volition/commands.
ベルが<ruby>鳴<rt>な</rt></ruby>るや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や、<ruby>皆<rt>みな</rt></ruby>が<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がった。
Mostly requires the same subject; emphasizes an immediately following action.
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>るなり、<ruby>寝室<rt>しんしつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>った。
Uses V-た; usually something unexpected; less written.
<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>ったとたん、<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>くなった。
～かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと／～かと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>ったら
Heightens the nuance of surprise; usually a subject different from the speaker.
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと、すぐやんだ。
More conversational; the “immediacy” is weaker than ～るが<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>いか.
<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>着<rt>ちゃく</rt></ruby>いたとすぐ、シャワーを<ruby>浴<rt>あ</rt></ruby>びた。

mistakes: Using a command/suggestion in the second clause → grammatically incorrect.
Choosing a durative verb for the first clause → loses the sense of “as soon as”.
Confusing it with ～たとたん(に): ～るが早いか uses V-る and has a stronger written nuance.
Putting a future conjecture in the second clause (“will…”) → not appropriate; use an event that has already happened.
1372.notes:
• Some common combinations: 見るが早いか／聞くが早いか／開くが早いか — the action “springs” very sharply.
• When the two clauses have different subjects, state them clearly to avoid misunderstanding: 先生が入るが早いか、学生たちは静かになった。
• Works well in narratives/news captions to add vividness and a fast pace.

examples.jp: 彼は部屋に入るなり、大きなため息をついた。
examples.tr: As soon as he entered the room, he let out a big sigh.

examples.jp: 電話の声を聞くなり、彼女は顔色を変えた。
examples.tr: The moment she heard the voice on the phone, her expression changed.

examples.jp: 席に座るなり、眠ってしまった。
examples.tr: (I) fell asleep the moment I sat down.

examples.jp: 子どもは父の姿を見るなり、駆け寄った。
examples.tr: The moment the child saw his father, he ran up to him.

examples.jp: 彼は結果を知るなり、笑顔になった。
examples.tr: As soon as he learned the result, he broke into a smile.

1373.explain:
Emphasizes “immediacy” and an element of surprise/unpreparedness.
The following sentence is usually an action/sign of emotion that occurs instantly (叫ぶ,泣き出す,笑う,驚く…).
Avoid using it with the speaker's commands/intentions; it leans toward describing events that have happened.
The past tense is usually used in the second clause (～た／～てしまった／～出した).

• Expresses two events that occur in succession, almost simultaneously: “just as/the moment V, …”.
• Nuance: written language, more formal than ordinary conversation; often accompanied by a surprising, unexpected result.
• Restriction: Usually not used for repeated habits; suited to single, sudden events.

rows: Usually the same subject; written nuance
ドアを<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けるなり、<ruby>叫<rt>さけ</rt></ruby>んだ
ベルが<ruby>鳴<rt>な</rt></ruby>るや<ruby>否<rt>いな</rt></ruby>や<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>した
Emphasizes speed; usually the same subject
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るが<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>いか<ruby>逃<rt>に</rt></ruby>げた
Emphasizes the unexpected; A is a moment
<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がったとたんめまいがした
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったかと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うと<ruby>止<rt>や</rt></ruby>んだ

mistakes: Changing the subject between the two clauses: × 先生が入るなり、学生は立った → use ～や否や／～かと思うと.
Using it for a habit: × 帰るなり、テレビを見る (for habits, use と/たら/といつも).
Using it for a command/volition: × 着くなり、電話して (unnatural; use ～たら／～次第に電話する).
1373.notes:
• Vるなり has a slightly archaic/literary nuance; suitable for reading comprehension tests and essays.
• Avoid using it for the future/volition: × 着くなり、連絡します (use ～たら／～次第で instead).
• Many materials require the same subject; when the subjects differ, prefer other patterns such as ～や否や／～かと思うと.

examples.jp: 新人が時間をかけるのは驚くにはあたらない。
examples.tr: It is no surprise that newcomers take their time.

examples.jp: 彼のミスは非難するにはあたらない。
examples.tr: His mistake does not deserve criticism.

examples.jp: この程度で騒ぐにはあたらない。落ち着いて対処しよう。
examples.tr: There is no need to make a fuss over something like this. Let's stay calm and deal with it.

examples.jp: 今回の成功は称賛するにはあたらないが、努力は認められる。
examples.tr: This success is nothing to praise, but the effort deserves recognition.

examples.jp: 彼は被害者でもあるのだから、彼を責めるにはあたらない。
examples.tr: He is a victim too, so there is no reason to blame him.

1375.explain:
Used to tone down the degree of a reaction/evaluation: “one should not overreact”.
Common with verbs of evaluation/emotion:驚く,憤る,心配する,非難する,称賛する,絶賛する.
Usually comes at the end of a sentence or before から／ので to state a conclusion/a mild recommendation.

• Meaning: Not to the extent of having to…, not worth… (an evaluation that the degree is “unnecessary”).
• Two common directions of meaning:

Not worth being surprised at/criticizing/worrying about: 驚く・非難する・心配するにはあたらない。
Not worth excessive praise: 称賛するにはあたらない。

• Not worth being surprised at/criticizing/worrying about: 驚く・非難する・心配するにはあたらない。
• Not worth excessive praise: 称賛するにはあたらない。
• Nuance: Formal, objective, often used in commentary, news and reports.

rows: <ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>するにはあたらない
<ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>くほどのことではない
Not to the extent of having to do
Leans toward “no need to carry out the action”
<ruby>慌<rt>あわ</rt></ruby>てて<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>するまでもない
Written; means “no need” or “not as good as”
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>するには<ruby>及<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ばない

mistakes: Understanding it as “must not V”: incorrect. This is an evaluation of degree, not a prohibition.
Using it with concrete actions that involve no evaluation: × 走るにはあたらない (unnatural).
Confusing it with ～までもない: that pattern leans toward “no need to carry out the action”; ～にはあたらない leans toward “not worth reacting/evaluating that way”.
1375.notes:
• Can be used as a modifier: 驚くにはあたらない出来事 (an event that is no cause for surprise).
• With nouns: 非難にはあたらない／称賛にはあたらない — common in legal documents and essays.
• The nuance is not prohibition, only “an evaluation that the degree is unnecessary”.

examples.jp: 住所も電話も知らない。彼に連絡を取るにも、どうすればいいかわからない。
examples.tr: I don't know his address or phone number. Even if I want to contact him, I don't know how.

examples.jp: 初めての街で道がわからず、駅へ行くにも見当がつかない。
examples.tr: It's my first time in this city and I don't know the way, so I have no idea even how to get to the station.

examples.jp: 資料が足りなくて、報告書を書くにも書ける状態ではない。
examples.tr: There isn't enough material, so I'm in no position even to write the report.

examples.jp: パソコンが壊れて、修理に出すにも店が近くにない。
examples.tr: My computer broke, and even if I want to take it in for repair, there's no shop nearby.

examples.jp: この予算では、新製品を開発するにも人手が足りない。
examples.tr: With this budget, we don't have enough staff even to develop a new product.

examples.jp: 証拠がないから、抗議するにも根拠が示せない。
examples.tr: There's no evidence, so even if I want to protest, I can't show any grounds.

1376.explain:
Pattern: Vる + にも + a clause expressing difficulty/lack of means/not knowing how.
Often used in written language and formal speech; natural when describing problems, in reports and mild complaints.
The subject is usually the speaker/the speaker's group; it does not express commands/requests.
The second clause avoids verbs of strong volition (〜ようと思う) unless stating “cannot/do not know”.

• Main meaning: “Even to V / when you want to V, … (it is still hard/there is no way/you don't know what to do)”. Used when lacking information or means, or facing objective obstacles.
• The “にも” nuance heightens the sense of helplessness and confusion: it puts the speaker in a situation of “wanting to do something but not knowing the way/being at a loss”.
• The second clause often contains: わからない, 見当がつかない, 困る, できない, 手段がない, 難しい, どうすればいいか.
• Describes a situation rather than volition; differs from the pattern of strong volition “Vようにも〜ない”.

rows: Even to V, (it is hard/one doesn't know how)
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>うにも<ruby>手段<rt>しゅだん</rt></ruby>がない。
Want to V but cannot V
Stronger nuance of volition; a structure of its own
<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようにもできない。
Emphasizes “wanting” (feeling) rather than “how to do it”
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いたくても<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>えない。
In order to V / To V, …
Neutral, often used to evaluate conditions
Does not emphasize “not knowing how/lacking means”
<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>つからない。

mistakes: Mixing it up with “Vようにも〜ない” or “Vたくても〜ない”: note that the second clause of Vるにも is usually “not knowing how/lacking means”.
Using Vたにも… × (does not exist). It must be Vるにも…
A command/suggestion in the second clause is unnatural: × 行くにも、早く来てください。
Confusing it with “にもかかわらず”: the two patterns have completely different functions.
1376.notes:
• After Vるにも, interrogative phrases are very typical: どうすればいいか, どこへ行けばいいか, 何をすべきか.
• In casual speech, the explanation can be partly omitted if the context is clear: 金がなくて、引っ越すにも…。 (sounds natural when the listener understands the rest).
• Do not confuse it with “どこへ行くにも” (wherever one goes) – this is “interrogative noun/pronoun + にも” meaning “also”, not the Vるにも pattern being studied.

1377.connection: Vる + にも + V potential form ない (泣くに泣けない)

examples.jp: 忙しすぎて、休むにも休めない。
examples.tr: I'm so busy that I can't rest even if I want to.

examples.jp: 電車が止まっていて、帰るにも帰れない。
examples.tr: The trains have stopped, so I can't go home even if I want to.

examples.jp: 涙が出なくて、泣くにも泣けない気持ちだ。
examples.tr: The tears won't come; I feel like crying but I can't.

examples.jp: 上司が目の前にいて、断るにも断れない雰囲気だ。
examples.tr: With my boss right in front of me, it's the kind of atmosphere where I can't refuse even if I want to.

examples.jp: 体調が悪くて、食べるにも食べられない。
examples.tr: I'm feeling unwell, so I can't eat even if I want to.

examples.jp: 道路が封鎖され、会場へ行くにも行けない状態だ。
examples.tr: The roads are closed, so we can't get to the venue even if we want to.

1377.explain:
Pattern: Vる + にも + the negative potential form of the same verb (or できない with サ変 verbs).
Emphasizes “the will is there but it is blocked”. Usually used in the first person, or to describe a general situation.
Nuance of lament and helplessness; more formal than VたくてもVられない.
The reason for the obstacle is usually stated before or after the sentence (with 〜ので/〜から/〜せいで/状況描写).

• Meaning: “Even if one wants to/intends to V, one cannot V” for objective reasons (busyness, circumstances, rules, suppressed feelings…).
• The structure emphasizes blocked volition: the first part states the “intention”, the second affirms “impossibility”.
• Pragmatics: complaining, explaining reasons, expressing a dilemma.

rows: Emphasizes volition blocked by objective factors
<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>るにも<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>れない。
Even if one intends to V, one cannot
Strong nuance of volition; more written/emphatic
<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようにも<ruby>手段<rt>しゅだん</rt></ruby>がない。
Leans toward the personal feeling of “wanting”
<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いたくても<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>えない。
Means “even having tried” rather than “want to but cannot”
<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しても<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>つからない。

mistakes: Wrong potential form: × 行くにも行かれない → it must be 行くにも行けない.
Confusing it with “Vるにも … (not knowing how)”: look at the second clause. If it is the negative potential of the same verb → pattern 167.
Using it with a command/suggestion is pragmatically wrong: × 行くにも行けないから、行け！
Dropping “も”: × 帰るに帰れない → in this pattern “にも” is mandatory.
1377.notes:
• Typical, natural combinations: 泣くにも泣けない・笑うにも笑えない・休むにも休めない・帰るにも帰れない.
• Spoken language may use “ら抜き” (食べれない/来れない), but tests/JLPT prefer the standard forms 食べられない/来られない.
• A reason can come first: 事情があって、出席するにもできない。

examples.jp: 無実の人を罪に問うことは、許すべからざる行為だ。
examples.tr: Charging an innocent person with a crime is an unforgivable act.

examples.jp: 研究におけるデータ改ざんは、看過すべからざる問題である。
examples.tr: Falsifying data in research is a problem that must not be overlooked.

examples.jp: 人権の軽視は、社会にとって看過すべからざる危機だ。
examples.tr: Disregard for human rights is a crisis that society must not overlook.

examples.jp: 信頼は、組織運営にとって欠くべからざる資質である。
examples.tr: Trust is an indispensable quality in running an organization.

examples.jp: 歴史的事実の捏造は、許すべからざる虚偽だ。
examples.tr: Fabricating historical facts is an unforgivable falsehood.

examples.jp: 安全基準の遵守は、製造業における欠くべからざる要件である。
examples.tr: Compliance with safety standards is an indispensable requirement in manufacturing.

1378.explain:
Used to modify a noun, creating a sense of seriousness; formal, written language.
The meaning of prohibition/judgment (許すべからざる,容認すべからざる,許容すべからざる) and the meaning of necessity (欠くべからざる) must be distinguished by the verb.
Not used in everyday conversation; replace with ～てはいけない/～べきではない in spoken language.

• Meaning A (common): “Must not/should not V; V is unacceptable” → nuance of moral, legal or regulatory judgment.
• Meaning B (idiom): 欠くべからざる + N = “indispensable/essential” (the meaning is reversed by negating “欠く”).
• This is a classical form, used often in academic writing, serious journalism, political speeches and regulations.

rows: Archaic, very formal, modifies a noun
<ruby>許<rt>ゆる</rt></ruby>すべからざる<ruby>行為<rt>こうい</rt></ruby>
Modern norm, also used in imperative sentences
<ruby>差別<rt>さべつ</rt></ruby>してはならない。
<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をつくべきではない。
<ruby>欠<rt>か</rt></ruby>くべからざる<ruby>条件<rt>じょうけん</rt></ruby>

mistakes: Mistaking “indispensable” for the general meaning: it is only correct with 欠くべからざる.
Using it as an independent predicate: × これは許すべからざる。 → A noun is needed: 許すべからざる行為だ。
Using it in everyday conversation makes the sentence too stiff; replace with ～てはいけない/～べきではない.
1378.notes:
• Natural combinations: 許すべからざる罪/暴挙, 看過すべからざる事実/不正, 容認すべからざる差別, 忘却すべからざる教訓.
• With サ変 verbs, the form “すべからざる” is more common than “するべからざる”. Examples: 看過すべからざる, 容認すべからざる.
• In newspaper headlines, particles may be omitted for conciseness: “許すべからざる虚偽、明るみに”.

examples.jp: 関係者以外、立ち入るべからず。
examples.tr: Authorized personnel only. No entry.

examples.jp: ここでの喫煙するべからず。
examples.tr: No smoking here.

examples.jp: 境内での撮影するべからず。
examples.tr: No photography within the temple/shrine grounds.

examples.jp: ごみの不法投棄するべからず。
examples.tr: No illegal dumping of garbage.

examples.jp: 火気使用するべからず。
examples.tr: Use of fire prohibited.

examples.jp: 試験中、私語するべからず。
examples.tr: No talking during the exam.

1379.explain:
Used as an independent sentence (the subject is usually omitted), placed after a place noun or a noun indicating time/target.
For regulations, notices and signs; not used when speaking to someone face to face in everyday communication.
Can be accompanied by an adverbial phrase:当駅構内での飲酒、 厳禁 ／飲酒 するべからず。

• Prohibition: “Must not V”. Used on prohibition signs, in regulations and serious notices.
• An archaic, strong, authoritative tone; rarely used in everyday conversation.
• Often used with action verbs performed on the spot: 立ち入る, 撮影する, 喫煙する, 投棄する, 使用する.

rows: <ruby>撮影<rt>さつえい</rt></ruby>するべからず。
<ruby>喫煙<rt>きつえん</rt></ruby>してはならない。
ここで<ruby>吸<rt>す</rt></ruby>うべきではない。

mistakes: Using it in conversation: × ここでタバコ吸うべからずよ → unnatural; use 吸わないでください/吸ってはいけません.
Wrong conjugation of a compound verb: × 立入るべからず → it should be 立ち入るべからず.
Confusing its nuance with べきではない (advice) → べからず is an absolute prohibition.
1379.notes:
• On signs, “する” may be omitted: 喫煙べからず is also seen, but the standard is 喫煙するべからず.
